To call SOMA unique would be to do it a massive disservice; instead I always open my discussion about this game by saying that its narrative seems like something better suited to a novel, but had it been relegated to such a format as opposed to the video game it was made to be, its marvelous take on existential dread and the fragility of life, experience and consciousness, wouldn't likely have been spread as far.
Avoiding spoilers, SOMA places you, the player, in situations where you're constantly forced to ask extremely uncomfortable questions about yourself, this world, and what it means to be what you are. In truth, as the story unfolds, the questions SOMA makes you ask (many of which are about feasible, or worse, already extant technologies and how they relate to the very concept of human consciousness) only get worse. SOMA's approach to horror is different even from other Frictional titles, in that it isn't meant to scare you, like the suitors in Amnesia or the spiders in Penumbra. It's meant to horrify you. The longer you think about the world of SOMA and how startingly believable it is, of course, the more the game succeeds in doing that.
My only gripe about the game is that the sections involving enemies seem a bit stilted, as if it doesn't really matter how sneaky you're being sometimes, they're going to idle right around wherever you happen to be, even if they haven't formally detected you. I also really dislike the heavy use of chromatic aberration and recommend you disable that in the settings before you do anything else in the game (it's listed as 'Color Separation' under video settings).
Another incredible title from Frictional. Play it.

Soma is my go-to game when it comes to describing video game storytelling. In all my years of gaming, I have never connected with such a protagonist (Simon). The fact that you are both tossed into the atmosphere allows you to not just embody Simon, but also sympathize and empathize with him. Feeling the anger, the frustration and the loneliness of the unknown.
While the game does have great story, environment, and atmosphere, it lacks in gameplay from time to time. The horror elements do get tiresome after awhile, but do spice it up every so often with a new creature, however, they can all be boiled down to "this one can't see, so be quiet around it", "this one can't hear so stay out of sight", or "this one doesn't like to be looked at, walk around."
The game does have moral decisions throughout it, yet they do not affect the story or the games ending.
In the end, I give SOMA
Story - 5/5
Music - 4/5
Gameplay - 3/5
Graphics - 5/5
Overall - 8.5/10

My opinion is that most of the people that had gripes about the gameply or function of this or that just didn't understand the gameply mechanics fully.  I read the reviews before I played the game and tried to keep an eye out for everything they said and just couldn't find many faults with it.  One might say they attempt to steal your tech too often, almost every turn actually, but thats why you build and maintain defenseive spies... and honestly its one of the best ways to get ahead and would not put it past a player to try to steal tech every round if it were possible for themselves.  It usually comes down to enemy tries this, but you counter with this, if you don't counter, you suffer.  I don't think the game should be rediculed on many of the points it lists when there is a perfectly viable and available way to counter the issue built into the game. I also didn't run into any issue where I couldn't overpower the computer if i chose to invest in military might or any other catagory.
As for command points, the maximum per colony is not 4, its 6 for the largest battle station, 1 for a command antenna and there are some other bonuses and techs to add more and you can even put bridges and cockpits to your ships to reduce the command point cost of them, in addition to this you can add 7+ points per colony, more colonies more points.  So if you have 50 cp you can use 50 cp worth of ships reduced by the bridge and cockpit modules if you choose to install them.  And all of that is on TOP of the multitude of free ships it lets you have.  For instance if you hvae 50 CP you might be able to have something like 30 corvettes and 15 frigates without even using one of those CP, then you can make a cruiser with a bridge reducing its cost by 1 and that would mean you could still make 25 cruisers before you ran outta command points. And that doesn't stop you, you can make more, it doesn't mean you have to stop, it just costs you money for maintenance after you pass your CP thresshold.  I feel like CP depicts the amount of ships you can control within your logistics capacity -  its simply a way to give you free ships... it by no means stops you from pumping out as many ships as your empire can support with money.  And this of course is not a new concept, many games use this in the strategy genre.
The game could use a few extra diplomacy options, and they do fall straight away to hatred if you expand too much, especially the races that have the trait expansionist, like hurt little kids if you take their candy... but I feel that just falls within their race trait and act accordingly.  I otherwise never had any issues with diplomacy and used it often with no issues.
The ship construction and design isn't found in any other game of this type to the degree that has been implemented and I thouroughly enjoyed that aspect of the game.
There are a few intereface changes I would make, but there are changes I always think should have been added in every game.  For instance, I would have loved to have 2 arrow buttons to slide between colonies onteh build menu, not just he planet menu, it would have saved a click or two.
Bottom line, I thoroughly enjoyed the game for the first 40 hours and intend to put at least 100 hours into this game.  I feel that its worth the 30 dollars but if your not sure youo can handle the extra bugs that are in fact within this game and you are very interested in what you see, well then take the dive when its on sale.  If your open minded and understand that nothing on this earth is perfect and you liked moo2 and its faults then you should really like this game too.
Thank you for reading.

Too much Civilization; not enough Ascendancy.
I've been looking for a successor to Ascendancy since it doesn't appear that Logic Factory cares to do much with the IP, and copies of the game are online-order only at this point (from places like Amazon).  After seeing the ship construction menu, I was hopeful that this game could fit the bill.  Unfortunately, it does not.
The early game can be quite fun, as are most exploration-style games.  Finding habitable planets and pushing through the tech tree to get bigger and better ship models and construction options is always great.  However, I find that the gameplay and mechanics beyond that (and even including those facets) is basically just a reskin of Civilization titles, and the aforementioned are really all the pros this game has.
As for cons, there are quite a few that make the game unenjoyable as a title.  This is a space game, but the map and battles are all 2-D.  The PC knows all the algorithyms, and plays at a high level, even on easier modes.  They expand faster, research tech more  efficiently, and have an endless number of spies, which the player can never hope to match.  They seem unrestrained by that which confines you.  And in a diplomacy game where races will declare war on you with little warning and even less provocation, the fact that there is no "alliance" option is really inexcusable.
Overall, it's a nice title if, and only if, you are a huge fan of Civilization and have some way of either running the game using the AI's algorithyms, or overcoming them in some fashion.  Otherwise, just buy Ascendancy off Amazon, as I intend to do.

If you are looking for a cheap, well made game on steam, this is the one. I recommend getting this game with the raising hell dlc because at the end of the game you will want more (plus the raising hell dlc is basically paying for the proper ending with another 6 hours of gameplay) So first of all, one of the unique things about this game is being able to control an army of minions that will kill and destroy things for you. All of the minions have a special attributes (except for the browns, besides them being the strongest of your minions) The reds will get rid of fire that may be blocking the path or stopping your minions from grabbing an item without dying. The greens can get rid of toxic gas that some plants emit and are also resistant to poison (the reds are resistant to fire) And The blues are the only minion that won't drown in water. This game will allow you to hold up to 50 minions at max which doesn't sound like a whole lot but it is. The combat is one of this games strengths, usually when you are about to be put into a difficult fight, it is best to strategize about what you are going to do with your minions, you can place some in a certain area to jump on your enemy and some other minions near that position to fire fireballs at the enemy, there are many ways to go about a fight I just named a simple example  (all of the minions have a different fight style, forgot to mention this earlier, reds can fire fireballs at enemies and when there are a lot of reds it will definetly do a number on your enemy, blues use magic and are the weakest of your minions, they also revive dead minions, greens like jumping onto enemies so they can attack them without the enemy being able to do anything about it and browns are your strongest fighters, doing the most melee damage and just running straight at the enemy) Items dropped by your enemies or items found in boxes, your minions can pick up to become stronger, like pieces of armor and weapons. Items your minions can pick up will usually have a shine on them and when you sweep your minions across it one will pick it up, when a minion picks up a item this will increase your minions horde power which just makes your minions stronger. You can also control your minions and move them around to get to switches that you may not be able to. At this point, you may think that I have talked a little too much about minions and that is because a lot of the game focuses on them and is what makes this game unique.
Now some other things rather than minions. This game allows you to customize your tower (Your base) You can forge different types of armor and use your minions to upgrade parts of it like defense and max health, you can also forge weapons and just like with your armor you can use your minions to upgrade damage and knockback ect. the games story is decent, nothing really special, not a lot of the voice acting is good, a bit cheesy but that is mainly from smaller npcs, most of the main npcs have better voice acting like gnarl and some others I guess. The minions are cool, they act and sound like what you would expect them to. The game does get a little annoying closer to the end and the final boss isn't amazing but is still fun. The ending isn't great either so buy the raising hell dlc to get the "proper ending." Welp that is about it, if you skipped to the bottom of this review all I have to say is buy this game and buy the dlc and you will have a great time. RATING: 8.5/10

There was something interesting about Seasons After Fall... something that called to an ancient part of my memories, maybe a story about the woods...who knows... but after spotting this game on steam and  watching a couple of gameplay videos,  I was certainly hooked to it  and  i wanted to play it.
I don't know exactly how to explain it, but there's something cool about a good platforming game, that, when it's done right, it is really great, no matter how many times you play it. Its like a great liberating experience/thing... and in other genres of gaming it can only happen a few times (make an original kind of game within a already well known style), but in this case, with the genre, i think its the opposite, the formula is old, but the the experience of playing it feels  new.
Sadly, this isn't the case with Seasons after fall...
It really saddens me to say this, but after playing the whole game i've got a bad impression from the "overall experience" and  that's what ultimately counts and lasts forever (and also, puts you away from coming back).
I have to say, the art direction for this game, is beautiful, inspiring even. It's also like watching a live painting move before you, it has that distinctive look from old. You are a fox, or a spirit inside a fox, but then you make your own way.  You meet the guardians of the seasons, and get to experience the seasons themselves, you control them at will, and you can change your environment while controlling them. In a way you are manipulating the elements, and it is amazing really...to a certain point, that is.
Then there are things that start to show up. One of the main problems with this game, maybe one of its greatest falls, is the level design, or map, or just plain simple (lack of) organization. Its not very clear (ever) where you are supposed to go. And no, i'm not saying you should be told where to go like a stupid, that's not necessary. I'm not telling to have a map with objectives either (although that could be nice) but the problem here is that really, the level layout is a mess. You start in one place, then go forward, but then  you have to go backwards (or forward depending on what you've accomplished) and you absolutely don't know where to go next you are just "guessing". There are no signs in the woods, no visual cues that makes a place feel or look different from another (aside from the four main zones) That's fine for half of the game. But then ,by the middle point you start to reach all these black points (of not knowing what's left to be done, (if you are missing anything at all, wich isn't always clear) and you realize you haven't kept track (i didn't write down how many things i've completed) )and so you don't know what you have already completed in certain places and what not. So you just keep checking and rechecking and theres no fast travel, no feedback from the game. That's one big mistake,  the players should have, some kind of feedback at all times.
It's a lack of direction and no clear level design that ultimately destroys all the sense of enjoyment you get from the first levels, the art design, the music (wich is recorded live, with classic musical instruments) and even the story at the beginning seems so interesting and compelling, but by the end its very convoluted and ends in a very weak note..
Also, another criticism i have, is that the game  seems empty at certain points. There are not enough things to do sometimes. Big spaces with nothing else except run.
The controls are at least nice, and playing the fox is very fun (I've played it with a gamepad).
The music is excellent, and is well placed, but also the voice actors are phenomenal in this game. (Personally, I've played the original language version, voiced in french) but from what i understand the english version is just as good.

Jazzpunk is a reviewer’s nightmare.  I’m serious - the game is built entirely on jokes and nudge-nudge-wink-wink pop-culture references, to the point that almost anything mentioned about the game is a spoiler.  The best way to describe Jazzpunk is that it is Let’s Play: The Game.  In a time where Youtube culture dominates such a large part of our lives, it is no surprise that games like Jazzpunk gleefully jaunt onto our Steam pages and present themselves like a fish supper desperate for sauce.
Gameplay: 8/10
That’s not to say that I didn’t like Jazzpunk – far from it in fact.  I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Jazzpunk, and for myself personally, the humour was excellent and hit the required pleasure centres of my tiny brain.  Far from the “Hey remember that thing you know about well I know about it too look Look LOOK AT ME” style of the turgid Duke Nukem Forever, Jazzpunk delivers its references tastefully and subtly.  Such was the extent of the classy restraint on the part of the development team, some references were even lost on me.  This may seem like an oddly backhanded compliment to pay a game which has built its foundations stoically upon references, however in my opinion it shows how unforced and unobtuse the game’s nods to other franchises were.  This, thankfully, doesn’t constitute the entire game’s content (I’m looking at you here Retro City Rampage).  Rather, the game has a ridiculous but surprisingly easy to follow plot running through the game.  Unlike its obvious influences, Blendo’s Gravity Bone and Thirty Flights of Loving, Jazzpunk’s purple-monkey-dishwater plot is clearly explained and actually makes sense in its own weird way.
Artistic Merit: 8/10
In terms of presentation, Jazzpunk does borrow some things from the aforementioned Blendo games, however the characters themselves differ entirely from Gravity Bone and Thirty Flights of Loving, and this helps Jazzpunk develop its own identity away from its obvious influences.  While not a GPU-straining, high-fidelity particle-a-thon, Jazzpunk’s art style is clean and effective, especially when being used in the game’s trademark humour.    Musically the game is adequate – the tracks are very quiet apart from during several set-pieces, and fit the overall theme and mood of the player well.  The issue I have with the soundtrack is that if you asked me to hum a piece of the OST to you or even recognise it from an identity parade of other pieces, I probably couldn’t do it.  The sound design fares much better with the voice acting and sound effects.  The latter are varied and always giggle-inducing - even the most mundane of sounds like swatting a fly becomes a joy while wearing headphones, while a certain Scarface reference made this reviewer have to pause and change his boxers.  The voice acting - for the most part - is a hilarious selection of regional accents, with The Director in particular always drawing a grin from the player’s lips.  My problem with the voice acting? The frankly abhorrent excuse for a Scottish accent by a certain hula waitress.  You’ll know which one she is.  Joking aside, the accents and vocal talents on show here are varied,  competently handled, and execute the game’s fantastic writing to a T.  The game also offers great variety in terms of its settings, with you as the hero Polyblank being whisked off to Russia, China, England, and a Tropical Island to name a few.  Each offers a completely new set of objectives and characters to complete and interact with.
Cohesion: 7/10
The game’s framerate was rock-solid, and I was extremely impressed by the performance in general (I even managed to livestream it from my 6 year old laptop).  It does suffer from the usual Unity pitfall in that the options menu is lacklustre in the extreme.  VSync, fullscreen toggle, resolution options, and key rebinding are your lot here.
Value: 4/10
My only real issue with Jazzpunk is that it’s just too damn short.  My Steam profile says 3 hours, and I ambled through the story mode, stopping to mindlessly click at everything like a lab rat waiting for another piece of gorgonzola to be bestowed upon me.  That horrible image aside, an experience which lasts all of three hours (maybe four if you want to go back and snaffle those achievements you missed) for me doesn’t really justify the £11.99 asking price.  It is a blast, no doubt, but once you’ve seen everything it has to offer the game won’t keep you coming back time and time again.
All in all Jazzpunk is something that I believe every gamer should experience in some form, however the asking price is not at all a fair reflection of the game’s length and the time it will spend entertaining you.  I didn’t get review code for this game, and bought it on release for the introductory price of £10.79.  Despite buying it cheaper than usual, I can’t help but feel slightly aggrieved at the length of Jazzpunk.  That aside, the game is some of the best 3 hours you can have this side of Luigi’s Mansion, and is absolutely worth splashing out on if you see it for a reasonable price.
Final Score: 7/10
Jazzpunk is a great, if short, experience that is only hampered by its lack of replayability and blink-and-you’ll-miss-it length.  One for the sales.

All-in-all, Jazzpunk is a must have for your Steam library, and nothing should ever change that.

Video Review:
For Honor is a third person action game that is quite different from other games in the genre. In For Honor you use a unique fighting system that involves picking a direction to block and attack, similar to mount and blade but with actual UI indicators instead of just player animations. You can play either a campaign or one of many multiplayer modes in which you contribute to your team's conquest of the world over the lesser Vikings and Samurai, because let's be honest. What's not to love about Knights?
The campaign of For Honor is set up sort of strangely, but it is amazing nonetheless. You get to learn a good number of the playable heroes while following a narration which has you switch between each of the three sides: Knight, Viking, and Samurai. The story is absolutely engrossing and commonly depicted through movie-like cutscenes that I have rarely seen outside of something like Metal Gear. You can find special items and earn special rewards for completing the campaign, receiving higher rewards on higher difficulties. This gives players a reason to replay the campaign if they enjoy the story because they earn steel, which can be used to upgrade and purchase things in the multiplayer. And with 2 player co-op? It can lead to some hilariously fun moments. There are some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t moments of the campaign though such as how this one viking king has these forever-spawning wolves that can dodge literally every single attack. But there are also some interesting on-rail parts where things get changed up that were a lot of fun. One downside to the campaign is that your AI followers, especially during the Samurai campaign, CONSTANTLY attack you while trying to attack an enemy. Friendly Fire works in some games, but in this game it would be nice if single player had an off button for it.
The gameplay of For Honor is really special. It's the first time I've ever seen an AAA title take on combat even somewhat similar to mount and blade. It also includes a special set of moves like a fighting game would for every single playable hero. The memorization is difficult for me, but it doesn't change how much I love getting the satisfaction of memorizing a moveset and using it to pull myself out of difficult situations. My only complaint gameplay-wise is that they opted for a cinematic lock-on system that restricts your movement and field of view rather than a regular lock on system. The game DOES have a pretty crazy learning curve if you're not used to combo-based fighting games, so that's something to keep in mind.
The multiplayer of For Honor is, some might argue, the point of buying the game. I personally wouldn't say that, but that doesn't change that I love it. You can play one of several game modes; my favorite being dominion where you fight alongside legions of NPC fodder troops to capture and hold points from the enemy team. It's marketed very much like Rainbow Six Siege in that you have to unlock your heroes and have the ability to customize. However, the customization here is a lot more filled with micro transactions. You either have to wait for gear to drop and then deconstruct the ones you don't want in favor of upgrading the ones you do want...OR you need to buy gear crates with steel...which guess what? Is purchasable with real life currency. And unfortunately gear is, if you build it right, extremely unbalanced and overpowered in the game's current state. This makes it so that if you aren't a microtransaction player, you're going to feel it when you're fighting someone that is.
This game looks amazing graphically with the exception of some occasionally janky looking animations. I have never seen an action game look quite as good as For Honor does, and the sounds are amazing too.  The soundtrack really helps set the intensity of the fights and the effects are very fitting and impactful.
The biggest flaw of this game as it stands is the fact that the multiplayer and even co-op campaign is filled with incessant disconnects that consistently ruin the gameplay experience. Well actually, even the single player. This game REQUIRES an internet connection just to play it by yourself. You can be booted from multiplayer games en masse, lose your co-op partner mid-boss fight, or even be fighting a bot in multiplayer and watch him disappear as a player hotjoins and then spawns behind you and kills you because you're almost out of health and he spawned with full health in place of the bot that you were just about to kill! But let's be serious, why on earth would Uplay base this game's internet connection off of what is seemingly the WORST server connection I've ever seen AND make the multiplayer run off of peer to peer connections where your lag is based on the connection of a host, instead of making dedicated servers!? The P2P system picks a host at random too! It even picked my friend who has the worst internet connection in history twice in a row. The first time he got DC'd and the second time everyone BUT him got DC'd. And they call that an "advanced P2P system". How is picking the most instable and slow internet conneciton in the entire match to host it advanced!?
Overall despite it's flaws, For Honor is easily my favorite game to release so far this year. I think this really set a bar for all the games that follow it in 2017 and if it had a stable connection it would easily be the first 10/10 ever given on Konglomerat. But the internet connection problems are everywhere and the pay to win aspect with gear isn't very good either. That being said, I still feel the need to stress how good of a game this is despite those two problems and so For Honor gets a 8/10. It's the most amazing game to come out so far in 2017 that I have gotten a chance to play and I would recommend it, even at the overpriced rates that are typical AAA retail prices. I had figured the developers might have gotten over their over-ambition and would be able to put out a game that's playable.  Instead, we get a game like the last one; too buggy and poorly documented to consider playing.
There's this disease going on with developers where they produce this involved game and don't tell you the rules, or they don't think they need to document them, so you have to spend hours and hours finding out how to play the game by exploring it in order to even have a shot at winning.  This is effectively a dumbed-down version of the pay 2 win business model for multiplayer games; the older and more experienced players know all these subtle tricks with the "product" they have bought.  When new players are brought into the game, it's advertised to them they are on-par, that all the shiney things the other players have bought are "just cosmetic" or some such hogwash.  The new players eventually find out that the next level is 100hrs of play, but it's 10 with the xp upgrade for $5.99, and they are continuously strung along one line of over-complicated crap to the next, filling their minds with rules nobody else knows all along.  I'm sure some actuary or analyst is literally sitting there figuring out how to profit-maxiimize players time, it's disgusting.  For multiplayer games, there's always a learning curve, you expect it, especially for good multiplayer FPS games that are not designed to be theatrical garbage.  For single player games, if you do this, your game is a bug-ridden mess.
The final straw was forfeiting a battle so I could re-do it as there's no pause button or speed reduce button as far as I can see, in order to do this I use the pre-battle auto-save feature.  Lo and behold, I found out the AI can do multiple combat actions per turn, and so after forfeiting my main fleet so I could restore the save, it immediatly attacks the tankers, which I retreated the same move, creating a new auto-save.  So I can't reatreat ships out of battle but the AI Can?  It's an AI, it plays at an advantage; I've got other AI's building literally a half dozen starbases at the border of my emprire before I've even discovered them.  I'm sure there's some involved explination as to why what the AI did was a valid move that will take 200 hrs of playing\bugtesting this game to find out.  The last version is the same thing.  I've got better things to do with my time than waste it on this crap.

Resident Evil 6 provides an interesting take on the journey this series has had throughout the years. While it looks slightly dated in comparison to games using DirectX 11, it still manages to mantain a fun experience across all the different campaigns.
Resident Evil 6 splits itself up into campaigns that translate roughly into different "eras" for the Resident Evil franchise. You have Leon Kennedy, while with the B.S.A. now, feels very familiar regarding the slower paced and claustrophobic gameplay of the earlier parts of the series. You have Chris Redfield, still capable of bench-pressing 600 pounds in his more action oriented and over-the-top military-based experiences. You have Jack and even Ada Wong as well rounding out the people involved.
The controls for the PC are a bit awkward, but thankfully it manages to provide for mouse support that hasn't really irritated me in any particular way. Control keys seem to be a bit awkward in their defaults and some keys are used for more than one thing which can cause some confusion in frantic fights.
One thing that really bothered me was the number of QTEs in this game. The "tutorial" consisted of no ability to save and had far too many QTEs which made the entire segment feeling much more like a zombie/explosive version of Dragon's Lair. Thankfully it eases up over time and while they are still a bit more common than I'd like, they aren't overbearing.
Weapon upgrades was another bit of disappointment for me as well. Instead of gathering money during your exploits and spending it on weapon upgrades specific to pistol X, Y, or Z; you pick up "Skill Points" and spend them on basic skills that improve things like extra pistol damage, extra rifle damage, round penetration and so on. This feels a bit disappointing since it reduces the impact your inventory has on how you operate in the game, meaning that instead every pistol of every time is suddenly better without any visual representation to show it.
On the multiplayer side of things, we have a number of different ways to play. You can essentially "infect" another player's game by joining in as a monster or creature with the sole goal of killing one of the human players before they manage to finish the chapter they're on. This is neat as it feels a little like Dark Souls, though lacks the heart-pounding result as it's declared and the human players are well equipped to handle it.
You have Mercenaries and the like as well, with Mercenaries also getting a Left 4 Dead crossover. It's the same Mercenaries game mode we've had for awhile with very similar rules. The downside is that the Left 4 Dead crossover feels hamfisted with the characters not really having anything special here as they feel like they were just reskins.
Despite it's flaws, Resident Evil 6 proves to be a fun enough game with various different paces to suit many different moods. The crossovers for the stories of each campaign compliments each other without getting in the way and gives you a reason to hop around the chapters once you unlock them all for a second playthrough.

This might be the best game I've ever played in this genre.
- Amazing story with great theories and concepts
- Fantastic voice acting
- Great character development and stories
- Incredible tension and often very frightening without the use of tropes or stereotypical events
- Sound design that was immersive and added exponentially to the atmosphere and tension
- A visually stunning world that loved making your senses tingle with anticipation
My only criticism was that it was a little linear for some people's tastes, and likely didn't have multiple endings.  But as an interactive horror adventure game, it was a very enjoyable world to walk through and a very fascinating science fiction concept.  I felt like I made my way through a novel written by the likes of Michael Crichton or Carl Sagan.  The fact that the graphics, sound, and acting were top notch far outweighed any criticisms I had.
I can't recommend this enough if you love adventure, horror, and sci-fi.

This game is Killer (see what I did there? lol) I am not really a horror fan, or a huge fan of these films, but this game is great! Its rounds are quick and engaging as hell. You will usually try to survive the night as a camp counselor, or at random be chosen to fulfill your bloodlust as the nearly invinceable Jason Vorhees! As a counselor you race around, using teamwork or solo effort to try and repair cars, boats or a phone to call the police in order to survive... As Jason you get a slew of horror movie trope abilities, like morph teleporting, shifting across small distances, sense perception and so much more! There are tons of unique deaths and kills as well as neat perks the counselors can unlock to help escape. Sure, it can be a bit glitchy and a little clunky with the controls, but to me this game more than makes up for it with it's high quality graphics and unique game mechanics. All in all I'm hella impressed, and as someone who knows only a little about the films even I find myself immersed in the lore and stories behind this games world. - The dark area was very annoying because it was TOO dark, you're ruinning blind for most of it.
Overall:
It's a fine side scrolling puzzler, and the puzzles (save for that damned bug puzzle) weren't too hard. Easy to pick up and beat in a day. Final Thought:
While I do very much recommend it for purchase to play, it's not a game I would replay after 100% it once.

We seem to have a motive for doing what we do, but halfway through the narrator also admits that "we should have dreams or something right?"
Gameplay is rather simple, with some puzzles that can puzzle you because you missed a crucial information piece, or did not see something particular. It is nothing revolutionary, but not too simple.
Gorgeous colors makes you wonder if I am liking the artwork or the light show. Artwork is also probably great. Colors overshadow the artwork.
Narration is unnecessary and breaks immersion, explaining more of the story where no explanation is needed.
In summation: a step in the right direction gamewise, I am looking forward to the next game this team produces, but I cannot recommend this particular one.

Man, where even to begin with this? I just finished it and I'm sitting here in a quiet house, trying to absorb that ending. No spoilers here, but it was pretty much perfect.
Game-wise, this is mainly a stealth horror title. Lots and LOTS of body horror in this. If this squicks you out, this is not the game for you. You'll come across monsters that you can only avoid, you have no way to fight back. When they're around, you know it. You'll have to sneak, distract, run away from, or otherwise stay out of their way. The visuals and sound design are spot-frickin-on. PATHOS-II is fully realized and looks and sounds amazing. Play this in a dark room with headphones and it might as well be a VR title.
Story-wise it deals with the nature of humanity, what it means to be "human". I'm already familiar with the concept of transhumanity, but the protagonist, Simon, is very much naive when it comes to ideas that challenge what it means to be human. What if you could upload yourself into a robot? Would you still be you? What if you could
yourself into a robot? Would there be two yous now? Are you both real or is one of "you" a fake, and what are the implications of either answer?
I'll get down off my soapbox and just say this: I loved this game and I loved the ending. Stay for after the credits roll!

The original rocksmith of 2012 was a great "game," although it wasn't just a game was it?  It was entertaining but also very educational and the latter was indeed the point.  2014 brought that same focus but with an updated user interface and tighter performance which makes it a definitive improvement over the original title.  Songs are easier to learn with the updated interface and with the optional inclusion of the songs from the first game, you have hundreds of dollars you can spend on tracks old, known and new as well.
I'm a bass player and I've practiced more with the game than I've ever had with lessons or trying to teach myself.  Ubisoft says that 20 minutes a day will make you a better guitarist, especially if given 60 days to absorb the techniques provided, but I find that I lose track of time and play well over 2 hours, every evening!  I know i've become better at playing songs from bands such as Radiohead, Chic, Chicago, Vampire Weekend, etc., but I've also become way more comfortable with the instrument and catch myself deviating from the notes on the screen and improvising with shapes and scales that I've learned.. And why not?  It's already paid for and it's not going to smack my fingers for not being a robot.
As far a learning an instrument is concerned, there are some drawbacks such as not teaching you notes (chord's being an exception) but just places to play the songs, but supplement this game with a cheap instructional book to work on your notation and reading simultaneously and IMO, you'll become a decently rounded player.  Musician?.... I don't know about that, but this game can definitely turn you from a music listener to a music player.

Funny how I felt more for these shapes by the end of the game than any characters in most AAA shooters.  However, without the narration and story, I'd say the platforming puzzles would be fun but forgettable; it's the combination of all factors that makes this game stand out for me.

This is a perfect game for winter. I played through it while the weather was below freezing and raining.

The graphics are stunning. Each atmosphere/ biome, color, and each character (Nuna and Fox) have a beautiful and cute style. The game really evicts emotions to the player. The girl and fox have a special companionship that is revealed to be based on a true story in one of the factual cutscenes. The companionship is so strong that if you ever dies the other starts crying then you're sent back to the last checkpoint which is actually really sad, but again it is interesting because normally I'm not attached to the characters in a game like this. As you duck and fight off the blizzard, it is truly heartwarming and wrenching how these two lost characters (both of which you can play as and have special roles/ skills) try and survive from the help of each other and spirit friends along the way.  Through the hardships in life and in the storm, they have each other.
One of the very interesting aspects of this game was the documentary/ cutscene aspect to this game. As you playthrough the game, you unlock interviews  and footage of the Alaskan people this game is based off of. Some of these scenes include the type of clothing they wear and how storytelling influences their culture. There are 24 of these documentary scenes, all unique and adding to the immersion of the player into the lives and culture of the people. It is quite fascinating to me at least and truly gave me a connection and context to the game.
The puzzles in this game are not incredibly difficult, especially if you are not a casual gamer and are looking for something more complex. However, this game is a unique, touching, beautiful, and immersive gaming experience that I 100 percent recommend.

I really want to recommend this game, because its graphics are so beautiful, its music is so sweet, and the story is so intriguing, but the player controller is awful. Right off the bat I have difficulty jumping from platform to platform because the fox is rather unresponsive and doesn't always jump when I press the jump button. In addition, it turns around slowly, requiring about a half second just to face the opposite direction.
These player controller problems coupled with questionable level design result in a very frustrating experience, especially if you're like me and have experience with tighter player controls, such as that in "Ori and the Blind Forest". Coming from that game, the controls in this game are very clunky. Anyway, the levels don't help. There are multiple places where missing one jump causes you to have to redo an entire puzzle from the beginning.
What's worse than missing a jump and falling to your death? Missing your jump and falling to a platform below, from which you have to spend 5 minutes getting back to the place where you missed your jump.
On top of that, the devs haven't posted anything since November 2015 (as of the end of January 2017), and haven't addressed any issues with the game since then.
I want to recommend this game, I really do. So much work has been put into it and it looks fantastic. But it's littered with game-breaking bugs that make it unplayable.

10/10 In every category.
Absolutely gorgeous game. The nuance of movement is stunning, from the transformation of a live geyser into a pillar of ice to the swish of the fox's tail. The music is incredible, and made even more so by the fact that it is played sparsely inbetween gentle stretches of simple ambient noise.
The puzzles start simply, and ensure the player has every opportunity to learn what effect each season has on the environment. The environment itself gives subtle hints to puzzle solutions as well: all you need do is pay attention. Even the most difficult puzzle (which is reached approximately mid-game) requires little more than a decent memory (or pad and pencil) and basic platform skills.
The ease of gameplay allows the player to fully relax into the story and enjoy the journey. While it does ask the player to think, it never puts them in a position where they lose immersion.
Addendum: Highly recommend players seek out The Bird achievement.

I don't think I'm even going to bother to write a "helpful" review here.
Instead, here's a little story.
Once upon a time, there was a very nice EA game called Stardrive. It promised to be so many good things to so many people, and to be a spiritual successor to MoO2, one of the greatest 4x games of it's time. Our young hero read many reviews that said "THIS IS AWESOME, IT HAS SO MUCH POTENTIAL!" and, not realizing at the time that "potential" almost always translates into "don't buy this♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; in non-review english, he decided to buy it.
Many hours passed, and because our hero likes starting 4x games more than finishing them, as well as designing ships, some great fun was indeed had. Soon though, cracks began to appear in the happy facade of his new game - memory overrun bugs would kill games part way through, unfinished tech trees robbed our young friend of satisfaction, and AI issues began to make things feel dull and drab.
"Why have I spent so much time playing this?" he lamented, "If only I'd realized earlier that there is literally no lategame here, instead of starting a thousand different games and only playing the first bit?"
He had to suppress a sob. "And why did it take me so long to realize that there's only one tactic you really need to use in this game? I'm supposed to be good at games, how could I have been fooled by the shiney ship design, when all I had to do all along was jam my ships full of cheap, first level missiles in order to ruin all?"
In the end, he was crushed. Where was this potential the other reviews had told him about? Where were  these promised features that never materialized?
Distraught, he turned to the forums. "Hi guys, I just noticed a few things about this game, and had a few questions." He detailed his experience, and his input, and made a few simple queries such as "How do I make my fighters actually land back on my ships?"
The response that await our hero was unexpected. No sooner had he posted than a wave of drama, anger, and malcontent rushed forward, flowing out of the screen of his ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop, and engulfing him. The force was so great that it nearly capsized his desk, and caused him to be lost in the swirling vortex of it's black waters.
"SUCKER, THIS ♥♥♥♥ING GAME IS GARBAGE AND BROKEN AND THE DEV IS A MASSIVE ♥♥♥♥♥♥", and "ABANDONWARE, NOOB, DON'T BUY IT", and "STFU YOU GUYS THIS IS THE BEST THING EVER AND ZERO IS MY BUDDY AND YOU'RE ALL♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, and "BUT THERE'S ONLY ONE DEV, SO IT'S OK THAT MOST OF THIS SUCKS", and finally, "Hello, I'm a moderator. The dev has essentially done all he can with this engine, and has dropped development in favour of StarDrive 2, which will be everything that was promised and more. Check it out, you'll get 33% off since you bought this game! Also, check out my mod which fixes some of the problems with the game you already own!"
Somehow, he managed to swim free from the maelstrom, and hit the vitriol release valves built into his computer room. As the drama-fluids slowly drained away around him, he vowed to write a negative review, forget about the experience, and never be involved with sequels or games with "potential" in general ever again.
Then, years later, he fatefully stumbled across StarDrive 2 in the Steam store.
Our hero fought the good fight for a time, but all the positive reviews speaking of "potential" (no, you fool! you say) and improvements over the last attempt by the dev began to haunt his every waking moment, invading his thoughts at work, while playing MoO2, and eventually, even began to snake into his dreams.
One night, awakening in a cold sweat from dreams of turn based glory, galactic conquest, ship design, and fighters that could actually land rather than being doomed to spend eternity floating through the cold vacuum after launching, he fell to the dark whispering, and clicked BUY.
The next morning, he realized what he had done, and was filled with sorrow. "My god! What have I done? Even with 33% off, this game is 66% overpriced for what it will likely contain." In shame, he did not play the game for quite some time, during which drama raged, DLCs were released, and countless empires could have risen and fallen.
the despaired internally,
But one day, the urge was too strong. "What's the worst that could happen? Besides, I already bought it."
Our hero, despite having grown wise with the years, foolishly decided to try the game.
"Gee, this isn't too bad. The new turn system is ok, and the ship design is slightly less ♥♥♥♥ed." While not "complete yet", the game was indeed a bit of improvement over the first iteration, and once the promised features of the first game and the new promised features of the second, combined with some of the new DLC, were all in place, it could truely be great. Several hours were spent playing, and our hero slept easy.
For some time afterwards, the game was forgotten, buried deep in the far recesses of the Great Steam Library, under an opaque pile of other games that fit the tag "space" or started with "s". While on a grand re-organization, our hero stumbled on it yet again.
"Hm, I only have 9 or 10 hours on this, and there's lots of easy looking achievements to get. I don't remember it being all that bad, really." And so, he began to play again. "This seems to be loading slower than normal. And appears to have more bugs than I recall. And wait... this is all hex based. Did the developer do me a solid as a former customer, and give me the DLC for free?"
Perplexed, he turned to the forums, and it was immediately evident that something terrible had happened to the denizens within. The place was nearly empty, the remnants of spam and flame wars splattered on the once stunning marble pillars being the only indicator of what may have happened. Through judicious exploration using his trusty torch and noble search feature, most of his questions were answered. There were indeed bugs, and some issues, and the DLC had indeed been given out for free, though apparently by accident.
One question remained, and so he shouted out in the dark to anyone who may still have lingered to hear: "Hi everyone. Been playing this again, it's pretty ok. I noticed that I seem to have gotten the DLC for free, which in my understanding is a bug. I was wondering if I now just *have* this, or if it's going to be patched out. Is there much point in me starting a new game right now?"
The question echoed around the empty halls of the Forum for some time, before a quiet answer was given. "Hello, I'm a moderator. The dev has essentially done all he can with this engine, and has dropped development in favour of...."
The last thing our hero remembered before his vision turned to darkness and his torch sputtered out was a howl, full of fury and pain.
"ZEROOOOOO!!"

Make no mistake, Resident Evil 6 is no longer a (survivor) horror game; it's a full blown action game with horror themes here and there. The story is rather poor (great characters interactions but overall the is full of cliches and most of the backstory is crammed into documents you get by shooting snake emblems) and the campaign itself is full of highs and lows. When it shines, it really does - you get great setpieces, boss fights, interesting over the top action sequences etc. But when it blows, man - it really blows: you will rage in frustration over instadeath QTEs, stupid design decisions, frustrating stealth sections, slow-walk sections (the whole beginning of Leon's campaign), camera control being taken away from you (while enemies can still move and hurt you), annoying vehicle sections... ugh, there's a lot of that.
However, the combat system is fantastic... once you learn it, because Capcom forgot to include a proper tutorial to teach you how to play the game. But when you do get how to play - it's marvelous. It's the most technical and versatile third person shooter that has been released in years, topped only by Vanquish. Forget about boring pop and shoot cover shooters that flood the genre nowadays; this game is all about slides, dodges, counters, stunning enemies and performing melee combos. :D If you spend most of the game hidden behins a cover or standing in place and shooting enemies, you're playing the game wrong. :P
Also, Mercenaries is the best bonus mode ever. EVER. Very addicting and time consuming and at the same time, very satisfying, mostly because it focuses on the game's strengths (the combat system), while throwing away everything else (those highs and lows from the campaign design).
The game is definietely worth checking out.

I think I got this game for free (or part of a bundle at some point) and figured I would try it one afternoon when I was looking to just kill a little time before going out. I'm not usually one for cartoon style graphics, but this game has a way of drawing you in!
I have been playing it for an hour or so every night for the last week and have to say that it has a lot of content and whilst the puzzles don't really require much thinking, it does require some planning as you regularly have to retrace your steps with a different type of minion (Poison, Water, Fire or Normal) in order to pass the next obstacle. It is very cleverly done in that way and so it keeps you engaged and actively looking for things that require you to switch your minions to progress.
When I first started playing, I was a little perplexed by the lack of a mini-map or compass but the more I play it seems like less of an issue. In fact, I am enjoying the exploration factor that you get from playing a game that doesn't have a map feature at all. I would say though that if you prefer a linear game where you don't have to retrace your steps, then this is not for you. Personally though, I am enjoying playing it.
Another thing that stood out to me is the fact that you are technically a bad guy, but can play through the game doing good things. What's more, I couldn't help but notice that you bare a striking similarity to the Witch King of Angmar from Tolkien's Middle Earth and so I enjoyed spreading a little bit of Chaotic Mayhem and Goodwill in a faux Middle Earth. I totally loved beating on the half-lings too, who also live in holes in the ground that are remarkably similar thanks to their rounded doors and tables full of food and beverages. The fact that in this game the Halflings are "evil" really made me chuckle too.
I have been playing the game with my Microsoft wired 360 pad and the controls feel very natural, as the game has a fairly simple interface. My only 2 bug-bears with this games controls however are the inability to seperate minions by class (unless you place multiple gather-points and juggle them yourself) and the fact that the game doesn't seem to have ever told me how to switch through my spells. At 8 hours in, I have discovered the latter by trial and error. Neither of these are a major annoyance though, and whilst the lack of minion sorting can lead you to losing a few every now and then (usually by drowning!), it is really not that hard to go and farm some more of the right life force to spawn some more.
The Crafting system seems pretty basic too, but so far I have not really had much call to change my equipment other than for aesthetic reasons (My Cartoon Witch King needed a sword!). It is nice to have the option to change a few things like that though and so I am glad they added it in.
I have to say that the game is worth buying for anyone who likes strategy rpgs and it's regular price of £3.49 is well worth it. Currently the game is on offer due to the steam summer sale (until 5th july 2017) and at £0.87 it is an absolute steal.
I am so very glad that I decided to try this game. It is very addictive!

At the default resolution the game was beautiful, but I did have some issues with glitching and button lag (which is not good in a platformer!). However, once I set the resolution a little lower, it ran flawlessly. The gameplay was worth the slight loss in crispness in the art.

Despite the annoying monster AI, this game is existential terror at it's finest.  It's highly recommended that you disable the AI with a mod, rendering it a "walking simulator"--but make no mistake: this is an story *everyone* should experience. It messes with your head LONG after you complete it. It sits up there on "Mindf$#k Mountain" with Bioshock and Limbo. Though it could easily be adapted into a horror movie (and, in the right hands, become a classic), a film would fall short in truly grasping the sheer *horror* the main character experiences. The isolation, the mystery of what happened to your predecessors, the *atmosphere*, and the revelations can only be truly experienced through the medium of games. Only a VR remake of this game would make the experience complete.

You like the idea of beating up peasants... and then having the better idea of having someone else do it for you.
Overlord is a remarkably clever and silly role-reverse title. Wreak havoc, pillage the local populace and bash in the toothy grins of the local do-gooders who usurped your predecessor. Punch a Paladin, harass a Halfling and punish peasants. A game that not only gives you full reign to be a complete git, but gives you an army of loyal minions to do it with.
And it's the minions which are ultimately what make this game, both in humour and the unique mechanics. Though you skulk about in your somewhat intimidating armoured frame, the minions do the heavy lifting for you. Whether it's fetching treasure, playing with levers or swarming over foes to bring them down. They're flimsy though, often pounded into dust by anything larger than a sheep - and that's precisely where the challenge lies: Strategic minion control. This gets especially prevalent later on when you regain the specialised minion types: Ranged, assassins and healers... and have to start taking down rock giants, Dwarven tanks and evil unicorns.
It's novel and very enjoyable, yet can equally lead to frustrating moments of losing large swathes of your army to mis-clicks or stupid errors. Playing 3rd person (with all the camera joys that brings)
controlling minions can be a fiddly process, especially in tense moments. Not a deal-breaker by any means, but there are moments later on where you'll need to hit a lot of keys... so make sure you're ready for it.
The crafting system is also a little basic, and can create a horrible grind later on when pushing for the best kit, which requires somewhere in the region of 1,000 minions to be sacrificed to fully upgrade. It starts beautifully, then loses pace near the later stages... but at the very least rounds to a satisfying conclusion.
The story is brilliant though, with some clever twists and turns. The general look-and-feel of the game is equally fantastic and fun, helped massively by the minion shenanigans with their gleeful cries of "For the Overlord!" and donning pumpkins as creative helmets (at least until they find something heavier to wield, like a zombie limb) - small details but one that give Overlord an undeniable warmth. It's all very silly, but satisfying - taking a refreshing stance in the classic human/elf/dwarf world... by utterly wrecking it.
It's stupid, it's clever and it's very unique. Still great after 10 years.

I picked this game up when it was on sale when the overall reviews were positive rather than mixed, and I have to say that I am really glad that I did, because it is actually a rather good game with a unique character and sense of humour running through.
Most of the negative reviews concentrate on the bugs and difficulty of the game.  I don't really understand this.  I get the occasional bug and have to re-load a save now and then, but it certainly is not bug-ridden as many reviews imply.
It is a hard game because your enemies will send massive fleets against you and if you don't manage to defeat them in the first battle and lose your entire fleet, chances are you will not be able to recover.  It is very satisfying when the tide of war turns in your favour.
Once you have learnt to design your ships effectively and understand the balance of research, construction, expansion and conquest, you will find progressing through the game very enjoyable because unlike most 4x4 games, it remains a challenge right up to the end.  The AI is clever enough not to engage you in battle unless it thinks it can win.
There are little sub-quests and unusual things to be discovered in the galaxy, which keeps you interested when you first start playing.  The ship design aspect is excellent and it's fun to see how the different weapon systems work out.  The aliens are varied and interesting.  Dipolmacy can be very effective and I find I use it a lot more than in most 4x4 games.
As it is such a hard game, I'll end my review with some tips.  Keep your ships fast and manoeuvre the fleet manually to avoid the initial barrage of rockets from the enemy.  If your ships are fast and manoeuvrable they can avoid a lot of the slow heavy rockets the AI often likes to use and you can run rings around their ships, attacking them from the rear with laser or beam weapon turrets.  If you have shields and your enemy doesn't, use hit and run tactics to give your shields time to recharge as their armour will be permanently damaged.  If the enemy has shields as well, then keep manoeuvring until they have used all their rockets then close for the kill.
Use diplomacy to get the technologies you need if you can't research them.  Shields and good engines will beat a slow and well armoured ship, unless that ship also has shields and equal beam weapons.
The Pollops are probably the easiest race to play as, because their ships have so much space for weapon hardpoints.  They are weak in ground combat, but you can blockade the enemy planets to stop them building fleets while you build up your troops.
The game is very much inspired by the old MOO2 game and it feels like an improved and modern version of that game.

There really should be a "maybe" option for steam reviews... Orwell is a decent game, just not the kind of game that is engaging for me.
Orwell is more a graphic adventure game rather than the espionage game it was advertised as. If you like Life is Strange, you'd probably like Orwell.
Sadly this is not my cup of tea. I want to actually think and *play* a game. If I want a story I'd watch a movie or a let's play... The story had to be deeper than this for me to be interested.
The good:
Orwell did a good job at designing the user interface. It's beautiful, functional, and believable. The artstyle is unique and pleasing to the eye.
You'd find that despite the handholding, you will have to make choices that will have separate story outcomes. Some choices are more "right" than others, There're be hints in the game to help you make the right choice, so the choices are at least not just random.
The bad:
However, just like the other reviewers had pointed out, the articles and character profiles are too simplistic, it doesn't feel "real" enough. This design choice is understandable since adding fluff and pointless information just for the sake of making the sites "real" doesn't help with immersion either. So I'm an intermediate guitar player that hit a plateau and stopped playing for the most part. Every once in a while I would pick it up and play around a little but I never really stuck with it too long. Then I decided to get RockSmith 2014 during the steam summer sale...
It took a little while to get used to the way the notes are presented but honestly, that didn't take too long and the easy levels are a good way to get used to it because they don't throw too many notes at you all at once. The game also gets progressively harder as you do well.
Along with the actual game, I also bought the surf pack mainly for the song "Walk, don't run" which is one of my favorite surf songs. If I were to find tabs of this, I would play around, get frustrated and probably give up, especially if trying to play along with the recording. With Rock Smith, the Riff Repeater is a huge help. I can slow it down and I still get the backing band and I can set the difficulty level and I'll spend hours practicing this one song. You can even select a section of the song to keep repeating. Trying to do this with tabs and mp3s is probably possible but would be a giant PITA to setup and you'll need special software to slow down the song and then you have to figure out where in the song you are in relation to the tabs and it would just be a mess. I will say that this song at 100% difficulty and 100% speed is crazy hard but I'm determined.
Of course, not all the songs are this hard, there are a lot of easier songs and of course multiple difficulty levels per song. Since you have the backup band it's still fun to play on the easier levels because you still hear the song.
I don't know how easy it would be for someone completely new to guitar but there are tons of lessons in there that I haven't really looked at yet but plan to just for completeness sake. (I mean, I don't really need to watch a video on how to put my strap on the guitar but I guess it's good for someone?) Hopefully as I look at more of the lessons I'll find some harder stuff I don't know but I've just been having fun with the game.
The biggest thing is that this game makes practice fun. Practicing scales and even just songs over and over again can get repetitious and boring. With this game, the backing band behind you and the ability to focus on smaller sections of the song at a whim, it makes it a lot nicer.
The one downside I've found so far would be that I'd love the ability to make my own selection to reapeat in the riff repeater rather than the pre-defined sections (of course you can include multiple sections, you just can include say the next two notes or split a section in half). I'd also like the ability to pause and step through. Sometimes the harder songs, even when slowed down, I'll miss a few notes and I'll just have to wait until it repeats again and if it's in a busy section of the song I might miss it again.
I have some other minor things about the interface that I wish I could change (like using the tones in tone designer is weird) but it's possible I just need to read up on how to do it.
All in all I love this game and there's so much to do. Between the songs, the mini games and session mode, there is enough to keep you busy for a long while. The best part is, all of it is designed to help make you a better guitar player. So I don't know if I'd use *just* this to learn guitar but it's certainly very complimentary to other lessons.

If you like quirky, unorthodox games like The Stanley Parable, you will certainly get some enjoyment from it. Similarly to The Stanley Parable, it's a game that's less about winning and more about wandering about and seeing what you can do. There are a couple of big differences though.
The first is that it's linear. There's only one path to take, and no amount of meandering through doors will change that. Instead, however, you are given large, open areas to explore, with a nice handful of jokes, minigames, and even the odd sidequest. If you try rushing through the objectives and getting to the end, you will miss out on most of the meat the game has to offer.
The other difference is, obviously, the style. This is much more cartoony, with a nice dose of slapstick thrown in there. The humour is certainly a lot more visual than lyrical, although there's some good dialogue in there too.
I would highly recommend this game if you're looking for something funny and quirky, a nice experience albeit short. On the other hand if you're looking for a traditional espionage game with stealth and whatnot, yeah this really isn't for you. Hitman this ain't. :P

Jason is back! And more powerful than ever!
Skip down a bit for the actual review: In Friday the 13 game Jason from the popular horror movie Friday the 13
comes back to kill one of many councilors you can choose for which variety of talents. Pick AJ or Jenny when hiding. Pick Kenny, Adam, AJ, Deborah or Eric if you want to be able to repair. Kenny, Vanessa, Chad or Jenny are made for fighting Jason better... From 4-10 players get thrown into a lobby with one randomly being Jason, and then Jason hunts them all down well the councilors have a few options: A: Repair a car B: If there is a boat on your map you can repair that and escape
C: Repair the phone and call the cops and escape with them D: Hide your way out (Do not try this very long especially unless your AJ or Jenny)
NOW FOR THE REVIEW!
PART 1 VALUE: Now I have seen quite a few people that say one mode is not worth $40. Well this mode is damn good at being fun over time! I have 90 hours and still have fun when I play.
PART 2 Luck?: Well people can spawn as some lucky **** that gets a shotgun and pocket knife off the bat. But the game stays pretty fun even if your stranded with crap and the map is relatively small so it's not that big of a deal.
PART 3 Being Jason!: When you start the game people watch that cutscene to see if they may get to be Jason.
And then when the game starts you get to take those pocket knifes off the wall and the hunt starts!
I'll also have a guide to both councilors and Jason at the bottom!
PART 4: Being councilor!: When you unfortunetly don't get Jason *Sad violin plays* You get to go into cabins and grab things to fight off Jason. Also it is so satisfying when you get a pocket knife and a part to repair with! Also even when you get grabbed a lot of the time you can enjoy the death and with a silly community. I've seen two very hilarious scenarios. One asked if I needed a Dentist checkup before bending my mouth until it comes off. One killed everyone with a hug. Awwwwwww cute little Jason.
PART 5: Glitches/Bugs: The game has a decent amount of bugs but the game isn't as bad as *ahem* Halo 5
But you run into them occasionally. Also a lot of the time if you get knocked out when your about to shift it can lock you in position and throw you outside the map... Also if you put multiple traps down you can get stuck (Not sure if it was fixed)
GUIDE!
Jason: Right away at the beginning of the game you should grab the pocket knifes coming out in the cabin you spawn in.
Then right away after you should teleport to the Telephone icon, and put Traps (R) in front of the phone (Be careful the traps do not go under the box or they will not work) Then you want to wait until you get sense and anything RED means people are nearby. For general purpose. The best Jason seems to be Part 6. I would say the worst one is Part 9 due to the lack of damage and traps. But most of the others are pretty nice.
Councilor: Right away you want to run into a cabin and lock the door and open the windows and search dressers for items
Then you want to move onto the next house when you can. Then you want to keep searching houses. If you find something roundish and tall (Hmmmmmm I wonder what Chad has been up to) It's the phone fuse. You want to ask in chat (Hold T) where the phone box is.
REPAIRING: Go up to whatever you want to repair you hold E and then you press left or right click depending on platform obviously. For the boat you need a propellor and Gas (Same one as the car uses) And the car needs Gas and the battery. Then you need the Keys to start it. BE CAREFUL! Jason can stop it by simply standing in front of it.
WHEN JASON ARRIVES!: Do not try to fight Jason like you can beat him. You will die unless you are in a group, then you can be more offensive. Also if you wanna be offensive. You need a character with high LUCK. Anything above 3 is fine (For stunning) (You don't need luck neccesarily) and ima teach you guys a few tricks
One: camping *****: You wait for Jason to break down the door then break the second the door falls down. Also putting a trap by the door is useful
Two: Dodge a grab or hit then whack him (Also a good trick for Jasons to abuse
Three: If you are about to be grabbed, Especially in close quarters: Try to dodge the grab and escape the house. It has worked for me many many times.
Strategy, chessing: You camp a window and wait for Jason to come then he will have to go all the way around.
FINAL REVIEW 8/10

Let me begin by saying that I didn’t know much about this game until recently, but since I found out it's being developed by some of the same guys who worked on S.T.A.L.K.E.R. I decided to try it out, especially since it's free.
First impression wasn't very good: I had some technical issues related to my video driver, the game kept crashing to desktop all the time and I was tempted to uninstall and forget about it. I'm glad I didn't though. Support was prompt to reply to my ticket and, following their suggestion, I managed to solve the problem and from then on the game works perfectly.
So, technical issues solved, I discovered a game that can potentially be a dark horse of online multiplayer shooters. But let's be clear about one thing: while it's obviously inspired by S.T.A.L.K.E.R. (after all it’s made by some of the same people), it's not a multiplayer version of it. I think some of the bad rep comes from the fact that, as I read, the devs announced a while a go that they'll include an open-world survival mode, which isn't there (at least not yet). But for what it is, the game does very well what it sets out to do: being a good competitive online shooter. Play it for what it is and you’ll discover a good game here.
At the moment, there are 4 game modes: Team Deathmatch (self explanatory), Battery Retrieval (where you have to go to specific points on the map and pick-up batteries to deliver to your base - pretty fun and allows some interesting co-op tactics), Research (where you have to conquer / defend certain spots on the map) and Artifact Hunt (where you have to be on the lookout for a randomly-spawning artifact and try to deliver it to your base).
Here’s another reason why some players may choose to rate this down: the waiting time for finding a match can be rather long (although it can also take a few seconds, depending on your luck). But a little patience goes a long way, since the gameplay is worth it and you’re not stuck on a waiting screen either. You can have a chat or manage your inventory, which has some interesting customizing and upgrading options. The gun play is solid (including bullet ricochets flying around), the graphics look good (some of the map areas are plain gorgeous) and the sound effects are very well done. Getting a kill feels rewarding, and while the maps aren't that many, they all have variations based on what game mode you're playing and also offer different time of day / weather effects, which add to the diversity.
In case you decide to try it out, take note that in the beginning you will only be playing against bots. I can't remember now if it's just the first match or the first 5 matches, but it's designed this way so that you can get a feel for it before taking on real opponents. Don't despair, you will get to play with and against other real people. However, you will still encounter bots because of the current small (but dedicated) player base, so a 5 vs. 5 can sometimes be a 2 vs. 2, with the rest of the spots filled by bots. But you will always have real people to compete against and If you like the game and progress to the upper tiers (5 and above) you will get to play Ranked Matches, which are 100% real players (although again you gotta have a little patience for the match to fill). Here’s another tricky part: as a newbie you can stumble upon experienced players which WILL tear you apart before you even realize what’s going on. I know because I’ve been there. But I guess, like in all games, practice makes perfect, so take it easy and have some fun while learning the ropes. :)
Oh, and if you want a detailed breakdown of your stats and matches, here you go:
(LATER EDIT: currently not updated for the latest version).
Also, in case you’re wondering, this is not P2W. Gold / Premium equipment, as far as I can tell, doesn’t have any unfair edge over any equipment you can eventually grind your way to without having to go through your wallet. And other things you can get for real money are purely cosmetical. Sure, you can get XP faster if you pay for a Premium account (which you can sometimes get for free by completing Daily Missions), but it doesn’t put you at any sort of disadvantage if you don’t.
So, bottom line, I really like Survarium and think it deserves a better rating than it currently has and a larger player base too. That's why I wrote this. For a free game it’s really solid and has plenty of potential. Give it a try, you might like it too. :)

Never written a Steam review before, or returned a game. And I'm fully in support of ANY lone developer, and the huge amount of effort it must take to get a game like this to market all on your own...
But seriously - £29.99 (price of DLC bundle), for this?!
I don't know or care if SD2 is a rich and involving 4X strategy (although on surface inspection, it looks like a forgettable and mediocre space-4X like many others). For me, the dumb and inherently buggy interface killed any enthusiasm. Considering the advances strategy games have made in this area in recent years, especially since the interface IS THE GAME in this genre, and not forgetting this is the Dev's 2nd attempt, I honestly don't know how they looked at ANY of this and thought "Yeah! Looks great!"
Again, credit where credit is due - apparently both StarDrive games are the work of a lone Dev. A solitary code-monkey who has clearly never used an interface in their whole life. Half of SD2 looks like placeholder art, with utterly dreadful layouts and spacings, 3-4 different typefaces in any single screen (most important text is... ugh... Arial). No consistency between buttons or widgets. If something looks click-able, it's 50/50 just meaningless. Somebody spent a lot of time drawing pointless "sci-fi" lines, dials and squiggles around everything, just to make the terrible layouts even fussier without any actual purpose... Mr Lone Dev: look at those stupid sqiggles, and now ask yourself: Why?
Tutorial windows that wouldn't close when I'd done as asked (restart); Windows obnoxiously overlaying windows, but still allowing clicks "through"; Yet more windows appearing UNDER other UI ellements; An "Are you sure?" message that didn't care I'd clicked Cancel (restart); Paragraphs of unedited flavour text that only labotomised chimps would laugh at; Tool-tips for EVERYTHING, as if having ANY useful information on screen is just a damning admission that Yes, we made a mistake with the Arial font...
In short, it looks unfinished, feels unfinished, and in the face of Stellaris and GalCivIII, most probably IS unfinished. Most other Steam reviews seem to agree, and there are plenty of conspiracists accusing the Dev of shenanigans.
I haven't played enough to honestly comment on the long game, or AI failings etc, and I do feel a little disingenuous returning a game this early... but sometimes you just KNOW you've wasted £30, and that is NOT a small amount of money. Nothing about the 1.4hrs I've seen was in any way enjoyable. I can't imagine suffering that interface for any longer - let alone the hours an average 4X takes.
Considering SD1 is still going for £22.99 (?!), was there really not enough spare cash to pay for a dedicated artist with a singular vision for the UI, rather than this hodge-podge? Sorry Mr Lone Dev (and I do mean that), but maybe you should employ a friend - if only to remind you that your s*** stinks.

There really should be a "maybe" option for steam reviews... Orwell is a decent game, just not the kind of game that is engaging for me.
Orwell is more a graphic adventure game rather than the espionage game it was advertised as. If you like Life is Strange, you'd probably like Orwell.
Sadly this is not my cup of tea. I want to actually think and *play* a game. If I want a story I'd watch a movie or a let's play... The story had to be deeper than this for me to be interested.
The good:
Orwell did a good job at designing the user interface. It's beautiful, functional, and believable. The artstyle is unique and pleasing to the eye.
You'd find that despite the handholding, you will have to make choices that will have separate story outcomes. Some choices are more "right" than others, There're be hints in the game to help you make the right choice, so the choices are at least not just random.
The bad:
However, just like the other reviewers had pointed out, the articles and character profiles are too simplistic, it doesn't feel "real" enough. This design choice is understandable since adding fluff and pointless information just for the sake of making the sites "real" doesn't help with immersion either. What would help with immersion is the compelling content; which I find sadly lacking here... I find myself just skimming through for highlights. It's too much hand-holding for my taste. Really, they could have made it so much better by just making the relevant text unhighlighted so we have to actually spend effort reading and playing the game as "intended".
