A full, immersive horror experience that goes far, far beyond the simple experience of the original. This game will ease you in with beautiful scenery, haunting music and a tense atmosphere, then gradually lead into the paranormal investigation into where the player's friend has gone and what the thing that took her is. From suspenseful searches through abandoned locations, to shortlived breather moments, to intense chases, this game has all the elements needed to excel as a horror.
There are some downsides unfortunately. A lot of the scares are jumpscares, the enemy AI can be cheap at times and there are some bugs in need of ironing out. The main problem is the jumpscares, which there seem to be a lot of, in addition to the moments of genuine horror.
If you can forgive some of its cheap scares and fully immerse yourself in the heart-pounding experience that is Slender: The Arrival, you will have a short but altogether riveting time playing. Choose to get the terrifying experience over with as soon as you can or spend time gathering clues as to what happened - which in itself is an extremely interesting story.
For horror fans, this is perfect. You will dread continuing on, in fear of what is to come. At times there will be nothing, at others your worst suspicions will be confirmed and something horrible will come at you from the darkness. But always the game will be gripping and have a lot more to offer past the first playthrough, from extra content to undiscovered clues.

Resident Evil is another franchise that to have any hope of enjoying now, you have to forget what it used to be. There is nothing for survival horror fans to enjoy here. Of the 4 campaigns, Leon and Ada try to pretend to be horror, but there's still too much action, and its pointless putting hidden key puzzles in completely linear maps. Leon also has to suffer countless unforgiving QTEs. Chris and Jake play like a standard 3rd person shooter, and therefore more enjoyable, if that's what you're in the mood for. Although they do have some frustrating running at the camera sections and dull turret sections. The story is okay but you need to play all campaigns to get the whole picture. One area I can't fault is value for money. It took me 24 hours to complete all campaigns, and only Ada's felt too short. Coop partner AI is vastly improved on RE5. My advice is to buy it on sale, wait until you're in the mood for a dumb shooter, then play Chris and Jake, and treat the rest as bonus content.

Before we get started, this is not Ori and the Blind Forest. It might look a bit like Ori, but it does not play like Ori. Don't go into this expecting something similar.
Seasons After Fall is a puzzle platformer by French developer Swing Swing Submarine. Unlike their previous games, which were also puzzle platformers, this one offers one big semi-open world, where more gets accessible as you go along and learn new abilities, much like in a Metroidvania game. It's entirely without combat though, all your powers just allow you to solve new puzzles.
Let's get the most obvious thing out of the way first, Seasons After Fall is absolutely gorgeous. The game has an almost hand-painted look to it, with makes good use of bold colours. Every single area is visually distinct, yet the game presents a coherent whole. The games main mechanic, changing seasons, makes this all the more impressive as each season is also visually distinct.
While not as technically advanced as some other games, like Dust: An Elysian Tail, the animations look really good in Seasons after Fall, and a lot of care seems to have been put into making the main character, a young fox, feel like a young playful fox. The animation show an impressive attention for details in how the fox moves.
The sound is no slouch either. The game has an excellent soundtrack that fits really well with the game. While it's probably not a soundtrack that will find its way into every cellphone & MP3 player out there, it works well for the game. The sound effects are also well made and fit well in. None feels out of place, and while they are clearly noticeable, they don't get annoying. That's how sound effects should be.
There's not a whole lot of voice acting in this game, but the voice actors that they found work well. There are two characters that are extensively voice, and I thought the voice actors did a great job portraying them.
The gamplay in Seasons after Fall is relatively simple. It's structured like a typical Metroidvania game, where getting a new power opens up more of the map, and you use this to get yet another new power, up until the end of the game. In Seasons after Fall these powers are the abilities to change seasons. Changing season makes some changes to things around you, like for an example, in spring the water levels will be higher, and in winter water freezes. In summer certain plants will grow and water levels will be lower, and in autumn mushrooms grow and winds will be stronger. It's a simple concept, but it works well here. If there's one gripe I have with the game then it's the fact that the puzzles are too easy. Not once did I feel challenged by the puzzles.
Movement of your character works like in most other platformers. One aspect that might feel a bit strange at first is how the character jumps. Your fox jumps quite high, and not as far as you might think it would. I suspect that they made this choice because they wanted the jump to feel like a playful pounce. The fox jumps like a young fox would jump when playing.

I really enjoyed my time with Seasons after Fall. It was a beautiful game and it feels like the developers had put a lot of effort into it. I previously mentioned the animators showing an impressive attention to detail. This extents to other parts of the game as well. How the fox moves, tiny background elements and heck, even the loading screen shows a nice touch as the direction you're moving in when entering a loading screen changes the direction of movement in the loading screen. It's a tiny detail, but it's a nice touch, and those nice touches really start adding up. The game is sadly not flawless, it's a bit on the easy side, and it's also relatively short, but what's in there is excellent, and I still feel that I can recommend this game to almost everyone.

[SPOILER WARNING: I discuss heavy story plot points and elements for the title]
You know, I gave the Seasons of the Fall a good shot. I originally bought the game based off two criteria: the art style and wanted to buy a casual game for my girlfriend and I to enjoy. I would have played Ori and the Blind Forest, but as she is not an “average gamer” it would have been too difficult for her to play; so how simple the mechanics for Seasons of the Fall are was nice at first, but as the game progressed we slowly questioned the purchase.
We attempted to understand and get behind the story, but we just couldn’t. We assumed we would be going on a cute adventure as some fox, but instead we are some spirit seed that possesses a fox over and over again for the narrator’s hidden agenda (someone call PETA lol). Your objective and purpose is also unclear for meeting the guardians of the forest and collecting these season shards. I understand the story is supposed to be unclear and vague, but without enough context it left myself and my girlfriend baffled as to what was going on and didn’t want us to continue.
The danger of the “angry” guardians was never present because as you meet them they help you right away with no context. And that is the key word, the game has little context besides the narrator giving vague descriptions that never become true. Like certain guardians being angry or unpredictable. Nothing is ever shown.
Some puzzle mechanics are painful, not because they are hard just because of how the fox and other objects are controlled. Even the fox jump will stutter quite often causing missteps or, rather, mis-jumps. It feels laggy.
I will admit we never finished Seasons of the Fall and I ended up watching a 100% speedrun by “StrawberrySpeedruns” on Twitch to see the complete story (I might add StrawberrySpeedruns narrates quite a bit of detail as he speedruns the game and is a welcoming change versus speedrunners who play music or don’t talk while playing). And after watching the speedrun I admit that the story needs to be vague, but I need to care somehow for the role I am playing at the beginning or that the story encouraged solving the mystery earlier on through the player rather than arbitrarily through game itself. In my opinion, the game has ten minutes to an hour to grab a player. If it doesn’t by then, then the developers did not do a good enough job. And even the speedrunner at times admits that the story is never complete or questions still go unanswered. The game leaves more questions than answers. And it’s just not a satisfying story overall.
I love the music and art style and how the world looked so dramatically different with each season change. However, because of a bad story (or story context) and some poor mechanics either involving the player controlled fox or puzzle elements I cannot recommend this title. The meat of the game is needs polish and the story needs to be reworked. It’s unfortunate because it seems like some love and care was put into the title.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is one of the most compelling, contemporary games available on Steam. Without pandering to any particular side, Orwell allows the player to explore the pros, cons, and grey areas of state-sanctioned surveillance. I also recommend this game if you have a busy life and can only play short segments at a time...and don't want to be caught dead with Candy Crush or Bubble Witch Saga at the top of your play-time list.
The only downside is that the game involves a lot (and I mean a LOT) of text. You're going to be doing a lot of reading. However, it's largely digestible because text is separated into news articles, web pages, and timelines (much like Facebook).
Orwell is worth the buy, even if it's not on sale. 8/10 would recommend.

Great game, I got it in the humble bundle monthly along with other games, and decided to play it because it looked interesting.
Describing the game, it's a very well made point and click adventure, but it's different from your typical point and click games because here you just use Orwell, an operating system designed to watch and monitor people, you can browse different websites and access all sorts of public and private information about your suspects, you go from page to page, phone to phone, computer to computer, device to device, as you try and look for useful information that may help you in your objectives.
The story is short but entertaining and exciting, you get the feeling of really becoming an Orwell 'investigator', the feeling is authentic, the websites, pages, profiles, articles, and that sort of stuff seemed believable enough to get you going into the story. Sometimes the story feels a little bit linear and forced upon you, e.g. pages that you need to look into for information will sometimes be spoonfed to you. but I get it though, if it wasn't though, many people won't know what to do next and get stuck, and they will need to add a lot more useless filler pages/information to make it a more realistic and harder experience. As typical with these kinds of games, there are multiple endings, all affected by your choices in the game. so it adds a bit of replay value.
I only hope they add more episodes/cases next, as the story is a bit short and there is potential for more storytelling using the Orwell system, I also hope they added in voice acting for the voice call tapping parts. so It feels even more authentic.
I'd also not recommend it for it's full price at the moment(IF they add in more free episodes/cases, then I will change my stance about this, a Season Two is coming though, but that's for another price unfortunately). if you can get it for 50% off, I'd say it's now worth it. Alright, this is going to be a long and honest review of the game. If you are planning to get this, please read my review first. It might save you from wasting your time or money.
I'm a "Survarium" Veteran and someone who knew about the development of the game, as early as 2013.
We were promised an authentic S.T.A.L.K.E.R. multiplayer, open-world high quality experience.
I took part in the first closed betas. The game was just PVP back then in small CoD-like maps. We were told that this is "just a place holder" and that we would get open world PVE very soon. We believed them, because the game back then looked and played amazing. The game was tactical and you couldn't go guns blazin without getting punished for it. You had to listen to footsteps and always go slowly. You had to use your camouflage to blend with your surroundings. (Unarguably the best game when it came to camouflage. No other game made it so rewarding to find a good spot.)
The graphics were phenomenal. High quality textures, thick vegetation that you could actually hide in, high-resolution anomalies spawning all over the map and great shadows over the distance. It was a masterpiece. All it needed was the open world update.
BUT.... once the game became an open beta, the updates started getting slower. With every update, the netcode worsened. OP guns were introduced in the game and tactical gameplay started getting weaker and weaker. With update 0.29 the game died.
The amazing and dense vegetation was completely removed and replaced with low-quality short grass that looked unnatural. It made camouflage and hiding completely useless.
Lighting became worse. Shadows became much lighter and softer. It made people hiding in shadows easy kills. It also made the game look kind of blurry because the lighting was so unnatural.
Sounds were changed. Everything regarding sound was just downgraded. Gun sounds weaker, footsteps weaker/random and ambiance removed.
KILLCAM added too, which made Snipers even more useless. Not only people now couldn't hide in the vegetation anymore, but they were also visible in the killcam.
Frequent game crashes.
Now, this might seem bad but trust me, it didn't just stop there.
After that update, the forums were filled with people complaining but the developers (Vostok) completely ignored us!!! Moderators STARTED BANNING PEOPLE AND DELETING THREADS!
The devs continued to add more stupid updates to the game such as low-poly weapon attachments that completely broke how shotguns and assault rifles performed. Gun condition was completely removed and people no longer had to pay a lot for grenades. With every update, the game was getting closer and closer to becoming a fast-paced low quality COD!
A few updates ago, the graphics became even worse. In distance greater than 90 meters, grass completely disappears even on maximum settings. Textures become even more blurry and the game looks terrible compared to what it looked like back in early 2015!
Armors are broken. You can have the heaviest 90+ kg armor equipped with two heavy assault rifles or a .50 sniper and still be able to sprint around endlessly. Now only people who go guns blazing with the fastest ROF weapons win! The game is no longer tactical and requires no thinking whatsoever!
And of course, the game is filled with hackers. The anti-cheat system is a joke.
If you thought Survarium was going to be a hardcore and atmospheric S.T.A.L.K.E.R. experience, please stay away from this game. Don't even bother downloading it. We want this game to die already. Their playerbase is rapidly decreasing and I can't wait for the greedy liars at Vostok to go completely bankrupt!

Conflict:  Orwell is an excellent game that is well designed and well written.
Conflict: Orwell is a poorly written game that is horribly designed.
Choose one.
Orwell is a game that would demand someone choose one of these options, and the problem is is Orwell is an very good game, that is well written.  It however has some horrible design choices that stop me from calling it excellent or perfect.  In fact these design choices are VERY problematic.
The entire game of Orwell is viewing webpages/conversations/phone calls and hunting down information and uploading it to a major database.  You're allowed free access to almost anything and you can upload almost anything to the database and play with it.  You'll get chastised for uploading garbage information, but it's also kind of fun.  Then the government who hired you to find the information will eventually operate on what you have found.   The story is told through these uploads and the results of your information gathering will change the story.  That's kind of cool.
And Orwell tells a compelling (if a little predictable) story.  However it ends abruptly and seems to think it's ending can be a lot more impactful than it ends up being.   And then it falls into an egregious hole of pushing replayability but not allowing players to replay part of the story.
But the thing is Orwell doesn’t really explain it’s gameplay.  The core of the gameplay is not what you upload, but rather what you choose not to upload, or how you choose to resolve conflicts.   But I really hate how it handles conflicts.  What it should do is allow you to upload conflicting information and have you choose how to resolve it explaining more “what do you think?”  Instead it makes this assumption that A or B is right and whichever you choose, they kind of operate on.  However that’s not how the world works, there’s conflicts in a single paragraph and the question is does the guy feel remorseful or does the guy feel responsible for the past… the answer is probably both, why make me choose.
Then there’s other conflics that seem to not matter.  But what’s really important is what doesn’t get uploaded, and that’s kind of the problem.
The first game you’re going to upload everything, because that’s what you think is right, but the game is VERY interesting when you don’t upload everything, you can change the game and the story minorly because of this.  You WILL end at the same point, but there is changes that happen.
Sadly, the ending is a trinary Mass Effect style choice, that feels a bit eyerolling, even the “this ending is only unlocked if X” doesn’t happen and the end is really two or three screens.   I just want more interactivity in the story.
The other problem is the final episode is actually excellent.  This is the episode where the game shines in a brand new way, it adds a new twist and limits the operator.  I almost wish this twist was added in day two or day three because it makes it much more intense to decide what you do, and I’d have liked to see the decisions on day 2 or 3 affect the ending, perhaps locking off the good ending if you fail.
You see, the game feels a bit like the Teltale games, low interactivity, always reach the same ending and while that’s true, it’s not the same.  In Telltale, the same things happen no matter what, but in this game, there is changes, I just wish there was bigger meaningful changes that persisted, or even changed the ending and I’m hopeful for the future of Orwell because of that.
But the story itself is good, if not as interactive as you like.  There’s good story twists, there’s good characters, and I actually like everyone involved in the story.  Orwell is supposed to be about the surveillance state, and even in that way Orwell shines.  And at 5 hours for a full gameplay it might seem expensive, but it can easily be played a second time.
However replayability does suck, almost the entire game is the same and you have to play at least 3 or 4 hours to replay it.  I wish each episode would be replayable separate so I could go get the three endings of episode 3 and 5 without the full replay.  I didn’t mind a second replay but the third is abusive.
Overall though I DO like Orwell, the litmus test for this game is “did I put season 2 on my wish list” and I did.  I liked it that much.  10 bucks seems high but I think it’s worth the money, and even if not you can get it on sale.  It’s a unique experience, and a fun and interesting take on the surveillance state.  But even my complaint about the design and the way the game really presents it’s gameplay doesn’t ruin and interesting and engaging story.
I’m hopeful, I want to see season 2 have more interactivity, I want to see season 2 involve more limitations on the user, and I want season 2 to be better, but for a first season of a rather novel game type, I’m pretty happy.  Orwell delivers what it intends to and I do adore how it does so.

Feeding Frenzy 2: Shipwreck Showdown is an arcade-style video game involving the marine food chain. It is also the sequel to the 2004 title, Feeding Frenzy. The game was developed and published by PopCap Games.

Gameplay
As in Feeding Frenzy, players have to control several fast growing marine predators who are out to uncover a mystery which is lurking in the ocean. The aim of the game is to avoid predators and obstacles while eating other smaller fish and creatures, eventually reaching the top of the food chain. Feeding Frenzy 2 includes 60 new levels which feature scenery such as new underwater worlds, coral reefs, deep sea caves, and sunken ships, as well as above water challenges. The story mode starts the player as a small butterfly fish named Boris. The player has to eat and chomp his or her way to the top of the food chain. Along the way, the player meets new creatures, both friendly and unfriendly.
Plot
The player controls different fishes. We start first as Boris the butterfly fish. In the end of each the 9th stage, the fish saw a dark shadow. After moving on and moving on until we reach Goliath the shark, Goliath reached the top of the food chain and battles the Intruder. He lured the Intruder to a nearby mine. When the INTRUDER explodes the mine, it stays stunned and we have to eat enough shrink shroom to attack the intruder. After defeating the INTRUDER, the alien fish shrunk and escaped, so we have to re-control the fish in the previous food chain to track down the Intruder. The stages after the first boss battle got more difficult, and each fish that we re-control have 3 stages only. However this is an exception to Edie the Angler Fish as the Intruder was said to be afraid of the dark. After we reach the last stage, Boris battles the Intruder in an ocean full of cuttlefish and poison fishes. After shrinking the Intruder for one last time, the Intruder was eaten by Boris.
Special abilities
The animals which the player controls have special abilities, although these are generally quite similar to those in the previous title. They include a "dash" maneuver for a quick burst of speed, the ability to "suck up" a large school of fish all at once, as well as an ability which allows the character Edie to light up her way.
Power-ups
The game features power-ups which can be used to gain instantaneous or short term effects. These include older power-ups from the previous game, as well as completely new ones:
Lighting Bolt: A lightning bolt icon which is usually stored in a bubble. The effect of this power-up is to provide increased swimming speed.
Shrink Shroom: The effect of this power-up is to shrink any fish whose size is bigger than the player.
Instant Illuminate: Lights up the whole screen for a few moments during the "Midnight Zones".
Looney Lures: This power-up is displayed as a hook icon. It lures and moves bigger fish off of the screen.
1UP: The player is awarded an extra life.
Golden Herring: This fish makes the player grow one level size, allowing you to eat the next biggest fish. This fish is fast though, and the best method of catching it is to use the inhale ability.
Plankton: Can be eaten by Edie for light in midnight zones.
Environments
Above water challenges
In some levels the player will be able to jump out of the water, catching several insects and bugs which wander near the surface. In the air, the player can use an ability which sucks a number of insects at the same time. The player can also do back flips to gain more style points, while a failed attempt will result in a belly flop. Also some are just in the middle waters of the ocean and are like midnights zones, only the giant difference is it has light.
Midnight Zone
The player will also come across several “Midnight Zones”. During these levels Edie the anglerfish's illuminating lure will be used to light the player’s way. However, eventually the power of her illuminating lure will decrease. Hence, Edie has to hunt for bioluminescent plankton to increase the lighted area of the level. A bulb icon power-up can be eaten for instant full screen illumination.
Playable characters
Boris - Boris the butterfly fish is the first playable character in the game. He lives in the warm waters of the Sandy Shoal, a beautiful area off the Frenzy Coast. He is the first to meet oysters that give pearls and sometimes power ups, and also meets starfish and sharks.
Layla - Layla the queen triggerfish is the second playable character in the game. She lives in the warm water of Paradise Reef and is the first to meet barracuda enemies and shrink shrooms.
Edie - Edie the anglerfish is the third playable character. Edie's levels are difficult because her several of levels are the "Midnight Zones". Note that the fish's gender has been changed to female due to the fact that only female angler fish emit light; this was a mistake in the original game. She is the only returning playable character from the first game.
Peter - Peter the pompano is the fourth playable character in the game. He lives in Buccaneer Bay, where the player will first come across cuttlefish, which shoot ink.
Harry - Harry the humphead wrasse is the fifth playable character in the game, the balloons are back after a while and you can again jump for bonuses out of the water. Also, he meets pelicans.
Goliath - Goliath the great white shark is the sixth playable character in the game. He is very high up in the food chain, and is the first to fight "The Intruder".
The Intruder - The Intruder is an alien fish disrupting the food chain. The player is required to fight it every 3 levels after Goliath defeats it for the first time. The player then moves lower down the food chain, playing as previous characters until The Intruder is defeated for the last time, after which Boris eats it. This completes the game. The Intruder is then unlocked as a playable character, and the player can then play through the entire game again as The Intruder.

I too got this game for nostalgia purposes. However, it has not aged well, at all. The first problem is the game's resolution. I know this game is pretty old, and super HD things weren't around back then, but the view you're given is so very very limited. There is no warning of any predators that are coming from off screen. Far too often you will find yourself swimming right into a fish. Another issue is that the game is crazy unfair. Most of the power-downs that prey emit are pretty much death sentences. Fighting the alien fish (5 times with no difference in the fight every 2 levels...) or a barracuda is pretty much impossible because they just turn around and eat you right away. Another big issue is your growth rate. You have to eat an insane number of fish before growing to the next level. This is hindered even more due to the fact you lose all of your growth bar for that level once you die. Finally, the concept of the game itself is pretty flawed as well. The game's level difficulty is reversed: it is easier at the end of the level than at the start. This makes the feeling of completing a level a chore rather than a rewarding experience.
Overall, skip this even if you've played it back in the day. It is not at all worth $10. $5 is a decent price, but only if you've played it before and are prepared to rage often.

As the Overlord you command a horde of minions which come in four colors, brown, red, blue, and green, Each have their various weakness and strengths. Brown minions are good at fighting, red minions aren't affected by fire, blue can swim and green are immune to poison. While this setup would normally add some depths an complexity to the game. Most encounters in Overlord can be summed up as using X type of minions; usually the brown ones and sending it against a given enemy or group of enemies, and picking up the weapons armors the drop rinse and repeat. The boss battles are a little more cleaver than this, but not by much. You can upgrade you Overlord by finding various items throughout the different levels that your minions will literally pick up and bring back to your home base. This is not a survival horror game, this is a action game. You play through three campaigns and once you finished those, you unlock another campaign. Each campaign will take you roughly five or six hours, depends mostly on your difficulty level. Plus there is also a New Game + setting after you finished the whole campaign. And there is also Mercenary mode and some other modes.  So the game should keep you busy for a while. Now, Ive been a Resident evil fan ever since I played the first two resident evil games. This game is nothing like that all, there is no horror to speak of, and the tension of  running  out of ammo is also gone. But does that make the game bad? Nope. Even though you do get a lot of quick time events, I really enjoyed the game. Especially the bosses, those were awesome, and they will take some time to take down.
So here are in my opinion the best bits about Resident evil 6
+Awesome bosses
+ Co-op is fun
+Long campaign, plus a New Game+ mode is always nice.
+Skill points which you can collect and spend
+Mercenary mode is still awesome, also the new modes included are fun.
+The the graphics of the game looks great
And here some things I didn't like about Resident Evil 6
- Lots of quick time events, after a while its gets tiring
- No horror to speak of
- The story is nothing special, it do hit some high points, but overall, I didn't like it much
-Some cheap deaths, you can't avoid unless you know the exact spots where suppose to be.

A full, immersive horror experience that goes far, far beyond the simple experience of the original. This game will ease you in with beautiful scenery, haunting music and a tense atmosphere, then gradually lead into the paranormal investigation into where the player's friend has gone and what the thing that took her is. From suspenseful searches through abandoned locations, to shortlived breather moments, to intense chases, this game has all the elements needed to excel as a horror.
There are some downsides unfortunately. A lot of the scares are jumpscares, the enemy AI can be cheap at times and there are some bugs in need of ironing out. The main problem is the jumpscares, which there seem to be a lot of, in addition to the moments of genuine horror.
If you can forgive some of its cheap scares and fully immerse yourself in the heart-pounding experience that is Slender: The Arrival, you will have a short but altogether riveting time playing. Choose to get the terrifying experience over with as soon as you can or spend time gathering clues as to what happened - which in itself is an extremely interesting story.
For horror fans, this is perfect. You will dread continuing on, in fear of what is to come. At times there will be nothing, at others your worst suspicions will be confirmed and something horrible will come at you from the darkness. But always the game will be gripping and have a lot more to offer past the first playthrough, from extra content to undiscovered clues.

Splain's View                                    For the full video review check here
Slender: The Arrival

Introduction – Slender: The Arrival is a true survival horror game that focuses on atmosphere, creepy audio and mystery to set the player on edge throughout the duration of the game. The mystery will draw you in to make you want to learn more about what you are getting yourself into. It sticks to a very basic control scheme anyone can use. You can expect to finish the game in 3 hours of play, but there is decent replay value.
1.	Story – 4/10 After fully beating the game once, I was still confused at what I just experienced. You read notes throughout the game which give little pieces of information about what is going on and if you do not collect a large majority of them good luck figuring this story out! I could make some good guesses at what I think the story is, but I could easily be wrong on these also.
2.	Difficulty – 4/10 While there is one particular area of the game I thought I might never beat, the rest was relatively easy. In fact the last half of the game I did not get a single game over.
3.	Visuals – 7/10 The graphics in this game are decent. If you run the graphics on a higher setting it looks pretty nice and adds a slight touch to the atmosphere which is always appreciated in a horror game. Speaking of visuals, your flashlight will be your best friend in this game. When it is dark, it is DARK!
4.	Audio – 9/10 This would have to be the best aspect of this game. If you really want to experience this game play this game with the volume turned up! The game is often quite and subtle which leaves the player feeling on edge as if something is about to jump out at any moment. When the pace picks up a little though, so will the background music. You will often here the antagonist movement long before you see him and in some scenarios hearing a baddie before you see them can be life or death!
5.	Replay Value – 7/10 The game is short, but there are pages of plot hidden throughout the game that once you find, are added to a scrapbook you can view at anytime. Items on the map are randomly placed each time, although it does not vary much. This game is also great fun with friends because face it, who doesn’t like to see their friends pee their pants in fright. There are also steam achievements and steam trading cards to be found in this game.
6.	Final Verdict – 6/10 The gameplay is very basic, the graphics are decent and the audio excels! The story is very confusing, but does not hinder the scare factor. Playing alone with the volume high is sure to give anyone some good jumps. It is a very short game but I enjoyed it all the way through.

The game gets increasingly frustrating as you get closer to the end, and most of the time spent playing the game is trying to figure out where you are supposed to go, or dealing with enemies that apparently do no damage... I would suggest playing with the classic mouse and keyboard because I had a very hard time with a standard gaming controller; the sensitivity is either too high or two low and learning the controls is a frustrating feat for such a short game. I would not reccomend buying this game UNLESS you are a die hard fan of the original Slender, or if you enjoy scaring your friends. Overall "Slender: The Arrival" was an experience I did find myself enjoying at the time, but now wish I had my money back to send on a lengthier game or DLC.

I have waited to review this game for so long but now I can longer keep quiet.
Ever since this game was mentioned before it was given the official title, I was very anxious to play and experience it. I backed the game, payed for Savini skin Jason and Counselor clothes before the BETA was released.
When the BETA was released, I had a lot fun with it save for some instances where people could ruin the game for you i.e Quick Play. It wasn't just 'trolling' because people could invite their friends into Quick Play lobbies and make what should be a fun experience miserable.
Some people in these forums turned a blind eye to this issue among others. Of course if you want something to get better you need to scrutinize it and say what should be changed. Some still did not care.
Flash forward to full release. Exploits, servers not up to par for allowing people to play, the same issue in Quick Play, bugs and other things that should not have made its way onto a full release. There were still people who didn't care about these issues in the Steam forum while others were trying to tell Gun Media what the issues were.

This game is atrocious.  Never before have I played a game that requires less tact, skill or effort in my lifetime, and I've played every Call of Duty game to date over various consoles.  The game works on a triad system of attacking and blocking with little more effort to it than that.
You block to the left, to the right, or up, and time your heavy attack button to parry an enemy's attack and stumble them.  Otherwise, you have light attacks which can be blocked by simply blocking in one of the three directions corresponding to your attacker.  Then there are heavy attacks which can be blocked but confer a stumble on your part and still allow slight damage to get through-  but the indicator gives you a flash of red to let you know exactly when to parry the heavy attack, effectively making them worthless outside of stunning, parrying, or running up to steal an execution from an ally.  You can cancel these heavy attacks to try and juke a parry (heavy attack) out of your enemy so you can parry them back.  Lastly, there are unblockables which can be used and abused in a chain of combos to stun and disorient your enemies.  Certain heroes make excessive use of these, and while all of them can be dodged, only some can be parried.
That sounds fun when you don't consider that this isn't how the game is played in any of the modes you see.  To effectively play the game, you must often pick the heroes with the right amount of easy chainable stuns, with examples being Valkyrie, Lawbringer and as of recent, the new DLC character, Centurion.  All of this can be avoided, I will admit, with the right timing of a 'counter guard break', to break their guard break on you.  However, the only indication of this is a white flash, and the window for the counter is so unbelievably small, I personally have only done it out of panic.
There are three gamemodes with two variants to two of the gamemodes and one being a ♥♥♥♥ing travesty that people like to play for whatever odd reason.
-Brawl
This gamemode features 1v1 and 2v2 respectively, and does not draw from item stat boosts.  The maps are usually smaller or cut-off variations of other maps from either Singleplayer or Multiplayer and come with various drops and traps to abuse to your liking.
-Domination
This gamemode is a 4v4 land-grab in which you battle for control of three points.  One point is often swarmed with minions that determine control of it, while the other two are simply 'stand to capture'.  In this gamemode, you must control points until one team's exceeds 1000 points, at which the other team will "break" and will no longer respawn after each death.  Capturing points from a team above 1000 CAN reform your team and give you a second wind, but you must still break their team to win.  In this gamemode, gear stats apply and often decide a game before it even starts.  These stats include things like building Revenge Mode in four blocks or less, or reviving enemies in a matter of a second, and horribly imbalance an otherwise """fun""" gamemode.
-Elimination
This gamemode is split into two variants- one of attrition and one of, well, elimination.  Attrition sees you fighting for points to break the enemy team while elimination is pure 4v4 fighting.  Buffs are scattered across the map and each player spawns before another enemy to duel.  I can't for the life of me remember if gear stats apply here, but this is the gamemode I remember having the most fun in.
The game is beautiful, and that's probably the best thing I can say about it.  Although, it does feel a little washed out- sorta like putting a red sweater in with a pair of white shirts.  The environments feel well-crafted and beautifully designed, and they did seem to put some effort into making them feel immersive to an extent, like there's a real battle going on around you.  Arrows flying, trebuchets firing mounds of rock overhead and into structures, as well as the odd minions haveing their own little duels.
The customization comes down to painting parts of your hero's armor and coloring it.  Outside of that, most of your customization will come from gear you'll find on the battlefield or from "scavenging".  Scavenging can be done with Steel, a currency you can pay for or play for, or can recieve from events.  The gear unlocked from these, however, also have stats to them that apply in Domination and become more complex the better the rarity and higher the prestige level.  You can upgrade these items to give yourself ludicrous benefits with little drawback- like sacrificing revival speed for increased Revenge Mode build or better overall damage.  Most of the time, these stats can determine the outcome of a game, and it's not exactly left down to skill- at least in Domination.  Too bad it's the most popular.  You can also purchase or unlock costumes for your character to wear with Steel or by playing.
Matchmaking is horrendous and the settings automatically broaden and broaden until you're left playing against laggy opponents with superior gear or skill comparative to you.  After about thirty seconds, the skill range will change from "Strict" to "Extended", to "All Skill Levels", at which point another 30 seconds will go by and then the game will resort to shoving you in an out-of-region match where stable connection is no longer guaranteed.  It's very possible players will leave halfway through the match, leaving your team with a buckethead AI, or may sometimes disrupt the game to the point everyone loses connection and nobody is rewarded.
The story is alright.  Nothing too impressive or to write home about, but it does a decent job of preparing you for Multiplayer.  At least, it did on launch when nobody understood all the combos and insane stunts you can pull off to leave your enemy at half health and with no stamina- I'm looking at you, Lawbringer.
The game is still very buggy and the gameplay feels incredibly unresponsive and clunky to me.  Sometimes, the game can't even keep up with my actions or the enemies, which has resulted in it stating the enemy is attacking to the right even though they're doing an overhead swing, or I'm still commencing a heavy attack even when I've cancelled it- only to still be parried due to the attack that I cancelled.  Most of the gamemodes other than Dominion or Attrition have queue times beyond reasonable, and the stat-based gear makes the game feel unfair and unbalanced if you get pitted against, or with, an ally rocking a 144 gear level.  Anyone can sit here and say I'm just bad at the game or haven't played enough- though a day and a half's worth is more than enough -The same argument can be said for any other negative review, yet this game is still rocking at 45% user score, which is under average, and horrific for a triple-A game.

For Honor was supposed to be one of Ubisoft's greatest multiplayer experiences, adding in a deep combat system with very intricate details that were imperative to your success against other people.  That, however, is not entirely the case.  When "For Honor" was announced to have a beta, people were losing their minds over what could've been one of the most played multiplayer games of 2017, but on launch day there were a few issues that brought the game's hype down to a fairly negative light.  To be clear, I did and still do find this game fun, but some of the preliminary bugs the game experienced most likely caused an early failure on the game's part.

One of the most prominent early issues involved the peer to peer connection system, which can be made good.  Nearly every match started with either one or multiple persons being disconnected from the match and having to search for a new game, only to have the problem repeat itself over and over again.  And for the people who didn't disconnect immediately after joining, they were met with up to a minute of "Host disconnected.  Searching for new Host..."  It was extremely tedious and was most likely the cause of so many people writing this game off in the early stages of patches.
To Ubisoft's credit, the game has been out for several months now, and they've fixed this system (for the most part).  However, they recently have added two new heroes to their roster of twelve, and I'll be damned if they aren't the most played and most complained about heroes I've ever witnessed in a multiplayer game.
One of the new heroes, the Centurion, is a part of the Knight faction and is a "Melee-Specialist" whilst being described as "Mix-Up Intensive".  What the game doesn't tell you about this hero immediately, is that the Centurion is a monster in any 4v4 gamemode (Dominion, Skirmish, Elimination).  Even if you don't take item stats into consideration, he is able to consistently output damage to anyone in his line of sight, as he is equipped with more than enough unblockable attacks to stunlock any opponent.  Revenge is basically pointless against a Centurion, as his kick punishes people who use it, knocking you out of the un-attackable state you are put into upon activation.  He's not impossible to play against, but he appears to be a bit too powerful in 4v4 gamemodes at the moment.
The second character released is the Shinobi, an Assassin for the Samaurai faction and is currently called "The most broken hero in existence".  Ask anyone who has fought a Shinobi in the first week or two of his release and they'll tell you about his kit and why he seems to be almost impossible to play against at times.  The Shinobi's kit is too diverse, I believe, and that allows him to be even MORE mix-up intensive than the Centurion.  The Shinobi is a monster in any gamemode currently, with his ranged guardbreak and his vortexes that he can execute almost endlessly.  If Ubisoft finds a way to somehow fix this hero even slightly, then it will be a bit more bearable to fight against more than one Shinobi.

The final point I have to bring up about this game is that it IS fun (for me personally).  You can have incredibly fun matches, as well as incredibly frustrating matches.  I would recommend you play this game with friends, since it is a very team-based objective game at its core.  Matchmaking-wise, here's some problems:
-Almost no one does the 2v2 gamemode anymore, as the population for this game died down quite a bit
-The largest amount of the player-base is doing either 1v1's or Dominions
-There is no true matchmaking system, everyone you fight from this point on will be very experienced in the game's mechanics, so you will have to learn from losses before you can truly understand how people play
-The Season pass grants access to the newest characters added to the roster, but to those who don't have $40 to spend mindlessly, or have the willpower to save up 15,000 steel (the in-game currency), they will have no way to look at the characters' movesets, lest they look it up online
Aside from all of these negatives I am posting, I truly do enjoy this game and have been playing it regardless of my win/loss ratio.  But it is a hardcore competitive multiplayer experience, so if you do not like starting out as a new player against a huge population of skilled players, then you might pass this game over in the long run.
I give this game an 8/10.  I enjoy the game, but it can be frustrating at times to fight people who can easily stomp you into the dirt.  Matchmaking is non-existant, the fanbase has dropped drastically since it's release in February 2017, and new(er) heroes can be unfair to play against especially if you can't find their moveset.

Just off its writing quality, I would not recommend this game.
I love many of the design features around this game, but honestly it just feels as though you are just scrolling down a page, looking for key words that are highlighted, and then dragging them into the information system.
In games like this, the writing needs to be particularly strong if the game wants to retain your attention, and sadly, it is not particularly strong writing. I will refrain from completely degrading the work, as I appreciate the developer and writing team's attention to detail in the spirit of world building.
Some moments which I really enjoyed were the conversations that you could overhear over a suspect's cell, though it is disappointing that there is no audio in these segments. The writers are successful in writing the story they wanted to write, but that does not mean that its perfect (but then again, nothing is).
Overall, I like this game, and I can see myself playing more of it, but I would not recommend it to many other people, as it is very niche. You really must be a person that is willing to read a lot of bland text in order to get a better feel for the world you're in. Ultimately, if you are interested in this game, you should be prepared to answer the question of whether your time reading in this game could not have been better spent in a good book, magazine, periodical, etc.

This game shows the tension between surveillance and freedom quite good. It's a better detective game without it being an actual detective game than most detective games...
Wrong conclusions because of too intensive or simply dumb surveillance is a big part of the game. These situations are easy to imagine to happening in real world surveillance, what is one of the biggest arguments against it. As there are a lot of such cases known in the real world, they wake you up and make you aware about the dangers of mass surveillance.
The gameplay is a bit lacking in this game. It pretends that you have a lot of freedom but this is only an illusion.
You play an agent which needs to collect information from all kinds of sources and put it into a system. This system then might or might not draw some conclusions from the found information. The conclusions are sometimes done by your supervisor who might trigger some action. These actions can be totally unintended by you and you might even think they endanger the investigation.
Sometimes there are pieces of information that you really don’t want to put into the system because wrong conclusions might be taken from them, but as the game seems to be linear (I haven’t been able to find a real alternative storyline yet, only small details that are different but not essential), you sometimes need to enter them to continue. The other way is true too, sometimes you got a piece of information in a source that cannot be selected to put into the system, while the piece of information is so basic you’re sure it’s missing and will be enabled later or entered from another source.
Although there are clear holes in the gameplay, the game is fun, and the freedom you get in the details let’s you still play a bit with how your targets need to live their lives.

Orwell takes sort of a visual novel framework and bends it until it looks something like a mass surveillance simulator. You're a foreign contractor working within a series of ethical safeguards to perform ethical mass surveillance (if such a thing is possible) for another country's government. And it's an interesting time to be an Orwell contractor, because The Nation is in the grips of a terrorist bombing spree. Your actions and possibly even inaction can bend the arc of the story.
Like most visual novels, your actions don't have major impacts on larger direction of the plot, but they change the details along the way and might make you more sympathetic to ending the game in one way or another. It's neat to go back and see how changes affect things and unlock other achievements, but it does get a little tedious since waiting through real-time chat and phone conversations is a lot less exciting the second time around.
Overall, I had a pretty good time, but most people will probably be one-and-done and put up fewer hours accordingly. Weigh that against how much you're willing to spend.
VERY interesting game, could use some tweaks. But, let's see where this goes.

Absolutely chilling. Orwell is proof of how frighteningly easy it is to collect information on an individual in the era of social media. 1984's surveillance state comes to life and flips the roles by positioning you as Big Brother instead of Winston- a slippery yet intoxicating slope towards unethical snooping in the name of 'safety'. Piecing together stray clues to form profiles on criminal suspects forms a satisfying progression system, and the well-paced narrative with multiple twists and turns will keep you on the edge of your seat until the very end.

Thomas Was Alone is without a doubt the most pretentious game I have ever played. It thinks it's smart, but it's not. It thinks it's unique, but it's not. It thinks it's funny, but it's not. The "minimalist" art style is banal and fails to give the game any character whatsoever through its environments. It's pretty apparent that this was intentional, but it's irrelevant. If you act stupid, people will think you're stupid. The gameplay amounts to either arranging the different rectangles into particular staircases over and over again to reach a point, or simply taking each rectangle individually on incredibly simple obstacle courses. Any interesting mechanics that may have emerged are never used in actual gameplay. Each level has one bland solution, And dear lord, does it drag. A two hour long game drags, by making the player perform repetitive tasks. The attempts at drawing the player in through story and humour are absolutely laugable. Everything that this game thinks it's saying about individuality or compassion or even AI research is at the level of a four-year-old. The humour is that of a three-year-old. The music is repetitive and does not contribute to the atmosphere. However, the use of shadows in a 2D game is sort of unique. But regardless. Do not buy this game, whether it's on sale, or part of a humble bundle, or anything. This is not the direction video games should go in, so don't tell the industry that anything like this is what you want.

Slender: The Arrival utilizes two basic gameplay mechanics: "find X of Y in this level" and "avoid this monster" which worked so well in the original Slender: The Eight Pages. Unfortunately, the execution of the second mechanic falls flat compared to the free predecessor: Slenderman often chooses to aggressively teleport in front of the player instead of silently stalking him - a small detail which ruins all the suspense that defined the original. Because of this new feature and several other "this is not fair" moments, the game alternates between being cheesily scary and annoying, with the second trait being a lot more common on more challenging game difficulties.
It also delves into it's own vision of the Slenderman lore, working hand in hand with the previous game - which could be interesting for Slenderman enthusiasts. Game's own share of secrets and Easter Eggs also helps.
Going commercial certainly helped Blue Isle Studios achieve it's goals, because the game looks and sounds amazing. I have a big screenshot folder which I made during the game's initial release back in March 2013. Unfortunately, the optimization leaves much to be desired.
Overall I recommend this game to the people who liked the original, because it's more of the same, and from purely consumer standpoint, it's really cheap. If you are unfamiliar with The Eight Pages but interested in the indie game market, I recommend you to play the original and dive straight into this.

Simple: if you liked Masters of Orion II, you will like StarDrive II. This game is a direct forward iteration of the timeless classic. I cannot stress enough how wonderfully refreshing it is to play a game in that same vein that grows upon it organically without overdoing it or trying to change too much. Stardrive also has a very refreshingly light attitude and a healthy sense of irreverent and sometimes self-depricating humor, which helps a lot during a long slog through a highly technical strategy game on high difficulty.
If you have not played Masters of Orion II, but you enjoy space turn-based 4X games, I highly recommend this one. The ship designer can be a bit overwhelming to do well at, and understanding the consequences of technological research takes a bit of getting used to, but as a spit-shine using modern engines and a fresh setting and story on what many consider to be the greatest space 4X game of all time, this one is well worth it.

This is a very good space strategy game, easy to pick up and challenging to master.  Built on—but by far an improvement over—a similar design philosophy to games like MoO, the depth added to gameplay far surpasses current offerings like the newest Master of Orion.  This game is arguably up there with Star Ruler 2, Stellaris, and Galactic Civilizations III in terms of both addictiveness and replayability.  The developer is responsive to the community and works continually to improve upon an already strong game.
EDIT:  The dev has become less and less responsive to the community since the initial writing of this review and has now essentially abandoned this game, with game-breaking bugs still abouding.  It seems to be a trend of his, as the first StarDrive was (according to other players) abandoned in a similar unfinished state.  Ultimately, this game has a LOT of promise, but that promise will remain unfulfilled, as the dev has moved on to other things.

This must be one of the most boring games I've played in years. Where Resident Evil 1-3 were all about horror, 4 more about action/horror and 5 more action than horror, 6 has finally come to the point where there's no more horror at all, and it's all about the action. Granted, it's campaigns are long and to complete them all will take you well over 20 hours (1-1,5 hours per mission). But I couldn't even finish the journey.
So far I've finished Leon's campaign and am near the end of Chris', but it's mostly shooting, with an awkward co-op partner at your side. The animations of Leon were wooden and there will tons of QTEs, yet Chris' animations were fine and his campaign had practically no QTEs. It's like they were made by entirely different teams. The Japanese influences can be seen in all of the campaigns and maybe that's what makes the game so boring. Instead of moving forward it looks like they went backwards when compared with Western developers. I can't really explain, it's just a feeling, and the fact that it's absolutely not scary at all, when, well, it should be.
I heard good things about the Mercenaries mode so I'll be sure to give that a try, and I might finish the campaign over the next couple of weeks/months, but for now it's just too damn boring.
Edit: I finished this later and unfortunately it never improved. So my original review still stands.
[Rating: 65/100]

You block to the left, to the right, or up, and time your heavy attack button to parry an enemy's attack and stumble them.  Otherwise, you have light attacks which can be blocked by simply blocking in one of the three directions corresponding to your attacker.  Then there are heavy attacks which can be blocked but confer a stumble on your part and still allow slight damage to get through-  but the indicator gives you a flash of red to let you know exactly when to parry the heavy attack, effectively making them worthless outside of stunning, parrying, or running up to steal an execution from an ally.  You can cancel these heavy attacks to try and juke a parry (heavy attack) out of your enemy so you can parry them back.  Lastly, there are unblockables which can be used and abused in a chain of combos to stun and disorient your enemies.  Certain heroes make excessive use of these, and while all of them can be dodged, only some can be parried.
That sounds fun when you don't consider that this isn't how the game is played in any of the modes you see.  To effectively play the game, you must often pick the heroes with the right amount of easy chainable stuns, with examples being Valkyrie, Lawbringer and as of recent, the new DLC character, Centurion.  All of this can be avoided, I will admit, with the right timing of a 'counter guard break', to break their guard break on you.  However, the only indication of this is a white flash, and the window for the counter is so unbelievably small, I personally have only done it out of panic.
There are three gamemodes with two variants to two of the gamemodes and one being a ♥♥♥♥ing travesty that people like to play for whatever odd reason.
-Brawl
This gamemode features 1v1 and 2v2 respectively, and does not draw from item stat boosts.  The maps are usually smaller or cut-off variations of other maps from either Singleplayer or Multiplayer and come with various drops and traps to abuse to your liking.
-Domination
This gamemode is a 4v4 land-grab in which you battle for control of three points.  One point is often swarmed with minions that determine control of it, while the other two are simply 'stand to capture'.  In this gamemode, you must control points until one team's exceeds 1000 points, at which the other team will "break" and will no longer respawn after each death.  Capturing points from a team above 1000 CAN reform your team and give you a second wind, but you must still break their team to win.  In this gamemode, gear stats apply and often decide a game before it even starts.  These stats include things like building Revenge Mode in four blocks or less, or reviving enemies in a matter of a second, and horribly imbalance an otherwise """fun""" gamemode.
-Elimination
This gamemode is split into two variants- one of attrition and one of, well, elimination.  Attrition sees you fighting for points to break the enemy team while elimination is pure 4v4 fighting.  Buffs are scattered across the map and each player spawns before another enemy to duel.  I can't for the life of me remember if gear stats apply here, but this is the gamemode I remember having the most fun in.
The game is beautiful, and that's probably the best thing I can say about it.  Although, it does feel a little washed out- sorta like putting a red sweater in with a pair of white shirts.  The environments feel well-crafted and beautifully designed, and they did seem to put some effort into making them feel immersive to an extent, like there's a real battle going on around you.  Arrows flying, trebuchets firing mounds of rock overhead and into structures, as well as the odd minions haveing their own little duels.
The customization comes down to painting parts of your hero's armor and coloring it.  Outside of that, most of your customization will come from gear you'll find on the battlefield or from "scavenging".  Scavenging can be done with Steel, a currency you can pay for or play for, or can recieve from events.  The gear unlocked from these, however, also have stats to them that apply in Domination and become more complex the better the rarity and higher the prestige level.  You can upgrade these items to give yourself ludicrous benefits with little drawback- like sacrificing revival speed for increased Revenge Mode build or better overall damage.  Most of the time, these stats can determine the outcome of a game, and it's not exactly left down to skill- at least in Domination.  Too bad it's the most popular.  You can also purchase or unlock costumes for your character to wear with Steel or by playing.
Matchmaking is horrendous and the settings automatically broaden and broaden until you're left playing against laggy opponents with superior gear or skill comparative to you.  After about thirty seconds, the skill range will change from "Strict" to "Extended", to "All Skill Levels", at which point another 30 seconds will go by and then the game will resort to shoving you in an out-of-region match where stable connection is no longer guaranteed.  It's very possible players will leave halfway through the match, leaving your team with a buckethead AI, or may sometimes disrupt the game to the point everyone loses connection and nobody is rewarded.
The story is alright.  Nothing too impressive or to write home about, but it does a decent job of preparing you for Multiplayer.  At least, it did on launch when nobody understood all the combos and insane stunts you can pull off to leave your enemy at half health and with no stamina- I'm looking at you, Lawbringer.
The game is still very buggy and the gameplay feels incredibly unresponsive and clunky to me.  Sometimes, the game can't even keep up with my actions or the enemies, which has resulted in it stating the enemy is attacking to the right even though they're doing an overhead swing, or I'm still commencing a heavy attack even when I've cancelled it- only to still be parried due to the attack that I cancelled.  Most of the gamemodes other than Dominion or Attrition have queue times beyond reasonable, and the stat-based gear makes the game feel unfair and unbalanced if you get pitted against, or with, an ally rocking a 144 gear level.  Anyone can sit here and say I'm just bad at the game or haven't played enough- though a day and a half's worth is more than enough -The same argument can be said for any other negative review, yet this game is still rocking at 45% user score, which is under average, and horrific for a triple-A game.

For Honor was supposed to be one of Ubisoft's greatest multiplayer experiences, adding in a deep combat system with very intricate details that were imperative to your success against other people.  That, however, is not entirely the case.  When "For Honor" was announced to have a beta, people were losing their minds over what could've been one of the most played multiplayer games of 2017, but on launch day there were a few issues that brought the game's hype down to a fairly negative light.  To be clear, I did and still do find this game fun, but some of the preliminary bugs the game experienced most likely caused an early failure on the game's part.

One of the most prominent early issues involved the peer to peer connection system, which can be made good.  Nearly every match started with either one or multiple persons being disconnected from the match and having to search for a new game, only to have the problem repeat itself over and over again.  And for the people who didn't disconnect immediately after joining, they were met with up to a minute of "Host disconnected.  Searching for new Host..."  It was extremely tedious and was most likely the cause of so many people writing this game off in the early stages of patches.
To Ubisoft's credit, the game has been out for several months now, and they've fixed this system (for the most part).  However, they recently have added two new heroes to their roster of twelve, and I'll be damned if they aren't the most played and most complained about heroes I've ever witnessed in a multiplayer game.
One of the new heroes, the Centurion, is a part of the Knight faction and is a "Melee-Specialist" whilst being described as "Mix-Up Intensive".  What the game doesn't tell you about this hero immediately, is that the Centurion is a monster in any 4v4 gamemode (Dominion, Skirmish, Elimination).  Even if you don't take item stats into consideration, he is able to consistently output damage to anyone in his line of sight, as he is equipped with more than enough unblockable attacks to stunlock any opponent.  Revenge is basically pointless against a Centurion, as his kick punishes people who use it, knocking you out of the un-attackable state you are put into upon activation.  He's not impossible to play against, but he appears to be a bit too powerful in 4v4 gamemodes at the moment.
The second character released is the Shinobi, an Assassin for the Samaurai faction and is currently called "The most broken hero in existence".  Ask anyone who has fought a Shinobi in the first week or two of his release and they'll tell you about his kit and why he seems to be almost impossible to play against at times.  The Shinobi's kit is too diverse, I believe, and that allows him to be even MORE mix-up intensive than the Centurion.  The Shinobi is a monster in any gamemode currently, with his ranged guardbreak and his vortexes that he can execute almost endlessly.  If Ubisoft finds a way to somehow fix this hero even slightly, then it will be a bit more bearable to fight against more than one Shinobi.

The final point I have to bring up about this game is that it IS fun (for me personally).  You can have incredibly fun matches, as well as incredibly frustrating matches.  I would recommend you play this game with friends, since it is a very team-based objective game at its core.  Matchmaking-wise, here's some problems:
-Almost no one does the 2v2 gamemode anymore, as the population for this game died down quite a bit
-The largest amount of the player-base is doing either 1v1's or Dominions
-There is no true matchmaking system, everyone you fight from this point on will be very experienced in the game's mechanics, so you will have to learn from losses before you can truly understand how people play
-The Season pass grants access to the newest characters added to the roster, but to those who don't have $40 to spend mindlessly, or have the willpower to save up 15,000 steel (the in-game currency), they will have no way to look at the characters' movesets, lest they look it up online
Aside from all of these negatives I am posting, I truly do enjoy this game and have been playing it regardless of my win/loss ratio.  But it is a hardcore competitive multiplayer experience, so if you do not like starting out as a new player against a huge population of skilled players, then you might pass this game over in the long run.
I give this game an 8/10.  I enjoy the game, but it can be frustrating at times to fight people who can easily stomp you into the dirt.  Matchmaking is non-existant, the fanbase has dropped drastically since it's release in February 2017, and new(er) heroes can be unfair to play against especially if you can't find their moveset.

Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna) is an atmosheric adventure platformer with some minor puzzeling aspects. It revolves around a girl named Nuna and a fox that desides to help her on her journey to find the source of what is overwelming her village with a never-ending blizzard. This can be played both single player and co-op (locally). It tells a traditional story of the Iñupiat, who are an Alaskan Native people, and gives video insights throughout the game to tell you more about the members of the Alaskan Native community's culture, values, and wisdom.
It took me about two and a half hours to get through the main game. An extra hour is me going through a certain section again to get an insight video that I missed, and to take some screenshots, as well as buy the DLC (Never Alone: Foxtails). The DLC is about an hour long and I got the rest of my time from going over the last section in the DLC to get more screenshots.
Overall, I really enjoyed the game, the art/graphics (while a bit outdated), still look fairly good considering the passage of time and the general budget of Indie titles. I enjoyed the story and getting to know more about the Iñupiat culture. I loved the connection between the girl and the fox and their personal journies through the environment. I've read a lot of people talking about the controls, and although I see their grievances to some extent, it never bothered me all that much. For the most part, I was able to do as I needed to progress through the game. There were times where I would die because I wasn't quite sure where to go, but I felt like it was either my fault for not getting it, or just a part of discovering what to do because the game decided to let you figure some stuff out on your own. That isn't to say it was completely hands-off either, because when I died on a particular part a couple times it would give visual hints of what I needed to do. There was only a very rare occasion where I knew what to do but couldn't do it but of how precise you had to be. These situations mostly happened in the last section. At that point I did get a bit frustrated, but it didn't even come close to overshadowing the good parts of the experience (which was a vast majority of the game).
The menu is a bit troublesome in my opinion because you have to use arrow keys, where with the rest of the game you are using WASD, so it was a bit unintuitive and confusing. There are settings and options for graphics, audio, ect. and it was all pretty standard so there really isn't anything to complain about there.
Despite the negatives I mentioned, I personally recommend this game, because I enjoyed it regardless of these minor (in my opinion) inconveniences. However, I would say you need to understand this game is more about the journey. If you are someone who gets frusterated easily you might not enjoy it because the moments where the game isn't flawless might blind you from seeing the rest of the game. Considering the game is only about three hours to complete (and giving the negatives above) I would reccomend it on a sale.

I only really found out what Jazzpunk was the day it was released, I knew PC gamer had given it a shining review but apart from that I knew nothing. After 10 minutes of Giantbomb's quick-look I was sold.
Jazzpunk is bright, bold, hilarious, confusing and garish at the same time. Mind, I don't mean garish in a bad way in this instance. It is a game best played completely blind. Some aspects are still fun and comedic the second time round, but a shock factor is a huge part of the enjoyment while playing Jazzpunk. With that said, there's no need to worry I won't be the one spoiling anything for you.
Jazzpunk is totally rife with references, be it games, TV or otherwise. It is obvious those familiar with the culture of video games will get the most out of this title. However there is still much to enjoy without the knowledge of anything it references. This is due to Jazzpunk being so utterly bizarre, many scenarios will leave you in a state of hilarious confusion. It really doesn't matter if you get the reference or not, it's random nature and constant moving forward won't keep you in an awkward state of "was that a joke I didn't get?".
For better and for worse there are times which can be very overwhelming. You are often presented with a large open space full of many interactions, the majority of these interactions are optional too. This could be a problem for those who don't have the patience to explore as huge sections of the game can be missed entirely. Of course this is great for those you that enjoy second play-throughs, or exploration but that isn't to everyone's taste.
While the surface value of Jazzpunk is enjoyable, but for those who like deep analysis of games there is something of interest here too. There is a huge amount of meaning behind some of the strange rambling characters. I don't think I've experienced a game which truly works on as many levels as Jazzpunk.
This is where we get to the general aesthetic of Jazzpunk. It is certainly something brilliant to behold, everything, even the blemishes seem with purpose. Somehow with it's multitude of video game references it's actually a very absorbing and atmospheric game. I wish I could tell you how this works, but believe me it's very easy to get caught up in the obscure world only to realize you're 30 minutes late for work. This is where everything truly comes together for Jazzpunk. It doesn't feel like a random mix of mini-games, it manages to stay consistently inconsistent.
In many ways Jazzpunk could make anyone laugh out loud or at least smile, but is 3 hours of gameplay worth £12? That's for you to decide.
I give Jazzpunk a "OMGWTFBBQ out of ten".

It's also good social commentary on the whole deal surrounding what makes an actual terrorist in today's world; This is immediately apparent as protesters early in the game protesting against mass surveillance because, well, mass surveillance, are portrayed as "anti-governmental terrorists" without much more context to legitimize that label.

You're the In-Between Brother, looking down on Little Brother, bossing him around; But in the end both you and Little Brother are in a complete chokehold by Big Brother - no match, not even close.
What I'm trying to say is that this game does a good job of portraying how

The game specifically portrays collection of information from social media as self-publicized, along with information gathered in general around the whole internet about a person, as this information is available when

Got this game in Humble Monthy not really knowing all that much about what it was or anything like that, but jesus christ this was one of the most fun and unique gaming experiences I've had in a long time.
You're basically an investigator who has access to certain tools to sift through people's lives and search their phones/computers, monitor their conversations, and search for information on various websites about them. Your goal is to find out who committed a series of terrorist attacks and put them behind bars.
Now the gameplay here is obviously not the strong point. The only gameplay is really clicking and dragging blobs of test to the left every now and again. That being said though, it's not like you're mindlessly dragging things over and not doing/thinking about anything. You have to be cognizant of what you're uploading because you could screw up some stuff and let bad more things happen. Your choices matter, and there are multiple endings and possible situations that can happen in the game based on your choices.
The only thing I can say about the game is that I wish it offered more freedom or at least more thought to what you had to upload. There were instances in the game where it was just a linear click and drag whatever you see because there was nothing else to search. Then you get to episode 5 and you have to be careful of what you upload because you have a limited number of datachunks that you can actually upload before the story starts to unfold. I found that last episode much more interesting because of the fact that it forced you to actually read the documents and search through everything instead of basically just being able to drag the first thing you see. That and there were people by the end of the story that we didn't even get to investigate just because they were viewed as unimportant. Even with them not necessarily being related to the case, I would have liked to investigate those other people as well. This could actually bring more gameplay and they could easily relate some of those people to the suspects and have them tie in when them somehow.
Overall, if you like a game with an intriguing story to follow with serious attention to detail, then you will most likely enjoy this game. I usually don't like games with a deep story, but this game has such a deep and interesting plot that I have to recommend it. I'll definitely be picking up the 2nd one whenever it comes out.
