The game's premise is fun, and it is fun at first. But then the issues start cropping up.
First off it's very buggy. The NPC's pathing is terrible and they can get stuck indefinitely making them literally useless. Often they just stand there and pick up and put down items continuously. Gathering resources from the forest is just frustrating and not fun at all; there's just too many zombies and they seem to always know where you are but you can only see them when they're close. They move slowly, but a lot of times you'll lose everything you collected in unfair ways. The controls are a bit clunkly as well.
The game doesn't explain things very well. It feels random when the NPCs come by and it takes too long for them to show up as if they were just trying to pad the game knowing the actual content is very minimal. Yet despite this, it uses up more resources on your computer than you would think for a game like this.
It's not exactly a bad game, though. If the problems above did not exist, it would be significantly more enjoyable.

Excellent game concept and friendly user interface. This is the new MOO2, imho. The game is VERY fun to play and some subsistems are excellent (ship design, random events, heroes, space battles). After 100 hours in, however, I can say that the game is still very buggy and has some design issues that sorely need fixing. There is a steady stream of patches coming from the designer, so I hope this game will eventually shine as it deserves to do. Right now, Espionage and Diplomacy seem to be the two sub systems more in need of an overhaul. There is a tendency for AI to build HUGE fleets that will smash right through anything you can send against them, and I suspect the command control mechanism in place to keep in check huge fleet building for the human player does not work properly for the AI. Overall, the game is more fun at the beginning, where exploration ad special events count more, than during late game where usually it becomes simply a matter of amassing production points to build a huge fleet or research points to win a tech victory.

Among the problems are the fact that most of the game settings won't apply when you play the game. A good example is the setting to keep minor races from attacking you. It simply doesn't work. Out of several games I attempted to play, I encountered the same problem every time. In many of the games, I had it set up with a single opponenet, that I never got to encounter. In the others, the enemy ended up being right next door. There was never a chance to get off the ground.
The one game I did make considerable progress with included several possible enemies but ended prematurely, and abitrarilly, because the game simply stops. It counts x number of turns and then notifies you that the game is over. What kind of idiot designed this into a game like this? Again, one of the settings is for game length and has an "Epic" setting. I doubt, like the other settings, that it actually works. The game should at least have an open ended option and finish only when a victor has satisfied the victory conditions or conquered the galaxy.
This is sad because this game looks like it has a lot of potential. That's why I bought it. The economics, tech advancement and colinization all work very well. It was everything I wanted in those respects, but the other aspects, as described above, make this one a real loser. It's too bad.

4/5 stars
Pros:
-Very pretty game -- This is by far the best quality to this game. The colors, the animations/fx, the season changes, all gorgeous!
-Music -- Very interesting music, if you like string orchestra, you'll like it =)
-Game Mechanics -- The game mechanic (solving puzzles and traversing by changing seasons to get to new places) is very interesting, and is overall easy to understand
Neutral:
-Story -- Story is a little weak, but still has an interesting premise. It would have been nice to have a bit more backstory and reasoning in the main quest chain.
Cons:
-No map -- This game REALLY needs a map; it's really easy to get lost, miss areas, and the story direction is pretty vague for the first 1/3rd of the game. The game could have also really benefitted from an indicator that could point you in the general direction to the next story checkpoint.
-Extras are a bit vague -- Throughout the game there are extra little things you can collect, but there is no indication of these existing until the end of the game. A map would also help in this case, to gain 100% completion.

I first started playing this game a couple of years ago, based on the tags of "open world" and "COOP", which I thought would be really cool inside of the universe advertised by the post-apocalyptic screenshots of the game.
Turns out THERE IS NO FREEROAM WORLD OR COOP IN THIS GAME AS OF RIGHT NOW, ONLY BASIC GAME MODES SUCH AS TEAM DEATHMATCH AND CAPTURE THE FLAG(battery).
So back to when I first played Survarium, I downloaded the game and realized that there was actually only a Team-deathmatch type gamemode and a couple of other basic PVE game-modes (capture the battery etc.) and found out on the forums that the open-world element was still being worked on and would be put ingame (soon!). So I shelfed the game for a couple of years figuring they would have gotten some basic free-world up and running by now.
Here is what I have to say about the game now:
* The graphics look okay for a non-AAA studio, but I can't say that I think they have changed much in the last couple of years which doesn't give me much hope for the future. I like the level design where there is a lot of nature and foliage(nothing to really hide in though), but I do not think that the game is optimized very well. My computer runs BF1 and other recent games on pretty high gfx settings, but Survarium feels choppy and sluggish at higher settings. Perhaps this is just something that I experience, but it is something to be aware of.
* The gameplay gets boring very fast. It is the same three or four maps (if even that many, I'm not sure) being played over and over, and after each round you get some xp that after a few hours unlocks some new weapons and gear depending on what level you are. It is the typical f2p microtransaction boogaloo that you would see elsewhere, where you grind for some gear, and if you want to stand a chance against the people who have put in 200 hours in this game you can pay a few bucks to get some goldmoneis to buy a better weapon NOW. (I wouldn't put in any money into this game as it is right now and I recommend you don't either).
* The responsiveness of the game makes me feel detached from it unlike other games. When you walk it almost "feels" like walking in syrup. When you fire your weapons you can't really "feel" it if you know what I mean.
* There are more things overall, such as the sound, that make me not superlike this game but I honestly don't feel like putting in any more time in this game even if that means typing out a much longer review.
My recommendations:
If you are looking for an open-world freeroam game, do NOT download this game, go elsewhere for now. If they haven't released anything big in this game after years of development while stating that they have YUGE plans such as coop, AI and freeroam, then I honestly don't trust that much is ever going to come. But then again, perhaps there is stuff going on behind the backdrops as the developers have claimed the last few years, but I would take it with a grain of salt.
If you are looking for a free-to-play team-deathmatch fps with okay graphics but no substance which will simply waste your life, go ahead and download this.

Jazzpunk understands video game humor.
From the get-go the player is faced with a stylistic and slick animation introing the game - it's simple 2D colourful style is reminiscent of several movie openings, Catch Me If You Can being a prime example. And from that very moment the game feels abstract and different.
There is much to say about Jazzpunk, but not much can be said without spoiling the game itself, as the beauty and charm relies heavily on situational humor, references, and player-induced gags.
To put it simply you are an agent tasked with fulfilling tasks for your "secret" agency during an alternative cold war era. Thus, you will be tasked with infiltrating a Russian Consolate to steal data, killing a target in a Japanese setting, and making a journey around the world into a holiday resort to steal vital information. Each of these cliched settings and quests is accompanied by a varied amount of jokes, gags, situational humour and dark comedy. The best part about them? Very few are shoved down the players throat. If you don't explore the environment, you won't get the jokes. If you don't interact with items/NPCs/backgrounds you will never know whether they have something funny to say or whether they will cause a chain reaction of absurd humour.
And absurd is an area very known to Jazzpunk - The characters exist in a reality where they semi-know they are inside a video game and are able to express insightful and hilarious commentary accompanying many of the jokes and gags. As you approach an agent-looking-man in a dark alley, the moment he begins talking to you the text "SIDE QUEST" appears underneath him on the pavement, mocking both the player and the game industry, and yet somehow managing to put a smile on your face. Text is one of the vital strengths of Jazzpunk, and one of the stylistic decisions I enjoyed the most.
The text is superimposed upon the 3D world as part of the charm. Almost every line of dialogue or activity is accompanied by a few small lines of white, bold, caps-lock text which further mock or create humor as appropriate to the situation.
Jazzpunk is also full of mini-games, each of them their own gig, their own sketch, their own gag. The mini-games make little sense and don't actually add anything to the games story or plot development, but they are hard to hate. (As an example if you explore enough you'll get to play "Wedding Qake" A wedding cake version of quake with AI pretending to be real players, and chatting to each other with phrases such as "lol ur pretty gud at this game, a/s/l?") This can be entirely missed and the player is never told that such a minigame exists, which makes exploration in this game all the more and valuable.
Since a lot of exploration games have been released recently - Dear Esther, The Stanley Parable and Gone Home just to name a few, Jazzpunk plays on a similar idea that The Stanley Parable utilized, except it does it better. Rewarding the player for his/her exploration isn't done with dialogue, with achievements, with new tasks or with arbitrary map unlocks or anything of the like - exploring Jazzpunk feels like exploring a Monty Python sketch, a basin of comedy waiting to splash you the moment you dip your hand in it.
There isn't a lot to critique about this game, maybe aside from it's length - I was able to 100% complete Jazzpunk in under 3 hours. Whether I saw all the gigs and jokes I won't know, and that's the wonderful thing about it too. It's likely that upon revisiting the game you will discover a lot of comedy you missed the first time around.
Overall it's hard not to recommend Jazzpunk as an interactive comedy experience. As a game it's a pretty simplistic first-person point-and-click with mini-games added for good measure, under the hood of a game though is a greater experience, one that brings the player into a bizzare world of comedy, pop-references, abstract voice acting and a ridiculous story, all tied together by playing on the basic human need of exploration and wanting to smile and laugh.
Since laughing is healthy, it's likely that Jazzpunk will extend your life by like 0.02 years, so you should probably get it for that.

This "game" is a must for someone who would like to start playing the guitar and does not know how to get into it. I did this and then started learning some music theory to, just to expand my abilities and understanding of music. It is rather a tool than a all in all guitar experience, do not fool yourself into thinking that you can be a guitar player just by following this simple yet addictive teaching platform.
Now, first of all, it does not have everything, it misses the human interaction but I guess, it excuses a real teacher from having to wait for you to get better. You can learn at your own pace without having to get distracted, it is just you and your will to learn. Now, that is fine as long as you do not resume your learning to just that of the game, it is fun, simple and addictive, but why not take it further and start learning music like a pro? You can do this but only outside the game, as Rocksmith 2014 does not teach music theory, only techniques define-related to guitar or bass.
The presentation of the game and menus are nice and they tell you exactly what to do, but it can get overwhelming sometimes, as too many representations of notes on screen will get you into believing it is all a sad joke. After a while you get used to the pace and start playing by memory because simple eye-hand coordination from the display wouldn't normaly be enough to play, it is that fast.
It has a guitarcade, an area of the game where you do stupid-fun games to further enhance your skills, these are fun laid back games, made for gamers. These minigames are difficult and they will better your dexterity and skills with the guitar, a nice addition to a good package.
It also has a session mode, where you jam with your guitar in different rithms and beats accompanied by other simulated instruments. The way you sing and the pace you give the play will make the instruments come to a good play and you can sing like this for hours. Great mode!
I will give this a 9/10 for minor bugs and crashes. The only downside is that it can only be compared to it's earlier version, Rocksmith. It is a great and simple tool to make you start playing the guitar. If it does this I guess it serves it's purpose.

An incredibly complete product.  If you want to learn guitar, this is for you.  If you already know but want to get better at specific techniques, or improve your reportoire, this is also for you.  Pretty much perfect

Slender:The Arrival had good atmosphere, and the "attacks" were well done, tense moments that occasionally startled me enough to get me to jump out of my seat a bit and get the ol' heart racing. Graphics are so-so, but sound design is well done. I am still not sure what the story was really supposed to be about, aside from a way to get you into a position to be jumped by some beasty or another. But, that is really what this is about - the scare.
So, I dont regret spending 10 dollars on it, and it was fun. if short. I would have been happier paying $5, but I would still recommend it if you like a good startle and would like to spend 3-4 hours getting it. Think of it as a movie, but one that is better than most of the sub-par stuff being passed off as horror in the theater these days.

To conclude, Slender the Arrival is an interesting but short-lived psychological horror experience, that's worth checking out if you like a bit of  tension and meaningless scares. The vagueness of the game won't be agreeable for some people, and for others, the lack of hand holding will be a godsend. On a technical level, the game could be better optimized and it's a shame some extra effects weren't used to add to the atmosphere.  That said, there's some genuine fear on offer here,which shows that the most simple of concepts can work but at the end of the game it's likely you'll be none the wiser as to what just happened.

Out of the several puzzles the game features (yes, sadly: only several), only one was really tricky (drawing patterns using multiple colours to reproduce shapes found in the backgrounds in obscure locations), all the others were a simple set of "control the water level", "unlock several objects, one leading to another" or "find item, bring to object, repeat 4 times".
Unlike a seemingly similar platformer, "Ori and the Blind Forest", this is rather a kids' game, than a full-fledged puzzle platformer. Savvy players who don't thrive on fairytale ambience and expect a tough challenge may find it disappointing.

I just finished this game. I like many of the latest reviews received this as part of a humble bundle. Unlike many of the reviewers I am no stranger to the concept of interactive fiction. As such I cannot say "WOW so unique." This game has many elements I found fascinating, and indeed I played through the whole thing in one go, a very do-able task. I think there are many things that would make me recommend it, but there are two glaring holes that I think bring it just shy of a general recommendation. I can say this, If you have never played an interactive fiction game, and the plot sounds intriguing, buy it. It is worth ten dollars. If you got it in a humble bundle or something similar, play it. You will have an entertaining few hours. If you do not fall in to either of those two camps I would recommend a pass.
The good -
Plot- Everything to do with the plot is great. The characters are interesting, and they do to some degree develop. The world feels complete and well rounded, The plot is where this game shines, as it should be as interactive fiction lives and dies by the plot.
The interface - For the most part is pretty solid. There are few idiosyncrasies. The one glaring hole is the need for a few hot-keys, if only Enter and ESC, would make this much easier on the wrists, but it is as a whole soundly usable.
The bad - For the bad I will go in to detail as to hopefully explain my point of view fully to the Devs.  There is at least one more season planned, and I would love to play it. Perhaps the Devs will hear this feedback and consider it. Before I continue though, if you have already thought “I kinda want to play this game,” do it and forget the ramblings of an old gamer.
Choice - If the plot is what an interactive fiction game lives and dies by then choice (or for that matter the illusion of choice) is what allows it to breath. In Orwell the idea of choice dies very quickly, and never returns. There are several pivotal moments which finds the player, through the narrative, put in a position to make a pivotal choice. All the relevant characters are obviously pointing at you and saying you decide. I never really felt like there was any choices to be made. Either The player is not given enough context to understand the consequences of that choice, in these cases you are just blindly choosing one of two options and made to accept the consequences. Or you cannot progress until you make the choice.
At the heart of this, in my opinion, is the engine for which you as the player progress through the narrative. You are told at the very beginning of the game that you cannot progress until you have uploaded certain information. Which pieces of information allows for progression is up to the game. The premise of games like this in which it is up to the player to provide or not provide information to the antagonist is a great juxtaposition to make the player feel invested, and in many cases responsible for the consequences levied on the characters in the narrative. Games like “Papers Please” and “Beholder” levy this mechanic very well. In Orwell you cannot progress without giving the Antagonist certain information. This kills the illusion of choice, and make the rest of the narrative lose it's bite. Because I cannot NOT provide certain information the consequences are not my fault. The game made me do it. Especially in those moments where you have several data points you can give, and you need to choose between them, but if you choose wrong the game does not go forward, you end up throwing whatever data points at the wall, even those bits of data you do not want to provide, in order to get the game to continue.
I realize why it was written this way. You cannot write a narrative which has ALL possibilities. So in order to move forward you need the player to trip certain triggers. An elegant way around this in my opinion would be to allow the information to be presented in "real time." This allows the narrative to continue while allowing the player more of a choice in the way it unfolds. I think this would greatly improve the impact of the game.
The Twist - (mild spoiler warning)
If you have read this far then I doubt this will really be a spoiler, but just in case, you have been warned.
There is a twist at the end. All good who-done-it's have them. This is no exception. My issue with the twist at the end of Orwell dove tails in to the idea of choice. There is no way you the player, let alone the character you play in the game, could predict it. There are no data points that I found that will allow you to discover the twist in game. Therefore it feels arbitrary. Once again the narrative loses impact because it does not feel like the player could intercede. The game is going to do what it is going to do and you are just pulled along to see what happens. that is what novels, TV shows, movies, and comic books are for. In fact I could see this story being a great Rashamon-Style comic, but as an interactive fiction I think this game falls flat.
Summery - In summation I think if you are interested in games as an art form, or are just curios about what happens in this particular narrative, then this is worth while. I look forward to see if any of these issues are fixed in the next chapter. I do not regret my time "playing" this game. but I think in the end, The impact of the events was greatly blunted by the mechanics with which the narrative is presented. That seems a shame to me as the story could be quit impact-full if only the illusion of choice was maintained through out. In a narrative the promise of the premise is key,
"Only the information you provide will be seen by the security forces and acted upon. You decide what gets seen and what does not, influencing how the suspects will be perceived."
and this narrative missed that promise.

An investigation game with an intriguing premises,
comes together as a unique experience that keeps you gripped with its narrative, despite fairly limited mechanics. Putting the player in the role of an investigator working with an information-processing system known as Orwell (referencing George Orwell's
), the game tasks you to search out information from a fictional set of websites (and later, live conversations and data on individual target personal devices) to investigate the aftermath of a bombing, to determine those responsible and various subsequent events.
The game's core concepts and the way in which the plot develops clearly link to recent contemporary developments, with surveillance becoming increasingly prevalent in many developed countries, and by the end of the game you're very much prompted to take the time to develop your thoughts on the merits of the 'real life' use of surveillance. In-game, this link to modern society serves to heighten the player's engagement with the game's mechanics and plot. Alongside this, there's a clean interface that minimises the friction in the information-gathering mechanics, well-judged use of music to emphasise key developments, and the ability to influence the outcome of certain poignant key events.

I had wanted to play this game ever since it came out way back when, and I think that if I had done so when it was initially released on Xbox 360 my opinion of it would be more positive.  Unfortunately, despite my efforts to appreciate Overlord for what it was then as I play it now, I find it difficult to review it in such a vacuum (I should also note that I played this game using the Steam controller).
Beginning with the positives, Overloard is set in a charming, comical, and vibrant world that flips the arachatypical approach of what would be considered a traditional "Western" fantasy kingdom.  In this Overloard certainly nails the aesthetic it was going for and comes off as a slightly dark and more twisted Fable derivative.  For what it's worth, the world is quite beautiful, unique, and surprisingly large.  The motley crew of characters you come across in your adventures fit the peculiar world and I found myself admiring everything from the music to the quirky animations of sheep frolicking in the meadows.
Unfortunately, gameplay and design fall short of the same mark in quality.  Managing your various colored minions (which is important for solving puzzles and overcoming obstacles) became way too much of a hassle.  The camera rarely ever wanted to play nicely with the target auto lock and I found myself frequently annoyed when approaching puzzles that required a level of resource management ("resources" here being you minions) of meager complexity.  That is not to say that the puzzles were themselves difficult to understand, but executing them became an exercise in frustration.  This was the first time in quite a while that I actually had a strong urge to throw my controller, even Dark Souls never was so mechanically burdensome to bring me to that point.
Along with the aforementioned issue another major problem I had was that too much of the game relied upon your minions as an expendable resource.  Regaining health and mana, solving puzzles, upgrading weapons and armor, using them as your primary "weapon" meant actively fighting with the poor controls and camera to direct your horde(s) and perform what should have been simple tasks.  What's more is that this heavy reliance inevitably required with it a very boring gameplay loop that forced you to grind for the life-force to summon more minions.  So much of the early game centered around amassing your horde while holding off upgrading yourself until the late game with equipment that wouldn't feel like wasted effort.  Nothing ever felt fulfilling, everything revolved around the minions, but because they were expected to be sacrificed even attempting to equip them with more powerful equipment felt wasted.
Sticking with it for a couple hours longer I was conflicted in my desire to continue exploring this gorgeous world while simulataneously never actually having that much fun playing it.  I eventually deleted my profile and uninstalled the game when I realized I was actively trying to convince myself that I enjoyed it than genuinely feeling that way.  Maybe if I was playing with a mouse and keyboard it would have been different, or maybe if I stuck with it just a little bit longer I would have gotten over that hump, maybe I was expecting too much out of a game getting on in years.  Whatever the case, I found that the frustrations I faced wasn't worth the time I was putting into it.
No, I certainly can't recommend this game, but a lot of people seem to enjoy it so there is definitely an argument here to purchase and play it.  There are a lot of genuinely great and novel ideas here which attracted me to play it in the first place.  On paper they would appear to be a recipie for success, but in execution they were cumbersome and I just don't have the time to fight with such issues.  As a MD student, my limited vacation time is valuable and I try to balance gaming with other recreational activities as best I can.  Others might find value here but I would much rather play something more immediately entertaining and with lasting appeal like Morrowind.

In Overlord, you take the role of the epinonymous anti-hero, recently resurrected by your hysterical minions to take up the mantel of your fallen predecessor. Very little backstory is provided and this is a little disappointing, but the humorous sequence through which your minions great you makes up for it. Apparently a band of nefarious do-gooders trashed your Evil Tower, and you've got to put it back together, strange the peasants into submission and get your revenge.
To do this, you are teleported into the first map area to pummel some bloated halflings (I never did like hobbits). The first map (and the ones that follow) is well designed and beautiful, with some creative ideas to keep it interesting and give you an open feel. You're welcome to explore at your leisure but, to accomplish your quests, things move in a fairly linear fashion. To the game's credit, however, it doesn't FEEL linear. I felt free to do what I wanted when I wanted to do it. But, tasks really must be completed in a certain order before you can progress. (Un)-fortunately, that precise order isn't clear until after some trial and error (which either leads to confusion or creates that non-linear sensation).
The primary tool in your conquest will be your minions. Your selection is limited but effective. You have your warriors (brown minions), fire throwers (red minions), assassins (green minions) and healers (blue minions). Ironically, your minions are the real star of this game -- not you. They run around, wreaking havoc on the land and indulging your every whim. They leap onto the backs of sheep and ride them like broncos and swarm over your enemies like a bunch of gibbering goblins. Constantly breaking loose funny little jokes and reverently presenting you with treasure and gifts, they really steal the show and I never get tired of them. Compared to thim, the Overlord is definitely the strong silent type -- individually he is far more powerful in battle, but your minions are far more powerful when used en masse.
Your evil-ness is rated on a scale of corruption. You can take the less "evil" path by helping your peasants and restoring the Elven race or you can be Evil by pillaging the village, killing the peasants until they're suppressed, and slaughtering the few remaining elves like the simpering fools they are. Reflecting your chosen path is a selection of two mistresses (a fiesty but well-intentioned maiden or a sultry and wicked seductress).
I found the gameplay relatively simple and not terribly challenging. I doubt it's supposed to be. The game is, first and foremost, about having fun. The game is riddled with little jokes and the minions have kept me chuckling and laughing the whole time.
The graphics are rich and beautiful, and the sound is also well done but not particularly remarkable. The real gem is the gameplay and the novelty of being Evil. Due to the linear nature of the quests, I'm not sure what the replay value of this game will be, but it is a fun and enjoyable romp.

Never Alone is an adventure platformer consisting of some light puzzle solving and a blatant disregard for solid gameplay principles. It's hard to control but easy to love.
Built on the rich Inuit culture, Kisima Ingitchuna encompasses art, story, language, characters based on the history and folklore of those peoples. The presentation of this is mostly done in a solid manner. Inuit art and language are used for cutscenes as well as the story being a traditional Iñupiaq tale. By playing the game, unlockable videos also provide insight into some of the concepts and items behind the game.
The gameplay takes place in a 2D tundra world where obstacles provide the meat of the light puzzle solving where not too much thinking is required. The basic concept here being switching between Nuna and Fox where both have their own skills to help the other. The theory being when you move one, the other will follow (if you opened the path for them). This however does not always work as expected as I found myself having to switch between characters frequently as the other would just not do what I wanted and sometimes even killed themselves. The developers did include a local co-op mode so the second character can be controlled by a human. I recommend you try that.
Controlling the characters is a whole other can of beans. Characters feel heavy when moving, shooting the Bola is imprecise, swimming is.. well lets just say Mario would win gold in Olympic swimming on his day off after he had too much to drink the night before, Luigi would be second, Nuna and Fox would be disqualified for drowning. Controlling the kayak (DLC) is basically impossible.
Never Alone does a beautiful job of presenting itself. It has an unique concept tied to it and the execution of its artistic values are done well. Technically, it's a bit of a mess especially in the controls department. Gameplay is passable but too shallow for my taste. It's weak in puzzles and platforming and can hardly stand on its own adventure. There's no real depth to anything apart from the story if you can delve past the ambiguity of it. It's a shame because it is artistically very pleasing.
I don't think the game is worth the full price but you should try it just the same. If nothing else, it does provide insight into Inuit culture and hey, you can play as a fox.

If this bait and switch method continues, I don't see much hope for the future of Rocksmith but rather your competitors who will see this as an opportunity to lure customers who want a one stop shop for all of they're music.
That being said, I definitely recommend this game to anyone who is passionate about playing guitar or bass. At this time there isn't really anything out there like it. There are some bugs and if your PC isn't up to par (2.66 Ghz) you will have some problems like crashing, effect tones disappearing, and lag between when you play a note and hearing the note. You may also score poorly because of this. The software thinks you missed the note or chord. This seemed to happen more often when I first started using it. I think alot of the "game's" resources are occupied by listening to how you play in order to provide you with a difficulty level which suits your playing ability. Once it has that, it seems to speed up a little. You can adjust the difficulty level yourself but only in the "Riff Repeater" mode. I spent months trying to get it to work on my new Gateway  (1.4 GHz) PC . Got it to only crash once in a while. I turn off all the exrra graphic features like shading etc... and play it in windowed mode and it's decent. The built in guitar effects are decent but, don't expect to sound exactly like your favorite band (remember, they have an entire sound crew and engineers...you don't). So, plug in, strap on headphones (or don't), and ROCK OUT!!!

This game has a couple pros and cons, much like any other, however my view is this game is quite enjoyable,
.
Pros:
-If you're a beginner, you're going to learn a LOT and likely develop better habits early on which will let you become much better in time.
-It's fantastic for practicing and learning songs, as well as developing and refining techniques in play.
-Has a lot of handy side games, a 'session mode' tool where you can just play with "a band", and a considerable number of lessons which are quite well done.
-It begins easy and gets more difficult as you successfully hit notes and such. If a section is overwhelming, or you want more practice, you can use "Riff Repeater" which lets you play sections repeatedly at various speeds, difficulties, etc, to help master it.
-It has a decent setlist, and a decent amount of DLC
-The tuner is handy...
-I'm a fan of the achievements, leaderboards, etc (gives you a goal)
Cons:
-The learning curve, mainly to understand which string shown is which... (it doesn't take long, it's just daunting at first)
-The game isn't ideal in ensuring you hit proper notes within chords or fast sections. You can have a string a fret or two off and still hit the chord (with the remaining fingers on the proper chord...)
-
: You pay for the game (so $15-60, depending), then you need a Tone-Cable (which is about 40 online), THEN if you want DLC you're pay 2-4 per song. Let alone the actual guitar. It all adds up very quickly.
-The DLC itself isn't ideal and is quite limiting...
(>They do, however, release one pack a week, on Tuesdays)
-While many have found ways to get custom songs on Rocksmith, yeah, the game itself doesn't let you do this.
(>As a fan of metal, I wish the game had more. Some Devin Townsend, perhaps...?)

After watching a couple of gameplay videos that came out after the Sector Zero DLC was released I finally decided to give this game a try when both items were on sale (pretty much the same as when I go watch a movie I already know I won't enjoy so much, but don't mind the price of the ticket thinking I'd rather be busy for the duration than the alternative). Just like Stardrive 1, I saw the potential of some of the features of this 2nd game, although in the same fashion I was almost always disappointed by their implementation, feeling like the developper sometimes did not even realize how good his own ideas could have been if just a bit more passion had been put into polishing those specific features.
There is - or there was? - a potentially very good game again in SD2 (as it could have been in SD1) but once more the fact the game is crippled by a sheer amount of bugs, a clunky UI lacking ergonomy, and that overall many of the features lack "that little something" that would have made them awesome. Also, while there are difficulty levels and several options to activate or not it is pretty clear there is a balancing issue (try playing brutal x4 without deactivating the attack events and you'll most likely get crushed by a master remnant fleet around turn 100 or something (6 shielded mid size ships using disabling EMP attacks and having very decent firepower), and if you miraculously manage to beat that fleet, good luck with catching up with the AI empires after focusing on building your military till that point in game).
While tons of references to "geek culture" in sci-fi/fantasy fields can be found in the flavor text, they sadly get old pretty quick (provided they were "fun" in the first place) and sadly don't add enough to the enjoyment for the player to forget or in some cases forgive the effort put in those instead of making the core game much more solid in every critical aspect.
But at the end, this 4X can deliver its share of fun and has a bit of replayability especially when you try to optimize custom races for some specific playstyles.
I would never ever recommend it on full price though (its simply too expensive for a half-baked product to fully back it), I could say it's a ok game game that could provide you with several hours of fun and is somehow challenging, at least if you don't encounter game breaking bugs (I did encounter mostly UI display bugs and UI functionality bugs on my side). But if you are tight on budget and want a polished game that will last in your shiny library, it would be wise to avoid this one which has big chances to end up in your bin (of shame?) at some point.

An investigation game with an intriguing premises,
comes together as a unique experience that keeps you gripped with its narrative, despite fairly limited mechanics. Putting the player in the role of an investigator working with an information-processing system known as Orwell (referencing George Orwell's
), the game tasks you to search out information from a fictional set of websites (and later, live conversations and data on individual target personal devices) to investigate the aftermath of a bombing, to determine those responsible and various subsequent events.
The game's core concepts and the way in which the plot develops clearly link to recent contemporary developments, with surveillance becoming increasingly prevalent in many developed countries, and by the end of the game you're very much prompted to take the time to develop your thoughts on the merits of the 'real life' use of surveillance. In-game, this link to modern society serves to heighten the player's engagement with the game's mechanics and plot. Alongside this, there's a clean interface that minimises the friction in the information-gathering mechanics, well-judged use of music to emphasise key developments, and the ability to influence the outcome of certain poignant key events.

SOMA is a first-person sci-fi/horror adventure game from the beautifully twisted minds at Frictional Games. Those familiar with Frictional's previous offerings, the
and
series, will quickly feel at home with the game's core mechanics and style. Similar to those earlier offerings, SOMA is a story-rich adventure with a thought-provoking plot that steadily unfolds throughout the game. The protagonist starts with minimal knowledge of the bizarre situation he finds himself in and must uncover the truth from documents, computer terminals and NPCs that are encountered during the ensuing exploration. The game adeptly employs psychological horror elements to conjure a deeply foreboding atmosphere but the persistent feeling of dread is not merely imagined. Very real dangers stand in your way, most notably the hostile creatures that relentlessly hound you if discovered. A familiar mechanic comes into play here; similar to other Frictional titles, enemies are impossible to defeat so evasion is your only chance of survival. Combat is not an option.
One of SOMA's strongest aspects is the power and depth of the story it tells. Unfortunately, this is not something I can easily expand upon as revealing too much would be a great disservice to potential players. I believe that the best way to enter this game is in exactly the same way as its protagonist; unaware of the immediate situation, obliged to cautiously explore the alien environment to discover what has happened and why. But without revealing any specifics, I will say that the story is an extremely well crafted and thought-provoking foray into existentialism and what it truly means to be human. The core themes are certainly not unique but their masterful presentation by means of the unfolding storyline in SOMA surely is.
In many respects this is Frictional Games doing what they do best - an atmospheric adventure game with a very strong story and effective use of horror elements, bordering on survival horror considering your helplessness in the face of the hostile lifeforms you encounter. This is standard fare for Frictional Games but SOMA refines and perfects the formula to surpass
and
in almost every way. The puzzle solving elements are logical and streamlined, providing a challenge without resorting to red herrings or burdensome inventories. Despite being unable to engage in combat with your foes, you won't be constantly dashing between hiding places; in fact, as you learn more about the nature of these monstrosities you'll discover that you're not
as helpless as you first thought. The story unfolds at exactly the right pace and is delivered in many different ways so it doesn't feel like a significant proportion of your time is spent pouring over random notes and journals.
Everything that brought critical acclaim to Frictional's earlier work is here but the weaker aspects have been carefully considered, refined and improved to the point of virtual perfection. This is truly their magnum opus and the absolute pinnacle of the "Frictional formula". This formula won't appeal to every gamer but SOMA still receives my highest recommendation, even to those who may have been underwhelmed by the developer's previous titles.
To conclude, I'll merely add that SOMA defies a simple "pros and cons" list so I apologise if you were expecting to find one down here!

Never Alone is a puzzle-adventure genre game that places you in a beautiful world on the brink of disaster. The story revolves around a child who becomes separated from her village during a devastating blizzard. Luckily, she's rescued by a seemingly magical Snow White fox. The primary objective of the game is to find the unknown source of the blizzard and stop it at any cost necessary. Throughout the game, you're able to switch between playing as the child and the white fox. Quite a few puzzles actually require you to do so in order to navigate through them.
While the gameplay is very straightforward, I honestly found the simplicity enjoyable and preferred in this scenario. During gameplay, you're forced to navigate through multiple puzzles that are thought-provoking and intertwined with the plot. Completing these puzzles will progress you through the story and unlock absolutely amazing cutscenes that further develop the narrative. Throughout the game, I had experience with controls occasionally being unresponsive and frankly unusable for a certain duration. Even though it's a disappointing defect, I found the game amazing nonetheless.
The narration in Never Alone is heart-wrenching and soul-defining. From the moment I started the game, I was hooked and unable to stop listening to the beautifully composed narrative. Furthermore, the music they incorporated into the gameplay is perfectly suited for the atmosphere that's demonstrated within the game.
Never Alone is a beautiful demonstration of how a puzzle-adventure game is done correctly. I was pleasantly pleased with everything the game had to offer, and while a few defects are present, I genuinely don't believe they're a significant issue. Overall, for the reasonable price of 14.99$, I would highly recommend Never Alone to anyone who enjoys a casual puzzle experience with a twist.

It breaks my heart to say this but: Don't buy this game.
I was so enthusiastic to find a game that embraces the culture and folklore of the natives.
Visuals of the game looked great, and the music played nicely with them. Character designs were cute, not the most unique, but nice. The first few levels are allright, because the game keeps it fairly simple. You (most of the time) have time to react to things, and can work out the fairly simple puzzles in peace. However, when the pace gets faster, the clunky controls really start to drag you down. You'll die multiple times, not only because of the controls, but because your character decides to jump on itself over the ledge, or the dumb-as-a-boot-AI decides to kill itself by stopping to a place where it most likely will be squashed between two platworms. When playing a single player game you don't only have to look after yourself but also the AI with an IQ of a vegetable. If those things didn't make the game unfair for the player, should I mention that the game is RIDDLED with bugs.
The biggest fault in the game however is its inconsistancy, in terms of both gameplay AND storytelling. This causes you to AGAIN die multiple times before figuring out that the game designers have had a complete brain fart, and don't remember how they introduced a certain game feature, and ended up changing it, without realizing that this might confuse the shaite out of the player. (Mind you, I did not watch the info videos, because I wanted to keep my immersion to the story as keen as possible, and I thought that the videos were only disturbing on that part.)  There were A LOT OF THINGS that made no sense. After beating the game I'm just left with a bunch of questions which I never got an answer to. What was the point of the Bola (other than showing the spirits)? Why did the bad-guy want itso bad? What was his role in all of this (more than be a filler), if the girl's town and family were going to be alright in the end anyway? But the biggest question at the end is: WHY WAS THE GIANT HAPPY after Nona literally WRECKED the thing that he was working on?! (Whatever that was anyway) There were just so many things that didn't make ANY sense. I could've forgiven the technical difficulties to the game, if they'd only delivered on the part of the plot but no. Sorry no, I just can't.
On the top of this. After finishing the game and quitting, the game decided to crash for the last and final time, like saying 'farewell' to me.

I would recommend this game to anyone who loves beautiful art styles, a calming game, puzzles where the only way to lose is by giving up, pretty good platforming, foxes, seasons, pretty colors, and good sound.

Simple and fun mechanics that can get down to the perfect amount of complexity that it really peaked my love for the game! It was perfectly balanced in fun and challenge in my view! Then the absolute beauty of the seasons never ceased to keep me going when I had to run back through an area to do something.
On that note, the game never felt rushed or stretched out longer than it needed at all. Every moment was spent used to do something important or give you pause while you ran through the forest to admire the absolutely beautiful art.
Something I hate about games these days is that they are stretched out so insanely past the main plot line that it usually can take up to a mouth or more to get everything done. I completed this game and got all of the achievements in a single day and after that I felt both complete and endlessly inspired! Few games these days let the player just finish so that they can get on with their lives and go back one other day and do it all over again (all of it) without it feeling like some kind of chore. I love to restart games and do something different with my playthroughs. Admittedly this game doesn't have really that potential, but because it's nothing like Skyrim with seemingly endless content I can enjoy it, not as a game that steals your life with a million options, but as a game that is like a gorgeous song that can be played over as many times as you want without getting tired that it never seems to end!
There were quite a few bugs and glitches that lead to either a crash or (in the case of falling through the map) a restart that I experienced in my playthrough. Worth it all (In fact it might have made me even more encouraged to press onwards... I'm not trying to encourage bugs in games to stay, but a game that is so wonderful that bugs and crashes make me want to try harder to continue? I could go back to that easily)!
If the art wasn't good enough I can be quite picky with the music I listen to and at the moment I write this I have only been able to listen to 3 specific songs repeating. And then I got the soundtrack and I'm off to falling asleep to it, even though I haven't been able to fall asleep to any other music at all lately! It too, is perfectly balanced in my view! Most songs are addicting (especially the good ones), too plain or just bad. These songs I could listen to over and over again and I would be able to stop at any time if I wanted to (in essence I get to choose to be addicted or not and I choose the former).
All and all I think it's an absolutely wonderful game and I eagerly await the next time I feel like playing!
I only wish I could help with the ideas for a sequal (a plot line and mechanics the for it have been running through my head ever since I finished)...

This game was a very enjoyable experience thanks to its thoughtful artwork and gorgeous music. Compared to other platformers, the world isn't large and confusing and you will usually have a rough idea of where you need to go. The controls are simple enough and the puzzles aren't terribly difficult. I occasionally got stumped but I figured it out eventually.
As far as story, don't be fooled by chipper, cheerful narrator at the beginning. It's not all sunshine and cinnamon buns—the story becomes more serious and dramatic after the first few hours; I definitely wanted to know what was going to happen next. (The voice acting is believable and well done, too. It also breaks up the monotony and drives you forward at times. I feel it fits without being distracting.)
For people looking for a casual, artful experience, this is definitely your game. If you are looking for a game with a Health bar, enemies to fight, extra lives and a skill tree you won't find it here. The appeal of this game is playing a lonely fox as it runs around the forest solving puzzles in a tastefully artful environment.

The amazing artwork sets this game aside from the blandness of modern gaming industry. This is essentially a puzzle game with a mysterious story and beautiful handcrafted environments to explore. Don't be misled by the apparent "fairy tale" tone of the game, by midgame puzzles are quite challenging.
The only minor negative aspect is the lack of a map, by midgame multiple tasks make navigation rather confusing.
All in all I give it a 8.5/10, hopefully navigation will be improved in the future.

So here's my review (from someone that has put at least 100 hours into this game).
This is a good game... a very good game however be under no illusion of what you are getting. This is a game made on a shoe string budget by what seems to be a single guy. He releases regular patches to fix the things he has broken in previous patches. The graphics are not going to win any awards and the gameplay at the end gets a bit repetitive. With all those negatives, this is actually a really really good game. I would put this in a similar league to tetris when it first came out. It's one of those games that will eat away at your life as you play again and again. The sight of your intergalactic empire sending out fleets of ships to defend against an attacking race is exciting. Will my fleet make it to the planet before I lose it to an invasion, will my state of the art research win the technological arms race and allow me to turn the tide of battle? This game feels how i imagine it must feel to actually control an intergalactic empire.
Buy this game but be aware it is not without its faults.

So to start, let me say that I started with the older version of Rocksmith. At first, it was a good enough program. It got me started, but somewhere about three hours in, I just could never move forward. I had never played guitar before that, and the premise of learning something new is kind of an exciting one. But the songs were difficult in my opinion, and relatively unknown to me, and interest faded, and I kind of, well, quit.
I saw Rocksmith 2014 come out, and it caught my interest. Right away, I noticed some of the differences. It wasn't entirely a game. There was little motivation in that regard. But the motivation turned to learning the songs now. The tools were intuitive, and soon, I started picking up new tricks, especially from the videos. I even learned to restring my guitar. (Don't judge me! I had watched one online earlier on and ended up having to go to the music store anyway).
So the question is... Does it work? I think so. I've picked up how to play, but I also learned how to read tab, too. The only thing I could suggest for them next time, is maybe teaching a little about music theory for people who have never done music before. You know, what is a quarter note, half note. What do they look like if I wanted to leave this game and learn more on my own. But otherwise, I'm learning new songs, and songs that I want to learn. I can now do it in front of others and it sounds good. So yes, I recommend it. After all, everyone should have something cool they can do. I can now break out a guitar and play a few songs. Why shouldn't you, too?

tl;dr - The bugs/design flaws made me want to rip my hair out at times, but the presentation and simple gameplay were enough to still make me really enjoy the game. A simple but enjoyable title, but I would wait for a sale, as $17 CDN seems a bit much for a game that I finished in 2 hours.
Never Alone is an adventure platformer, with inspirations from games like Limbo from the way the game progresses and its ominous atmosphere with bits of puzzles and action sprinkled throughout. I highly recommend playing it with a friend. Not because you like your friend. But you need someone to take control rather than letting the AI sit and drool. Also make sure they take Nuna. The fox is much more fun.
The game overall
fun, but honestly, I would recommend this game as I grind my teeth. I don't regret playing it, and will probably come back to it later just to snag the last few achievements and play Foxtales, but that'd be it. The puzzles are mediocre, the platforming can be incredibly frustrating at parts, and there are a few bugs here and there that can halt the progress at times.
As I was saying, the gameplay itself is alright. I found myself really annoyed with the wind mechanic, as even though there is a pattern to it, it does occasionally change, or sometimes, because of the level design, it can basically make you over-jump a gap and end up dying anyway because you flew right over the platform you were aiming for. The magnet mechanic to try and help you avoid falling over the edge can also be a pain, because at times it can make trying to make moving around a bit clunky as you might end up sticking to the edge for a moment and lose some momentum. Overall it's not terrible, but it feels like it could use some polish.
Also mentioned before, choose the Fox if you have a
friend to
help. He's a lot more fun and feels better to move around with. I understand why Nuna doesn't move around as much, given her giant parka she's in, but nonetheless feels more fun to be able to leap around, wall-jump and get to do some of the more interesting work.
This was probably my favourite aspect of the game. I really love how the game presents itself. It does have that Limbo sort of feeling with the calm and quiet atmosphere, which is a refreshing feeling and change of pace. You don't feel too rushed and you can enjoy the scenery. The spirits that help you along the way are simple yet charming, Nuna and the fox are simple in design but look really nice. One character that I thought was a little off was
I understand he's supposed to be bad and therefore unlikeable, but I feel like he just stood out a bit too much. Overall though, I love the look of the game. It doesn't try to be anything extravagant, and that's okay. It's simple but charming presentation is beautiful and definitely pleasing to take in all throughout the game.
This is the part where I almost considered giving it a thumbs down, but I do feel it wasn't bad enough to sour my whole experience. When I played with my girlfriend, we'd find that sometimes Nuna would get stuck on platforms when she's climbing on spirits, I got glitched off and would fall to my death. I also mentioned in the gameplay section how the wind screwed me over occasionally as well. There is usually calm air with - I believe - a rhythymic gust that comes along every so often. One thing that I found, however, is that during some parts there's also this tiny little blow of wind that can impede your momentum, which isn't really used for anything. So I had a few instances where I was going to leap for a platform, and it's like the game poked me during midair and said "lolbye." I had this happen a few times and it just felt annoying.
The camera is fairly solid, but there were I think two areas where it wasn't really clear where I had to go, and ended up going towards a small platforming area where I needed the fox to show the spirits before we went. There was one spirit rope that you would fling across, but there was a second one you needed to reveal to make it to the other side of the gap. We thought that maybe you just needed this stupidly precise jump to be able to clear it, but after we went back a little bit and checked out the area above,
it showed up, despite not doing so before.
Another thing was the Insights. I couldn't actually play any of them because it would just result in a black screen with nothing going on, so I simply restarted the game. There are 20-some of them and they look interesting, but I can't even check them out, which is unfortunate. I had to go on YouTube to see them.
Despite my incessant whining, I really did enjoy Never Alone. I'm usually playing a lot more hardcore games, but I got Never Alone as part of a bundle, and I think you should do the same, or at least wait for a sale. It only took me 2 hours to beat the game, and if I wasn't dawdling, I could have probably finished in an hour and a half. It's a lot to pay for so little gameplay. If you do get a chance to get the game for cheap, I would definitely recommend it for a quiet night where you want to wind down with a simple story and relatively calm progression.

This really is a very unique game in the gem/color-matching casual puzzle genre (is this actually a genre?).
Where Puzzle Quest combined the puzzling with some RPG, Tomb of Tyrants combines it with tower defense and some strategy.
And it is FRANTIC!
You match varying colors to give different bonuses to your minions (which defend your tomb), traps and rooms.
At the same time, you are building rooms and recruit minions to place in said rooms to defend the rooms from the ever growing tide of heroes trying to slay you.
You reorganize the room layout and need to really optimize where to put each minion (certain minions work better with others, some rooms give benefits more fitting to other minions, etc.).
And you have to be FAST about all of it - thankfully, there is a pause button that you will learn to use frequently.
You will lose a lot, but usually each run gives you some lasting bonuses which carry over to the next run so you do get stronger to withstand the waves longer and longer - while also becoming better at the meta game.
The game is really fun and for the price absolutely recommended.
And it gets a big +1 for supporting linux.
But there is one glaring problem:
You get thrown right into the midst of it, having no idea why the game layout is so weird and what the hell is going on. There really is too much happening at once in the game. Just look at the negative reviews, most are by confused people after a very short session of playing.
The "tutorial" actually adds to the confusion because it is just pop ups appearing on top of all the chaos already happening.
There really should be a better tutorial, maybe only including parts of the game to explain the first steps. And then slowly introducing other concepts.
As it is now, I can see a lot of people giving up quickly in confusion.
Highly addictive. Highly recommended.

TL;DR: Beautiful, stylized game with LOTS of charm and potential, ruined by TERRIBLY IMPRECISE CONTROLS; and completely DUMB NARRATION which ruins the ambiance.
4/10
Complete Review:
I fell in love with the art style, look, and feel of this game and was really looking forward to playing it and enjoying it. Sadly, the controls rained on that parade soon and hard. And before you think it's me, my controller, or my computer, I finished both Rayman Origins and Rayman Legends (both titles at 90%+) with the exact Logitech controller/PC/config I am using to play this Seasons after Fall. I am by no means a platforming guru, but I am not a complete dolt, either.
This game lacks the required precision, in part because...
1. The fox "hops" when it moves (and you cannot jump mid-hop), making it impossible to time running jumps with where platforms end;
2. It's very hard to tell where platforms actually end and begin;
3. There seems to be no internal consistency as to whether the exact same action performed in the exact same way will be successful or not.
All that makes it very frustrating to play. Before it is stylish and charming, a platformer MUST HAVE ROCK-SOLID CONTROLS (especially a puzzle platformer which requires elaborate setups to get a series of platforms in the right conifguration to be able to progress). A game has to be a game FIRST; especially a platformer. PRECISION IS KEY. Without solid playability, a game just isn't...well...PLAYABLE!
The second thing which ruined the game for me was the narration. Like Blade Runner, The Director's Cut, this game would have been MUCH better without the stupid hand-holding voice of--whomever--ruining the amiance, mystery, beauty, and magic of the world created. These are spirits and animals. LET THEM BE, and LET US PLAYERS DISCOVER BEING THEM. We don't need all that inane exposition tearing down the third wall and completely booting us out of the game world. With such a beautiful art style and animation, there are so many ways to SHOW us the story rather than TELL US.
SO MUCH POTENTIAL...squandered. Very, very disappointing. It's been a while since I was so eager to play a game based on its Steam video only to be thwarted so utterly by the actual game. Very sad. The developers need to go back to the drawing board with this one.
Fix the controls; get rid of the narration and tell the story using the visuals and music. Then you will have a 10/10.

I'll be honest, this one surprised me! And I actually had decent expectations to begin with. After playing the demo I figured it'd be a well done pick-your-own-adventure sort of deal, dressed up as something more intricate, but I'd say this went well beyond that. Simply put, the demo really is just a taste of what comes later. The game does a lot with the limited gameplay it has available. The story handles the subject matter fantastically and actually managed to surprise me (and it's quite a relevant tale these days). The final chapter was genuinely tense and left me constantly reconsidering my options. I'd have to play it again to see how much of the choices were an illusion, but it did feel like actions genuinely had large and unforeseen consequences.
I have small niggles, like I sometimes felt that I should be able to override the conflicting data chunks or felt stuck while the game waited for me to upload chunks for which I didn't feel I had enough justification to upload them, but some of that is part of the story and some of it is just the limitations of a narrative like this. Overall, they're fairly minor issues.
I can wholeheartedly recommend the game at full price and I'm looking forward to the sequel.

The game designers who implemented the interface desrver credit for the ease of use (despite a few minor bugs) and ease of learning. You will understand game mechanics after finishing the first chapter.
One might also consider Orwell as a training simulation for future employment posibilities. Somone needs to keep track of Uplink agents and the like.

Jazzpunk is a wonderful game that really is horribly short. The beginning is a great introduction to a world that is reminicent of a 60's spy flick mixed with 80's cyberpunk. Oddly, the biggest failing of this game is it's exploration, in that there simply isn't enough. One entire level is merely a night version of an earlier one, and it possesses the same jokes and side events as the day version. Also, there where at least two occasions when I wished there was an alternative action or possibility than the ones you are forced into in order to proceed with the story. A cliched lapse in judgement brings about a briefly, inarguably unfunny event that amounted to the plot getting in the way of the fun. I never saw the point of the rhythm games you played with a small plastic "guitaresque" controller. I always thought it'd be more worth my time to learn to play an actual guitar. I just re-bought it again on Steam to take advantage of the sales on DLC and I don't see the next version coming to PS3. To me this is more than just a game, it's an investment. This is something that can teach you not just how to play the basics, but how to play multiple songs of various genres. It's going to provide you with an invaluable foundation to learning guitar overall. Make no mistake, this game is amazing, but it will only provide a part of your guitar education.
It won't teach you how to read music or even tab. It also provides very little by way of music theory. It teaches you the how, not the why. A library and/or Google can help you find resources to help make up for the games few shortcomings. If you have the money, try your local guitar shop and see about some lessons. Some advice for when you start practicing outside of the game, get a tuner and a metronome. Either buy them or get an app on your phone/tablet. Use them every time you play without the game. By staying in tune your ear will develop faster than if you played out of tune. The metronome will help you keep in time so you can play consistently.

PROS:
+ You can control different types of civilian vessels, from small tugboats to huge cruise liners
+ You can walk around your ship in first-person mode
+ A wide variety of missions are available
+ A mission editor is included so you can design your own routes and objectives
CONS:
- Options menu is bare bones (three non-descript settings for graphics and an audio slider that controls both sound and music at the same time)
- Graphics are on the low end and except for the odd suicidal AI-controlled ship, the entire world seems lifeless
- Music is incredibly annoying
- Physics and handling of ships feels a little off
- No freeplay or sandbox mode, just scripted missions (unless you use the mission editor)
- The mission editor is overly complex and very unintuitive
- AI-controlled ships won't adjust their course, so if you happen to be in the way (even if this means you're simply docked), they will ram you
- Crashes to the desktop so often it's unlikely you'll ever play through an entire mission without losing all of your progress at least once
VERDICT: As much as I wanted to like ESS, I just couldn't. Even if I could forgive some of this game's faults, the constant crashes and restrictive gameplay are just too much. Unless you find this game as part of a package deal (on Humble Bundle, for instance) or at an extremely low price, I'd have to say "No, don't buy this game."

So. Whats a tyrant anyway?
The games name implies that you, the player, are a tyrant. By matching 4 or more runes of a color you gather ressources. You use these ressources to build rooms, vertically downwards, that are filled with different creatures. This creatures don't ever leave your inverted tower ...which makes you a landlord, more than a tyrant.
Well, maybe the tyrant is in the way you treat this creatures. Sure, you can asign them a workplace, but more often than not, they are free to stay where they are. The most successfull of them will likely work close to you. The ressources you get from matching 4 or more runes allow you to grant benefits to the creaturs working in your not-tower, like healing their wounds, mending their clothes or just refresh them. Well, you can even bring them back to life, should some kind of workplace injury claim them. ...that's more than most CEOs do for their employees, that doesn't sound like a tyrant.
Who could be the tyrant? Who would bring harm to this so called tomb and its inhabitants?
Well, it's trespassers. They wander in, start slaying the creatures and if they are not stopped, they even kill you. At least, you can bring down your collapsing downwardstower on them, and burry these monsters! Yes, you can make this a tomb for this tyranical murderers!
Just match 4 or more runes.

Tomb of Tyrants is a Match 3 (technically 4) / RPG hybrid with the twist being you're matching tiles to create a deadly dungeon. Depending on what tiles you match, you create a deathtrap filled with different rooms, cunning traps and angry minions in order to fight off those pesky adventurers that want to slay your tyrant. You roll the row to make a match (in a similar style to 10mil / You must build a boat), but you can also move in multiple directions in a single move and when a tile is used blocks can fall as well (physics matching?), tetris style. There are a fair few tile types, but thankfully you get a mouseover on each one because it would be a nightmare to remember everything. Less thankfully you have to squint at the screen to actual read the text most of the time.
It's a deep strategy game from the very first playthrough. Deceptively hard, it really took me a little while to figure out, so despite being a match 3 game it's really not casual at all. I'd definitely recommend having your coffee (or tea, if you're British like me) before you launch this in the morning.

Orwell was an enjoyable, but very flawed game. I struggle with recommending it to anybody, because I can't imagine a particular audience falling in love with it. Gamers looking for a great narrative may find Orwell's offerings lacking, as I have. Gamers who are fans of the works of George Orwell may get what they're looking for, but as a fan myself I find the game's vision lacking. George Orwell's works were a denouncement of totalitarianism, yet his most well-known fictional books were either set in the real world or clearly based on real events and people. Orwell the game instead opts to take place in the wonderful setting of "The Nation" in which "The Party" exercises total control in a fictional world.
While the setting certainly lacks creativity, I was pleased to see that the plot and characters of the game improved as time passed. Orwell places the player as a worker for a state surveillence system looking for the perpetrator of a series of terrorist bombings. The player is tasked with reading various articles, profiles, and personal conversations and sending this information to the authorities within The Nation's government. This sounds more interesting than it plays out, however. In the beginning I was given a suspect who was very clearly not the bomber. I resented my superior for being so brainless for assuming they were responsible. While this suspect inevitably had some connections with people who actually did know more about the bombings, I was frustrated that I had to investigate the suspect in the first place. The gameplay also lacks for imagination. While I enjoyed reading some of the articles and the suspect's internet profiles, conversations, and e-mails, the text that you upload is already pre-determined. It ultimately boils down to a scavenger hunt. There are some choices to make things interesting. Sometimes you will have to chose between two pieces of data to upload to the authorities, as there may be conflicting data. Sometimes this decision is a moral one, and others it's more based around what the player things is more accuracte information. There are even a few times where uploading too much information will lead to unforeseen consequences. Regardless, for the most part the gameplay is very linear and will ultimately turn off many gamers. The gameplay gets more interesting in the final chapter when the uploads you can make are limited and the pressure is heightened, yet this improvement comes too little, too late.
Orwell is a game I want to love and there are moments of quality within. The general conclusion to the story was pulled off fairly well and there are consequences for chocies that many probably would not have anticipated being held accountable for. The characters and their interactions amongst each other are far more engaging than the uncreative setting. I hope for the sequel the developers be more bold with their setting, their message, and ultimately make the gameplay more interesting for a wider audience.

I received Orwell as part of a Humble Bundle and thought I'd give it a go. My play time is 6 hours and that's with a couple of hours when I just left the game open to answer a call or get the door. Overall it was a quick game.
I was interested in the concept of it, and they executed it very well. I was drawn into the characters, and their complex lives over the course of the 4 hours of play time. It's purely text based, but they still managed to bring these characters to life. Details like small misspellings, people overlapping each-other when they spoke over the messaging systems, and the way they lied to each-other, all make them feel like real people.
Ultimately you're faced with a choice at the end and, while I didn't play the last chapter twice to find out for sure, I'm pretty sure you can pick your ending based on your actions.
If you're looking for something interesting but quick, and want to spend a few moments thinking about the implications of state surveillance programs, then pick this up. I am not a big fan of text-only games, but this did convince me to play through it to the end.  If you’re looking for action, graphics, or even voice acting, look elsewhere.

Le numéro 6 de la célèbre série suit très bien les traces de ses prédécesseurs tant pour l'histoire que pour ses vidéos léchés. Les graphiques en jeu sont aussi dans les standards auxquels Capcom nous a habitués au fil des ans.
Le bas est au niveau de la jouabilité. Depuis le 4e jeu, les aspects horreur et survie ont été relayés à l'arrière plan au profit de l'action.  Si cette action était bien gérée dans le 4e et 5e, elle est tout simplement ridicule dans le 6e. Les actions sont imprécises, le nouveau "recoil" des armes rend leur utilisation pénible, les boutons d'actions apparaissent souvent lorsque le temps alloué pour les utiliser est déjà en parti écoulé et les angles de caméra, surtout lors des scènes animées, rend certaines parties du jeu frustrantes, voir enrageantes. Lors de parties multijoueurs c'est problèmes sont doublés.
Somme toute, le jeu n'est pas injouable mais pas à la hauteur des attentes malgré son contenu varié et ses multiples défis.
