When I played the beta for this game, I was very excited. I was extremely hyped for the official release of this game, and to be able to play a fun little "party" game with all of my friends.
Unfortunately, when the game was released, I didn't realize I would be playing an even buggier, lamer game than the beta was. Launch day was a mess; there was an incredible amount of bugs and various problems, and this was just for the Steam version. I hear console was so much worse.
Continuing to today, there is still way too many bugs. I played ONE game yesterday to see if it was any better, and I ran into about 5 or 6 different bugs while playing as Jason rendering the game almost unplayable.
As someone who backed this game, and encouraged all of my friends to purchase it on release day, I feel betrayed. This game is awful on a million different levels, and I wouldn't recommend buying it even if you had all the money in the world to spend.
Reason 1.) Bugs. Obviously this game has more bugs in a game than I've ever seen. More than when I used to play DayZ. More than any pre-release game I've ever played. You will run into bugs in almost every single game you play, and a huge portion of these bugs are game breaking. I think I have seen a couple of patches for these bugs in the past, but there still always seems to be just about the same amount of bugs as before. You will run into map glitches such as falling under the map, getting stuck in a hiding spot, players getting out of the map, and players hiding in a spot where Jason cannot kill a counselor. Important items such as the phone box fuse may fall through the map. Jason will sometimes teleport with a counselor in his hands to take them away from a group of people. (I once witnessed Jason take a counselor who was fixing the phone box, and teleported both him and the fuse to an unknown location to kill him.) Sometimes when a counselor hits Jason, he will be put in a situation where he's supposed to mash a button to get back up/snap out of it, but Jason will still be able to walk around despite it. Sometimes Jason will be flown backwards in a direction for hundreds of yards for no known reason. A few times, I've seen players get stuck in the car for a full 15 minutes, unable to move, and unable to be killed by Jason.
Yesterday, I was trying to change a video setting and my mouse cursor disappeared. It took me about 5 minutes to manage to get out of my settings screen. These reasons listed are just a microscopic look into all of the bugs that lie within this game, and you will run into a lot of these bugs 5 minutes into launching the game.
Reason 2.) Speaking of video settings, this game has some pretty trash video settings. For as bad of graphics as this game has, you would think it would be easier to run it, but no, it's actually quite demanding out of your PC. You will likely have problems running this game well unless you have a great gaming PC, and even then, who knows? There is probably still more issues beyond the surface.
This game genuinely looks like it was made by high school students who have made their first game ever in Unreal Engine. It almost looks like something out of Gmod. Actually, this game would fit better in Gmod.
Reason 3.) Game mechanics. Are. ♥♥♥♥ING. GARBAGE. It's hard to believe, but I have never played a game with worse mechanics in my life. Jason grabs feel very weird and unnatural. Counsellor fighting stances feel the same way. You can do cheeky sprint/crouch combos to save stamina and reach longer locations, but it makes it extremely unrealistic. Driving in this game is a joke. Playstation 1 games have better driving mechanics than this game does. Boat is the same way, but driving the boat is easier since your only obstacle is a few rocks and just water-- but even then, you'll still somehow run into a rock while driving despite the rock being 2 feet away from the boat. When driving the car, sometimes you will crash it into some object or player, and the car will just flip for no reason. Gravity is inconsistent in this game.
A huge issue I have with mechanics though, is Jason. Players playing Jason can choose to just chop everyone in combat stance, completely ruining the point of Friday the 13th: cool, gorey, scenic murder. This mechanic also makes the game very boring to any counsellor facing this chopping Jason, and probably quite boring to the Jason player as well. Not to mention the buggy-feeling grab kills from Jason. Jason can reach unreasonable lengths to grab a counsellor and kill them a millisecond after grabbing them. I'm not sure why the developers thought this would be a fun mechanic.
Reason 4.) Story mode-- Oh, sorry, I mean single player mode. A highly anticipated mode by most of the fanbase. Unfortunately for these people awaiting single player mode, they probably don't realize that this mode is literally going to be nothing more than VS AI Mode. I don't even want to think about how buggy and boring this mode is going to be.
This is a reason since myself and a lot of other fans had the belief that Friday the 13th was getting some sort of Story Mode, but this was not the case at all. The developers just failed to make a public statement letting their fans know that we weren't getting a Story Mode, but a VS AI mode instead. They have stated it now as far as I'm aware in respone to a few people on Twitter, but this is hardly a public announcement. No one asked for a VS AI mode unless there was a Story mode to go along with it, and I doubt anyone is going to enjoy this single player mode.
EDIT: After looking through their Twitter, it seems there is going to be a few aspects to single player; one of which being "Virtual Cabin." This sounds like it has some chance of being decent, as they state it will take you into a first person experience, and give you a chance to uncover lore and secrets and what-not. (Although this contradicts what they said on their Twitter. See Reason 5 for context.)
Reason 5.) The developers seem to be children when it comes to any form of criticism. Allow me, right now, to take a look at their Twitter profile.
Someone replied to a Twitter thread upset to learn that "Story Mode" is actually not happening, and instead, single player AI is. F13 responded by saying "We never announced a story mode. F13 films aren't really "known" for their strong narrative." (Again, when you announce "Single Player mode coming soon," your followers tend to think STORY MODE. Be specific in the future.)
What F13 said is what contradicts with their upcoming "Virtual Cabin", that seems to be some type of Single Player mode that will involve lore and secrets. Why would you basically say that F13 has a trash story, then follow it up with lore stuff?|
Someone responds further with "And you guys aren't really "known" to fix and stabilize this game."
They respond with a petty "Appreciate the kind words."
The developers do not seem to be very smart when it comes to announcing upcoming projects for the game. Pretty much every single time they have announced a new thing, the date of said thing is pushed back further, and when it does finally come out, it's trash. Take for example, THE RELEASE of the game. Now take for example, their summer counsellor outfit DLC.
Reason 6.) Paid DLC? Really? This is a joke, right? When you hear paid DLC, you usually think of something huge, like a big new influx of items, maps, characters, or whatever. F13 recently announced Spring Break outfits (probably originally called Summer Blast or something like that.) They won't be released until Autumn. Why? Why is this something anyone should pay for more importantly? Your users already paid $40 for an awful, buggy, almost unplayable game, and you give us counsellor skins that we have to pay for?
There is so much more for me to say, but I've run out of room. Take note of how much more I could say if I had the room, or time. Do not support this game. Do not support these developers.

SOMA is an awesome game. It is not a horror or a survival game, but a linear adventure game with a few horror elements. You will not be in for a jumpscare like Deadspace or F.E.A.R.,but it tells a very good story, with good progression and at the end it will make you think: What are we? What is death and what is to be alive? The most notable thing is that you do not get bored playing it. You may finish it on your first session and it is not a small game... It took me almost nine hours in two sessions to finish,but if i could i would have finished it the same day it was installed.

This is from the same people who brought us the horror subgenre of "you have no weapons and can only run or hide" with Amnesia: The Dark Descent. Is there a shorter name for that type of game? Anyway, SOMA is a huge step forward in terms of story, while preserving the essential feeling of helplessness and expanding it beyond mere fear of dying. This is a game that examines the very nature of identity, and raises some extremely disturbing questions. There are monsters, yes, and they can be scary, but they do occasionally get frustrating. Luckily, there is a new option to turn them off, so that you can focus on the fantastic story, which is the heart and soul of the experience. Anyone who's ever thought about consciousness and what exactly defines it should absolutely play this game ASAP.

The worst part of this game is the learning curve - and I mean that as a compliment.
I wasn't impressed with Tomb of Tyrants when I first played it - I have the discussion threads to prove it - but that's because this game is so packed with game mechanics, I initially had no idea what I was doing. The tutorial does its best, but because many mechanics interact with each other, you're best off if you pause the game, open up the Glossary (those little icons to the right of the pause menu), and read through the entire thing.
Once you get over that initlal hump, you will find an amazingly deep, lovingly crafted game that you will only appreciate more as you continue learning its ins and outs. And when I say that you'll continue learning, I mean it - I was discovering new strategies nearly right up until I 100%ed it.
Don't be intimidated by my hours logged; I estimate you could probably 100% this in under 20 hours. More importantly, once the mechanics click, it's a game that's very easy to put down and pick back up again. It appears to autosave automatically, and there's no real loss of progress when you "die" (I 100%ed it on my 20th Tyrant).
This game is probably in my all-time top 10 on Steam. Highly recommended.

Okay, so this is one of the weirdest match-3 (or match-4, rather) games I've ever played. You're playing some evil dungeon master (or a Tyrant, if you will) and you're building your tomb by expanding it downwards. In order to build new floors you have to unlock them and spend resources to place. Unlocking takes time, pre-requisites (special conditions, like having some specific floor active, or making matches, or killing heroes, etc.) and resources. Resources are gathered by making matches. Performing rituals (making matches of a specific shape) expands your resource cap.
And so on it goes: you're unlocking stuff, building your tomb downward, repel heroes attacks, and eventually die, leaving your successor a few troops and a few floors (if you managed to lock them in, by performing specific conditions, which change every new round).
And that's only tip of the iceberg, since there are also things like unit management, traps, usable items, god knows what else (I'm only a few hours in, so I don't think I unlocked even half of the stuff in game).
I know, it sounds *very* complex, but it really isn't. You'll get the hang of the game in around an hour, and you'll like it a lot, if you're enjoying match-3 games (I am) and you're not scared off easily by pixel graphics (I'm not).
There is a downside to the game, of course, and it's the UI. I can't say it's extremely bad, but the most time I've spent getting to know the game was getting used to the UI, which is sometimes very clunky. There is, however, an active pause, which you'll be using a lot, especially on later waves, when enemies become much stronger and you'll need to manage a lot of stuff quickly.
- - - - -
In conclusion, I can say that I'll definitely recommend you to at least try out this game, since mechanic is pretty unique and the game is constantly updated with new content.
Overall, I'd rate this game
and recommend it to fans of pixel art, casual strategy/RPGs and match-3 games.

I bought this game knowing full-well that it was a work-in-progress.  I waited a full year and 20+ hours of game play to give the developer a fair amount of leeway before putting this review down.  Get two Tylenol ready because reading this review is going to make your head hurt.  I know writing it made mine positively throb!
Essentially this game is trying to be too many things at once and it really makes very little sense how it all fits together.
There are so many areas to focus on at one time: a tile-matching game which allows you to gather resources (this game also has a special pattern-matching meta-game embedded in it), a dungeon-building game, and a 3 vs. 3 team combat game.
With all of this going on at once, you're just sort of thrown into the game with a paucity of instruction and expected to figure it all out.  You're told in the "tutorial" what things are but not in an ordered way, and not in a way that gives you an understanding of HOW you're supposed to play.
You'll spend time in the tile area swapping tiles to make matches of 4+ same-colored tiles, which makes them disappear and gather the corresponding resources.  As you clear out the tiles you make room to build "floors" of the dungeon.  These floors apparently create space between the invading Heros and your avatar, the Tyrant, as well as spawn monsters that will fight the invading Heros and their minions.
Depending on what floors you build, you'll get different monster types.  You will have no idea why you would want to build one floor vs. another floor - the tutorial is limited in this area to basically "you can build floors by clicking here".
You can then see the invading Hero troops and your minions engaging in battle on the floors you built.  You are told that you can pause the game to strategize these battles, but again, you are left with no information on exactly WHAT that means or HOW you are supposed to go about doing that.
You can drag the minions to different places in the dungeon and watch them run willy-nilly, or re-arrange them in a fight.  You will have no idea why you would do this, what troops are appropriate, etc.  Nothing is explained.  You can roll your mouse over them to get a popup rollover window, which contains an array of microscopic, completely meaningless icons.  That is, if you can figure out which minion is yours and which is the invader.  You can't bleeping tell until you roll over each one.  There is literally no visual way to distinguish troops, they all look like pixelated blobs.  The option to outline good guys in green and bad guys in red is great in theory- too bad the highlights only show up when you roll over which is so useless the feature might as well not exist.
All while this is going on, different tasks will queue up at the top of the screen demanding that you complete certain number of swaps in a specified time frame, or other task like "don't spend resource X", other times alarms go off and then fade out of existence before you know what they said.  There are different banners you can assign to your Tyrant which gives your troops various bonuses/penalties.  Each resource type you gather does things like grant experience, fatigue points, wards, etc. Yeah could this game get any more complicated?  Does any of this make sense?  I can't even keep it all logical enough in my own head to write this.  TRY PLAYING IT!
Given all the different things to split my time and attention on, I never had a clue what I was supposed to be doing at any given time.  No clue whatsoever what play strategies will result in the most success.  Just swap like a madman, build floors higgildy-piggildy, click-res your minions when they die, and try to de-scramble WTF is going on.
The UI of this game is a hot mess.  I'm not talking about the graphics, I'm talking about the User Interface.  Every single thing you can do is crammed onto the screen all at once and it constantly reorganizes itself on the fly!!  Clickable interface elements pop in and out of existence and graphics overlap each other all over the place.  Instead of things like floors and minions being self-contained interface areas that are organized into radial wheels, lists, drop-downs, or whatever, they're all just crammed into the UI at once. There are popups on top of popups on top of popups.. Look at this - it is atrocious:
And for some reason the tile matching area is displayed in TWO different areas of the UI at the same time, but one of them is only partially-functional because there always seems to be some rollover impairing my ability to interact with it!
The thing is, none of this has gotten better since I bought the game a year ago, it has just gotten all progressively more muddled and confused.  Rather than streamlining the game and the interface, the dev has focused on adding more floor types, more minion types, locking tiles, color-changing tiles, more gobbeldy-gook. Meanwhile the core gameplay is totally unfocused and non-intuitive.
While the developer is a responsive person eager to shape the game into what his audience wants, it is abundantly clear that there has never been a clear design philosophy or goal behind this game. This game seems to be a playpen for the developer where he iterates new concept after new concept, heaping one half-baked idea on top of the next.  I'd love to see the storyboards and interface design documents for this game - I doubt they were ever made.
This game suffers from "everything and the kitchen sink" game design, and needs deep, nay, severe editing.  Half of the gameplay needs to be torn out, automated, or completely overhauled, the UI needs to be demolished and completely rebuilt from the ground up with input from a UI specialist, and the game needs to move beyond the "proof-of-concept" mire that it is currently in.
All-in-all, I cannot recommend this which is sad, because I feel like there is enough novel here that it could really be an innovative game.  There are just too many concepts, they are all too jumbled and confusing, and the UI is an abomination unto God as it relates to communicating meaningfully and clearly with the user.

UPDATED REVIEW 24/07/2017
Just going to preface this: This was a skill-based game. Now, it is an unbalanced grind and a experience-based game. What do I mean by that? Once you learn what combos work the best, you basically just exploit them and wreck the other team. Here's some current problems:
1: Armour is basically worthless. Even if you survive a shot from a sniper rifle, it will likely make your character bleed out in 2 seconds. Armour doesn't prevent bleeding like one would expect.
2: Armour slows characters down to a ridiculous level because the devs replaced the 'weight' with 'slowdown'. So, if I wear some very light armour with speed bonuses, I can run around the map like a super soldier, which is really effective when you consider:
3: Changes were made without understanding the impact on a latency dependent game. If I run around like a super soldier, I'll beat everyone else because I'll have seen and started shooting at a player before their side even recognizes that I've appeared. And, if I have heavy armour, it takes longer for me to pop in and out from cover than it does for a player to reload.
4: Weapon balance is out the window. There are guys using LMGs, SMGs that have a 4x scope and virtually no recoil. Despite shooting from a distance or suppressed, those weapons only need about 3 body shots to get a kill even when wearing the max amount of armour.
5: Players who pay can skip the grind. It is still possible to get the weapons and unlocks, but only after months of playing and you wouldn't even get all of them. Why do I still play it then?
--------------------------------------------------------------------
+The best gunplay I have ever experienced. Bullet physics including ricohets. I once got a headshot when I shot a guy with a sniper rifle, and the bullet hit his arm and deflected up into his head.
+Team-based. If your team sucks, you can still do well, but you probably aren't going to win.
+Not pay to win. The upgrade system benefits the premium players, but it's not an unfair advantage at all. It's paying to avoid the grind.
+Great anti-cheat system build right in.
-Not as many players leading to wait times to get into the game
-It is a huge grind. Think prestige-ing like 10 times in COD.
-Incomplete/beta

PROS:
-Very diverse cast of operators that all have different weapons and gadgets. There are 33 operators in this game, all with different abilities
-Because of all the different maps and operators every match feels new.
-Unlike the CS:GO matchmaking, you actually get paried of with people in your rank in ranked. If you're gold, you will, most of the time, get paired with other golds.
-It's very easy to rank up and derank, so you won't be stuck at one rank for 2 weeks straight.
-If you cooperate with your team, you will do better.
-All of the operators are pretty balanced.
-It is very easy to learn how to play the game, so it attracts new players. However it is also very hard to master, keeping people around to get better.
-Very fun with friends.
-Good for casual and competive players. If you're just looking for a fun FPS, you can play casual. Or if you are a very competive player who only wants to win, you can play ranked.
-The DLC operators add new ways to play the game, without being too powerful and change the way the game plays overall.
CONS:
-In ranked, if people leave, you don't get a bot or a another teammate, your just down a teammate, and since this is a very team based game, someone leaving can lose you a game, sometimes causing you to derank.
-Peakers advantage. I won't go on for 3 paragraphs about why it's a huge problem in this game, but if you want to learn more about it just look up a youtube video.
-The netcode can be really janked sometimes. Sometimes you can shoot someone 40 times in the chest and not kill them. And at other times, you can shoot someone in the foot and get a headshot.
-The starter addition is a straight up scam, it says it exists for people not sure if they want to spend 40$ on the full game. But in reality it's an incomplete version of the game that makes you either spend money on all the operators, or grind for an insanely long time.
-The R6 "fun bucks." Whenever you want to buy something in R6S, like a new operator or a cosmetic item, you can't straight up pay for it with money, you have to go through a long process to buy "R6 credits". First of all, half the time an error occures while trying to buy the fun bucks, so you cannot buy the credits. And you can't buy a specific amount of credits, you have to buy pre-set amounts. So lets say you're 10 fun bucks away from getting a cosmetic, you can't just buy 10, you have to buy 5$ worth, which is 600 fun bucks.
TL;DR: This game is really fun and worth the money, it does have some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t wrong with it, but if you can get pass that, it's a really fun game. Also remember, DON'T BUY THE STARTER EDITION.

Long Review

Gameplay
This game would have received my praise if the amount of blocks I had to control was reduced by 3-4. This is not a decision made off of difficulty, but more of a large inconvenience. About an average of 3 blocks (Rough estimate) will be worthless for half (Rough estimate again) of the levels that they appear in. You can just move them to the doorway and complete the puzzle with the remainder. The reason this was probably done was because of the story they wanted to tell. I believe the this still could have been done if they put the blocks in separate groups instead of all in one badly controlled bundle.
Story
The story and voice acting in this game is good. I found it easy listening to the narrator every level, but if you ever messed up, you had to listen to him again. I would say, for a blocky-platform-puzzle game, this story was probably the best that you'll ever get.

The game is short though and can be finished in about 3-4 hours but that won’t take away and fun or experience. The $15 price tag is a little high but if you catch this on sale pick it up because it is a great game to experience. I would have loved to play more and hope maybe the devs will put out some add-on content or maybe a sequel. Probably won’t happen but I can always dream. Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna) is not just a game. It is a story.
It isn't a new story. Instead, it is very old. Never Alone is a game that comes from the cold Arctic, made and written by members of the Iñupiat people (an indigenous group to Alaska and Canada, sometimes called "Inuit"). The story comes from that culture, and as you progress through the game, you will receive video clips of interviews that inform you about the Iñupiat culture, history, and lifestyle. As you play, a narrator tells you your story, speaking in the Inupiaq language, making you feel as if you are around the campfire with him. All the snow and wind on screen made me begin to feel chilly, as I braved the blizzard with my canine companion.
This game is filled with history and love. There are almost no games that delve into indigenous American cultures with so much passion, and so few games produced by natives. I am always supportive and ecstatic to see other cultures represented in games, and this is a beautiful and heartfelt example.
The gameplay? The game itself is acceptable. It is average. It gets the job done. It's not very fun single player, so it's a good idea to find a friend or family member to play with. It's a little clunky, and certain parts can be frustrating, but it gets the job done. The importance of this game lies in its history. You are here for the story.
This is an excelent co-op game to play with kids. A platformar with minimal combat, explaining the story and culture of Innuit people. Controls can be a bit clunky sometimes.

So this game is a classic sidescroller with a lot of story driven content.
It's supposed to be like a story is told throughout the game as you advance.
And I think the story is supposed to be "real" in terms of that they've shared it through generations of their people.
So because of this, they're using someone who talks the story in the native language to enhance the "feeling" for the story. Which I guess it does, but definitly not for me, it actually threw me off more than it enhanced my experience for it. But that's just a nitpick. The scenery in this game is really beautiful!
Now for controls, the game is just like a regular sidecrolling platform game, and the controls are very minimal, which is not a bad thing. You got your, jump, crouch, throw and thats all (and a swap character button, we'll get into that more later), it works good, but they controls feel abit clunky and "sluggish", nothing grave or anything but just a tad.
Now this game can be played solo, or local co-op. and I played this game solo, which works good, but while I was playing I was thinking all "this would be so much more fun if I was playing with a friend.
Because in this game you control 2 characters, and if you play solo the other character becomes a "AI" and you swap the control between these with a simple button.
The characters have different traits ofcourse. But here's the deal with it for me, while it works in solo, it becomes more tedious work while playing together with a friend it would be just more smooth gameplay.
To sum up the game in few words as possible.
Everything in this game feels average or just above that for me, the game is quite short in terms of hours. (I finished it around 3 hours)
I still recommend the game, but preferly if you play with a friend.

The initial impressions of SD2 are positive. It is exceptionally similar to MOO2. I know it is common to say that when discussing any space 4X game but it is really true in this instance. The pace of the game, the way research is conducted, the complexity and scope of the game is almost exactly like Masters of Orion 2. There were a couple of good ideas from Stardrive 1 that carried over including the factions and the ship builder. I love the graphical style too.
If that impression held throughout I would give StarDrive 2 a firm "good" rating. I've never played any 4x that evoked so much from MOO2 which is generally a good thing. The feel of the game is very similar to that classic game, down to the research options. The art style is wonderful, the ship builder is exceptional and the AI is more than competent (in fact, it's brutal). There's a lot to like in the game.
But it falls down in a few areas and could use quite a bit of work.
The middle to end game is not very good. Every game will devolve into the same pattern - at some point you'll expand too much, your neighbors will get upset and it's just all-out war at that stage. There are no really cool random events to upset the balance of power and no distractions to occupy the player's attention elsewhere. It's a drudgery of cycling through building on planets, pushing units around, auto-resolving battles and repeat. This is a common problem in 4x games but it's magnified here because there is only one victory condition - extermination. Thus the entire endgame falls apart and the whole game breaks down.
Which brings me to the next problem...
...the Victory Conditions. The player has no choice and it becomes very tedious. Instead of building a consensus or achieving enlightenment or fighting some external foe, I'm forced into a policy of being a ruthless warmonger. That's not a lot of fun IMO.
The random events are exceptionally limited. Usually it's me getting .5 fewer food per farmer. Big deal. Where are meteor showers or a comet to explore? Where's a powerful earthquake that changes the orbit of a planet, a new resource to be discovered, a really cool derelict ship to add to my fleet, an uprising by an alien species or things like that? The "?" in space tiles seem to be exceptionally limited and not very interesting.
The diplomacy system needs work. That's putting it nicely. Diplomacy is a train wreck. I like the fact that we can't spam requests to rob the AI blind, but often I'm so hamstrung I have an option of either a non-aggression pact or a trade agreement because there aren't enough points to get both. Considering I have to do this every 30 or so turns, this part of the game feels woefully underdeveloped. There aren't any options for long-term peace, coalitions or friendships which then leads to the train-wreck ending of extermination because nothing else is possible.
I also think the spy system needs work too. I don't feel like the AI is playing the game game when it comes to esponiage. It seems that they have far greater opportunities to take techs from me whereas I have to wait far longer. My spies seem to get caught almost immediately. So this part of the "game" it just shunted aside - I build a half dozen spies, put them on defensive and ignore this aspect. Why? Because building enough spies to accumulate 500 points and THEN using land troops to steal a tech is a heck of a lot of work. Nice idea, but the reward just isn't worth it.
Finally, I'd suggest making the actual building portion of the game a bit more interesting. One good thing from Gal Civ 2 were the special tiles that were on planets - some gave more food, others more production, others more science, etc. It made building more strategic in nature and helped foster better planet specialization. I'd love to see something similar in SD2.
SD2 has a good foundation. It's just that Zero never expanded upon it - and when he finally did, it was to charge for DLC to fix fundamental, core problems with the base game. SD2 is one of the biggest disappointments in my library because it is so close to being so good but never fulfilled that promise. Thus the base game can not earn a recommendation. Your money is better spent elsewhere.

I received Orwell as part of a Humble Bundle and thought I'd give it a go. My play time is 6 hours and that's with a couple of hours when I just left the game open to answer a call or get the door. Overall it was a quick game.
I was interested in the concept of it, and they executed it very well. I was drawn into the characters, and their complex lives over the course of the 4 hours of play time. It's purely text based, but they still managed to bring these characters to life. Details like small misspellings, people overlapping each-other when they spoke over the messaging systems, and the way they lied to each-other, all make them feel like real people.
Ultimately you're faced with a choice at the end and, while I didn't play the last chapter twice to find out for sure, I'm pretty sure you can pick your ending based on your actions.
If you're looking for something interesting but quick, and want to spend a few moments thinking about the implications of state surveillance programs, then pick this up. I am not a big fan of text-only games, but this did convince me to play through it to the end.  If you’re looking for action, graphics, or even voice acting, look elsewhere.

Orwell is a game where you step into the shoes of an "Investigator"; an individual specially chosen outside of the dystopian-like nation simply titled "The Nation" to interact with a big-brother type software that allows you to track and keep tabs on every single person in The Nation. You take control of yourself, your name, your info, you. You've been specially chosen for reasons unknown to yourself or anyone else, per the exception of a secretive few, to be hired at Orwell. Your new "Adviser", Symes, is going to show you the ropes of international and domestic espionage, only this time, you aren't taking down super villians or having a martini "shaken, not stirred" as per the classic spy movie or game, Orwell instead hits close to home....a little too close.
Orwell is a Story Rich, Dystopian, "Choices Matter" Indie game made by Osmotic Studios where you "Investigate the lives of citizens to find those responsible for a series of terror attacks. Information from the internet, personal communications and private files are all accessible to you. But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences.". When Osmotic says that choices matter, they really do. You feel as if you're truly in this dystopian world, helping, or harming, The Nation's citizens. You get to look through countless web pages, trace and listen to countless phone calls, emails, text message and otherwise, even hack into citizen's computers or mobile phones to gain access to information stored on there, such as browsing history, photos, files, and even deleted files.
For an example (spoiler free); You will be investigating certain citizens, and obviously need to find certain clues about them, their age, phone number, email address, face id, street info, parents, siblings, workplace, links to them from other sources, and you can even go as far as finding medical info from The Nation's hospitals.
Now let's say I have a citizen I'm investigating, I can start with their relative name, go from there to their social media pages, find out their DOB, address, friends, maybe even mobile number. let's say I need to (or want to) take it further, I begin to suspect they're somehow a threat to The Nation. I can do a little research, Get in contact with friends, trace their calls and emails,  find out information that was never meant to be seen by hacking their computer by getting their PSI address or their IP address, or find ways into their workplace, or even goof off and research their background, what their favourite colour is, or who they're in a relationship with.
Orwell does an amazing job at immersing the investigator (you) into dystopian earth, into The Nation and it's surrounding countries, the citizens who inhabit them and even smaller things like a simple webpage for a local university or a humanitarian organization. Once I started the game, I honestly did not have high expectations nor did I think it was going to be something i was going to enjoy, since it just didn't look or seem like the type of game or genre that i liked, but once i started investigating and learning more about this country, it's citizens and the lore about this world I simply couldn't put it down. I played all the way through, read tons of webpages, information, emails and texts.
That being said, the game is roughly 3-4 hours long, maybe shorter if you (somehow) speedrun it, but if you really want to get immersed into this game world then it can take a lot longer.
This is one of a only video game worlds and lore that I genuinly became interested in and invested in as time went on, it truly made me feel like I was impacting the citizens and world around me, mainly because I actually was.
One of the reasons this game resonated with me so much (and one of the reasons I am recommending it) is because in reality, this is not very dystopian. Things like this very well happen in real life and seem so real it's almost disturbing. The amount of dialogue in this game is astonishing, from everything to simple text messages to elaborate corporate emails, everything seems completely geniune, and feels that way too.
Orwell is a masterpeice at storytelling and really making the player truly become immersed and feel like there are consequences. Season 2 of Orwell is coming out sometime soon, and I WILL DEFINETLY be purchasing this game. I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes immersive game worlds, spy type games, choice matter games, or just mind-f*ck type games. Absolute great game. 10/10

Lately I've been finding myself bored with many games. I got through the motions without any real investment in what I've been playing... So, I decided to play something different. In comes Orwell. It's unlike any of the games I've toiled mundane hours hacking and slashing away in any random RPGs that I have on rotation. I've been engrossed in it for the past day getting familiar with the intricacies.
This is a different kind of spy game. One that might hit on reality a little closer than I'd like to think. Even more so if I was prone to ideas of the government watching our every move, which is why I'm an active VPN user. But I digress, Orwell is still just a game. A game where you play a data miner looking into the lives of who you might consider dangerous terrorists to a fictitious nation. I should mention there's quite a bit of reading. This isn't your mindless run and shoot game, or hide from the enemies and kill in secret game. It's not even graphically inspiring but the ideas and execution is solid. 
As you're uncovering terrorists and their plots you get deeper into the lives of those you think are involved and have to feed information into the Orwell system to determine their threat level. The game has you scouring through newspapers, blogs, and social media feeds to gain as much information as possible. It would be overwhelming if the interface wasn't so simple to navigate. 
While progression in the game is pretty linear you do have the ability to impact significant events based on what you choose to feed into the system. There is also an abundance of conflicting information that you will have to make judgement calls on what you want to submit. Orwell do a good job highlighting these inconsistencies. The only thing I might have qualms with is there's no "undo" feature. So if you do happen to make a mistake and upload something you'd rather not you don't have a second chance to fix or update your mistakes. The system for all it's abilities has a permanent function. Like most things once it's out there it's there for good. 
In all Orwell is an engaging game where you play big brother and stop terrorists a different way. It's got a solid story and characters and an easy to use interface. It may or may not resemble some truth to life but in the immortal words of Harold Finch "It's not paranoia if they really are out to get you" and in this game you're out to get everyone.

TL;DR: Cheap, fun, time-waster match 4 with dungeon-building and rogue-lite elements. For fans of 'No Heroes Allowed'.
A fun little time-waster for your library that combines games such as '10,000,000' with 'No Heroes Allowed'. You play a match-4 puzzle game to gather resources, then build rooms for your dungeon to hold back invading heroes. The premise is simple but the execution is deep.
There's enough strategy to keep things interesting and the game does a decent job of giving you the tiles you need, when you need them. Rogue-lite elements stop failure from being frustrating, playing unlocks new rooms and items for your next run. The more you play, the further you can go.
The pixel art style won't please everyone and the interface is initially overwhelming. It's also a very visually 'busy' game, it's hard to know where you should be looking and what's important when you first start playing. It's no so bad when you stick with it, but it could be offputting for a new player.
Pros:
- Low price
- Simple to pick up, match-4 gameplay
- Well executed pixel art
- Tons of progression and unlocks
- Expansive options
Cons:
- Visually noisy
- Overwhelming interface

Tile puzzle/roguelite game where you slide tiles to match them and get resources you then use to build floors of a dungeon or revive minions to fight for you.

Some things are unclear, but once you get the hang of it, it's really fun and exciting.

So everybody knows our favorite "Match Four" games, like Bejewled and all of that. But this is just about the best one I have ever played. Think of an RTS alongside a match four, and all of your resources are obtained based off of your successful matches. Complete special matches known as rituals to increase your limit of resources, perform a set of tasks like complete a number of matches, don't use a resource type, etc in order to lock a room to your current tomb, allowing it to stay when you are defeated and carry on to your next tomb, and unlock new rooms with new abilities or units to use in the current and all future runs. Summon creatures, slay heroes, and make the greatest dungeon you can is all the point of Tomb of Tyrants, and it is definitely worth a bit more than its price tag.
Interesting monsters, a rather complex but well-thought and constructed game-mechanic and truly wonderful pixel art.

***NOTE*** My "Raising Hell" review is separate of this one. If you want my opinion on it, check Raising Hell's steam page.
TL;DR: I recommend the game. It's not good, but it's not bad either. I'd give it a passing 5/10. It's a great concept for a game, and "Overlord" with its pros manages to rise above its cons for an enjoyable game. So get out there and think evil, breed evil, and control all!
When I was a kid I always wanted to play the bad guy, and why wouldn't I? They had the coolest lairs, the most badass armor, the most killer weapons, the hottest babes, the most powerful magic, and a host of minions and henchmen ready to do their bidding. As I've matured that preference has changed quite a bit in video games but my enjoyment of fun little self-indulgent romps like "Overlord" has not! When the first bits of hype came out for this game on IGN back in the day I wanted the game instantly. I followed it like a hawk on a rabbit for months until it finally released, and I played it to absolute death. I remember going through it three or four times all the way. But is it as enjoyable as I remember it now that I'm older? The short answer is kinda. The long answer is, eh...
In this game you play as the titular Overlord, struck down after you were ostensibly defeated by a band of heroes who after beating you went back home as heroes to rule their respective homelands. Now back from the crypt beneath your Dark Tower, it's time to rebuild, reconquer, and reclaim your rightful place as the one ruler of the land. To do this with you not only have your own strength to rely on but that of your minions who you control in a very Pikmin-style to do what needs doing as you navigate the domains of the seven heroes, reclaim your plundered posessions, and kill those meddling heroes.
If you were hoping to be the one sole evil, I'm afraid you'll be disappointed. All the various heroes have fallen into their respective vices and have become self-serving tyrants or apathetic hedonists. This, ironically, leads the peoples of the world to almost welcome the marauding Sauron wanna-be and his army of bloodthirsty gremlins with and appetite for booze only equaled with their love of destruction. You can take advantage of this gratefulness and reap the rewards, or you can just butcher them all and use their souls to make more minions and their loot to enrich yourself. Really, the "Evil" route is the one you'll probably take. Since all the lands until the very end of the game regenerate at each loading screen you can plunder their endless bounty to make yourself ridiculously bloated on resources and your endless minions armed to the teeth. As you might suppose from that sentence there is a light grinding element to the game and you're rewarded for visiting your wrath upon your dominions. How it's executed is genius, though; it's fun to go forth and plunder and pillage idyllic farmlands, elven temples, and dwarven halls. You don't feel bored until the end of the game, once various "moral" choices have thinned out the zones unfortunately making slaughtering villages less of a fun activity and more of a "find-the-villager-way-out-there-so-you-can-get-that-lifeforce," type thing. You even find yourself going to specific zones for certain types of life force and resources, making you see how each realm will fit into your evil empire. Is that a light roleplaying element I see? Well done, Codemasters.
Being just one bad guy amongst many I feel detracts from the game a little. There are very few moments when I can just relish in being a High Fantasy villain like I was hoping to be, though all the boss battles are fun, challenging, and satisfying. Revenge is its own reward! There's a genuine sense of progression as I obtain more and more of my old Overlord trappings and powers and my minions swell from a humble horde to a mighty host. Unfortunately this evil army's greatest enemies aren't hobbit warriors or armored knights, but pathing. "Sweeping" is far too sensitive, the camera is sometimes uncontrollable, and minions sometimes get stuck on things irretrievably unless you want to reload the zone. But these problems don't crop up very much, just barely enough to warrant a mention. There's reports of game-ender bugs but there are only two I know of and neither have happened to me on any of my playthroughs.
The plot is about as sturdy as a rickety rope bridge, but it's serviceable all the same. There are some things you'll want explored more or that arguably don't make sense and sometimes zones feel unfinished compared to others. But the overrall narrative is strong with a twist you realize had quite a bit of foreshadowing. There's always something you'll feel like your missing, something going on just out of the corner of your eye, something that just feels off... the reveal is definitely worth not spoiling. Go see for yourself! In the end it's the humor that really greases this thing along; Gnarl is a delight and the dialogue is very well-done. You'll truck along just to hear Gnarl's musings on everything.
Your Dark Tower is hyped a lot in promotional material, and while cool it is a bit underwhelming after a short time. You'll be wanting there to be more to it or wishing you could explore more of it, and choice of Mistress unfortunately boils down to if you want your tower to be an imperial monolith or a torture palace - and the one who gives you the fortress to rival Barad Dur is unfortunately far more interesting than her sister who has all the personality of a High School Civics textbook. Unless you really don't like spikey stuff, it's not a hard choice.
Upon finishing this game again, I felt the same I did when I first finished it: satisfied but wishing there was more to do, wishing the scope was bigger, and eager for a sequel where I could expand my dominion. It's by no means a great game, but it is good and remains a cult classic. Pick it up when it's on sale and be sure to grab the "Raising Hell" DLC. As for the others? Well, see me at the other Steam Pages.

Not necessarily a DISCLAIMER: I played it on Linux (Ubuntu 16.04 x64). Below is my personal experience with this specific port.
Pros:
- A lot of fun, interesting concept.
- A rather mysoginistic approach. I mean the jokes are Ok, I laughed a lot, but female players might just get a bit ... angry ;-)
- It has a Linux port
- The DLC not only brings new content, it also "fixes" some issues in the code of the main game (see Cons)
Cons:
- No Windowed Mode
- I tried to change the keyboard bindings, to suit a different set than the default (WASD, etc). It turned out that many of the new key bindings were simply doing nothing (keys changed but with no real effect on the game control). I had to revert back to default.
- I played/finished the game without installing the Raising Hell DLC. At some point, during the game, I noticed that voice over tracks simply dissappeared. I only heard the voices of many game characters on YouTube, while searching for some clues. I decided to ask for technical support so here I was, on Steam, trying to post a ticket. Surprise... the Steam support for this game asks us to ask Codemasters for help. So I sent an email to Codemasters, describing the problem. Guess what ? After two or three days I got an answer from Codemasters, telling me that "support for Linux" is provided by Virtual Programming. Really !?! What is this ?! Ping-Pong ?!
- From the very start, Gnarl (the Minion Master) guides the player through the game. Yet, at the very end of the DLC, at the final quest, he gives absolutely no clue. The quest itself is the pinacle of an entire "out of the pattern" set of quests. Some players might argue that not knowing what to do, trying, guessing for hours is, overall, a positive thing. Well, it's not ! I always hated games with quests which have no minimal logical explanation of "what to do". It's all like "Ok, I just gave you a new car/plane/submarine/spoon/trombone/OS/etc, the rest is up to you, I don't really give a s...t if you don't know how to drive/use/play it". This is a big "NO-NO!" to any devs (but not limited to).

Ryzen 7 1700 CPU average utilization >98% (8 cores 16 threads maxed 100% most of the time). Radeon GPU RX-470 4GB avg utilization <10%. Note that most of the time, GPU is running at 0%. Conclusion - DO NOT BUY! if you're using AMD GPU. The above stats are typical regardless of what resolution and graphic detail you select. Incidentally there are only 3 settings in-game; low, medium and high. Resolution can only be set at the launcher wih Alt-click of the play button in Steam.
I'm changing recommendation to an emphatic NO because i'm tired of games pretending to support AMD GPU hardware acceleration when in reality it's more akin to software acceleration because frame rates of below 20 fps is just not acceptable by any standards!
My bad, I'm now unsure that poor frame rates is due to under-utilization of AMD GPU because of a simple fact; other dissimilar games that out-performs on equivalent specs also exhibit under-utilization of AMD GPU. So this might just be a case of poor general optimization.
It now seems apparent that the low frame rates is due to under-utilization of GPU and unrealistic minimum system requirements - i3, seriously i3? More on this later. ESS is heavily dependent on CPU processing. Nearly 2 years ago i played this on i7-2630 QM laptop with Radeon HD 6770m 1 GB GDDR5. Playing and recording gave absymal frame rates that frequently fall below 30fps. The game world is very large and feature many 3D objects and some ship like the container ship is humongous! It's the reason why i couldn't complete the first mission (actually 12th in the list of missions) that involve this ship. It would crash at random points, usually while changing camera views and sometimes crashed for no apparent reason. My guess is the GPU ran out of memory even though system RAM was more than adequate.
A few days ago i fired it up on my new Ryzen desktop and monitored vital system stats b4, during and after playing and i found out that this games utilized all 8 cores and 16 threads up to 100% nearly all the time while the Radeon RX-470 GPU was at 0% half the time. So the i3 minimum spec is misleading; this game would probably use as many cores and threads as is available to the max! Although the memory requirements didn't seem to scale-up.
It's apparent that this game doesn't make full use of AMD GPU evidenced in the fact of low percentage utilization and the fact that basic feature like Anti-Aliasing is purposefully ignored. Why? Because even when i set the AMD Crimson driver to use 4x AA, the game would pretend that AA feature doesn't even exist!!! WTF even games in the 90s already use AA. This is totally unacceptable; i dunno how this game treats Nvidia GPU but
Take at look at this proof; mission #14 can only reasonably run at 720p and never reach 60fps. Frame rates fluctuates wildly and averages IMO slightly above 30fps.
Tried to run previous mission #13 in Full-HD and i got occasionally 30 fps, more often @24 fps
while GPU was still being under-utilized.
Score amended: 3/10 for AMD GPU users (not recommended); ?/10 for Nvidia GPU users (who knows?). This website claims that it can run at 200+fps on GTX 970:
Well who knows? Clearly something is very wrong somewhere. Well at least it makes full use of Ryzen CPU unlike Dirt Rally which refused to run on more than 4 cores.

Seasons after Fall is pretty as all hell. Its environments are beautifully rendered and the animation is mostly smooth. That said, I can't recommend this game in good conscience because of the ridiculously glitchy state the developers have released it in. You will (there is no maybe) find yourself falling through the scenery because the game hasn't loaded properly, or find yourself stuck in the scenery.
There is a KNOWN PROBLEM THAT HAS NOT BEEN FIXED with a particular section in the summer part where after you have destroyed an obstacle, it can take upwards of thirty tries and thirty minutes to get it to recognise said obstacle is gone and allow your fox to grab onto the ledge. Given that you have to use this ledge at least twice, this becomes a rage inducing nightmare which has had nothing done about it.
Add in the controls, which are looser and even less responsive than Ape Escape for PS1 (if you've played that you know what I'm on about), and the actual gameplay is a mess.
Stick with Ori and the Blind Forest.

Seasons after Fall is a relaxing platformer with a short but sweet story, a great visual design and beautiful classical music.
This game is all about the exploration of the world. On your search for the Guardians of the Seasons, you have to travel through 4 big areas (each with a few sub-areas). Using a season changing mechanic, you have to solve different puzzles and pass platforming segments. When you have unlocked new powers, you can revisit an area to further explore it.
Apart from a tricky puzzle near the end and searching some secrets, the game never gets very hard. There are no enemies and you can't die. The worst that can happen is missing a jump and having to pass a platforming segment again. On the one hand, this makes it easy to just lean back and enjoy the world and music. On the other hand, you may get bored if you're looking for a challenge.
The controls are a bit slippery, you will miss some jumps, but you get used to it pretty quickly. In the ~5 hours it took me to 100% the game, I ran into a small bug twice where I couldn't interact with an object. Quickly leaving and reentering the area or just quitting to title and reloading the save fixed it and I could continue.
A friend gifted me this game. I was going to buy it soon, though. After finishing it this quickly, I'm not sure it's worth the full 15€, but I definitely would pay ~10€ on sale.
Pros:
+ Sweet, fairytale-like story
+ Beautiful graphics
+ Great classical music
+ Relaxing gameplay
Cons:
- Very short (~5 hours to 100% for me)
- Way too easy if you're looking for a challenge
- Some small bugs
- Controls a bit slippery

This game is visually stunning, using a gorgeous hand painted art style that's paired with a beautiful classical score. Despite complaints I've heard about the story, I found it relatively clear and well delivered. I do have one complaint which I can't give without spoilers so I'll leave that to the end, but overall this is a great game that isn't overly long (about 5 hours) and I'd encourage you to give it a shot.
The obvious point of comparison for this is Ori and the Blind Forest since both see you playing a fox-like character platforming through gorgeously drawn and animated forest environments to a beautiful musical score but the two are very different games. While Ori is an occasionally very challenging, intense action puzzle platformer, Seasons has a much more laid back, relaxed feel to it. You aren't fighting enemies or dodging bullets or anything. It wants you to take your time, enjoy the scenery, and solve some puzzles along the way. You do revisit areas but in that way where you have new abilities and things have slightly changed so there are new puzzles to solve and things to uncover. It never bothered me but I've seen complaints in some other reviews.
Story wise you're started more or less "in medias res" where something has clearly happened and a voice is telling you to do things and you piece together what's actually going on over the course of the game. It doesn't answer all the questions but everything eventually comes together clearly. It's a style I quite enjoy but your mileage may vary.
This leads me to my complaint. This requires spoilers so I'll put it in the tags.
So it's a visually beautiful, well made game and I'm giving it a recommendation because overall I enjoyed it. But be aware that there are some story elements you may find uncomfortable.

Seasons After Fall is a 2-d, side scrolling, puzzle-platformer. In the game you play as a wild fox who gains the power to manipulate the seasons and alter the life of the forest. You can change to any season at any time for any reason. You can use the Spring season to give life to plants which will allow you to progress further into the beautifully drawn out world. Use Winter to freeze lakes and rivers allowing you to get across them much easier. Use all of your powers to save the forest and solve the mystery behind a young seedling's odd disappearance.
As I mentioned before, this game is simply gorgeous. The art style of the game is only further enhanced by an equally beautiful soundtrack making the game great for unwinding while still exploring a perfectly made game.
Seasons After Fall is a must play game, not only for those of you who like puzzle platformers but any indie game fan. This is how indie games should all be made.

Alright here we go, with mostly negative reviews at time of writing and mixed overall this will be difficult to say without getting flamed. But this game is amazing, not everything about it is perfect but overall it is just amazing.
Pros:
-Community (yeah you read that right) I can agree that about half the community are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and that can get annoying but I think people forget that mute buttons exsist. You do not have to take anything they say at all, you can 100% ignore it all by muting them, I cannot understand why not using a mute button is seen as "this game sucks". I can however, understand people only using OP heros and stupid strats thats where I agree that people can be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ If you really wanna be able to counter it, play 1v1 2v2 its better its how the game was meant to be played. "but you only get XP from dominion" ok well that's only for customization since gear is disabled in 1v1 and 2v2. Sure you may not look badass but hey dont bash the game cause you wanna look cool and the only way to do that is by playing dominion.
-Gameplay it's so much fun, I do not think i have played a game so frequently in my life. I cannot stop coming back, learning a new hero is addicting and the want to get better makes it so rewarding when you finally do. It's one of the only reasons this game has positive reviews from people who say toxic community.
-Campaign The whole campaign is just one big meme now and it is honestly so funny. The devs no doubt did it on purpose too which makes it so much better. From awkward things to funny lines in a serious situation and the repition of a single word it is the funnies campaign I have ever played (with an OK story too). The campaign served me as an extended tutorial and actually really helped for getting simple things like parries and blocking and combos down. I do recommend playing it, just don't take it seriously at all, just sit back play, and enjoy the memes.
Cons: (more like community complains)
-Servers? Yeah they suck sometimes, and it is very frustrating to not be able to complete one game because you get kicked half-way through it. People constantly complain about P2P when they know absolutley nothing about netcode, trying to say dedicated servers are soo much better cause it works for the other games they play. I hate to break it to you guys but P2P is not the issue at hand, if For Honor used a system like dedicated servers the game would be unplayable, the timings required in order to fight in this game are so tiny (we're talking about miliseconds here, characters have been buffed by giving them miliseconds less recovery time) that anything BUT P2P would be impossible to play on. To put it simply, client -> server -> other clients vs. client -> client. Which do you think is faster? Now this is the con part, which do you think is more stable? Yeah the P2P can break and kick everyone out if one person has♥♥♥♥♥♥connection or leaves, thankfully now they have a leaver penalty and it has made a lot of my matches better. People need to stop obsessing over P2P it is a very streamlined P2P at that, giving no player a host advantage (looking at your Gears of War). I understand the outrage over the seversm but yelling P2P over and over doesnt solve or even address the issue at all, the devs know the problem and have even given compensation for some of the outages. It is being activley worked on as of now and will continue to get better. Keep in mind these people brought Seige back from release. :)

It is hypocritical to complain about issues then complain about low playerbase ♥♥♥♥♥♥im doing that now arent I)
DLC- Well technically its not DLC its just in game currency but yes the DLC heros are a little crazy right now, many people scream OP but the truth is that its not OP its just new. They havent been there since Day 1 and therefore they are harder to play against, having not played against them as much. The devs will address any actual OP mechanics (like they have at this time) and fix them.
Pay to win- Someone calculated how much money or how long it would take to get ALL the customizations in this game and people freaked out saying pay to win and calling Ubisoft money ♥♥♥♥♥s (not defending other Ubisoft titles just this one ;) ). I cannot comprehend how looking badass (buying all customizations) and winning duels (not even based on gear score in 2 different gamemodes) is paying to win. It makes no sense to me, no you do not pay to win. You dont even have to pay to look cool, steel is very easy to get and with just a little dedication completing daily orders gives you 600 alone. Yes it can be a grind (some stuff is a little over priced) but no it is in no way shape or form "pay to win".
Learning Curve- Yes there is a pretty steep learning curve, especially coming into the game now where only the most dedicated people are left. I personally try to really help newcomers and I want more community and less ♥♥♥♥♥ing and moaning. It can be challenging, and it will be frustrating, but personally that is much more fun than a game that has no learning curve and allows you to walk all over people from day 1 no matter how many hrs they have. Some of the best games have learning curves.
Conclusion:
If you have intrest in this game, have watched some videos on it and really liked the game, have the ability to MUTE people, and enjoy a challenge then you should buy this game. I can agree that 60$ is a bit much and I would recommend buying it on sale if possible but it is an amazing game. I could very easily see myself putting 1000 hours into it no doubt. If you do not think that you will be able to play this game enough to get your moneys with I honestly dont blame you, its very difficult (yet rewarding) and can be extremely frustration when it comes to DCs and getting cheesed. If you can be a patient gamer you will enjoy this game.

. For Honor is very frustrating to play upon new installation, but offers many different playstyles due to its roster of characters. For Honor is a challenging, unique game which got caught in an unfortunate hate bandwagon. Not for casuals.

In this game you play as a little girl named Nuna and/or her pet arctic fox, through a series of puzzle platforming levels. The gameplay is very solid either in singleplayer or through local as co-op. It has a very fluid feel to it all, as well as a beautifully crafted story.
The story is based off the Alaskan natives known as the Iñupiaq, and the game has very strong cultural undertones. To be more accurate the game is based off of the stories that the Iñupiaq people tell eachother and pass down from generation to generation. As you play throughout the game you can discover these hidden little owls that unlock short movie clips (about 2 minutes each) that explain the culture and traditions of the Iñupiaq people. There are 24 clips in total, with 5 additional in the DLC known as Foxtales.
It was a absolutely beautiful experience I had playing this game, and would reccomend it to anybody looking not only for a fun platforming game, but also for a fascinating learning experience of a different culture.
The base game took me roughly 4 hours to beat and would score it a 4/5.
The DLC Foxtales took me 1 hour to beat and would score it a 5/5. (This DLC is a masterpiece)
The last hour was spent watching the 29 clips in total.
So for 15 dollars (19 if including Foxtails) you're getting about a 6 hour experience full of fun and laughter and challenges along the way. It's also a game you could definitely come back to again and again because of the fun to be had through the local co-op.
So in conclusion GET THIS GAME. It's 100% worth your time. I definitely recommend it.

I love the creative direction of this game. It is an E X P E R I E N C E. From the art to the soundtrack, the presentation was high quality, and these elements delivered a cohesive vision about the spiritual connection that humans have with the world around them. There is something so lonely yet comforting about the game and its embodiment of this message. Just thinking about the title screen, I can feel a tug on my heartstrings, and I can hear the soft piano track playing in the background. The high production value also manifests in other aspects of the game. Everything just looks really nice, from the art to the level design to font choice and to the documentary videos that you unlock as the story progresses.
With that said, some people may be turned off by the game-documentary-game-documentary format that is pushed by the developers. I didn't really mind it when I was playing it, but I do think it limits the "fun" of the game in a sense. On one hand, the short videos explained cultural elements of the levels, making my experience more enriching. Because of the background provided, the storyline and hocus pocus stuff made sense. On the other hand, I was less likely to play the accompanying Fox Tales add-on because of how much more mental effort I felt that I needed to contribute to the game in order to do the Inuit culture justice.
Characterization was a little lacking; I didn't even know Nuna's name until I saw it on gamefaqs. You don't really get the antagonist's reason for being evil, either. Both simply exist because legend said so. I think the devs deliberately made this trade off to push the educational aspect of the game. Personally, I don't see why they couldn't do both. What I will commend them on, however, is fostering a relationship between the player as Nuna and her fox without having them say a word. This animal is your only companion in a bleak and grim world. It reminds me of Wander and Agro from Shadow of the Colossus.
In terms of level design, the game was easy to medium difficulty as a puzzle platformer. I felt that the solutions were intuitive, and you would quickly learn what to do and what not to do when interacting with spirits. There were only a handful of times where I got stumped to the point where I looked the answer up. I will say that the whiteness of the snowy backgrounds did make it hard to see: A) the solution and B) death-inducing parts of the environment. I can't tell you how many times I acidentally jumped into icicle spikes, thinking those were in the background.
Regarding my frustrations, I was mainly more upset by the controls, as I found it extremely easy to fall off and die if you did not climb juuust high enough before jumping off a ledge. Keep in mind, however, that I am FAR more jump-death prone than other gamers.
Mildly frustrating due to clipping through the terrain, but that was only at one or two points in the game. The game brought me 3,5 hours of fun (didn't watch all the videos), absolutely loved it!

Orwell is a really unique experience - mix of a point and click game and trying to find information on the internet. Recommended for anyone who is interested in these topics or enjoys an investigation story. The game Consists of 5 chapters/days, each about 2 hours at first play, and each episode can be restarted or revisited, keeping save data only from the previous chapter(s). omg i immediately got sucked into this game. it just pulls you in with its twists and turns. idk how this is done tradiitonally so i'm gunna wing it.
genre: it's a slow-paced political/espionage thriller about working for the wrong side. for some reason, i was reminded of counterfeit monkey in how the world felt in this game.
story-telling: best part of the game. it's all told through reading articles, websites, medical records, phone calls, private emails. this game got me feeling equal parts paranoid (about my own online data) and guilty (about how obedient i was in being an oppressive surveillance tool). it just kinda... slowly built up. there were twists and turns galore!
actual story: draws pretty heavily on the 1984 book in terms of central themes, but i feel like it definitely updates it to the present. some parts were pretty hokey and implausible, but eh. but some parts were actually kinda scary and real. idk, there are fears i have when i go about the internet and this game left quite an impression on those fears.
visuals: pretty serviceable. probably the only thing that annoyed me was how small the window got as your network grew. but i enjoyed the geometric art and the almost facebook-like interface.
gameplay: it's actually pretty simple yet also kinda inventive. you feed an advisor "datachunks" that help their investigation. they can talk to you, but you can't talk to them. it makes you feel like an alienated observer almost, except you're definitely not because you're basically trying to crush opposition to the government. reminded me of the miller obedience studies a lot, idk. (Edit: Okay, i played this game three times overall to get all achievements. It was pretty fun! I spent a lot of time trying to figure everything out and consider all the thematic elements!!
overall: i feel like as a work of art, it's 9/10. i would definitely show this game to people and it's left a real impression on me. put this game with the likes of this war of mine, papers please, and counterfeit monkey. however, just like those games (except counterfeit monkey), when you play this game you're either on the edge of your seat with your nails between your teeth or you're feeling like an office drone trying to put these details together for your boss. this game isn't really something you play so you can have "fun" as such. it's an experience.

I didn't think much of the orwellian gimmick after the first few interactions with the system, which is something I thought I'd fault the game for, but in fact I think it's better this way because the insidious nature of the surveillance at hand feels ickier when you suddenly realise what it is you're actually doing. So in the end, I quite thoroughly enjoyed the story and the message, and I'm looking forward to the sequel.

Farm for your life should be commended for combining genres and mixing together lots of different play mechanics. It definitely stands out from among the dozens (hundreds? thousands?) of zombie games on Steam. After you play through this game for an hour or so, though, it's hard to miss the conclusion that there just isn't anything original about it except for the combination of thoroughly derivative game play mechanics. What's worse, none of the core mechanics are particularly well executed.
The tower defense aspect is clunky albeit serviceable, but the lack of combat is a bit odd when your character is literally holding a hammer and an axe. Similarly, the restaurant management aspect of the game works, but lacks anything particularly interesting to make it addictive in the vein of Diner Dash or Miss Management. The recipe creation minigame is a poor match to mouse play and is highly derivative of Fruit Ninja... probably would have been smarter to copy Chocolatier's factory efficiency minigame instead.
A derivative game can be fun if they nail the gameplay, just as a creative game can really carry subpar game design... this game lands in the middle of both, putting it in a no man's land that's not really worth visiting.
