The single player is worth about $19-25, it's playing with friends that really makes this worthwhile: Resident Evil 6 is a great Co-Op game. It's got an entertaining story that intersects through the 4 campaigns. The wide range of  difficulty levels allows even the weakest of Co-Op partners to still enjoy the game. You can do split-screen on lan and control the game with one keyboard/mouse and one Xbox controller, or two Xbox controllers.
Multiple copies of the game can also play Co-Op over the internet, and you can invite people off your steam list to join you provided they own the game. If you are playing an online game, you may find certain sections where 2 online co-op partners may also join your game for a 4 player story-based event or boss battle.
Regardless as to whether you are playing Split Screen or Internet, you have an option for your game called Agent Hunt that will make the game harder if you decide to turn it on, explained below.
There is one and only one REAL downside to this game that I have experienced, QTEs or QuickTimeEvents; the release for this game was blasted in reviews for it's QTEs where you'd have to mash buttons during cutscenes. If QTEs are not too your liking you can enable "Auto Action Button" in the menu as of a recent update, yup, they fixed it!
For players whom want to be competitive, there are two mutliplayer modes in addition to Co-Op. The most well known is Mercenaries where you can fight in Deathmatch against one another...
However where the fun really came in for me was in the AGENT HUNT mode, where you join another player's campaign as a zombie, and you and your fellow zombie players are tasked with hunting down and killing the human player(s). You naturally move a LOT slower than them, but you can make up for that with quick-travel vents and other holes that human players can't move through. How you win? MAKE THE HUMAN PLAYERS DIE OR FAIL!
If you choose to register at residentevil . net
it will keep track of all your player records, and you will earn EXP toward "Agent Levels" that can be used to unlock costumes and other bonus content. The website will also host "events" every week that players can participate in. The winner of an event will have that win permanently placed on their profile.
As with many, many other games the true value in it is using it as a social tool, co-op, death match, or agent hunt all make the game great.

If you like platformers and are looking for something more on the relaxing side I would definitely reccomend this game. It's very charming. The dialogue is fun, the graphics are beautiful and the soundtrack is amazing.
The gameplay istself is simple yet intuitive. There are only a handful of controls you need to know; jumping, barking, and manipulating the seasons as you aquire them. However despite the simplicity the puzzles involved are challenging enough to be fun without getting frustrating. There is no dying mechanic so if you've been getting annoyed at harder games like me this is a great change of pace. It basically the opposite of dark souls. No dying, not hard, and it's fun.
The story is lighthearted and engaging. It feels very welcoming and friendly without talking down to the player but becomes more in depth as you go. I'm only about 50-60% done and I've really enjoyed it so far.
If you are looking for a more challenging platformer I would say consider something else. This is a game made for stopping and smelling the roses, so to speak. Without a dying mechanic or health or enemies the most challenging thing is maneuvering the map, which becomes easier as you go since you revisit the same areas a few times.
Overall I'd say this is a great game that seems to be flying under the radar. Even the minor sound effects should be appreciated. The small tink of frozen water when you walk on it or the sound of rain on leaves. The detail of this game really stands out. And how can you not love adorable foxes?
This game has great graphics and a cute story. Some directions are unclear the small puzzles can be difficult, but I would 100% recommend this game to someone, Buy it!

I've put several hours in now and I have to say it's a chilled out and enjoyable experience - another gorgeous looking and charming indie title with a few minor flaws. However, Seasons After Fall is something you play if you've had a rough week. It's relaxing and looks beautiful and won't take up too much of your time.
I have to say the controls are a bit annoying - this isn't NES era horror story stuff, but making jumps can be tedious as the fox often doesn't respond and you drop to the floor. So you have to practice to get it all together, but it's such a short game so it's not exactly ideal. You're left with far too many swears as you drop down and make your way back up again.
Other than this it's simply a relaxed experience and the music is a unique touch, although it sometimes doesn't sit comfortably with what's going on during the adventure. Maybe that's me being pedantic, but I think a David Wise type soundtrack would have suited it more. You can compare this game with the glorious Ori and the Blind Forest and its soundtrack is simply perfect and seamless, whereas here it's occasionally jarring.
Other than a few gripes, there's a big thumbs up all round for Seasons After Fall. I've found it quite joyous at times, and annoying at others. It's absolutely worth your time, though.

Fierach's Reviews:
Tl;dr: For Honor is a flawed, but gorgeous game. Worth buying if you like the premise, and are into fighting games. If not, pick it up on sale.
The Good: It is the age-old playground question. Who would win in a fight? A viking, a knight, or a samurai? The devs at Ubisoft Montreal have crafted an absolutely beautiful game. Anachronism stew though it may be, it is clear that they paid close attention and detail to both fantasy, and real life tropes for the characters depicted in For Honor. You feel the weight of the Lawbringer's poleaxe, the calculated swift strikes of the Orochi, and the savagery of the Raider in every step, swing, and animation. The devs have crafted a uniquely compelling fighting system, the Art of Fighting for their interaction. The game boosts a short, but meme-worthy and fun single-player campaign that is just the tutorial for the multiplayer, where the game really begins. Online there are a variety of modes versus players and versus AI opponents (who differ enough in strength that they can give veteran players a run for their money), earning wargear and customization options to personalize any of the heroes you picked to fight as. Modes range from the single, and honored 1v1 Duel, to more chaotic 2v2 Brawls, and 4v4 deathmatch-like Elimination and MOBA-like Dominion modes.
The Bad: This is a fighting game, and Ubisoft has never really made a fighting game before. Balance isn't the best. Some ideas put into the game (for example, such as polearms and larger weapons taking longer, and with a slight delay on rapid guard switching), might sound okay on paper, but can prove frustrating in practice. Their peer-2-peer networking scheme causes problems for some. While I also experience disconnects now and then, it is a matter of opinion whether this is a dealbreaker or not. Do be aware that p2p will not go away however, and will not be replaced, since it would need a total overhaul of the game's netcoding.
The End: For Honor has had many problems at its start. Much like the other Ubisoft title, Rainbow 6: Seige, For Honor has had communication issues, connectivity issues, and well, almost any sort of problem you can think of, it had it. However, the game overall is stable now, barring a few disconnects by salty players in the larger 4v4 modes possibly dragging the rest down. The developers host a weekly talk and showcase to talk about upcoming updates and current issues brought to light by the community, and the game is much improved from its release thanks to several updates focused on balancing, bug fixes, and improvement of the netcode. Could it still be better? Absolutely. There's still work to be done on adding more features, expanding customization, and balancing certain heroes, but the community and devs work hard, and work hand in hand to bring new content and address issues on an at least biweekly basis.
If you enjoy fighting games, or just running around as a badass Viking, Knight, or Samurai, you owe it to yourself to consider buying this game.

Overpriced and overhyped cash-grab.
Now I have mixed feelings regarding this one, as I really had fun playing it for two nights. Unfortunately, that's where it all ends. I would recommend this game, if its price was around 15 bucks max, but since it's almost 40 bucks, you'd expect a top-tier game.
After playing F13th, I purchased "Dead by Dawn", which is by far a superior game, both content and quality wise. And cheaper! And you can play as Michael Myers and Laurie Strode!
What's wrong with "Friday"?
- Glitches and bugs. The game feels completely unfinished. As a matter of fact, it feels so buggy, I got the impression (I'd like to believe, that it's wrong, though) like the development budget was split in 4, with 3/4 ending in fundraisers' pockets while 1/4 went to some Indian or Ukrainian freelancers, who barely started to learn Unreal Engine. Graphics look dated, even for an online game, gameplay annoys you with loads of bugs and the amount of texture glitches is unforgivable;
- Game process is samey, repetitive and replay value is close to zero. There is not much you can do in this game, really. There are three camp maps, which are basically the same night time camps with different cabin layout. That does not matter, since actions, that you can perform inside cabins are ridiculously limited. Unlocking new Jasons and counselors does not help either, as they hardly vary. "Fatalities" are neither creative (even context ones) nor glitch-free most of the times. Counselors do not have any special abilities or personality traits. Jock, nerd or goth girl - it hardly matters as only random irrelevant stats vary. No wonder, online multiplay has a lot of trolls, as gamers quickly get bored doing same things over and over again.
- Biggest issue - if you do not have many gamer friends (who have also purchased this game) with whom you can arrange a private session, you hardly get to play as Jason. Yes, you heard it right. In a game about serial killer, you hardly get to play as one. Out of 50 matches I played, the randomizer only gave me control of the masked killer twice. It is really random and not obvious to the player, when he gets to play as Jason. Developers could have introduced a queue algorithm or a visible randomizer (e.g. match drawing or rock-paper-scissors). Don't think, that offline bots will help much as their AI will most likely be glitchy and stupid as hell.
- Another one for me (not everyone gets it) - push to talk does not work in this game. It really ruins any fun, that I could possibly get long-term from this game.
In short, I feel like I'd been ripped off. I realize, that you also pay for a movie license, when you purchase this game, but this feels like a total cash-grab.
If I were a kickstarter backer, I would definitely ask for a financial report of the funds raised and rather raise a question, where did 600 000 bucks intended for development actually go.

You begin the game as Simon Jarrett, a 20-something living in 2015 Toronto who was recently in a car crash that is causing his brain to bleed uncontrollably. His only option for extending his life is participating in a graduate research project in which these two students scan Simon's brain, recreate his brain as a computational model, and run thousands of simulations on that model to find the right treatment plan. The scanning visor lowers onto Simon's head, and when it lifts up, Simon finds himself in a research facility at the bottom of the ocean in the year 2105. There are robots all over the place that think they are people -- and not in a "robots can have humanity, too" sort of way, but rather that these robots think that they are specific people who worked in the facility. You have to figure out how a man can suddenly be transported 90 years into the future, what this research facility is, why do these robots think they are people, and what you can do now that you are stuck there.
If this premise, the first twenty minutes of the game, hooks you and you feel it reeling you in, absolutely play SOMA. This game is all about story. Unlike some other narrative-focused games, like Gone Home or Dear Esther, you do have challenges in gameplay with puzzles and the occasional monster encounters, but the puzzles are fairly simple and those rare monster encounters often feel like they detract from the game somehow (enough that there are mods to remove or pacify them). The real meat of the game is in the path the characters take and the questions that are raised not only on the nature of humanity but on consciousness itself. What makes a person unique? Can an imitation be as valuable as the original?

Never Alone, also known as Kisima Inŋitchuŋa, tells the story of an Iñupiaq (ethnic Alaskan natives) girl named Nuna, and her fox companion. The game allows controlling the two characters individually, and is a platform puzzler. The game is notable for combining a traditional cultural story into a video game layered with authentic artwork and narrated in the native tongue. There are several in-game videos that can be unlocked to know more about the cultural background of elements found throughout the game. Though the gameplay feels somewhat unpolished, the overall experience is that of an interactive story, and is rewarding as a co-op adventure. The entire array of narration, artwork, and design lends an amazing credibility to the story and feels authentic. It somewhat reminded me of Studio Ghibli in a very distant way. The puzzles are interesting, but not the focus of the story. Playing them is one way to enjoy the story rather than simply click to move forward. There is a DLC called Fox Tales, which follows another short adventure with the same characters, and is as enjoyable as the first.

I am quickly finding that there are quite a lot of games that we’re covering in our Indie Spotlight and Early Access Insights that I want to continue playing long after I’ve written a Steamified in a Nutshell for it. Unfortunately, with the pace of the website and with a lot of plans in the works in the not too distant future that often becomes an impossibility. Prior to our second launch I figured that starting Steamified would enable me to spend more time playing games but it just hasn’t turned out that way yet. I’m hoping to remedy the situation by hiring some aspiring writers who can provide quality articles on the site to further your entertainment and knowledge.
One of the games that I really want to spend a significant amount of time playing is Tomb of Tyrants by Jake Huhman. Once you dig into the tomb you will quickly discover that it’s much deeper than your standard – and casual – match 4 type game. Yes, the base mechanics in the game would make you believe that it is in part your base match four game but once you delve deeper you quickly discover the amount of strategy and skill required to be successful with the game.
The aim of the game is to overcome the AI’s heroes that are attacking you. You can do this by building an underground fortress that is constituted of traps and minions/monsters among other things. You gain these through the match four gameplay mechanic. However, rather than it being a typical match four game where quickness is rewarded deep strategy is rewarded with gaining higher multipliers. This makes the game not necessarily slower but definitely more methodical. Intelligent game play is consistently rewarded above the taking of obvious but not necessarily more efficient matches. This process moves the game away from being a match four and into a tower defense, strategy, RPG puzzle game. It’s a very impressive mixture that is done incredibly well.
The only thing that I would disagree with developer and self-publisher Jake Huhman on is that I would argue against it being considered a casual game. Yes, if you so choose the game can be played in a casual manner but I would argue that players will never see anything near the best that his game has to offer by playing in such a manner. This is why I would love to – and will – be spending significantly more time with Tombs of Tyrants. It’s a fantastic game that can be deeply rewarding.

This is a yes, but with a few caveats:
The game is fun, and has a good combination of mechanics. It's got a good, consistent look/feel to it, and the music is reasonable. The interface is rather good too - not too much guesswork (apart from stuff below). Overall, it feels pretty polished.
Now to get to the caveats (in this case, the bad stuff):
The game kinda falls apart after a few hours (of total play). There just hits a point where you don't know whether you're progressing or not, and there's a metagame mechanic (the legacy system) that isn't very well explained and kind of breaks stuff more than anything else. You can even designate the standard 'Tyrant hangs out here' room you get every game as a legacy room, which means you just wasted a legacy slot. Bit of an oversight.
The other thing that basically falls over, is the ritual system. While it's nice to see the concept of a 'match four' system where orientation and position are important, sadly this one requires you to match shapes that are far too complex to be reasonable.
There's a codex which is meant to explain things, but a chart would've been better (also, it only shows you what you already get from the alt-text which renders it obsolete and useless).
The game gives you a lot of choices, but ultimately since you don't really tend to look at your dungeon (ever), these are pretty meaningless (really, what's the difference in the rooms? What impact will they have? It's not very apparent). The dungeon/base building aspect of the game doesn't give you any form of progress assessment, so you never know how well you're doing.
The final part where the game falls apart, is the combo system. Sure, no problem - match more than four tiles or get more than a single match with a move, get a bonus. No worries - except in this one due to the often lack of resources, you just can't get more than four tiles together regularly. Forget about trying to set up multiple matches. I felt like the size of the horde was a crippling restraint.
So, what we have is: a fun game that you can play every now and then, but with a broken metagame, combo system and progression. Fun for a few hours, which honestly is fine for a few bucks.

So, gotta say, I am actually sorry I waited until the Winter Sale to pick this title up.  There is a lot of fun to be had with this engaging match-4 game, and I like the use of theme combined with the mechanics of how you collect and use resources.
I love the legacy aspect of the game, playing multiple times to unlock new floors and completing goals to retain resources for your next play-through.  It pulls inspiration from a lot of sources without being a knock-off clone, but remains familiar enough that you can pick it up quickly.  This is a casual game you can play to unwind, but one which keeps finding new ways to surprise you if you play long term.
Is it perfect?  No.  Pixel based graphics might be offputting to some, and I actually would like to see a slightly higher resolution be implemented for the game (nothing major, I'm not expecting rendered 3D or anything... just closer to Super Nintendo graphics than NES).  I also think that there needs to be some refinement for when the game gets played on larger monitors.  However, the dev has proven that he is looking to do significant post-release support, so take these as constructive criticism rather than reasons to turn away.
In the end, it's just a whole lot of fun, and I look forward to seeing what else this dev has in store for this title and anything he does in the future.

A few people have noted that this is a 'neglected classic', although it was well received at release as seen in it's metacritic score of 81.  It also seems to be liked here on Steam and now that it is available for all platforms including Steam OS you've never had a better reason to pick up this cult classic and unleash your bad side.  I'd also recommend getting the Raising Hell expansion too as it offers a worthwhile chunk of extra fun and is integrated into a new playthrough quite well. Story: Overlord casts the player in the silent (real heroes/villains don't need to blabber to the nines) role of the eponymous Overlord, an evil villain who has been defeated and your tower destroyed by seven good heroes.  This simply won't stand, so you head out to wreak revenge on the world with a mob of chatty adorable goblin/gremlin things, leaving not a sheepie or pumpkin in your wake.  The game plays with all the tropes of fantasy games/books with affection; greedy dwarves, soppy elves and large spiky suits of armour are all featured.  The game offers two routes, broadly classed as lawful evil vs chaotic evil (or benign despot vs crazed psychopath for those who don't do the D&D classifications).  There is a bit more to say but for spoilers reasons it is at the very bottom of this review.
The Game: Overlord is a RPG (ARPG possibly since there is no classes and min/maxing and such like) and you can attack enemies directly with weapons and spells which are upgradable/findable.  Your main weapon though is a pack of goblin minions who overwhelm your foes in a wave of stabbing and insults then upgrade themselves by dressing up in whatever they destroy/kill.  It knows it's being cute but damn it is cute, like a pack of trainable ultra-violent kittens.  with little hats.  You can upgrade yourself or your horde as you play so some variance in playstyle is possible.  You play through different environments exploring fantasy type environments (Elven forest, Paladin's Castle etc)  and rebuild your tower growing stronger along the way.  There are choices to make but this isn't Deus Ex, the choice are more about playstyle mentioned earlier than unlocking/locking parts of the game.  Minions come in four flavours Brown (general melee), Red (ranged, immune to fire), Green (melee, great at backstabbing) and Blue (Heal, immune to water).  These are introduced is a gentle learning curve that offers plenty of scope for you to get the most from each class and if they all get squashed, well there is plenty more where that came from.
Technical points - I had no difficulty playing on Win7 and Linux Mint.  Also worked with xbox360 controller.  Sometimes the swarm of minions can lag a little bit or be otherwise fiddly and I have drowned a few by accident.  But these were minor hiccups and most of the time grand sweeps of destruction were a delight.

Pros:
- MOO2 Rip-off: This is better MOO2 than the original MOO2 ever was. Basically all of the orig game mechanics are there, but all of them are slightly enhanced (in the way that you think this is what is should have been in the original). Some of the mechanics seem to be new (ground/troop combat), but overall, very good design and approach for those players, who strive for a new and deep MOO-type-of-4X-game.
- Very good overall graphics/sound design: Light, but effective, pleasing one's eyes. Some menus are very well organized so e.g. the empire management is thus very effective, even with lots of colonies.
- Very good ship designing: Create multi-purpose or very specialized ship designs; mix fleets in a way that fits your gaming style. In general, there is a great variance of ship's weapon and module types.
- Good ship2ship combat/battles: Ship design plays a big role in combat, but certain tactics are necessary and are a definitive advantage. Still, tactics are not the core of battles, it is mainly techlogies and ship design. Ships get various medals/bonuses for certain combat achievements and retain these for life; these are also upgradeable. Battles are also very well graphically designed to please one's eyes. Thus, some battles can be quite epic.
- Well designed diplomacy: You know exactly what they think about you and why and what you did good to help the relations, what you did bad to harm them. You know exactly where your current diplomatic limits with each of the races are. Spying is yet another game concept which reminds of good old MOO2, but is nicely extended, so that a player has a better control of offensive actions.
- Additional in-game candy: You can build Space/refueling stations whereever you need them on the map. Exploration of space anomalies - some trigger combat, some additional research; all provide various in-game bonuses and content. Various planetary enhancements, generated randomly ad-hoc as a result of certain long-term situations (sport resorts, merchant guilds, private shipyards, ...). Space-creatures. And a dark story, affecting the whole galaxy...
Cons:
- Diplomacy: Despite diplomacy being very well designed and informative, it seems its purpose is not to seak diplomatic victory in this game (e.g. a concept of permanent alliances is missing). Diplomacy does not need an ovehaul, but an extension to have even more possibilities.
- No SpaceStation designing: This is a "minor" issue; but not possible to create customized space station designs. Neverteheless, space stations use the best tech the player has available.
- Groud/troop combat: Although developer put quite an effort into modelling of this concept, it is a bit dull. It has a great potential, but it feels like it does not work as originally intended. This is overhauled in DLC.
- MOO2 Rip-off: This might not be ideal for players ho seek new, unorthodox approaches to 4X gaming.
- Some bugs: From time to time, there are small bugs/glitches in the game, usually not gamebreaking, but sometimes quite annoying. The number of bugs went down quite a lot just before the DLC release, on the other hand, DLC release might have introduced new ones. Anyway, the (only) developer is working to fix those too.
Verdict: 8/10

I brought the DLC and it's an vast improvement for StarDrive 2. I'm very happy with the way he has set it up. I actually like the hexagon style gameplay and the game has been more streamlined. For example:
1. Ship Design - it is a ton easier to design a warship and not have to worry about the secondary systems or having to line up everything perfectly. Hours could be spent in here but thanks to the streamlined process, I can design the parts I want to mess around with and let the "behind-the-scene" nerdy people figure out how to power it and etc. Excellent improvement.
2. Freighter - this entire process has been automated and I'm vastly relieved as this was too much micro-managing. The AI now does it for you, provided you build enough feighter ships to transport the necessary items to the colonies.
3. AI - the AI has been vastly imporved and I LOVE LOVE LOVE having to deal with pirates, space monsters, and etc. This keeps me on my toe and I can't just send all of my fleets of warships to the border but actually have to watch within the terroritory and intercept any troublesome pirates/space monsters and so fourth. Just a fantastic addition to my gameplay
4. Colony Management - this has been streamlined by a huge margin. I do not have to try to micromanage each colony but I can still set a theme of what I woud like the "AI Governor" to follow in building up the colony, such as focus on Science, Food, and etc. Furthermore, I do not have to bother with managing the tile management but only mindful of the total number of buildings there are and plan accordingly. Huge burden been taken off and managed by the AI. However, you still have a lot of control over the colony management but can automate it, if needed.
5. Space Battles - I do think this is an improvement over the StarDrive where we had fighting occuring on the strategy map and that was tough to juggle. Now, it's more streamlined and allows me to focus one thing at a time. I do think there's room for improvement but it's an improvement nonetheless.
I do think there's some issues but the developer has been intent on hearing about it and working on fixing it. However, it is far less buggy than it was with the original game. The developer have made it clear that this is just the first release and will continue to improve it. If this is a sign of what's to come then I feel very good about the game improving even more with more content.

I've put several hours in now and I have to say it's a chilled out and enjoyable experience - another gorgeous looking and charming indie title with a few minor flaws. However, Seasons After Fall is something you play if you've had a rough week. It's relaxing and looks beautiful and won't take up too much of your time.
I have to say the controls are a bit annoying - this isn't NES era horror story stuff, but making jumps can be tedious as the fox often doesn't respond and you drop to the floor. So you have to practice to get it all together, but it's such a short game so it's not exactly ideal. You're left with far too many swears as you drop down and make your way back up again.
Other than this it's simply a relaxed experience and the music is a unique touch, although it sometimes doesn't sit comfortably with what's going on during the adventure. Maybe that's me being pedantic, but I think a David Wise type soundtrack would have suited it more. You can compare this game with the glorious Ori and the Blind Forest and its soundtrack is simply perfect and seamless, whereas here it's occasionally jarring.
Other than a few gripes, there's a big thumbs up all round for Seasons After Fall. I've found it quite joyous at times, and annoying at others. It's absolutely worth your time, though.

Seasons After Fall is an average game wrapped in top-tier visuals. I suspect that this will drive a lot of sales and honestly, good for the developers. I would hope that their next game tries to be a little more ambitious, however. I give it a thumb up but this review will mostly be critical :I
The amount of repetition in the design almost evokes the old Alan Wake American Nightmare spinoff, where you go to the same areas three times. What you do each time is different, but it's not very exciting to be told to go back to an area you've already been to twice. To add to that, there are moments where the game is fun and puzzly and moments where the game is on autopilot, and I felt that the game was on autopilot for way too often. So going back to an area and not really feeling challenged while doing so, is a combination built for boredom.
One thing that's nice is finding the dreams will take some work and some smarts, in order to get the bonus ending scene. The season changing elements sometimes led to good puzzling, but not enough for what I was expecting. A lot of it was just plain busywork.
Another issue that I had was input lag. There is a small bit of delay and it got more and more noticable the longer I played the game. I don't know if this is just my experience or if anyone else will have this problem. The character is also slippery and air control is not very good. I would miss ledges because I couldn't gracefully hop to a ledge in one direction and then hop to another ledge in the other direction because the fox was slow to turn. The platforming is not very devious and there are no real hazards to speak of in the game so these issues are not a killer, but I hope that Swing Swing Submarine can work this out for whatever their next game will be.
Visually, there are few indie games that stand alongside Seasons After Fall. I just wish the gameplay could match it.

LOLNOPE your friendly bot is gonna walk into it,kill himself and lose you a respawn point. The bots will also give away your position if you're hiding. They always know where you're at 9/10 times. There's a good game buried here. It's a diamond in the rough. I tossed em 30 bucks as athank you for continuing the Stalker idea,but this isn't STALKER. Don't fool yourself. This game made me think more than any game has in recent memory. It's labeled as horror and while I do not disagree with that descriptor, anyone expecting Amnesia 2 is going to not only be disappointed with SOMA but come away disliking what I would consider a stronger story, though maybe a weaker game.
The trailers do not do the game justice and, without spoiling anything, I do not believe that any snippet, any fraction of time, could. The game is about coming to a haltingly horrific realization about what the protagonist has gone and continues to go through and the further epiphany that while this might be science fiction in the early parts of the 21st century, how we answer the questions posed by this game are not as far into the future as we'd like to hope.
Sure, there are nasty creatures that chase you around and if you don't outrun them/hide, you'll be eaten or killed or...whatever. That takes a backseat to the ideas planted in your mind. As the credits rolled, as I tried to sleep that night, the thing that kept me awake, that kept nagging at me and demanding attention, was not the eldritch horror of what lay under the ocean: it was that perhaps there is no solution to the questions asked by this game and that the entirity of humanity will very soon be suffering an extreme identity crisis.

Stanislaw Lem WISHES he had come up with this. SOMA takes all the best parts of Amnesia: The Dark Descent and improves upon that game with a story that is as fascinating as it is disturbing. The monster encounters can get a smidge repetitive but the rest of the game is so incredibly good that I didn't care.
A very sobering and insightful experience. The story and atmosphere are near-perfect. The monsters may be a bit uneccessary, but it was totally worth the existential crisis.

If there was one thing I would describe the game as, it's "psychological torture".
This game makes you ask questions you've never asked before, and leaves you at the end, utterly bewildered. It will leave you with a deep pit in your stomach at many intervals and make you think "Is the person I am talking to really themselves Am I really myself? What is being alive?"
No game has ever made me ponder my existence as much as SOMA did.
Also a fair warning: The ending is both incredibly straightforward and incredibly subjective. Whether the ending is a good ending or a bad ending is up to you and what you percieve as someone being youself (for a lack of better words)

I know what happened with Dilly and Cyndaquil but I'm not going to let that effect my opinion on the game. It will be based off the game itself and not my stance on that issue. Alright, Friday the 13th is a horror movie fanchise thats been going on for about 30 years. Now this is Friday the 13th: The Game, a love letter to the series made by Illfonic. In the game you either play as a counselor or Jason.
As a counselor your objective is to survive. You have 4 ways to do this, Escape with a vehicle (boat or car), Call the cops, Wait until the timer runs out, or the hardest one kill Jason. In order to do any of these you need to check houses for important items like gas, batteries, and the fuse. you can also pick up weapons to defend yourself against Jason. Most of these are melee like a machette, pipe or baseball bat (the best one) however there are some ranged ones like the shotgun and the flare gun. All the counselors have different stats with some being more useful than others. One of the most useful is repair which makes it much easier to repair things like the car or phone box. You also have perks which you can equip on anyone and all have strengths and weeknesses. Some make you stronger but decrease your stamina while others can make starting up a car much faster.
Now on to Jason. As Jason you have one objective and it's a pretty obvious one, kill all the counselors. And you have a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of ways to do it. You can slam their head against a door, punch their head off, drown them in a toilet, and make them one with the bird bath amongst other things. You start off with traps and they do exactly what you think they do, trap counsolers. You can also pick up throwing knives around the map so you can injure them a little bit. You have six Jasons (7 if you backed the game and one coming soon) from most of the movies to choose from and all have different stats. Some have amazing water speed but a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ sense while others will give you more traps but a terrible shift. Speaking of sense and shift Jason has four abilities up his sleeve shift, sense, morph, and stalk. Sense lets you see counsolers nearby, shift makes you invisible and makes you much faster, Stalk lets you turn off the scary music that plays when Jason is nearby, And Morph lets you teleport anywhere on the map. Jason also has a grab ability which lets you pick up those pesky teens by the throat and preform an execution.
Ok so whats good about the game? Playing as the counsoler is tense as ♥♥♥♥ and can lead to some nailbitting moments when Jason is right on your♥♥♥♥♥ Also you can communicate with other players via voice chat making teamwork a viable option for counsolers, when Jason comes though, They will be going nuts, but when you finally escape and hear that satisfying music play, it's awesome. Playing as Jason is the best part about the game though. You feel like a Hawk diving torwards seven unexpecting rabbits ready to kill them all.
Now lets go on to the bad. The game is buggy as hell. I haven't encountered many of the gamebreaking bugs myself but definitly a fair share. there was this one in which none of my abilities as Jason worked so I had to quit. Jason is also the most unbalanced part of the game, making him both the best part and worst part. His grab range is way to long
and his abilties can be absolutly broken. The fact that he can grab you the minute he exits morph or shift means as a counselor you have almost no chance of escape unless the Jason goes for an enviornmental kill or you have a pocket knife. Also Sometimes attacking Jason when he's holding a counselor doesn't make him drop meaning Jason gets a free pass and can kill the survivor.
However even with all those issues the game is incredibly fun and devs seem to care about the game because we're getting more Jason's, more maps, and single player. I would recommend this game but only for a price drop. 7/10

seriously don't know how to start this review. There's so much to say about this game. I think I should start by shouting huge cheerish THANK YOU! To Jake Huhman, the game's sole developer and publisher. Not only because he made an amazing game, but because he's a great friendly guy, really caring about his game and it's players. The amount of work he put into his game is astounding, fixing bugs, releasing frequent updates and inserting loads of references and little details and jokes anywhere where's some text.

ow finally to the game. Let's put a quick
At the first look the game looks like a simple tile matcher puzzle game, and it truly is one, but I guarantee it's the best one ever made. It builds upon the simple concept and expands it to a strategy genre. For matching tiles, you get resources. For resources, you recruit units or build floors. To build floors, you have to make room in your Hoard, the stockpile where Loot falls from dead enemy Heroes, defeated by your minions, and after building a floor. Loot which you match to get MOAR RESOURCES. All this in quick cartoonish package filled to the brim with humour.
on't get deceived by it's cartoonish pixelart look, though the game graphics are very creative, detail and expertly  crafted to finest pixelart, all staying in the cartoonish theme of the game. Nice element is you can customize colors of resources.
n the core, this game has a very complex systems built in which offer tens of hours of just explorating what Units can you build, going through Phropecies to "building" your own game style, possibly retaining it through multiple playthroughs using the Legacy system. This system allows you to keep hero minions, items, floors and resource capacity in exchange for completing time limited quests, which range a lot in variety and difficulty. You progress through the game not only on the level of a single "run", but also on scope of multiple ones, as you unlock new Floors through Phropecies, which for example require you to build several floors (sometimes ones which block each other), and recruit some amount of units. Each floor you unlock falls under a specific Tier, which form trees of possible combinations of units you can use to defend your dungeon. And as they are trees, to climb some branches you have to give up some units, because some floors block each other, as I mentioned before. Some floors work as traps, other allow you to recruit Mounts, which can your Biped minions use to roam the dungeon, offering considerable  advantage.
xpecting your question "and what are they for?" I will explain. Your minions are defending you, because you are an extremely evil person and all righteous persons want to hang your head above their fireplaces. And they group at the dungeons ground floor, waiting for it to open, forming waves of trouble waiting at you periodically. All units travel around the vertical dungeon using elevators, and as heroes descend by one floor at a time, your minions can travel freely, patroling the dungeon in meantime.
ranted is, Heroes will sooner or later be caught by your minions, and when this happens, the combat happens. It is turn based and works on cycling heroes in party, each taking one attack and defense at a time. Both minions and heroes have great variance of attacks, abilities and perks, some working as buffers or poisoning enemies.  Those perks don't serve only for combat. If you have a general "theme" in your floors and units, specific heroes come to defeat you, for example necromantinc dungeon resulting in holy heroes.
xpanding the system even more, sometimes you can find items in your hoard which upon collecting serve either as passive effects to the game, active items affecting Hoard with for example spreading a specific resource or shuffling the hoard, or even serve as Potions on a specific floor, taking some time to recharge after each use. Another hoard element is that you can build specific tetromino-and larger- shapes to raise capacity of a specific resource stockpile. And if you need some more to fiddle with the game. there's possibility to move floors, even with enemy heroes in them, for a little price. Needing specific resource and your hoard is almost empty? You can refill it for a price of a little chunk of each of your resources. Want another? You can unlock Banners, which give you specific bonuses to your game, for example granting more mouse slides per move.  And if you still arent satisfied, don't worry, Jake improves the game at a regular pace.

I don't really understand why this game gets sh** on so much. I've been a fan of the Resident evil series since its inception, and have had to grit my teeth along with the rest of the fans through the movies and games like Raccoon City. Resident evil 6 may be flawed, but the PC version is a true successor to RE5, let me explain.
Many people's main complaints about RE6 are either the bad AI, the muddy graphics, or that it is a poor console port. Anyone who has played RE5 recently will recall just how bad the AI was in that game. Playing single player would mean that you would have to call Sheva 5 or 6 times to get her to help you open doors or do objectives. Sheva would constantly get knocked down or held in place, and she would knock you down with her attack reaction. The zombie AI in 5 was also pretty terrible, where J'avo would climb up things and then immediately jump off in order to attack you, or they would get stuck inside each other because they wouldn't understand where to go. In RE6, I feel like I never have to worry about my AI partner, and the enemy AI always keeps me on my toes(on Professional difficulty) with their new running leaps and ground grabs, and the large numbers of regular zombies make them feel actually threatening.
Though the graphics/ textures may be muddy at times even on the highest settings, the shaders and effects are great. and the underwater effects in Ada's campaign may be some of the best I've ever seen in a video game. That being said, there's not much of a graphical change from consoles to the PC version. Whats also important to realize though, is that Capcom has tried very hard to rectify their mistakes from the console versions, and has added tons of new options that will help tweak the game play to your preferences.
The story is in a similar vain to the RE5 story, where it's mostly action, losts of Quick-time, and some exploration. This time around, there are 4 campaigns, and though they may be shorter than RE5's full campaign, they keep the action varied and prevent it from becoming stale. Unfortunately, the action-oriented nature of the campaign seems to confuse some players, as if they forgot how much action/Quick-time that RE5 brought to the table.
The difficulty this time around has really increased. I vividly remember RE5's Professional difficulty being somewhat of a pushover, with zombie's movements and attacks being perfectly telegraphed and predictable. This time, Professional mode really increases the survival horror feel, as being grabbed or missing a dodge can spell death for your character. As I mentioned before, zombies have new attacks like running jumps and crawling grabs, and the special zombies can ruin your day quite easily.
All and all, the game is the next evolution of the RE series, which in my opinion is a great installment (we should be thankful they didn't continue to go the Raccoon City route). The new crossover instances and Agent attack modes can be fun, and are great ideas that I hope they continue with in the next installment.

A game that provides a 50/50 experience: it's either rather fun and enjoyable, or frustrating you with broken mechanics and connection issues. Some say that the gunplay in this game is excellent, and to those people all I can say is: where the hell are you coming from?
One of the fundamental rules of fps games universally is that at the very least the first bullet you fire down sights should go where you want it to, and this basic principle is trampled over in this game. Aiming down sights is only a marginal improvement to shooting from the hip, considering how messed up the aiming manages to be.
Oh, the "ANOMALIES"? They might aswell not be in the damn game, they pose absolutely no threat and as far as I can tell do nothing other than spawn "powerful" artifacts, of which maybe a grand total of two are mildly useful.
Other than that, even though the game hides behind it's WORK IN PROGRESS or EARLY ACCESS or WHATEVER banner, manouvering around the main menu hub is extremely awkward, with it often misinterpreting the things you want to actually do. Multiple disconnects, connection issues, crashes and what not are present, as expected, but are definetely not something to overlook.
None of the games I've played have I been put into a proper PvP game. It's usually been 2-3 people per side, with the remainder of the slots being filled by one of the dumbest bots in any video game I've ever seen. We're talking spinning in circles, staring the enemy dead in the eye without action, standing still and doing nothing dumb.
I think the only positive thing to be said about Survarium so far is that the music is nice and climactic and the guns sound pretty damn good. Other than that, the game feels pretty bad when it comes to everything else it does.

For Honor is getting a lot of hate - some deserved, a lot undeserved from just very angry gamers. Long story short: do I recommend you buy For Honor? Yes, I do.
Pros:
Innovative new gameplay styles.
Incredibly addicting combat.
High skill roof.
Complex enough for hundreds of hours of gameplay.
Graphically beautiful.
Continously updated.
Cons:
After 4 months, the game still has connection issues. Can be quite frustrating.
Minor balance issues - however, in a game like For Honor, even minor balance changes can feel massive at times.
Somewhat small PC playerbase makes matchmaking sometimes take a few minutes, and limits proper skill-based matchmaking due to lower player numbers.
High skill curve makes it a bit unforgiving for new players.
Very salty playerbase.
Here's the thing, For Honor has technical issues. Yes. Are they gamebreaking? No, not for me, and to my understanding, not for the majority. Are there balance issues? Yes, but they are HARDLY as bad as the many critics make them out to be - it's a L2P issue mostly.
Look at the negative reviews here, and look at how much NOT THE GAME they are critizing. They hate Ubisoft. They hate season passes. They hate you can buy in-game currency with real money (but really, unless you wanna madly pimp out your character day-one, you in no way need to, and it has no real effect on gameplay). The list goes on, but rarely do they actually have valid criticism of THE GAME.
The worst thing about For Honor is it's whiny and salty community, that will complain about everything and anything.
The best part is... well, the game. The game is goddamned amazing.

Browns are your basic melee soldiers who are pretty tough and can take more beatings than the other species.
Reds are your fireballs throwing artillery, and thus die pretty quickly, they also absorb fire.
Greens are your assassins, they love to jump onto the enemies and stab them for tons of damage. They aren't as tough as the browns, but they can take more beatings than blues or reds. They also absorb poison.
Blues are your healers, they are terrible at fighting and die quickly, but they will resurrect any fallen minions.
All in all the game has a lot of interesting creature designs, is pretty funny sometimes, and you can forge sweet new weapons and armor for your overlord.
The only downsides is the minions have a tendency to get stuck in the scenery in one small part of the game.

Seasons After Fall is a charming and vibrant 2D platformer that captivates the player with its unique art style, gorgeous music, and intruiging story, ultimately leaving a lasting satisfaction in the heart and mind.
This game features a variety of puzzles that are solved primarily by utilizing your Fox's  ability to switch between the seasons on command. These puzzles are indeed simple to solve, but that does not detract from the enjoyment of the experience, since the true joy of the game comes from the exploration of its varied and enchanting environments. Instead of using puzzles to challenge its players, Seasons After Fall uses them to engage the player in interacting with how each piece of the level design changes with the seasons. Likewise, the game focuses moreso on expanding your toolkit for exploration, while increasing difficulty at a gentle, casual pace.
Regarding the game's story, it is simultaneously simple and mysterious, obscure yet fundamental. This is largely due to how the game keeps the player in the dark for majority of the duration, and only begins to reveal itself in the second half. Consequentially, the player comes to understand the true nature of this world just before the climax of the story, therefore amplifying the strong emotions of the game's beautiful ending. Just like the nature itself, Seasons After Fall feels intuitive and familiar while also retaining an undeniable sense of mystery and wonder.
Overall, I highly recommend Seasons After Fall, especially for its low price point. I could feel the love that went into every minute detail of this game, and, while it is not a flawless work, it feels complete and satisfying.

This isn't so much a game as it is an experience, more akin to an interactive movie, or rather an interactive tv show that wouldn't be out of place in an Adult Swim lineup. The whole game is basically a massive fever dream disguised as an adventure game, with inexplicable stuff happening for no apparent reason, and there are a handful of mini-games hidden throughout the game for you to find and briefly amuse yourself with (my favorite would definitely be the wedding themed Quake clone "wedding qake"). Besides the brief and ultimately meaningless mini games, there is no real "gameplay" to speak of besides walking around the levels looking for more surreal scenes and jokes to trigger: in fact if you ignore all the secrets that can be found, the game is incredibly linear and short, with whatever puzzles required for the plot taking no effort to complete whatsoever. I bought this game today, and I beat it in 2 hours despite wandering around aimlessly looking for secrets and replaying mini games. The voice acting supplements the humor perfectly, but as for the humor itself, it's a matter of personal taste; the humor is basically surreal slapstick in the vein of aqua teen hunger force (which, surprise surprise, happens to be an Adult Swim favorite; it's almost like this game was published by them *wink wink*), and if you're into that kind of humor, you're in luck. If you don't like this kind of humor however, you should probably pass this up. So for those who do like this kind of humor, should you buy this? Yes and no. This game is an amusing experience while it lasts, but it ends far too quickly with very little replay value, which stings even worse when you take into account the $15 asking price. So yes, do buy this if you like this sort of humor, but if you can wait, you should probably wait for a sale.

Orwell is a really solid visual novel. The plot is engrossing, with the right number of twists and player choice moments to keep things fresh over it's 5 episodes. Some enjoyable ambient music gives Orwell some much-needed atmosphere.
One slight disappointment was the gameplay, or at least player input in the game. While there are a few moments where your actions directly affect the plot, for the most part it is a case of finding the right entry or 'datachunk' in a given document to keep the story moving. It is extremely linear in that regard. For the purposes of the plot that is no bad thing, although it should be pointed out that the game itself has less player input than advertsied.
At £7.19 I was a bit disappointed with the game's length. Less than 3 and a half hours was enough for me to finish the story: I felt like I read most/all entries in that time, and did not feel I was rushing.
In a sale, I recommend Orwell for a good plot and treatment of surveillance issues. Be prepared for the game to influence you, though, rather than you influencing it.
definitely recommend.

Absolutely recommend the game. If you get into it - and if you are attentive, you will - you will be faced with moral dilemmas which are very fun to experience. The good sides are a captivating, neat story which provokes thoughts regarding the real world, especially mass surveillance. It's not entirely presented as black-and-white, either, which is always a bonus. You understand that the Orwell system can be very useful against any crime, but that it has unparalleled capacity for abuse, as well. Without giving spoilers, that's all I can say.
The one thing which irked me was the difficulty of distinguishing between what datachunks are necessary, and which ones are not. While I wouldn't have an issue with this, the judgements you make can have consequences. ...Hey, that's actually a good thing!
Definitely recommend. Even has replay value.

I honestly don't remember buying this game but I was looking through my library trying to put some time into my games and review them all and deiced this gem would be the pick of the night. It is an amazingly addictive little game that I got sucked into almost imediately. After playing it from some time I already have 50% of the games achivements and am definantly going to be playing more of this gem. I recommend it to people who enjoy match 4 games and resource management/Building.

It's match-4 meets base-bulding, and my gosh is it addictive! You play as the Tyrant, having opened a tomb of endless resources (gold, gear, rubble, herbs, scrap, bones) to make your evil lair with. Heros notice you right away, so you must match colors to gather resources, and use them to build rooms. Your sanctuary is always the bottom floor, so your room goes deeper and deeper underground as you build rooms, where its safe from heroes.
Monster rooms spawn monsters, which you can spend resources to respawn them with. Trap rooms are filled with traps, which break with each use, but a few resources can fix them straight away. Items REALLY help, and sometimes you can carry them from round to round to get a better score. The Midas Glove, for example, grabs all the gold squares, and the milk bottle will spawn in more bone blocks to use.
Simple rooms take a bit of a couple of resources, and big advanced rooms take a lot of three resources. Its very carefully balanced and well-thought out. The rooms are arranged in a tree, though, so building certain rooms will cut off your ability to build certain other rooms.
So you build, build, build and match, match, match as long as you can until a lucky hero finally gets down to your sanctuary and kills you. Your reward is your high score, and the ability to lock certain rooms, items, and monsters as your "legacy", to be passed on to your next tyrant. So it very much encourages you to play for multiple rounds.
=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=
+Excellent Match-4, Base-Building Gameplay
+Lots of monsters, rooms, unlockables.
+Fast and furious gameplay, you REALLY have to abuse the pause button if you want to succeed.
+Rituals (match this shape with your blocks) and Plots (complete this circumstance) grant you extra rewards.
+Beautiful, well thought out time-waster of a game. :)
+/- Games can range from 5 minutes to 1.5 HOURS, depending on your skill level and what you have unlocked.
+/- The achievements, save one, are complete child's play.
+/- Endless mode is the only mode, so a high score is your only goal.
-The tome that has the glossary of the games rooms, monsters, and items is GARBAGE, you'll be doing a lot of experimenting to figure out what does what. What does this symbol mean? How is that item actually used? It's awful!
-It is possible to run out of rooms to build, since they're arranged in a tree you can write yourself into a corner.
=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=-=
All in all, I'd call this a stocking-stuffer, a birthday gift, or a rainy-afternoon sort of game. I got 10 of the 20 achievements in my 4th round. I also had to do a lot of "translating" to figure out what the symbols and indicators in the glossary tome actually MEANT. But it's an addictive match-4 game with plenty of easter eggs, unlockables and awesome base-building gameplay.
This is a buy! :D

Farm for your life is a sweet little gem of a game that takes the elements of a few classic games (referenced above) and somehow manages to pull it off.
You begin your life on a pretty sweet looking farm in the middle of the cutest little Zombie apocalypse ever, lose it all to a storm and refurbish it all from the ground up.
Plant your crops, harvest and rennovate a restaurant that caters to other survivors that will trade you goods for food, allowing you to upgrade and improve.  Reinforce the farm, build corn cannons, slingshots and pumpkin catapults to fend off the hungry (and cute) undead.  Attract survivors to live on your steading and help out with the tasks you assign to them.
Farm for your life is a regular jack of all trades, yet master of none.  For what it is, it pulls it off brilliantly and delivers hours of enjoyment.  There's something here for the casual and not so casual gamer.
The game isn't without it's faults here and there, but nothing that can't be easily overlooked (especially for the price of the game + bagging it during the Halloween sale).  The farm itself isn't huge, the buildings and upgrades are pre-determined in their positioning, removing most of the customizable options for those that would be seeking it.  Some of the dialogue in English has been misspelled due to translation (which is a tiny complaint, owing to the fact that it's like 98% fine.)   The most amusing translation error is that "Grass" is labeled as "Gras."
When altering your character's appearance at the house, it has a tendency to randomly alter beard/hair colour (which is easily fixed by going back into the house and selecting the colour you intended.)
Full plates of food/beverages can get stuck on the tables in the restaurant and become non-interactive at times, which I've only noticed happening when I've set my character to perform a task that a worker suddenly attempts to perform at the same time.   This is easily fixed by saving, exiting to the main menu and returning to the game.
Nothing game breaking that I've run into, yet.  The flaws really do feel so minor to me that I don't even notice unless I'm forced to recall them (like writing a review).
It's hard not to love a game that pays homage to existing classics and owns up to in the achievements.  One of the real winning points for me was that I noticed you have the option to play the game without zombies in it.  My girl's very phobic of zombies, yet loves games like this.  It was great to know she could play without having to worry about that, which turned out it wouldn't be a problem anyways.
The zombies in this game are adorable, they don't even eat people.  They're vegetarian zombies that bust down your fences to eat your crops.  There's not a gun in sight, you defeat them by lobbing corn husks at their heads, or letting your automated defenses finish them off for you.
A concept that might seem a little blasphemous to viscera chomping, plague spreading, Romero-esque zombies that I've been a fan of all my days.  But, jeez... just look at em!
Farm for your life is triumphant!   Stop reading and buy it already!

The guardian of winter has a fabulous voice.
More to the point, the game as a puzzle platformer is a very charming experience. I couldn't take a break and beat it in one sitting, which took 7 hours. While the puzzles aren't the most difficult for experienced brain gamers, it can still serve as a good introduction to the genre.
The music is good from beginning to the end, and brings about a similar atmosphere as Journey. While lovely to listen to, the songs seem to do only a single loop after activating an event. This leaves the game rather silent if you're stuck wandering, though many sound effects do keep a minimalistic atmosphere going.
The art also stands out as every sprite and background looks handpainted. The effort is clearly seen and pays off in the visual image of the game.
Regarding the gameplay, the game might feel a little repetitive to some people. You have four general areas and you visit each 3 times as the story advances and the objectives change. Each round gets a little more challenging as new puzzle elements emerge, but there are many points where simply moving around requires repeating the same puzzle over and over. Luckily shortcuts emerge, but they don't skip all of these situations.
The controls work quite well, though one could complain that the responsiveness is a bit slow, but not so much that it would hinder the experience. Changing the seasons with the mouse also tends to mess up if you try to do it quickly. (Could be the player's fault though.)
Probably my only issue with the game is that the only reason I ever got stuck anywhere at all was because it was a search puzzle. The moments where I couldn't find 'that one missing puzzle piece'. Rather than being stuck by difficulty, getting stuck by a search quest is rather frustrating.
I also found a pair of bugs:
1. sometimes the rolling branches stop responding after swapping season, but reswapping fixes it.
2. Sometimes while falling the fox gets stuck inside a mushroom for a second.
Overall I very much recommend this game. Despite the minor nags, it's a great experience to any fans of puzzle and platforming games.
And seriously, the guardian of winter's voice. For all I care, I'd have him narrate my life.

An excellent first-person espionage adventure game kinda thing. Though there's lots of self-aware comedy and surreal interactive weirdness thrown in too, kind of like the movie Top Secret or The Naked Gun meets the games Panic! and The Standley Parable. Sort of. Honestly, Jazzpunk is unlike just about anything I've played.
You play Polyblank, an agent for some kind of agency, based in an alternate-universe cyberpunk Cold War. Oh yeah and there's some random jazz thrown in there as well, hence the name. Random seems to be a word thrown around a lot when describing this game, and for good reason: it's all over the place in its references and absurdist humor. And while it feels a bit ham-fisted at first, like it's trying to set a world record for most pop culture references per square meter, I found the experience to be thoroughly enjoyable after I completed a mission or two. So yeah, what happens is that you'll be given increasingly bizarre missions every so often, which is done in increasingly bizarre ways. Sometimes it'll be as simple as infiltrating a soviet installation or tailing an American, other times you'll have to do something like catch and roast a robot pig or exterminate rogue microchips in a kitchen. While you can just go from point A to point B completing your objectives, you'd be doing yourself a huge disservice, as it's all the stuff in-between that really makes Jazzpunk a worthwhile experience.
Being in a cyberpunk world filled with robots, the references to nerd culture are all over the place. Gaming culture as well, with minigames like Wedding Quake, an homage to Quake III Arena where you shoot wedding party members with champagne and collect prenup agreements. And a reference to Street Fighter II's car-smashing sequence, but done in the first person and with just a bit more humor. Things like this are every few steps in this game and it just put a huge grin on my face. Most of it's not laugh aloud kinda stuff, but I can't help but love bits where you find a 3DO console in the sand, or have to pour coffee onto a Commodore PET to proceed. Granted, it risks alienating some players if they're not familiar with these in-jokes, but with as wide of a spectrum as the comedy covers, chances are you'll find something in here to make you laugh, or at least exhale sharply and chuckle to yourself. I honestly don't have any noteworthy complaints about the game, just a couple minor things like some objectives being a bit obtuse to figure out and the humor being hit or miss depending on individual preferences. Also, there's the game length. You can complete it in about an hour if you just speed through it, but you'll miss a ton of awesome stuff. It takes two and a half to three hours if you take your time, so Whether or not the game is worth the asking price of $15 is up to you. Personally I found the game to be a breath of fresh air and I had a blast just wanting to see what absolutely freaking strangeness was coming up next. So if you see anything you like here, why not give Jazzpunk a shot, especially if it's on sale.

This was a very well-meaning game that should have been a documentary or a kid’s show or something, because it was a terrible platformer with possibly the worst control layout I’ve ever experienced. Road to hell is paved, etc etc.
The idea with this game was to tell a Native Alaskan folktale with the input of the actual Native Alaskans. That’s a lovely sentiment, and indeed the game is interspersed with video of the people talking about their culture. These videos, dubbed “Cultural Insights,” were really cool and interesting, and were easily the best part about the game (edit: except in that they had to be unlocked by triggering random waypoints, which was really annoying when they were the highlight).
The art was also very nice, though the 3D models themselves were awkward.
The problem is literally everything else.
First of all… okay. So you move around with your left hand and the normal WASD controls. But the “interact” button is the left shift key. Not either shift key, not the right, the left. This meant that to interact with the environment, you either had to cross your right hand over, take your hands off the arrow keys, or contort your hand so that you could, say, hold W, D, and LS at the same time. I have small hands, but I am confident that after hours of this anyone would be uncomfortable. I literally was still in pain the day after I played, not joking.
Meanwhile, You use the space bar to jump and the left mouse button to attack. So while your left hand is playing Cirque du Soleil, your right is hopping back and forth between the mouse and the keyboard, all in a vain effort to play the damn game.
MEANWHILE, the key to toggle character modes is Q, while is right next to W, so as you’re flailing around trying to jump and drag and walk to the right at the same time, you may just accidentally swap to another character somewhere else on the map. Then you die.
Like… I know this may not sound bad because I’m not sure how to describe four hours of increasing pinky pain and utter frustration, but I don’t think this is a complaint I’ve ever made on this blog before, or in my life before, so try to give me the benefit of the doubt.
Meanwhile, when the controls did work physically, they were incredibly clunky and unreliable in the game. Often I had to press the mouse button several time to get one attack off, jumps seems to execute whenever they felt like, and the physics were just not. This game is ostensibly a platformer, a genre that is predicated on quick, precise controls. Between the unreliable nature of the characters’ weights, jump distances, and speed, the question of whether or not button-presses would work, and the ridiculous layout, the game was almost unplayable. Forget about something like timing jumps. It was so ♥♥♥♥ing frustrating.
Meanwhile, so, there’s two player characters. At all times, one of them is controlled by the single stupidest AI ever, and if the AI dies it counts as a death. So much of my time was a race to the next save point before the AI committed suicide. So. Much. There were also parts of the game where the two characters had to be close together or the platforms would disappear. The AI seemed to get great joy out of wandering off and letting me fall to my death. Over. And over. And over.
The game is also really buggy. Sometimes when you’d jump to cling onto a wall, the sprite would hit the wall, flail in the air for 10 seconds, and then die, even if there was ground right underneath. There was a whole area of wall-climbing that was just the most Sisyphean exercise in futility. There was also one point where I was standing on solid ground waiting for a platform to come close, and I just fell through the ground into the level below. Just, plop, into the hillside and out the bottom.
Another big issue is that there was very little sense of gameplay progression. Large swaths of the game are just walking through barren snowscapes, and every once in a while there will be a platform you have to jump to. There’s not much of an increase in difficultly as things go on, and new mechanics are introduced very sparingly. Then there’s the narration that actually tells the story, which is really, really widely dispersed. Every fifteen minutes or so the narrator would spout of two “And then this happened…” lines and then disappear forever, something no doubt made worse by the billion times I died. Then there’s the cultural videos, which are a few minutes long apiece.
The end result is that the pacing is terrible. I’d love to see the entire script for the game; it’s probably just a few pages. This game took me four hours to play, and virtually nothing happened. You’d think that working with folklore there’s be a lot of interesting and exciting plot events to throw in, but the vast majority of the game was just walking in silence. It never really feels like you’re getting anywhere; the protagonists don’t feel like they’re accomplishing anything. Hell, it feels like they’re at the whim of the narrator, not the setting itself; they have no real agency or personalities, no real emotions we’re shown, they just walk, then stop for two lines of narration, then walk some more.
One thing I really don’t think the game considered is that these stories that come from oral traditions are meant to be experienced all at once. When in between the old woman (well, man, but I picture it as a woman) dramatically giving her monologue you intersperse (frustrating) video game, you lose something that I think is really integral to the experience. The whole thing is disjointed, as though the game, the storytelling, and the real people we’re seeing on video all have nothing to do with each other.
I guess I’m just kind of confused about the way this was told. Why doesn’t the girl get any lines? Why doesn’t the villain? Why not make her, the character, the way through which this story is told (as one would expect) and use the narrator as a bridging event, for time jumps and to skip the “walking through barren snowscapes” thing that sucks so much? I think whoever was behind this had the idea of what they wanted to do — Alaskan folklore, with the Alaskan people, in video game form — but really had no idea how to weave those things together in a coherent whole. The result is something that even awful gameplay aside is less than the sum of its parts.
So… yeah. Skip the game. But go watch the cultural videos, I’m sure they’re online somewhere, and they’re wonderful.

Orwell is a really solid visual novel. The plot is engrossing, with the right number of twists and player choice moments to keep things fresh over it's 5 episodes. Some enjoyable ambient music gives Orwell some much-needed atmosphere.
One slight disappointment was the gameplay, or at least player input in the game. While there are a few moments where your actions directly affect the plot, for the most part it is a case of finding the right entry or 'datachunk' in a given document to keep the story moving. It is extremely linear in that regard. For the purposes of the plot that is no bad thing, although it should be pointed out that the game itself has less player input than advertsied.
At £7.19 I was a bit disappointed with the game's length. Less than 3 and a half hours was enough for me to finish the story: I felt like I read most/all entries in that time, and did not feel I was rushing.
In a sale, I recommend Orwell for a good plot and treatment of surveillance issues. Be prepared for the game to influence you, though, rather than you influencing it.

Finished in 3 hours, did not replay to look for alternate choices.
You play as a character who works for the government and has complete access to internet, phone calls, text messages, etc. Your job is to investigate people, collect evidence, and solve (and prevent) terrorist crimes. You're the man behind the camera in the all-seeing surveillance state.
The way the surveillance system is set up is that you collect the information and pass it to an analyst. The analyst looks at the information and decides whether it is sufficient to arrest somebody, or enough to indicate another person is a person of interest that you're allowed to investigate. Over time the network of people you're investigating grows, and it's harder to keep track of their history and relationionships.
If you collect the correct information, you might be able to prevent terrorist attacks. It is possible to get enough evidence to arrest people who aren't actually dangerous or ringleaders.
Sometimes, you see conflicting information (such as when one person is lying) and you need to make a decision. You can't submit both pieces of evidence, you can't delete evidence once you've submitted it (silly, but a game mechanic to make your choices more meaningful), and sometimes it's not clear which one is correct. You sometimes can dig around and find out which piece is correct, but sometimes you need to go with your gut and what you think the people's motivations are.
Other times, it's not clear that you're making a choice. You can always choose to submit or not submit information, and it could lead to different results. The only way to know this is to replay the game and deliberately not choose things that led to bad outcomes. At first I was just grabbing and submitting all the information I saw, but you're intended to put a bit more thought into it. Is this relevent information? Do you want the analyist making a decision based on this information? Is this quote being taken out of context? Are you encouraging your analyist to arrest a harmless person?
My only complaint about the game is
I know it's a smaller indie type of game, but a few more cases to establish what you're doing, how significant your choices are, and so on BEFORE it reached that point would have been appreciated.
I did enjoy this game. It involves a lot of reading, and a lot of thinking, in order to enjoy it properly. It's not a good game for people who want to click through the boring stuff to get to the exciting part. In a way, it's more akin to the visual novel genre than it is to more traditional games.
