There's a key phrase that aptly describes Resident Evil 6:
"Flawed, but fun."
This game takes its' predecessors pedestal of being the most polarizing entry in the series, although it may divide players more than ever. Each of the 4 campaigns present will appeal to certain players and not so much others. The same can be said for some of the features in the game such as the intersections, Agent Hunt, and the co-op mechanics. The real safe bet is that if you're an action fan who likes to play with friends, Resident Evil 6 is an easy recommendation. It's not the greatest action game and it's definitely not a good horror game, but there are some fun moments and good replay value to keep you coming back for more.
However, if you come at Resident Evil 6 expecting another Resident Evil 1 or Resident Evil 4, then you will not only be severely disappointed, you will hate this game immensely. This is a game for open-minded players who like action, players who are willing to take the time to adapt to its' systems, and players willing to overlook the flawed design choices and story to have a good time.
There is a lot to enjoy here, but only if you're willing to sit down and enjoy it.

An EXCELLENT game, wherein you are a tyrant. As this character you gather / produce resources and build / expand an underground dungeon as a classical dungeon master.
At first glance it looks a lot like those decades old pattern matching games like bejeweled in a fantasy setting, but with a twist. The blocks you gather are in fact resources, which you can use to construct the next layer in your dungeon, buy single use items or recruit new units, which you have to unlock with another layer of the dungeon.
Constructing one room of a certain dungeon room disables you to construct a different one from the same tier. As such, you really need to think about what kind of rooms you want and make effective combinations to defend your dungeon succesfully, as hero's will come in not only to loot your resources, but take your life / unlife as well.
So if you choose to focus on the undead (skeletons, zombies and necromancers) you'll have a tough time also maintaining an army of goblins, beasts, mercenaries or ritualistic dark elves with all the pro's and cons that come with each path. You can, but it won't be easy.
The graphics look very simplistic, but they complement the game itself remarkably, showing that graphics do not need high end rendering for game to be this great. The sound could use an upgrade, but isn't terrible. Online scoring system (if you're into that sort of thing) and very good integration with Steam.
All in all, highly addictive, very interesting and a challenge to form that specific combination of monsters that make your score go WOW!!!

How do you describe this game?
This game has so much complexity into it:
­- The meat of it, is basically a match 4 game where you can only slide rows left and right.
- The 2nd part of it is a "tower defense" style where you have to build rooms to slow the enemy
- The 3rd part is the management part of it, you need to manage resource, use items, and manage your space for more rooms
It's complex, casual, and addictive-
When you lose, and you will lose, the game goes so seamlessly to start the puzzler over, this may sound so trivial but it made me spend time playing it.
Issues that I hope got addressed in future versions: (and I got faith because I owned this for 2 days so far? and there're already 2 patches to fix bugs)
- The main one, I feel like this game need better tutorial/manual- I was so confused (and even still on the details of what room does what, the 'tech tree', etc)
- The interface- it looks intimidating, so much information on screen (again I reckon some of them need better explanation: what are the resources for, what produces what, etc), also sometimes important things on screen got covered by other window (yes there are different placements of the interface but I dont think they're ideal at the moment) It feels weird criticising the interface as some parts are very intuitive
- Sometimes it can be difficult to tell which ones are the enemy, and which ones are your allies
- Minor complaint- music, only 1 looping track?
All in all, once you get to the flow of this game, you'd be surprised at how indepth the experience is, it has its minor issues, but my god, what a fun little gem. I haven't enjoyed a casual matching puzzle this much for awhile considering how saturated the market it is of it. Give it a go :)

is a very cute game based on Native Alaskan folklore where a girl and an Arctic Fox team up to take on the elements and save their village from destruction. It plays very well as a local co-op game and I encourage everyone to play
together as the dynamic of girl and fox is much more fluid with a friend by your side. I played through with my wife and it was much preferred to playing solo.
The visuals and audio are as adorable as each other. The sounds of the fox, especially during the accidental death of either character, are so heartbreakingly cute. There were a lot of unintentional deaths though, mainly due to how poor the controls are in this game. The wonky physics also contributed a significant amount to our demise as we would often be launched into the stratosphere or violently teleport all over the screen after becoming stuck on a ledge. Despite these issues it only took us roughly 4 hours to play through both the main story and the expansion. I don't think I could recommend
at full price so it's worth waiting​ for a sale.
The portrayal of these indigenous people and their culture is fantastic. I loved unlocking and watching each little piece of footage that provided further exposition to the game, to the history of its story, and to the people it is based on.

tl;dr: The game is good. Buy it if you like block puzzle games. It's not Tetris. Don't expect Tetris.
So, Anode. One thing above all others to remember when looking at the screenshots is that this game is not Tetris. Its similarities to Tetris are superficial. The only things it has in common with Tetris are that it has falling blocks of varying shape and that the playfield is very restrictive. What it's actually fairly similar to, but not exactly so, is Bombliss/Tetris Blast. It also has similarities to games like Puzzle Fighter and Lumines in the sense that blocks can only be cleared with special detonators of the same color. The mechanics at work here are a bit different, though.
While this is a review and not a game summary, it's hard to review this game without actually reviewing the core mechanics. You have tetronimos made up of different colored cells. Unlike Tetris Blast or Bombliss (but like Tetris,) blocks are placed exactly as they land, which means space management becomes a vital part of the strategy when you're playing Endless mode or the longer Time Attack modes. This, however, can be worked to your advantage when making long chains. The other thing you'll notice immediately is that the colored blocks can be connected diagonally as well as parallel. This becomes a vital thing to remember when setting up for chain detonations later on.
What actually sets you up for the largest scores are, though, is the proper use of couplers. Couplers are special blocks that link two sets of blocks together regardless of their color. This means you can link two chains of entirely different colors together with proper planning and clear them with a single detonator for a large amount of points. You are scored on the size of your chains, the amount of them you can cascade together and how quickly you can actually set them up. Once a chain is detonated, a timer is started that gives you a stacking multiplier to your future clears. Each subsequent clear resets the timer. If you go long enough without clearing a chain, the multiplier resets. Speed, thus, is just as important as long, cascading chains.
Due to the presentation of the game, your first instinct is to play it like it's Tetris. That's the first habit that needs to be broken, but it's one that really only takes maybe about a half hour of play to transition out of. The playfield will feel very cramped indeed with the size of the blocks used - especially before you really start utilizing the couplers to their full advantage. Like Panel de Pon/Tetris Attack, though, once you get used to the game's mechanics, cascading clears will become fairly easy to set up and the game will become more or less instinctive to play. The only thing there will be how fast you can actually perform. The later levels of Endless mode will especially test your speed.
With that all out of the way, the tl;dr of my review is: "It's a great game, especially for $5."
The game doesn't really do anything new. It takes ideas from its many predecessors and puts them together in a single game that actually manages to have an identity of its own. It adds just enough of its own thing (particularly with the couplers and simplistic, but demanding scoring mechanics) to be engaging for the person who likes to chase after higher leaderboard placement. There aren't too many people actively playing the game, so you might find it easy to hit top ten within just a few hours of play (I personally, at the time of this writing, have a top 3 spot in each Race leaderboard and I feel it certainly isn't because of my skill,) but that rarely stops people from wanting to improve for their own sake.
From a technical standpoint, it's rock solid. It's very simple with simple graphics and simple animations that have a good amount of color to them. It feels like it was intended to be a game for mobile made in Unity (mostly because it is,) but actually done correctly. It has enough eye candy to make detonations satisfying to watch, but not enough to really distract you. Screen shake can be a bit annoying after an hour or so of play, but that can thankfully be turned off. Same with controller vibration if applicable to you.
The soundtrack is pretty alright too. It's a dynamic soundtrack of otherwise repetitive techno that amps up in tempo as you reach the top of the screen. Repetitive, in this case, is not a bad thing; it helps keep you focused and zoned into the game. That said, you'll probably end up turning it off after an hour or so and just listening to your own music. If it gets a mobile port, though, the music is a pretty good companion to the game.
There are a few caveats, though. Design-wise, the game isn't as 'tight' as Tetris. The size of the blocks compared to the size of the playfield doesn't always make it conducive to making the types of chains the game really wants you to make. It can be very hard to actually link couplers together as a result of this; a lot of the time, you end up having to bury a coupler under the blocks because you simply don't have room to utilize it.
A lot of this feels due to the block generator. In Tetris games, especially later ones - especially the Sega/Arika ones - the block generator actually isn't random. It is randomly seeded to give you blocks in a specific order, but the blocks all have an intended placement for perfect play. Anode doesn't seem to have this. It feels completely random (at least as random as a computer can get) without any real rhyme or reason to it. It is entirely possible to get three detonators of the same color in a row. It's possible to three couplers of the same shape in a row, just in different configurations that make them even harder to use.
Sometimes your success really does feel like it's up to the RNG on whether or not you'll actually be able to keep up your multiplier. Planning your chains, of course, helps this tremendously, but there is only so much planning you can really do until you have to bury your plans with blocks of different colors because that is literally all you're actually getting. If the playfield were two spaces wider, I feel this would be significantly less of a problem, but maybe there is something I'm missing and simply need to play it more.
I have not been able to try multiplayer mode. The lack of online multiplayer is actually a pretty big issue since this game seems perfect for it. Hopefully we'll see it in a future patch.
Overall, Anode is a great game and especially so for its price. I think it would be even better as a mobile game, but as a PC game, it's still a good buy. The core mechanics are solid, all of the standard puzzle modes are there. With online multiplayer, this would honestly be a no-brainer purchase for people who enjoy block puzzle games of this sort. Even as it stands now, though, it's absolutely worth trying for what is basically the price of lunch.

So, the funny thing about Overlord is that originally I never really finished it or saw a need to finish it. The premise is great: play the bad guy, kill the corrupted heroes. It's a pleasure to play overall, but trying to keep your minions alive is a pain and before long I lost my save file to an accidental hard drive failure. I just recently came back to play Overlord after playing Pikmin 2 again and was a little sad that I never really gave it another chance.
It's inevitable that I'm going to compare this game to Pikmin so let's get that out of the way right now. This is evil fantasy Pikmin, just with a little more story, morality, and a ♥♥♥♥ton more strategy. You'll be gathering resources to spawn hundreds and hundreds of your four typed expendable minions, using their vast numbers to decimate the enemy, and get large treasures for yourself in a large fantasy world with many different "hubs". This is where the simularities end. Unlike Pikmin, Overlord is more forward with the fact that your minons are expendable and are going to die en masse. As you move through the areas, you'll find many opportunities to replenish your dwindling minion supply though you don't always get the choice to what minion types you can replenish. Typically the game will put out brown or red minon pits as to say "You're going to need tanks and ranged warriors up ahead" and that's as far as the hints go. From there the game throws everything at you when you least suspect it, decimates your well-equipped army, and forces you to fight your way back to the last pit with the knowledge of what to expect next time you make a run through that area. While losing a few minions isn't a big deal, losing a lot can be more painful, as minion survival and attack power is based on little items they collect as you break things and the spines of your enemies. Meaning a party wipe means that you'll need to grab more equipment or be disappointed in how squishy your new forces are against the incoming threat.
I think my favorite part of Overlord however, is just how strategy oriented it is. While your minions are dumb, they're typically not dumb enough to outright kill themselves (typically) or attack things you don't want to attack (typically). Your job is to manage your horde in such a way to best succeed in every situation. I went for the straight in brown rush as browns are the toughest of your minions. But I could have used greens to flank enemies or clusters of reds to pick off enemies as they approached. You're given a lot of tools  to make the best of every situation you're put in no matter your strategy and it was something I truly enjoyed in this game.
Last bit which may have been stronger at the time but more meh now, is the corruption mechanic. You can go balls to the wall evil and just destroy everything while taking things for yourself, or you can be pragmatic in your conquering and try to be nice to the locals in exchange for other benefits. Neither option is truly bad, though going 100% corrupt takes a lot of effort and is probably more trouble than it's worth. Each path will lead to different ultimate spells. A completely evil Overlord will get spells that scream "screw subtlety!" and promote a chaotic scorched earth playstyle, while a more reserved one will get spells that do a fair bit of damage but not accidentally harm your loyal worshipers in the process.
Overall Overlord is a good game, and one I'm glad I gave a second chance in playing as ultimately I enjoyed it more than I did the Pikmin games. Sure those games are cute in their own way, but Overlord's gameplay is a complete improvement, feeling like a more advanced Pikmin (albiet more about fighting recklessly than managing your limited number of troops for long periods). I can easily recommend it for full price since the game's been out for a while and sells for peanuts, but I probably would have recommended it at full price if it wasn't anyways.

Orwell is an investigative game akin to a visual novel. You play as The Investigator, someone whose job it is to use the powerful Orwell surveillance system to solve crimes – or in this case, solve a particular crime. You see, a bomb was set off in Freedom Plaza in The Nation, killing three people, and it is your job to try and catch the bomber before they can kill anyone else.
Orwell is more like an interactive novel than an ordinary video game – the game is wholly centered around reading text for about four and a half hours, and while it has more meaningful interaction than most visual novels, the actual gameplay itself is very simple and not very action-oriented. It is a very cerebral experience, and if reading lots of text isn’t your cup of tea, this is not the game for you.
You start out with a single person of interest – a young woman who left the Plaza shortly before the bomb went off. She was a protester who had been arrested for attacking a police officer, but who wasn’t prosecuted for it due to lack of evidence. It quickly becomes clear that not all is as it seems, and it seems unlikely that she personally was the bomber – but she has past associations with a group known as Thought, an anti-government group which often engages in extremist rhetoric. But are they really the sort of people who would kill people? Or are they just innocent bystanders coincidentally caught up in the investigation?
Orwell is a very ambiguous game, and it is precisely this ambiguity which really makes the game work. Thought is upset about living in a surveillance state, but it is clear from your perspective as The Investigator that the system is designed to be humane in many ways – the investigator passes on information to someone else, whose job it is to analyze the data. You cannot investigate people who aren’t targets – unless someone has been designated as suspicious by actual data, you cannot collect data at all them, nor are you allowed to go snooping through their things. But if they are a target of interest, you have nigh unlimited authority to go snooping. And while the state is clearly a bit authoritarian, it is also clear that the system works – crime has gone down, and you can catch several criminals over the course of the game who really did do bad things. The person on the other end, who helps to determine whether or not the data is really indicative of wrongdoing, is a genuinely nice person who cares about people and who urges you to collect more data. The leader of The Nation appears to genuinely be trying to help out neighboring states.
But all of this is muddied with the ambiguity of the fact that not everyone in the government is nice, and the general sinister nature of your surveillance. Your actions do have consequences, and it is clear that if you made the wrong decisions, you could potentially feed people bad data and get people put in jail – and the choice of whether or not to feed people bad data, and the impression you leave the government on people, is dependent on what data you give them.
The game, thus, is a combination of an investigation and a moral choice system – you are not only investigating who might be the bomber, but also deciding what is and is not relevant, what should and should not be part of the investigation, and you have the power to wrongfully put people in jail or put people in danger. The very simple gameplay of choosing what pieces of highlighted information to put into a database from various documents, webpages, emails, and phone and text conversations thus takes on a great deal of weight, and makes you think about what you’re doing in a very different way from other investigatory games, as you think of it not only in terms of true/false, but also whether the information morally belongs in the hands of the government.
The game’s gameplay also shows how a system like that can lead to paranoia, as you see people engage in a lot of extremist rhetoric and it is easy to jump to conclusions and morally convict someone in your mind who didn’t do anything worse than complain, as well as how easy it is to prejudge someone in the opposite direction as well, making you think more positively of them than they truly deserve. And it puts stress on the player as well – you cannot take back your actions, so if you incorrectly present someone as a dangerous criminal, you can’t fix it and have to live with the consequences.
How humane the system is – and who is in the right and wrong – is a complicated question that the game ultimately doesn’t answer for itself, but which the player answers via their actions throughout the game. Like “The Lady or the Tiger”, the way the player responds to the story really reflects as much on the player’s own evaluation of humanity, and how they weigh the risks and benefits of a system like that. Rather than being preachy about how evil the system is, the game also shows why people might like a system like that and want it to be implemented. It is perhaps the most even-handed presentation of the subject matter I’ve seen, and it achieves this by putting the player in the seat of someone who might be a part of such a system and showing just how ambiguous the system can be and how much power they wield, both how dangerous it can be if misused but how beneficial it can be if used appropriately.

Let me start off by saying this is not a scary game in the usual sense, I got actually scared around twice on it and I can't play Scratches. It's also not 'fun' in the sense that a book is also not fun. You won't fight monsters or solve hard puzzles, there's almost no skill involved. It is however a very creepy and very well-thought out horror game, and one of the best story-driven games I've played.
There are other reviews or places where you can look up the story. You shouldn't if you haven't played the game, but let me tell you it's good. I'll give out just enough of it to explain one of the things I loved about SOMA: right at the beginning there's a disconnection-like experience (I was in one place, closed my eyes, now I'm somewhere else entirely) during an experimental procedure got a brain scan, and so the first thought is "ok this abandoned leaky place must represent my damaged brain and I have to fix it". The developers know what you're thinking, and the actual story is much better and less metaphorical.
Also, this isn't a quest for your own gain. Quoting someone somewhere else "there's no hope in the world of SOMA". This feels reflected from your interactions with monsters: you'll never beat them, at most you'll survive. You're not trying to win anything or make life better for you, everything you do should be for the sake of someone else. Which is actually one of the big gripes I had with the story, because while we the player understand that our actions are for the sake of others, the main character seems lost on this: right at the end (literal seconds before the credits) the main character revealed how little he understood of what he was trying to do, despite having had it explained to him and actually having done it before. You realize you spent hours playing as someone who couldn't really get why he did what he did, and while this isn't a necessarily a flaw - nowhere does it say you have to play as a smart character - but it does breaks immersion.
The level design was actually very good. Due to the setting, there was no need to include an invisible wall or wizard-made fence you can't climb over, and the limits to where you can go feel more natural. The levels themselves seemed larger than they were and to me that usually indicates good design. This is where the horrifying-not-scary factor comes into play: everything (the sounds, the lighting) makes you fear going into the next room even if you know it's fine, even if you've been in that room before. Not because you're on edge due to jump scares - in fact I like that it barely uses jump scares, and when it does they don't come off as cheap thrills at all - but because it's designed to make you feel worried about turning a corner. You're at the top of a staircase and you can hear banging down below, where you have to go. There are also situations with a more usual type of fear, usually scripted events where a monsters chases you or something is behind a door/hallway, but these are a handful and like I said above don't feel cheap.
I liked how the monsters all had different ways to sense and so different ways to counter. Some attack when they see you at all, others when they see you move, some when you look at them, others when you look around. It was fun how the game kept playing at your memory - oh you learned how to evade this enemy? Here's an enemy that behaves in the exact opposite way.
I don't know what to say in terms of graphics. It looked very good and it's hard to compare it to anything because graphics-wise I don't know anything that looks similar.
The story itself makes you think a lot about what it means to be human, or a REAL human, and what a conscience is. This can lead to excellent several-hours-long pub conversations. Your choices have pratically no interference with the game, but frankly I preferred it that way. It made me do what I think was right instead of googling for which choice gave the best loot. By the way, there's no loot or inventory. It makes you explore to the information, not to make your life easier.

Every now and then, one gets the itch to descend into a tomb of madness and arcane power, delving ever deeper into the earth while fielding a veritable army of minions to keep impudent heroes at bay. This game scratches that itch very effectively in a combination of base defense and puzzle gaming.
And it also shows you why evil overlords tend to go mad, since unless you can blaze through the puzzle part, a lot of the challenge is the fact that it's hard work to stay on top of it all. You have to clear the puzzles to get resources, but then you have to spend those resources just as fast to expand your base and rehire minions as they inevitably die to the blades of the heroes who intrude upon your lair. As heroes die, resources rain down to refill the puzzle grid... blocking downward expansion until you clear them, but rebuilding your puzzle resources. You get potions to buff or heal your minions, but while you're using them, you're not solving the puzzles, which means you're not getting resources to resummon dead minions... and if you don't solve the puzzles fast enough you don't get the space to build expansions, but while you're solving the puzzles heroes keep attacking and the grid is full again and aaaaagh how did heroes get down to the sanctum level?! Guards! Guards!
Having to continually switch contexts keeps the game from feeling stale during a playthrough, and it's easy to pick up, though some of the mechanics like potions are more challenging. The 'match colored blocks' style puzzles should be familiar to basically everyone by now, and if you can do that, you can figure out everything else through play.
Great potential in this game, even in "early access".

Want to be EVIL? (C'mon, you KNOW you want to!) Want to smite pesky do-gooders who invade YOUR realm? Want to relive the glory of being the Horned Reaper or that oppressive Overlord with his Merry Minions? Then this game is for YOU!!
Join Jake Huhman on his diabolical adventures in hoard-pillaging, tomb-building, and !!Hero-Mashing!! Unlock an ever-expanding range of murderous minions, blasphemous buildings, alluring loot, and archaic artefacts! Be the best Tyrant that ever lived...well, until you die! But EVIL is never truly defeated! Empower a new Tyrant to even loftier heights (of score) and foul play - if you dare!
On a more serious note, it really is a wonderful game, with a highly dedicated developer. New content is rolled out on a weekly, if not daily, basis. If you have questions in the forums, he WILL take the time to talk to you and help you out. He has incorporated many good suggestions from many people, and the game has become that much better for it.
You are cast as the anonymous Tyrant (presumed Lich) who sets up shop under a remote mausoleum (the Tomb). You begin with only your Sanctum, with an endless well of resources from previous Tyrants yawning down below your feet. You slide rows horizontally in this hoard and match regions of four of the same type. There are many - Ruins, Treasure, Equipment, Mechanisms, Flesh, Bones, Arcane, etc. Each match you make earns you a given amount of that resource. Making matches in specific, predefined shapes will increase the maximum storage of the resource you matched. This allows you to focus on the resources you'll need, if you are careful.
The game does have build paths. Many floors (aka rooms) are mutually exclusive. You cannot build a Portentous Portal (Imps) and a Wicked Workshop (Gremlins, and produces Mechanisms and Equipment that drops into the hoard below) in the same Tomb. The monsters each floor gives have their own unique abilities, traits, and uses. Some are used as Hunters who will pursue enemies wherever they go. Others merely follow a patrol route, fighting what they encounter on the route (which is down to the Sanctum, then back up again, repeated). So having that Lupine Lair (wolves) or Gossamer Gallows (giant spiders) gives you very useful hunters. You will need them.
From your first slide of the Hoard puzzle, a timer begins counting down for a wave of Heroes. They will emerge one by one from the mists of the forest and camp on the surface until the timers reaches zero, at which point they invade the Tomb en masse, intent on getting to the Sanctum (and YOU) and putting an end to your Evil Reign. Kill them quickly as the next wave comes sooner than you'd like in each case. Each floor that hosts a battle will have a maximum of four monsters and four heroes slugging it out in initiative order. If more heroes or monsters enter the floor, they bypass the fight by moving through the background and continuing on until they themselves get into combat.
As you fulfill certain objectives, known as Prophecies, you unlock further floors and artifacts for use. Artifacts are earned by matching them up in the Hoard when they appear. They give an ongoing benefit as long as you have them in your item bar (inventory of a sort). For example, once you unlock King-sized Kibble and match it up, all of your monsters that have the trait "Beast" will gain a permanant +2 HP from that point on. I refer you back to the part about Giant Spiders and Wolves. They have the Beast trait.
One of the great things about this game is that entirely new floors are being added all the time. Traps you can place on floors just got implemented. There are already floors (the Harrowing Hallway) that are nothing BUT a gauntlet of traps to slice and skewer those weak heroes who pass through them. Along with the new floors come new creatures, with new possibilities. Bear in mind, they game is still early accesss, so imagine, if you will, how much new content Jake can pile into this game before he considers it to be version 1.0. Even then, I'm sure he won't stop adding even MORE goodness to the game. Bosses, checkpoints, tricks, more traps, legacy traits and items that carry on from one Tyrant to the next. Oh, the possibilities!
You know what, readers? Buy the game. You'll have plenty of fun with it, and for the price of $8.00, its a bargain. Think, thats about 3 Quesoritos at Taco Bell. Not so pricey, eh? As for myself, I'm done talking about it, now i'm going to go play it...

Shorter: A clever and deep mix of tower building/defense, puzzling, and strategy with a sense of humor that can be very addictive.   Well-supported and being constantly improved by the creator, the game is a must-buy for puzzle/strategy hybrid enthusiasts.
Tomb of Tyrants' idea is simple - you're a tyrant in the Tomb of Tyrants, using your hoard of good to build a deeper and deeper dungeon to keep pesky adventurers away.  As you build more floors to the tomb, you get more monsters and options to deal with the various do gooders.  As you build, use resource floors, and defeat adventuers, you add to your hoard.  Oh, sure the adventurers will defeat you eventually, so how long can you hold out?
Tomb of Tyrant's tower defense element is also simple - add floors with traps, resources, and monster spawns, buy minions, and use equipment to defeat a continuing stream of fantasy tropes.  Where it does one different is the hoard mechanic.  That big pile of gold, equipment, ruins, bones, flesh, and so on is a giant match-four puzzle - you have to match up the things in your hoard to acquire resources.
So, in short, as you build the tower, you're also playing a matching-tile puzzle game.
This puzzle element adds a certain something to the game.  This could be just agame of tower planning, minion summoning, and hero-mashing.  The puzzle element means that you break out of standard mechanics and resource management, and have to apply several set of skills at once. It also avoids (but doesn't remove) the inevitable wait-for-the-attack games like this can have - usually as heroes gather you're busy taking advantage of what the last group of heroes dropped.
The game also has a sense of humor, with amusing names, jokey flavor text, and a pixel-graphic aesthetic.  It's charmingly light-hearted and has it's own personality.  There's something delightfully fun about the whole affair that feels good-natured . . . well good-natured for a game of killing adventurers.
The game requires a lot of strategy.  You have to decide which floors to build  (some of which may exclude or be required for other floors).  You have to choose what minions to summon - your choices in floors determine what minons are available.  You have to choose what items to use - and if you want to buy or sell them depending on the dungeon you've built.
Adding to all of this are the unlockables.  You complete "prophecies" (reaching certain achievements) to unlock even more floors and thus more options in the game.  These unlocked items become a permanent part of your inventory, so the next Tyrant can take advantage of them.
The game has a few flaws:
* The music is lackluster.
* The help guide isn't that  helpful, but is being improved.  There needs to be more information on the game creatures, rules, and features.
* There are some controller issues, but I understand that's not high priority right now.
It's hard to criticize the game as it's quite clever and well-done even in early access, and fun enough to be compelling (first day I got it I played it for 3 hours).  Most additions to the game are a mix of UI improvements and even more content around an already solid game.
The author (apparently it's written by one person) adds new content as it develops and is enthused about feedback - in fact he even responded to this review, which shows a fantastic level of ownership.  The author also posts reguarly in the forums and even shows screenshots of new ideas.
The game is already highly entertaining and well done - and is still getting better all the time.
Now excuse me, the adventurers are knocking at my door, and the Blasphemous Basiilica isn't going to desecrate itself . . .

(please note that I decided to write this review is interspersed with comparisons between this Ship Simulator and the older Ship Simulator by Vstep)
Bit of a mixed bag this one, frankly not very impressed with it, espesially given that I myself am a sailor (though by no means a captain) with a little boat handling experience.
When compared to Vstep's long abandoned Ship Simulator series this one's got quite a lot of catching up to do, even though the Vstep shipsim has numerous faults of it's own.
First thing I noticed about this game that kind of set the trend for what I was expecting of it was the poor terminology used in the manual, for example referencing to the 'Front Engine' and 'Rear Engine Throttle' controls, the proper names for these being the Bow and Stern Thrusters.
As far as I can tell this game has only two features better than that of the Vstep shipsim. The first being the inclusion of independent control for port and starboard azimuth steering units, as found on the Tug, though unfortunely let down by the clear fact this game's developers obviously don't know exacly how these units work in real life. The second, possibly more obvious one, being the distinct lack of bugs which were a notorious problem with the Vstep simulator. As far as thing go thats about it for being ahead of it's (dormant) competition.
Where graphics are concerned this game isn't too bad, all things considered, it's fairly level with the Vstep one, though I would consider Vstep to be slightly ahead. So far I can't say I've found much in the way of issues with the physics, but I may be wrong. However there are a few things with the physics and general effects that could do with attention, such as for some reason the ships seem to create a bow wave when going astern (reversing), and one thing I found when I came along side the cargo ship in the first tug mission, I lightly brushed the side of the ship with the side of the tug, a move that would be fairly common place in reality, resulted in severe damage and caused me to sink. In reality the tug would be fitted with rubber fenders, as can actually be seen on it's sides in the game, which are there to dampen any very light brushes resulting in minimal damage, if any.
This game has a little more in the way of interactive/functional controls on the bridge, though frankly their functions being fairly unrealistic, such as light and horn switches. The horn seems to operate on a repeating pulse setting when turned on and won't stop until turned off again. Personally I think they missed a trick here as they could have opted for a selective horn signalling system as used on real ships, one-uping Vstep. The lighting is something they really put no though into as it only turns on a few deck lights, not the more obvious navigation lights.
The steering isn't that great, though thankfully is much better than the horrible control setup of Ship Simulator:  Maritime Search and Rescue. One rather nice touch with the controls is that both the throttle and steering are set so that they take time to complete their movments, as in real life, rather than just instand full rudder or power. The steering/rudder angle on the featured ships only goes up to 10 degrees in either direction, both poor and unrealistic as the typical maximum rudder angle for the average ship is 40-45 degrees, as reflected in the Vstep game. As I mentioned before, the developers of this game decided to include the use of azimuth steering units with certain vessels, as did Vstep, but unlike Vstep did have enough of a brainwave to program in individual steering control, but unfortunately They don't actually know how these units work, where as Vstep do. Just to clear up, an azimuth unit is effectively a pod fitted with a propeller mounted under the ship which can be rotated though 360 degrees thus eliminating the need for a rudder or reverse gear and giving the ship better agility than with a conventional rudder and fixed-shaft propeller setup.
Just like the Vstep shipsim, this on comes with a mission editor. At first it seems quite simple to use but I still haven't got the hang of it, so I suspect looks may be deceiving, also not really helped by the camera being in a fixed birds-eye-view, only the height above ground being ajustable. Good luck to anyone who can figure it out.
To sum it all up this game does have potential here, but I'm not convinced by it. The best thing the developers of this game could do is have a good long shot with Vsteps (now possibly abandoned or furgotten, jugging by their website) Ship Simulator series and see where this game has to improve. So I don't recommend this game, at least not yet.
Instead I recommend you try out one of the Ship Simulator series from Vstep, The newest one Ship Simulator Extremes (2009 release) being available on Steam, but be prepared for bugs/glitches which are likely to appear.

This game is fun.
But holy hell is it short and stupid. The campaign only took 5 hours.
You normally wouldn't expect stellar writing in a high-octane action game, but characters change their dispositions and motivations mid-sentence.
"I'm BETRAYING YOU! I'm gonna kill a bunch of people! .... UGH! You've defeated me..."
"Don't you die on me! We are friends even though you were literally just trying to kill me and millions of other people and start a war for economic gain!"
"Friends to the end! But get out of here! You have to finish YOUR mission that contradicts my own! That's an ORDER! I'll blow myself up and kill the other soldiers I'm supposed to be allied with to cover for you!"
A lot of it aside from being super inconsistent is just tone-deaf or is trying to set up some kind of big conspiracy that it never explains.
That all said it runs alright and is fun for the most part. Kinda frustrating how fast your boost runs out, and when it does run out you're left walking at 70% speed for a few seconds, which will happen a lot (also happens whenever you melee attack or if you take too much damage). It's also littered with QTEs and overly long and campy cinematics. The game doesn't feel like it has the level of flow it was aiming for.
But, in spite of all that, it's still an entertaining romp. You blast your way through hordes of enemies using a variety of weapons in a mindless spectacle of bullets and missiles. Grievances for the plot don't matter as much, and the debuffs and QTEs at least aren't deal breakers.
It's nothing stellar, but an okay purchase if you can grab it on sale. (Probably not worth it at full price.)

Take 2 parts Pikmin, 1 part Lord of the Ring and a dash of humor.  Shake and serve cold.
Overlord is a unique game.  You play "The Overlord" a dark and mysterious figure served by "minions".  Not the yellow twinkie shaped minions from Despicable me, but impish shaped creatures.   The player gets the ability to chose what type of overlord will he be, either good or evil, and that's really the weirdest part of the game.
It's not that morality systems are necessarily bad, it's just that the "Overlord" in this game usually has the option to be benevolent or evil, and even when he's evil, it's quite tame.   The sequel will eventually figure this problem out with "Dominate or Destroy" morality choices.   However for this game, the choice is usually something like "do you give the food to the villagers or keep it for yourself.
The problem with this morality is neither is really that interesting.  Keeping the food doesn't give a noticeable difference other than less farming to do, which would be useful but by the end of the game, you can easily gather hundreds of minions with minimal work, and the game isn't hard enough that being selfish sounds good.
There is one morality choice that offers you to choose between two mistresses for your castle, and that's about the only choice that really matters because it decides what minions to power up.  The "good" choice though outweighs the bad choice.  Who knew being evil was so hard?
The point of this diversion though is that while the Overlord idea is "you are the villain".  In actual gameplay.  You're not really, and that's kind of the flaw of this game.  You're never as evil as you could be.  Yes you can be eviler than a "hero" but overall it's a pretty milquetoast version of evil.
However with that being said, the game is actually quite good.  In 2001 Pikman came out and was a fantastic adventure game, and then took forever with sequels, apparently the creator of this game saw this market barely being serviced and stepped up to fulfill the need, and to be honest they did.  Overlord plays like Pikman though better, and with no time limits, solving the big complaint about Pikman.
The player is able to summon four types of minions each with different strengths, and using the minion in various ways he has to make his way through levels.  The minions can be controlled in a few different ways, from sweeping the minions left and right, to tasking the minions directly.  The minions are smart enough that placing them in a location they'll intelligently fight with enemies, or when sweeped around an interactable item, they'll figure out what to do (with a few exception, but exceptions for the right reason).
The Overlord himself is quite weak, but over time (and forging) will gain a great amount of power to the point that he'll eventually be able to stand up to enemies almost solo by the end of the game.   In fact the weak form at the beginning of the game feels very different from the end of the game where the player feels like he doesn't need the minions as much (though of course he does)
As for the story, it starts off feeling like a rip off of Lord of the Rings,  with the character clearly being influenced by Sauron, the first town being named "Spree" and the first enemies are halflings.  There's other clear Lord of the Ring mythology lifts (Elves and dwarves of course).  but after Spree the game seems to diverge from Lord of the Ring and finds it's own fantasy story, and does well with it, though borrowing heavily from other mythos.
The thing is though, the game works in all the right ways.  There's never an extremely annoying part of the game, and the game lasts at least 15 hours, probably closer to 18.  While there's some padding to this number due to the length of dungeons, you're never in the same environment for very long.  There's a decent amount of exploration, and a few alternate paths that give different result.
Players will likely need a guide at some point due to a weak quest system which doesn't tell the player exactly where things are, but at the same time, it's not a horrible system and only once did I miss a major area.   Still this is 2007, so a lot of the handholding that modern games do is missing.   That's not necessarily a bad thing, but can make this game frustrating if you find yourself in that position.
Overall though, this is a game which barely got noticed when it first came out, and probably deserved a bigger audience.  I really liked Overlord, and the fact I put 20 hours or more into it speaks to that.   If you like Pikman, like quasi "evil" or just like to play something a little different, I would recommend Overlord.

I may not have any time put into the game on steam during the writing of this review, but rest assured my experience with the game is vast.
I've played this game since it's inception years ago when I was still in High School. The game isn't something you're likely to spend hundreds of hours playing, but it's a blast to play with friends. You get a mouse that you name and then get to costomize with hats, glasses, scarfs, and a vast many other accessories. You can unlock these customizable items with cheese, which you collect as you play the game. You're essentially guaranteed to get cheese, as it happens the be the actual goal of the game. You take your mouse over, through, and under obstacles in an attempt to collect cheese and make it back to your hole. Pretty simple concept, though the game it's self can be challenging at times.
Not only are there tons and tons of base maps for you to play on, community created maps are also thrown into the playlist. The variety of maps to play on is virtually unlimited, and if you think you can challenge people even further, you can create your own maps as well. The other challenging aspect to the game is the Shaman. The more cheese you successfully bring back to your hole the quicker you get to become a Shaman. Your duty as Shaman is not to collect cheese, but a completely different dynamic. You are given the power to either aid your fellow mice to victory, or cause chaos and dispair. The Shaman gets the ability to build objects on the map which can either assist or hinder your fellow mice, either by intention or accidents. You get skill trees that you can allocate points into to better make use of your shamanistic powers, and you also get to customize your Shaman with different colors as well.
You can even form Guilds to keep your friends together and keep in contact through your guild chat regardless of what room you may be in. Which is ideal as it happens to be a rather sociable game. Unfortunately, there happens to be quite a bit of stupidity. Though there tends to be hackers, which don't really impact the game as they usually use their hacking to ensure their capture of the cheese, people will sometimes call you out for hacking and may also attempt to report you if you happen to beat them to the hole. This is what can happen when you have a racing game with a map by map leaderboard. It doesn't happen all the time, or everywhere either, so it's not that big of a deal in the grand scope of things.
The last thing really worth mentioning is that there are a myriad of game modes to choose from. Switch from type to type or stick to one depending on preference. I won't go into as much detail into the game modes, and I'll just let you guys delve into the game and test it out yourselves. Remember, the game's focus is all about being silly and having fun. Don't take it seriously and you can have a blast. And remember, trolling is apart of the game, so don't get upset if you get screwed over. It's all apart of the fun. ;]

I bought Seasons After Fall on impulse (what with it being the only recent thing on the Steam new releases page that looked like anything I'd actually want to play) for its decent artsyle and good soundtrack, but every indie platformer on Steam these days looks nice and has a good soundtrack, so what sets Seasons After Fall apart from, say, Ori & the Blind Forest or Thomas Was Alone?
Well it's certainly not its deep and compelling story. It's fairly basic, but not particularly bad, just does enough to hold everything together. There's no combat, which I felt was kind of a missed opportunity, as it would have been cool to use the Power of the Seasons (which is a great mechanic that I've never seen before implemented well) used to defeat certain bosses, not that a game needs combat to be good and it certainly isn't a deal breaker, just might have been a cool little addition. There's also a lot of backtracking through the same 4 environments (albeit opening different areas at different times so that the puzzles don't become stale).
What I like about this game is the puzzle aspect of the puzzle platformer. As said before, the Power of the Seasons mechanic is used very well, as the environment around you reacts to whichever season it happens to be e.g. geysers will be frozen in winter so you can reach higher ledges, mushrooms open up in the autumn etc. There are some puzzles in here that get you thinking. The main one that stands out for me is one with fireflies in the "summer" portion of the game, but there are a few others as well.
Overall, certainly worth a go if you like these kind of platformers. Not particularly challenging, but puzzles are satisfying enough to keep going to the end.

Seasons After Fall is a 2D puzzle platformer. In Seasons After Fall you play as a newley born seed of the forest. You're supposed to restore the seasons and the forest sanctuary itself but being just a seed, you can't really do all that without a proper body. So you possess the body of the animal closest to you, which at the time, happens to be a fox. It's possible to play using a keyboard but a gamepad is preferred. Works fine with my rock candy xbox 360 controller, I can't vouch for any other controller but I know it with that one for sure.
The graphical artstyle is stunning, reminds me a lot of Ori and the Blind Forest and in my opinion is just as gorgeous. At the time of this review there is some issue with the audio mixing. If you're using the English voice over, it gets drowned out by the music sometimes making almost impossible to hear. So I recommend using subtitles until that's fixed. There's only 1 slider for the main volume and none seperately for BGM, Sound FX and Voice...yet. It also includes German and French voice overs.
The gameplay is pretty solid, the controls feel tight and responsive. There's no death in the game, you can jump and bark to interact with objects. The big gimmick this game has is being able to change seasons in order to access new areas. For instance if you switch the season to Autumn, you can grow dormant mushrooms into platforms so you can get to higher areas. Seasons like Summer and Spring change how other foliage grows and raises or lowers water levels. In winter you can freeze water spouts and climb on them. Those are just a few examples. It gets considerably more complex once you have the ability to change every season. The game does have achievements and although they were broken at first, I did find some help in the forums about how to fix them but sadly I had to start the game over again to get the earlier ones I missed. There are also some unlockable extras that are earned from discovering flower patches. After you walked through enough flower patches you'll unlock pictures of what the game looked like during the years of its development. Very interesting to see how the game progressed since the first picture in 2009.
It's not the game for you if you're looking for some crazy action, it's a very relaxing game to play. Sometimes a little frustrating if you haven't figured out where to go next.  It's an experience that will last 6-7 hours or more depending on your skill level and whether or not you're an achievement hunter. I think this game is well developed and damn near perfect for the kind of game it is (except for the audio issues). The developers are active and helpful on the forums too. I recommend it.

Thomas Was Alone is a game that I can honestly say surprised me. I picked it up in a bundle and played it due to boredom one day. From a gameplay standpoint it is a relatively simple puzzle platformer that requires you to switch between various characters and utilize each of their special attributes to make it to the exit of each level.
The interesting thing is that each character is nothing more than a block of varying color and size. The puzzles are never too difficult and the game moves at a decently quick pace and that is good because the story is told well at the pace the game allows you to progress through it and that is where the game really surprised me. Story.
For a game that consists of very basic 2D graphics and a cast of characters that are nothing more than various blocks it had an amazing story. Each level starts with a small bit of narration, very well done narration. It is through this narration that the story is primarily told. (a bit of information is garnered from text between sections, but the real heart of this story comes through this narration.) This works very well because the narration is very good. It allows to you see each of these colored blocks as a living being with its own hopes, dreams, feelings, insecurities and aspirations and allowed me to care more about the fate of a colored block than I ever thought I could. I found myself right from the start referring to the characters by name, they were always “Thomas” or “Chris” or “Paula” never “The Red One” or “The Orange One” or “The Purple One”. I felt something for these characters.
I also have to give the game credit for how it develops the story. The story is tightly connected to the gameplay, and because of the nature of the story I feel like this tale could only be told through a video game. It would not work as a book or a movie because you feel how these various blocks move, you control them and guide them to their destination and, as the way these characters handles is intrinsically tied to their personality I feel like it adds a great amount of depth to the story.
Also, special mention has to be given to the music in this game. It is fantastic, it conveys the feeling that the story is aiming for perfectly. There is little more to say about it, the sound works outstandingly well.
All of this, driven by the narrative, keeps you moving through each short stage and leaves you eager to get to the next one.
I would very much recommend picking up this game and playing it all the way through in one sitting.

First, European Ship Simulator was not created by the same development team that brought you Eurotruck Simulator. Arguably, there was an effort by the Euroboat team to make it appear that way. Unfortunately, with European Ship Simulator, what you get is a shallow experience at best without any campaign mode, meaningful objectives, or even a sense of immersion to say the least.

I've completed 4 of the missions so far, successfully I might add, and it wasn't challenging at all. You have a short selection of "Missions" along side a mission editor. I started off with a tug boat mission. The tug boat itself was sufficiently detailed and breaking into open sea from the harbor was satisfying, the choppiness kicked up and there seemed to be correct current physics to deal with. That, unfortunately, was about all there was to be impressed by.

Dropping the tug was a simple press-this-button, which displays a bunch of balloons around your boat. All I had to do was select one of my ballons, and click on the balloon from the ship I would be towing. This easy process connects the two balloons together with a rope, instantly. At this point I'm ready to tow. The massive tanker's front end would dip inappropriately into the sea while towing, which was weird. The physics aren't perfect but I can get passed it. There is no complicated mooring procedure either once you get to your destination. You simply float to the next arrow and you're done. Congratulations. *yawn*

Later, I tried the speedboat. A speedboat mission! My objective was to drive my speedboat to a yacht and pick up a rich lady in distress. On my way, I clipped through just about every bit of ocean, I was practically a submarine. Additionally, the reaction of the boat to the choppy water felt so unauthentic that it made me feel like the developers included this irritation just to force me to press the A and D keys a whole bunch of times and not fall asleep.

To spice things up, I tried the cruise liner. I figured, this should be a challenge. Wrong again, and that brings me to my conclusion. European Ship Simulator is a disaster at the price it is asking. I've played more complex and immersive sims on the iPad. I don't know how some people came the the conclusions they did by recommending this game, it really does make me wonder. The game offers you nothing in return for your effort. It is over-simplified, unrealistic and broken. Wait for the massive content update it needs and in the meantime there are better boating simulators out there.

Overlord Review.
Intro, Overlord is a cult classic original series created by Codemaster's in 2007. Its a very unique game where you control a 3rd person overlord then command an army of minions kind of like an RTS.
Pros
1  The game is a personal favorite of mine a one of a kind game that has one of a kind gameplay. The only other game that is like this is overlord 2 and if you ask me the first was far better than the second. I just have never played a game like this wanting to make an army and gearing them up for tough battles. The game also has a legendary difficulty that I have not managed to beat yet.
2 The game has amazing sound, I don't think most people have tried the 3D audio, surround sound of the game but it sounds amazing. The game has wonderful conveyance, so its difficult puzzle filled nature isn't such a pain to figure out when you have gnarl a well written character by the way, give you instructions and advice often. The games story is wonderful interesting and fresh, after all how many stories do you get to play as the villain in a game? If you have bought a new soundcard, speakers or something like that and you want a game to take full advantage of that overlord will sound great and you will be able to hear the environment.
3 The game is full of content, replay value and puzzles and has many different game modes. The game even has split screen multiplayer, lan and used to have online multiplayer. The split screen gameplay is lots of fun with a friends and the single player content is multiple hours worth as it will take time collection all the missing tower objects and finishing all the worlds and many levels.
Cons
1  The game has no mods, for being on PC for so long and for being such a classic and original game it is shocking that there are no huge mods to the game if it had official support or not. This may be a minor issue but I have bought the game more than once, and I was hoping to mod the game but nobody has made any mods for the game.
2  If you don't like puzzles the game isn't full of it as much as a puzzle game but it will constantly challenge your mind as you need to figure out how to do things, how to use your minions, what tactics and formations to use and how you will build your overlord. The game is also a huge pain when you spend a long time gearing up your minions only to have then all or almost all of them die in one attack that you didn't see coming. The game isn't the most casual and relaxing game because after all there is evil to be done.
3 the online multiplayer is 100% dead. It was not a huge part of the game, I never played the game online myself but I did play it locally and it was quite fun so it will be missed a little but to be honest the multiplayer is not that great it fun to play a few times but it loses its charm quite fast.
To Conclude overlord is a unique one of a kind classic with great sound, full of content and has good conveyance. While the multiplayer is dead, there are no mods unfortunately, and the puzzles and tactics filled nature of the game is not very easy to get into its still an excellent game that I would recommend to anyone wanting a new game. The game even has controller support. I have played the PC vanilla version on disk, then I have played the console xbox port with the raising hell DLC and I have played the steam port with all the DLC legendary difficulty, that costs money on the xbox port.
Do I recommend you buy this game? To put it bluntly, Yes for 19.99$ the game is worth it and for, 5.49$ the game is well worth it. I would recommend you get the raising hell DLC and see my review on that.  (note: my hours spent playing the game are not shown because raising hell the expansion is the new launcher and my game time is shown on the DLC)

When I was a kind in the 90s, there was a popular idea of "edutainment" - games that are entertaining, and also teach the player something goold, like math or spelling. Most of the attepmts failed at both tasks: they were neither educative nor entertaining. It was a rarity to see a game that did both parts right.
"Never Alone" is a rare beast: an edutainment game that doesn't suck. Sure, the gameplay is nothing to write home about: it's a simplistic puzzle platformer that doesn't really challenge either your reflexes or your mind. But it's made competently enough to help convey the main content of the game: an interactive documentary about the Iñupiat people, their way of life and their fairy tales. And this part is done beautifully: the visuals are very cute, the sound design helps build the atmosphere, and on the top of that there's an authentic voice of a storyteller, narrating the tale in its native language.
A short and beautiful game that helps you broaden your cultural horizons a bit.

Having played guitar for nearly seven years now in rock, metal, blues, and jazz, I was really needing something that put interest back into playing, like a new piece of gear. I found that in Rocksmith, and played it nearly 35 hours in my first five days of owning it. I love having the callouses back. That being said, the game is not perfect. I'll make a simple rundown of pros and cons for simplicity.
Pros:
- Definitely inspires you to play and learn songs. Whether you find your own style of playing before or after you learn a steaming pile of songs, it's always good to learn said steaming pile of songs. Rocksmith will definitely help you do this in a fun, relaxed, pseudo-Guitar Hero environment.
- Has a nearly flawless session mode where you can construct your own band that has a wide variety of styles, sounds, progressions, and can play in all the basic modes and scales with all 12 roots. It also has a very helpful and changable neck layout to show you exactly what scale they recommend you use. This is like a loop station +4, people!
- Songs have a fluid difficulty. If the game sees you rock, it'll make the next bit a little bit harder. If it sees you're having a lot of trouble, it'll dial it down. This spans from pretty much root notes only to having every note be invisible. This game has an infuriating way of making you learn songs ;).
- Has a sometimes helpful section repeater for every song.
- Has a MASSIVE amp emulator where you can try out digital versions of generic and some name brand gear to see what you want for a new song or purchase. These are all dependant on the quality of your computer speakers of course, but it's still nice to have a reference.
- You can change your tone in the middle of a song if you despise song's preset tone.
- An interesting pro, this program's DLC and price per song is generally roughly the same if not cheaper than sheet music, and you get a lot more. You get to hear the song, see a visual representation of how it's played, get alternate lead, rhythm, and bass parts, and a preview of how the guitarist got their tone with the amp emulator. Plus you get to beat the snot out of it over and over and score points.
- There are several other little pros scattered throughout, but these are the big ones.
Cons:
- My worst complaint with the game: Some of the ways this game has you play songs are ABSOLUTELY RIDICULOUS (yes, I mean to shout), and there's no way to change what frets it wants you to play from what I can tell. Fortunately, the game is just based on tone recognition, so if you can play it on a different string and it's easier for you, do it that way. Problem is, you have to ditch the way the game wants you to play at that point, so there's no on screen reference. For example, Are You Mine by the Arctic Monkies has you sliding all around the neck. I have learned to play it to where I hardly have to move from the second fret. Ultimately, this is kind of beneficial, as you should be learning the way you want to play, and hopefully that's without having to watch the Rocksmith screen. On a similar note, some of the rookie ways of playing songs can actually be harder than the advanced way because you don't know all of what's being played. This is a problem for me as an advanced guitarist because it's easier for me to play by chord names rather than some stepwise building of chords throughout the song.
- The other pretty unfortunate bit of this game is that it has a serious case of death-by-interface when you're first starting out. Everything the guitarist played on the song has to come down this alley at you and convey, in it's entirety, everything about that note: string, fret, duration, slidel vibrato, bend, temolo picking, harmonics, tapping, hammerons, pulloffs, anything that the guitarist could do has to be contained in that one tiny note flying toward you, and it's one of several at a time. The game will modulate this problem a bit by removing some of the extra things like bends and tremolo, but this is still serious information overload, so be prepared to have some difficulty with reading what's happening for a pretty long time.
- The nearly flawless session mode's one flaw is that it changes dynamically with how you play, which in terms of musical expression, is not always the best way to do it. Do you want to rip a screaming solo while the band lays back? Ehh... This will have problems figuring out what you want. Conversely, are you trying to rip a screaming solo, and the band's dying away? This happens too, especially when your guitar is producing rather low output like with tapping. It may be great to change with the band, but when you both follow each other, pretty soon the band stops playing 'cause you're too quiet.
- The riff repeater can slow down parts and manually change difficulty, which is good, but all these parts are pre-determined by the game. If you have a problem with one part at the very end of a solo, it's very likely you'll have to play through the whole solo a billion times to get it right and understand what you're doing, which may or may not be a good thing. Also, and this is infuriating, the slowing down of a song has no metronome or click track that I can find, and past about 80% speed, the audio quality is so bad you can't tell what's happening anyways. Good luck finding a tempo here. You're better off just watching what is happening at slow speed and trying to master it at full speed from there.
- The tone recognition isn't perfect, and it never is. This is extremely frustrating if you're going for note streaks, mastery score, and basic video game statistics. I've missed chords in the middle of strumming a long line of the same chords just because the game herps a derp (It was punk rock. 1/8th note power chords? Don't tell me I randomly missed one lol).
- A few nitpicky things here: On the minigames, the notifications can seriously get in the way of what you're trying to see so you can play the right thing. The score attack sounds are also extremely distracting when you're trying to rock your awesomest.
- And a technical note from one player to another: Always tune up. The game seems to hint that as long as you tune down to the right note (say for drop D), you're good. This is not always the case, especially if your strings are a little too thick for your nut. They can stay just a hair too tight on the playing end compared to the segment after the nut. This means that as soon as you bend or play one of the strings, your tension will equalize and you'll be slightly flat. So remember: Always go below the note you want and come up from below it. This could concieveably make you slightly sharp, but if you're having that much problem with string tensions, you need to get your nut slots widened for your apparently super-thick monster-tendon He-man/Hercules strings.
So, on the whole: Is it awesome? Yes. Will you learn guitar? Yes. Will you learn songs? Yes. Will you happily lose track of hours of your life? Yes. The review officially ends here, but I have a few personal notes for the dedicated reader.
Just remember while you're playing this game, take the time to learn what's comfortable and right for you. Just because Rocksmith says you should play a song a certain way doesn't make it right. You'll love guitar that much more if you find your own voice on it. This game will definitely teach you to play if that's what you're looking for, but always try to put your own spin on what you learn afterwards. For example, the game doesn't recognize if you play more notes than are in the song, so I always add my own licks, fills, and harmonies when my part gets quiet just so I can get a better feel for what I would want the song to sound like. By all means quote songs you love and guitarists you idolize, but don't become a riff junkie who brings nothing new to the table. Put your own inflections on their ideas, because that's what makes your playing interesting.

Was hoping that developer will do better this time, but he failed. Again. The game is out for 9 month already, and what do we have? Stardrive decided to become more MOO-like, with a few interesting ideas, but it failed at implementation.
Space battles: realtime "wall vs wall" style with no tactics involved, you just stand and shoot with arty while your fighters keep enemies occupied. There are abilities, 2 of them, both useless cause you have to activate them for each ship separately. No formation moves. No random stuff like asteroids or junk. Selection often bugs out and selects the wrong ship. There is a slow-mode, but no fast-mode, so in the lategame i just alt-tabed from battle and went for a tea/surf net/whatever. And with lots of stuff in battle it drops to a few FPS, so why didn't he either optimise it or make a turn-based one - i have no idea.
Ground battles: oh god. Why did you  even put it in here? It is the most basic turn-based tactical combat I have ever seen. With a separate loading screen. With a really strange battle system, when you have to wait till enemy comes closer so you can shoot a salvo (if you go forward, you will shoot only once). And it lags even more, so you get lags with only a bunch of people fighting.
AI: that one is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Declares a war when he has no fleet, demands tribute and uses his fleets REALLY bad. In the first game AI could just raid you everywhere, now he just cheats. Every his planet has a negative income, every his fleet is over his limit (2-5 fleets of that size would eat really A LOT), but he somehow manages to get even more of that stuff.
Empire screen: if you copy something from another game that was good, why not to copy ALL the features? That screen lacks half of the functions you would want and expect.
Visuals: the only thing that is good and not bugged in that game, but really, how can you make a buggy graphics?
Diplomacy: well, already mentioned it in battles and AI section, it is simply ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Races: MOO set of traits, that was, imho, done worse. Why do metal-made creatures eat food and not production? No idea.
Planets: a beautiful screen from GalCiv without GalCiv functions. Why would you even bother to do that hex-based map if it is just a simple list of buildings and provides no bonuses for special tiles or connections? And yeah, automatic management of colony is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ too, it places people on farming when planet DOESNT EVEN HAVE IT!
Ship design: well, it may be called somewhat good. Except that it is worse than original. And weapons dont show you their DPS.
Oh, and I forgot: game is so bugged that even after killing every other race (there are no other win conditions anyway), you dont win. Why? I dont know.
The game tries to be a "jack of all trades", but it did not only become "master of none", but it actually failed to be average in every field. In my short time with this game I've infiltrated the Soviet Embassy, devoured countless pharmaceuticals, committed insurance fraud, played miniature golf, stolen a top secret cybernetic kidney, and boxed a sedan to the death. Jazzpunk is filled to the brim with personality, humor, and enough WTF moments to make even the most seasoned adventure gamer blush.
The setting alone is worth the price of admission; Imagine Mad Men meets Blade Runner written by the folks who brought you Airplane and directed by Tim Schafer. Sure, it may only clocks in at four hours; but it never ceases to be utterly engrossing as well as hilarious. I've not played something so memorable, so provocative, so weird as this in quite some time.
If you're a fan of spy movies, satire, adventure games, cyberpunk, copious amounts of alcohol, or simply want a fresh experience then JazzPunk is your most certainly for you.

The spiritual successor to Lego Island and an incredible tribute to the classic spoof movies of the 80s (Airplane!, The Naked Gun). The game is a rollercoaster of ridiculous gags and an oddball setting that is three long, twisted steps away from James Bond gadgetry and cyberpunk. The game is never challenging and can be rushed through quickly (but what the ♥♥♥♥ is the point of that); the levels can be thought of as environments to explore and interact with to find secrets (a la Gone Home or The Stanley Parable). The scope of these secrets is immense, ranging from short slapstick gags to entire games-within-games that have to be seen to be believed.
If you're not the kind of nerd who gets pissy about short games, Jazzpunk is absolutely worth your time and is one of the great examples of the finally-growing comedic game genre.

After playing this game for well over 100 hours, seeing the good and the bad, I can say with confidence don't buy this game. At least, not for 40 dollars. Developers rush updates to 'fix' small bugs in the game while creating new ones, instead of fixing the game breaking ones. These updates also bring severe lag or frame drops to players making the game unplayable. They remove features of the game to 'stop' trolling/griefing while at the same time making it easier to troll/grief; moreover, making the game feel like less due to removing of said features. There are no penalties for players leaving mid-game after being killed by Jason or not being Jason. The game crashes at random points with no reason other than saying there's been a fatal error. The game feels like it is in a beta state with no Early Access label on it with a full game price. You can still glitch out of the map months after the glitch was discovered. Finally, plans for single player have been out for months but the next DLC/update is going to be cosmetic base with swimsuits.
Is the game fun? Yes. Is it fun with friends? Yes
The game at its core is very fun, especially with a server full of friends. However, with all the problems above, it's not. There's too much wrong with this game to be worth 40 dollars besides just being fun. Maybe in the future the developers might redeem the game by fixing some of these problems. But, in its state at the moment, just save your money and don't buy this game.
