Vanquish is ridiculous in every sense of the word. It's over-the-top and it knows it. Platinum looked at all the other serious shooters around it, and said "Now let's give it a try. I really enjoyed my time spent with this game, and I would say that if you're slightly interested in Vanquish, you should play it. It's a more-than-worthy addition to your steam library.
Yes, the game is short (I got about 7 hours out of it while other say they got 4-6), but it's enjoyable all the way. The story is pretty much just there to give you a reason to shoot some dudes, but I personally don't see a problem with it - not all games need complex character arcs. The rocket-sliding, slow-motion mechanic was pretty engaging for me, and I found myself waiting for the next time I could kick-flip a robot into the air and shoot it as the world around me came to a crawl. I liked the simplicity of the weapon upgrade system, and the animation for changing your current weapon is pretty sick.  The environments were actually pretty memorable in the sense that, if you showed me a still of the area, I could tell you where in the game it takes place, and what's happening.
Personally, I would say that this is one of my favorite shooters I've played, I'll probably be replaying it soon.
To sum it up:
If rocket-sliding, kick-flipping, slow-motion-headshoting a huge robot sounds like a good time to you, get this game.

Vanquish has a tortured history, and was traumatically birthed into existence when PlatinumGames walked in on Halo and Metal Gear Solid having what can only be described as the least colourful Seven Minutes of Heaven ever since the official text adaptation.
So while it might seem a bit cynical, embracing bloom harder than Orlando Bloom's most stalkerish Legolas fans, Vanquish rises above to laugh at its divorced parents and invite you to have a pretty fun time, sans broom closet.
Playing as a DARPA researcher turned slip n slide enthusiast, you Max Payne your way through a campaign that's full of generic setpieces, slightly less than generic setpieces, and shooting every not-Covenant identical bug robot between you and the other side of the arena.
Combat involves trying to string together stylish moves and shots, aiming to pump out damage safely inbetween constantly repositioning yourself on the arena. It's fun, fast-paced with your exploding knees, and never stops for a smoke break unless you want it to.
Now this isn't strictly a run n gun, in that unless you combine your exploding knees with roly-poly business then staying out of cover is a very bad idea. But you can, which is just one of many exploits.
This is a game of exploits. Learning to kick off the side of cover to launch into slowmo, or disc-launchering to instantly disable Romanovs, or learning to give the Bogey's tracking laser/s the ol' truffle shuffle. About pushing your ARG guage to its near breaking limit and using EMPs and the ball-buster to disable and destroy entire crowds.
You can plink away with the upgraded Assault rifle, sure, but that is a different game, a not fun one in the slightest. Your stylish abilities are decided less by cutscenes and animations, and more about how well you know the gameplay.
Now the gameplay isn't without its problems. If you do "overheat" your suit's AR meter - and let's just call it what it is, a stamina bar - Sam Gideon gets the vapours and has to lie down, desperately sucking down Gatorades and cigarettes. Obnoxious as mechanics come, especially with your melee attacks instantly setting you into that state.
Now the biggest outright flaw is that Vanquish has delusions about how good of a story it actually has, and will constantly interrupt you to deliver dry exposition on plot elements that nobody in their right mind cares about. Over and over. Making you walk while it drones. Not skippable in the slightest.
There's an arcade score meter too, so why they're so gleeful to break the pacing is anyone's guess.
Course the best part of the game is tackling the Tactical Challenges anyway, so there's your balancing act. 6 stages of 5 waves of enemies that you'll breeze through before promptly getting stomped in the gut on the sixth. Other optionals include GOD HARD, limits your Max Payne juice meter to 3 seconds and not much else.
So all that and a bag of chips, and you've got a fantastic, experimental and polished game with a sense of humour hiding under some obnoxious monochrome visuals.
Yeah, I'd recommend it. It's as short or long as you want it to be, but keeps the mechanics explosive and legitimately fun for the whole ride.

Vanquish is a very unique third person shooter, it's fast-paced, has a slow-mo mechanic, giant mech bosses and more. Before I played it, I knew next to nothing about it except that it was developed by Platinum Games. I got it on sale for $9.99 and the game only took 12 hours to beat on Hard Mode.

Well, very rarely do I pkay a third person arcade shooter which pits me in a situation where I tell myself "Okay, I need to think ahead of the a.i here I know to get everything precisely planned out or I will die." Dare I say that Vanquish is the Dark Souls of the third person shooter genre. That's not to say that there could have been a few things left to be improved upon a sequel.
My only complaints were:
-Cgi breaks up the gameplay too frequently
-Some enemy blind spots where you can cheese a boss
-cliff-hanger ending
-the muted color pallete

The game isn't underrated, it's just overlooked. I can see how the fact that the main character is a literal mix of Solid Snake and Raiden certainly made people cringe at the time of original release. Also, the fact that so many cover-based shooters were releasing at the time. Now, I expect a few fanboys to see my review and tell me how I'm wrong and that's okay. The game is great, it's fun and I enjoyed myself through the campaign. Will I return to it? Not anytime soon but it was a crazy ride, an adrenaline rush for sure and one that everyone should experience.

Ok Be Advised! The Nether is not for frightened little girls!
You will DIE a lot in this game and when you DIE you will lose everything in you're:
> back pack inventory.
> all perks are lost - reset to zero.
> a percentage of your ready cash in the bank is lost (%10 I think).
And of course you lose your dignity in front of your family for crying out loud "NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO" and then slowly weeping like a sad little girl.
Things you WILL DIE from:
> YOU - you will kill yourself more often than not.
> Nether - you will DIE when they swarm you.
> Other Survivors - They will KILL YOU for what they think you may have.
> The Developers - "unintentional" but a fire escape landing at 12 stories that has not had its physics enabled is a DEATH      TRAP and you will DIE.
> Friends - They will at some point KILL YOU maybe by Friendly Fire or maybe because they are not your friend?.
> YOU - I think I cannot stress this enough, I have killed myself more times trying to leap to other buildings while not having a glider in my backpack.
Note: in Single-play you will not have to worry about friends or survivors.
Bugs:
There are quite a few but as Nether was in Beta and still is so, I expected that and I have not found a game breaking bug as yet.
The game over all:
I am told the game engine is Unreal 3, however it reminds me more of a Unity Build graphic wise, simular to Beasts of Prey (Bop)
> In game entities are good and makes the post-apocalyptic very real.
> Map is quite large and well laid out.
> The textures are reasonable.
> Enemy AI - When you first start, these guys are SCARY and unpredictable, and of course then you DIE, see "slowly weeping" above.
Game Play:
> Perk System - works well.
> Clan System - I am of course in the STALKER Clan :D
> Open world - do what you want when you want to.
> No story to follow as such, which I like.
> Escort missions are available (more than likely you will DIE).
> Transportation of goods missions are available.
> Killing a nasty kind of Nether missions are available (more than likely you will DIE some more).
> Defending missions - the Safe Zone (yeah you will DIE).
> Searching for everything - Not a mission but necessary to survival, no food guess what :) YOU DIE!
> Loot Drops -  not a mission but provides some great free stuff (yep DEAD AGAIN if you're not careful)
> Hunting other players - not a mission but provides an income (you may DIE or not).
OVERALL:
I enjoy this game!
There is no grinding or running all over the map to get things done, day in and day out. No daily missions you have to do.
So just take your concrete pill and harden the XXXX UP! Just get in game kill or be killed! Or survive until you DIE.

I've seen this game pop up in my suggestions list several times, but never really gave it a second look until a rainy day at home a few days ago.
The overall premise is different, placing you as the tyrannical dictator who is happy to sacrifice your minions to get upgrades to your armor, destroy your enemies or just for laughs. As you complete quests you unlock different types of minions who carry out your bidding on the battle field, and also restore your looted and dilapidated castle to its former glory. You are encouraged to be evil, which is a nice change of pace from the games that give the tired option of choosing good over bad (i.e. Fable, KOTOR, etc). Sometimes, it’s nice to have a linear story line that takes you down a specific path to show you something fun.
The game play is addicting, though a little buggy when trying to control your horde, and the control mapping wasn't ported very well to my Mac (namely the function keys which have operations assigned to them through mac os). But you can map the controls yourself and find a way to play the game that works best for you.
The game also crashes periodically for unknown reasons, but I'm sure an update will fix that in the near future.
For the price, Overlord is worth your time.

I loved the original Rocksmith. Case-in-point, I put in 140 hours. There were things that could have been better that were improved in this iteration and the experience is richer as a result.
Take Riff Repeater, for example. You had to navigate the main menu to activate Riff Repeater and you weren't able to make adjustments on the fly. The new version is much more robust, being able to dynamically control sections, mastery, speed, and many more options. The ability to effortlessly switch between Riff Repeater and Learn A Song is my favorite improvement.
Mastery Mode is tacked onto Riff Repeater as an option, which turns on and off depending upon your mastery of a section. I liked the all or nothing proposition of Mastery Mode, but I can see the benefit of "hiding" well known bits of the song as well.
Session Mode is new and it's pretty cool. You can build a backing band that will follow you as you play. Haven't used it too much, though. My skills on lead are wanting.
The new Guitarcade games & Score Attack modes are fun, but I still miss the old games from the original. It would've been cool to include the old ones as part of the import tool.
Just get it. It's worth the money, even at full price.

I've been playing guitar for 25+ years. I got Rocksmith 2014 on a whim and I have to say, I haven't played guitar this much since I started playing in the 80's!  My hands are about to fall off and I love it.
Riff Repeater is an excellent tool to work out tricky riffs and intimidating solos. You can slow down the song and progressively build up to full speed.
One tool that routinely gets bashed in the forums by other guitarists is the use of Dynamic Difficulty. It takes away parts of the song and slowly adds more notes as you progress. Yes, at times it is very tedious but I have found that using Dynamic Difficulty has greatly increased my timing and makes me think about what i'm playing.

Farmville meets Harvest Moon meets Plants vs Zombies.
Surprisingly good.
IS GOOD.

Short version: The zombies aren't zombies; the gameplay's a joke; the graphics are horrendous and look like a product from ten years ago; the story is sickeningly unoriginal; the entire game is a cross between three much better implemented casual games which are much cheaper at the same time and the characters are about as interesting as cardboard. Don't waste your money.
Long version: This review is based entirely on some of the key features which are listed, so get ready for a rant.
"Combining elements from farming, tower defense and time management genres" - now I agree with 2 out of 3 of these points. Because this game is literally Farmville, Plants vs Zombies and Fruit Ninja smashed into one - and considering the price for this really unoriginal idea, it's much much cheaper to find and play all of these separately. So really, this game isn't claiming anything new - especially when it wears the zombie apocalypse t-shirt.
Now this really could be forgiven if it redeemed itself through the story or the characters or the graphics. On all three of these points it fails miserably; the story and characters are non-existent, each person that gets hired or visits the restraunt you own is literally a robot that has decent AI but has nothing compelling about their characters despite looking different from the rest. The models are unique enough to give some sort of personality, but when absolutely none is given, it completely destroys what little story there is. It is literally a point A to point B step by step proceedure and despite clocking in a fair amount of hours I don't feel like I'm progressing or enjoying any moments that I wanted to or expected to.
"Protect your farm by building mazes and towers. Our zombies are vicious vegetarians!" ... So? This is a very particular problem that desperately needs addressing because there are no stakes. All that happens when zombies 'invade' your farm at night is that they eat your produce. Obviously you don't really want this as the food is literally the only way you can progress, but you need to attack them with your produce anyway, and additionally - these are zombies! Zombies eat brains not food like us, that's the one fundemental thing that zombies do - eat people! Vegetarian zombies aren't zombies, they're just rude vegans! And it would be slightly more interesting and tense if they went to your AI partners; it would be slightly more interesting and tense if they went for your customers waiting for food that you didn't have the produce for - but they just ignore them! They just go straight for the produce! So what? I can just grow more, why do I need to waste food to protect the food that I'm wasting! That makes no sense!
"Original soundtrack" Yep. You can count that as a key feature of this unoriginal, boring mess of a game. It has it's own original sountrack. Oh yes, and when they say that - they mean one song that plays during the day over and over again until your ears start bleeding. One song isn't a "soundtrack" guys! And the effects are about as generic as you can get as well.
So no, I can't reccomend this. I wouldn't reccomend this game to a brick wall. I'd prefer actual zombies to gnaw on their balloon heads until they explode, which would be a million times more interesting. Hell - I'd prefer staring at the brick wall that I'd reccomend this for, at least it'd give me time to rethink how on Earth I managed to think that this would be a good game to buy with my hard earned money. Why people are giving it good ratings and are calling it one of the best games ever completely baffles me - it's unoriginal and isn't a game that belongs in 2014. I'd expect this POS to be around ten years ago, but nowadays?! No way!

If you like farming & cafe simulations in a similar vein to Farmville and Cafe World (minus the social media element), then you'll like this game. It's a lot of fun, and strangely compelling despite its bugs and lack of storyline (the storyline mode is at best a thin sprinkling of plot and really isn't much different to endless mode). The bad news is that, for what basically amounts to a casual sim game with unlockables, the game is woefully short. The story mode is at best 10 hours of play. Endless mode isn't much better, and whilst you can theoretically go on forever, you'll find that you have everything unlocked and nothing to do but hoard very quickly. The achievements are also bugged - several are impossible to get due to not being awarded despite completion in-game (such as the golden scythe). The audio is also irritatingly bugged if your character commits actions (such as chopping wood) off screen, and the A.I. helpers leave something to be desired. I recommend trying this game if you manage to pick it up in a sale, but be forewarned that there's only about 10-20 hours of gameplay in it before there's nothing left to do, and the game has a lot of bugs.

BACKGROUND
Got the game in the October Humble Monthly.
I'm not sure if I've played something like this before. The closest I can think of is Papers Please, but that feels like a slight stretch.
TOTAL TIME PLAYING
Just over 3 hours. That was enough for me to personally beat the game. the average time on HLTB is 4 hours.
SPECS FOR PLAY THROUGH
- AMD FX 8350 @ 4.0 GHz
- GTX 1080
- 8 Gb DDR3 RAM @ 668 MHz
- 7200 RPM HDD
- LG Ultrawide
PERFORMANCE
The graphic style isn't demanding (that isn't to say it's a "bad" looking game). I was able to maintain full 60 FPS the entire time, and I'd be surprised if any modern day machine cannot do the same.
PROS
+Amazing story. I played through this in two sittings and all I could think about in between the two sessions was going back and playing the rest.
+ As soon as you start to feel overwhelmed with the massive influx in characters, the game ends. This could be viewed as a con, but I don't think a game like this would benefit from character-over-load.
+ As I mentioned earlier, the graphics are pretty interesting. Everything has a flat look to it. Really interesting.
CONS
- Orwell does a lot right. Unfortunately, I feel like it held my hand far too much. Instead of looking through a wide range of documents, the game was constantly pushing me into specific documents. This would be super hard to work around, but towards the end the choices and clues became very obvious and the game lost it's "detective" feel it built up so well in the first half.
- As far as I could tell, you can't get anything wrong. Sure some of the "conflicting evidence" could be misdiagnosed, but
from my play-through adding useless information just got a sarcastic response from your boss. No real consequences.
CONCLUSION
Alright. So I really liked the game. It was great and a pretty phenomenal gaming experience. At this time I am going to recommend it if found on sale around $5. It's far too short to be worth $10.
I'm really hoping a sequel or an entire new story comes out. With that new game I really want the choices to be less linear. Hold my hand less, let me mess things up, and let things pivot around my mistakes.

I would recommend this game, but not to everyone. If you enjoy dystopian settings and stories, this game gives you a unique perspective in that this time you are Big Brother's informant. You spy on civilians and you decide what information to pass along.
This game is a lot of reading and linking bits of information together. It is not very action packed, though there is plenty going on to read about. Getting a handle on the controls is pretty straightforward and easy. It makes you have to decide what kind of person you want to be: one who follows orders and sticks to the rules, one who picks and chooses what rules they want to follow, or one that defies orders and stands for their own beliefs.
My biggest complaint is that the story felt somewhat short. It is designed to feel like the events are happening in "real time" as you play, but I feel like there was a lot of background that could have been brought forward and utilized to extend the story a bit. Overall, though, the story as it stands is still pretty intriguing.
I really enjoy this game! There is some replayability in that the choices you make do affect a lot of the events in the story, and the final outcome. If you're an achievement hunter, they are all easy enough to get in a few playthroughs. One playthrough took me I think around 5-6 hours, and that was taking my time deciding what I wanted to do.

SOMA is a very philosophical horror game. Made by Frictional Games, the same developers as Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
However; their goal with this game was not to create a jumpscare funhouse carnival ride (looking at you, Outlast).
They wanted to ask a question of the player:
What is conscienceness?
The player is offered many choices that are only there to make the player think. Many choices to not change the outcome or environment.
The gameplay revolves around figuring out puzzles, environmental story-telling, and avoiding "enemies". It is quite the atmospheric experience and really draws you in with its fantastic art design and audio effects. The graphics in this one are quite amazing to look at. Audio logs are quite prevelant as the most obvious story giver, but paying attention to the environment will reward the player. The creatures all have different quirks to them (reacting to either sight, sound, or both). Avoiding them is easy enough, albeit with a few scripted chase sequences. Item managment in an inventory is gone, as the player is really only carrying a few things ar a time anyways.
I personally enjoyed the experience and atmosphere, and the audio terrified me more often than the creatures did. Should definately be on everyone's list of games to play.

This is the one game I've played for nearly 5 years now and which I still enjoy. It's the perfect combination between casual fun on one side and the ability to communicate with others on the other side. This game is highly community driven thanks to the Map Editor, the LUA integration, the possibility to voteban people from the room if they're annoying. It's even possible to play moderator if you wish and check out reports other players made using the tribunal.
Sure, it's a pretty simple 2d game and it may not be as immersive as more elaborate games. But that's sometimes exactly what you should be looking for as it gives you plenty of time to chat up with other players. If you ask me, that's where a lot of other games go wrong. Not everything is perfect here and occasionally there are server issues or bugs, but in the end they get resolved and at least that means we get to laugh at Tig (one of the creators and known as a troll).
Do I recommend this game? Yes I do. I've found it to be the perfect place to make a lot of good friends and that to me is extremely important in a game. So yes, go make friends!

StarDrive 2 has the same vices as StarDrive, though to a lesser extent. There are peripheral areas of the game which feel rushed or unpolished, not for lack of effort as I understand it, but lack of manpower. Unlike SD, the mechanics and overall gameplay is SOLID. I liked SD but there are segements of that game which were flawed.
Diplomacy is much more responsive and worthwhile in SD 2. The different factions in StarDrive have a lot of character and its something you actually want to engage in.
Not feeling the need to slow down time to a crawl in order to micromanage every detail of a star-spanning empire, is great. While I miss combat actually happening on the stategy map, turn-based allowed the rather spartan and unwieldy management aspects of the game to flower.
It can almost go without saying that StarDrive's defining aspect; ship design and combat have been developed, honed and polished to outshine any other 4X. It moved ahead in leaps and bounds, and it is fun, fun, fun. The are more options and everything is really slick. On top of that, there are special technologies and components you acquire outside of the actual scientific tree through various means. Some are stellar, others feel gimicky - which isn't a bad thing. The only addition I don't like is the proto-molecule device which is underwhelming - not because it underperforms, but because it is pretty superflous and there is a sizable build-up to actually getting it. Also because the mechanics which underpin it are perhaps the one weak point in SD2's fleet combat
It highlights the one real complaint I have with shipboard weaponry in the game. Ships can carry massive Subspace Artillery and Mass Drivers which by any yardstick should be able to get the job of bombarding a planet done. Instead ships have to carry a seperate arsenal of otherwise useless weapons, which take up precious space, in order pummel planets into submission. It is extremely arbitrary, especially one one considers that tactical and strategic nukes are available form the very start of the game - long before any sort of ground-based counter is available. A doom fleet in orbit, armed to the teeth with kinetic weaponry and only able to 'blockade' is a sorry spectacle. Maintaining planetary defenses on more than a few planets seems prohibitively expensive, even of it wasn't useless because most of the AI strategy is based around landing troops anyway.
At times playing on defensive boils down to playing wack-a-mole with invasions fleets amongst your holdings. That will probably be alleviated somewhat by wormhole junction forts and other defensive options in the 'Sector Zero' DLC.
Planetery invasions were unwieldly (in capital letters) in SD1, and while massive focus has obviously been put into tactical ground combat in StarDrive 2, it feels tacted on and doesn't really add much to the experience at this point in time.
Overall though, the game is fun which is to say that what it does well, it does really well. The feature set it touts is there and it is solid. It is the little things where this game looses ground. I dwell on the little things a lot, but that is nitpicking. This game deserves a much better rating then it has.

A MUST OWN. I love Platinum and this was the first system I got to play Vanquish on, it's absolutely the best way to experience it.
The good:
-Combat is really fluid, you can combo into multiple enemies as long as you have enough boost, and guns are easily some of my favorite in recent memory.
-Graphics/performance are 1000X better than the console versions, and being able to play it at 4K is glorious.
-The boss fights and setpieces, as well as general level design (though sometimes a little on-rails) are what really makes this a true Platinum game. Some of the best in class, not surprising coming from this dev.
-One of the only linear single player games from the last 10 years I can think of that I would play through more than once.
-Controls on K&M are FAR superior and much easier than a controller.
-Most fun credits screen I've played since Smash Bros Melee
The bad:
-Story only took me about 4 hours on my first run (minus the cutscenes). This isn't so bad if you plan on playing through again, and definitely not bad considering it's highest price point is $20, but still it's worth noting.
-The story honestly made no sense, maybe until the very end? then I still really didn't get it... It was fun to sit through, but it just felt like a thousand things were left unanswered. The good guys are the bad guys, but then not really, but we're the --- whatever...
Buy it without hesitation, even if just to play through it once, it's absolutely worth every dime.
It's Vanquish. You know what it is. Just get it.

The marriage of the most American hard-a$$ plot with the super-over-the-top action of Japanese games/anime with a little bit of Max Payne in it. It's the Independence Day of videogames.
Imho it's only worth it on a sale. It's short (4 hours), the levels and bosses are very forgettable, the slo-mo makes it too easy even on harder difficulties and the progression system is
absent.
You upgrade weapons by picking up more of the same gun, but at full ammo (otherwise it picks up ammo). Each upgrade will increase some kind of stat on the weapon. The only really meaningful upgrade is the big max-ammo upgrades which you pick-up separately and the magazine upgrades, because that means you won't run out of ammo during a slo-mo. If you ever swap them for something else you lose some upgrade levels when you pick up the same gun again elsewhere. It doesn't matter though, it's not like you notice the stat increases. Level 1 shotgun is just as good as almost max-level shotgun.
Also some of the biggest issues I have with this game is the feedback. The indication of how much health you have is very vague. Even more vague than the bloody screen in CoD games. All you know is that when you've taken enough hits to trigger the emergency slo-mo where the suit saves you is your limit. The next hit will LIKELY kill you, but it might also heal you enough that it... doesn't? A lot of things are vague in this game.
While sliding with a nitro pack on your butt might seem fun at first, it gets old fast without the progression. If you skip this game you really don't miss out on anything and that's why I'm not recommending.

All you really need to know is that Vanquish is a prime example of the sort of game where everything except the gameplay is generic at best, but the gameplay is so good that the other stuff doesn’t even matter.
To go further, Vanquish is a distinctive and solid good time with excellent movement and controls. That and some delightfully tricksy setpiece/boss battles. A Third person Shooter that pushes the player to  get up and out of cover. To move around with smooth glide and slow time effects. There is even a happy lack of snap-to gunplay. It is a different and fresh take on the style.  It feels good to break apart your shooter muscle memory and give yourself to its new ways, and I only wish that element of it could somehow be transplanted into a game with a less bland/macho personality. In the absence of that impossible possibility though – yep, play Vanquish.

Sometimes a game's like a hamburger with weird "secret sauce" you get from a small burger joint. It needs a lot of polish (or ketchup, you know) for you to say that it's amazing, but you still really end up liking it. That's basically Overlord.
Overlord is essentially the result of Pikmin, the original Fable, and Sauron being thrown into a blender. It has gameplay elements of the first, the charm of (and clear inspiration from) the second, and you take on the role of the third.
The gameplay is pretty good, for the most part, but it definitely needs some refinements here and there. You're the titular overlord, and you have an army of minions at your disposal. These little guys serve a range of different purposes, ranging from basic cannon fodder to being needed for progression in certain areas. They have their own classes, and each class is separated by their color. Browns are brutes, greens are assassins, reds are fire mages which act like archers, and blues are mages that can revive your dead troops.
The Overlord himself initially needs these minions in combat for survival, with strategic minion usage in the early hours of the game being the difference between life and death. Later on he's able to do alright in combat on his own, but that doesn't make combat as the Overlord very fun. Melee combat has laughably poor animations, and just feels awful. Magic combat is a bit more fun to use, but quickly drains mana at higher ranks. There are some neat details, though, like fire magic burning fields. You can unlock different spells (and different ranks of spells) by finding different totems throughout the world.
There's plenty of totems throughout the world, and finding them is pretty satisfying. You'll often want to revisit previous areas after gaining new minion types to look around for totems, as some of them are the only way to boost your health, mana, and maximum minion count.
Actual level design is fine... for the most part. There's a point (fairly early on in the game) where you're going to need to get through the first couple segments of both areas available to you at the time to get the minion types needed to clear both, and it isn't obvious at first. Combine that with the fact these areas are fairly annoying to beign with, and you have a negative stretch close to the start of an otherwise good game.
The story is also an enjoyable romp, even if the game seems light on it. There's a lot of hints dropped throughout the game about its finale, leading up to a story heavy ending. The finale's good enough that I'd recommend not spoiling it, but it's not like the game will be ruined if you know what it is or anything. There's multiple routes, too, which allows you to end up with a pretty happy ending. You could also be a murderous maniac, if that's your thing.
Overlord in general needs a lot of polish, as previously mentioned. Combat is unsatisfying, there's really annoying levels at the start of the game, and the boss fights are annoying because of how bad the combat is. It's a game that could be a lot better than it is, but I still really do enjoy it. It has a ton of charm, has decent length, and still kept my interest for almost all of its 20 hour length.
TL;DR/Wrap-up: It's $5 for a good (albeit flawed) game that should take you 20 hours to go through. On a buy/sale/don't buy scale, this is a definite buy.

Jazzpunk is a comedy in the burgeoning sub genre of first person games like Gone Home or Thirty Flights of Loving that seek to tell a linear story in a non-linear experience by shepherding the protagonist with incentives. This review is the hardest review I've ever attempted to write. Being a comedy, and a video game, many of the jokes are deadpan and are uniquely structured to the levels of the game. Because of that there were levels that hit the mark, such as Wedding Quake were hilarious. Often times though there were jokes in levels that matched that were nearly identical to each other in structure, cadence and delivery right after each other that were not only not funny but actively served to make subsequent new jokes in that level less funny.
This fault of the game seems to be a result of the non-linear structure. Due to it being a non-linear game there are many chances to miss things. Due to this they would reuse minigames and even types of jokes. That said reused jokes can be funny. There are multiple instances where you are sent through a zombie pizza hut minigame trifle, and each time it gave me goosebumps and it would cause uncontrollable laughter. Most of the jokes are not given as much car as the pizza hut gag or Wedding Quake and are mere stand-up routines. There are instances when multiple non-player characters in levels will give similar routines but not quite the same, and these jokes fall flat.
Jazzpunk in many ways is a stark realization that game developers growing up playing Nintendo 64 games are now making games of their own. It’s a weird artifact from an era that went in a different direction, when minigames dominated and there were a torrent of incentives deployed at the player character to get them to complete a non-linear environment in a linear way. In the end, what this boils down to is a unique refreshing experience that's comedy doesn't hack it the whole way through.
Awesome awesomeness. 'Nuff said. Buy it. Enjoy it.

To describe Jazzpunk to someone who has never heard of Jazzpunk is almost like trying to explain joy to someone who has never smiled. The best way I have been able to describe it is this: "Take a Mel Brooks or Leslie Nielsen movie, and blend it with a video game.", and even that falls short of the indescribable pleasures of Jazzpunk.
To put it bluntly, Jazzpunk is the worlds first comedy video game. Yes, sure, lots of games, especially recently, have been funny, but the jokes are told to you in a stand up manner. You sit there and wait as the game delivers the gag, and you move on. Jazzpunk is different. Rather than making you the audience, the jokes are incredibly interactive.
A frog needs your help to steal WiFi from Starbux, a rich British man wants you to spray Cheez Wizz into his mouth, secret agents beckon you to smuggle pigeons in your stomach, a game of virtual reality tennis is played... on a real life tennis court.
By no means are any of the jokes, gags or visual puns in Jazzpunk "high brow", but rather, they are the dumbest, silliest things, on par with the strangest episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus. You might not find a joke funny, but don't worry, 10 more incredibly different jokes are coming in the next 3 minutes.
The visual style is a mix of the brilliant visual designer Saul Bass and the hyper-real, gross-detailed bits from John Kricfalusi (Ren and Stimpy), that forms a world that is so distinctly Jazzpunk. By sticking to a visually distinct art-style, the gags and the game form a believable world, where things like robot ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s make TOTAL SENSE.
Jazzpunk is a game designed with a singular goal: to make you laugh. And it will achieve that goal in its unfortunately short 3 hour length. However, after those 3 hours, you feel like you may have missed out on hidden gags, and you probably did, bringing replayability to an already great game.
I want to see more games like Jazzpunk, its a breath of fresh air to have a game that doesn't give a toss about the actual gameplay, but rather the filling around the gameplay.

Played since near release. Some pros and cons for people considering buying this:
[Pros]
- Unique, fast paced, and skill rewarding combat system
- Generally high skill cieling
- Rewarding level progression given by playing vs. bots or other players for casual and more competitive players respectively. ( Playing against people gives more exp, but not by enough to make vs. bots unviable for those who wish to avoid more competitive matches. )
- Suprisingly in depth character customization
- The majority of the community in pvp matches outside of dominion just wants to fight honorably
- The two newest characters are balanced way better than cent and shinobi
- It is generally easy to get gear for your character, be it getting steel from challenges and play, drops from after a game, or free scavenger crates from certain challenges or community events
- Everything in the game, including the cosmetics and premium status, can be bought with currency earned through playing the game and is all set at a reasonable price. ( The only things set a bit pricey are the characters added after vanilla. )
- Dev team cares about patching and balancing
[Cons]
-  The dishonorable duelists throwing people off cliffs meme is very real
- The devs are heavily biased on which heroes they like and the balance (and patch note dev talk) shows it
- Note the date of youtube footage you may have seen. The game has changed wildly since vanilla
- The most recurring nerf in the game is to the speed of a character's attacks and the recovery window. This can and has made certain fast attacking characters of the assassin category attack slower than ones in the vanguard category.
- Emblem editing is limited to less than a handful of layers
- You'll need to log on to Uplay when you want to boot up the game. Hope you like logging on twice to play one game.
- The gank memes are real
- Sitting back and blocking until you get super sayan mode for a health shield and super attacks as a strategy is real (Yes in 1v1)
To sum it up, the game was heading in a pretty bad direction for a bit, but it is getting a bit better and shows promise again.

Never Alone could have been an outstanding showcase of taking games beyond their cultural norms, into the realms of documentaries and educational medias. It does everything right; appealing visuals, characters, music, documentaries. The one thing it lacks though is actual gameplay.
Never Alone is a simple platformer with some unique puzzles thrown in. That alone, would have been enough to make this an outstanding game alongside everything else it offers. What troubles this game though and why I can't recommended it is the controls. For a game with such simple platforming mechanics, the controls completely failed and/or brought about numerous bugs. Oftens times I wondered how much time went into testing this game. I quickly lost drive to learn more in the documentaries seeing the total number left as only a countdown until I would be done with this game.
If you feel like you can stomach the sluggish, unresponsive controls and glitches in this game to experience the novelty that's offered, I recommend it, I played it after all. But if you want to play a game that's enjoyable on all accounts,  specifically the main one of moving through the world, I'd pass. The controls bring this game down far too much.

Never Alone is an enchanting educational co-op platformer. Overall, I would recommend getting it if you intend to play with a friend 'couch co-op' -style and apparently with controllers. If you intend on playing single player, I recommend waiting for sale or price drop below $10.
Pros:
~Art and soundtrack are fantastic.
~Writing, design, and voice acting are fantastic.
~Interviews with Alaskan natives become available mostly by completing levels; some require extra effort to unlock.
~The game doesn't interrupt your play to show you them, but rather gives you the option to watch at any time, which is perfect.
~Frequent background autosaves make game challenging but not punishing.
~Fun to play co-op and experience with a friend.
~Story was surprisingly dark at times
~Gameplay more challenging than I expected, though partially due to imperfect mechanics.
Cons:
~Some problems with glitching, but possibly due to Steam Link.
~Some problems with movement mechanics, even using controller.
~Not as fun playing singleplayer - switching between characters somewhat interrupts flow and breaks immersion.

Not a fan of platformers (though this is less traditionally so) but I really loved this game! It's very cute and has a lot of native and cultural inspiration. My favorite part about the game is how much research they put into this game and how much it shows. Watching the insights really gives you, dare I say, insight on the background of this game. The environment and story and characters are relatable and brings out your inner hero(ine) and make you feel immersed in the game. I started watching the insights for the achievement in all honesty, but when I actually listened, I felt a connection to the indigenious people and their culture as well as the game. After playing this game, my eyes were opened to a new way of life and thinking, and I appreciate it so much. I loved the impact that this game had on me.
Moving onto the game itself, it's a bit difficult to master the controls, but you get used to it. I would probably reccommend using the co-op mode (which I wish was not only local) because I think it would be easier, and also mirrors the connection between Nuna and her fox friend (though I personally have not tried it). The graphics are simply stunning, very simple yet so detailed. The relationship between the fox and Nuna is so important because as the title suggests you never feel alone, and really the title suggests more towards the spirits that guide us and are always around us. In such a technological age, it's nice to feel that connection.
The interaction with the spirits is unique and I love the appearance of them all. Whenever the game shows a story, it is depicted in an art style that reflected the Iñupiat's and it was so lovely to see.
Pros:
+ Heartwarming story
+ Addresses an issue of climate change
+ Characters feel real
+ Lovely graphics
+ Soundtrack
+ Narrator (no dialogue)
+ Real-world inspiration
+ Immersive, impactful
Cons:
- Sometimes scary (I get scared easily though)
- No online co-op
- Some areas are difficult (resulting in lots of death and death noises)
- Controlling Nuna and the fox at the same time can be difficult (single-player)
- Controls are admittedly slow
- AI Nuna/Fox could be better
tl;dr If you like seeing cultural influence and spirits fascinate you as much me, I reccommend it! If you like crisp controls then maybe not

I never bought Siege because I've always assumed it was a rich man's CS:GO (I'm a poor little boy), what a mistake.
PROS:
-Extremely intense matches, emphasizing CQC.
-Interesting and fun "Operators" (Basically Heroes/Champions)
-A lootbox system that actually is 100% in game currency
-Varied maps
R6S is really ♥♥♥♥ing fun, I haven't been this addicted to a game in a long time, especially a FPS. Overwatch and CS:GO had their honey moon periods, but R6S seriously grabbing my focus and keeping it.
That said this game has some serious flaws.
MIXED:
-Operator cost
This one is an iffy point, honestly, if I buy a Triple A game, I would typically expect all the characters to be unlocked, in R6S you have to unlock all the operators using in game renown. However, it was so easy unlock the base operators it was almost a non-issue (Standard Edition) The problem comes with year operators, If you want to play the game to its fullest potential some grinding will be required or forking over minimum of 50 bucks (20 for Year 1 OPS pack, 30 for Season Pass) This doesn't bother me that much but will hinder the experience for people not expecting to get gimped by who they own. (Do not get Starter Edition! It makes unlocking Operators significantly slower)
-COMMUNITY:
With any online game, you'll meet some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. That's just part of it. Rainbow Six Siege suffers from the same problem every competitive online game has, toxic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, but also actual nice normal people who will help you learn.
If you've played CS, it's so far, a better experience but eerily similar.
CONS:
-Matchmaking is a nightmare
This specific point is something I want to address. The matchmaking in this game is ♥♥♥♥ing bizarre. Most games will have long queues but will end up finding you an equal match, R6S goes the opposite direction and throws you into a match almost instantly (Good!) but puts you against people who seem to have almost hundreds of hours of experience. (Bad!) I'm not a little punk, so I can take it, but I can see how it would be frustrating for inexperienced players, trying to learn all the nuances of the game, getting bodied by Year 2 OPS with no indication on what just happened other than a killcam.
This was my experience with Casual MM at least, I'm waiting to see what Ranked is like once all my friends hit its level requirement of 20.
-BUGS
The game still has some major bugs that really shouldn't be in a 2-year-old game at this point, especially one that is coming from one of the biggest studios in gaming. Things like having problems getting everyone in the party or having people join different games despite being in the same party. A major one is the insane amount of tries it takes to get into the game, sometimes it will launch just fine but other times you'll be greeted with an infinite loading screen. (Must restart multiple times) Some visual inconsistency in game and bizarre frame drops which could easily be on my end as well.
VERDICT:
The game rocks, has some issues that can be solved and from what I've seen, the devs really do listen to the community and love this game. The constant stream of content and operators is very uplifting to see and seems the like pro league for R6S is doing especially well.
For sure get this game if you're thinking about it, especially on a sale!

Fantastic learning tool.
I've been playing guitar for a few years, learning by myself.
This has made me use my little finger more often and opened up a whole new realm!

I saw a guitar teacher in a video on the Internet say that it takes about 3,000 hours of practice for someone to really become decently competent at the guitar. His point was simply that there was no substitute for putting in the time, and no real shortcuts  - though of course good instruction (such as his own) would help.
RS2014 went away from its more "gamey" style predecessor to become more of a full-fledged training tool for the guitar. This was a good move. It's easily three times better than the original Rocksmith at meeting this goal. Everything is much, MUCH more instructive and convenient. It gives you lots of tools to learn popular (and not-so-popular) songs... really learn them, to the point where you can completely play them from memory. From the basic "Learn a song" tool to the flexible "Riff Repeater," which allows you to practice a section of a song over and over again, to the ability to test yourself at various skill levels in Score Attack - which is a lot like classic Guitar Hero / Rock Band type play. But it also includes dozens of lessons - many with practice tracks. And a number of "Guitarcade" technique games to take some of the boredom out of common drills.
You can simulate a large number of amps, cabinets, and effects to simulate all kinds of tones and use the game like a sound system and amp - and to learn how your favorite band got a particular tone for a particular song. `There's a "Session Mode" where you can practice jamming and improvising with a computer-controlled band. The game supports lead guitar, rhythm guitar, *AND* bass techniques - including a "bass emulation" mode to learn to play bass on a regular six-string guitar. And there's multi-player (really 2-player) capability, so a friend can plug in (with another cable, which currently runs $30) and the two of you can learn songs together, jam together in Session mode, play a duet with different song parts for a high score, and go head-to-head in a competition at the same difficulty level and part to see who is the better player.
The game isn't perfect in detecting the notes, and will allow some sloppiness in your playing that does not sound good to the human ear. Unplugging or adjusting the mix and really listening to yourself is a must, or you could develop some bad habits because the game will let you get away with it.
Ultimately, the success of the game is dependent on how successful it is at teaching you to play guitar. It's supposed to be "the fastest way to learn guitar." I don't know if that's exactly the case. But I will say this - it's helped me make more progress in the last six months than I had in twenty years on my own, so that's a good sign. I've been playing about 45 minutes per day, on the average, and it's really made a difference.
But the important thing to remember is that it doesn't work miracles. If you think you can master the guitar in the time it takes for you to master Super Mario Brothers, you are going to be disappointed. You won't go from being a beginner to playing like Eddie Van Halen in 60 hours. That 3000 hour thing is not super flexible. The game does help in two ways:
1) It can provide lots of feedback and support to help make your practice time more efficient. This may yield somewhat greater improvement per hour of practice than doing so unaided.
2) It can make your practice time more fun, which may encourage you to practice more, and stick with it.
And that's really all it can do, though that's awesome. In the end - if you want to learn to play guitar, you are going to HAVE to put in the hours. There's no way around that. If RS2014 makes those hours more productive and more fun (and I believe it does), that's a win!

Overlord
Let’s get this out of the way: Overlord is a blast to play, sure time has taken it’s toll on the game but the charm still remains intact. In Overlord, you play as an evil guy who has to pillage various villages and take back his lordship with the help of his mighty powers and the cute but loyal minions.
The story in Overlord is a just a way to give way to chaos. The main meat of the game comes from the evil things that you do. Overlord has garnered a cult following in the timespan it has been released and with good measure. It is a game where you truly feel like you have been granted the powers and you are the best the demons have to offer.
The gameplay of Overlord is fairly simple. You can either attack yourself or send your minions to plunder the wealth of innocents. There is no better joy than to seeing your minion bring back coins and just drop it at your feet. You can have a limited amount of minions jogging around at a time. You can respawn them for a price once they’ve fallen into a battle. They are pretty easy to spawn again and again which makes for a enjoyable play. You don’t have to worry about minions dying in battle because of this reason. Now, that’s not to say that you yourself are underpowered. No, not at all. In fact, as you move up in levels, you get far too much overpowered for anyone to stop you. At that point, you don’t even need to use your minions as the work is pretty much done by your much more quickly and efficiently,
The Sound design in Overlord is pretty good. Minions have the usual chirpy, jittery kind of voice which gives you a sense that they want to keep plundering around with you. When villagers run and scream, it brings a gleeful smile on your face. The music is spot on here.
Since the game was released more than 9 years ago, the visuals look pretty dated. But along with games like Bully, Overlord holds up pretty well. Nothing will surprise you, but there is enough detail in the environments which will keep you coming back should you enjoy the gameplay.
Overall, Overlord is a game that is worth buying simply because you get to experience the evil side of a story. Also, the minions. Don’t let the old release date fool you, this is a treasure waiting to be plundered.

If you’ve ever wanted to have an army of loyal goblin minions willing to do almost anything to serve your evil needs, then Overlord is the game for you. The game stars you, the Overlord, whom has recently been brought back from the dead by a mysterious creature looking for a new master to spread evil across the land.
The game pushes you out into the village of Spree where you are tasked with summoning various minions to harvest souls from living creatures (such as sheep or monsters) which serve as a sort of currency for summoning additional minions or upgrading weapons and armor. Minions come in 4 different flavors: brown, red, blue, and green, and each of these has their own special strengths and weaknesses. Though you start with brown, you will need to venture to various locales and dungeons to unlock the other 3 variants.
Minions are basically your “army” and are needed in order to fight the majority of the enemies you encounter as you play. Minions can also be sent to areas that are inaccessible due to narrow passages and they will be more than eager to flip remote switches and carry heavy objects back to your castle via the various warp gates scattered across the land. There is also an array of magic spells to assist your minions, protect yourself, or do heavy damage to single targets.
Another factor in the game is your “corruption” level which grows as you do extremely evil deeds (murdering innocent civilians, choosing gold over saving lives, etc) although it seems that the only purpose for this metric is aesthetic, meaning your armor and castle are just more spikey and evil looking. Speaking of your castle, you can upgrade various parts of it to your liking but these upgrades are also mostly just for cosmetic appeal.
The game’s learning curve is a bit on the easy side, and I found myself clearing many areas simply by having a large number of minions and holding down the “send minions” button while waggling my view around until they had killed/looted/activated everything in the general area. Fortunately, the game does increase a little bit in difficulty in the later chapters where using such tactics will result in losing almost every single minion. If you want a real challenge, you should forego any armor or weapon upgrades as getting the arcanium armor and weapons with full upgrades turns the last part of the game into a total cakewalk.
The story also wrapped itself up rather abruptly (without spoiling much, you’ll suddenly feel like you’re at the end of the game without some necessary exposition). That being said, I really enjoyed the concept and will probably pick up the sequel sometime in the near future and I would recommend this game to anyone looking to try being the bad guy for once instead of the goody-twoshoes hero role we are so often shoehorned into in gaming.

According to indie developer Necrophone Games, Jazzpunk is a “comedy adventure game set in an alternate-reality cold war world, plagued with corporate espionage, cyber-crime and sentient martinis,” fused with gameplay supposedly inspired by spoof classics such as Airplane and Naked Gun. So, with a description as above, it is fair to suggest that I had no idea what to expect when I ‘cyberjacked into the netrix’ for the first time.
Published by Adult Swim Games, whose notable successes include the absurd, quasi-addictive Robot Unicorn flash-game, it was always a reasonable guess that this title would be somewhat lacking in real-world sensibilities. By the time your character has consumed his prescription ‘Missionoyl’ medication (Guidelines for usage: take one capsule per mission until reality is sufficiently augmented), your assumptions are confirmed. Jazzpunk is Christian Bale crazy.
You see the world through the eyes of Polyblank, an espionage agent of sorts, who, under the instruction of a peculiar gentleman known only as The Director, must infiltrate the Soviet consulate to obtain a top-secret data cartridge.
Except, when you arrive at the location of your first mission, it doesn’t take too long to realise that the ‘storyline’ itself is as tenuous and stringy as overcooked spaghetti, it is purely the vehicle that transports the player from one fast-paced escapade to the next. This is not to say that there isn’t a vague storyline in place, but, to be playing this game for its storytelling narrative and character depth would be to miss the point entirely. Jazzpunk is intended to be a light-hearted poke at, well, pretty much everything.
It is an ambitious notion, particularly for an indie games development team consisting of just two people. The good news, however, is that Luiz Hernandez and Jess Browse have succeeded in their primary aim, to make people laugh. After a promising but sluggish opening chapter, Jazzpunk really begins to gather pace, providing several genuine laugh-out-loud moments, generally involving pigeons.
However, Jazzpunk isn’t just the quirky chick that nobody wants to take to the prom. She’s pretty, too. A vivid cartoon landscape adorns the open-world environment, and Hernandez himself has composed an original soundtrack, which wouldn’t sound out of place in a 1950’s motion picture.
Help From a Few Friends
Those hoping for a little more than an interactive comedy can also rest assured, Jazzpunk is not short of good old fashioned gameplay. Mini-game appearances from favourites such as Frogger, Fruit Ninja and Space Invaders creep up on you when you least expect it, as well as an incredible wedding-themed parody of Quake, in which players must use champagne corks as projectiles in order to avoid the prospect of matrimonial doom.
The game builds to a resoundingly triumphant climax. An Olympic style multi-format duel with the story’s main antagonist, The Editor (or ‘The Man with the Horn Rimmed Glasses,’ as he is originally introduced), continues to raise the ridiculousness stakes, and an epic gravy boat race (yes, that’s what I said) closes the battle magnificently.
Jazzpunk, a nominee for the grand prize at this year’s Independent Games Festival, is a thoroughly enjoyable experience from start to finish. It shares some similarities with fellow IGF nominee The Stanley Parable in its ability to not just break, but smash the fourth wall, yet still remain exciting. However, where it stands apart from TSP, and the vast majority of other computer games to date, is its steadfast commitment to being absolutely mental.
Too Much of a Good Thing?
Of course, the off-the-wall nature of this title will mean that it will not be for everyone. If you are expecting an experience that follows traditional gameplay protocol then you will be confused, let down, and most likely irritated. Jazzpunk is wacky, in a way that is simply incomparable to anything else I have ever seen. It is an explosive compound of equal parts satire and slapstick, noir and nerd, sublime and ridiculous.
On the whole, Jazzpunk seems to completely merit its reception as one of the best independent games to be released this year. In terms of replay-ability, it is very solid. Having completed the full-story twice, I was able to find plenty of content that I had missed on my opening play-through, which kept it fresh and engaging.
The humour is likely to be hit-and-miss, based on personal preference. But, for this soul, Jazzpunk is an extremely funny and refreshing piece of work.

Played since near release. Some pros and cons for people considering buying this:
[Pros]
- Unique, fast paced, and skill rewarding combat system
- Generally high skill cieling
- Rewarding level progression given by playing vs. bots or other players for casual and more competitive players respectively. ( Playing against people gives more exp, but not by enough to make vs. bots unviable for those who wish to avoid more competitive matches. )
- Suprisingly in depth character customization
- The majority of the community in pvp matches outside of dominion just wants to fight honorably
- The two newest characters are balanced way better than cent and shinobi
- It is generally easy to get gear for your character, be it getting steel from challenges and play, drops from after a game, or free scavenger crates from certain challenges or community events
- Everything in the game, including the cosmetics and premium status, can be bought with currency earned through playing the game and is all set at a reasonable price. ( The only things set a bit pricey are the characters added after vanilla. )
- Dev team cares about patching and balancing
[Cons]
-  The dishonorable duelists throwing people off cliffs meme is very real
- The devs are heavily biased on which heroes they like and the balance (and patch note dev talk) shows it
- Note the date of youtube footage you may have seen. The game has changed wildly since vanilla
- The most recurring nerf in the game is to the speed of a character's attacks and the recovery window. This can and has made certain fast attacking characters of the assassin category attack slower than ones in the vanguard category.
- Emblem editing is limited to less than a handful of layers
- You'll need to log on to Uplay when you want to boot up the game. Hope you like logging on twice to play one game.
- The gank memes are real
- Sitting back and blocking until you get super sayan mode for a health shield and super attacks as a strategy is real (Yes in 1v1)
To sum it up, the game was heading in a pretty bad direction for a bit, but it is getting a bit better and shows promise again.

Never alone is a game with a powerful message. A message however that could have been delivered in a better way.  At a glance may seem completely harmless, but even with the aesthetics and tone of the game, it is a flawed experience.
Soundtrack
Sound is nothing even worth mentioning here. It has tone that fits but is very half-hearted if you ask me.
Gameplay
The gameplay is not fun at all. The controls are sluggish, and the terrible character AI movements will result in a lot of unwanted deaths. Frustrating, clipping glitches all throughout the game make it hard to trudge on. This game follows a lot of 2D Sidescrolling Puzzle-Platformer tropes. I liked that you had videos to subsidize and compliment the game but I ended up skipping them because I was more invested in playing than watching which usually I don't skip cutscenes. However here I was already not very into it and felt like I could just watch them after. I figured it would be like pieces of a documentary that are parted out and could be watched all at once later to become a complete set. However when I later went to watch them after playing the game I had no idea what they were talking about since there is no continuity between them. You pretty much have to watch them as you play or play it all then watch it all in the same day to know what is being talked about.
Story
I did not enjoy this element in the game.  Folk tale or not I walked away knowing jack all about what was happening in the game. The presentation is quite weak. Anytime I was interested I was ripped out to be educated in video format. I'm playing a game for a reason. It  was an interesting idea but for the same reasons above I was not on board with whatever this story is.
Graphics
The aesthetic at first was appealing but the more I saw the more I felt like it was just low effort for the sake of resources rather than an intended choice.
There is something to value in that it is trying teach you stuff in a puzzle platformer but the puzzles aren't as interesting and there is a lot of real boring platforming and running away from stuff. The game wants to give you an adventure, but the poor controls and the stuff mentioned above make this game below average at best. It's a hard no from me.

This is a hard one. I could say I recommend the game or I could say that I don't recommend the game, and both sentences would not be a pure truth.  It's somewhere in the middle. I enjoyed the trip along Alaska, among Iñupiat people and get to know their culture a little better. The game visuals are beautiful. But that's not enough. The gameplay is just not very good, and sometimes is just bad. This game had what many games don't: A good background history and theme to explore, a different and interesting subject, some interesting art vision. But the delivery failed where it couldn't fail: the gaming experience.
This could be a positive review. I've given positive reviews to games that are at this (average) level. In the end, it was the sense of seeing such good potential going to waste that made me decide on a negative review.

This is another in a spurt of artistic puzzle platformers with twists. This one sees you playing two travelling companions: an Alaskan Native  Iñupiat girl separated from her village and a white fox who she stumbles upon. The two become in separable. And they each have unique abilities that are essential to the pair's survival. I'll start off by saying the characters are SOOOOO appealing. A mix of cartoon and slight realism, especially for the animals. There is a fierce polar bear too but he kind of wants to eat the both of you. Yet still totally huggable. (before he mauls your face). Now lets get to the gameplay. They can both jump and climb very well. The controls are very usable on the keyboard. The fox can call spritis to help them in their journey as well as has a little more nimbleness, able to ricochet off of walls to get to higher places. The girl, fluffy parka and all, can attack things with a bola...usually ice chunks essential for the fox to use his trickery. You do become attached to the two rather quick. And the whole thing is authentically narrated by an Alaskan native as well. Like Nihilumbra the narration supports the story and sets up each puzzle screen. These two get out of the frying pan into the fire a lot we'll just say. I will also say that at times this game IS really hard. Not unplayably hard tho. That's kind of good as it gives you MORE than just the story. There are actually tricky puzzles that force you to actually do the moves correctly. Knowing is only HALF the battle after all. It DOES kind of hold your hand a LITTLE too much perhaps but that's also helpful. If you can't get past a screen in a few tries, it illustrates via picture which character should be acting next and where they should be. That is nice for screens that you get stuck on. Myself, if I am stuck, I turn off a game and try the next day. If I'm still stcuk after more tries then I look it up. This kind of short circuits that whole getting stuck thing...and still...even when you are presented with those hints for where you should be...you STILL have to do the moves. And it doesn't tell you exactly all the moves. Just nudges you really hard. So that IS satisfying. And man I'm SO SICK of that polar bear. He's likely to join Limbo's Spider in the animal villain Hall of Fame. And again....THANK you Limbo for bringing this kind of game to the forefront. I expect I shall have many delightful hours crying about my dead Alaskan friend....as I HAVE to play the fox as much as possible, ya know. (and it IS really sad when one of them dies. Because the other character DOES start crying! ;( )
edit: I've made it much further in this game now and realize what people's gripes are about. The gameplay sensitivity is pretty bad sometimes. spacebar is notoriously a bad jump button for sure. Sometimes it is very very unclear as to what you are supposed to do simply because it goes against some of the principles it set up originally. And with some bad areas it could offer more checkpoints so you don't have to keep redoing.

Story may be fun, mechanics are stupid though. Either its totally boring "run from a to b, then jump" or it's just plain annoying "guess the ghost magic trick we thougt of in this scene". Also, if you or your companion dog dies, there will be whiny noises which are probably supposed to make you care but did quite the opposite for me.

Come si può vedere dai trailer, questi frammenti permettono di passare da stagione a stagione. Questa meccanica è fatta MOLTO bene! "l'animazione" di cambiamento della stagione è veramente bella da vedere e molto veloce quindi se dovete fare dei puzzle molto veloci non avrete problemi. Ma ovviamente non è tutto oro quel che brilla quindi parliamo dei difetti (non parlo delle altre cose positive perchè sarebbero spoiler, anche se piccoli): i comandi non sono la cosa più reattiva del mondo e bisognerà prenderci la mano prima di poter "rushare" il mondo di gioco senza problemi-alcune animazioni della volpe sono letteralmente tagliate a metà e sembra quasi che si teletrasporti, ovviamente questo si nota solo se si concentra sulla volpe e sui suoi movimenti. E qui una cosa che si trova a metà tra un difetto e un pregio: la durata di questa opera d'arte: non dura tantissimo e se si cerca di fare tutti gli achivement allungherete il gioco di massimo un oretta. Ma questa fine e fatta proprio nel momento in cui il gioco stava per iniziare a essere noioso e ripetitivo. In conclusione, un applauso ai creatori di questo piccolo e solitario gioiello.

I bought this game expecting a fun, spooky horror game to play as a part of my developing tradition of binge-playing scary games during October-November. What I got instead was comepletely unexpected, and absolutely marvelous.
SOMA takes place in a dilapidated complex of buildings at the bottom of the ocean, where you are stalked by various nasty things. That's all you need to know going in, and anything more would be spoiling it.
Seeing that it takes place in the ocean was a big hook for me, because I am deathly afraid of that abyssal unknown (Subnautica is still the scariest game I've ever played). For some reason, however, this game didn't trigger that fear in me. In fact, it didn't really trigger that much fear at all.
Because it isn't all that scary.
It's tense, sure. It does a great job of maintaining a constant eerie atmosphere that keeps you on edge at all times. But terrifying, shaking in your seat, jumping-at-the-slightest-provocation
? Not here. At least for me. So if that's what you want out of a game, look elsewhere. But if you're in the mood for a smart, beautiful, emotional, atmospheric, ridiculously immersive
, SOMA will blow you out of the water (heh).
The basically nonexistent HUD, silky smooth animations, wonderful sound design, and continuous story-telling (there's not a single pre-rendered cutscene that I can remember outside of the literal beginning of the game) add up to one of the most immersive, if not THE most immersive game I've ever played outside of VR. I felt myself getting sucked into this world. Every time I turned it off, I felt like Neo awakening from the Matrix for the first time. The animators, texture designers, modelers, sound designers, and everyone else who contributed to how this game
deserve a hats off. It's half the reason it works at all.
The gameplay is simple, but highly enjoyable. Mostly solving puzzles, exploring, and being sneaky. I found some of the stealth segments to become boring after a little while, but everything else was very satisfying. The most intriguing thing to me was the way gameplay was interwoven with storytelling through out the game, which leads me to the next part.
The story is brilliant, and to me is one of the greatest examples I've ever seen of how a game can use the inherent interactivity of its medium to convey thoughts, messages, and emotions. You will be forced to do bad things, and the fact that it was YOU doing it, not just some character you have no control over, will hit you square in the gut again and again. It will bring up very profound concepts, and use interactivity and subversion of gameplay and player-game relations to deliver them in interesting and effective ways. I'd love to gush more, but I seriously don't want to spoil it for anyone. Just play it.
In summary, SOMA is a breathtaking interactive experience that you should play. I got it on sale for somewhere between 10 and 20 bucks, and got 10.5 hours out of it. At that price it's an absolute steal, and if you want to promote semi-indie devs making amazing single-player titles, I'd reccomend buying it at full price. It will suprise you, move you, and may very well change your outlook on life.
So get it. It's good.

I know that a lot of other people love this game, but for me:

Like their earlier game Amnesia, only without any resource management (in Amnesia, light was a resource in the form of tinder and lamp oil). What's left is an adventure with pretty basic puzzles and a story that thinks it is deeper than it really is. The player's character throws tantrums because he doesn't understand it, long after you've figured it out and come to terms with it.
A few times, the monsters you must avoid refused to leave the hallway I had to enter, forcing me to get "killed" by them and limp onward after waking up (they wander away a bit while you are unconcious, hopefully away from where you are headed but sometimes not).
Other areas you must wander for a while in the dark where they are also wandering, and the tension eventually gives way to annoyance because you cannot get away and have to wait, wait, wait for it to randomly go somewhere else over and over again.
It's pretty short, with my stats saying I have played for 11.7 hours, and I did finish it.
On the plus side, the atmosphere is perfect, with detailed, foreboding environs. The survivors and recordings you find are excellent for fleshing out the story. There is a lot of tension, but it is paced well, because you cannot be on edge all the time.

A surprisingly enjoyable casual game blending influences from titles such as Harvest Moon, Animal Crossing various tablet and social media games to produce a fun resource management game.
The three key aspects of the game are upkeep of the farm, management of a makeshift diner and repelling zombie attacks. This encompasses watering, fertilizing, harvesting food, chopping wood, pounding rocks, management of livestock, fulfilling food requests and general progression through upgrading your farm using resources gained mostly through serving customers at the diner and harvested crops.
An example of the upgrades is the recipe system, these are purchased from the town merchant and are then learned via a fruit ninja style mini game. Various upgrades such as seating capacity, food storage, tents which allow the recruitment of helpers and even a bridge to access your stranded cow all require the use of resources to unlock. All but the most basic seeds also need to be purchased before you can set about farming them.
An enjoyable game with content and longevity being the only obvious stumbling blocks.
