This game has good ideas and in some parts it is really strong, but it loses its charm because of it's many flaws.
I really liked the first part. It felt buggy and weird sometimes but it also felt somehow right and had a lot of good ideas. I never got to finish a match though, because in the end there were always some flaws which made it impossible to continue (always attacking remnant fleets for example which felt immensly like a bug but I couldn't say it was).
The second part is similar but loses its real-time focus. In some parts this felt worse: for example my favourite moment from the first game was when ships warped out of a sector and this is gone. But when you play a little bit you get to like the turn-based, more "strategic" command of your fleets. Battles are not taking place in the "real" map, but in special battle areas, similar to the game Gratuitous Space Battles. This is fine I think.
But how these fights get started feels often very strange, for example when an enemy fleet is attacking one of your planets and you put your whole fleet there. On the way, however, the enemy is passing another of your planets. The AI clearly didn't intend to attack this other planet, but since it's in the proximity of this planet it starts a battle and you lose a planet. It's strange and there are a lot of those moments in this game.
One other example is a remnant fleet attacking your planet, but since it doesn't have ground troops it just blocks it. Now, I don't know if I'm maybe just to stupid to find it, but you can't stop freighters from transporting food. So this planet was constantly spawning my empty freighters and the remnant ships destroyed them instantly. All in all I feel like there is a lot of options from the first part missing (for example the dialoge with alien races) and replaced with strange other things (like the AI television show). All of this feel like it was put in with a lot of vision but it lacks in execution.
I couldn't finish a game there either. I played on easy but the AI constantly spammed me with ships which was just so annoying that I stopped playing. Every round in the end-game was micromanaging for me. And not the fun kind. Sorry StarDrive, I really liked your premise and I really hope you improve. I will stay tuned, but in this state I can't recommend you.

This game directly appeals to Master of Orion and other space 4X games fans.  There are a lot of interesting aspects of this game, but unfortunately there are also too many fatal flaws.  The infantry combat is so bad that many players avoid it altogether.  It's basically a crappy isometric turn-based combat minigame that would have been sold on a Wal-Mart multipack floppy disk ten years ago (I'm serious, it makes the original final fantasy tactics look amazing).  The other fatal flaw is the sheer amount of interface glitches.  I can ignore and work around a lot, but they are everywhere.  The third fatal flaw is that you cannot give verbose commands to your ships in combat.  The ship combat is very interesting, but it's incredibly limited.  There is no formation move.  You cannot queue commands.  The battlefields are always the same boring grid, etc.
The dev has patched it many times, but it's still a broken game, and he is already moving onto his next project.  He hard coded many parts of the game so it is very hard to fix/mod, so this game will NEVER be fixed.
Do not buy this game, and be careful about supporting pre-releases!
With great sadness I remove this once promising game from my library list.

Ah, a not too complex blended real time with turnbased strategy game, thoroughly fun to be sure. The turn based method of colonizing planets and tending to your growing civilization is well executed, as the real time space battles are fun and a visual feast, but perhaps lacking in complex strategy. The characters that represent the various factions are all fun  to interact with and play as. The true meat of the game is in designing the various starships you make fleets out of, this is what really defines battle strategy and is very fulfilling when you can build your next evolution of ship for your fleet. Where this games sees some major downpoints is a lack of multiplayer, and some difficulties late game as the number of ships in battle can reach  in the hundreds per side as the game needs to calculate trajectories for every shot and damage for every piece that makes up the ships you design. another annoyance is that while you can redesign your ships as you aquire new tech, the other factions do not and are relegated to predesgined ships that simple dont put up much of a fight. the game makes up for this as the enemy may amass giant fleets, that will cause the game to stutter as i said before. This is great fun and hours of play go by as the 'just one more turn' syndrome hits hard.  the characters are all fun, the game plays great, but despite some late game issues and a lack of multiplayer, its still a recommendation. The full price of the game is fair, but if it drops in price with steam sales and such, its a definate buy.

I think I can sum up the game in one word: tedious. StarDrive 2 is a modern remake of Masters of Orion 2. It adds some neat features, like placing modules in specific quadrants of the ship but takes away on some of the others. I'll try to break down some of the main areas.
Colony Management - It's very tedious, much like MoO2. There are some auto-builder scripts you can select from to focus on food, research, or production. But, when I pick one like production, the manager often moves some of the people off of production and over to research. If I try to correct this, the colony goes back to manual mode. Also, you may inadvertently get technology for colony buildings you don't want (some have drawbacks), and these will get rolled into the build queue by the colony "AI".
Ship Combat - Actually the best part of the game. It plays similar to Homeworld, but without the bells and whistles that make Homeworld cool. You can't pause combat, which makes any kind of tactics pretty much impossible so you end up charging in with everything you got. Fighters are essentially unselectable as they flit about the main ships of your fleet. Still, it's satisfying to watch your enemy ships explode into debris.
Ship Design - The design is another aspect of the game that is fairly good, but still lacks something. I found that at the end of the game, lasers were still on par with the best tech in the game. Either my math was way off, or there's really no reason to try new guns. In MoO2, it was fun to try out different weapon types, especially boarding enemy ships. But, I just didn't feel the same enthusiasm here.
Ground Combat - Very very tedious. Similar to ship design, a lot of the tech you get for ground combat is useless. The skeletal upgrade gives +20 max HP but leaves your soldier wounded by 20 HP. Since they don't naturally heal out of combat (until late game), the upgrade is pointless. Guns like the fusion carbine will do 20% more damage against unarmored foes, but 86% less against anyone with armor, which is pretty much everybody. The AI is really stupid too. You can stand still and let the enemies exhaust themselves walking into your firing line of fresh troops. However, if you press Auto before combat, you're likely to lose a ton of troops than you wouldn't lose by playing out the combat. Also, Mech Units are very disappointing. They are very slow which makes me just want to use regular troops more. (The dinosaurs with lasers are pretty awesome though I must admit). Also, you must equip every single troop. If the enemy invades a far off planet and you didn't equip those troops with the latest tech, they are likely to be holding stupid worthless knives and get rolled. All the clicking involved here is very tedious, it would be nice to set a master template automatically used for all new troops.
Research - Sad. I don't recall ever looking at a research screen in a 4x game and thinking "wow, I don't want to research any of this". Not until StarDrive 2 anyway. Many of the "upgrades" come with drawbacks. Like, you can grow food on radiated planets but it makes your people mad. Or the aforementioned carbine rifle, or pretty much any ship weapon. Some of the colony upgrades are very useful, but incur heavy upkeep fees which force you to raise taxes so much that you lose any additional productivity from the buildings. If the upgrades didn't have so many drawbacks, it would be so much better.
Spying - I didn't try this much because it seemed too slow to be useful. You send spies in and they gather intelligence points which you use to plant a mole... which then gathers research points... which finally delivers enemy tech to you. But the enemy's spy network can destroy your mole fairly fast meaning you probably never steal any tech. It's far easier to just assimilate it or trade for it.
Diplomacy - It's not great. You can trade for tech, but it raises this intolerance meter which requires time to cooldown. The other races are quick to declare war, on Normal difficulty, even when you have great rapport with them. This is something I expect at higher difficulty levels, but not Normal. I do like how the items offered in trade have point values so you can quickly tell how likely they are to accept.
GUI - Sometimes my fleets would split up, especially after an invasion. One time I saw a fleet that said it would arrive in NaN turns (not a number!) and just froze in space. If you click on a planet from too far of a zoom, you won't be taken to the colony even though it highlights. The GUI just feels like it needs too many clicks to get what I want done.
Overall - The game just feels tedious. I got to where I owned half the galaxy versus three small remaining alien races. I could tell it would be another four to five hours of clicking to finish the game when I decided to just uninstall it. It seems like it has a lot of potential though, and there aren't a ton of bugs. Fix the colony AI, add troop auto-equip, make the tech more enticing, UN-balance the ship weapons and I think you'd be on to something.

Despite me only having 15 minutes logged at the time of the review, I have been playing this game on and off since late 2010. What I can say is that the game is an average game at best with okay physics but a lack of necessary features and some bugs can make the game rather grueling to endure.
The game's premise is simple: collect the cheese by using wasd or arrow keys and then return to the mouse hole to earn points. In time, you become the shaman with the ability to build platforms for the others to traverse. You also get skill points to then use in a skill tree to get more passive abilities as shaman or completely new abilities. It's a solid concept and it is enjoyable. There are also multiple room types. Regular rooms have a normal map rotation comprised of official maps and then permanent community made maps while vanilla rooms only uses the official maps made by the developer. Furthermore, the business model is sound, using in game purchases only for cosmetics rather than game changing effects.
However, there are no rebindable keys to speak of. This will turn off quite a few people. Secondly, the tutorial is clearly lacking, completely omitting any sort of shaman tutorial.  Being a decent shaman is rather difficult and the community will be quick to call you names should you fail. Finally, the steam client is a little choppy. You're better off using the official site or downloading the non-steam client for the time being.
All in all, it's an okay game. The lack of key features will make the game not as appealing to most but for a free game, what are ya gonna do?
Also the community can get to CoD and Dota 2 levels of hostility.

According to indie developer Necrophone Games, Jazzpunk is a “comedy adventure game set in an alternate-reality cold war world, plagued with corporate espionage, cyber-crime and sentient martinis,” fused with gameplay supposedly inspired by spoof classics such as Airplane and Naked Gun. So, with a description as above, it is fair to suggest that I had no idea what to expect when I ‘cyberjacked into the netrix’ for the first time.
Published by Adult Swim Games, whose notable successes include the absurd, quasi-addictive Robot Unicorn flash-game, it was always a reasonable guess that this title would be somewhat lacking in real-world sensibilities. By the time your character has consumed his prescription ‘Missionoyl’ medication (Guidelines for usage: take one capsule per mission until reality is sufficiently augmented), your assumptions are confirmed. Jazzpunk is Christian Bale crazy.
You see the world through the eyes of Polyblank, an espionage agent of sorts, who, under the instruction of a peculiar gentleman known only as The Director, must infiltrate the Soviet consulate to obtain a top-secret data cartridge.
Except, when you arrive at the location of your first mission, it doesn’t take too long to realise that the ‘storyline’ itself is as tenuous and stringy as overcooked spaghetti, it is purely the vehicle that transports the player from one fast-paced escapade to the next. This is not to say that there isn’t a vague storyline in place, but, to be playing this game for its storytelling narrative and character depth would be to miss the point entirely. Jazzpunk is intended to be a light-hearted poke at, well, pretty much everything.
It is an ambitious notion, particularly for an indie games development team consisting of just two people. The good news, however, is that Luiz Hernandez and Jess Browse have succeeded in their primary aim, to make people laugh. After a promising but sluggish opening chapter, Jazzpunk really begins to gather pace, providing several genuine laugh-out-loud moments, generally involving pigeons.
However, Jazzpunk isn’t just the quirky chick that nobody wants to take to the prom. She’s pretty, too. A vivid cartoon landscape adorns the open-world environment, and Hernandez himself has composed an original soundtrack, which wouldn’t sound out of place in a 1950’s motion picture.
Help From a Few Friends
Those hoping for a little more than an interactive comedy can also rest assured, Jazzpunk is not short of good old fashioned gameplay. Mini-game appearances from favourites such as Frogger, Fruit Ninja and Space Invaders creep up on you when you least expect it, as well as an incredible wedding-themed parody of Quake, in which players must use champagne corks as projectiles in order to avoid the prospect of matrimonial doom.
The game builds to a resoundingly triumphant climax. An Olympic style multi-format duel with the story’s main antagonist, The Editor (or ‘The Man with the Horn Rimmed Glasses,’ as he is originally introduced), continues to raise the ridiculousness stakes, and an epic gravy boat race (yes, that’s what I said) closes the battle magnificently.
Jazzpunk, a nominee for the grand prize at this year’s Independent Games Festival, is a thoroughly enjoyable experience from start to finish. It shares some similarities with fellow IGF nominee The Stanley Parable in its ability to not just break, but smash the fourth wall, yet still remain exciting. However, where it stands apart from TSP, and the vast majority of other computer games to date, is its steadfast commitment to being absolutely mental.
Too Much of a Good Thing?
Of course, the off-the-wall nature of this title will mean that it will not be for everyone. If you are expecting an experience that follows traditional gameplay protocol then you will be confused, let down, and most likely irritated. Jazzpunk is wacky, in a way that is simply incomparable to anything else I have ever seen. It is an explosive compound of equal parts satire and slapstick, noir and nerd, sublime and ridiculous.
On the whole, Jazzpunk seems to completely merit its reception as one of the best independent games to be released this year. In terms of replay-ability, it is very solid. Having completed the full-story twice, I was able to find plenty of content that I had missed on my opening play-through, which kept it fresh and engaging.
The humour is likely to be hit-and-miss, based on personal preference. But, for this soul, Jazzpunk is an extremely funny and refreshing piece of work.

This game parodies a lot of games and movies from the 80's and 90's and does it in style. I must admit that I wasn't impressed by the graphics of the game when I first saw the screenshots, but after having played it it looks really sharp and clean. The NPC's are still roughly modeled, however, and I think they could've done a better job here, but that's debatable.
There are so many little details, scenes and easter eggs to be found that you can't help but smile if you understand a reference. I don't think a lot of people will be laughing out loud, it's just all too random.
There are, technically, 4 levels to complete (if you count the mini levels it's a bit higher, of course) and each of them can be completed in around 30 minutes. So it isn't a long game. In fact, I think you can finish it within an hour if you just rush through it, but trust me, it's worth it to touch/activate/etc. as much as you can, and just play around with stuff.
For a game this random I was surprised to actually find a semi decent story here. It won't blow anyone away, but considering the context of the game it's kinda fun.
If you like weird and random games play Jazzpunk. It's also good if you want to relax. You can take your time doing things, and you're not being pushed forward every 2 minutes. Yes,... yes, I think I like Jazzpunk.
[Rating: 76/100]

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW:
So far, the simulator seems to be scratching an itch that hasn't been scratched in ages.
I love the attention to detail, and how they really bothered in making the ships. I love ferries but I fell in love with the fishing ship. Life huh!
I also love the water, although I feel it needs a bit more love as in transparency (side of boats and docks and depth) refraction and reflection. But I would also love if we had proper ship wakes. A few games that managed to nail wakes, that I've seen are Silent Hunter 3/4/5, Deadliest Catch: Alaskan Storm(dynamic wakes) and Spintires(Dynamic wakes), and I would love to see that beautifully well-formed foam around the ship, giving a sense of movement, or that you are displacing tons of water.
And the developer's approach to the community and how they are handling criticism, suggestion and even the comments are very commendable. I think this simulator has shown a lot of promise, and I can't wait to see the developer’s dreams over this simulator come true.
I also like how the light reflects over the surface of the ship, tiny things like that immerses you more than you can imagine.
In other words, it is still Early Access, bare bones, probably pre-alpha, and still needs a lot of work, but what it already has is fun and worth the money! So, if you like simulation and ships, this is definitely something you should buy!

At the current state, I can recommend this game only for die-hard ship simulator fans. For these people, it'll probably be like heaven. At first. Currently there are only a few missions to play but since this is an Early Access-game, it's totally understandable. Some missions have a time limit, if you exceed it by 1 second, it doesn't matter if you played for like.. 2 hours. Mission failed, that's all, plus an immediate return to the homescreen. The graphics are still quite buggy and unoptimized. But hey, it's Early Access.
What really annoys me though is that the developer seems to focus on new content, not on bug fixes. And of course, it takes a loooot of time to create new content. Meanwhile you have a buggy game with a couple of missions, and perhaps every month a new mission. That is what I see here right now. CTDs are quite common, happens to me 70% of tries to play a mission, it crashes within the first 10 seconds.
What I fear is that the game might become like the other ship simulators. Buggy, repetitive games with minimal content in terms of different things to do on the vessel.
Also, there are only the Steam Forums to communicate with the developer and well, I haven't seen him responding to any recommendations whatsoever on what to change in the game.
I think it is great that there's finally someone who wants to bring a new ship simulator to the market, but at the moment, I cannot recommend the average player to buy it, especially at this price. Wait a couple of months until major enhancements have (hopefully) been made so that you can see in which direction the game goes: the old Ship Simulator games or something new and really different.
// Update: 13.02.2015 - I was quite astonished when the developer announced that the game will leave early access next week, which means that it'll be on steam as an officially finished game. Although the developer said that they'll "continue to work" on it, I do not think that this is a good way for a game. It still has minimalistic content and is very unoptimized, containing disastrous bugs such as the horizon which is full of weird blue lines, flickering around and destroying the game's atmosphere. They have not been able to fix these for months. And how can you say that the game is finished when even the menus of some indie games made on unity look better than this one?

*Disclaimer* I played this game co op, with controllers, so I did not encounter any single player AI bugs, nor did I have any problems with controls. If you have read any negative reviews about the controls or the AI being buggy, just play it with a controller and co op and you'll be fine. Also, playing through this very few bugs were encountered, only one was, and that was not being able to watch the final cutscene in Foxtales (the DLC), which wasn't even in the main game, and we just watched the cutscene on YouTube.
Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna) is a beautiful game, not just in graphics, but in everything about it. The educational value of the game, the co op gameplay, and the resistance to being Westernised were all great reasons this game is amazing!
The educational aspect of this game is very well done. The more you play, the more videos you unlock. The videos are people speaking about their culture, stories in their culture, and explaining what exactly is going on in the game. This is a perfect way to learn about different cultures, as it gives the marginalised a voice for talking about their experiences, and it gives us context. Never do the videos feel like they are interupting the gameplay, as the videos are often found when you are not doing anything particulary important. Nor are the videos a chore to find, never while playing this did we have to look up a guide for the videos. The videos also were never a chore to watch, but always a pleasure, as it gave a nice little bit of context to what you were doing in game.
The gameplay itself was amazing, especially playing co op (I have played only up to the fox being introduced singleplayer, the rest I have played co op). The game was made for being co op and works best that way. No single character is used more or less in the game, and each player feels like they have an equal and important role in the game. Despite this being my account, I even played second player myself, because animals are awesome! While my co op buddy played Player One, and at no point was I bothered. I quite enjoyed playing second player, as the fox has so many great roles, such as moving spirits, wall jumping, and
But player one also has so many great roles, such as throwing the bola, pushing things (and paddling in Foxtales, which my co op buddy told me was a lot of fun). Despite the controls being very minimal, the game never felt constricted or empty.
Although I, myself, am not a part of any cultural minorites, the game not letting itself be Westernised was a very important thing. The whole game is not in English, instead it is in the langauge of the Iñupiat people, but with English subtitles. I personally don't mind subtitles, and eventually get used to reading them, so this provided no issues for me, but did do a really good job of giving the native people an actual voice instead of giving it an English voiceover. Other ways that the game refused to Westernise was that the entire plot of the game was derived from an actual Iñupiat story, and the story wasn't changed to make it more interesting to a modern audience, because it didn't have to be changed, as it was perfect. As well as the beautiful story and the language, the game also had lovely art cutscenes, as well as the game cutscenes.
Overall, it was a very unique experience to play a game made respectfully and made beautifully such as this one. I loved learning about a culture that I was very unaware of, I loved the co op gameplay, as it made me feel good to share this wonderful game with someone, and I loved the authenticity of the game. Even if I tried I could not find any reason to hate this game, no bugs did we encounter, we did not get stuck too long while playing, and we both had a brilliant time while playing it. I would recommend this game to anyone who has: an open mind to learning about different cultures, a controller, and an IRL friend to play with.

Never Alone is a single player (and co-op) platformer based around Native Alaskan stories. The major focus of the game is on the story itself, which is told with beautiful visuals and environments.

-Puzzles relatively easy but still fun to solve
-Lots of check points
Cons:
-Controls were a little frustrating,
-Certain parts felt not adapted to single player. (For example, I needed Nuna to hold a box while I moved the fox up to the platform, but Nuna let go when I changed characters making the puzzle extremely hard)
-Died a lot
-Pretty quick to finish
-Not a lot of alternative paths/exploration
For an enriching storytelling experience, I would recommend this game!
Excited to see if any more stories are released!

If you enjoyed Tyrian 2000 from way back in the day, you're likely to love this game, as it plays fairly similar in both in game play and the ability to customize your ship to your liking (though this one is more intricate).  I loved being able to design my ship from individual parts, it allowed for a massive degree of customization, and the fact that I could sell back parts at full value meant I never felt afraid to try new things because I knew I could always undo them if they didn't work out.
While the random drops of equipment can be kind of annoying, I found later that I actually liked it, because it can force you to make interesting choices.  All your plasma cannon drops lately have sucked, so do you deal with a massive ship of weak but high quality weapons, a small but overpriced ship of powerful but relatively low quality weapons, or switch to other weapon types entirely that you're less comfortable with?
I actually found myself using exceedingly old weapons at one point because it had a rare quality that let it be fit on the smallest ship parts, so even though it was a bit expensive and weak, my ship was absolutely tiny because of it.
The difficulty seemed about right, though I found some of the latter levels too easy, and I hadn't even spent time harvesting some of the prior levels for additional scrap like I could have ahead of the time limit. "Just one more level and I can upgrade this subsystem..."
It's one of those games. You know which ones I'm talking about. "Just 5 more minutes..." turn into "Why are the birds so loud this late? Oh...".
So, what is the game about?
Basically it's a 2D arcade-style side-scrolling shooter with 2 game modes (campaign&survival). What sets it apart from the generic shooter, apart from being quite polished and having rock solid gameplay&controls, is the upgrade/weapon handling. Between each level you are able to modify your ship more or less from scratch. Layout, engine, energy generators, energy storage, weapons, defensive systems and lots of other addons like tractor beams or loot magnets are at your disposal. And that's about it.
What makes it work is how well it comes together. The gameplay itself is solid (if somewhat repetetive), the levels are just about the right length not to get boring, the upgrade system offers lots of stuff to play with but is really straightforward and easy to use.
That said, there is room for improvement. The variety of enemies is fairly small, the level design is rather basic and while gamepads are supported there is no option to configure it properly (some buttons can be mapped ingame but that doesn't help much). As steam offers a controller remapping it's not a big issue but an ingame configuration would be nice.
Overall I think this is a really enjoyable, above-average shooter with decent replayability. I wouldn't necessarily recommend it to hardcore bullet hell fans (if I can beat it casually it's probaly too easy ;) ) but to anyone who enjoys a decent arcade shooter with lots of customization options. Would definitely buy it again.

I've been playing StarDrive2 for a long while now and I've neglected to add a review until now after seeing its Mixed rating which I feel is undeserved. I would like to list off the games major stengths and weaknesses.
Strengths:
- Extremely customizable galaxy (How many stars, liklihood of life in each system, several different patterns to place them in that have significant gameplay consequences for each one)
- Excellent execution of the 4X concept (Explore fast to get a few treasure systems with plenty of buffer systems between them for protection )
- 9 species with customizable racial traits (Personally I was happy with their presets and never changed them)
- Beautiful digital graphics and fine character art
- Stradegy in unexpected places (Most battles are decided by how well you built your ships and each race has a favored stadegy that requires a tweak to your fleet to come out on top)
- Great replayability (I'd swear I would be sick to death with this game and after a two-week break I play as a new species and conquer the galaxy all over again!)
- Crazy ideas (I've made talking elephant citizens, T-Rex shocktroops, and dropped zombie virus nukes on planets!)
- The developer is good about fixing bugs or performance issues that get brought up (Crashes have been rare for me)
Weaknesses:
- Not much story in the campaign ( I've never played a 4X game brimming with plot )
- The space battles dont require a lot of stradegy (Its mainly decided by the quality and size of your fleet)
- The game really slows down in the epic 100+ ship battles (Patches have since made it tolerable)
- The ground battles are stiff and slow in contrast to the fast and fluid space battles ( The troop limits on special missions keep it challenging though )
-  The only way to win is wiping everyone else out ( Develepor claims there will be more victory conditions later )
My personal score - 9/10

An absolutely amazing game for RPG and Real Time Strategy fans. Control a horde of minions across five worlds to assert yourself as the ultimate overlord. While you're out, you will find a mistress to call your love, investigate a zombie outbreak, and defeat seven fallen heroes that destroyed your tower and killed your predecessor.
TL; DR: Fun Game, Awesome gameplay, godawful voice acting and story.
Pros:
*Simple, yet tight controls- Controlling minions is as simple as selecting a target and clicking the mouse to send them on their way. Your own combat skills are not as prevalent because you have minions to fight for you, but using yourself to soak up damage and dishing some out while you’re at it feels satisfying.
*Good Variety- The usage of four different minion types keeps for a large variety of possibilities in the game. Keep your Red Minion's in the back as they throw fireballs, sweep your Green minions onto the backs of larger foes and watch them fall, and let your blue minions come and sweep up the mess, resurrecting dead minions and conserving valuable resources.
*Interesting Puzzles- With each minion having a special skills and abilities that mean only they can do specific tasks, it opens up for a huge amount of puzzles, many of which will give a sense of satisfaction upon completion.
*Humorous- I wouldn't say that Overlard has the best humor at all times, but in between your elderly minion master being rejected by just about any female that he comes into contact to, and the antics that your minions get into whenever sheep are involved is enough to brighten up anybody’s day.
*Simple Story- Not exactly an Oscar winning story, but a simple and satisfying story about a man with control over a massive horde of minions invading the world. It has good pacing, and you feel like you're making progress with the semi-open world filled with things to do, and kill.
Cons:
*Short- I blew through the campaign (Goody-Goody run, more on that later) in about twenty hours. I went back and played the game as an evil jerk, but that ended up being even shorter, only around ten hours.
*The Voice Actin' Guvnuh!- The voice acting is bad. Like, unbelievably bad. I can understand that they only had eleven credited voice actors, and admittedly some of the voices, such as those for the Minions and the Mistresses, are rather good, but the peasants and the fallen heroes are just cringingly bad.
*Pathfinding- Gnarl, your minion master, regards rather late in the game that your minions have small brains. However, the player could have guessed that by then due to the horrible pathfinding, where minions will often go up to a ledge, stop for a second, and come back without even looking at the ramp right bloody next to it!
*Unnecessarily unforgiving- There were many points in the game where I almost gave it up, most notably near the end. One enemy, a sand worm that pops up from the dirt and devours anything that is standing nearby, made me quit the game around 5 times because it ate 35 of my minions without so much as a chance for me to get them out. When it takes forever to grind enough minions to either upgrade an item or to proceed in the story, it's easier to just leave the game and start at the last save point.
*Ending/Moral Choice System- In Overlord, how evil you are depending on your corruption level, which you can increase by killing innocents and being a general♥♥♥♥♥♥ It really only changes the function of a few spells, so having two runs through is kind of useless. That being said, it also changes the ending that you get after you kill the final boss, and both endings were absolute tripe! You're either Pope Magnificent the still somehow "Evil" or Darth Sidious and Godzilla mixed together, both portrayed in a two-minute cut scene and neither of which felt like it did the game justice.
With all of the pros and cons listed, I still wholeheartedly suggest looking at Overlord, as it's some of the most fun with an RPG that I've had in a while. It's where you want to go for pure catharsis and cruel glee, not where you want to go for a good story.

Despite many glitches, bugs and exploits, I'm still having fun with Friday the 13th The Game.
Many people consider Jason to be a very strong character, and for the most part, it's true. However, I don't necessarily consider this a problem. "Friday the 13th" is the story of a crazed maniac slaughtering 100s of people, and not a story of how a bunch of teenagers outsmart a buff, grown man with a love for sharp edges and masquerades.
Playing as a counselor, you will die. A lot. It's even emphasized in the achievements. You gain achievements for completing 1, 500, and 1000 matches, both as Jason and as Counselors. On the other hand, you only have to escape about 40-50 times to gain all the achievements related to winning a match. Why? Because winning is meant to be difficult.
Being on the wrong end of a shift-grab and instakill is a frustrating experience, and I do not condone it. But in general, it is only natural that people get aggressive in such a tense and competitive environment. The fact that you need to stay to the end of the match in order to get 500 points (this is a stupid mechanic, I agree), makes death as a counselor seem uninviting and a source of bored waiting. On the other hand, you have people that finally got to play Jason, perhaps for only the 10th-30th time. They want to make the most XP in their matches, and go to desperate ends in order to win.
At level 31, you have unlocked all characters. When I reached this level, I began to relax. XP didn't matter anymore, so I quit as soon as the kill animation was done and entered a new match. There was no need for me to wait, and I got a lot more playtime. As Jason, I had always been pretty chill. I only went for environmental kills (unless I had to let someone go several times or there was nothing remotely close), and noticed that most of the time, I won just like those that use controversial and cowardly methods. Even if the matches got longer, it only became more rewarding. I was able to chitchat and roleplay (god that sounds kinky) with the survivors, as well as have an exciting gameplay session as the arrival of the police or car repair ticked closer.
My point is, that if you think you are going to invest a good couple of hours in this game, take it chill. You will reach level 31 eventually, and don't be afraid to leave matches once you're dead. You don't have to let the survivors win, just give them an extra chance and fool around a bit. Chances are you are going to be able to kill them later on. This way you get a more enjoyable experience and have more matches done in less time. The gameplay is good but drags on unless you have some cool people to play with. Feel free to mute TS and/or Discord in order to get a more exciting gameplay experience. Now that the achievements are working (mostly, I guess?) you have a motivation for further grind.
And HEY, there is a lot of new content coming, so you might as well stick around for a while.

i beat this years ago on the ps3 and remember liking it a lot, thought i'd replay it for the steam port ($10 right now)
wow!!! wow!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! it's everything i remember and more. i played on hard difficulty which was the perfect balancing imho - i died lots but out of those deaths there were few that really made me frustrated. the controls are just about perfect, the only complaint i had is using the dpad to change weapons can be weird when you're speeding around, but using the boost feature is very satisfying and you can pull off lots of neat tricks like boosting toward an enemy, kicking it in the air, and entering bullet time to shoot the ♥♥♥♥ out of it. there's also a weird mechanic where you can smoke a cigarette behind cover and throw the butt to distract enemies. i never used it much but it shows the charm and detail put into the game. weapon progression seemed odd (even counter-intuitive) at first, but when you get the hang of it it adds another layer of strategy to the game. there are two methods of upgrading: random (not to mention rare) upgrade cube drops from enemies, and  collecting ammo for a weapon when its ammo is already full. the former is fast, but the latter requires 3 surplus ammo packs to get the next level. as a result, if you have a gun you really like, you'll have to use it less if you want to improve it. BUT, you hold 3 different weapons, so you can use the other two to attack and then use your preferred weapon in particularly hard spots. you have to approach encounters thinking "do i use this gun to make is easier, or do i use a lesser gun in anticipation of a harder battle later on?" which is subtle but adds an incredibly satisfying sense of risk/reward. there are around 12 different weapons in all, so you have freedom to mix and match to find your a comfortable loadout (i stuck with rocket launcher and assault rifle, emphasis on upgrading the rockets, using the third slot to pick up different weapons as available). enemy types are generally varied and areas are arranged in a way that keeps combat feeling fresh. the boss fights use the same mechanics as regular combat, but requires you to rethink what you know to fit the arena and offending move set. these tend to make the best boss battles in video games, in my opinion at least.
i skipped most of the cutscenes, as the story isn't that important and scenes usually drag out with you trying to find an exit, but then something unexpected happens and you need to find a way around. the soundtrack is about what you would expect from a game of this type - lots of pulsing techno and hard rock. nothing amazing, but it works within the context of the game. the graphics are nice and the game runs at 60 fps (thank you sega!!!!!), and the character design is great all around.
the game's length was probably its biggest issue at launch - it's only around 10 hours, and even with the replay value i can understand being hesitant toward smacking 60 bucks down for it. the steam port is basically improved in every way, and its base price is $20 (i got it 50% off from the autumn sale), so there really isn't any reason to pass it up if it looks appealing to you. it excels in everything it sets out to do, and i could easily see it finding its spot in my top 5 all-time favorite games. play this goddamn game!

The game's online interactions are a mess. Disconnects are relatively common, loading screens take forever, matchmaking is allegedly pretty messed up (though that's mostly based on gear numbers and rep levels, which you shouldn't pay as much attention to as most people do, as they're hero-related), and the community is up there with the worst you can find. Constant♥♥♥♥♥♥talking, trolling and whining when people lose. Single player on it's own is not worth much, it's a decent way to get to know the heroes and get the basics down, but that's about it.
With all that said, I don't regret dropping 60€ on it. Objectively it's probably not worth it, but I've had so much fun with the game I don't mind, and probably will continue to do so for the foreseeable future. The combat feels exactly like the game you've always wanted, you know the one. Fluid as ♥♥♥♥, Dark Souls-esque requirement to commit to an attack, feints, mindgames, parries, all that stuff. On a mechanical level it's relatively deep, but doesn't cross over to actual fighting game territory with their frame-perfect input nonsense, so skill-wise this is an upper middle tier I'd say. You still need to perfect your moves and get comfortable and deliberate with your inputs, but mechanically things don't get that complex. There's been some mumbling about hero balance but personally I've never spotted any glaring problems. There seems to be a counter for most things, and team-play is always a thing if you don't have the answers yourself.
I will leave a thumbs up because I genuinely think it does well what it sets out to do, and this very well might be the game you've always wanted, but with a word of warning. Be sure you know what you want from this game before you drop that big an amount of cash on it. There are flaws, and first getting into the game might be a bit daunting. Oh, and preferably bring a friend. Playing alone is fine if you're training or just want to spend some time, but the game absolutely does shine most with friends.

8.5/10
+ Unique subject matter and location. The game takes place in Alaska and is about Iñupiat people. I wish there were more video games about little known cultures and folklore. This to me is the strongest point of the game.
+ The game includes short documentaries ("cultural insights") that unlock when you meet owls. They are interesting to watch and don't disrupt the flow of the game.
+ The art style is beautiful and the animation very well done.
+ Not too long, which in my book is a plus.
- The game is a bit thin on story and a tiny bit too heavy on puzzle platforming, even more so in the Foxtale DLC. I would have preferred it to be the opposite, with a more engaging story and some more twists.
- Controller bugs. If the controller disconnects (e.g. due to depleted batteries) there is no way to continue. The game suggests to press Space to connect, but that doesn't really resume functionality, with only a couple of the buttons working. I always had to close the game and start it again to resolve these issues.
- I played singleplayer and it's clear that the partner character is a bit AI-challenged, sometimes managing to get itself killed in situations where a human player would easily survive. I'd assume local co-op is a smoother and more satisfying experience.
- Some cultural insights are less easy to unlock (I must have missed a few of the owls). This seems pretty pointless to me, so instead of replaying segments to get them to unlock, I just watched them on youtube.
The game is unique, interesting and fun to play. I definitely recommend it and can only hope to see more games like it.

My wife and I enjoyed playing Never Alone (and the Foxtales DLC) together as a couch co-op.  It is not long, not hard, and has visuals and a narrative that we both enjoyed.
I think that it is best played in this way as opposed to single-player (in which you switch between controlling one or the other character).  In co-op, each player has something to contribute, and the one truly needs the other. If you are interested in truly playing "together" (as we were) ... instead of playing against one another, then you may find this game to be a nice diversion.
My wife appreciated the fact that the game wasn't overly "stressful" or had much in the way of "destruction" (i.e., where the means of accomplishing a goal was essentially to hurt, break, or destroy something else).
The game has some bugs that sometimes resulted in our not being able to unlock every single piece of bonus content (i.e., if we failed a jump at the very end of a chapter, the chapter might advance anyway, without giving us an opportunity to try again).  Also, I found that the Cultural Insights bonus videos would not play on my machine when I launched the game through Steam's "Big Picture Mode".  However, if I launched the game outside of Big Picture (i.e., by directly running the Never Alone icon on my desktop) the Cultural Insights would play fine.  So yes, there are some quality issues ... but not too frustrating and not enough to make me not want to keep on going.
I played as fox ... which I enjoyed quite a bit.  The movement and animation, while perhaps "simple", was still fun to watch and control.
If you are looking for a pretty casual little game to play together on your couch with your friend or significant other, then I think you might want to consider this game. We got it on sale for $6, and we think it was worth the experience at that price.

Wow. What an amazing visual novel.
Orwell begins as a simple story about an investigator following up on a crime, but deviates into a darker story asking the player if what is for the greater good truly is ethical.
There are a few choices that will change the story significantly, and these choices will create different endings, allowing you to play through the story a few times as different investigators before the game truly "ends" so you can get the whole story.
The only con, a large one in my opinion, is that the game babies you and holds your hand. All answers are highlighted to you. Large red (!) signs appear when there is a pertinent piece of information in that story. NON-STORY SPOILER:
For a game that has the feeling of a detective thriller, you are practically on rails to what is already being laid out for you.
Overall, this is a masterpiece of a novel, it emulates the fearmongering that comes from modern technologies, and has the potential to give you goosebumps from the twists and turns you, the lone investigator finds on the trail. While there are a couple choices that cement the final ending, the majority of the game is spelled out for you, but that's okay, this is an amazing story and worth the hand-holding.

I purchased this game on Pewdiepie's Water Charity bundle. I really did not know what to expect as the title did not reveal much: only that there was a character named Thomas and that he was alone. But I booted it up and was pleasantly surprised!
How Thomas was Alone can be described is as a puzzle solving platformer. You use different characters and their abilities to complete puzzles and physical challenges in order to make it to the next level/world. The gameplay mechanics are extremely smooth and very simple to operate. I find that a lot of the time; platformers are very difficult to play on a computer, due to the keyboard being awkward for one's hands. I have to admit I did have to take some breaks for my hands during playing this game, overall I haven't much to complain about.
The story is absolutely adorable, and the narrator really brings the story to life. How he portrays each character is a lot of fun to watch and a lot of fun to listen to. He reminds me a lot of Stephen Fry from The Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy.
While the game does have replay value, I don't see it being on the same level as Mario or Megaman's replay value. But overall it is a timeless piece and hopefully the game will gain well-deserved popularity.

This is a very unique open world apocalyptic survival game. The antagonists are called Nether. The Earth was hit by an extinction level Solar Flare. Most of the population turned into various forms of Nether.
There are many elements in this game that are in most survival games. You can loot, craft weapons, upgrade character stats as you level up, you have to monitor your food/hydration and health levels, trade, buy & sell items as well as join Tribes (or clans) to gain extra money and experience.
There are side missions like Escort packages to safe zone traders, loot drops, Securing Safe Zones from Nether, Trade Packages between traders for money & experience, collect Nether body parts to trade for items & weapons, Tribe Land Grab missions. There is A LOT of PVP, KOS on this game. If you want to PVP, there are plenty of servers to join. If you want to play a little more casually and/or want to play with others without fear of being KOS, you can seek out a PVE server, although there aren't many.
Overall it looks very nice graphically, it isn't too demanding on the GPU so it runs smooth yet still looks amazing, has a very well done eerie end of the world feel with very unique antagonists.

I am writing this review to help guide others, like me, who are seeing the "Mixed" rating, and wondering whether to take the plunge.  I read the reviews, and saw that the developer was busy fixing the many bugs, and decided to take the chance that the game would still be buggy.  A little background first:
I love space games like Master of Orion 2.  I bought this game when it was 66% off, and right after patch 1.2 went live.  With that said, here are my thoughts:
Pros:
-This game is basically Master of Orion 2.1.  To say that this game is inspired by MoO2 would be the understatement of the century.  The gameplay is copied, the tech tree is copied, and even the race customization options are copied directly from MoO2.  This is not a bad thing, but it was surprising.  I really love MoO2, but this game is only slightly different and expanded compared to MoO2.
-The art is pretty good.  Better than MoO2.
Cons:
-Buggy as hell.  And not in the weird technical-glitch kind of way.  Simple stuff that should have been caught by the bug-checkers.  Your planets will be invaded, but you won't have any troops, so there is no way to start the battle.  You must exit and load an auto-save.  Enemy ships fly off the edge of the screen in space combat mode.  You must retreat (lose) the battle.  You conquer an enemy civilization but somehow the planet doesn't get captured.  It just sits there, uncolonizable and unconquerable.
-Interface is really finicky.  When zoomed way out, there's like a 2x2 pixel range on which you have to click to select a planet.  Lots of other little stuff like that that makes the experience less than seamless.
Conclusions:
DO NOT BUY.  Wait for the bugs to be fixed.  This game is at Alpha level at best.  The good news is that the developer is actively fixing bugs.  The bad news is that they are also working on an expansion.  This is going to seriously detract from the bug-fixing, and will probably introduce a bunch of new bugs too.  Not a great sign.

If you own an electric guitar or bass, own any of the supported systems, enjoy playing rock music, you MUST own this "game".  It is everything that Guitar Hero and Rock Band want to be, for those who can handle a real fretboard.  I do have just a few complaints... but I list them more as motivation for improvement (hopefully in patches, but at least in future versions)...
A few interface navigation issues.  Generally "back" should return you to where you were.  That's not true 100% of the time.  Generally crossing between "Learn a Song" and "Score Attack" needs to have more attention devoted to it.  I think it works correctly if you access "Learn a Song" for a song from the Score Attack menu (IE, if I'm on "Some Song: Score Attack", select "Learn a Song", then use "Back", I'm at "Some Song: Score Attack"), but the inverse isn't true.  If I'm at "Some Song: Learn a Song", then select "Score Attack" and use "Back", I'm in the list of songs for Score Attack.
Fine-tuning could be a hair easier.  I noticed on some songs when I got into Drop-D on my bass that I needed to tune the open D down a hair for the first three frets to be closer... don't know why... but I was failing hard on the 2nd-4th frets of the low string until I did. It may be different in other modes, but at least in Score attack, once it decides your string is in tune, it moves on, and there is either no way, or no easy way to keep measuring the one string before moving on.
Lack of desktop UI optimization.  This is incredibly frustrating...  the game was obviously designed for a least-common-demoninator interface... so we have a UI that was meant for a simplistic game pad, even when using superior interface devices on a Windows or Mac PC. I think the best illustration is in sorting songs.  If you're on a device with a mouse (or touch for that matter), why not have drop-downs?  I tend to try to sort by tuning to see what to play next (I want to play them all, and don't want to retune between each song).  Tab, tab, tab, tab, tab, tab, "Crap, passed it", tab, tab, tab, tab, tab.....    WHY??  A search box would be great too...  we can certainly type a name if we're using console buttons remapped to a keyboard.  Oh... mission to do a particular song.... tab, tab, tab, tab, "crap, passed it", tab, tab, tab, tab, "Starts with 'B'? Great, I'm in the 'W's... ", up-arrow... hold.... hold.... hold...........    Search box...   click (search box entry), b, possibly a second letter in the title, click.  Done.   Even better.... if the mission is very specific, hyperlink the objective.  Actually, in most of the missions I can think of, you could give a button to go for it... or at least get closer (and that'd be even better for the consolers).  Next Mission: "Achieve 5% Mastery in Some Song", Press [whatever] to go to Learn a Song: Some Song.  Even with "play a new song" or "play x new songs", you could use that button to either randomly go to a new song, or open a list, filtered to unplayed songs.
I could go one all day, but perhaps one more: Learn a Song, Riff Repeater, setting difficulty.  It'd be really helpul to have an easy way to tune the song's difficulty to matching the score attack levels (easy, medium, hard).  I figured out pretty quick that I need to try to get Platinum on Easy and Medium before using learn a song, because if I'm pretty good at the full studio arrangement, seeing the simpler arrangements screw me up.... but sometimes I'd like to use riff-repeater to nail the medium-level version (and on a few rare songs, the "easy" version).
I've heard Zeppelin and Metallica are out because the record companies won't get on board. I'm guessing AC/DC is in the same boat. Here's some great DLC that may be easier to license:  Cake, lots of Cake...  SUPER bass lines, decent guitar riffs... I think that'd be fun stuff good starter pack may include "Hem of Your Garment" (awesome bass throughout, good rhythm through most of it... don't think there's a lead 6-string part in this one), "Sheep Go to Heaven" (something for everyone), and "Arco Arena" could be a really fun, short instrumental.  Ok... now here's something you're REALLY missing out on.  Music software for gamer geeks...    and NO JOCO?

Really wanted this to be a bit more polished than it is, and maybe it's just me, but it falls short for a few simple reasons.
The biggest is how you can't save design templates, which can take a long time to get the way you want. If you die, that's it - game over, start from scratch. I've died from some really, really stupid circumstances and buggy physics, too.
So what's the point in such a complex customization if you lose your design every time you die? I could see having to save the scrap to remake at least the physical structure in a future run, but anything less I would have assumed would be unthinkable.
If this absolutely can't be implemented for whatever strange reason, then there should at LEAST be presets or something equivalent.
I've played Gradius, R-Type, Ikaruga, RayForce, Touhou and on and on since I was a child. I'm not new to the genre. At all.
I'm using a controller, and PSR STILL feels like you're an ice cube sliding across a floor also covered in ice, shooting at snowflakes. Difficulty spikes and dips violently - it's either a little too easy or murderously hard (and I've tried several different routes with different difficulties). Blueprints are too random, so you're either OP early on or totally underpowered for the majority of a run.
There's a way to die without a run immediately ending, and revert to the previous system you were in to choose a different route, but I have no idea how this is triggered and there's no indication of how to earn 'lives' nor is there a counter of any kind. It happened to me once, and I was totally lost as to how it happened.
Some blueprints are way, way, way too expensive (I've never even seen what the black hole generator looks like, despite being frugal on scrap expenditure) and once you clear the campaign, your save just loads back to the mission before the end - so that masterpiece you've spent all that time building up and tinkering with basically gets shelved.
That's no fun at all.
It's an awesome concept. I feel like there was a lot left to experience, but the reward is not commensurate with the investment.
The campaign ending is brief but has a shocking and dark twist, hinting at a much deeper universe than we're shown...but there are no achievements or unlocks or anything for clearing it. At all. You would think there would be a NG+ system or something, or maybe a sandbox where you could test wacky builds, but no.
I can only hope some of this stuff comes as DLC. I know I would actually pay for it. For what it is, though, I recommend it just for the Saberhagen-esque experience.

I'm really not sure why this game has 'Mixed' reviews. This is truely one of the better 4X games out there and definitely one of the best produced in recent history. I can only assume that at least part of that is due to the fact that StarDrive II is totally different than StarDrive I. I didn't like StarDrive I personally so I would say thats a goood thing. If you liked SD I then you may feel differently. StarDrive II is a true classic 4X space opera title.
Ship customization is a real standout with this title. You can pick all the systems from weapons, shields, hanger bays to powerplants, C&C systems, and medbays and place them on a wide variety of ship sizes and shapes. Which adds another minigame type aspect that is well done and adds to the enjoyment and variety of the game. Each playthrough you can tweak and scheme to build ships that are a little better.
The real-time space battles are great with a well done variety of weapon effects (lasers, projectiles, missles, point-defense, etc), the ability to launch fighters for defense or offense, give standing orders, manually direct ships if desired, deploy mines, engage planetary stations, zoom in or out, whats not to love here?
The atmosphere is engaging and quite complete with a solid and well thought out lore. The races have real 'personality' and quirkiness that actually makes them standout and be remembered long after you play the game. This for me anyway pushes this game towards 'classic' quality. The custom race generator is quite excellent and balanced and allows you to make well balanced custom races that cater to your own playstyle.
The AI is above average for the genre. Clearly if you, like many of us that enjoy the 4X genre, have been playing these games for 20+ years the AI will rarely 'beat' you but it will give you a reasonable challenge. I have not seen the AI doing truely stupid thing like sending fleets to attack fleets twice their size or leaving planets undefended as I have with other 'bigger name' titles.
The diplomacy system is well done with many options to trade; money, treaties, trade, technology, planets, etc. The diplomacy screen gives you immediate feedback of the 'value' of both sides trades so you can clearly and easily see the likelyhood of making a successful offer. The races traits even affects what types of goods/technology they value more than others. Well done.
The graphics are quite varied and interesting. Not ground breaking but well above average. Different races ships look quite different. The universe scale map is quite nice with attractive atmospherics. The UI is well done and presents all the information needed to make decisions in an attractive and functional way without menu surfing.
Planet development is standard faire for the genre with a wide variety of planet sizes, types, and environments. The varied environments interact with various racial abilities. Planets can be mono or multi-racial with associated ups and downs depending on your technologies. A wide variety of buildings can be placed to upgrade your basic production values of industry, food, reseach. Your tech tree selections provide more than enough options for specializing your planets and giving them different roles within your empire.
The tech tree is perhaps not as deep as some would like but it is more than amply long for all but the longest of games in huge universes. The mechanic to pick one of three techs at each technology upgrade is innovative and ensures that on each playthrough the tech is varied and plays out differently from game to game. The tech tree can be easily modded if you really desire more.
Some people complain about the ground combat but I actually find it quite a fun 'mini-game'; sure it's not C&C ground combat quality but its a great way to break up the monotony of moving fleets and setting build orders. It's 'fun' not 'deep and complex'. Many of the ground combat scenarios are interactive story missions giving the game at times an RPGesque aspect which is nice and fairly innovative for this genre.
The game is fairly moddable so I love being able to easily tweak and mod minor annoyances in ways I prefer. Compared to the many other recent 4X games this is the one I would recommend over many of them.
In my 80+ hours I have seen few (if any) bugs and the game runs extremely stable which seems to be a rarity in todays world of 'early access' drivel.
Overall, I strongly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the classic 4X space opera genre.
If you have a choice Between Star Drive 2 or Stardrive, I suggest getting the original Stardrive over this one.

European Ship Simulator is exactly as the name states, it is a simulation of what it's like to take control of a variety of European style ships. It's in early access so there is still a ways to go for this game but it does show some promise.
Graphically the game looks mostly top-notch. The interior of the ship's cabin are well detailed with high resolution textures and great quality models. You'll find all the small intricacies that you would in a real ship, switches, knobs, GPS, etc, which helps with immersion. The water and weather effects are also some great stuff as well. Though the ship's interior, and the ships them selves show some good quality, the game isn't 100% consistent at the moment. Some of the environmental models, such as buildings, the docks, and streets, are very low polygon and features low resolution textures. I'm hoping that these lacking elements in the visuals are just place holders until a later / final build. Audio wise I got no complaints as the sound effects are realistic with great background noises from the boat's motor and the sounds of the ocean itself keeping you company.
As far as gameplay goes, It's surprisingly easy to learn and to get adjusted to, as the main controls is "WASD". Some ships will feature the option of more intricate controls with the num pad, allowing you to manipulate each of the ship's engines individually. Even at it's early stage, the game does a good job at simulating what it's like to drive a ship...for better or worst. I say this because, though the game achieves good results as a simulation, due to what it's simulating it may make it an incompatible for some gamers. Unlike Euro Truck Simulator, where you have the micromanagement of traffic, following traffic laws, avoiding cars, etc, European Ship Simulator is mostly "set sails to full" then auto-pilot straight. There will be lulls where you are simply doing nothing but watching the waves as you wait for your ship to arrive in a straight line to your destination. For enthusiast of simulation games or sailing, this won't be an issue, as that demographic probably already understand this before jumping in, but for the average gamer who is just curious to this game, know that this is a simulation before it's a game.
Currently at the time of this impression (version 633), there isn't much in the way of options, graphics, or audio, and there is only 4 missions available with no linking campaign or side features. This is early access I do understand, but at the same time I think it's fair to let people know that in it's current state, it is the bare minimum.
Overall, European Ship Simulator shows a lot of promise, that I think will shape up to be some thing quite interesting. But currently, it does feel rather unfinished. If you are a simulation game or ship/boat enthusiast, it might be worth your cash to check it out, even in it's early stages, but for every one else, keep an eye on it, but wait for later versions or even it's final release.

- Subject matter might not be as universally appearling as Euro Truck Simulator

It's an ok start, but too early for being on sale. Criminally unstable and buggy, and I say that not because I don't expect an alpha game to be buggy, but it often makes to where 5% of my mission attempts actually let me finish a mission without crashing or locking up. There is also no save function(manual or automatic, so you will lose your progress.)
There is also effectively no settings menu. Low, Medium, and High and none of them seem to affect how the game looks. No vsync, reflections, distance, AA, nothing.
The game certainly looks pretty, water reflections and physics are nice. Sitting inside the tug boat out in the ocean feels very realistic, however the actual buildings and cities a long the coast look like something from HotWheels Crash. It performs really well on my system, but that's something I'd expect, again looks nice, but not amazing.
The game has nice sounds, the roar of the engines below and the horn on the ships all sound fitting, though that's mostly all you'll hear. That and seagulls for hours because the skip time function will probably break for you as well.
Like I started with, it's a decent start, but under no circumstances would I suggest a casual player to purchase this. Only someone who is a big fan of ships and ocean simulators. Even then, they will probably go through all the content very quickly.
Launching February 2015 seems pretty soon, wait for launch before taking the dive off the starboard.

This is an excellent example of a narrative platformer. So far so good - but that it is a sweet and touching story (if it tapers off a bit with an inconclusive ending in a third act that doesn't feel as well written) so much the better.
Graphically, it is an excellent example of a very simple looking platformer whose simplicity has nothing to do with any retro affectations - just clear unambiguous shapes, but like nothing you'd see on a SNES. The primarily strings and piano compositions for the soundtrack suit the ambience perfectly and the actual platforming is fairly simple, just about frustrating enough to keep me engaged (so I imagine veteran platformers will find it all quite easy.)
This is a relaxing and well executed game, a standout among indie platformers. I recommend it.

Nether brings together an amazing graphically detailed post-apocalyptic world sprinkled with some addictive PvE elements like: skill leveling, quests, trading and weapon crafting and tops it all off with an optional PvP component that allows you to stalk and kill other players on top of the A.I. controlled nether.
Its STALKER aesthics meets Fallout (3 & NV) style gameplay.  Singleplayer content maybe a little lacking for someone who enjoys both games however.  Yet this has to be one of the best "unfinished" games Ive have the pleasure [and frustration] of playing.  There isnt that much the game needs to take it from being very good to great.
The learning curve at the beginning is pretty tough.  So much so that I almost gave up playing the game.  Gameplay diversity is fairly limited but conversely addictive as you try to build-up your character and their equipment.  Once you've played the game for a while you may perhaps miss features that other survival games provide like base-building.  It certainly doesnt have much of a dynamic past completing missions and boosting your equipment, other than staying alive ofc.  The game has also received a recent re-boot by the original developers, so content and features have been reset to an older build.  They intend to add modding and possibly PvE but what exactly, remains to be seen.
That said if you can look past the shortfalls in content diversity, the yo-yo development tract, the customary spawn-campers, kill-on-sighters and cheaters there is a veritable enjoyable post-apocalytic, survival experience to be had.  In single-player or PvP. But are you brave enough to try?
Online open-world, sand-box, survival PvP FPS, with optional singleplayer.
A decimated post-apocalyptic Earth where most of the population have been transformed into mutated forms called the Nether, by some otherwoldly event called 'The Cull.'
These monsters hunt the vestiges of humanity who try to survive in technologically protected safe-zones, as they attempt to kill as many Nether as possible and scour for loot across the once majestic cities of civilization.
Predominately PvP but most of the gameworld mechanics are PvE.  There is a single-player mode but some of the gameworld features are not balanced for this mode.
Nether boasts a wonderfully conceived and well-designed gameworld. It possesses a raft of features and artfully incorporates them into a beautifully atmospheric, greatly detailed and extremely immerisve gameworld that is not only a joy to play but addictive to.  There is one map of a large city containing safe-zones. Dynamic events such as escort missions, air-drops, and hostile Nether surges occur to mix things up.  Anti-nether devices can fail rendering safe-zones ineffectual.
The game uses a common gameplay cycle: Equip yourself. Explore.  Fight. Kill. Loot. Undertake missions.  Earn money.  Buy better equipment.  Rinse and repeat.  There are diversions which spring up dynamically: Escort packages to a safe-zone, take packages from A to B, sell junk combinations or nether parts at the appropriate vendor.  For which you receive a combination of XP or credits.  XP levels your character, credits enable you to buy the equipment required for prolonged survival in the wastes.  You can also craft better firearms to kill the bigger threats: players and reapers.
You can level up your character skills: Guns, Stamina, Survival, Strength, Stealth and Melee.  There is a max level so not all aspects can be maxxed out but you can customize the character to the way you wish to play.  PvP just adds another layer of gameplay by forcing you to fight to stay alive.  Where its kill or be killed.
The game expects you to die and lose you characters skills.  Unless you had a buddy you will respawn with only a knife, whatever is in your global inventory (which is not much) and the game bonuses that your account level gives you.  It is this cycle that will frustrate you at the start but it what ultimately keeps you playing.  Indeed the account level is critical and makes a huge difference the higher it is.  To increase it ofc you need to keep playing.
Has only a handful of distinct enemies from low level dog-like hunters, to alert screaming sirens, brutal golems and spine firing hunters.  Biggest threats are Reaper.  The name says it all.  Dont go hunting these brutes without the firepower or manpower to bring it down.  In PvP however the main threat is from other players.  Some of which wont even give you a chance to draw your weapon.
There is a reliance on having mostly fix spawned enemies so the A.I is fairly limited. It does an able job however for once you are spotted you will be attacked by any local Nether.  Get a screamer near you and it will alert many more Nether than you are able to deal with.  Once alerted unless you can outrun them to hide or get to a safe-zone they will not stop coming after you.
Standard mouse and keyboard.
Attention to graphics detail is what brings Nether to life.  Even though they may not be top notch I found skulking through the gameworld during the day or at night sheer bliss.  Unless I was too busy running away from Nether.  The ruined cityscape is hauntingly beautiful.
There is no real soundtrack but a low continous haunting humming sound provides a constant companion as you trek through the post-apocalyptic environment that perfectly adds to gritty atmosphere.  Nether enemies have their own distint call, wail or roar.  Weapons have decent sounds also.
None.  But those of you with teamspeak can listen to some banal player communications in your head-set! :p
Has a painful learning curve at the start of the game but once you start playing and understand that equipment and weapons equals survival you can make dying that little less painful.  At least in single-player.
Slight lag on my Core i3 at 1280x720 with most options off. Issues are minimal with some interface design and game-world clipping issues.
There are no achievements for this game.  No need to distract players from the enjoyment of staying alive.
No dlcs currently.
Havent experienced much of cheating since the early days of this game when there were many hackers and cheaters that culled alot of eager players such as myself.  There are fewer now but that doesnt mean they wont come back with a vengeance.  Safe-zone campers and Kill-on-Sighters are also present but its hard to know how many.  Admin capabilities are being added so servers can be policed.  But unless you are prepared to put up with dying and restarting alot dont try PvP.  You will hate it.  The biggest plus is modding being added to allow servers to be customized.
Single-player will appeal to anyone who enjoyed playing Stalker or Fallout out.  At least to some degree before too much repetition of gameplay sets in.  If it does those of you bave enough can try PvP.  Anyone who enjoys survival games or hunting other players in a sci-fi setting would enjoy this.
Unless you are a pro survival game player it will take you upwards of ten or so hours to get to grips with the early game, 40h to get self-sufficient if youre me.
Im not one for much PvP yet in single-player it has an underlying addictive quality that compels you to one more safe-zone to safe-zone run.  On balance I think it has just enough content and features to be worth £7.

Anybody who has read through George Orwell's 1984 will recognize many prevolent themes throughout this point-and-click adventure. While many movies and games struggle to rival their literary counterparts, Orwell does a spectacular job of demonstrating the themes prevelant in George Orwell's story. While the actual story of the game is different from the book, focusing on the player rather than Winston, many of the aspects are still the same.
I only had a few minor gripes with Orwell that did not take too much away from the story or my immersion. The only real problem that I had with the game was the fact that you had to open each file up to add data to them, rather than just dragging and dropping them onto the character web.
A compelling story with many twists leaves the player hungry for more, available through multiple playthroughs of the game. A second season to Orwell would be very difficult to achieve, due to the ending of the game. I will not go into depth about what this is, as I cannot without spoiling the game.
I strongly reccomend you play through Orwell if you have read the novel 1984 or are interested in games with themes of censorship and/or a malleable story.
