Orwell, in a not-so-subtle nod to George Orwell's criticism of totalitarianism (*CoughCommunismCough*) 1984. I've actually read 1984. It's not bad. It's not great, and quite frankly I think it's more of an observation than a story which in my eyes weakens it. It's also an incredibly quick read so I do recommend you check it out. On a scale of 1-10? Probably a 7. Amusing, but not the best. Slightly better than average.
Anyway, the gameplay of Orwell is unconventional and reminds me greatly of Papers, Please. Which is another game I should write a review on and I do recommend it. In it you scan documents for information and upload this information into a mega-database which contains details on everyone under investigation (at this time). Presumably, Orwell would be expanded to cover all citizens. In the name of peace, surely! Everyone can trust the government to know every detail about them to make sure that they're entirely safe! 
Light Spoiler Warning: Orwell is a narrative, a visual novel of sorts. I'm going to do my best to avoid spoilers.
Throughout the course of Orwell you follow the individuals of an organization called 'Thought' named after some German poem. Thought is an alleged terrorist organization. Your job is to follow the members of this organization to prevent terrorist activity. The first person you investigate is a woman with blue hair and problem glasses because of course she is. Which now presents us with our question. What scale of authoritarianism would be acceptable in the name of protecting people? As the game progresses, it gets to the point where almost the slightest connection to someone (perhaps eating lunch or seeing a movie together) is grounds for investigation. Authoritarianism seems to have a very tough job reigning itself in from being conventionally oppressive. 
You know, I could not help but giggle with glee as I listened to phone calls of people and other people got blamed for things that I did. It was glorious! And it kept happening! I felt no guilt at all for doing my job. Perhaps that's the point of the game. Thinking.jpg
The art style is... quirky. Not bad. Just quirky. The music is pretty okay too. My (small) gripe (I guess) is how long I had to wait for responses when it came to monitoring calls and SMS. I get that it's supposed to be realistic, that's the point. Not really a point against the game, I just felt that it was sometimes a little long. 
Overall, excellent game. Quite a nice length for the price ($10 at the time of posting). Of course, cheaper is always better. I think my first playthrough had a run of about 4 hours and there are multiple endings (all of which, I did not explore). It's a thumbs up from me.

10 Days after is a product of the Unity Engine, that is very clear upon initial load and play.  When I attempted to launch on Steam, an executable could not be found, so it simply wouldn't start.  I navigated into the local folder, found an executable, and used that to start the game, but Steam didn't track my playtime, so...  When I finally got into the game, I must say that I was very amused by the music played during the loading screen... Something about that tuba...  However, when I loaded into the world, after taking just two steps, I got stuck and had to relaunch the game.  This should allude to the state of the robustness of the game itself: very buggy from what I've experienced.  And this is to be expected, because the game is in version 0.09 I believe from what the menu told me?  Anyways, I talked to a few characters and killed a few zombies, ran really far to meet a player, ran all the way back to the central hub, did a few quests, then got stuck again and had to restart, lost all progress, and here I am writing this.  This review is mainly to offer a few suggestions to the devs, who appear active by their recent update about a week ago.
The car wasn't so obvious, so I didn't know about it until after I ran all the way to Josh.  I thought that was a huge waste of time, especially when nothing happened when I got there.  You should have included a zombie ambush or something, that would have caught my attention :)
The car also ultimately broke the game from my perspective.  When I got in it, I couldn't use the menu anymore.  I also didn't know how to get out of it; I still don't, I just mashed buttons until I escaped it's greedy clutches.  Also, when I was in the car, the "Press F to get in" wouldn't stop flashing in the upper left.
The zombies...  I laughed.  I'm sorry. :D  They're animated so poorly, it's quite unrealistic and a bit game breaking, but I could live with it if the next point was addressed.
The world is so empty at this point.  I was really interested when I came across the other towns, but getting there... It's so empty.  Maybe this is because it would be difficult to render a bigger environment?  There was a significant amount of lag, only from what I could imagine are too many assetts trying to render at a distance.
Finally, the dialogue is quite slow, although the writing isn't too bad.  I would speed up the text as it appears on the screen and make the option to skip it more obvious, since it took me several conversations to figure out that you can press esc. to skip through.
Those are the current suggestions I have for the game.  It's a good concept, but it's been done before very well by several games.  If you can find a better way to stand out above the other competition, then I will continue to support the game.  I'll hopefully be back to update this review when there's another update.  Looking forward to continuing with this product!

Pretty good game overall. Somewhere in the middle between GalCiv (strategic, planet management), Sword of the Stars (combat depth with some physics) and MoO (ship design and management on MoO2 level). All in all, I'd say - It is very fun. Has a lot of small, nice events that add up to the general gameplay too. Tactical combat is interesting enough with ship design being amazingly fun.
That said, it has a little bit more bugs than you'd expect, and of a sort you'd not expect. Most notably:
- Fast fleets tend to overshoot their destinations - and then try to get back and overshoot again. This circus can for last a few turns if you're unlucky.
- You can't enter the purple wormhole right after researching it. Need to wait for a new one to spawn. And then to not overshoot it ;-)
- Very rarely, but sometimes you control the wrong ground force during ground combat.
- Very rarely, (happened to me only in corvette-only fights) forces refuse to engage and you do not seem to have control over any of the ships.
- Leaders appear so rarely that it's entirely possible to have a complete playthrough without ever encountering one
- A lot of the weapons are not really much of an improvement over their predecessors - effective dps seems similar.
- Auto resolving battles kills ships that would have not a single chance in hell of dying had the battle actually taken place.
I would also be happy with a bit more documentation on weapons while placing them in the shipyard. It's not trivial to remember at first which weapon is 'beam', which a 'particle beam' etc, and if installing, say, a particle capacitor makes sense for one.
The game's also a bit too easy. I have not lost a single game ever - even the new brutal modes seem to only give the AI more resources, but don't really make it any scarier. I think you can safely ignore any difficulty below 'hard' even on your first playthrough.
All that aside - I would recommend to friends. Which I am hereby doing. Cheers!

I recommend the game to any people who enjoy strategy 4x space. That said I share the disapointments among the community.
There are bugs, interface bugs are the ones that I have noticed the most. I feel like the game hasnt had enough testing before release. It is still playable at least for me.
My biggest complaint about he game:
There are tons of different research options and weapons in the game. Most of the time you speed through research before even needing to use the things you have unlocked. I guess what happens is that you move along this research path too fast. By the time you get to fighting you never used those missiles, or that powerplant because now you have way better ones. Almost as if the research to those things served no purpose. It is like you can skip from tier 1 weapons to tier 10 weapons before you actually need to fight anything.
Also the pirates and the aliens that attack you are pretty ridiculous... They dont attack the ai as far as I can tell only you. The ground combat is poorly coded from what I can tell. The longer you are on the ground view the more memory gets leaked or whatever it is that is happening. The defensive base cannon does nothing.
I mean the list goes on and on. Shady development is what it looks like. Cutting corners here and there to rush something out.
Either way it is still a 4X game and it has a lot of cool things about it.
The exploration of new systems is good. The ship module builder is great. The combat is eye candy. Lots of great stuff but the overall balance and feel of the game needs work and the bugs need to be sorted out. If it is just one developer then perhaps the developer would consider spending some of the fortune on some help.

Just finished the game and well, it kind of left me in a 50/50 feeling. I'll go to the good things first.
The ship customization is ingenious! It gives you all the freedom to create a ship that suits exactly your taste. This includes the shape, weapons, weapon directions, energytanks and so on. You can even assign different keybinds to different parts of the ship. It is easily the best part of the game.
Also destroying enemies feels great and satisfying. The music fits in the game quite well, though I only liked maybe one song. The songs resemble those annoying chiptune songs too much, but that's just my opinion, I don't count it as a flaw in the game. Graphics are also nice and flashy, kind of what you would expect from a space shooter.
While the ship customization is fantastic, along with some smaller things, the rest of the game isn't that tempting.
Starting with permadeath. Yeah you read it right, this game has permadeath, which affects many other things that ultimately lead to an unsatisfying gaming experience. Permadeath happens if the enemy wave reaches your position on the world (star) map. This means that you have about 6 lives, as every time you die, the wave moves closer to your position. This means no free exploring and collecting various items on the map, that you would maybe want.
You have to keep moving forward towards your goal. But you cannot move towards it too fast, since the levels are too hard compared to your level, so you always have to take the "easy", "medium" or at maximum the "hard" route. This means that you have to zigzag your way through the map. This then leads to a situation where you are only a couple of steps ahead of the permadeath wave at all times (so maybe 2 lives).
This then affects to your decisions regarding what weapons you'd like to equip. When you've found something that works, you cannot really differ from it, since if you try out a new setup and it doesn't work, you're back to your previous setup with maybe one life remaining. So there goes all the fun of trying out new things. Also you don't get to keep the items and scrap you collected before you died, which means no extra boost after death.
The enemies and levels are all the same, with the exception of enemy movement and bullet patterns. Every enemy and boss is the exact same red wireframe thing. Bosses have some kind of pattern, but mostly they just shoot masses of bullets everywhere. And yeah, don't expect any difference in the last level or boss either. Playing the levels just get boring halfway into the game. And the ship's acceleration and deceleration are more annoying than good game desing, though it does help with small movements, but I'd rather have none or very tiny values on those.
It's a damn shame, because the ship customization is so well done here, but the negative things really outweigh the positive. It's just annoying and frustrating most of the time to play this game. There is really nothing memorable outside the ship customization system. But this gives potential for future releases, I have to give it that. A slight thumbs down from me.
- Ship customization (10/10)
- Graphics (8/10)
- Loot system (9/10)
- Permadeath (1/10)
- Level variety (2/10)
- Enemy & boss variety (2/10)
- Difficulty curve & forgiveness (3/10)

Never Alone turned out to be an unexpectedly powerful game to me, despite some weaknesses in the controls and mechanics.
The main purpose of Never Alone is to paint some images of Iñupiat folklore and culture. The Iñupiat are an Alaskan Native group of people, and some of the developers of the game involved are actual members of the culture, with stories throughout the generations being passed down.
Nuna and Fox, a little girl and an actual fox, are setting out to learn what is behind a blizzard that is destroying her family's village. To play their adventure, you control both of them, or can play co-op with someone else.
In order to get around, the game is a 2.5D platformer, with some pretty nice graphics for nature and beings you come across. Most parts of the gameplay are nothing that new for platformers, as you switch back and forth between the characters to use a small number of unique abilities - i.e., Fox can wall-run and wall-jump, while Nuna can move objects or throw a bola (a netting of stones), to name a couple.
Most of your time is spent solving little puzzles to move forward. Many are easy, as they just involve having one of the two characters get to a place the other can't, then opening a path. Though there are some more unique challenges here and there to get through, such as non-material platforms that can be moved around with special capabilities. At a few points in time, the game also has some chase scenes which are enjoyable, but later ones in the game get to be a little picky and the flaws of the game's mechanics show up there a lot.
Speaking of, let's get into the gameplay flaws. While you should be able to complete the game in a few hours and not have that many problems, there are definitely a handful of places in the game where you will suddenly get angry. Certain places in the game require perfect jumping with the winds, for instance. But the game seemed to be inconsistent with the physics. You will clearly see when the wind is blowing in one direction or another, but sometimes the game will still keep the physics of the wind direction even when no wind is moving along the screen. When that happens, it will easily lead to you falling down, sometimes to your death.
The reliability of moving along the platforms is also finicky at best. Sometimes the character will glitch out and act as if they can't grab the ledge, usually ending with their death again. And even worse, the AI (whichever character you are not controlling at the time) will follow you along on its own, but sometimes move or jump at the wrong time, causing itself to die and making you restart a section.
I definitely got more frustrated as the game went along with the above issues happening more often, especially in slightly more challenging sections. Nevertheless, I was able to push along and still complete the game. Even the most glitchy sections did not hold me back that long.
But the only reason I did the above was what I mentioned at the beginning - the folklore, culture, and style. I believe that the developers made the game efficient in showcasing that, but by also making it connected as a game. It is not like you are just sitting and watching a documentary. Which is funny, because as you play the game, you unlock "Insight" collectibles, which are actually videos of developers, Iñupiat family members, and other people being interviewed about the game and the culture. Some clips and photos also show the areas of Alaska in modern times as well as from mid/late 1900's, it seems.
And yet I never felt bored or like I was just sitting through information. In fact, I felt emotionally attached to the story. So, I recommend Never Alone for a more unique style of game wearing the outfit of a traditional platformer.

SOMA is brilliant. It is an incredibly atmospheric horror game where the horror comes far less from overt scares and more from atmosphere, biting tension, occasional confused terror, and the implications of all the little story details you find here and there.
This is a rare horror game where the monsters are far, far less important than the story, and indeed, many people believe that the monsters actually detract from the experience; yet even these possibly-unnecessary monsters are really well done. I don't think of myself as very easily scared, but at two points in the game, I just had to stop playing for a while because I
The fact that probably the scariest part of the game is one in which there are no monsters is testament to the overall quality. In sound, especially, the game just excels, and will more often than not make you extremely nervous.
In terms of length, the game is just perfect - it's long enough to feel satisfying but doesn't overstay its welcome. If you want to come back for more, there are quite a few custom scenarios, most of which are very high quality, but none really have the same grip as the main story so I haven't gotten too far into them.
I give this a very strong recommendation. The only qualm I have with this game is the price - maybe I'm thrifty, but 27.99 Euro is perhaps a little bit excessive given the length of the game (10-ish hours or so), but on any sale, and perhaps even without, my shining seal of approval goes to SOMA; probably one of the best gaming experiences I'll ever have.

If you are looking for an amazing story-driven masterpiece, look no further.  SOMA isn't a very difficult game (though an objective or two took a bit longer than I'd like to admit...), but what it lacks in direct challenge, it makes up for with a whirlwind of emotions and bouts of self-contemplation.  Don't get me wrong, the horror elements of this game can get you out of nowhere, but it's rare that a game makes you reconsider your values and assumptions.  This game has adventure, suspense, exploration, and interpersonal relationships that are brought to life through intriguing story telling that will keep you playing to learn just a little bit more each time.
I play a lot of video games on multiple platforms, and this is one that will stick with me forever.  It will definitely have a lasting impact on who I am as a person, and not many games can do that for me.  I can't think of many short comings aside from the lack of difficulty (but again it challenges players in other ways) and the fact that nothing seems to go right for Simon Jarret (I'm a terrible speller, so if it's wrong... sorry), but that is something that most great stories tend to use in order to keep it interesting.  If I had to compare this to another game, I would say that this game is like a no-holds-barred bioshock level story for folks that may have played bioshock years ago but are now ready for something to quench a more mature thirst for intriguing storylines.

Orwell, in a not-so-subtle nod to George Orwell's criticism of totalitarianism (*CoughCommunismCough*) 1984. I've actually read 1984. It's not bad. It's not great, and quite frankly I think it's more of an observation than a story which in my eyes weakens it. It's also an incredibly quick read so I do recommend you check it out. On a scale of 1-10? Probably a 7. Amusing, but not the best. Slightly better than average.
Anyway, the gameplay of Orwell is unconventional and reminds me greatly of Papers, Please. Which is another game I should write a review on and I do recommend it. In it you scan documents for information and upload this information into a mega-database which contains details on everyone under investigation (at this time). Presumably, Orwell would be expanded to cover all citizens. In the name of peace, surely! Everyone can trust the government to know every detail about them to make sure that they're entirely safe! 
Light Spoiler Warning: Orwell is a narrative, a visual novel of sorts. I'm going to do my best to avoid spoilers.
Throughout the course of Orwell you follow the individuals of an organization called 'Thought' named after some German poem. Thought is an alleged terrorist organization. Your job is to follow the members of this organization to prevent terrorist activity. The first person you investigate is a woman with blue hair and problem glasses because of course she is. Which now presents us with our question. What scale of authoritarianism would be acceptable in the name of protecting people? As the game progresses, it gets to the point where almost the slightest connection to someone (perhaps eating lunch or seeing a movie together) is grounds for investigation. Authoritarianism seems to have a very tough job reigning itself in from being conventionally oppressive. 
You know, I could not help but giggle with glee as I listened to phone calls of people and other people got blamed for things that I did. It was glorious! And it kept happening! I felt no guilt at all for doing my job. Perhaps that's the point of the game. Thinking.jpg
The art style is... quirky. Not bad. Just quirky. The music is pretty okay too. My (small) gripe (I guess) is how long I had to wait for responses when it came to monitoring calls and SMS. I get that it's supposed to be realistic, that's the point. Not really a point against the game, I just felt that it was sometimes a little long. 
Overall, excellent game. Quite a nice length for the price ($10 at the time of posting). Of course, cheaper is always better. I think my first playthrough had a run of about 4 hours and there are multiple endings (all of which, I did not explore). It's a thumbs up from me.

Fantastic little game for what I paid for it.

Very little in the game is explained unfortunately, but it doesn't ruin too much of the experience as you can always google some of the answers. More than half of the achievements don't get unlocked for some reason, but who cares about that. There are some very minor detailing issues which could have been fixed but instead were overlooked, again, nothing worth complaining about though. Character customization feels a little bit weak and everything available in the customization minus hats and glasses, you see in the game on NPCs, but at least you have some customizing options which is nice. The game is much better played using the keyboard to move the map around cuz side scrolling gets irritating as the GUI prevents the scrolling. The some of the recipes training is annoyingly difficult to get 3 stars (fastest cook time) but at least once you get the stars, it's permanent unless you get even more stars, and 1 star is simple and easy to get... just take your time and get it done. The helpers do a pretty good job with the restaurant and farm, but there are still things they cannot do, like cut grass, milk the cows, make the deal with the customers, and they sometimes glitch in an annoying way where they pick up and drop something about a dozen times while they wait for more work, they also put the basket down in weird places making you have to search for them every time you want to use them. Since I muted the music cuz I tend to play for many hours at a time and music usually becomes repetitive and annoying (no idea if this one's any good though), the game ends up really lacking in sound effects... like when I throw the potion at zombies, no sound, you never hear birds and wild life in the background, etc... still not game breaking though. In this game, there is always too much to do and never enough time to do it which really keeps your mind sucked into the game trying to rush into everything and you can easily spend several hours into the game without even realizing it. The ending of the game was a little disappointing and too simplified as you basically cure the old man and he thanks you in a bubble text and the end credits appear. Also, the game froze after the end credits during loading (at 86%), probably bringing me back to game menu? Other than that, the game is very stable, plays fine on my gaming rig without having to hack the game apart in order to force it to work like some EA and Rockstar games out there...
I definitely recommend this game to anyone who is into farming and time consuming games. Zombies are optional as you can disable them. The depth of this game will sneak up on you.

Some tips:
The green arrow on the map points at where you need to go, not the direction of the ship (which is the black underneath). You can hit 'P' to get a waypoint marker, but it's usually off-map, and the green arrow is less obtrusive.
Learn the keys - they aren't that complicated (basically WASD and keypad) and it makes it much easier to control the ship precisely.
When you do the tug mission, click 'T' produces some markers on your boat. You then need to drag a line to the vesselyou are towing to connect a line. Don't make it too short like I did, otherwise you end up pulling the front of the vessel down as you tow it :-) You can also push with the tug boat.

Survarium is a game that tries to base itself in a world that was built by the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series.
Visually, Vostok has gone far beyond my expectations. Details, colors, lighting, effects... All of it works exceptionally well together, especially when you consider it's an Early Access Free-to-Play game. Although, this does come at a cost when the lack of optimization causes frame rates to struggle on certain maps.
For sound, again, Vostok answers the call and delivers. Gunshots sound snappy and powerful. They ring out in the distance like thunder and the echo reminds you that the enemy is somewhere out there. And the rain.
The interface and menu mechanics take some time to learn and get used to, and it doesn't help that I've seen it change drastically several times in my experiences. Granted, it's still Early Access, so I can't really fault them for making changes like that.
Equipment is varied over several factions and performs differently depending on how you choose to play. Pistols, SMGs, LMGs, assault rifles, sniper rifles, shotguns, frag and smoke grenades, claymores, bear traps and more. You also have extra items to provide a certain stat boost or to heal yourself with.
The gameplay itself is a multi-player competitive match-based shooter. Different maps have different sizes, themes (bridge, jungle ruins, city buried in sand, etc.) and amounts of players. Modes include Team Deathmatch, Battery Retrieval (sorta like CTF), Artifact Hunt (also like CTF), and Research (like King of the Hill). The matchmaking has come a long way, though the lacking playerbase and continued poor handling of the system still results in frequently long wait times and unbalanced matches.
Now, I can understand if you're confused as to why I would paint a generally positive picture while also not recommending Survarium. Well, here's why.
The atmosphere caught my eye as being familiar to the Stalker games. Reading more, I discovered that although the game was a match-based PVP game at that point in time, there were promises of an open world in development with AI and everything. I gave it a shot and, for a time, I was surprised to find out that I actually enjoyed the PVP. So, even though I had heard some unsettling things about the game and the developers, I let myself believe that this was the game I was waiting for. That the PVP was their way of testing various mechanics on the front end, while implementing those mechanics into the open world.
Eventually, that blind optimism faded. Major connection issues. Low player counts. Forced migration of NA players to EU servers. Being forced to re-synchronize 80 times in a single match. Constantly unbalanced teams where high level players with high level equipment were spawn-camping and simply obliterating the under-equipped players. The broken spawn system. No afk penalty. And then Vostok somehow has the brilliant (/sarcasm) idea to start up Leagues? Competition events? With the game in that state?
The promise of a consistent open world had morphed into a timed session with the same number of players as we had already grown used to. Basically, open world was going to be what we had already been playing (or trying to play). And then after... what? Two? Three years? They announced that it was not going to be possible on that engine.
Their communication with the players has been questionable. As I understand it, their communication with each other has had a history of being questionable. They have broken promises, fumbled every step of the way and pushed for features and Leagues while the game was still broken and bleeding.
But, at the end of the day, it is your choice to take my words to heart or take them with a grain of salt. Based on my experiences, the concept and atmosphere have been amazing, which is why it hurts me to know that I cannot recommend Survarium. It is a game I truly wish I had never played.

Awesome, uh, game? I'm not so sure this should be considered a game. To me, a reasonably experienced guitar player, this is a tool to direct practice. Anyone new to guitar will find it great, and those who've been struggling to find not just the time, but quality practice will find it endlessly useful. In short, this "game" will teach you how to warm up, practice, and shred.
Currently, there are some issues with the 60-day challenge tracking progress for many users, and Ubisoft is apparently on vacation for like six months. Who does that? But don't let that hold you back, this is a great piece of software.
One of the problems of the self taught guitarist is finding things to practice. Finding new scales, new chords, new progressions, jam tracks, and keeping them interesting. Well, this has all of it, and it is a ton of fun! So easy to use.
The mini games have a cool 8-bit charm, and you interact by using techniques like bends, harmonics, and chords. They're fun ways to teach you all the technical parts of the games.
There are tons of lessons with practice tracks. It has really too many features to cover. A huge amp sim, automatic jam tracks, tips for what to practice to ace a particular song. There is nothing you could ask for that isn't included.
It plays a bit like Rockband, but with your actual guitar. Maybe a bit like Guitar Hero but looks more like Rockband, for those familiar with both. The coolest feature of the game is that it scales the difficulty as you get better, and it features a Riff Repeater that gradually lets you learn a song chorus by chorus and verse by verse. Tough solo? The software will ease you into it, gradually speeding up and adding more notes until you ace it.
The song selections are fairly limited and DLC is $3 a song which could easily turn an initial $200 investment into $400, depending on your musical taste. I would like to see a broader variety of styles of music. Its heavy on the rock, nothing wrong with that, but they could have landed some (more) country, surf, even classical arrangements for guitar, like Fur Elise, or flamenco. Orwell had me on the edge of my proverbial seat more than once. I played the game from start to (one) end in one sitting. I observed myself become careless, abusing my power as the investigator. I made mistakes, and I felt shame because the game made me care about the characters. I made right choices and figured out secrets, and I felt excitement and pride because the game did not make it easy.
Sure, some passages were a bit linear and less eventful, just like in a book or a movie. But there are many things to learn and discover, and everything is so perfectly arranged, down to the advertisements on the in-game websites you read. Everything has an explanation, there are virtually no plotholes (at least none that I noticed). Ultimately, I felt like I had real power and my decisions mattered.
While Orwell is obviously a very story-driven game, the art was also quite appealing to me.

How should we EVALUATE Orwell?
Is it an anti-fascist salute to the famous novel, a revelation toward our digitalized lifestyle, or just simple satire to the authority?
This ultra-realism game is based on actual events that happened in the passed decade. The player acts as an investigator to wiretap multiple POIs in order to investigate and prevent bloodshed. And there is the old question of ethics. You know what this typical pop-cultured question is, and please don't spit that 3 line of words from our beloved author because this game is going to completely obliterate that old-fasioned image of mass-surveillance of yours.
Because in this game, just like how emergency works in reality, freedom is at stake, and so does lives, integrity , security, and pretty much everything that make the nation stands together instead of falling apart are hanging in the balance. Things were not and will never be that simple.
Also in the same game, you will make your best decisions based on what you believe in reality. You can be the detective, the judge, or the executioner, but unforturnately you shall never be the big brother, because he's not here and he never existed; because behind the monitor, every investigator and their superior is just common, living and breathing people that has little attitute toward his or her world, like those they observe. Never has an interactive story about anthropomorphized rectangles been more fun and compelling.  A devilishly clever puzzle-platformer already, Thomas Was Alone also has a surprisingly well-developed story behind it, one that will have you rooting for the colored blocks you're navigating through obstacles and hazards.  A lot of why it's such a good story comes down to Danny Wallace's excellent job of narrating the whole thing, giving it a mostly light, humorous tone that manages to shift to the dramatic when necessary, all to exellent effect.
As a puzzle-platformer, Thomas Was Alone does not disappoint.  The puzzles themselves range from easy to truly confusing, but never feel cheap, and most importantly the levels are never frantic timed events.  This is not Super Meat Boy; you are not going to end a session of playing Thomas Was Alone with shakey hands and a lingering adrenaline buzz, but rather a pleasant feeling of accomplishment.  Sure, you CAN blaze through the levels as fast as possible, but slow and steady will do just fine, too.  Play the game at whatever pace you're comfortable; the satisfaction is the same either way.

Edit:
So I returned to Nether and the game was pretty fun. I didn't know what I expected, but there have been a few changes to the game.
For one guns seemed very hard to get and I only got a single 9mm pistol and katana, which I used to reach level 31, the level cap. Previously, years ago, I hit lvl 28 on my all time high.
So singleplayer was added to the game and that was great, but now it feels sort of pointless. I now see why there has been nothing but multiplayer available for a while now. The game is fun until you "beat it", aka hit max level. After that it's sort of pointless because the AI is too easy to beat. 2 golems, 3 screamers and 6 dog-like zombies? No problem, I could beat them all while standing still. The same can't be said for a multiplayer experience, since players would be attracted to your situation, and would likely kill you.
Back to weapons. I was 31 for a while, exploring and then I finally got my first 2 weapons... then my 3rd to 5th weapon, and my 6th, then 7th and even my 8th-11th weapon. All within 15 minutes. It seems like weapon drops had originally been removed from the game to only drop weapon parts, but I was wrong. It's however a little strange to have so many weapons spawn in an area I was circling. Still no SMG or sniper though, even after 10-20 hours of looking. It seems I'll be stuck with my shotguns, 9mms and katanas until I hit multiplayer.

Okay so here goes the long version.
Is the game fun? Very.
How would I describe it based on other games?  A
good mix of Sword of the Stars and Endless Space, but single player.
A bit more detail on the gameplay... there really needs to be some form of diplomatic victory.  I was actually very surprised to find out the only way to "win" the game is to annihilate everyone else.  There aren't even alliances so to speak.  I mean you can make another race love you to pieces by throwing gifts at them constantly or making real good deals with them but in the end you
turn on them and kill them.  I really like the "masters" (not oging to spoil it) aspect because it's something new.  Other than that it's another new 4X space game that is made very well.  A lot of people complain about the ground combat, it is somewhat buggy but not terrible.  Think Heroes of Might and Magic for the ground combat and you get the idea.  Minus the hero.  Now ground combat... what's the point exactly?  Other than doing some side missions along the way you never need ground units.  You can nuke the planet from orbit and given the right wepons there won't even be any fallout or anything to deal with before you sprout a new colony there.  You
take over the enemy colony through ground combat and keep their workers and such but it's better to just grow your own over time so you won't have conflicting race issues killing the happiness.
Balance wise.. it's kind of sad when you figure out your best bet is to slap on as many Disruptor Cannons((turret version) which are pretty low tech) as possible and the only thing really better is the "ultimate weapon" I won't spoil.  You'll want a few beams to take out "pest" ships like fighters but other than that... Disruptor Cannon spam FTW.
For the bugs, oh boy..    Here's an example.  There's a construction ship you can build and (without tech) it can deploy into one of two things.  Either a refuling station which is kind of obvious or a listening post which is basically a large area stationary scout.  Now when your ships run out of fuel they automatically make a bee line at half speed for the nearest planet or refuling station right?  No no, apparently the listening post will also fuel your ships and never run out either soooooo.... what does the refuling station do again?  Maybe I'm missing something but I can't see how this is intentional.
Another bug I have often is the inability to refit ships.  You can select a ship you have and select an updated model and send it to the nearest planet for refitting but I have a bug often where it just won't let me refit them, instead of doing anything when I hit the button to refit it just unselects them and nothing happens.  Reloading the entire game fixed this once but not always..
Another problem I ran into that was extremely frustrating was I got into a ground combat at my planet where, right in front of my starting line, was an incline which blocked line of sight completely for my
defense turret, making it completely useless because it couldn't even fire on the square in front of it.  The LOS issues are real bad due to random(I think?) terrain layouts being seriously against you.
The tooltips need some major work too.  There's a structure you can get through tech that deploys from a construction ship and acts as a "space highway" to move your ships around faster.  Only the problem is the description leads me to believe you deploy two of them and it's a "start and end" scenario and you can redirect them (selct a new end point I guess?) based on the tooltip but that's not at all how they work.  How they
work is you deploy them all over the place and they have an "area of effect" that your ships move super speeds through.  Which actually works out better I think but redirecting them does absolutely nothing so there's no point and the tooltip is way off for what it actually does.
By far the biggest tooltip issue I have is the readout of how much power your ships use up per second, it is so far off it's amazing.  Weapons have a power "requirement" and an amount of power they "use when firing" and the first appears to be spot on, it won't let you make a ship loadout that doesn't have the power to use what's on it.  The second however is terribly off, you basically have to look at all your weapons individually (which there can be 30 some odd on a titan) and add them all up to see if your power output is going to cut it.  Sorry but I don't really think math problems (even simple ones) should be part of designing a ship loadout when it's supposed to be calculated for you.  For instance I can have 4 beam weapons that all consume 100 power when they fire and the information will tell me I'm generating +300 power per second more than it's using and the "time until power is fully drained" is "infinite" but no, not at all no.  What really happens is two of the beams will fire and I'm out of power for a few seconds and by the time the other two can fire the first two are off cooldown.  So that needs some serious tweaking.
There's some more issues I can't really remember at the moment but the game has them for sure.  Is the game worth buying?  Heck yeah it's really fun, there's some good humor in it and it's a solid 4X game.... or will be once it's fixed.  It's very playable, you just have to figure out what the issues are as you go and work around them.  Currently there is no way to achieve the "ending" that I'm aware of, it seems to have been glitched out in the last patch, sad.  However, the game is certainly not worth $30 right now.  Get it on sale for under $10 or wait until you see someone make a review saying it's fixed or something.
On a final note, T-Rexes with lasers strapped to their heads are amazing, this is the only point in ground combat.

TL;DR: Controls are a downside, AI is utterly useless at times. Weird letter-boxing on 16:10 screens. Otherwise fantastic little platformer.
In this game you play two characters, Nuna and her fox. You can swap which one you play (Q) and each has unique abilities. The fox can run up walls, jump higher, control spirits, and is generally more agile. Nuna can throw her Bola to break ice in some spots, activate spirits, and use opposable thumbs to climb rope. The story is well written and the lore is rock solid. Both are in the game at the same time and whichever character you aren't playing as is controlled by artificial intelligence. That term used lightly, of course as countless times the AI has killed itself due to being completely inept at anything. If you play with two people the experience would be better, but I have yet to test that. With that possibly being remedied there is one other looming issue. The controls are garbage. No other way to dance around that truth. Even with a high end keyboard (BlackWidow X Chroma TE) I feel like I am telling a deaf man what buttons to press via postage. Yet somehow the Bola controls are worse. I have to literally slide my mouse along my desk to get it to aim down a little. Also, as a Mac user, my screen is 1440x900 which is a 16:10 aspect ratio. The game doesn't seem to have support for that and thus letterboxes the game. That is a huge eye soar and will not ever leave my mind while I am playing. No other game in my library does this, not even other Unity based games. The game's engine, Unity, seems to behave itself for most of the games, and the graphics are pretty good for Unity. All in all it is a good game I am happy to play.

Rocksmith 2014 is both a game and learning tool for use with a real electric guitar or bass. You plug in your guitar to a USB port with a special cable and can play through step by step guitar lessons, learn specific songs and riffs and play a variety of arcade style games with your guitar as the controller.
Everything the game does is done in a very incremental, adaptive and intuitive way, from the games to the lessons, everything is designed to help you retain information about notes, chords and scales, etc, as well as building up your muscle memory to improve your skill at playing guitar. It’s obvious a lot of work and research has gone into making Rocksmith 2014 a powerful education tool that can teach anyone to play guitar while still being fun.
The lessons try to teach you how to play in the way a real guitar tutor would; by explaining techniques, showing you how they are played and then giving you a go while gradually making things more advanced each time. The practice riffs also slow down and let you do things at your own pace if it thinks you are having trouble.
There are also a decent amount of ‘Learn a Song’ songs that come with the game that start you off by getting you to play the very base notes that hold the song together, the game reacts to how well you are doing and gradually adds in more notes if you are getting everything right, eventually the notes will become chords and with enough practice you will easily learn how to play a song from start to finish.
The arcade games are designed to make you remember specific aspects of guitar playing as well as increasing your reaction time, muscle memory and being able to play without looking at the guitar neck. One game has you shooting ducks by playing the right note as they appear in front of different frets, another has you strumming entire chords in a zombie rail shooter. I found all the games to be both fun and very helpful.
Some other nice features Rocksmith 2014 has is a full tone designer where you can create your own digital sound using a variety of pedals, amps, loops and more. The real life equivalent of this kind of equipment is really expensive so I found it really fun to be able to play around with this kind of stuff. There’s also multiplayer modes, online leaderboards and session mode where you have an automatic band accompanying your guitar as you play.
I don’t have many bad things to say about Rocksmith 2014 other than the song selection not being entirely to my taste, but a few DLCs fixed that for me. I also had an incredibly hard time getting a Rocksmith RealTone cable in Australia, all of the retail stores were sold out for over a month and I had to order one online. Some may also argue that the game is too repetitive, but with learning any instrument, repetition is the key to success and I think this game really makes the repetition as fun as it can possibly be.
If you have a guitar sitting in the corner of your room which you don’t really play because you’ve given up on learning it on your own, then I highly suggest you try Rocksmith 2014, you will almost definitely improve at playing guitar, learn some new songs and have lots of fun. If you want to learn guitar on your own, this is the way to do it.

Is it an anti-fascist salute to the famous novel, a revelation toward our digitalized lifestyle, or just simple satire to the authority?
This ultra-realism game is based on actual events that happened in the passed decade. The player acts as an investigator to wiretap multiple POIs in order to investigate and prevent bloodshed. And there is the old question of ethics. You know what this typical pop-cultured question is, and please don't spit that 3 line of words from our beloved author because this game is going to completely obliterate that old-fasioned image of mass-surveillance of yours.
Because in this game, just like how emergency works in reality, freedom is at stake, and so does lives, integrity , security, and pretty much everything that make the nation stands together instead of falling apart are hanging in the balance. Things were not and will never be that simple.
Also in the same game, you will make your best decisions based on what you believe in reality. You can be the detective, the judge, or the executioner, but unforturnately you shall never be the big brother, because he's not here and he never existed; because behind the monitor, every investigator and their superior is just common, living and breathing people that has little attitute toward his or her world, like those they observe. Thus mass-surveillance will never be mass-mind controll. So RIP Orwell, prism,electroscreen greatfirewall,
or anything that attempts to turn security tool into A.I. bigbrother. Your service will be remembered.
But why do instrument of oppression such as these still exists? This game will give you, your own, answer.

Psycho Starship Rampage is an interesting combination of a shmup and roguelike that I found fun for one playthrough, but lacks replay value. The game starts out feeling well balanced, with most enemies not feeling too bullet spongy, but still providing a good challenge. About halfway through the game, I discovered a beam weapons that made the game far easier. By the end of the game I'd slapped 5 beams onto my ship and was sweeping up and down the screen instanly wiping out anything as soon as it spawned, and occasionally wiping out the entire screen with a black hole for good measure. It was a lot of fun to be massacring the enemies that were previously such a challenge, but it made the last half of the game far too easy. Even the bosses would die in 5 to 10 seconds of sitting under my beams.
The game randomly generates waves of enemies and debris as you progress through the level, as well as a random boss at the end of each level. After a while I noticed the same waves repeating, and the levels started to feel very repetitive. The bosses are all very similar to one another as well - they all move in roughly the same pattern, with the guns being semi-randomized each time. I was disappointed when I got to the final mission, only to see that the last boss was just another of these generated bosses that died in 5 seconds rather than a climactic final battle. It's also worth noting that the game isn't really a roguelike if that's what you're looking for. The game features the same map from FTL with the fleet slowly advancing on you. When you die, you don't start over, the fleet only advances a little further and you start the level over again.
Despite these flaws, the game feels good to play. The controls are a little floaty, but otherwise solid, and binding different weapons to buttons of your choosing is a core feature of the game. The game's best feature is obviously the complete customization of the ship. You can make it take any shape you want to, and the controls for assembling the ship work well with a controller. Components like generators, guns, and shields can all be bought with the scrap you collect from dead enemies, and placed anywhere on the ship. Guns can even be pointed in any direction to shape your bullet patterns as you please. It's offers a huge amount of customization without being overwhelmingly complex like other games that have attempted to put in similar features.
Graphically the game looks good, though not amazing. The art style is unique, bright, and makes it easy to see where everything except small bullets are. The bright red enemies are easy to keep track of, but this also makes it nearly impossible to tell enemies apart from one another and prioritize targets accordingly - until you have beam cannons that is, and just annihilate everything on screen.
The loot uses Diablo style system with affixes and randomized stats, though most loot you find up until the endgame is useful. The UI for collecting loot is bad, however. As you go through the level you picking up loot boxes. At the end of the level, you get to choose from one of two items from each box. The problem is that the screen doesn't show you the stats for any of the items as you are choosing between the two, so you can't tell if either of the choices is an upgrade or not. You also can only see the current item in the list, not the rest of them. You might end up choosing a generator instead of a cannon, and hoping for another cannon to appear, only to find 2 more generators and no cannons - something you wouldn't have done if you were able to see all the choices rather than being forced to go through one by one.
Despite it's flaws, I found the game to be a lot of fun, and I'll probably go back for a second playthrough at some point. There are no difficulty settings, however, which restricts the replay value of the game once you've nailed down the boss patterns and more or less memorized all of the spawn waves. Whether the game is worth your time at it's current price depends on you, but if you find it on sale, I'd highly reccommend picking it up immediately, as I very much enjoyed the time I spent on it.

Good Lord in Heavens, I can't recommend this game enough.
Yes, it is fairly short - about 5 hours for the main game on second difficulty, + about the same for NG+ if you want to, + about the same for co-op Vendettas if you REALLY want to keep on with new experiences, but those 15 hours are gonna be packed. First off, because this is an FPS, take a look at quad-wielding Darkness mechanics. They are well-made, polished, and gory as hell. You grow more powerful throughout the game, which in some part also has a narrative effect. Speaking of the narrative - the story is pretty good. For an action movie, that is, but this game is nothing more than an awesome action movie. Nonetheless, it does its job really well. The characters aren't cardboard, they are at least somewhat alive, AI in enemies isn't too bad either - I'm not the best shooter player, but unlike some games, I rarely felt power-stomped. Instead, most of the deaths I had were the result of being outplayed with the light. Most of what you do, ♥♥♥♥, EVERYTHING you do in the main game ties into the narrative one way or another. And while the ending was a bit shallow, a playable part of the ending was an awesome crescendo of a great game.
Graphics add up to the athmosphere, being cell-shaded they can allow you to feel the violence in first person without being repulsive, and the choice of music may seem a bit strange at first, but give it some time... The music actually is more right than in any other game.
In other words - simply because it lacks in playing time you would feel bamboozled if you buy it for full price. Grab it on any sale at any time, though - although it isn't for everyone, if you do enjoy a good story and an example of maybe not a spectacular, but noticeably well-made game, grab The Darkness II any time and savor the experience.

Now, I am not a betting man, far from it, yet even I would bet that this game will never be finished, it is far, far too bland and ambitious for 1 person to even consider, let alone achieve. If you combine that with it's current state being riddled with inexcusable bugs, regardless of EA (Early Access) then you have a recipe for disaster.
After a quick playthrough and seeing how broken the game was, I decided to record the experience, the following is a raw, unedited (and no voice over, don't worry) look at the game from title screen till end.
End being Alt+F4 by the way as the escape menu has no such feature (shown in the footage, the audio might be quite loud too, so please be aware of that)
As mentioned this is EA, bugs are to be expected, but what you don't expect to find in a product
are the following:
"There you are, I'm going to feed you your own ♥♥♥♥ing arms", with no audio direction to lead you to the person shouting it, that is, if he even exists.
That is what I found after less than 20 minutes of gameplay, I can only shudder at the though at what lies further into the game.
Now, let me stop you right there, before you go any further and state the obvious "It's Alpha/EA", you are correct, it is, but the game has also been patched, ignoring several of these bugs that are blatantly obvious when you start the game, requiring no hunt at all, if that doesn't show incompetence then I don't know what will.
Proof of this can be seen in the video linked at the end, you can clearly hear the dialogue repeated despite this being a build or two behind the version I played.
Quite frankly, there isn't a game to play, remember the early Eric Chahi point and click games, that had you quite literally pixel hunt for objects? Well this is a 3d version of that, only with less direction and more frustration. I am apparently supposed to exit the first area (3+ floors of an apartment complex) but when reaching the door, it didn't open, turns out I need a key.
Off you go then! No minimap, hints as to where the key may be, nothing, it just dumps you in and expects you to have fun in a sandbox full of cat♥♥♥♥♥♥
The level design itself is very bland, it is quite literally corridor after corridor that repeats rooms with no indication of level or distinguishable factor from one to another, and if I am to understand correctly, this is just the first area and there are several more for me to explore, something I imagine that would be a true joy!

Most of these characters are fairly realistic to a point, with the exception of a few things. The obvious one being Revenge Mode, highly unrealistic aspect of the game however forgivable for it being a game and all. This will activate mostly if you're in a position where you are fighting against more than 1 enemy at a time, however, this ability turns sour when you rank your armor in such a way that you can keep pumping out revenge mode. There has been a nerf to it which makes it a little less common to be activated, however there have been a number of times where someone will just turtle their way through and keep activating revenge, they still die, it's mostly a waste of time.
Another highly unrealistic thing is their removal of the difference in running speed between the characters. It's insanely odd to see Lawbringer, a man with a heap of armor, and Shugoki, a fat sumo, run the same speed as a Nobushi, a lightweight character.. Ubisoft has removed the ability to rank up your running speed which made things more realistic, and also more balanced in most situations.
Now, the most unrealistic thing of them all, is Shinobi. Not only is this the only character that actually gets a running speed boost ability from the get-go, but this character literally disappears into thin air and reappears (rather quickly) in it's moveset. For a game that tries to go for some sort of medieval fighting accuracy; having this in the game is pure stupidity.
There are a decent amount of maps that have a nice general design, and some are very pretty to look at such as Temple Gardens. However they are packed with WAYYYYYYY too many environmental kills, where a player can very easily bait you into being thrown off, OR a lot of tight areas where you can be cornered very easily and fights just aren't very elaborate because of this. I can already see you typing "JUST GIT GUD" -- Yeh I agree somewhat, but with how crap the matchmaking is, new players are put up against experienced players and this doesn't give them anything to learn by, and learning with Bots isn's the same as real-player situations as the Bots aren't as adaptive, more randomized.
Manageable
The moveset is diverse and has a decent amount to learn. Very swift and calcuated character. What ruins it is during gank situations they will constantly shove, or flip you (which is not blockable) while thier teammate is hitting you, you get put in a constant stunlock and die.
Slightly Abusive
Basic moveset, which ruins it. There isn't much to do with this character. Furthermore what it does have, is a constant unpredictable 50/50 move which is highly annoying.  It's a shoulder bash much like lawbringers shove- one part of it you can't block and they get a free hit in, and the other part of it is if you dodge they can grab (guardbreak) you and get a free hit in. The warden can change what it's going to do half way through doing the move, 100% unpredictable. They will also spam the shoulder bash during ganks to stunlock you.
Somewhat Abusive
If this character gets you into a tight area where you can't dodge the shieldbash move it does, then game over they will spam that until you die. They can also spam this to stunlock you in gank situations.
Manageable
Ubisoft has nerfed this enough to make it manageable. Moveset is diverse and takes a bit of finesse to pull off properly. Nothing particularly overpowered about it except the speed in which it's quick attacks come at you. It's often unpredictable which direction you have to block in, and once they get one hit in they get another free hit because you can't change block position fast enough.
Balanced
Diverse character with a moveset that allowed to to combine them in a lot of ways. Character armor looks ugly though.
Somewhat Abusive
The Cockrochi has a diverse moveset and is very satisfying to use everything and dismantle your enemy. However tryhards (not me) will use 2 moves, overhead quick attack, and zone attack. They are very fast and hard to parry. The zone attack starts off with an overhead red indicator making you think it's going for an overhead quick attack, that needs to be removed.
Somewhat Abusive
Moveset is linear, but has a decent amount. Shugoki gets hyper armor which lets it shrug off 1 hit and continue with it's moves. The Shugoki is very good in team situations, kinda over powered actually.
Balanced
Basic moveset but diverse in ability to use it. Not overpowered in any way at all. Probably the most perfectly designed character in this game.
Manageable
In a 1v1 situation this character is kinda annoying but manageable. If you get put in a close quarters situation and they spam a move that trips you, then you're dead. This move is often spammed which is just boring to fight against.
Somewhat Abusive
Moveset is linear, and like Warden, has a move where it can 50/50 you and is totally unpredictable and performs fast.It also stuns you getting rid of your HUD.
Balanced
The moveset is easily telegraphed but be careful not to screw up. This character excells in trying to throw you off ledges, has an insane throwing distance. But it's manageable, play smart.
Balanced
Relies heavily on feints to confuse you, takes some skill to do properly and the payoff is good. The only bad thing about this is how much damage it's overhead heavy attack does, way too much for a character like this, and it gets hyper armor during that so it cannot be interupted.
Manageable
You can counter a lot of what Centurion does, but if he gets you, then you're likely a goner if the user knows how to play. This character is beyond overpowered during gank situations, they will constantly kick / punch / stunlock you. Activating revenge mode won't even stop them.
Highly Abusive
Comparing Shinobi to every other character makes them look easy to go up against. This character is not easy to use, I'll give it that. But once you know how to use it, you'll essentially be unstopable. Ubisoft seems to think that slapping a small amount of health on it makes it okay. But nah, every move combination this character can do will utterly destroy you. And just the way it performs, moves, acts, is beyond unrealistic. It's recovery time is faster than any other character, and the kick move that it has cannot be interrupted by anything at all and will get a free heavy hit in after it. It also has ranged attacks, and the ability to be hidden from HUD / Radar. If you're fighting someone else, they can come in and get free hits on you from afar without you knowing where it is, and unable to block it unless you're accidentally blocking in that direction.
No one cares..
You can complete it in about 4 or 5 hours, there is no character depth, the plot is thin, but it's a good way to learn the game I suppose.
It gets a point for being pretty to look at and feeling fluent in how you interact with everything. And it gets a point for trying to be something great, but it fails miserably in it's attempt to balance.

StarDrive 2 is a refreshing game to the old 4X genre and I really would like to recommend and here are the reasons why.
The main reason, for not recommending it, is that I feel it is incomplete. Both in features and bugs. It is a shame though because the game is surprisingly well done. The UI is fluid and pleasant to look at (contrary to Galactic Civilizations 3). It has both tactical space and ground combat. It has beautifully rendered planets and the map is organised and does not become cluttered when you zoom out (again unlike Galactic Civilizations 3). But where it fails is in two areas.
The game is incomplete. The ground combat is woefully underdeveloped, diplomacy is not very well done, building starbases is almost useless (except getting command points) and it takes way too quick to max out research techs which makes the game almost feel like a rush-type 4X game. The tactical combat, although refreshingly good for a 4X game, is not balanced and the different weapons and defence system can range from really good to practically useless.
Then you have the lack of variety of ships where every race has only one ship model per tier.
And then ofcourse you have the bugs. The worse is probably when you invade a planet and sometimes you are in control of your enemies(!) units instead of yours. It is nothing that can't be fixed but still reduce the gameplay quite a lot.
That being said there are a lot of good things with the game. I already mentioned the good UI and tactical combat and how you fit your ships is really nice with a lot of cool weapons and utility modules. Sadly though that the rest of the game has so many problems because this is truly amazing game if you take into account the fact that it was developed by only one person.
That being said, I found it well worth the money because you can replay it quite a lot. So despite the lack of bugs and incomplete areas, it will still give you some fun for your money.

The good:
- UI and graphics are appealing.
- Ship design and space combat are fun. But very easy and exploitable once you understand the insights.
The not so good:
- Far too oriented to war, but the mechanics of space warfare are not especially deep or rewarding.
- Research and tech tree are counterintuitive, although it opens some diplomatic possibilities.
The bad:
- The ground combat is, to keep it short, completely and utterly terrible. And unskippable because the "auto" function is a slaughter for your troops.
- AI is idiotic, treacherous and, at the same time, completely predictable.
- Because the AI is how it is, and the space combat is easily exploitable, you can "game the system" to win against the odds.
- Forget any playstyle besides warmongering. War up to extermination is the optimal response to everything in this game.
- Very buggy and glitchy. Nothing game-breaking but it feels like an unfinished product (for now).
- Big empires require to much micromanaging in my opinion.
I think Star Drive 2 fails to deliver innovative concepts/ideas or a well balanced/polished "classic" 4x game. I had some hopes that the game would improve through the months, and I've seen some improvements, but overall is not specially fun or challenging. It's not worth the time nor the money in my opinion.

Very beautiful game. I love the thought and purpose behind this game - it teaches so much about Inupiat culture (in a very interesting and non-intrusive way, I might add). There's a lot of good wisdom there. The story is interesting, the characters are charming and sweet. I feel like it has just the right amount of player involvement for the length and plot of the story. (i.e., a good balance of emotional investment for like... 4 hours of gameplay).
I really recommend watching the videos that give more information about the Inupiat people; they're all really short and made the game a lot more interesting. You can tell the developers really put their hearts into the purpose of this project.
This game is sometimes a little exciting, but overall it's not a heart-pounding ride. If you need extremely action-filled games to fill your adrenaline addiction, this probably isn't for you - it's basically a long, pretty sidescroller maze where you have to time your jumps and movements just right to avoid death.
And that's my only complaint about this game: There were some places where I died repeatedly just because I couldn't switch deftly enough, or move quickly enough, or make the jump or whatever. And there's no health bar. You die instantly! So I'd have to do them over and over again. That happened in a few different places, to the point where it was laughable... but I managed to get through.
Like everyone else says, play with a controller on co-op if possible. Using a keyboard on single-player was... trying, at times.
But worth it. :)

Very nice homage to George Orwell while still being its own unique experience. The characters involved are multidimensional, and neither side is distinctly good nor evil -- a second playthrough really made that clear to me. There are multiple endings depending on the choices you make and the sides you take, so it's a really fascinating exploration of censorship in the Information Age.

Which is odd, because the story is actually quite touching. It's nothing deep, it's no Metal Gear story or anything crazy like that, but it is a story that'll play with your emotions quite a bit. This game needs a lot of work before it can be considered playable:
- Enemies clip through walls
- Enemies only use a limited number of character models (so you're often chased by up to three identical looking enemies) and I'm not just referring to their faces, but identical clothes as well.
- I can stab enemies through walls (handy, but shouldn't be possible)
- Enemies have no path finding ability at all, they are completely unable to walk around a wall or through a doorway. The enemies in Doom (1995) were much more adept at attacking me.
- No interaction with the environment (can't open doors, search cupboards, turn faucets on and off etc.)
- All rooms are furnished similar, there's three different wallpaper designs and everywhere you see the same cupboards, closet, couches, chairs, tables etc. everywhere. This is not how normal people live.
- I can't enter any of the bathrooms (there are invisible walls in front of them) yet zombies can enter them. Why?
- How did people live in these rooms, there are no electrical appliances anywhere, no tv's, no radio's, no lamps, no toasters etc. There aren't even any candles or something similar to provide light yet the player has a flashlight with unlimited battery life.
- There is nothing to indicate which floor you are on and also no numbers or names next to appartment doors. Real flats do have these kind of features so that their inhabitants don't get lost. The lack of appartment numbers and floor numbers makes it extremely hard to navigate.
- No map (see remark above).
- Some objects (TL lights, light fixtures, power outlets etc.) are visible even in complete darkness. Before discovering the key to turn on my flashlight (why use L instead of the usual F?) I thought the game had horribly crashed.
- No onscreen indication of the amount of bullets/clips left. There have been other games with a minimal UI but in those games the player character would at least shout out the amount of clips/bullets left. I also think there is a good reason why only very few games have UI's which don't display the amount of ammo available. It's highly annoying to have to open the inventory to see how many times you can fire your gun.
- Magical health regeneration. Cool, apparantly I have nanobots in my bloodstream healing me after a few seconds. To bad other people don't have access to this technology then there wouldn't have been a zombie apocalypse.
- I understand why zombies attack me, but why do healthy humans attack me and I mean each and every one of them? Shouldn't at least some of them be trying to work with me instead of shooting me on sight? Rember games like S.T.A.L.K.E.R.? Most normal NPC's would start out as neutral towards the main character instead of opening fire immediately.
- No option to reconfigure (gamepad) controls.
- Many buttons on the gamepad are not used, yet no buttons to activate the flashlight or open my inventory.
- I'm not a fan of automatically picking up weapons or ammo by walking over it. But the finesse necessary to pick it up using a gamepad makes we wish I could pick up stuff automatically.
- I had several enemies shouting at me at a time where they could not possibly see me. There were several walls in between us. Yet he still found it necessary to shout threats in my direction. This also makes no sense. Remember the original Doom (1995)? Enemies would not react until they either saw or heard you.
- I was unable to leave the appartment because I hadn't found the key yet. Why not simply display the text "find the key first" or have the main character simply say something like "I need to find the key first". I had to go to the forum in order to discover that this wasn't a bug.
Deep, deep down I sense some hidden potential in this game. But it needs a lot of work. Right now I would suggest you leave it alone until at least three quarters of the problems I've mentioned are solved. There are better and less buggy games available.

+ Halfway competent voice-acting : You can tell this is from an indie studio. The voice acting is a little off at points, but it's there, and from what I've heard of it, it's not strictly bad.
+ Dialogue trees : I suppose I can put this as a plus, there's some decent dialogue trees in the game, a lot of it seems to be voice acted, though mind, I'm not far in the game, I cannot vouch for in-depth VO.
+ Communicative dev team : From what I'm seeing in the forums, the dev(s?) are very communicative and pro-active and open to criticism. It makes me hopeful that they'll use the EA model right, somewhat. (Update from 10/12/2016, putting this as a plus point now makes me laugh.)
Cons, and oh lord there are a lot:
- No initial tutorial : When you begin the game, you're thrown into a room and are immediately set upon by zombies. If you're not quick enough, you're gonna get torn to scraps immediately. If you're unattentive, you're going to miss both the knife and the gun in the room. If you don't search every corner of the building, you're going to never escape this first level. From what I do hear, they're releasing a path that will "re-vamp" the first level. I'm unsure what this means, I'll come back to it when it's released and revise it. By the time they finally showed me where I could find the controls, I was out of the first level. Press F1 for controls. Yeah. Gimme that at the start.
- Poor optimisation : This game looks something like a game from 2006. Maybe Stalker at a stretch, though I wouldn't say it gives anywhere near the same atmosphere. Yet, I found myself repeatedly dropping to sub-30 fps. No, I'm not running on a potato, I should be getting consistent 60+
- Bugs, bugs, bugs : Repeating lines - I swear I listened to the same guy tell me he was going to rip my arms off and feed them to me about 50 times over the course of my "exploration" until I found the existence of the guide. Invisible walls, zombies being stuck in objects/walls, floating objects, AI ignores line of sight, corpses still existing on reload, zombies with 10 foot arms, the list goes on. Yes, I understand this is early access. That does not mean a consumer should not be informed.
- Poor graphics, no artistic consistency : I touched on this earlier, but it looks like something from 2006 if even that. There is no very little consistency between models, and a lot of them simply don't fit together. And there simply isn't enough variation in the amount of models, I've seen the same ones over and over. I'm assuming these are placeholders, and if they're not, I would advise reassessing.
- Features advertised in trailer unimplemented? : I give a question mark here, because maybe they have a trigger to be activated, but the hunger and thirst bars just aren't there for me.
- What IS the story? : Looking at other reviews, there's a backstory to this - on the website. Not the place to have it, really, because for me, currently, it's down. I don't know how long the site has been down, but it doesn't give me good feelings.
- Absolutely grating sound : Once you're out of the "tutorial" (I reluctantly name it so) level, you're greeting by grating, repetitive groaning... It sounds awful, it doesn't belong, I could barely deal with it long enough to get into the next section. Once in the hospital area, there was just noise that gave me a splitting headache. White noise? I'm not sure how to describe it.
- Buggy, unappealing menus : The option menu has a graphical glitch over the audio slider, and the font used makes it rather unclear and irritating to navigate the menus in general. They're a chore to use right now, and there's no exit to main menu as far as I can see.
All in all, I feel this game launched into early access way too early. Pre-alpha is not where you should be launching your game into the service - alpha, maybe. That means you've got your core concepts down and you're starting to implement features. Beta is ideal, as there's a fairly complete game riddled with bugs which the community can feedback and help you fix. From what I hear, they are taking feedback from the community which is good to hear. Hopefully, this will be worth the purchase in future. There's potential there. I just don't feel it's worth that purchase right now. Wait and see, it needs a LOT of work. The dev(s?) seems open and communicative, and it's my hopes that things do turn out well seeing this.
