Jazzpunk is a game that defies allocation to a traditional genre.  At it's essence it is an absurdist comedy intermingled with puns, computer jokes and various mini-games.  There are moments where you will laugh out loud, others that make you smirk and some that may just go straight over your head.  It's a comedy experience, but one that may not be suited to your tastes or the entry price point.
The game is delivered in a 60's style TV/film presentation - flashy colours, big stylised letters, obtuse and poorly explained events and an over arcing plot of being a spy in a 60's interpretation of a somewhat cyberpunk world.   While cyberpunk depicted today is body augmentations, guns, guns, guns and a high body count. This is a depiction of late 50's early 60's sci-fi, robots and crazy gadgets in the world of tomorrow!  The presentation is very good and it conveys it's unique attributes very well, I haven't seen this style of introduction since the old No One Lives Forever games (another 60's spy type game).
Gameplay wise the game is very simple, you cannot die and the pay off is in exploring everything to elicit the jokes hidden around or to even create them yourself.  It is best to avoid following the main quest until you have explored everything.  On my first play through (approximately 3 hours) I didn't discover everything and I made the mistake of going to pick up on the main quest again while doing side quests and then suddenly finding myself ending the level and missing out on the additional exploration.  You can interact with a surprising amount of the world and things felt rather intuitive in terms of control.  There were some blocks to gameplay though such as when I discovered a door a tried the ye olde tried and true knock that it didn't do anything.  Once I discovered the trigger for the area it was the exact same knock required on the door that I had already performed.  I felt that perhaps it would of been rewarding to have accidentally discovered that rather than being led directly to it.  The minigames are rather frequent and range from mundane to excellent, though I found that the better games were all towards the end of the game, perhaps to counterbalance the reduced humour in the latter stages.
Replayability wise there is perhaps not so much there once you have discovered anything, thankfully the best mini-game by far is unlocked for you automatically when you complete the game - Wedding Qake.  It's actually a highly enjoyable rip-off of the old Quake experience, albeit fighting bots (who moan and complain in chat humourously) rather than other players.  I would guess that the short play experience is probably quite beneficial to the game overall as prolonged humour can make the player continually expecting increasing funny events which is very hard to maintain.
So if you like absurdist humour you may find this game right up your alley, if you find such surreal things annoying or particularly unfunny then you best avoid this product.
One last thing to point out, currently on Steam this is listed as $14.99 USD, quite a steep price for the short length of play and amount of content.  If this goes onto a Steam Sale I would definitely recommend it as a purchase (ie if it's around the 7.50 or lower mark), but at it's current price point it really is best value for those who enjoy this sort of humour.

A pretty solid 4X. Takes the Master of Orion formula and adds a modern spin.
Pros:
- Pretty good racial diversity
- Ship designing is amazingly fun
- Plenty of planet variety
- Random events are cool
- Modding community is decent (Check out the official forums)
- Loads of options for customizing your race
- Capturing resources feels important
Neutral:
- Research tree is... fine. It's okay where it is, but it's nothing special.
- Very stable. Haven't run into any crashes. I put this under neutral because this should be expected, not surprising.
Cons:
- Space combat is fun to watch your first time, but gets bland quickly. Ships move so slowly and so inaccurately, it's like playing with paper boats in a rain gutter. During a hurricane. While on morphine.
- Ground combat is mind-numbingly boring. Imagine playing chess, but with only pawns (and as many queens as you can build, as soon as you get mechs). When it shows up, cover is useless. Micromanaging 15 guys, one after another, on a square grid isn't fun. Would be much more enjoyable if you could disable movement/attack animations and just show the damage markers.
- DO NOT USE THE AUTO-BATTLE. I've lost massive fleets to lone frigates that were using early-game tech, while I had max-tier shields and weapons. Add this to the problems with combat, and you'll be finding more fun in smashing your keyboard through your screen.
- Usually too difficult early on and far too easy in the late game. Even on hard, I was able to completely curbstomp a species that owned 75% of the galaxy because they refused to use their massive tech advantage, and kept building the same ships they'd been building since mid-game. This was AFTER the AI ship overhaul.
- Trade with other factions feels pretty pointless. You can get (or start with) a tech that lets you capture enemy tech when you take their planets. It's usually cheaper to conquer an enemy's planets and steal their industry alongside their tech.
- No satisfaction from beating the snot out of the AI. They barely try to defend themselves or barter for their own lives. Even if you've kicked their asses back to their homeworld, they'll still try to short you on the peace deals, then get uppity when you tell them where to shove their pitiful Tier-1 offerings.
Despite its problems, I still got several hours of entertainment out of it. I'd only recommend if you buy it on sale. $33 is way too steep for what you get. If you want a similar experience, and can tolerate older graphics and UI, try Master of Orion 2.

This is an amazing space strategy game with an unfortunate amount of bugs. I enjoyed it enough to give a thumbs up, even with all the issues.
Bugs I’ve run into:
When you use fighter squadrons, the post battle process can take 10-15 to finish loading.
The post battle process can sometimes crash the game after large fights.
The fleet ownerships were once switched between myself and the NPC during a battle. This was actually kind of funny at the time (I mad their ships turn around so they couldn’t shoot), but it’s a bug none the less.
NPC ships will sometimes fly outside of the battle screen (out of your view) if they are being defeated. If your ships aren’t fast enough to catch them, the battle never ends unless you forfeit.
Good things:
The game has one of the best ship designers in my opinion. It’s simple to understand but difficult to master. Ships must be constantly redesigned/improved as the technology in the universe gets better, or risk being left in the dust.
I generally ignore diplomacy managment in space games, but it’s actually very useful here.  As you progress through the various technology trees, you will leave some research behind. For example, you may opt for a new type of ship armor instead of advanced fighter technology.  Diplomacy with other cultures allows you to trade for this technology, which would be lost to your civilization otherwise.

This is an excellent game for a semi-professional / amateur-enthusiastic player.
This is the game closest to a real simulator among all I played. The cars are responsive but not unrealistically, react to bumps on tracks, the speed is about average, there is room for minor mistakes but not too much. There is even some randomisation, tire sets have different behaviour a little bit (most noticeable in Monza). There is a possibility to tune (balance) your car to some extent, but you can get along without it.
GT Legends is one of the few games supporting long races (up to 60 laps, 2-3 hours), which I find incredibly fun. Also night driving. I bought this not much after seeing a bit of Le Mans in 2013. This was the first game in which I actually enjoyed being in the middle of the pack.
The graphics are somewhat simple but overall very well done, the effects scale nicely with the resolution (so the cars look nice) and trackside trees are lush enough. I love the distant mountains, the night sky with the moon and the darkest hours, the morning / evening sun overbright.
There are no weather effects, unlike in its predecessor (GTR 1), either for performance reasons (back then) or the fact that cars are slippery enough. Lighting is pretty cool, works well for night races - not to forget the lamp posts and light in various buildings.
Used to play it in 2013/2014 without problems on a GTX 560 Ti, but on my new GTX 970 Ti it kept crashing. Got better over the months, but there are still some momentary freezes.
Administrator mode (or some tinkering with security settings) is required.
The only downside I would mention is how the progression feels slow. Tracks unlock by completing short championships in the top 3, cars must be purchased with championship earnings. Cash can be farmed, but if you get distracted by custom races or an obsession to run races at a tougher difficulty, well...
Given its price, I'd say it's a bargain. Pick it up, have fun for a few hours, be prepared to get hooked.

Never Alone is a fun little platformer, for the most part there isn't alot to say about the gameplay since it's as simplistic as it can get with you literaly just running, jumping, pushing and pulling. The game is playable either solo or in co-op with the player switching between the human character and the wolf at will in the former or each player taking control of each character in the later.
Later into the game some small aditional mechanics are introduced but going into them would spoil the story of the game.
Visualy the game is very atmospheric and looks overall very nice, with good design choices and its cartoon style. The music is very well composed and for the most of the game is so subtle that it blends well with the game's atmosphere, however something that might slighly put off some players is due to the fact that the narrator of the game speaks in Inupiaq meaning that most of the time players will have to stop playing in order to read the subtitles during gameplay segments.
The story isn't anything that hasn't been seen before in other mediums, it especially feels like something that has been seen in a Studio Ghibli movie however, the game does make use of Inupiat lore for its story and extends a lot of cultural insight of the Inupiat people so one can't fault it for that.
The game can be beaten in 3 or 4 hours although I feel as if the length is just right for what the game is going for, especially since it ends before it can get boring.

The game isn't outstanding nor revolutionary but it is stil a fun experience, if you can pick up the game on a sale I urge you to give it a shot since you mostly likely won't be dissapointed.

I found this game in early 2015 and stuck around with it for a few months, till around June 2015. The performance back then was horrid and I had to edit an .ini file to get a custom resolution of 848x477 in order to be able to play the game with above 20 FPS. And my computer isn't that bad as it can play all new games that came out in the last few years.
Even at 848x477, the performance was so bad that I had adjusted myself to the game's crap factor in order to be able to even remotely play it. Around the end of the spring of 2016 there were some updates releasing a new rendering engine for the game for low end PCs and as it got more and more optimized, I managed to eventually play the game with some smooth  FPS above 30 or even 40 with everything on lowest, it was then that I realized how flawed and broken the game is. The mouse smoothing was horrible - at too low, it took great efforts to rotate the camera with the mouse and at too high, it would make it both laggy and super sensitive at the same time. So this whole time I thought I sucked at the game because of how poorly it was optimized, this was a lie. In fact the game is still as broken as it used to be.
Now let's review the game play mechanics and aspects of the game. The progression is too steep and unrewarding, the scavenger hunt that happens every time after a match ends its basic RNG and it literally shoves in your face the fact that you need to buy VIP status in order to get the better rewards. Because of the graphics the game has, it's sometimes impossible to see an enemy camping. There is one map with like an underground reactor or something and at the spawning point of one team, on the other side there is a ruined building, snipers can hide there and just farm kills and you can't do anything about it to kill them. You can't see them and you can't get close enough to kill them. The aiming is really broken, laggy and unresponsive, making the feedback really different from what is actually going on.
The game feels like a Call of Dutyu/Battlefield knockoff with really broken mechanics and a post apocalyptic theme. The developers have been promising Free Roam mode, which hasn't been revealed for years and for more than one year of me knowing about this game, only one new map was released.
I would not recommend anyone to play this game, play this instead:
The game gets monthly updates with new content - maps, weapons, characters and skins. It will have PvE/co-op mode and after following it for 1 year and having about 400 hours in-game I can assure everyone that the PvE mode will come faster than the Free Roam in Survarium.

First off, I'd like you to take a look at my hours.  I don't have many hours as of 5/25/2017, but I plan to put more into the game.
FOR HONOR™ is a game that has 3 active factions that are at constant war with one another: The Knights, the Vikings, and the Samurais.  In the game, you play different gamemodes for a battle over terroritory for the Faction you have chosen.  The gamemodes compose of Duels & Brawl for 1 versus 1 and 2 versus 2 combat.  Dominion for 4 versus 4 combat, control points and a center point that must be cleared of minions before capture.  Elimination for 4 versus 4 combat and one life (unless revived).   And Skirmish for your usual 4 versus 4 team deathmatch.  Every factions warriors play and mechanically work differently.  No matter what faction you're on, you can still play a warrior from another faction.
In all honesty, I wish I could recommend this game to people WANTING to buy and play this game, but there are things that keep me from recommending it.  If medieval combat tickles your fancy, I'd rather recommend you play Chivalry : Medieval Warfare on Steam.  However, if you prefer more mechanically advanced games, then this game is for you.  HOWEVER, note there are several issues with the game.  For starters, the game will blackscreen a lot and nothing will show up which forces you to relaunch the game all over again.  Sometimes, the game won't even launch up and will immediately crash before even opening so you have to open it several times before it FINALLY opens.  The game is also not very welcoming to new players.  Since the game has lost a large quantity of it's playerbase, the queues are sometimes INCREDIBLY long and takes forever before you end up in a game.  Eventually, after the queue becomes so long, it will pair you up with someone who is probably fifteen times your level and they will likely beat you because the game pairs you up with people who are far more skilled than you are.  Sometimes all that time is lost because the Ubisoft Servers are like an irresponible driver and crash CONSTANTLY.  Don't EVEN get me started on the new heros in the game.  They are quite literally the most broken heros of the game.  Centurion can perma stun you and keep you exhausted with no Stamina to work with.  Shinobi can teleport attack and can perma combo you.  Don't even bother with this Campaign if you're looking for a good story, there is none in this game.  The game has about as much story as the game Happy Wars.
The game is seriously fun and mechanically advanced, which means you'd have to dump countless hours into the game to actually be half decent.  I would definitely recommend this game if the issues in this game weren't so largely common and didn't happen every 30 minutes - 1 Hour.  Also, do not accidentally bind your game to another friend's uplay account, because Ubisoft Support sucks a** and takes forever to respond on any issue you may be having (take it from personal experience).

Overlord is one of those games that certainly changes the way you look at how to approach a game. Overlord is what happens when you mix a third person slasher with a very light resource based RTS. Your primary striking force for the vast majority of the game is your minions, and you can spawn increasing amounts as you become more powerful. Each type of minion has different abilities and strengths, and utilizing them correctly can be the difference in total victory or total annhilation.
There really isnt much to complain about when taking into consideration the age of the game. Released in 2007, it actually plays pretty well for a game nearly a decade old. Because of its age, the graphics suffer a bit, and there are only 2 movement speeds: walk and walk faster. Something else that could have helped, but wasn't really necessary was the inclusion of a map. Other than that, my only quip is that once you get the hang of how to play the game properly...it becomes very easy.

This game is FUN!
The map designs are nicely laid out, especially later on in the game when the puzzles start to get trickier. You'll find yourself perhaps just on the edge of your last bit of health and most of your minions dead, when you'll come across a  summoning spot or a crate with health in it. It is challenging and rewarding to play, and the humour is fantastic.
If you're not a fan of grinding, make sure you take the time to learn when to recall your gremlins back at soon as you notice they might be in trouble - like drowning, or a boss about to do a strong attack. Losing too many will deplete your amount you can summon, forcing you to go back to old maps and grind down to collect life force. The good news is, most of these 'grinding' locations are very close to the map entrances, so you won't be there for too long.
Interesting gameplay mixed with an interesting story. I would recommend doing research on this title before purchasing.

A game hasn't made me laugh as much as Overlord has in a while.
Overlord is Pikmin if it was rated M for mature. An extremely fun game where you play as the Overlord and get to control a small army of minions with different abilities. Your various minions are used for combat and for solving simple puzzles. The game controls kinda like an rts but is also a 3rd person hack n slash game. Your main Overlord has spells and can fight but the majority of your strength will be coming from your minion horde. The story has some choices where you can decide whether to be a benevolent dictator or a true evil overlord.
The graphics are starting to show their age but the art style and world design are still more than capable of presenting some pretty cool environments. Overlord is set in your average run of the mill European Medieval fantasy setting but that doesn't stop it from being a very fun world to explore as you look for upgrades or gold. Animations for your Overlord are stiff but the minions on the other hand are all full of life. The music and voice acting are also both really good at bringing the world of Overlord to life.
My only gripes with the game are that there is no map which isn't really needed but would still help. Multiplayer has been shutdown and is now only playable through 3rd party tools such as Hammachi and that the game only saves your progress once you go back to your evil dark tower which is like your main hub that you can upgrade and decorate. This means that if you die in the middle or even the end of a mission you will lose all of your progress.

Some games you play because you want to unwind, or you want to build things, or you just want to win against other people.
This isn't one of those games. This one forces you to think about the new age of media and how information is stored and processed.
I don't really want to talk about the things in the game, because I don't want to spoil the experience for you. This isn't really a game where you have familiar mechanics, or great graphics. It's mainly a story told to you in a way that forces you to act in how you view the concept of power. If you haven't played the game yet, don't read the next paragraph.
I feel the issue with this game is mainly how much you care about being in control and in power. If you are living in a country that is democratic on paper but just shy of being a fascist nation, you prefer to be in power. There is no safety for you unless you think and act like 'one of them'.
And that is fun. For me, the end of the game was largely focused on that. It was too fun to spy on people, too fun to find clues and watch them squirm. It was so fun, in fact, that the peoples whose lives you hurt mean nothing, and not only in a video game way. In the end, they were just images and phrases in a social media site out of thousands, and they all had the same issues and favourite colours and likes and dislikes. The breach of privacy that we feel stems only if we are not the ones making the breaches, and if you think about it, we all do it in a way. Stalking is exactly that. It is the power to follow someone on a social media without them knowing.
I wanted to gather my thoughts a little bit more to write something more focused but I'm not sure I will be able to.
TLDR: This is a game about control and power. It makes you experience it and think about it. It's short but fun in it's own way.

The Darkness II is a first-person shooter video game developed by Digital Extremes and published by 2K Games which was released in 2012. The game is the sequel to 2007's The Darkness which you might not know because it was Console Only release.
In TD II we are stepping into a boots of a Jackie Estacado,after 2 years since the events from the 1st game. Now Jackie is a Don of a Franchetti family,and holds his Darkness from releasing.
Nothing last forever tho,as we have to free Darkness power to survive a hit,find out who hit us,and of course kill him.
So let's start from less important things.
Graphics.In short,it looks good,a little comic,like in Punisher or Borderlands.From Docks to our mansion,it is well detailed,polished,and good looking but i don't think you should really look at graphic in that game.

A TLDR at the end if needed.  The Darkness 2 is a solid, enjoyable game.  It is a good adaption of the comic book of the same name from Marc Silvestri and Top Cow Studios.
THE STORY:  You take on the role of Jackie Estacado, the current host of the dark force known as The Darkness, who inherited it from his father.  The story takes place some time after Jackie has inherited the power and having learned how evil The Darkness is, has found a way to supress the evil creature and it's accompanying desctructiveness, also allowing Jackie to lead a somewhat normal life as a Mob Boss.  The action begins when some unknown group attacks Jackie's gang with Jackie himself being their target.  In order for Jackie to survive, he is forced  to release the Darkness and allow it to come how and help him fight.  What follows is Jackie's road to revenge and eventual discovery that the initial attack was meant to bring out the darkness and the "unknown" group's intent to steal the power of the The Darkness for thermselves.  This discovery eventually leads Jackie to trying to save the woman he loves, and who he thought dead, but is actually still alive (in a sense).
Much of Jackie's, and The Darkness', background (e.g. the woman he loves, family, how he became gang leader, etc) is told via flashbacks, "dreams" and monologue style cut scenes between levels  (all skipable if desired as long as it's dialogue).
Eventhough I stopped reading comics a few years after The Darkness comics showed up in the comics scene, from what I can tell the story and atmosphere feel very faithful to the comics.
THE REST:  The graphics are good and game play is really fun.  It really feels like you're playing as the darkness.  While you can use regular guns and such since Jackie is a mobster and used to those things, you use the Darkness as your way of meleeing enemies.  With the Darkness you can grab, rip and shred your enemies.  YOu can use the darkness to grap guns and ammo that aren't near Jackie.  Using the darkness you can also grab objects for use as shields or throw them as weapons impaling or slicing enemies in half.  The darkness is able to grab enemies and objects at a medium disance, but if can be difficult to close the distance a lot of the times.  You often have to accept quite a bit of damage in order to close the distance to use the more enjoyable and satisfying Darkness melee abilities.
Jackie can also learn a number of abilities.  Many of the abilities enhance his use of guns, but other enhance his slash and trash abilities in melee combat.  There are several ultra-violent finishing moves that allow recovery of health, ammo, shielding or regenerating special abilities that are on timers.  IMO, Jackie's coolest ability is the abilty to occasioanally create a "Black Hole" when he kills someone.  This Black Hole can be picked up by The Darkness tentacles and thrown at other enemies that result in a huge Black Hole that sucks other enemies into it.  Most of the game environment will turn to chaos as enemies and objects are pulled to their destruction, even trying to pull Jackie in too (though I don't think he can be hurt by it).  It's a real neat and satisfying ability to use.
The only real downfall for me in gameplay is that when I was getting shot, it can be difficult trying to find out from where the weapons fire is coming.  Many of my deaths were caused from trying to find where the gunfire was coming from or getting behind cover so I can look only to find out where I hid didn't actually give any cover because I made a bad guess where to hide and was actually still in the line of fire.  This was especially bad playing the hardest (Don) difficulty.  A bad guess for cover always resulted in death because of the increased damage.
That is my only issue.
There is one technical issue involving gameplay.  When you are in sections of the game where Jackie has to crouch to progress, or when controlling the demon in air vents, the characters are prone to get stuck due to clipping issue.  In order to keep moving forward you have to press the jump key a bunch while moving forward to get "unstuck" and continue.
For others, a possible downer of the game is that the story campaign is fairly short.  (less than 10 hours of you skip dialogue)
This can be extended a little bit if you play the Hit List and Vendetta compaigns.  The Vendetta campaign is quite interesting and gives additional background into the history and abilities of The Darkness itsself.  Also when you play the Hit List and Vendettas, you don't play as Jackie, but have a choice of 4 other characters, who I assume were introduced later in the life of "The Darkness" comics.  The characters have unique weapons and abilities linked to The Darkness, but also don't have as many abilities or powers at Jackie.  This suggests that while they also possess the Darkness, they aren't the perfect matches that Jackie is to the evil power.  The unique weapons are pretty cool and they all have unque finishing move animations, several of which are really cool.
Sadly, the story suggests there should have been a sequel, and said sequel would also include an encounter with The Witchblade, Marc Silvestri's other awesome comic series that eventually spawned The Darkness series.  Ths is sad because I have never heard anything about a 3rd Darkness game making it unlikely, which sucks because this was a very enjoyable game and it would be fun to see a Darkness VS Witchblade sequel.
TLDR:  Good story,   Good graphics.  Really feels like you possess the awesome powers of The Darkness.  Worth the purchase.

SOMA presents narrative quality matched by few in the industry in a package that consists of mediocre, unnecessary horror gameplay. It's incredibly frustrating how excellent the story plays out in SOMA when its gameplay not only average, but tacked on and occasionally actively detracts from the narrative experience. Ultimately, I do recommend SOMA for gamers like myself out there who value narratives, especially narratives heavy on themes and big ideas, over gameplay.
SOMA is very thematically like NieR: Automata and to some extent if you were a fan of the latter I would especially recommend SOMA. The quality of the story in SOMA stems not only in the richness and depth in the storytelling, but also the maturity in its presentation. While I would argue that NieR: Automata presents its themes in an overall more powerful manner, I can't help but wish it carried the subtler creative designs with SOMA. While I am generally not a fan of the idea that environments alone can tell powerful stories, there are quiet and somber moments in this story that are alone melancholier than moments found in games with more bombastic music and dramatic plots. Simply but, SOMA tells more with less and its artistic design deserves heavy praise.
However, such narrative excellent did not need to come in the package of a horror game. The enemies in SOMA are often not very scary as there is little variety, and more importantly player response is limited to hiding or running away. What compounds this frustration is when enemies get in the way of exploring SOMA's intriguing setting. There are scenes where you would wish to read more logs, or listen to a sound going off in another room, only for another monster to appear necessitating the player's evacuation. Furthermore, the story explaining the monsters in the setting is easily the weakest part of the narrative. While labeling the gameplay overall as mediocre may come off as heavy criticism, I can largely forgive this shortcoming considering its narrative excellence.
I highly recommend SOMA to gamers interested in great stories. Horror junkies and challenge enthusiasts may be disappointed. For the future, I do hope frictional games can evolve out of the horror genre or utilize it more effectively as seen in games such as Detention. SOMA would have been more enjoyable as a walking sim such as Edith Finch or Tacoma.

Overall I give a positive review of the game. Is it perfect?  Well no, but it still gave me several dozen hours of fun (and the developer intends to support the game further).
The game's biggest flaw is that as it stands (and this is intended to change eventually) there are only two victory conditions (one official,
).  Diplomacy as it stands cannot be used to form long lasting alliances and the end goal is always conquest.  The player can mentally set their own goals, such as controlling and containing all threats, or getting friendly with as many other civilizations as possible, but there are no built-in alternate victory conditions yet, and the ability to win by forming an alliance would add another facet to the game.
The ground combat has a very mixed reaction.  Personally I like it, but I can see why some do not.  The developer does want to improve this eventually.
Just like the first game, ship building is a huge aspect of the game's fun.  To summarize, I think it's a really good game but focuses a bit too much on the aggressive side of 4x play, but as I said the developer is accepting feedback and does want to fix that.  I do not feel an imperfect situation is enough for me to give a negative review.
As far as how the game looks and feels, for the most part I think it feels quite well done.  Perhaps my play time speaks for itself.  My stance is if I put this much time into the game, how could I at least not recommend it?

StarDrive 2 is so much fun - it feels like a much newer version of Master of Orion and totally worth it. After 127 hours I definitely haven't explored the entire game, but I do feel like I've exhausted most of the appeal. Hopefully they'll fix a few of the things below and then it will be even more awesome.
***Things I've liked about it***
You can customize your ships by placing individual components onto the hull at different locations, and you have to consider the cost, power, weight, size, and hitpoints of different systems. Not all the components are the same size/shape, either, so designing a ship is a lot of fun.
In battle, ships acceleration matters - you can't accelerate to maximum speed instantaneously and can't turn immediately either.
There are many styles of weapon - beam weapons with essentially infinite speed (but still limited range), artillery with long range but no guidance after they're launched, and rockets with good range that home on enemits, plus many, many other weapons and/or variants.
Ground combat is interesting and doesn't feel contrived - there are lots of different weapons, and the units have actual coordinates during ground combat, allowing for more strategy.
You can customize your race at the beginning based on whether you want to boost research, production, combat, and lots of other things. Each race also has a few race-specific technologies and/or abilities that can't be customized and add a little more flavor.
The tech tree is interesting because there are several branches that are independent. Also, each branch has tiers of three technologies where you can only research one of those three technologies before moving on to the next tier. This leaves you to get it from another race (by trade, extortion, spying, or assimilation), or to live without it.
***Things I don't like about it***
The battle arena prepares you for a much harder game than this actually is. Once you design a sufficiently good ship to win the battle arena, that ship is probably roughly 12 times as powerful as another AI ship of similar cost, and then the normal game gets pretty easy (you can build no military, wait for them to declare war on you, and then quickly build a ship to wipe out their entire fleet by the time they arrive). The way that I'd like this to be fixed would be for the AI to more clearly pay attention to the kinds of ships that it knows/expects that you have, and to build ships designed to beat those ships. I'd also like for it to design slightly better ships in the first place.
StarDrive 2 has the same problem as lots of empire-building games where as your empire grows, it takes more time to micromanage all of it if you feel that urge. Unfortunately, if you don't assign a planet to build anything then it doesn't build anything, and the game doesn't remind you that some planets aren't building anything. There are notifications when a planet finishes building its latest building, but sometimes those notifications dissapear if other things are happening in that turn too. The way I'd like this to be fixed is first for the turn to not allow ending if planets are idle, and second to allow the user to set a default build order that planets follow if they have no planet-specific orders.
The AI doesn't know how to evaluate the ships that I build. When I try to autoresolve a battle, the AI is much more likely to favor the opponent than if I were to actually fight the battle. That's understantable, but it's unfortunate when combined with a bug where in some battles (perhaps 2%), if you click to fight the battle then there never appears the button to actually start the battle, and the game is then stuck. Usually this can be fixed if I reload the game from a save, but not always.
When forming a team for ground combat (which is a lot of fun (unlike what I expected); good job guys!), sometimes characters will be designated as starting the battle with fewer than their maximum hitpoints. This can be reproduced if you have two preset loadouts, one having the Bone Weave attribute and one without it. The steps are 1. Restore the character's equipment from one preset loadout. 2. Restore the character's equipment from the next preset loadout. 3. Toggle the presence of the Bone Weave attribute by clicking manually. Note that now the character's starting hitpoints has adjusted by 20 (positive or negative depending on which way around the loop you went). It looks like someone else noticed this at
and was even able to make a unit whose starting hitpoints was negative (presumably by going around the loop three times)
The zooming could be a bit smoother - I wish that the zoom would spend less time animating and instead would adjust more quickly.
Sometimes colony ships will get stuck on the strategy map and won't respect orders to colonize the planet that they are at, but if you tell them to move away from the planet and move back to that planet then they are willing to colonize it.
The AI's don't have as good of an alignment between their diplomatic goals and strategic goals as I'd like them to have. Mostly it feels weird that they tell you upfront how much they value each technology, but they don't adjust their valuations based on circumstances. I've been able to give some unimportant economic technology to an enemy who was about to take one or two of my four planets in exchange for a peace treaty that bought me more than enough time to build up a much bigger army. The AI diplomacy doesn't really bother me that much since it's a very hard problem, but it's still another opportunity for improvement.
In some special-mission ground combat battles (but none of the important planet-taking or planet-defending ones - don't worry) , the zoom prevents the leftmost column of squares from being visible, so I can't select my units and therefore can't fight :(

Had to contribute my two cents to the opinion pool, and it is basically this:
Anyone who gives this game a negative or even milquetoast review is out of their flipping mind.
I can understand muted enthusiasm if they played the old console port and were unhappy about the lack of the addition of new content.
In reality this game is the most white-knuckled, action packed third person shooter I have ever played, you get all the good of the genre (gears, etc), with a speed Infused sense of Mobility that I've never seen in a shooter.
The game runs perfectly and looks beautiful at 60 frames a second....  Or faster.
While I appreciate the graphic Innovations of recent years and have a machine that's more than equipped to run them, I recognize how well made this game was for the time that it came out. Some games age well, Batman Arkham Asylum or Arkham City still look beautiful today, and Vanquish falls into that category.
The graphics aren't the most advanced thing ever created, but they are gorgeous, epic in scale and more than adequate for the gameplay they are crafted around.
I never played this game on a console, this port is my first pass and it played flawlessly with a controller.
I've heard from other reviews that some of the intellectual content inside the story seem like a rip-off of other franchises, but taken by itself everything in the game works beautifully, whether it's an original idea or not.
I felt very much the same way about 40K Space Marine, another game that didn't limit you solely to running for cover in a third person shooter environment.
Another important issue, is the wonderfully ethical price structure attached to this port.
I purchased this port at full price, yeah a "whole $20".  I feel Sega/Platinum should be rewarded for pricing this game as a remaster should be, they did the same with Bayonetta and I applaud them for it.
When you compare this practice to gearbox's insane $50 price point for the Bulletstorm remaster, The $15 price point attached to this game as I write this review, should feel like an absolute steal, Because even without a sale it's worth every penny.
Last but not least to any game gods that may chance upon this review, this game falls into a special category for me. That category would be "most desired sequels": Along with Bulletstorm, and Space Marine, I would LOVE to see a sequel for this game, and would happily pay for a pre-order.
Bottom line, if you're a fan of shooters or action games and you've never played this before, Buy It Now, no matter what the prices is.

Vanquish is directed by Shinji Mikami, and it is the only title he had done under PlatinumGames. A third person cover shooter that plays very differently among its genre thanks to the emphasis on
, sadly, the story wasn't the focus, weak character writings is also present and obvious. Slide boosting will have you traverse in high speed within a battlefield, and AR Mode allows you to dispense enemy in slow-motion. Mixing high-speed and slow-mo, you have this tool that'll let you pull off cool chain of tricks in a short period of time. The short length of the game does not undercut it's value. It is a through and through high-energy, high-octane, adrenaline filled shooter. Playing it with Mouse and Keyboard feels great. In my opinion, M&K replaced the controller for this game.
For players who cares about score attack, 1 of the biggest problem the game had was its scoring system. Although they showcase every categories of scores, the game doesn't have enough context for players to know which category contributes into the total scores, or not. You'll have to do some experiment to figure out which action to avoid and which to approach for score gains. But replaying the game for the spectacles is worthwhile.

This is the sim racer I have been looking for, good selection of classic cars from small fiats to big american muscle. Has a decent selection of tracks, ai drivers are a decent challenge where they will try pass other drivers in smart places and not just push you off the track like a horny moose.
The biggest thing for me is that this game has great driving physics. Cars handle like you think they would. When you drive a small front wheel drive car you notice how nimble it is through the corners and has very little understeer and the bigger american muscle cars feel heavy with lots of torque. There are close to 100 different cars and you unlock them as you play through the career. You can adjust almost everything on them either with simple sliders for oversteer/understeer, stiffness and ride height to more advanced setup where you can change camber and so on.
Graphics are ok with decent textures and nice lighting effects for the time. Exterior damage modelling is very minimal but collisions do feel like they have some weight to them even though sometimes side to side collisions can feel a bit akward, but still you can push cars and make them spin. Very playable with older hardware and newer aswell. Also supports 21:9 aspect ratio monitors. Driving feels nice even with a gamepad, though oversteer can be difficult to control with such sensitive controls. I would recommend a good FFB wheel with this. I have not personally tested how it is with a wheel but support for all kinds of wheels and controllers are there and are very configurable with sensitivity, dead zones and so on. (I will try to add my thoughts later on about how it feels with a wheel since at the moment I don't have a good place to install my Fanatec CSR wheels, pedals and shifter.)

My favorite moments from the game are when you are playing the "david vs goliath" on career mode where you have to drive with a small and not too powerfull Lotus Cortina against big muscle cars like The Mustang. In the straightaways you get passed easily but if you carry lots of speed through the corners you can almost oversteer past them.
The game is very moddable, nogrip and other forums has a ton of beatifully modelled cars and tracks, period correct of course.

Intro/Graphics: If you love old cars (or just cars) and challenging racing, this is for you. This game is from 2005, so the graphics are outdated, although that doesn't bother me. I find the tracks and landscape suffer the most, but the cars themselves look great! The lighting is particularly good on the cars and everywhere else. You can race anytime of day, and night races are fun (I always end up breaking a headlight tho *oops*). Though, you cannot race in the rain unlike GTR2, however this is okay because driving these 60s/70s cars in the rain would be a struggle.
Controls/Difficulty: I got this game a long time ago before I was even old enough to fit in a driver's seat (much to the disdain of the elder British lads that I wrecked in multiplayer long ago), but I enjoyed it oh so much. If you are playing it with a keyboard, good luck racing on professional or semi-pro mode. With a keyboard, you pretty much need traction control, automatic shifting, and anti-lock brakes, therefore you can only be competitive on amateur difficulty. If you have a wheel and pedals and a shifter, then it'll be awesome, especially if you have a clutch pedal and H shifter. There's really no need to play on novice or beginner difficulty unless you really are new to racing games or are just a young kid. (Fun fact: it took me until this year to learn how to pit, however you won't really need to until the endurance races)
Physics/Realism: The driving physics are rather good. The crashes are very unrealistic however and it's very easy to flip your car and roll about five times before landing on your roof (and still being able to drive afterwards). Glitches are pretty fun, as well.
Gameplay: You go through a career mode where you race from 2 to 8 circuits per event and accumulate points and win a trophy if you finish between first and third in points at the end. You start with a Mini and a Lotus Cortina and race up to faster cars (Mustang, Elan, Corvette, Pantera, 911... etc.) by either winning them or earning enough credits to buy new (old) cars. You also unlock more tracks along the way. I haven't played multiplayer in such a long time, but back in the day I used to joyride in my Ford Falcon on the grass & dirt (on purpose) at Donington Park. The Europeans loved me.
tl;dr ~
You can drive (wreck) cars that are now worth millions!

Unimpressive, confusing, and riddled with errors and design flaws. You're better off spending your money and time elsewhere. (There are no Steam extras either, so you're really not missing anything.)
The story (if you can call it one) is all over the place. You're on a planet outpost and fix your ship to head back to Earth to save your injured boyfriend. You then fail miserably at piloting and crash-land on a unknown planet where you take it upon yourself to to heal their princess (completely ignoring the fact that you were initially drugged on sight and tossed in a dungeon to rot), as well as save the entire civilization from an asteroid by using all the tech lying around that people "forgot" about. I don't even know why the boyfriend was tossed into the plot, because he doesn't matter in the least.
The inhabitants of the unknown planet dress and live as if it's a medieval-era kingdom, yet there are high-tech machines scattered everywhere (and a robot barkeep o_0). I wouldn't say it's Steampunk, because it's really not. Just imagine if you brought a crapload of science equipment and factory machines to a Renaissance fair, installed or dumped them in various places, and instructed everyone to ignore or pretend none of it exists. I understand the idea was to create an anachronistic vibe for the civilization, but it's
sloppily done.
All that combined looks like the game is having a genre-identity crisis. It starts out as a sci-fi on a spaceship, then suddenly it's ye olde fantasy, then back to a more dystopian sci-fi. The story jumps from one thing to another like someone rambling in unrelated phrases that only connect or have context in their head. There's just no cohesive plot arc, and the end of the game bears little to no resemblance to the beginning. The only thing they have in common is that there's a meteor involved, and even that element is poorly used as a plot device.
Regarding the writing, it's painfully clear that English is not the original language. Awkward ESL sentence structures plague so many lines of text that I began to find it shocking when the grammar
correct (albeit stilted). The general meanings got through alright, but it was easier to just pretend the characters all spoke in broken English from the get-go.
I can't count how many times I wanted to facepalm while playing the hidden object scenes in this game. It's not just for one reason, either.
The number of mistranslations is astounding. The strange flavor text comments are bad enough, but the actual word lists are worse. A lightbulb is not a 'lamp'. An hourglass is not a 'clock'. That kind of thing.
Most two-step items are not indicated. Some words are in bold yellow to show it's a two-step item, but there are many, many non-yellow words that require combo actions too, and you'd never know without hints or pixel hunting.
Some HOGs are the "find then use" types, but you have to constantly switch between two tabs (list and inventory), which makes things needlessly frustrating.
Completely nonsensical scale and placement. There's no sense of proportion, some of the graphics are outright skewed, and objects practically hang in mid-air or stick to things at odd angles like someone got a little overenthusiastic with a tube of superglue.
Overly-precise hitboxes (which also applies to puzzles).
Some of the puzzles were decent, but very difficult on average. If you're a casual player who doesn't like thinking-type puzzles, you probably won't enjoy these at all. Several are actually
obtuse, or repetitive enough to become a pain to slog through. I admittedly skipped a few out of frustration (there are no "no-skip" achievements to strive for anyway).
A handful of puzzles are
badly designed. One example is a healing potion you have to make based on a recipe. The recipe sheet is a vague diagram with arrows, but the actual actions needed don't match the directions at all. Plus 3/4 of the ingredients aren't even shown on the paper, so I had to blindly click around till I found combinations that worked. Not fun.
When you solve a puzzle the window IMMEDIATELY closes, so it's nearly impossible to catch what some of the solutions look like (even with quick screenshot reflexes). That's more of a personal pet peeve, but I'm noting it in case I'm not the only weirdo who likes to see what they did correctly (or at least relish the solving for more than half an eye blink).
On the point-and-click side of things, there are quite a few unintuitive item uses and combinations. For example, if you have a hammer and chisel, in most games you place the chisel first, then use the hammer on it. Here you can't use them separately. You have to first combine them to get a "hammer with chisel" and THEN use them.
Not bad, but nothing special. The backgrounds are nice, but character design is a little odd and active/HOG objects don't look like they belong, like images slapped together from unrelated sources. Very poor resolution as well.
Meh. The main theme is mildly catchy, but annoying if you play for long stretches of time. I don't even remember what the SFX were like. No voiceovers to comment on.
Space Legends may seem like the kind of game you can just spend a few hours on as a change of pace, but don't be fooled. The cons far outweigh the pros, and the confusing storytelling, genre hopping, terrible translations, and bad puzzle/HOG design is not a fun combination in the least. With no cards or achievements to sweeten the deal, you're better off skipping it altogether.

Though this is a casual point-and-click adventure, it's actually quite challenging. The puzzles and even hidden-object scenes will require you to think methodically and logically. Some reviewers commented that the challenges are obtuse, but I believe you can crack all of them by paying attention to detail. And if you get stuck, there's always the handy hint button.
The world is vibrant and exciting, brought to life through excellent graphics. It's rare to find a good science fiction hidden-object games, and this one is actually not purely an adventure in space: it mixes in medieval tech through a twist in the story (no spoilers!). I think it's managed very well.
Unfortunately, the story is not well fleshed out and the characters are very one-dimensional, all leading up to an abrupt ending. But, despite this deficiency, I'm sure fans of hidden-object game will enjoy this one, especially if they are up for a challenge.

Stardrive 2 is clearly another attempt at a modern port of the old classic Master of Orion 2.  I've been waiting for years for someone to do this right... and unfortunately I'm going to have to keep waiting.
What's befuddling and frustrating is that after almost 20 years and umpteen attempts, no one has been able to improve on the original's turn-based combat resolution engine.  Every game that tries -- and there have been MANY -- insists on implementing a real-time combat resolution engine -- because, ya know, real-time is better than turn-based, right? -- but all they ever end up giving us is a muddled mess.  In this case, every battle unfolds exactly the same way: every ship charges across the battlefield to point-blank range, and then flies in tight loops back and forth across its target (no collisions in this universe) until one side or the other is completely annihilated.  High-tech weapons and defensees with varied effects seem to make no dfference whatsoever on the AI's tactics.
Oh, how I wish some developer would use their brain some day and realize that a turn-based combat engine would be better in this case.  After all, the whole rest of the game is turn-based, so you think they'd recognize the virtue in it.  It's a shame, too, because otherwise Stardrive 2 is pretty good -- mainly because it sticks to the script and slavishly copies MOO2's gameplay.  But the combat resolution engine is the heart of the game, and like every other clone, it just drags Stardrive 2 down from "good", past "mediocre", and straight into "disappointing".

Stardrive 2 is amazing in so many ways. The scale and diversity of the gameplay is fantastic. The integration of space battles, land battles, stragegic play, creativity, DESIGN! diplomacy, both realtime and turnbased aspects is something from a gamers dreams. The fact that this is mostly one mans creating is mindblowing. Stardrive is mechancially more ambitious than AAA games like civilization finding a perfect ballance of deep mechanics but simplistic and easey to undersand delivery. Here are some examples of thigs the game encompasas: optomizing planets for specific puposes (food, production and science mainly) which gives them strategic value adding to the turnbased strategic play. Engaging in diplomacy and espionoge to try to give yourself an advantage over the other free-for-all combatants in the galactic rat race to the top. Taking the information you learned to design ships that help you to win the real time battles. Control of space allows you to transport your  troops safely to take the enemies planets in turn based tactical battles. Now that you have a planet we are back to the beginning although ingame you can have at a hundred systems with nine races to do this all at once with. So cool, soo much fun.
A few things worth noting:
The AI is pritty good not terrible!!! unlike other  AAA strategy games which is a huge pluse
The diplomacy is really well done and ballance except on brutal difficulty where it is supposed to be hard
The facty one person made this sometime shows with minor graphical buggs inconvienances like things on top of each other
The ground battles are not super fun and easily the weakpoint but still not terrible or even without stragety just not geat, I suggest using auto rezolve as there is little point to many of the battles where one force is 3 times the strength of the other, however I have had some tense battles that were importand and I was trying my hardest to win against poor ods.
Load screens can be slow and performance although improved is not amazing, of course that is in battles with thousands of units I was able to run this on my gpu-less laptop
Buggs happen but not too much.
There is a learning cuve and you will loose some games which is a good thing. I think some people get angry with this game because they don't understand this kind of strategy well enough and perceve the game as unbeatable or think the AI cheats like crazy. (In this type of game, difficuly has to be added in the form of better AI start locations, More units at start and lots of modifiers to their economies).
In conclusion this is so worth the money if you have any interest in any kind of strategy or 4X games. It is challanging in many ways but fairer than many strategy games. Designing ships is soo cool and addicting and the realtime battles where you get to put them to the test with your own skill commanding is just and amazing gaming expeience. The ground battles are the weakpoint but can be dealt with with bombing and then autoresloving the boring ones. My number one complaint is that there is no multiplayer not because the AI is bad my any means but because the gtame is soo enticing to my strategic side and creates such epic situations that I want to have that experience in a free-for-all galactic war with my friends.

If you have not played StarDrive 1 this is a good 4x to pick up. It's fairly easy to start as the creator has a fully voiced tutorial and the game is a little less complex than it's predecessor (be warned if you jump around menu to menu while in a tutorial the tutorial will end and leave you helpless). If you have played the last StarDrive and really wanted this to be a good game, I have bad news and good news. Good news the game isn't broken like the last one and playing for several hours (as I normally do) caused no framedrop or resources hoging. Bad news the game is now a turn based strategy instead of one big realtime. This may not be a bad thing for all of you but it's something to consider, because it is a turn based strategy fleet battles now occur on a different screen. This once again is not really bad but the strategies you can use are limited since you always start on opposing sides and pretty much just clash in the middle every time. The ground combat is dull and managing your foot soldiers is a pain. This combat pops up often and it is rather dull with very little strategy besides shoot the things and not get shot by the things. Certain ground enemies are also really hard to kill for arbitrary reasons and will often cost you a well equiped group of soldiers. Talking about equiping soldiers it's impossible. Soldiers spawn with random gear and more likely than not the worst gear you have. There doesn't seem to be a way to say how many of each soldier you want or to even to limit their selection of items to make sure they spawn with more than a combat knife.
All this said I have had a lot of fun with the game. Ship building is what I spend most of my time on but I just wish a few more QOL things were in the ship builder like the health and shields of the ship. Managing your empire is simplified with one screen that shows you ever planet you have, what they are building, worker allocation, and so on and so forth. Tech is kept interesting with multiple routes that you can take. If you take one tech you lose the others and are sort of herded toward using diplomacy to gain the ones you missed or the spying system. Subterfuge is rather simple but does the job with multiple missions that your agents can be sent on.
I give this game a thumbs up and I think anyone who enjoys the one more turn mindset of Civ 5 will have a blast wtih this game.

StarDrive 2 is not by any means, a bad game. That being said, it is incredibly small for a 4x game. After one short play through you will have experienced all the random events and found all the strange anomalys. It's ship designers is a direct downgrade from StarDrive 1, which is a real shame considering that was one of it's best features. The AI isn't horrible, but it also does not act naturally or organically by any means. It will provide a challenge, never researching the wrong tech or mishandling it's economy. The ground combat is a direct improvement over the first game's, with chess-like turn-based battles that are satisfying but easy to win once you know what gear to use and have one of the few heroes who mop the floor with ground based units. The game doesn't take itself seriously enough, with the dialogue of your enemies simply being silly and somewhat childish, which is a unique twist when it comes to the genre but in my opinion not a good choice. Rather than introducing a universe and advanced species with a lot of lore and depth, we get plant like creatures who act cute and cuddly, space bears who act like japanese samurai, and space lycans who act like dumb evil dogs who miracuously managed to get into space. The space battles, although in theory would be fun, are unplayable without a CPU with the minimum power of 3.5 GHz quad-core (even then you will lag with the largest battles) once the AI creates fleets which numbers are in the hundreds, all firing 20 projectiles a second. Late game, this issue renders the game unplayable for a lot of those who have purchased the game, including myself. This is the game breaking issue for me, because although the base game is somewhat underwheling in comparison to other 4x games, if I were able to play into the late game without lagging to death I could add some pretty great mods to turn this into a game I put a bunch of hours into, as well as continue my support for the developer. So overall, the game isn't terrible, but I would not recommend paying more than $15 for it, and that is only if you are really itching for a new 4x game.

I would love to recommend this game, but I can't. While I was a huge fan of Stardrive, the sequel just rings hollow.
The first title was born of Steam Early Access, and gave the developer a large swath of suggestions, criticism, and feedback during its cycle. The developer would later make it pretty clear that he wasn't terribly fond of getting feedback during development, that there were too many voices in his first game and chose to develop Stardrive 2 behind closed doors.
Unfortunately, this is the result of a developer and his hubris stuck in an echo chamber. There's no one to point out flaws in design, resulting in poor decisions being reinforced as good ones inside one's own head, where they become entrenched.
Ship design is still good, but not quite as dynamic as SD1. There's far less freedom to build.  Faction customization is expanded. The tech tree is improved, but still not great and leader missions are fun the first time, but grow stale.
Outside of that, everything just falls flat. Ground combat is half-baked. Colony management interface is poor. The AI leaves a lot to be desired in both strategic and tactical combat (mathematical advantages are applied to make up for it). Diplomacy is even less useful. The move to a turn-based strategy map has taken away the immediacy of naval engagements.
Even with all the bugs, which I can forgive, this culminates into the two most damning critiques of this game:
* The game is shallow and has no spirit.
* It's flat out boring.

A while back, when I saw the trailer for "Thirty Flights of Loving", I was excited by the abstract, highly stylish visuals.  It looked like a seriously unique, undeniably "indie" experience, and I couldn't wait to get my hands on it.
Players heaped praise on the game, finding deep meaning inside the painfully short experience.  I was not one of those people, unfortunately.  I found "Thirty Flights..." to be a shallow proof of concept, at best -- something the developer himself seemed to admit from the commentary track.  I walked away from the game bitter, having felt duped by popular opinion.
That said, I very much liked the IDEA of "Thirty Flights": an interactive book.  A way of telling a unique, linear story, letting the player guide the narrative along at their own pace.  (Adding VR into the mix will take this immersive idea even further, but I'm getting ahead of myself.)
As it turns out, the game I was hoping "Thirty Flights" would be, is what "Jazzpunk" actually *IS*.
Both games are very strange, unique, linear short stories, but "Jazzpunk" gives you a bit more freedom to explore, with side-quests and mini-games here and there along the way.
What separates the two further, is that "Jazzpunk" is straight up hilarious and wonderfully strange.  More times than I can count, I found myself wide-eyed, staring at the monitor and going "whaaat!" with a huge smile.
Additionally, there are numerous references, both popular and obscure, to old technology (Captain Crunch's famous 2600 whistle, for example), and the culture around them.  Raymond Scott's unmistakable trademark musical style heavily influences the proceedings (not to mention directly referenced here and there).
While I damned "Thirty Flights" for being criminally short for the price, I found "Jazzpunk"'s short length to be JUST long enough without overstaying it's welcome.  A $10 pricetag would probably be more comfortable than $15, but the effort and love that was clearly put into this...well, I wouldn't at all feel ripped off if I'd paid full price.
I'd absolutely love to see this expanded into an ongoing series, with each installment being just as short but sweet.
4/5

Being a comedy videogame is rough. Not only are you subject to every single individual playing your game's unique sense of humor, but there's also the fact that not a lot of videogames are very funny.
Jazzpunk is pretty funny. From the get-go, it fires off visual gags, humorous audio, and strange dialog and rarely ever lets up. With the frenzied pace, the game could have easily spread itself too thin, but almost all the material in the game is executed very well. Sometimes far too well. Sometimes a completely innocent and almost throw-away joke will spiral out into a complete mini-game of its own. I'm hesitant to spoil anything simply because I feel the jokes and random asides in the game should be witnessed first hand, but I will say that it'll be hard to think of wedding cakes the same way again.
The game thrives on the absurd and your willingness to poke around each world to find that absurdity. If you just rush through each stage's set objective, you'll be missing the point, and all the fun entirely. The Achievements List is a fantastic way to get as much as you can out of Jazzpunk as it encourages that kind of exploration over simple "progress" based objectives.
If you enjoyed last year's The Stanley Parable, then Jazzpunk is most definitely for you. If absurdist humor, dark comedy, and anti-humor aren't your thing, it may be best to pass this one by.

Full review:
Well, this was one of the more interesting titles I’ve played of late. Certainly one of the most humorous games I’ve played in my life, that’s for sure. There’s just so many things right about Jazzpunk.
Jazzpunk is a first-person comedy-adventure game set during the cold war, in an alternate reality. The game places large emphasis on open-world exploration, which can be seen immediately in the first level. I spent the majority of my time in the game exploring, rather than actually playing through the main story, although I did manage to beat the entire game in about two hours. The game’s length being my major complaint. For such a great game, I’d like more than just two hours.
Unique. If I had to use one word to describe Jazzpunk, that’d be it. The game is full of references, side quests, and plenty of areas to explore in the various chapters. I even helped clean a guy’s massive ear out when he was unable to hear. Just one of the silly things that can be accomplished within the several chapters. Oh, and the dialogue. Fantastic. Simply fantastic. A lot of the characters in-game spoke like robots and it seemed like there were new accents everywhere I went.
Jazzpunk is heavy on its comedic appeal. There are several instances in the game that serve no purpose other than to make you laugh. I ran into a shop at one point whose door simply said “closed for no reason”. There’s plenty of new things to find when exploring the worlds of each chapter, and, like I said, that’s where I had spent most of my playtime, looking around. It’s overwhelming at times, the amount of stuff that you can find whilst exploring.
The game uses an interesting art style. I want to say its cel-shaded, but I don’t know if that’d be correct. For the most part, it does look like its cel-shaded, which is always a art style. Nothing to complain about in terms of the game’s graphics.
If you’re going to pick up Jazzpunk, don’t expect much in terms of length if you just play through the game’s story. Instead, spend some time exploring about. You’ll find yourself laughing at the numerous scenes scattered throughout the game.

Never Alone is an atmospheric side scrolling platformer that tells us the touching story of Nuna and Fox as they search for the source of the eternal blizzard which is ravaging her community. The story is based on an old Iñupiaq tale, a symbolic legend of a civilization that has been dealing with nature's hardships for centuries.
An amazing game with a heartwarming story. I enjoyed every second of my playthrough, especially the cultural insights. I believe I learned more about this fascinating culture through playing this game than I would have reading a book about it, simply because you hear the stories from the people themselves. Through the chapters, you will encounter several collectibles. Each of them unlocks a short video - a cultural insight featuring people from the community talking about what it was like to grow up in the region's unforgiving cold.
The game length is around 4-6 hours, depending on your skills, but for the 4-6 hours you are playing it, you are transported into the Alaskan way of life with the stunningly beautiful graphics as well as the narrator telling the story in his native tongue.

Orwell is an intriguing game that does not let you get away with bad jokes. The player will have to use rationality and puzzle together the real story from reading other people's perspectives on the same events, and one must be careful what information you hand over to Big Brother.
The game lets you choose whether you want to let people get away with things or if you hand every piece of information to your superior, and it's easy to let yourself be brainwashed and forget that one surveills real people and not just stains in the system, which the game is really good at making you believe. In addition to this, the game had good sound effects which kept you on the edge of your seat, as well as having many plot-twists and unexpected elements to it.
Not to mention the witty references to the novel 1984 by George Orwell, which effectively added an element of familiarity to those who are acquainted with the novel.
I recommend this game to both people who know 1984 and to those who don't (and possibly want to), as this is a good introduction to the novel and it gives you an interesting perspective in how it feels to work for Big Brother. Therefore, I give this game a rating of 10/10.

It's a 10/10. Not only is Vanquish the best shooter ever made (imo), it's also PlatinumGames' finest product (imo). Shinji Mikami's proven he's the man time and time again (Resident Evil 1, Dino Crisis 1, REmake, Resident Evil 4, God Hand, Vanquish, The Evil Within), and this time is no different.
Full disclosure, I'm not a fan of the slow walking sections. But, I don't actually have any other complaints with this game.
I got every Steam achievement in about 15 hours, using the 'mouse and keyboard' scheme, but this is a highly replayable game. There's also much cooler stuff to do that isn't tied to acheivements (God Hard difficulty, for example).
Other highlights, the unlocked frame rate and resolution bring a tear to my eye. This version of the game also includes all of the DLC from the console version (Anti Armor gun is too good).
If you don't like short highly replayable games, pass on this. It's campaign is no longer than 5 hours, for even the most inept, and if you're competent to any degree you'll finish it in 3 hours.
Caution:
Vanquish does boast some unique mechanics. Although they are always useful, you can painfully grind through the game without them on difficulties below Hard. It is for this reason that I'd highly suggest that you put the game on Hard your first playthrough. Even then, Vanquish takes time to learn. If you're looking for an end goal, you may have an idea of what you're doing by the time you finish Tactical Challenge 6.
Still, can't recommend it enough. Especially at this price. It's ideal for when you feel like playing a highly entertaining game with no filler. This game was made for leaderboards.

Nullysun is a very primitive game. It's about on par gameplay wise as an early-2000's flash game. Despite this, it has the most charm out of any small indie game I've seen on Steam, even if some of it is basically stolen from other popular indie platformers. Even though it is most likely a person's first attempt at making a game in Unity, all of the assets are original and the cutscenes are actually quite good, and it even has an original soundtrack. Unfortunately there's some jankiness, and that's to be expected of a beginner's work in Unity, but underneath the jank and the questionable design choices, there's a cute little game that obviously had a lot of care and effort put into it. Although I would have liked it to be more polished and complete, the game that's there is enough to hold your attention for a little while and make you smile a bit at some of the minor things it does well. The first level captured my attention well and I thought I was in for a small indie game obviously inspirsed by Inside, but after that it turned into a pretty generic platformer. Again, for a novice attempt I'm actually stunned how well the first level and the cutscenes are done, and I would have liked to see more focus in that area than gameplay. I would recommend purchasing on the sole purpose of supporting a guy who seems like he just wanted to make a fun little game after being inspired by other fun little games. It's objectively not a very good game, even by flash game standards, but it's just unique enough in it's artstyle for me to feel confident in my purchase.

If you enjoyed/enjoy the sweet masochistic nature of DBD then you'll love this game, but that's about it. To sum it up, this game was delayed several times throughout its development, and it shows. There are bugs and glitches galore, most of which were present during the intial release, now many months later there has been no fixes.
Counselor: The gameplay is rather boring and monotonus; all there is to do every match is open drawers, lock doors, fix one of three things, but usually they are so trapped that you'll never get to them. Items glitch into the ground mesh upon death so it creates a non winnable game for the other players. Then there is buggy animations for just about everything aswell as hit detection problems *cough cough Jasons grab range cough* and while all the Counselors have different stats, other than Stamina/Strength/Repair, the rest don't really matter much. Savini Jason, if you keep up with the game, you'll notice that intial backers of the game were able to buy a special "Skin" of Jason, but really it's not a skin but a whole other character with the greatest strengths and the most useless weaknesses, making him a literal pay to win game killer.
Jason: You can go days without getting to play Jason in pub matches since it's all random, but when you finally get that great honor, let me list you what can go wrong during your match.
1. Counselors leave mid kill animation, so you get no points. In retrospect you actually caught and killed 8/8 Counselors but you're only going to get the points for 2/8.
2. The bugs oh the bugs;  you can easily get stuck in grab animations and if a Counselor hit's you at the right time, it can literally send you out of the map or below it.
3. The glitches. Counselors can get places Jason can not and can also get out of the boundaries of the playable map, rendering a stalemate until you quit as Jason or wait for the 20 minute timer to tick down.
4. Players leaving at the beginning. You got picked as Jason, but as soon as the match can even start, two or three players leave, making your game already off to an amazingly awful start.
Then theres the price tag. [First Developer Meeting]
"Let's make a HO/puzzle/adventure game!"
"Awesome, but lets do sci-fi, there aren't many sci-fi HO/puzzle/adventure games."
"... but maybe there aren't many sci-fi HO/puzzle/adventure games because people don't like them?"
"hmmmm, ok, let's do a sci-fi HO/puzzle/adventure game but have it take place in medieval times."
"Medieval?"
"It's a safe genre."
"OK, lets do a sci-fi/medieval/HO/puzzle/adventure game!"
"With steampunk elements."
"What?"
"Steampunk is really popular right now."
"OK, lets do a sci-fi/medieval/steampunk/HO/puzzle/adventure game!"
"and post apocalyptic."
"Seriously?"
"Yea! Mad Max is coming out next year, Fallout 3 is awesome and Fallout 4 is being hyped right now."
"OK, lets do a sci-fi/medieval/steampunk/post apocalyptic/HO/puzzle/adventure game!"
"........."
And that right there is the biggest failing of "Space Legends: At the Edge of the Universe."
Don't get me wrong, it's a good game. The graphics are top notch, sound effects and music passable, but both story and game don't know what they are trying to be. It's all over the place. From an astronaut scientist, trying to save your boyfriend and get home, to a prisoner in a medieval dungeon, to trying to save a princess, to trying to save the entire planet, except it's not medieval, it's steampunk, oh wait, nevermind, it's post-apocalyptic! My hair is turning gray just trying to keep up.
Whatever it is, it's still an enjoyable game, even though it doesn't meet the expectations of it's title. Some relatively easy HO scenes, not too many, mixed with a lot of fiendishly difficult puzzles distract you from the wtf?!? moments within the storyline.
If you are into HO adventure games, this is definitely worth checking out.
(or medieval, or post apocalyptic, or steampunk, or sci-fi) ;)
