I was excited to take a look at Space Legends - Edge of the Universe because it seemed to be that rarest gem among the HOG genre - a hidden object adventure set in an outright sci-fi millieu. With most HOGs leaning towards supernatural horror, crime-solving, or some kind of fantasy/faery nonsense, Space Legends seemed like it would be a breath of fresh air. Little did I realize how quickly things would take a turn for the bizarre and inept.
The game starts off promisingly enough, establishing the main character as part of a two-person research team investigating a far-away planet. After a storm severly damages the station, the base, it's up to the main character to stabilize her love interest's injuries, gather their data, and fly back to Earth for medical assistance. This section is fairly solid - a logical threat bearing down on the player in an interesting and novel setting. Then the player blasts off and crash lands on a medieval planet, and everything goes straight to hell.
For reasons I can't fathom, the developers take the one unique thing that the game had going for it - a non-standard setting, and then decided to throw that away. By moving the action to a standard fantasy kingdom, complete with magic swords to repair and stricken princesses to cure, they make the game far less interesting by degrees - especially since the fact that the main character is from a far more technologically advanced civilization doesn't factor into the majority of her interactions once she arrives on the planet. What's worse, the one interesting mystery that the kingdom has to offer - why does a low-tech world have robot bartenders and industrial lasers lying around - has its solution spoiled by the game's map, of all things. Just minutes after arriving on the medieval world, the player gets access to a fast-travel map that depicts not only the castle they're trapped in and the surrounding village, but a secret monorail beneath it which leads to a futuristic city destroyed by a cataclysm sometime in the past. This is not how you build a curiosity, developers.
Now, on to the HOG criteria!
Criteria 1: To what degree do the puzzle screens look like a thrift store vomited on my monitor?
This is absolutely a problem, especially since the game has such a paltry number of Hidden Object Screens, most of which need to be visited twice. Absolutely no thought was put into the logic of what might items might be found in a particular location. The main character's closet on the research base is absolutely overflowing with the kind of random tchotchkes that one would expect to find in another game's haunted mansion. This raises the question of why someone would cart all of this junk halfway across the galaxy space. Naturally, the answer is 'the developers couldn't be bothered to conceptualize the type of junk that would be in a space closet, so they just went with cliched items'. Even worse is a subsequent scene in which a jail cell has a shelf in it fulled to bursting with random junk, much of which proves useful in planning an escape.
Criteria 2: Are the searches justified by the premise/story?
Only in the most basic sense. From time to time the player will need to find an item to unlock something, and then a standard HOS will pop up, allowing them to look for it, as well as fifteen other items that they don't need. Space Legends tries to make things a little more interesting by having items which require assembly,  and while that livens things up a little, it can't cover for the fact that the main character has no use for a target with a bullethole in it, so taking the time to load and fire a flintlock pistol at a piece of paper seems like something of a waste of time. Just once the game attempts to colour outside the lines and offers a multi-stage HOS, in which the player has to find items and use them right there on the screen to unlock the next set of items and task, but the objectives are so poorly explained that it proves more frustrating than innovative.
Criteria 3: How well do the various puzzles and object searches meld together to form a coherent whole?
Try as the game might, it can't make the puzzles and searches feel like a part of the story. Not that it tries especially hard. Most of the puzzles on display are of the most generic type imaginable - move blocks to slide a crate to the other end of a hall; spin knobs, but doing so causes the other knobs to spin as well. Most egregious is the cloaking device the player is asked to turn on by doing a jigsaw puzzle. It's hard to get more thematically irrelevant than that.
In addition to all of the design failures, the game's presentation is inexcusably sloppy. While I'm aware that the game wasn't developed by English-speaking people, I can't let translation that affects gameplay slide. A brush is not a 'comb'. A lightbulb is not a 'lamp'. An hourglass is not a 'clock'. There are another dozen examples I'm not going to list here. Beyond the bad translation, some of the puzzles are just poorly explained. At one point I was asked to brew a potion by following the steps in a recipe - except three of the ingredients I'd been told to gather didn't appear in said recipe. Which forced me to resort to trial and error to figure out when they were supposed to be used. That's just sloppy.
Here's a puzzle that perfectly illustrates the nonsense players are expected to put up with in Space Legends: The main character must use a crossbow grappling hook to snag a rope bridge so that she can cross it. But she's so bad at shooting that she hits the ceiling instead, knocking down some rocks, as well as the thing that was hidden behind them - the key to a cabinet in the princess' bedroom which contains insulating tape she can just to build a brace to allow her to fire the crossbow more accurately. Why was a key lodged in the ceiling of a secret cave that no one ever goes to? Why does a medieval princess have a roll of insulating tape? Did I seriously just have to go through a series of puzzle steps because the character I'm playing as doesn't know to fire a crossbow at the thing she wants to hit, rather than straight up?
With contrived nonsense, terrible presentation and generic settings ruining all of the goodwill built up in the game's full hour, Space Legends is a nearly-unplayable mess. In a sad final note, the game's end credits offer a possible explanation for its shoddiness. They start with an 'in memorium' photograph of a man who the credits quickly identify as the game's designer and scriptwriter. So it's entirely possible that all of Space Legends' problems owe to it being partially unfinished at the time of its release. That's tragic, but maybe they would have been better off simply dropping the project rather than releasing something this bad.

Space Legends is a decent hidden object/point & click game. You are in control of Elizabeth, who is trying to save the one she loves. You move around to several locations in a big effort to get back home.
The story is lacking in depth and background but…really isn’t that bad. I was still driven by the story to continue on and find out what happens.
The puzzles are good and varying in difficulty. Although the lack of direction and understanding some puzzles caused a little frustration.
The hidden object scenes were great and I always looked forward to them. The hidden object(s) may require several steps before you can collect them (obstructed, not complete, out of reach, etc). However, there weren’t enough of them! For the handful of scenes they had, they were used more than once in each location.
Environments were nicely detailed and the music seemed to match each environment. The only time I noticed the music is when it abruptly stopped and started over again.
This game was definitely translated over to English as the grammar and spelling is incorrect in multiple places. Although, I could tell when they were trying to go for in those situations.
One last point, the ending. It’s abrupt and I was taken by surprise. I would have been fine with a cinematic of how things turned out, etc. But it’s a 3 second ending and then the credits roll.
+Great hidden object scenes
+Detailed environments
+Puzzles were good and moderately challenging
+Not enough hidden object scenes
+Bad English translation
+Story lacking a bit
+Hint button can accidentally be pressed
+A few backtracking points
+Abrupt ending
I can ONLY recommend this if it’s on a .99 sale or you get it in a bundle. The $9.99 price is way too high for the content you get. Otherwise, it’s a decent hidden object game that will keep you engaged for a handful of hours and test you on some of its puzzles.

Now, I was expecting a whole lot from this one, as I can even see that Jim Sterling recommended it. After beating it I can say it's not bad at all. If you liked Fabel, you will love this. You play a rescued Overlord who is made to rule over his minions. The gameplay is alot like a hack and slash RPG meets Strategy. The games currency is split into Gold and Life force. You need lifeforce to spawn minions, so you can expect a bit of grinding....
Yeah the game gets that whole "Third Person action game with RTS elements" right, unlike Brutal Legends. Controlling minions takes a bit of learning, but once you get the hang of it, it's not bothersome at all.
The real joy is the core parts of the game i.e. the minion controlling and puzzling. The remaining parts of the game aren't exciting...I'm talking about the action, story, upgrading and customizing part. The Upgrading and customizing part are More like "They're there so I'll take it". The Overlords combat mechanics are silly, but minions make up for it.
Lastly, the part about you being Evil. It doesn't get portrayed well. All you feel is Anti-Heroish. It always comes out as you are a jerk who does good and is saving the world.

Overall, Overlord and its expansion provided a fun and memorable gaming experience. It surprised me how a 7 year old game can still offer the same caliber of entertainment that one can expect from current titles. I found the bizzare storyline, comedic fantasy atmosphere, humorous art style, and music to be the most notable aspects of the game. But just like any game, it is not perfect (see my critique below).
The Good:
- Ridiculously funny story line and art direction
- Decent mix of action & strategy
- Interesting character & enemy models
- A bizzare and outrageous depiction of the "fantasy" genre
The Bad:
- Some things felt unfinished or lacking
- Almost linear story line
- A few awkward cinematics
- Minions can be a burden to control at times

This is a gem of a game.
A steep learning curve and a few combat & diplomatic balance issues mar an otherwise delightful exercise in grand and tactical strategy.
Space is unforgiving in Star Drive 2. A wrong choice can cost you a planet in the the blink of a few turns, and random alien and pirate attacks are only slightly more dangerous than your own poor choices when it comes to colonization, research focus, and ship construciton.
My favorite thing about this game, and I why recommned it to any 4x-Space fans, is that Star Drive 2 comes closer to modeling real space colonizization (at least the way I imagine it) than any other game of this type that I've played. Despite the seemingly small number of star systems, space is big and you don't have enough ships to protect all your borders. As with other excellent military strategy games, SD2 starts you off with barely enough power to defend a single front. Overextension is as a dangerous as too little expansion. And if you designed your ships poorly, well ...
Beyond the challenging strategic (and tactical! w/ ground units) military aspect, the game has a difficult, frustrating, potentially rewarding, and potentially disasterous diplomacy system. I love it. Never has a game come closer to modelling something as futile and hair-pulling as real international diplomacy. Some of the time, you can get 1/4 of what you want, and it usually comes at a cost that makes you nervous about repurcussions down the road.
The writing is funny. The tech tree is challenging, rewarding, and full of great literary and film sci-fi references that made me smile. The music is solid, and the map is pretty. Races can be customized, and difficulty can be greatly upscaled to match increased knowledge of the game's tech and combat loopholes. All of this to say, re-playability is high.
TLDR:
This a funny, atmospheric, and surprisingly difficult game that required me to think more than most 4X games.

I would definitely recommend this game. Forget the trollish reviews--a lot of people are reviewing the game not its own merits but by posts by the developer or experiences with a prior game (SD1, which is a different beast, but related).
Yes, the game is HEAVILY indebted to a classic 4x space game, Master of Orion 2. It's not quite as good as that game (but what it is, eh?), but with some polish and an expansion pack, I think this game might surpass it.
What you should ask yourself is this -- do you want a space 4x game with a turn-base strategy and a RTS tactical map? If so, SD2 is for you. Really, there are not many hybrid 4X games out there. There's the Total War games, Sword of the Stars series, and . . . ? Most game companies don't do these type of games--they either go turn-based all the way, or RTS all the way. Why? It's really hard to program two-games in one and figure out the proper way the two should mix.
SD2 manages to pull off this hybrid approach really well. On the strategy side, you colonize planets and build buildings that help improve the economy. There are many buildings that can help improve industry or science or food. you can then use trade to boost these variables.
On the tech side, the tree is deep enough but not too much to allow individual techs to feel unique and useful. There's still some balancing to do, but the nice thing is, lower tier techs, mostly the weapons, still have their place. You're also limited by your race and your choices, so nearly impossible to get the entire tech advances in one game. This offers some interesting strategic choices up front--do I choose better weapons or better buildings or research options?
Combat involves an RTS game where ships duke it out. Lots pew-pew here with cool weapon and shield effects. Some battle can get pretty crazy, especially when there are lot of ships. Sometimes, the RTS mode can be buggy, and when you ahve a lot of ships on screen, the game lags. The developer is working on this problem and has posted some potential fixes.
There's a lot more to this -- included is a scenario and campaign editor. You can also experiment with a "battle-only" mode, where you can design ships and see them duke it out. No reviewers mention this! It's such a great idea, and i can't think of any modern game that includes this option.
Give this game a chance --it's a one man developer, and you can surely get a good 50-60 hours of this game, if not more if you mess around with each race and the scenario editor. There's a ton of content to play around with--don't get sucked into the negative hype. The game is well worth your money.

Good version of MOO II.  Good tech trees.  Interesting species. Similar character traits.  Thats where my pros end.
Boring, slow, space combat. "Tolerance" keeps politics from reaching its full potential.
Poor AI makes for horrible automated fights especially for planet invasions. Fight all your battles yourself.  That said the land battles are painful to be part of.  They are unintuitive, difficult to work through and unrewarding.  I feel like they are punishment for invading.  If you choose "auto" resolve be prepared for ridiculous consequences.  In land combat, Its very common to grossly outnumber your opponent by 50:1 and lose all your troops, and then have the game crash.  I assume its because there is only so much space to place your troops the computer automatically kills them before battle begins.
As for space combat, mass driver cannons are overpowered and take out any thought or development from ship creation.   You will need to micromanage your own ships as the AI really is not bright at all and you will find your overpowered ships pulled apart by an unintuitive computer admiral.
Overall, not very polished and needs to be updated with some of its bugs adressed. With all of these bugs and oversights I think the worst has to do with pathing.  The pathing problem keeps ships from entering refit queues as they "hop" and "skip" over the planets they should be docking at, this same pathng problem occurs when trying to attack planets or passing fleets.  Of course this is only a problem if you can actually select the ships themselves which is an ordeal, the only thing harder than that is trying to mouse over several ships at once.  A process that works 50% of th etime.
Another issue that annoyed me to no end was the "overlays".  When a new menu, map or option was overlaid upon another you could still access the GUI under it, so while trying to build something on a planet economy screen I would actually click the queue on the main map listing all of the items created on the turn before.  Annoying.
All of these problems make it nearly unplayable as these bugs often cause game crashes, forcing me to reload an "autosave", only to lose the last 4-10 turns and the hundreds of actions that likely went with them.  I play it not because I love it, but because for the price point it sucks less than the alternatives out there.
In the end I think I should have saved my money until the problems were adressed rather than having it forced through like so many other "indie"games only to have updates added later.
There's a reason it has dropped to half its price and put on sale so many times in two months.
Edit ** The first two patches have actually made the game more unplayable.  You can no longer choose to NOT send in your leaders in planet auto combat, so now they die.  THIS MEANS THAT YOU CAN NO LONGER "AUTO COMPLETE" GROUND COMBAT!!
-Fleets will now randomly disappear and become unuseable. THIS MAKES GAME COMPLETELY UNPLAYABLE
-Added "governnor control" is poorly implemented and far from potential.

Full review:
Well, this was one of the more interesting titles I’ve played of late. Certainly one of the most humorous games I’ve played in my life, that’s for sure. There’s just so many things right about Jazzpunk.
Jazzpunk is a first-person comedy-adventure game set during the cold war, in an alternate reality. The game places large emphasis on open-world exploration, which can be seen immediately in the first level. I spent the majority of my time in the game exploring, rather than actually playing through the main story, although I did manage to beat the entire game in about two hours. The game’s length being my major complaint. For such a great game, I’d like more than just two hours.
Unique. If I had to use one word to describe Jazzpunk, that’d be it. The game is full of references, side quests, and plenty of areas to explore in the various chapters. I even helped clean a guy’s massive ear out when he was unable to hear. Just one of the silly things that can be accomplished within the several chapters. Oh, and the dialogue. Fantastic. Simply fantastic. A lot of the characters in-game spoke like robots and it seemed like there were new accents everywhere I went.
Jazzpunk is heavy on its comedic appeal. There are several instances in the game that serve no purpose other than to make you laugh. I ran into a shop at one point whose door simply said “closed for no reason”. There’s plenty of new things to find when exploring the worlds of each chapter, and, like I said, that’s where I had spent most of my playtime, looking around. It’s overwhelming at times, the amount of stuff that you can find whilst exploring.
The game uses an interesting art style. I want to say its cel-shaded, but I don’t know if that’d be correct. For the most part, it does look like its cel-shaded, which is always a art style. Nothing to complain about in terms of the game’s graphics.
If you’re going to pick up Jazzpunk, don’t expect much in terms of length if you just play through the game’s story. Instead, spend some time exploring about. You’ll find yourself laughing at the numerous scenes scattered throughout the game.

Jazzpunk: a wacky adventure game stuffed full of gags, pratfalls, and jokes. Like many of Adult Swim Games' works, Jazzpunk's gameplay is supported mainly by its comedic factor. The end result is a somewhat shallow, yet still entertaining game. As Agent Polyblank, you travel the world collecting sensitive materials, thwarting other spies and engaging in general mischief. Though the sidequests offered by the game are enjoyable, the main plot itself can be finished in an hour or so, a glaring example of Your Mileage May Vary. None of the puzzles are remotely challenging and the game is more or less a Walk To Goofy Setpiece simulator with a few minigames that merely distract. Though the game ends quicker than a run to the Post Office, the jokes are somewhat funny in that Adult Swim brand of humor. Once again your mileage may vary and after the humor the game really doesn't have much going for it. The art style is abstract and engaging, but the world itself is more or less dead and roughly the size of a football field. Before you know it the level is over and even the few 'sidequests' in the game add little substance. That being said, the game is pretty funny, but it begs the question "Why did I pay for this?" Even at $15 (or $12 at the time I write this) Jazzpunk seems way too expensive for what it is and feels more-suited to the Flash Game crowd rather than a standalone title. In conclusion, not a bad game, but not worth the money.

If I have to give direct comparison, this game has similar style (albeit a much better graphic) to Limbo and Deadlight - especially the latter. It's more like a side scrolling game, nothing revolutionary, with emphasis on action and less on puzzle. The real value though, it's the cultural insight. There are many games, but very few in terms of ratio that really dig into its background, let alone being narrated in a very unique language (Iñupiaq) giving us a valuable first-hand experience.
Graphic wise, it's still relevant by today's standard, and friendly to laptop guys. My 840m can do this game all maxed without any FPS drop. The scenery is really beautiful and well rendered, except... if you hate snowy environment and/or frozen tundra then it's surely your problem (lol j/k) as the game is all about snow.
This one is best played coop, if you have buddy or family member to play with you then ask them. Perfectly doable solo, however. Overall it's not a long game, a few hours even if you watch the movies in-between the chapters and a narrated story, perfect to be played together.
Be reminded though, that the game is best played with controller. Yes you can use keyboard, but as usual platformer will be a bit awkward when played with KB/M.
Overall it's a nice little game with low level skill cap.

(REVISED) Some issues with the "sim"-ness of the game aside, this is one of the most satisfying racing games I've played. That's largely in part to the huge mod content available.
Compared to the hundreds of cars that games like Gran Turismo and Forza have ballooned into, even the modding community can't offer a comparable volume on that front, but it makes up for that in the quality of many of the car liveries (or "skins") and sheer volume of race tracks. You won't find a console racing game or many PC ones that offer the volume of race tracks you can download for GT Legends (and presumably its sister games, too). At the moment, I have more than 100 tracks installed, and there are lots more available. Not only can you find different tracks from around the world, and a few made-up ones, but some classic tracks -- such as Le Mans, Spa, Monaco, Nurburgring, and others -- offer some of their various incarnations over the years. In short, I've never seen a racing game offer more opportunites to race the tracks you've always wanted to race.
The visual quality of the tracks varies, some looking plain and dated, with textures like roads and trees looking painful old in some, but pleasantly realistic in others. This is also true for the creativity of the "fantasy" tracks, some a little bland, but others achieve what they advertise very well, like the "Moorlands" track looking like it came right out of Wuthering Heights.
Besides the mods, the game offers suprisingly good-looking cars and still some of the most impressive natural-light effects, particularly at dawn and dusk and how the light looks on the cars.
The "sim" aspect is also mixed. Having never raced real cars (much less any like these old ones), I can only compare the sim authenticity to my instincts and the closest game equivalent I've played -- namely, Forza. It feels a little overcooked in parts, with certain physics seeming oversensitive, like the grass and sand feeling more like ice; some cars getting lost in a slide that renders counter (or any) steering ineffective; cars flip too easily and overreact to some contact; some cars' inability to hold a straignt  line under braking. Not only do they feel overdone, but vindictively so, too often pushing it beyond challenge into unbearable irritation. In short, while some of the over/understeer and other physics are impressive and satisfying, there seem to be just as many elements that make this as aggravating as often as it can be fun.
Perhaps some of the over-fidgityness of the cars are avoided by using a racing wheel instead of a controller, like I'm using (PS3), which also doesn't recognize any rumble/feedback.
Also vexing, on the single player side is the poor balancing of AI and grid competition, and the relative uselessness of many cars in a mixed grid. That means that the number of actually usable cars -- in terms of being able to win the races on the harder difficulties -- is limited. You are stuck with whatever car you pick for all the races in a particular "tournament", so there are really only two or three choices (at most!) to give yourself a realistic chance of winning on pro or semi-pro. I imagine you can find (or create) online one-make races, though, that would allow you to drive all these nice classic rides.
Ultimately, the well-aged visuals, the mixed but overall still adequate sim-racing experience, and the gobs of mod content (most notably, the tracks!) makes this a must-have for  serious racing game fans.

It's very hard to write a review of this game. First of all, if you do buy it, do it in a sale, but even then I don't know if it's worth it. The game is a compilation of great ideas done extremely poorly in a super-edgy manner. I'll divide this review in Gameplay and Story. I played it on hard, and I found the difficulty adequate. Never run into much problem.
Gameplay: Using the Darkness as another pair of arms is very interesting. You have to dance around the battlefield, eating hearts, to replenish health, doing executions to regain ammo or giving yourself a shield, punching with the darkness. In some ways is similar to Doom (2016). The game has different kinds of enemies, powers, and there is a very interesting mechanic where you lose your powers (and sight) at light, so enemies use flashbang or flashlights to weaken you.
But that's where the good things end. Almost all enemies have hitscan weapons, so you almost always getting hit, so you hide on cover. In later areas, using melee attacks makes you so vulnerable that it's a disservice. Dancing on the battlefield makes you dead. You end up shooting behind cover using your guns and never your powers. You end up eating hearts to replenish health only AFTER the battle is over. You can use darkness to pick up objects and throw at enemies, which is very satisfying, but after the first half, it doesn't kill in one hit, making it easier to just shoot the enemies.
There are stealth sections that, my god... They are extremely easy, don't get me wrong, but they are insultingly bad designed.
Sound design and music is awful. Nothing packs a punch. Enemies become bullet sponges. Some animations like executions are long, and the enemies reposition while you're stuck (melee enemies gets close). End boss is much easier than the earlier ones (although all boss battles are interesting, since they don't use hitscan).
Story: You have to be careful not to cut yourself with the edges. Dialogue is sexist and I don't have any depth. It's cringy at best. But at least the cutscenes where Jackie talks alone, and the stuff that the Darkness talks to Jackie are interesting.
Everything that happens in the story is not very interesting (aside from being a mafia-boss, but even then...), until the end I was going through the motions, being more annoyed than interested. I only finished the game because I knew it was short.
There is one thing that kinda saves it though. The parts where you start questioning reality. Hallucinations and everything, with the darkness teasing you along the way. It almost makes it worth buying the game just because of that. At some point, I wasn't certain what was reality.
I really dunno how to recommend it. Story and gameplay has much more negatives than positives. If it's cheap and you don't know what to play, well, get it. It's not terrible. It's just extremely average, or worse, with some very bad spots and a few good ones.

Space Legends puts you in the shoes of Elizabeth, a human sent on a mission on a planet to explore it. When something bad happened to her lover Steve, she's forced to espace into space where she crashes on another planet. And well, now, the countdown is activated because... a comet is coming straight at her.
The story is full of twists. I never expected to crash on the planet that was supposed to be destroyed soon. Also, while there are some plotholes, I can't complain. I mean, you're in an advanced base, then into a town that looks like being in a steampunk environnmenent, yet looking more like medieval and then in a destroyed city that is similar to a human city. So, I can't say that there is a problem in the graphics.
The problem lies in the fact that you don't know where to go. I mean, you know what to find but you don't know where. Despite the map, in casual, showing you where you have to go, sometimes, there is no indication. NO INDICATION! Because every scene isn't shown on the map, that's why! The kitchen or the princess's room aren't shown for example.
And while I could do the majority of the puzzles, I've to skip some. Or I didn't understood what it needed from me, or I didn't see something because it wasn't clear or it was too "huge" like the scale in the tower with all these weights. And I found a terrible problem with the mold puzzle. I mean, I tried to put the item needed on it but it didn't work. I had to zoom on the chest in reality to find some mold on the wall like on the main screen. Why zooming when you can already do the work like that? The HO scenes aren't difficult, though it would have been great to have a better idea than put the text in black with effects. I had an hard time to read.
Space Legends isn't bad. It's just suffering from the puzzles. Only recommended to the hardcore gamers. I wish you had a middle ground button, because the game is barely passing the positive review (I enjoyed it - that's why I put a thumb up).

Space Legends is a gorgeous, but lifeless, uninteresting hidden object game; a typical bundle fodder.
Space Legends: At the Edge of the Universe is the only game created by Russian indie developer Red Hedgehog. It promises a thrilling sci-fi adventure on a faraway planet in the form of a hidden object game. And it is true.
For the first twenty minutes.
After that you suddenly find yourself in a medieval kingdom, where you need to save the life of a princess. Doesn’t sound too science fiction? It isn’t. Even though the plot eventually realises this mistake, by then it is so hopelessly uninteresting you barely recognise that it ended in a three-second cut-scene.
As a hidden object game, it is just… generic: generic hidden object scenes with mediocre amount of items and stunning visuals, generic casual game puzzles with low difficulty and long completion times.
If you happen to bump into this title in a bundle, it may be worth a try for its graphics, but otherwise you could spend 2-3 hours on better activities.

The writing in this game is fantastic and hilarious, the narration by Danny Wallace reminds me of Little Big Planet for all of the right reasons, and the gameplay reminds me of the fantastic puzzler Lost Vikings in a number of ways. Thomas Was Alone is a reminder to modern gamers that graphics are not what make a game great. That being said, the minimalistic graphic style that this game has actually isn't all that minimalistic, and its polish adds to the charm.
Pick this game up (at a sale if you don't like the price) and enjoy a relaxing puzzler with witty banter driving you to play it to completion. It's really cool, surprisingly so.

In terms of the quality of this PC port, it's honestly outstanding and feels even better to play it on PC than it did on console all those years ago. The gameplay is truly classic with it's bullet-time mechanics and movement feeling almost like a mecha-anime-dark-souls kind of deal. The difficulty, at least for me, is similar to that of DOOM whereas the standard difficulty is not unnecessarily hard but still poses a challenge.
What holds this game back are the problems with its story. Yes, going into a game like this, one shouldn't expect much of an intriguing story to follow a game praised for its arcady action, but what is disappointing is how much potential there was given the setting and scenario presented.
It's largely about a war between Russia and the U.S., with the player taking control of an advanced robotic suit to be deployed alongside U.S. Soldiers. This also takes place on a centrifuge-like colony floating out in space, full of different railways, dams, and all sorts of cool buildings. The soldiers you accompany, one character in particular, are all about getting the job done, no matter the cost, which leads to conflicting ideals between the two leads.
Given all these components, the story sounds interesting enough, right? Well, unfortunately, this story is taken on too many wrong turns, with certain cutscenes being entirely unimportant because the characters aren't given enough to them. By the end of the game, the script pretends that the player has built some sort of relationship with all the other characters, but for their time spent together there was no emotional payoff. The missions seem to follow in these footsteps as well, the context of each level being often unclear. The player will find themselves meandering through the colony, sometimes feeling like just another pair of boots on the ground, and sometimes feeling like their objective is something greater. It's unclear even by the end which one it is as all the time spent journeying through the colony didn't build to much by the end.
I wish I could say that the awesome boss fights and stylish gameplay made up for the poor story, but occasionally even the gameplay slows down for areas that you feel should have dialogue, but don't. This holds it back from being its best, and I'll have to give it a 7.5/10. However, if you're not easily distracted by story and just want a shooter that spices things up with its gameplay, then I still have to recommend this.

All that said I love this game. A lovely way to spend a couple of hours and I would recommend to all.

At first glimpse, this is simple platform game where you'll guide 4-angled heroes from point A to point B, where each hero has different jump ability. Each level will be played with different number of heroes where you'll need to combine their jumping abilities in order to pass obstacles. Funny thing is, this game has an interesting story which is narated during gameplay. Every hero-object has its name (for example, main character is called Thomas) and there're different relationships between them.
Game is short but fun, worthy to be completed.

The narration was catchy and amusing, the puzzles were fun and remained fresh throughout each stage, and the pacing was brilliant. But most of all, the level of emotional connection that I found myself developing for these wonderful, brightly colored polygons, left me in awe. “Thomas was alone” is a tremendous boon for not only the field of gaming, but for storytelling as a whole. I cannot recommend this game enough.
Update (11-2016)
I'm glad to find that even as time passes, this has proven to be a game that becomes somewhat like a form of comfort food. I've never seen a game get so much depth out of such limited assets.

Do you like platformers? Do you like puzzles? How about using your brain to actually play a game? What about good writing.. do you like that? Ok. Give Thomas Was Alone a try. Clocking in at around 3-4 hours, this is a great game to spend a few nights in. A great minimalist aesthetic and some of the best music I've ever heard in a game.

Guitarcade (the "game" section of the game) is a great way to develop your technique (harmonics, chords, scales, etc) while not becoming bored by dull and repetitive exercises.
Don't let veteran guitar-snobs discourage you from using this wonderful program.  Lessons from a professional are 20-60 dollars an hour (TX); this game plus the cable is about 84 dollars after tax with an approximate lesson/practice time of 100-1000 hours.
You also get to enter for a chance to win an Epiphone Les Paul guitar, which is an added bonus.
Check out the system requirements and shoot for the recommended specifications to avoid any tragic lag while playing.

I have previously enjoyed the dark souls series as well as games like Monster hunter. this game is perfect to scratch that particular itch. The combat is (for the most part) fluid and fun, without being so complex as to exclude novices. There are sparks of stunning design in this game that make it truly unique; such as the indescribable feeling i get after winning a 4 v 1 encounter. There are issues however; those being gear issues, difficulty in tackling multiple enemies, and most importantly, terrible connection issues.
The problem with gear in games like these is that if you are picking this game up now, most players encountered will have such powerful gear as to stack the deck further against you. The benefits of this gear supposedly is countered by downsides; but good luck consistently taking down a player that gets revenge every 4 hits. This gear only applies during certain matches, but the non-gear score game modes are sparcely populated at best. In short, while not impossible; the deck is heavily stacked against you until you put lots of time into the game.
The game excels in 1 v 1 combat, and even works rather well aginst multiple attackers sometimes; but certain characters are infuriating in multiple encounters. The strategic combat somewhat breaks down when one of your attakers is capable of completely immobilising you even through revenge.
These are small niggles that somewhat spoil the game for me, but you may not find is an issue. The one issue that truly breaks this game is the atrocious connection issues. i write this review after i have just had 12 consecutive disconnects from matches. given the 10-15 minutes taken to que up each match, the majority of time that i have put into this game is in waiting for a match, before being cut off. There is continued developments and additions to this game, but none of them fix the connection. It doesen't matter that there are 2 new characters and new rare types of gear if you cant even finish a match. i really enjoy this game but i will not continue to play it. if you enjoy waiting for 15 minutes before getting 3 minutes of brilliant action and then being thrown out of the game with no progress then this is for you. If you want to actually play a game that you buy, then do not buy it.

English review (polski jak zawsze, niżej)
Watching the Never Alone's ending credits I realized how much I am grateful for growing up during the 90s. Not for the bragging rights though. While many people criticize this game for clumsy and irritating controls (and not without a reason I must admit) I have seen the early platforming games with barely minimal physics and collision model inferior to what can be created in 20 minutes with the help of contemporary tools like GameMaker or Clickteam fusion. Truth be told, while I've seen much worse, Never Alone controls rather slow and switching between the game's two protagonists can be frustrating - especially in the final chapters of the game where the time limits are introduced. Consequently, if you are looking for a platform game with tight and responsive controls there are plenty better titles out there on Steam - the new Rayman games, Hell Yeah, Knytt Underground, the Shantae series or Odallus just to name the first few that come to mind.
With that out of our way, how about some reasons to actually give Never Alone a try? First of all, while technologically rather simple, the graphics - aesthetically - are pretty charming. That is if you like glaciers and various shades of blue, and even then Ori and his Blind Forest beat Never Alone effortlessly. Music on the other hand is enjoyable and perfectly fits the game's mood and tone.
Having mentioned that, the game is saturated to the brim with the folklore. The characters' designs , cutscenes resembling animated paintings, unlockable insights into the native Alaskan culture and beliefs or the storyteller narrating the entire adventure in the Iñupiaq language (accompanied by the subtitles of your choosing) - they make the entire game feel more like an interactive folk tale or fable.
The gameplay and challenges are surprisingly varied and ( while only about three hours long) the game stays fresh and entertaining for the entire time. The special mention goes to the final two boss battles - or, boss puzzles, to be more precise. Shame the entire experience is hampered by the, above mentioned, controls.
Long story short, I believe Never Alone deserves a chance, but definitely not at the original pricetag. It feels too short and clumsy for that. On the final note : if you enjoy the folklore games, may I suggest getting familiar with the Year Walk - also a folk - inspired game available here on Steam. Only much, much darker and more evil. Also, cheaper.
Polska recenzja:
Oglądając zakończenie Never Alone zdałem sobie sprawę jak bardzo się cieszę z faktu że dorastałem w latach 90tych. Podczas gdy wielu ludziom przeszkadza niezdarna mechanika tej gry (i trzeba przyznać, jest coś na rzeczy...), ja widziałem wczesne platformery posiadające ledwie konieczne minimum fizyki i model kolizji gorszy niż to co obecnie można zrobić w 20 minut w GameMakerze albo Clickteam Fusion. Dzięki temu, przez większość czasu Never Alone nie irytowało mnie przesadnie. Trzeba jednak przyznać że szybkość z jaką dwójka bohaterów reaguje na komendy gracza mogłaby być lepsza – szczególnie w końcowych rozdziałach gdzie gra wprowadza limity czasowe na pokonywanie przeszkód. Jeżeli więc do czerpania radości z gry potrzebujesz szybkiej i precyzyjnej mechaniki, jest pełno lepszych gier na Steamie – wszystkie Raymany, Hell Yeah, Knytt Underground, seria Shantae czy Odallus – to tylko kilka które przychodzą na myśl.
Najgorsze z głowy. To może jednak warto dać Never Alone szansę? Pierwszym argumentem za jest grafika – z estetycznego punktu widzenia potrafi być naprawdę czarująca. To znaczy jeżeli lubisz lodowce i szeroką gamę odcieni błękitu, ale nawet wtedy Ori'emu z jego ślepym lasem może skoczyć. Muzyka za to świetnie wpasowuje się w kolejne rozdziały gry i pomaga budować nastrój.
Skoro już o tym mowa: twórcy stawiają na klimat. Never Alone jest wypełnione po brzegi i dokładnie nasączone gęstym folklorem natywnych ludów Alaski. Widać to w projektach postaci, po przerywnikach filmowych stylizowanych na animowane malowidła skalne, nawet narracja prowadzona jest w języku Iñupiaq(od początku do końca, z napisami w jednym z 16 języków – w tym polskim). Wszystko to sprawia wrażenie uczestniczenia w interaktywnej opowieści, czy może baśni – jeżeli lubicie takie klimaty, będzie to spory plus.
Sama rozgrywka jest ciekawa a stawiane przed graczem wyzwania zróżnicowane (choć gra kończy się w mniej więcej trzy godziny, więc gdyby w tak krótkim czasie nudziła nie było by chyba większego sensu w ogóle zawracać sobie nią głowy. Z drugiej strony jeżeli graliście w Tulpę...). Szczególnie świetne są dwa ostatnie pojedynki (czy raczej łamigłówki umożliwiające pokonanie...) z bossami. Szkoda jedynie że wspomniane wcześniej sterowanie znacząco je utrudnia.
Podsumowując; Never Alone zasługuje żeby dać jej szansę, choć zdecydowanie nie za cenę 15 euro. Jest na to zdecydowanie za krótka i momentami irytująca. Jeszcze jedno: Jeżeli lubicie gry eksplorujące obyczaje i tradycje zerknijcie na Year Walk, dostępną na Steamie, podobnie śnieżną, podobnie folkową, podobnie krótką ale dużo, dużo mroczniejszą i bardziej krwawą grę. Również tańszą.

What a beautiful culture.
Not only is this a charming and interesting game based on the Iñupiat people, but included are “insights” that you can collect which unlock various clips from a documentary with said people.
I played through the game first and watched the insights afterwards and although I didn’t really fully understand the game, it was very enjoyable to hear these people speak so passionately about their culture and their love for their way of life.
Whoever made this game put a lot of love and respect into what they were trying to teach us about and I actually love the fact that the documentary side to this was included. You can tell that this game was made to be as true to the culture it was portraying as possible.
I played this game as a local co-op and honestly can’t really imagine trying to play this on my own. Given this games theme of community, companionship and togetherness, I don’t think it would have been as fun to me playing on my own.
The music and narrative is great and the graphics are beautiful. I especially like that the narrative was in the native tongue and translated with subtitles, as to give it a more genuine feeling. The general glow and contrast is really nice and with all these things together it gave off a nice atmosphere.
There are puzzle elements to this game and it’s at these parts especially that I can’t imagine playing on my own. Me and my boyfriend had to co-ordinate and get certain timings right to be successful in some of the puzzles. Although they weren’t all that difficult, they still take some planning and quick execution.
As an overall, the game itself I can’t say was one of my favourites or particularly powerful to me, but I love everything that was put into this game and having those insights definitely redeemed it for me.
Last of all, achievements. Unfortunately this is a game that you actually need the DLC to be able to 100%. Apart from that, it’s an easy one to complete. It took us around 4 hours to get through and is a fairly enjoyable game.
All in all, this is a beautifully charming game and if you enjoy “for the experience” kind of games I think this is definitely worth trying. If you want something with a deep, plot twisting, life changing story, or something with crazy mechanics or puzzles, than you are better off elsewhere.
TL;DR : Based on a beautiful and interesting culture, a (best in) local co-op game with beautiful graphics and a short unlockable documentary on the people it’s based around. An easy 100% and a fairly enjoyable game.

Yea, this is an okay game. It's a decent 3 hour plus game. It passses but it is not an AAA game. It is basically a co-op/single player platformer where you try to solve various jumping puzzles in pairs. You will use a little girl and her snow fox companion. You will find that it is reminescent of games like Brothers : The Tale of Two Sons, Wolfe, The Cave and Max : The Tale of Brotherhood. Unity 3D is a common tool for games like this, there is a common style.
The main gist of Never Alone is the tale of a young Inuit girl and her snow fox trying to figure out why their village was burned down. In their quest for answers, you will meet an Owl Man who has lost his drum to little people, get lost in the stomach of a whale, run away from hungry polar bears all while avoiding ice floes and strong blizzard winds. Your Snow Fox is in tune with nature and will guide friendly Spirits to aid you in your journey. However, not every Spirit is kind and you will face Spirit People that grip you and send you to your doom.
During your journey, you will discover that the perpetrator who burned your village is a horrible man who is able to toss fire and he burned your village down whilst searching for something. That something is oddly your magic bola which fires an infinite number of shiny blue bolas. Watch him snap the neck of your snow fox and keep on watching to see what happens after that. I'll not spoil this part for you.
The ice giant and his adze story is very interesting to playthrough and for those of you who prefer a more difficult game, Foxtales gives you the much needed challenge.
Conclusion? This is a must try. Remember to watch the cultural insights with interviews with actual Inuit people.

WASD keys, L-CTRL, Q and Spacebar. I play this game with 1 hand. The only time you need to use your other hand is to aim the bola with your mouse.
3. Owl Videos/Cultural Insights
You get to view videos of another culture that is rarely talked about. This is very interesting. THe videos about the Inuit are very high quality and are worth watching.
4. Interesting Stories
Beautiful to read about. E.g. The Owl Man, The Ice Giant and his Adze
5. Wind Jumping
I like the part where you have to jump with the wind. It's so much cooler.

Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege is unlike any other military shooter game. There's no real campaign (just situations, but they're more like tutorials), there's no character bond, there's no linear gameplay, and there's no respawns. The main basis of this game is it's multiplayer servers. You join a game with nine other people, making a five versus five situation. There are three game modes (randomly chosen): bomb, hostage, and secure the area. Each different situation calls for a different strategy and/or skill set. Some operators (the characters you unlock to use) are great for bomb and secure the area situations, but not great for hostage situations and vice versa. People either play the objective or they make it a team deathmatch game, but either way, it's still fun and exciting. Every game is different from the last because you're playing with new people every time and everyone has their own strategy, their own technique, and their own specialties. After each round, the teams switch from Attackers to Defenders, each with their own operators. Overall, it's one of the most fun shooter games I've ever played, and I've played almost all the Call of Duty's and Battlefield's. The main reason is, you have to think before you shoot, you have to strategize, you have to communicate, and you have to be fast because once you die in a mulitplayer match, you don't respawn until the next round.
I'd happily give this game a solid 8 out of 10, the only reason for docking off two points is because I can confidently say that at least 50% of the gaming community is negative, putting a crack in the once solid gaming community. But if you have a few friends to play with and you don't need to listen to the open mic with loud music in the background or the level 50 player who thinks he's the best player in the universe yell at you when you get sniped, then you'll be fine.
Nevertheless, I'd still recommend this game to anyone with patience for the game and the community.

(This review is copied from my Overlord Raising Hell review, which is the same game plus added missions)
(My playtime on this shows low, but I played the Raising Hell edition for 40 hours.)
Glee is the word that comes to mind when I think of this game. Two words would be "gleefully mischievous." Imps and goblins usually annoy me - like the sidekick in The Darkness II - but these little fellows manage to be endearing.
Anyway, this game has its tongue firmly pressed to its cheek, in a good way.
It parodies LOTR - except you are playing as pseudo-Sauron, sweeping your minions across halfling villages and elven forests with an evil grin on your face.
You (the Overlord) are slow and lumbering, but your minions - whom you can guide with an invisible hand or more precisely assign tasks to - are fast and fluid.
It's sort of open world - open enough to let you revisit previous (respawning) locations to replenish your gold and Souls.
Negatives: Lots of backtracking. No way to sprint or speed up your Overlord character. And no mini-map of any kind. These three problems are a big no-no in an open world game.

Survarium is a post-apocalyptic FPS with RPG elements and character progression.
You have a level, and a faction level (I will get to that later). Per normal level up you gaine one experience point that you can put into the current 3 skilltrees that determin your weapon handling, your thoughness and your knowledge and resistence to anomalys (yes, similar to the ones in S.T.A.L.K.E.R (I will get to them later)).
Ok, now to the factions:
The game has a progression system that revolvs around 4 factions:
The Scavengers, that are the hunter/sniper faction with mashine pistols, compact rifles and sniper rifles, but only with light to medium armor(your gear won´t take a lot of hits, but you are faster so be sneaky).
The Black Market, that are short range badasses in leather with a gang/biker vibe. They mostly use western weapons and seem to have role of raiders. (they have quite good armors and shotguns so go guns blazing).
Renessaince Army, they have heavy weapons and armor, which interferes with their mobility. So if you enjoy to be a hard hitting, but slowly moving tank, these guys are for you.
The Fringe Settlers, the Shaman/tribic people that have good array of  mp´s and shotguns but very few assault rifles. They also seem to go for many russian sub sonic rifles like the VSK-94 or the GLORIOUS VSSK "Vikhlop" sniper. They use anomalys and anomaly resistant gear to be able to use both in a way the other factions can´t (having an extraordinairy amount of anomalies that enhance your stats, or can be thrown like a grenade, their armors can also grant almost or even complete imunity to anomalies, but again can't take that many hits).
Ok, now that we covered the factions, we can move on to the price model this game has:
This game is not pay2win. It is pay2skip, since all weapons (ecxept the Barrett, but that should get fixed) are the same one that you can grind. The only diffrence is, that the "premium" weapons have camos and all attachments unlocked, with normal guns you have kill to unlock attachments).
So you can enjoy every facette of this game without spending money on it.
For the hackers: in the lates patch (0.44) Battle-eye was introduced, so there should be no more hackers around.

I give this game a "recommend", but only if you're a fan of the hidden object & puzzle game genres.  This game has far more variety of puzzles than just hidden objects, most of which I quite enjoyed.  (I had to skip one due to a very poor control scheme.)  Hints were available frequently enough that I didn't keep beating my head against a wall waiting for them, but also weren't often necessary.  And if you try to use a hint and there's nothing left to do in the room, it'll just point you out without using up the hint (I completely missed one exit towards the end of the game until a hint pointed the way).
The plot is surprisingly complex for a game of this type, although if you're coming from most other genres you'll probably find it lacking.  Part 1 is a pretty straightforward "get off the planet" story, with some really weird headscratchers (why would you hide a piece of your ride's keys
a dangerous fan?).  Shortly after you fly off, you land on a medieval planet, get captured... and soon find a piece of high technology.  Figuring out
the discrepancy exists is quite intriguing.  Parts 2, 3, and 4 all take place on this second planet, and are distinguished by having some of the old rooms shut off and gaining access to new parts.  The overlap between each part ensures a nice continuity.  Again, this is all in comparison to other puzzle games - if I was playing a RPG or a classic point-and-click adventure, I'd have given up long since.
However, it's clear that the game was translated by someone for whom English is not a native language.  Some of the hidden object clues were entirely obscure (when you want a "comb", you have to find a hairbrush, for example), some of the dialog was awkward, and there are places where sentences run together.  It's never impossible to figure out what was meant, but it's jarring.
Overall, I enjoyed the ~3 hours I spent beating this, and I don't regret buying the bundle that I bought it in.

I need a "meh" button instead of just "Yay or nay".
If it's cheap, sure, get it. It won't hurt you or anything, but you might want to prepare a walkthrough to help you when you're stumped.
The game isn't that bad, it has very positive features, but the bad parts are just too bad.
Decent voice-acting (instead of none) would improve it so much...
The ending sequence is VERY quick - I think there is a travelling scene that takes longer than the whole ending.
The story is not exactly epic either, it's nice and if you view it as a "not everyone is a hero that battles unimaginable monsters", it's OK.
It got better after the research station, IMO. At first it was too much "Oh no, I can't do that. That was Steves job." all the time. (Which I'd accept as realistic - if one is a medic/botanist, one doesn't necessarily tinker around in engine rooms. But reading it every few clicks gets annoying. Besides, in the end she is doing all that stuff anyway.)
A very positive feature of this game is the map which shows you which "rooms" you have been or can go to, and even indicates where you still have work to do. Very handy - instead of clicking half a dozen times to retract your steps, you open the map and are instantly in the other room.
Too bad it sometimes doesn't indicate rooms where you have things to find.
The biggest problem is that many of the puzzles are - at least to me - ungraspable. I have no idea how I should have come to these conclusions, or why I would do that in the first place.
At least once I ended up in a puzzle without knowing why - I wanted to click something different, suddenly I'm in a puzzle getting a quest item as reward. Where from? Why? No idea. I guess the character bet against an NPC, but we're not shown.
A few times the character knows more than it should - saying things like "This is on the list" when we don't yet have the list.
Fortunately, all the puzzles and games can be skipped.
The music is nice and the graphics are quite pretty - they're creating an interesting environment, too bad you don't know much about it.
So, as I said - when cheap, grab it. At worst you waste a few hours, but all in all I found it quite enjoyable.

I want to love this game but it won't let me.  Numerous bugs, bad UI, rare crashes, half baked ground combat.  This game is unfit to be called a finished product.  A good beta maybe.  Needs polish, lots of polish.
You can tell that love went into this but it did not come with an equal measure of design skill.  Fleets will frequently overshoot their targets without engaging/parking.  Ground battles will sometime bug out, switching control of you and the AI's forces.  Real time space battles are unforgivably disorganized and nearly impossible to command in any meaningful way without 10+ minutes of pre battle formation micro management that you have to do every-single-battle.  Save your formation?  Nope, F U.  Simply clicking on a ship and telling it to "fly here" is absurdly difficult when large fleets are present.  Planetary production Governors?  Nope.  All micro.  Insta scroll game text with a click?  Nope.  Get used to watching the letters crawl across the screen like a legless orphan eating crayons.  Enemy transports will bug out in/near wormholes, becoming permanent, untargetable fixtures until their race is annihilated.  The music is awful and may as well not exist.
In it's defense, smaller space battles are fun and pleasing to the eye.  The random events/missions scattered about the galaxy are fun and interesting.  Ship designing is lots of fun but probably poorly balanced.  A colorful cast of aliens, even the 1 world minor races, Art and writing fluff did their jobs at least.
Really, if everything worked properly and had a decent UI, I'd say StarDrive2 is slightly above average.  But in this state?  Unacceptable.

Yea, this is an okay game. It's a decent 3 hour plus game. It passses but it is not an AAA game. It is basically a co-op/single player platformer where you try to solve various jumping puzzles in pairs. You will use a little girl and her snow fox companion. You will find that it is reminescent of games like Brothers : The Tale of Two Sons, Wolfe, The Cave and Max : The Tale of Brotherhood. Unity 3D is a common tool for games like this, there is a common style.
The main gist of Never Alone is the tale of a young Inuit girl and her snow fox trying to figure out why their village was burned down. In their quest for answers, you will meet an Owl Man who has lost his drum to little people, get lost in the stomach of a whale, run away from hungry polar bears all while avoiding ice floes and strong blizzard winds. Your Snow Fox is in tune with nature and will guide friendly Spirits to aid you in your journey. However, not every Spirit is kind and you will face Spirit People that grip you and send you to your doom.
During your journey, you will discover that the perpetrator who burned your village is a horrible man who is able to toss fire and he burned your village down whilst searching for something. That something is oddly your magic bola which fires an infinite number of shiny blue bolas. Watch him snap the neck of your snow fox and keep on watching to see what happens after that. I'll not spoil this part for you.
The ice giant and his adze story is very interesting to playthrough and for those of you who prefer a more difficult game, Foxtales gives you the much needed challenge.
Conclusion? This is a must try. Remember to watch the cultural insights with interviews with actual Inuit people.
1. Wondrous Imagination
I love reading the different races in the game, they are so imaginative. E.g. Owl Face Man
2. Simple to Pick UP
WASD keys, L-CTRL, Q and Spacebar. I play this game with 1 hand. The only time you need to use your other hand is to aim the bola with your mouse.
3. Owl Videos/Cultural Insights
You get to view videos of another culture that is rarely talked about. This is very interesting. THe videos about the Inuit are very high quality and are worth watching.
4. Interesting Stories
Beautiful to read about. E.g. The Owl Man, The Ice Giant and his Adze
5. Wind Jumping
I like the part where you have to jump with the wind. It's so much cooler.
6. Foxtales
Lovely higher difficulty levels. The story of the Giant Rat was beautiful.
1. Repetitive Platforms
Some parts of the game are repeated, like a cut and paste. You jump on a ledge, move and jump on a ledge. This same sequence is repeated later in the game except with a different skin.
2. Short Playtime
Finished it in 3 hours.
3. The Bad Guy looks like Nigel Thornberry from the Wild Thornberry's
I like Nigel Thornberry, why is he the villain?

Let’s start out with two points:-
For the basis of this discussion,
defines ‘simulation’ as: -
The representation of the behaviour or characteristics of one system through the use of another system, especially a computer program designed for the purpose.
It defines ‘arcade’ as:-
An establishment, public area, etc., containing games of a mechanical and electronic type, as pinball and video games, that can be played by a customer for a fee.

Despite the odd controversy over the banning a few months back, this game is pretty good and stays very true to the movies. I went and watched the Friday the 13th movies after buying this game and in many cases the movies and maps are nearly 100% identical.
Currently, there are three maps, 8 Jasons with unique traits, and 10 counselors with different stats. Maps sometimes changes up one or two cabin locations that spawn, everything in a cabin drawer is randomized with certain objects spawning within a certain distance of a goal, and the game objectives spawn random within 2-3 different locations. Once you have played a lot you will mostly know where to check when you are looking for something specific.
Players are randomly chosen to be Jason out of a 8 player lobby. The 7 counselors must then find a way to escape by fixing a 4 seater or 2 seater car, fixing a two seater boat, calling the cops and waiting for them to arrive then escaping through one of two exits, or flat out living the full 20 minutes. Jason has enormous power and can't be killed by normal means. Counselors must kite, evade, or delay Jason so they can get the objectives done.
Friday the 13th has this uncanny ability to set up situations that make your heart pound. Risk and reward is huge in this game. If you find the gas right away near the 4 door, do you try and put it in before Jason shows up or do you lay low and deal with any traps he puts down? If you fix the car do you stop to try and save someone or do you get out of there before Jason appears and wrecks the car? Every game feels very different even though the maps don't change much. Maybe one game everyone works together and speaks english to coordinate. Other games no one talks and you get hunted down one by one. Maybe this game it's a bunch of Russians but they know enough words to work with you.
On that note, the community is either hit or miss. Many players label themselves as "Jason players" so if they aren't Jason they leave the game leaving the counselors short handed. Other players leave the game when Jason grabs them depriving the Jason player of Experience which is used to buy things. They recently patched out team killing, but that was a huge issue with many players just running up to someone else with a shotgun and killing them without a word spoken. Team killing carries a 1,000 exp loss, but this didn't dissuade many players. In other instances they would hit you just enough to leave you weak and slow moving, then run off.
Pros:
Exciting Gameplay
Good variations between Jason's and Counselors
Proximity based voice chat, improved with getting a walkie talkie in game
Effective Risk/Reward situations
Game is being updated often
Cons:
One Jason is locked behind a DLC only made available for kickstarters. Many people consider Savini Jason the best Jason which makes him a paywall and timewall pay to win.
Maps get old and predictable when there is only three.
Do you get one Hour of gameplay per $6 paid?: Yes even at full price.
Ease of 100%: Very Hard. Some are luck based. Like killing a counselor hiding in a tent as Jason. There's no telling when the time you are randomly chosen to be Jason will be the time you stumble onto someone hiding in a tent. There are also very rare cassette tapes that only spawn once per game if at all.

And I was not disappointed with this, it was in depth and definitely hard hitting where it counted and the only aspect of the game that I knew about when going into it, was the collection of information on people.
First things first, and quite briefly because there isn’t much to say about the graphics of the game. It is based on a user interface that you interact with, whilst it does emulate the use of an actual browser and its contents, it is very clean and takes the realistic nature away from it with its low poly style photos. This was a nice feature as I could focus more on what the story was offering than what the characters looked like and if the modeling of said characters worked with the rest of the interface. The only time there was animation was in the first cut scene where you were introduced to the game, however, this could be either 2D or 3D with flat colours and a low poly style to keep in with the theme. The only thing I was somewhat disappointed with was the fact that there was very little camera work, the game revolves around being monitored everywhere and it is constantly referenced to that cameras are a big thing, yet we do not experience this even though it was shown that they were capable of doing this. It did not, however, subtract from the story that there weren’t any cameras, it just would have been a pretty cool feature.
The graphics made it easy to navigate around the game, making the mechanics for the game very simple as you just had to click and drag certain pieces of information into a data bank, it was simple and easy to get to grips with, it just meant reading and doing a lot of problem solving. That, however, was the allure of the game, filling in the pieces and finding out just what was going on. Due to the dragging of information, you could affect the outcome of the game depending on what pieces of information you decided to let through, this was the coolest feature, I love multiple endings.

I'd describe this as a very niche game, if you're into point and click, this is perfect for you. The entire game is presented to you through the Orwell system, where you look into people's data and collect things on them. The game rarely leaves you at a point where you don't know what to do, as important information is highlighted for you, whether this is insane hand holding or reasonable is up to you, I think it's a good thing to have some guidance as to do next.
The story revolves around a government called simply "The Nation" controlled by "The Party(real creative, devs.)" creating a system known as "ORWELL" after a bombing. Along with that, The Party had recently passed something known as "The Freedom Bill" which gives police the right to arrest, interrogate, and detain simply on suspicion of a crime. Basically, The Nation is an authortarian government, it is obviously not as authortarian as Oceania is in 1984, as there is still plenty of resistance to the government, but it is pretty powerful.
You play as an investigator recently hired by The Nation, living outside of it's borders, tasked to collect information on individuals suspected of the bombing to bring them to justice. Throughout the game, there are several points where you can either choose to be defiant of ORWELL and enter embellished or false information into the system, or choose the blunt option. There are five episodes, and they are all very gripping, the game can actually be reletively creepy at some points as well.
There are multiple endings, as well, which is cool. I won't spoil anything though.

This is a really neat combination of Adventure and Hidden Object games. Most of the time you're adventuring with punctuated periods of Hidden Object finding. The Hidden Object stuff is better than pixel-hunting as things are usually out in the open. When they're not, it's because you have to perform a series of actions to create the necessary object. (e.g. load a pistol with a bullet to fire it at a target so that you can pick up a "target with a bullet hole".)
Perhaps the most interesting aspect is that some of the objects you find are important parts of the plot. This is MUCH more satisfying than your classic pixel-hunt nonsense that ultimately made adventure games so unpopular.
The story is chick-flick/romance clap-trap for teenage girls and lonely women, but if you can look past it you'll have some fun. You start in a space setting (fun!) but eventually move to a medieval setting after you "crash land". Again, just chillax, don't take it too seriously, and you'll have a good time.

Other than the basic information listed above, here is some useful information I gathered about this game:
•	The Steam version was censored in November of 2015.
•	In January of 2016 both the Steam and non-Steam versions of the game were updated.
•	 In March of 2016 future updates were announced for the game on Steam. The future updates were said to included content such as new maps, new costumes, improved “parkour” even a School Life simulator update.
However, I own both versions of the game, and as of the date of this review none of these updates have been implemented in either the Steam or non-steam versions of the game. You should consider that these updates are behind schedule before buying this game.
I think the game is fun and the idea, albeit perhaps not the implementation, is cute. The game has also gained attention for being a victim of censorship. So I think the game was worth the buy, its cheap and has the potential for improvement. Just don’t expect anything phenomenal, or time consuming for that matter.

Somehow (I have no idea how, otherwise I'd be rich and currently making an amazing game) the developer makes you feel for the characters and understand their emotions, in a way which most games don't. You want to know what happens to Thomas and his friends, you want to make sure they're okay.
If you like what you hear, just spare a little money and you'll get to have the experience too. It also helps the developer make more great games for you to enjoy.
The developer is currently making Volume, which I look forward to with all my heart and my tingly feels.    :D

This is another game among the best I have ever played.  I have never felt more emotional attachment to a square or rectangle than I have in Thomas Was Alone.  The Narrator rivals Rucks and the narrator from the Stanley Parable.  The game weaves a beautiful story of love, sacrifice, friendship, brotherhood, betrayal and freedom told through the personalities imparted to all variations of rectangles.  The platforming itself is also excellent, and forces you to take each characters unique abilities and dimensions into consideration as you puzzle your way through the levels.  A game for the ages, and a definite buy.

It is a Master of Orion remake.
Its graphics are polished up, the combat is real time, but it all boils down to the simple fact that this is Master of Orion.
If not for the hefty price tag, I would definitely recommend this game.
Other points of concern:
Combat
The space combat is entertaining in the beginning, but becomes a chore in the late game.
With large numbers of ships, the battlefield is crowded from second one, it does not scale well over time.
The load times before and after battles make the automatic battle resolution even more tempting. But Ships do not seem to get XP from automated combat...
(Also, combat pre-load and after-load times are horribly long, even with newest Hardware)
Diplomacy
The diplomacy is really broken: It is easy to keep other empires entertained or urge them to trade stuff with you no sensible human player would ever think of trading.
The diplomacy mechanic seems superfluous to the eventual military conquest, there is no "diplomatic victory" of any sort, nor deeper mechanics known from other 4X games.

If you are looking for a real time 4X this is not one.
Diplomacy is impossible because the Ai WILL randomly want one of your planets and start hating you over time with nothing you can do about it.

When I bought this game I was initially very impressed because of some superficial resemblances in the research tree to the classic Master of Orion 2 and thought the developer was inspired by and trying to make a worthy successor to that game.
Now my view on the developer's intent is somewhat more cynical.
After playing the game for a while it seemd to me that much of the research tree is not well thought out and balanced but just thrown together willy-nilly with a superficial resemblance to the original MOO2.
Much of Stardrive2 strikes me this way: hastily thrown together design decisions, numbers arbitrarily plucked out of thin air and various pieces of code cobbled together with little thought of balance and overall design.
Much about the game design is astonishingly poorly thought out, such as the massive imbalance of ship design layouts between races and the huge investment in time and preparation to perform even simple espionage missions(I could conquer the entire civilization militarily in less time) as well as the incredibly overpowered Mass Driver weapon.
And let's not mention the horribly repetitive and childish ground combat.
I have put a lot of hours into this game; aspects of it are quite fun for a while.
I stuck with it as I was finding ship design interesting, even as I was hoping that the developer would address some of the game's many design flaws. However, it became apparent that the developer had little interest in doing any more than fixing some of the glaring bugs and has more or less abandoned the game's development.
Much leaves me wondering if the author ever actually sat down and played the game.
Uninstalled.

StarDrive 2 is an excellent tribute to the classic Master of Orion II. This review is based on patched version 1.1a.
A few comments:
Stability and completeness: I've played this game for 40 hours. It never crashed. All features are present and complete...I assume the "this is a beta" reviewers were playing an earlier, unpatched version, or that I simply haven't encoutered the severe bugs they have. For comparison, every Bethesda RPG I've ever played had more and worse bugs than this game, even in GotY editions, and SD 2 is a one-man-show that cost me $30 undiscounted. It's not a beta.
Space combat: emphasis in ship design is on tactics, not customizing appearance. I love this...that's why it's a MOO II tribute game. The real time combat does allow you control of targeting, movement, and some special ship abilities, but it's simple enough that you can resolve a large battle expediently...unlike MOO II. Much better tactical combat than Galciv 2 or Endless Space, with or without extensions.
Ground combat: it's a simplified variant of Heroes or Age of Wonders style combat on a grid. You can customize troop loadouts, deploy shields, etc. Early in the game there are some nice ground combat missions that give you a challenge and reward early on, but once I figured out some simple tactics I found planetary invasions a bit easy: the AI is weak here. Personally I prefer the combat grid to the dice roll that is common for combat in 4x space games, especially in the early game.
AI: Challenging, at least in the early game. I need more playthroughs on harder difficulty to assess this properly, but so far it's better than the really stupid AI in competing games, including Civ 5, etc. I suspect big publishers know the player wants to win, even if he's rubbish! I do think the AI needs some better ship designs in the late game.
I've played the following similar games: MOO II, Galactic Civilizations 2, Endless Space, Sins of a Solar Empire. I actually bought Distant Worlds: Universe at the same time as SD 2, but opted to try SD 2 first...it's a good time for 4x gamers!
