Few games are simply this beautiful; from the wonderful art style, the crimshaw cutscenes, to the voiceover in the native Inupiaq language.  Even though the original intention was to bring the culture of native Alaska to the new generation, it still feels welcoming to outsiders who want to learn more about the peoples and lifestyle.  You are essentially playing a fairy tale.  That being said, the controls do leave a little to be desired, with some sections of the game bordering on the maddening.  But that is easily forgiven when you feel the satisfaction of solving a particularly difficult section.
However, what is easly my favorite part is actually the collectables.  Rather than having chests, or items that grant in-game bonuses, the collectables are a series of owls which, when found, unlock a documentary clip.  Those documentary clips serve as the perfect companion piece to the content of the game, featuring interviews and explorations of life in the far north of the United States.  It remains one of the few games that made me want to collect everything.
As a side-note, if you want to read more tales from the Inupiaq, as well as read the one credited with inspiring the game, I highly suggest checking out "The Dall Sheep Dinner Guest: Inupiaq Narratives of Northwest Alaska" by Wanni W. Anderson.  It is a collection of tales by native storytellers, including Wille Goodwin Sr., whose family were involved with the creation of "Never Alone."

From the man responsible for RE & RE 4 comes Vanquish, a fast paced action game that mixes elements of third person shooter and beat em' up.
Vanquish is a scifi game that tells the story (or should I say, long streak of cliches?) of DARPA op Sam Gideon, who along a future US army will try to retake a recently captured space station by the Russians. The story has a very 80's premise, full of cheesy lines, short but lots of fun.
It should be noted for Platinum fans that, as always, the gameplay is the real thing for these kind of games.
+Pros:
Smooth experience: No game breaking bugs nor inconsisten framerate (the infamous framerate damage bug has also been fixed).
Solid mix of genres: This game might remind you of Gears of War, don't be fooled. This game is not trying to be a third-person cover shooter, but a space marine version of Dante with robot instead of demons.
Cheap: For 20 dollars
-Cons/personal ranting or nitpicking:
Too short: You can finish this game in less than four hours.
Few extras: There's not much to unlock in this game besides the challenges and a god mode, so anyone looking for lots of content might be disappointed.
No multiplayer: People looking for a competitive experience might want to look elsewhere.
Also it must be noted that this PC port is superior to the Xbox 360 version because of higher framerate (Xbox 360 version was 30 fps capped as far as I know).
In conclusion, this game is very recommended for gamers who want to try a different kind of shooter, Platinum fans or gamers who like single player experiences.

First of all, thank you Sega for bringing Platinum's Vanquish to Steam; I hope other publishers do the same with their games. Now the
Bad:
- The writing (story and script) is poor. Basic story about America and Russia with some double crossing; it's OK, but not at the level a single player focused game should be. The script is just laughable at times. I felt no real reason or motivation to fight the baddies due to the lack of a compelling story.
- There is very little character development (a reflection of poor writing) masked by moments of character comradery.
- Lack of enemy and gameplay variety.
Good:
- Combat that will make the back of your eyes balls hurt and want more; it's so awesome to watch Sam slide around eliminating baddies in AR mode; or even punch them to a pulp!
- Game mechanics and UI are on par for the game's style. Platinum's game design skills are second to none, and it's present in every aspect of Vanquish's high octane experience! The ease of leveling weapons is perfect, with no need for a complicated UI to take you out of the action. I love this!!!
- Sam's Augmented Reaction Suit (ARS) is just a masterpiece! Every bit is detail was well executed, down to the equipping of weapon; I felt empowered af.
- PC optimization is excellent; well done Platinum. I was able to play with at 60 FPS @1440p with a 980Ti on high with no issues. It can run on many entry level GPUs/PCs with respectable settings, which is a plus. Frame pacing was good as well; I'm glad it was for the fast pace action!
- The graphical fidelity is great, considering that this is an old game with reworked textures; it does have the occasional flat, brown cardboard box like look of games from the early 2000's at times.
- The interactive credits is a nice way for players to appropriate the devs, and take their frustration out; lol.
Verdict:
Please buy Vanquish; you will not regret it!

Well this has been a long time coming.
I originally planned to leave this review as a positive one but due to recent experiences with the game and some more thinking I don’t want to recommend this garbage truck on fire ploughing through an orphanage of a game.
Let’s start at the beginning. When I initially bought the game I was hyped to play it like so many others. During my first few hours of the game it was just pure enjoyment and glee. Running around frantically, darting in and out of buildings, through the door then out the window whilst on the most tense scavenger hunt of my life. All this whilst avoiding big scary hockey mask guy.
In those first few hours of the game you feel scared but joyous as you, some fat nerd with enough chins to level a skyscraper and some brown-haired bimbo race to fix a car/boat or call the police in an effort to escape.
Then you get to play as Jason for the first time and the real fun begins. Getting to grips with Jason is easy and soon you’ll be hacking down doors with an axe, a machete or even a fishing pole in hot pursuit of fear-stricken, zit-covered, play-doh faced meat-bags, cowering under beds and diving out of windows just to escape your wrath.
Unfortunately the game wears thin after the first few hours you play. You realise how little there is to do in the game. You’ve already done most things. Escaping in the car doesn’t seem appealing anymore. The terror you were once filled with upon seeing Jason has completely evaporated. Instead you find other things to do. You attack Jason with the other players, continuously stunning him in an effort to kill him (you can kill Jason, I’ll leave a link to a video telling you how to). You begin to troll your fellow counsellors by killing them or deliberately getting them killed, soon hearing a 10 year old call you a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ over voice chat as a result.
It’s worth mentioning voice chat now. In my opinion the best/worst feature of the game. Some of the people who speak in game are hilarious, role-playing as Jason and the various counsellors. Others will come up with random funny nonsense in life or death situations and some will just play Thomas the Tank Engine ear♥♥♥♥♥♥through their mic for the entirety of the match. Of course there are those who play the game seriously to try and win the game too.
I’ve never really been the one to use my mic in general but this game has encouraged me to do so and I’ve actually made a few friends through F13. However it’s not always begonias and rosebushes.
Without a single doubt this game is the worst I have ever played when it comes to receiving abuse over mic. You’ll have your fill of young children carelessly mouthing off the N-word but now and again you’ll come across that one player who really gets under your skin. But what is worse than having one player being a♥♥♥♥♥♥towards you for no reason? Having 3. I was playing a game with these 3 guys who started to spew abuse at me for no reason. Starting by making fun of my name (I did come up with it when I was 11-12 but it’s always stuck :P) then eventually graduating to more nasty insults and killing me in game for fun.
I want to say I’m all for killing other players. It can be hilarious running over a friend with a car or point-blank shooting them in the face with a shotgun and I’ve had it happen to me many times but I draw the point at harassment. The example above is only one of my accounts. I am not looking for sympathy here but I am warning you that this games community is quite toxic at times.
Technically the game could be better and that’s an understatement. The car is janky when driving it; there are still a handful of annoying exploits and Jason’s grab distance feels like it has the range of a ballistic missile half the time. The game needs some more paint and polish as the rust is already begging to bear.
If you have the patience then yes. The game will go on sale or become cheaper. It will also have more content and from a technical standpoint be improved.
I don’t believe that the game is worth the current price and there is simply not enough content to back it up.
I am not saying Friday the 13th The Game is bad but you’ll probably enjoy the more updated version in the future than the current version, although if you do feel you want to buy it now you will find some fun to be had. It’s also more fun with a mic and a friend or two.
Thank you for reading and I hope I could be of help.

I'd describe this as a very niche game, if you're into point and click, this is perfect for you. The entire game is presented to you through the Orwell system, where you look into people's data and collect things on them. The game rarely leaves you at a point where you don't know what to do, as important information is highlighted for you, whether this is insane hand holding or reasonable is up to you, I think it's a good thing to have some guidance as to do next.
The story revolves around a government called simply "The Nation" controlled by "The Party(real creative, devs.)" creating a system known as "ORWELL" after a bombing. Along with that, The Party had recently passed something known as "The Freedom Bill" which gives police the right to arrest, interrogate, and detain simply on suspicion of a crime. Basically, The Nation is an authortarian government, it is obviously not as authortarian as Oceania is in 1984, as there is still plenty of resistance to the government, but it is pretty powerful.
You play as an investigator recently hired by The Nation, living outside of it's borders, tasked to collect information on individuals suspected of the bombing to bring them to justice. Throughout the game, there are several points where you can either choose to be defiant of ORWELL and enter embellished or false information into the system, or choose the blunt option. There are five episodes, and they are all very gripping, the game can actually be reletively creepy at some points as well.
There are multiple endings, as well, which is cool. I won't spoil anything though.

This game had a lot of potential but was ruined by bad connection issues & a disgusting imballence with the hero's.
I'm wrting this review 5 days after season 2 launch. I had some fun times with this game during season 1 but i had to also deal with a lot of issues. I have been playing this game now for multiple hours (+- 300 hours) and have mained the conqueror (even after the nerf i still love this guy to death ;)). Following are top reasons why you should NOT buy this game if you know nothing about network config or just want to enjoy a fun game to relax or play casual.
***The connection issues were really bad. With proper router config I fixed my NAT so that I could be the host most of the times and have a decent connection during a match. This solved most connection issues for my & everyone in my game. But before the router config I'd get kicked 2/5 matches at random (could be at the end, middle, start of match). To this day most people still experience the same bad connection issues.
***Imballence with hero's: during revenge mode some moves of certain characters give now a knock down ability which gives a free downed heavy on opponent. Some could even spam link this untill you are death. Still possible with a lot characters today. Some characters have move sets that are far superior then other characters. I will say with practice you can learn how do deal with this cheese a little but even the devs had to patch multiple times certain characters because it was too difficult to deal with for the casual players.
***You need to play this game daily to remain or get good. Now a lot of people like myself probably can't play everyday since we have other stuff going on in our lives. I myself can mostly only play during weekends so my first day is always a bad gameplay day :), after that it get's better. => if you are casual player then you will lose only so I can only recommend to play VS AI if you just want to play casual and don't have tons of time to get really good.
Now for all of this I can still live with this game and still enjoy it. The devs gave me the impression that they were dealing with the imballence of the heroes since they nerfed a lot of the top-tier characters and buffed some of the lower tier ones but seeing the direction this game is going with season 2 I can definitely say that you should not buy this game because the devs themselfes are ruining the community. They are clearly implementing the "pay to win" strategy. With the release of 2 new characters in season 2 (cent, shinobi) we have the pinacle of imballence for this game.
---Shinobi: gathers up all the spam & annoyance that peacekeeper, conqueror, warlord had. I will admit that shinobi has low HP to make up for that so the hit & run tactic I can live with, the double dash kick I cannot. You cannot do anything to decently punish this spam, which could also give you a 33/33/33 situation
---Cent: to be honest I expected shinobi to be a peacekeeper of sort but worse, but the centurian takes the OP to the next level. This character has all the possible move sets that all other characters partially have. He has stun, long combo's, heavy mixups, unblockables, push move, fast grabs, a way of draining your stamina, knock down move. Normally a character only has 2 to 3 of these moves but this guy has it all which he can do in 1 never ending combo that pushes you into exhaustion mode and then the match is just over.
If this will be the formula for every new character released then the game will be flooded with spammers instead of decent players and will basically break & ruin the game. My prediction will be that cent & shinobi will get their "kick" nerfed in the near future (which will reballence a lot) but i'm guessing with every new character it will be the same story all over again.

Survarium is an FPS game that isn't arena style shooter, but more of a tactical area style shooter with multiple in's and out's to flank or out flank your enemy. There is a slight learning curve dealing with the environments, the character progression and the skill tree. You may want to do a trial and error with resets on the skill tree to find what you like and don't like. The control layout is generally the same as any other FPS title.
Pros:
1. Graphics and textures are pleasantly pleasing to the eye for a free to play
2. Sound FX does the job for a free to play and the music is alright and fits in with theme.
3. Up-gradable character weapons and armor to where the player can have bonus stats put on to them through the use of spare parts and game points (gp) with a random success or failure.
The use of cash is optional for a guarantee results without wasting spare parts and having no failures, which can be seen as pay to win.
4. Being able to choose four different factions which offers different strengths and weaknesses. You are only able to level one faction at a time and use any available equipment that you unlock in that faction. You are also able to mix and match any equipment (as long the faction you level is unlocked) to make a more custom built character.
“Or” The use of real money to unlock + weapon's and equipment which offers pre-bonus stats and offers a permanent exp or gp percentage booster.
5. Weapon customization's which limited to 3 types, barrel (front), fore grip (under) and sights (top) can be unlocked by making kills with that weapon.
“Or” The use of the real money to unlock the customization's without the need to grind to unlock it.
6. Knyazev's Tools is a great to have, I have used it and I believe all FPS Games should have a similar program like it. Link below:
The Con's:
1. No team auto-balance before the match or auto-balancing during an active match.
2. No in-game vote kicking of players example: team killers, AFKers, or hackers...etc
3. Movement is clunky:
A. Crossing the terrain isn't smooth, the player may get some hang ups or stuck on static mesh on the map.
B. Traveling near guard rails or stairs the character will either pop on top of the rails without cause / warning or up and over which will fall to your death
C. Jumping over or onto 3D models like boxes, branches, vehicles, tanks or just general rubble  isn't smooth and awkward. The act cause's hang ups or sometimes having to remake the attempt again or several times.
4. Match making is a waiting game with wait times that can very from 2 minutes to 15 minutes. The max I've experience is almost a 30 minute wait time.
5. Limited game modes “4” Limited maps “9”, it can get boring fast.
6. Rendering issues, I've experience “Missing 3d Models” like building, tress, vehicles...etc. Would have to shut the game down, restart the program wait for a match and hopefully it would load and render the game properly
Some rendering issues like “Smoke Grenades” can be exploited by other players by changing their game graphic options to where they can see through the “Smoke Effect” easier. Which in turn they are able to take advantage of “unknown players” in a unbalanced game match.
7. Ping and Delay's: If your a NA player playing in the NA/EU server and playing against an RU player, say hello to bullets sponges. It is so bad it makes the game almost unplayable and not worth it
8. Random Game crashes
9. Pet peeve of mine:
Early access game's full of bugs and issues wanting real world money from the player-base with the use of cash-shops / micro-transactions with the promise of completion.
If a game or any game that is truly in "BETA" closed or open, or “Early Access” I believe that there shall be no "real money" cash shop allowed.
If the company wanted too there are other ways; they could offer a one time Founder's pack for early access until it was complete. They could start a kickerstarter, gofund page ....etc to generate the funds needed.
Remember the $10.00 potato salad on kickstarter.
Now if they re-move the early access, then I have no problem with the company having a cash shop.

I absolutely love this game in a way I wasn't expecting.
It has the right amount of humour and always in places you never expect to find it. You never know what you're going to come up against next, but you're guaranteed to laugh. Of course you could probably run straight through the game, do the tasks and finish it, but then you'd miss everything else going on. It's a game where you feel rewarded by looking at every little detail because so much of it has extra things to offer. It's not all in your face either, constantly forcing you to be in a typical funny situation. In fact a lot of the comedy in the game is quite subtle and you have to steer from the path in order to find it, but it makes you appreciate it as you play through. The attention to comedic detail is quite marvelous.
The gameplay is nice and simple. You walk around, interact with objects in often fun and ingenious ways to complete puzzles and make your way through the story. The graphics are very cartoony but still maintains a great atmosphere with all the music and extra sounds going on. It suits the tone of the game perfectly.
It's something nice, different and random. Nothing like I have played before and definitely a great experience. Would recommend.

A simple but still fun little indie gem (got to stop using that term) that harkens back to the days of gaming when the mechanics were simply 'go to the right, do not die or die as little possible'.
You pretty much help a handful of different coloured pixels with their own dash of personalities and one unique ability (higher jump, double jump or floating on acid are a few examples) through a series of challenges each one uniquely modeled to encourage you to use Thomas And Friends together to get through. The background storyline is narrated by a man with a soft pleasant voice and the games background music is equally pleasant to listen too.
Although six hours long, once you complete the game you can play through every mission in every scenario and try to catch up with the achivements. I had good fun and I'm usually the type that shys away from old school platform jumping. Think of it as the Indie Game Portal.

Once again this is probably the best game of ubisoft's that I have played and if you are a fan of shooters.

Orwell depicts a utopian setting where individual privacy is constantly violated thanks to public cyber-surveillance in form of an eponymous system, and justified through an ambiguous "Safety Bill" that sanctions "investigative methods" in order to "protect the freedom of The Nation's citizens."
Just how the knowledge about the individual characters' degree of criminal implication does retroactively affect your choices at the different decisive moments of the game makes the second playthrough the more interesting one: if at first you might have been well-intentioned enough to help the surveillance masterminds spying on your fellow citizens, you might be more inclined to rather try sabotaging the system on second thought, at the risk of course, to become yourself a "target" at the end.
That the game makes you second-guessing your "datachunk" choices is its biggest achievement, but that your superiors leave it entirely to you to distinguish between important and irrelevant information is Orwell's patent weakness since too ingenuous fiction-wise, though you need to contribute pertinent data in order to make the story progress, what can also be taxing at times.
It might not exactly be a totalitarian setting but it still is shocking to realize that the monitoring of both telephone and Internet communications is something also the citizens of democratic countries are faced with, and the game does a good job in showing the use of this type of top-down espionage. Worse still, it is yourself who is doing that closed-circuit observation with Orwell as your user interface: only once a person becomes a “target” related data can be extracted from the different documents and uploaded to Orwell's servers.
Orwell's approach might be simplified but it likely is how tracking persons in the Cyber Era does work, even when using a variety of sites, personas, and devices. This way the very conflict between public security issues and private data protection is well laid out, albeit far less preoccupying than in the famous Orwellian dystopia.
The five different episodes can be replayed separately for the different endings, though repeatedly going through the same dialogues quickly loses its interest during replay. Given the subject's topical interest there might be stuff enough for a sequel, unless your investigations did lead to Orwell being canceled altogether...

Stardrive 2 is an unapologetic Master of Orion clone that seeks to stay true to the classic standard of space 4X games. Besides a great number of direct references (Kulrathi? Really?) mechanics, buildings, and technologies taken directly from Master of Orion 2, there are more subtle parallels such as the occasional menace of the "Masters", which appears from sudden and inexplicable rifts to harass you for no apparent reason and give you problems in case you're not busy fighting anybody.
And surprisingly, it stacks up pretty well. The array of different races are colorful and the differences between them are substantial. The space combat is fun, and expansion requires difficult and meaningful choices.
Two areas in which Stardrive surpasses Orion is in ship design and diplomacy. When making ships, you don't just decide on modules and heap them onto a ship until some arbitrary "mass limit" is reached. Rather, ships each have a footprint, and modules - which include everything from weapons to engines to less obviously useful "capacitors" take up space, energy, and have mass, which slows the ship down. There are a lot of implications resulting from this, but the simplest is that you can choose to focus on speed, defense, or firepower without having specific technologies specifically suited to each area. Just pile on more armor, more engines, or bigger guns. Diplomacy is quite streamlined, with each offer being given a straight value that needs to be matched or exceeded for the deal to go through. Meanwhile, a species "tolerance level" keeps you from making very large deals, which is a very interesting and thoughtful cap on inter-empire trading.
Other areas in Stardrive 2 fall a bit short of their promise. Ground combat consists of a clunky lineup of a handful of soldiers in simple, turn-based combat, and it's quite hard to imagine such small and low-octane encounters deciding the ownership of entire planets. The technology tree also seems a bit stunted, and could use a few tiers that only offer one technology to research; some very important technologies simply should be acquired as a matter of course, such as battleships and terraforming. Nobody would seriously give up a larger ship footprint for a larger starbase or improved armor plating. It's also strange that there's only one ship footprint for each ship size, which changes from species to species. It's hardly unthinkable that ships built for different purposes would have different basic frames, but we have to settle for simply filling them with different modules. Also missing from Stardrive is a government system; all races apparently have the same system of managing their empires, modified by their species. Finally, BUGS. Lots of bugs. And not in the sense of an insectoid, hive-mind species (curiously, the Klackons didn't make it into this MOO clone). Things like ships suddenly taking on the appearance of other species' ships, fleets vanishing, sometimes being unable to name new ship designs, and - my favorite - being assaulted by an enemy race and then being given control of their troopers while the computer controls my soldiers. None of them are game-breaking, but you're not going to get through the game without finding a few of your own.
There are a lot of other things that could have simply used MORE. The planet types are stripped straight from MOO (toxic, radiated, barren, desert, all the way to gaia) with no interesting new alien-ish worlds on offer. There are neat little mini-quests and mysterious objects in space to explore, but they're exactly the same from game to game and quickly run out. Space combat is a lot of fun, but ships could use more tactical settings other than "frontal attack/broadside" and "sit in place/move". There's an engagement zone setting, but the blasted thing resets from encounter to encounter, so if you have a preferred setting (plasma cannons are infamously useless at long range) you have to reset it in each new combat. And as far as I can tell, there are no sudden galactic events that affect all players equally, such as space monsters or subspace shutdowns. A missed opportunity.
That said, Stardrive 2 is still a great game, and stacks up to its ancestor admirably. But I'll be looking ahead to StarDrive 3 (and hope that in that respect it is NOT like Master of Orion).

Cons:
-The game itself is abandoned. It's an early access title that was last updated by the developer on 15 March 2016 (according to SteamDB)
-The insanity meter and flashlight deplete way to quickly, leaving you with an infuriating experience as you try to walk through the dark and eventually die
-Still a lot of bugs and glitches which will never be resolved
The game had promise, and I wish I could see the final project, but that will never happen. Not worth getting as it'll never be complete.

I don’t know where to begin with Demented. I bought it as part of a Groupee’s bundle a bit ago, downloaded it, and the game never worked on my computer, so I wrote it off. Once it was on Steam, I decided to give it another go, and it worked fine. I don’t know what happened there.
As a fan of horror, I couldn’t really help but try Demented. I like the look of it, and it has an intriguing concept, but is it fun? Yes and no. While there aren’t a lot of issues in its current early access state, what issues exist are pretty big.
Big issue one: the game is ridiculously dark. I understand it’s supposed to be dark, but it’s a bit extreme here. Not helping issues is a completely useless flashlight, which you’re not even told how to use (it’s not found in the very minimal controls section, nor is it given as a tutorial). I did press F out of curiosity, and it didn’t work, but as I was wandering around, the light suddenly came on. Ironically, in a well lit area. I tried F again, and the light went off. So, F is the toggle for the flashlight, but apparently it didn’t want to activate right away.
Big issue two: sprinting wobble. Your head sways extremely quickly as you sprint, which makes locating items or even just seeing a hassle. Whether your character was intended to run this chaotically or a bug, it’s quite disorienting. I don’t suffer from motion sickness, but I imagine playing this enough will give it to me.
I’m torn on this game, and titles like this make me wish Steam had a neutral option, because Demented is neither good nor bad.

Looking to invite comparisons to titles as lofty as Amnesia: The Dark Descent is no bad aspiration for a game to have but the framework of DEMENTED is a dizzying mess.
The overbearing problem here is also unfortunately one of the game's major hinges; its sanity meter requires constant topping up from pills and your own health bar, killing you off should you ever allow it to hit zero. It is constantly running, plunging ever downwards which should produce an exhilarating panic in the player as they face untold horrors in a bloodstained facility. The reality is that this mechanic has been insufferably bolted on to a handful of fetch quests that DEMENTED would have you do largely in the pitch black, thanks to the impoverished lifetime of your flashlight. Coupled with a sprint that is unavoidably necessary to use despite being useless for spotting anything thanks to its obscene head wobble, it feels like the game is hellbent on punishing you for exploring or, at the very least, forcing you to play it as a kart racing game whereby you have to learn the correct route to stand a chance.

Long, long ago, in an era occurring only slightly after the death of the last dinosaur, there were these ancient artifacts called - wait for it - "text adventures".
They were among the very first "video games", even if they barely resembled the infinitely more snazzy products we now refer to by that name. The earliest examples of this genre of gaming didn't even have GRAPHICS, for cryin' out loud! They were no more than words...on a screen...which you interacted with by typing MORE words on the screen. Crazy, right?
But it's true: there was indeed a time in our darkest past where, if you wanted any level of immersion in a game deeper than one white bar hitting a dot towards another white bar (hello, Pong!), you were pretty much stuck with your imagination doing ninety-nine percent of the work for you.
Let's face it: it was practically child abuse, by today's lofty standards.
Fast forward to the year 2017, and what's this? Some game developer calling itself No Code (a double entendre, I presume) releases a four-episode game called Stories Untold, which at least partially carries on in the spirit of such text adventures...before adding some significant multi-genred twists, and a substantially more varied and modern visual interface.
The most common viewpoint given in the first three episodes, at least, is that of the player themselves seated at an old-school desktop computer into which you can type commands, and for the first of the four episodes that's literally all that you can do. As the episodes progress, however, the player's interactions expand to other objects/machines about their workstation, which must also be fiddled with to make headway.
It's all quite clever, really; even if I ultimately found myself favouring the first and most "traditional" of the bunch, a spectacularly spooky number entitled The House Abandon.
I first played this episode as a standalone game/demo quite some time ago, at the behest of a friend who generally plays neither horror nor text adventure games. It was available for free on a game-sharing site, and my friend (who had only been brave enough to watch a YouTube walkthrough) thought it might be well up my alley. He certainly wasn't wrong; though I at first suspected he might have been, especially in his assertion that a hardened horror game addict like myself might find it genuinely SCARY.
A text adventure? Scary?! I may well have wondered what drugs or alcohol this friend of mine had been scoffing, if I didn't know him as an all-but-teetotaller. He even mentioned a few occasions when the girl he viewed in the video visibly JUMPED in fright at what the game threw at her. Haha, indeed, I thought. Young, hysterical girlies on YouTube is one thing, but I'm a man in his forties and a hardcore horror fanatic, darn it all to Hades. Sure enough, a slightly harrowing twenty-five minutes later, I was tucking my tail between my legs and confirming to my friend how very right he had been.
Unfortunately, this tone of terror gradually subsides as the episodes of Stories Untold progress, and the parser-based typing largely makes way for more familiar adventure game puzzling and even a bit of first-person wandering. It's still very well-done, and there's still a consistent aura of dread to proceedings; it's just a shame that the seat-of-the-pants intuitiveness of the first episode is replaced by no end of tricky code-breaking and pedantic instruction-following, placing the last three-quarters of the game in the territory of a more familiar and contemporary adventure-gaming style, as opposed to the sheer green-screen era goodness of the game's earliest moments.
Or, to put it another way: if you're as bad at puzzles as I am, you'll happily stumble your way through the first episode without needing to peek at a walkthrough, while constantly referring to one for all that comes after.
It's also a shame that the brilliantly enigmatic ending of The House Abandon is not only explained, but almost OVER-explained by the end of the four episodes. The storytelling still remains strong throughout, but a part of me can't help but feel that the attempt to "link" the four episodes together into a singular storyline was a somewhat misguided effort, and it may have been better if they'd just told four unrelated tales.
It's still an excellent game, overall, and can hardly be faulted for lack of invention. I'm certainly intrigued to see what No Code get up to next.
Verdict: 8.5/10.

This review comes from a die-hard STALKER fan and veteran !
For those of you who don't know what STALKER is, STALKER is a survival FPS with a glimpse of RPG and horror-type FPS set in Ukraine in a fictional 2nd post-cernobyl disaster, where nature and fauna are suffering from mutation and odd things happen as a consequence. It is a very unique game and very good, often compared to it's rival, Fallout series, which is it's closest comparisson. *Metro may be second*
Now, Survarium is considered to be it's successor, even considered as "STALKER 2" ; only, that lacks singleplayer content as in the moment. it's beta stage and the game keeps getting developed with content as the time passes.
Survarium is a solid FPS, with lots of close combat and long range sniping like, featuring big maps where players are fighting for control or slaughter. Beside combat, you will also have to face anomalies on the battlefield, which may grant you specific bonuses if you collect them, or make your game harder by blocking paths etc  This game offers a huge range of weapons and armor to choose from 4 unique factions, which can be upgraded to fare better. Also, you can customize your gear with different symbols/ insignias/ ribbons/ marks and camos.
So far, this game offers classic team deathmatch and capture the flag types. More content will come as the devs promised ; including the most-acclaimed and waited, open-world game mode as Day Z.
The graphics are very good and pleasant to the eyes, with many next-gen features to tweak on. Music, sound ambience and gun sounds are very top notch. Maps are nicely designed, and offers suitable possibilites to be played with different classes/ guns.
Survarium is NOT pay-to-win. Don't listen to those idiots who cry "p2w", they don't even understand what that means. Yes there are some premium guns which offer extra incomes after battle, but they don't have increased stats/ dmg/ range/ precision/ so on. Premium items have only income and xp rate increased, which won't affect the course of the battle.
The only problem this game has, so far, as it is still beta-stage, there are kinda many cheaters/ hackers, especially in the high-tier, BUT, the game is so good, that I personally keep playing it. Sure I get mad and rage sometimes, but I still keep on, as the game is fun and challenging to play, even with some retar^ed hackers. :D
But if you play on low-tiers, the game is much more enjoyable and with less cheaters, in my oppinion.
I DO recommend this game, especially to other STALKER/ Metro/ Fallout fans. For those who like run&gun type of games, like Call of Duty or Battlefield, you will like this one as well.
So, "get out of here Stalker !", from the store page, and get in the game !

In this game, you are the government employee spying on civilians. You read their private posts, listen to their private calls, collect and disseminate information about them, until you have a full picture. It is invasive, horrifying, but might also save lives.
Although, at what cost?
George Orwell and Aldous Huxley would be proud; not in what our society has become, but in what this game truly illustrates what we have learnt from their novels. This is not a university lecture, but a fun game... but at the same time also a game that makes you reflect.
Instead of simply reading about the dangers of how information is used, you get to experience it first-hand, and make your own decisions. Do it well and you prevents horrible things from happening.
But would you be comfortable with powerful - possibly corrupt - governments doing this? Is it worth the danger of being abused?

I will be honest, I haven't even finished this game yet and I feel that I have already got my money's worth from this. It's an extremely unique comedy experience that delivers on its promise of fun. Interact with as many things as you can and you will be rewarded in spades with smiles on your face.
Let me put it this way: there is an entity you may encounter who is a direct parody of Rita from Power Rangers, Chikita Banana, and Fruit Ninja. You also get to degauss pigeons in a level. There are even items that take you into mini games when you interact with them.
The comedy is fast-paced and doesn't wave itself in your face in an annoying "DO YOU GET IT?" way. The joke comes and goes fast enough for if you actually don't get it you'll get to see something else and laugh at that instead. It's also worth reading signs too, even small ones and labels. Quite frankly, a game that includes "Deep Fried Katamari" as a menu item in a place and will allow you to miss it really "gets" this brand of comedy and won't drag you down.
Also, there's no pressure to do anything in a timely manner. I like that in this type of game.
I highly recommend it, particularyly to anyone who knows quite a bit about technology, are at least slightly familiar with the aesthetic of 1956-1960, and/or are a bit aware of Japanese culture. If you're not familiar with any of that, I'm sure you'll find the visual humor entertaining still.

I enjoyed SOMA for the story, the atmosphere, and the message about transhumanism. I didn't enjoy SOMA for the enemy encounters. I recommend the game for sure though. If you've played Amnesia: The Dark Descent, SOMA takes the same sort of storytelling and mechanical approach but flips the setting to science fiction.
I was able to predict the plot of SOMA in broad strokes very early in the game, but the way it unfolds, how it deconstructs humanity to get at the essence, is remarkable. There is raw emotion in SOMA, and there is enough of it to make you ponder on what it is that makes something or someone human. I was enthralled from the beginning to the end.
Unfortunately, SOMA does suffer from one element, and that is enemy encounters. They are kind of unnecessary, and I feel they detract from the overall experience. I'm not sure if it's the way the enemies behave or something else, but I never felt like the monsters were important to the setting or the gameplay. I would have preferred an exploration-only game with puzzle solving rather than mundane and boring hide or be chased segments. That said, enemy encounters are few and far in-between, so it's not all that bad.
I waited a long time to get this game on sale, but I think it is worth the full price.

Sega has done some sketchy things in the past but their recent ports have been surprisingly decent.
It is definitely a Japanese video game with a hyper view of American culture. Incredibly cheesy, flowing with internet references along with action movie tropes and it’s fun to watch. Diet metal gear.
Gameplay is fast paced with emphasis on cover and mobility by using the suit to drift around. A fun and often frenetic arcade action shooter. The enemies are well designed and they actually respond when taking fire even to the point where certain mini-bosses can lose their limbs and flail about helplessly. Some enemies become more dangerous as they take damage and others running at their last spark will throw themselves at you. Not much can be said about the friendly AI though as their real function serve as distractions or as rescuable damsels that pop out ammo/upgrade rewards.
Gunplay is damn enjoyable with disks that hack off limbs from bigger enemies to machine gun that staggers or sniper rifles that slaps enemies back on their bums.
Performance wise, there’s a bit of stuttering at times but it has never crashed on me. Levels are quick to load and everything else runs fine.
A fun shooter and well worth the price.

A long while ago, I was given this game as a present. To me, it looked so sweet and particularly interesting because I have a very big soft spot for animals. While the game does live up to these two things, being sweet and a treat for anyone who appreciates animals, Never Alone is also something much more than that.
This game is a simple 2-D platformer with a storyline that was based on very old folklore. The developers of this game really took the time to immerse themselves into the words of the people who made this folklore and created something brilliant with it. Throughout the game you are given snippets of videos showing them interviewing people about their folklore and what exactly it all means. In the end you discover that the central idea of these stories was to unite people in the belief that you must respect all forms of life no matter how big or small.
There are a few really nice challenging parts of this game that I think also make the game very worthwhile. The plotline takes and unexpected shift and gives you a whole new sense of gameplay. If you buy the DLC, you will find that it is also a great addition to the game.
Overall, I think that this game is a lovely pick for anyone who is looking for something that isn't too challenging but has an interesting and thought-provoking ending. I recommend watching all of the videos as well because they help you to understand the developer's visions through the eyes of the people who inspired them. It also has a very soothing soundtrack.
I am happy to say that I got to experience this game and even more thankful that it was given to me as a present. It truly is a wonderful game.

It pains me deeply to give this game a negative review but there is so much wasted potential here. I truly love this game (or rather, what this game could be) and I wish it was developed more and with much more care and attention.
The gameplay is your standard survival genre, scavenge for food and weapons while hiding from monsters called 'Nether' and other players. The nether mechanics are buggy and frustrating to play against, giving everything a teleport mechanic is just a lame way of saying "we don't know how to make different enemies so we'll just re-model the same enemy and adjust it's health and damage". The guns are good and have a nice feel to them, ammo is a pain to get put into one stack and the weight limits are just too restrictive. You have a global inventory which acts like a bank but again, you can only store a certain weight and size limit of items meaning you feel the need to keep your best weapons safe by leaving them there instead of using them, making them rather pointless. The graphics are actually very good considering the state of the rest of the game and the lighting is great apart from metalic surfaces being a bit too reflective in my opinion.
Overall, this game is 10% of what it could have been and that's a damn shame.
If you have a couple of friends who'd buy this game, it's worth the small £7 price tag but otherwise - as much as it pains me to say it, I'd stay clear of this game.

This review is spoiler-free.
I picked up Orwell because I love games that put you in the role of a detective. I previously played "Her Story" and hoped this would be along similar lines (albeit with a different interface), going through data and gaining clues in order to pinpoint suspects.
After playing the game, I was left fairly satisfied and definitely had an enjoyable experience with it, though I did find it lacking in some areas.
The good:
I loved the unique art style, and the whole set up of how you feel like you're logging on to this system as a detective. The music is great and very suitable for the game too, changing in tone dramatically when something in the game changes. I love the overall Orwell theme and how it makes you think about things like government surveillance and whether it's a good or a bad thing. The characters were fairly interesting to me (though mostly unlikable, but that may have been the idea). I enjoyed the way the game is structured and how gathering certain bits of data about a person unlocks more data such as relevant URLs or documents.  I found it intriguing and I wanted to keep on playing after each chapter (there are five chapters in total).
The bad:
The game is pretty short, lasting about five hours, however I do feel like the price point is good for the experience you get.
I felt like the mechanics of investigation had some excellent ideas but that they could have gone further with it. The game always highlighted where new information was available, and although I suppose that did stop you sifting through all the old documents you had, I kinda wanted to have to do that sifting - as a detective might. It felt a bit too hand-holding as to showing you where to look next, and sometimes that just made it feel like I was just following a path of "look at the new informatiion", "drag it to the person's profile", "look at the new bit of information"... and so on. I think maybe if it wasn't always so obvious which information to go back to, it would have been more fun to find it yourself.
I think in general, I just wanted more of the game, it was definitely a good start, but I would love to see more chapters, or a new story. And maybe an option to not have the right bits of data or documents highlighted, so you had to figure some more stuff out yourself. I think then I would have felt like a more clever detective!
But all in all, I enjoyed the way the story wrapped up, and a lot of the ideas and mechanics, such as deciding between conflicting information, deciding what to submit and what to ignore to determine what light you put somebody in.. and I enjoyed the end of the game too.
I think it's a 7/10 for me, an all-round good experience, but lacking in some areas that could have made it more fun/satisfying.

StarDrive 2 is a game where core mechanics are mostly superb, but it lacks features required to make a truly good 4X game.
Quite frankly, this game focuses way too much on "exterminate"-part of the 4X, which makes it seem shallow compared to it's peers.  This is not a game where you try to win with a peaceful empire by intrigue, colonization, science and diplomacy.  While these parts are certainly a part of the game, they have habit of getting into one another's way.  Given that, the game's focus tends to be in ship design, logistics and space battles.  But most of all, this game lacks diverse content that is usually a requirement for any 4X game.  The game's pacing also feels like it's not been thought out, with research, exploration, and conquest all working on their own pace, instead of supporting each other.
The good parts of the MOO2 are there, no doubt, and they will suck you into the game for a good 10 hours or so, before the flaws start to shine through the gaps in the awesome.  The alien species that seemed varied at the first sight, start to all feel more same-y with only a slight twist after a while, the short tech tree is past future-tech at the point around third of the galaxy is explored -- I haven't even met all species before the tech tree is done, and I am quite certain this problem will just seem all the more clear if you like to play research-centric species, which I do not.
On the other hand, the random-ish events and whatnot give some background into the galaxy, and fill some gaps nicely.  The worlds slowly turning into core-worlds, ski resorts built into tundra worlds and beaches of the ocean worlds all give nice flavor to your empire's worlds.  Designing ships is also fun, and quite likely the best part of the game.  Only thing I would love to have in the design is more options later on, but in the early-game, there were more than enough.  The problem there comes only later on, when you can just cram some full of long-distance weaponry and near-impenetrable shields, at which point any opposition just gets obliterated.
The diplomacy mechanics of the game are also good, which is a pity, since every alien you meet will want to murder you, however peaceful they claim they are (they usually don't).  The only empire I have ever managed to hold peace with, was the one trying to constantly steal my technology, to the point where I wanted to murder them instead.  And this is the problem with the alien species.  While they seem like really cool ideas with built-in shout-outs, you will soon see a certain pattern there.  There are Cthulhu-esque theocrats that want to murder you for not worshipping their gods, wolf-like evil warriors who want to murder you for the evulz, space-bears that want to murder you for honor, mind-controlling molluscs that want to enslave you out of boredom, robot hive-mind that want to murder you for lebensraum and plant-like "peaceful creatures" that quite likely just wanted to enjoy the gentle optics of my laser beam arrays on my ships.  The tendency of everyone trying to murder you, combined with AI's suicidal optimism and overconfidence about their odds about winning a war tend to lead them declaring war on you just to get horribly murdered instead.  And while this was fun the first time, it grew old fast.  There simply aren't any aliens that like to win the game, instead of giving you excuse to fight to showcase the game's combat mechanics.
The space combat itself seems OK, and ship designs seem to really matter.  The AI seems to just move towards you guns blazing though, regardless of its ship designs.  The UI is good enough, if sometimes a bit annoying, especially if you like to use fighters, since selecting ships is sometimes not as straightforward as it should be.
The absolute worst part of the game is ground combat.  It seems like an afterthought and the UI makes it constant misclickfest at it.  It is skippable, but the automagic resolution doesn't do as good job as you would with some equipment, so it becomes just a chore to be done before you can continue on the fun parts of the game.
In the end, the focus on the extermination and conquest strip the game of many of the strategic elements it should be capable of.  The space and ground combat lack good enough AI to actually showcase the best parts of the game -- the ship design.  The replayability also suffers when every game ends up in a war with only slightly varied opponents.  That being said, the game's strategic mechanics are excellent, and most of the bigger problems COULD be fixed with patches.  Even with all its flaws, this is probably one of the best space 4X games after Master of Orion 2.  The problem is, I still rather play MOO2, which currently costs quarter of this game's prize.  If this game would cost 10€, I would recommend it, but for this cost, it just doesn't offer enough.
tldl: If you can look past some flaws and/or have infinite money to spend, this is a good grab.  Not worth 20€, probably not even worth 15€ at 1.1 patch.  If you can get it sub-10€, get it.

Watching 10 minutes of Jazzpunk will let you know whether it's for you or not. Its brand of humour is hyper-specific, trading on James Bond, conspiracy theories, William Gibson and a dash of Blendo Games' work. If that type of humour appeals to you then stop reading, buy Jazzpunk, play Jazzpunk.
Jazzpunk may be the funniest game I've ever played. Humour is brutally difficult in games because the player is in control of the timing. Jazzpunk nails it, almost effortlessly. It's a game that rewards you poking at everything, and everything you poke is guaranteed to have a joke attached. The concentration of lunacy is consistently dense. The number of jokes per square metre in this game is ridiculous. There's so much to find and so much to discover. A few jokes fall flat but the majority of them work and work well.
Jazzpunk is essentially an adventure game. Often you'll be asked to collect certain items to combine with other items to progress. It sounds dull but virtually every puzzle is a clever joke or a stupid premise. Jazzpunk's objectives embrace the non-sequiter and the punchline and weave them into everything you do.
Remember
Recall the end scene? Remember the Applebees? Jazzpunk's puzzles and easter eggs rival that moment in their sheer audacity every two minutes.
It took some incredibly intelligent people to make a game that's so smart about being dumb. Even if it seems like it's not for you, you should play this game. It's a delight.

After my negative review of Stardrive 1 I thought I'd review this to set the records straight, this game improves on SD1 in every way, every little problem I have with the first one is resolved and more:
+ It's stable! Not a single crash, laggy moment or instability.
+ The research system is vastly improved and adds a few features I've not seen in a 4x game, including a system that makes diplomacy and espionage very important.
+ The ship varieties are nice, the game is very pleasant to look at.
+ There's even a little X-com like tactical game for your ground troops
+ Random events and regions of space can trigger special research projects that can help your empire
+ Freighters and cargo transport has been hugely streamlined, this used to be very frustrating in SD1 having to micromanage all of your freighters.
+ Good variety of planet features that give extra depth to the colonisation system including some nods to classic sci-fi.
All that being said, there are some things that could have been done a little better:
- The sound design suuuucks! from random 'sci-fi beeps' on the tactical map and cheesy 'pew-pew' noises in battles, the sound design could have been so much better, honestly can't remember what the music is like other than I turned it off pretty quickly.
- there is a max 100 system limit. the galaxy doesn't feel particularly big, gets crowded quickly with more than 3 opponents.
- A couple of balancing issues could use looking at
All in all though, this is a solid 4X game that improves greatly on it's predecessor, pleased to have bought it.

This game is NOT recommended for one reason, and one reason only, but I feel it is a very important one.  The game is the first I have encountered that abandons support for 1024 x 768 and lower resolution.  This may sound trivial, but I believe it may be the start of an ominous trend.  Because of this withdrawal of support gamers using still good gas plasma displays will not be able to play the game.
If the game succeeds in getting away with this move it could be the beginning of the end for all players using gas plasma displays.  Other developers will quickly follow suit, and soon GPD users will find that their computer rigs are useless for any and all new games.   This progression will soon follow to higher and higher resolutions, finally leaving players in a frantic and never ending quest to own systems with the highest possible resolution.  What Microsoft has done to operating systems, games like this will do to monitors.  Each new game out will see a new set of resolutions and monitor types rendered obsolete.
This movement needs to be squashed before it has a chance to take root.  I urge all prospective buyers to refuse to purchase the game until it extends support to all currently used resolutions.

is a platform, adventure game that takes place in the harsh climate of the tundra while facing a catastrophic blizzard that perpetually weighs you down as you trod through the frozen tundra in order to stop the blizzard from destroying your village. You play as a girl named Nunu and her companion, an all-white coated Artic fox. Fox were believed to bring joy and be excellent companions in the Alaskan climate to guide and aid people away from danger.  You use what is called a Bola, an ancient weapon that was used by Native American tribes to hunt for duck which an elderly man humbly gives you, the bola, as a reward for finding his drum he lost. Drums are considered the pinnacle and way of life of Native American tribes, the Iñupiat.  The spirituality and belief in pantheism, that all living things and animate objects possesses a soul and a nature of some type, is represented in the early parts of the game through spirits controlled by the fox that helps you get to heights, ledges, platforms, cliffs, ladders, and hills you are unable to reach typically in the game playing as Nunu.
Nunu is an emotionally devastated and vivacious girl. How would you feel if in real-life you were from a native tribe and someone who was a foreign alien, unwelcomed as an adversary, destroyed your hometown including all women, men and children alike? You would be distraught just like Nunu is at times. Nunu is at a loss because this fox seems to be her one and only companion. We don't know the whereabouts of her parents nor if she has any siblings.

is based on a genuine and real tale of Native American tribes, Alaskan natives to be more accurate whom have experienced severe forms of climate change throughout the aging of glaciers and a great devastation of a blizzard, which at the beginning of the game, has been coming from an unknown source. You will battle your way through your adversaries of an opposing tribe wanting to take you hostage, attempting to kill you, forcing you always to be on the run from imminent danger.

Even though it took them seven years, I'm glad that SEGA & Platinum were brave enough to finally port a modern light gun game to the PC. Of course, you might look at Vanquish and be bewildered, confusing it for yet another generic console port cover-based third person shooter. Everything about Vanquish seems to emulate an arcade experience, from the walls of enemies thrown at you, to the neon green HUD & cheesy sound effects, to the frenetic campaign & cutscene design. As expected of any good arcade game, nothing going on really makes sense; the plot is just an excuse to create new locations and introduce bosses.
Follow the adventures of Sam Gideon as you rocket-slide from cover to cover until you somersault-kick a Russian space robot in the face and spray LMG bullets into his allies in slow motion during the fall back to the ground. Sam's movement is purposefully clunky, with loud mechanical grinding and slow animations, giving him a unique feeling from other Platinum Games characters that is more mecha than dancer. The only complaint I have about the combat is landing a melee attack will deplete your Augmented Reaction gauge. Normally when you enter low health, AR (slow motion) will trigger until your remaining gauge runs out, giving you ample reaction time to kill a few enemies around you and/or get to cover. Getting down to low health without the AR available will quickly result in you dying because of how many enemies are attacking you at once in most situations. This however is a small nitpick and the only negative I can think of when it comes to anything in regards to gameplay. Melee combat's effectiveness varies wildly depending on the situation and is often more useful for making yourself airborne by kicking off of terrain. The complexity of combat slowly unfurls itself as your struggle to survive causes you to innovate with mechanics. This is yet another Platinum masterpiece that is easy to learn but difficult to master; watching YouTubers pull of complex maneuvers is as exciting as watching a DMC or Bayonetta playthrough despite the vastly different gameplay design.
Vanquish does everything it can to defy your expectations from a third-person shooter. While the music, SFX, and voice acting are all mediocre, everything else about this wild ride of a game elevates the experience to something special. Yet again, Platinum created something unique and memorable out of what could've been just another cover-based shooter. Even though it's seven years late, Vanquish is still an excellent experience that shouldn't be overlooked.

This is more than a game.
Rocksmith 2014 (RS14) is amazing for beginners, amateurs or pros, alike. RS14 WILL make you a better guitarist.  If you've never played guitar, this will teach you. There are dozens of features and mini-games to help anyone become a better guitarist. With each song, it has 'Authentic Tone' which is the exact sound of the original song.  No more tinkering with pedals and amps, just playing, aw yeah! Or, it has amps, pedals, effects, pre-amps and just about everything a budding guitarist could want so they can create their own tones!
Right from the get go, it will teach how to tune the guitar, and it gets really nitty gritty with tunings.  Most songs have standard E or Drop D kind of tunings, but every once in a while, a song will have a weird tuning, like A447.  It simply means the string tunings are slightly sharp, and before playing the song you will have to retune, bringing up the tuner and won't proceed till the guitar is in tune.
Starting with simply Learning A Song, it takes it easy, and builds up to your level of play.  Then it starts to challenge the player.  Once the song is completed, RS14 will offer tips regarding the song, from video lessons about techniques, to playing games (more on these later) to Riff Repeater!  When the song is finished, the game will offer a congratulatory statement that's always positive, then record your accuracy, longest streak of notes and mastery of the song.  At 100% of each of these, the song is played as recroded, and mastered, giving an achievement.
Riff Repeater will bring up one section of the song, slowing it down to 75% (by default, but the player can adjust this between 1% and 100%), and a Mastery Level ranging from 1% to 100%. Mastery Level is the notes of the song, at 100%, you're playing the song the way it was recorded. Riff Repeater will build it up piece by piece.  If all notes are hit, it will 'level up', adding more notes or speeding up the recording to full speed if Mastery is maxed.
Session Mode allows for the player to add drums, bass, keyboards, second guitar, etc, and just do a freeform jam within specific keys.  Just pick the key to play in and as long as the player sticks in that pocket, the backup band will keep time and jam along.  There are different modes for playing: Jam, 12 Bar Blues, Progressive, Radio Friendly and Changes, and it allows for tempo  and 'groove' for the backing band, as well as picking the 'venue sound' for playing (from studio to arena).  It's a great way to just fart around on the guitar and have a band playing along with you.
Non Stop Play allows the player to add a bunch of songs, and just play continuously without stopping to reload a song.  Just queue them up and play!  This can be done from Favorites from the catalogue the player has favorited, or just randomly picking them.  I personally keep in the same key to prevent retuning.
Guitarcade is where it gets very interesting.  The Guitarcade is nothing more than games to help the guitarist learn techniques or go head to head with other players in scoring on playing songs.
Technique Games:
- Gone Wailin'! is a noise game.  It helps beginning guitarist learn to make noise by bashing on the strings and learnign to mute the strings.  For such a basic game supposedly meant for beginners, it's actually really tough and requires some finesse.
- String Skip Saloon is a game to teach string skipping, duh.  Simply play the strings as the game tells you to. This is done by 'shooting' the bad guys that come at you along the screen corresponding to specific strings.  It seems easy enough, but as the game goes on, it gets rather challenging.
- Ducks Redux is all about hitting notes on the strings.  Basic game of shooting ducks by hitting the right notes on the right strings.
- Ninja Slide N is a play on the name Ninja Gaiden, duh.  Simply slide from Fret to Fret to build up sliding technique.
- Scale Warriors is playing scales to beat up bad guys, ala side scrolling fighting games of the 80's.  Every conceivable scale is included, the faster the scales are played, the faster the bad guys go down!
- Return To Castle Chordread is a zombie killing game where Power Chords kill the zombies!  Hells yeah! It can't be explained any better than Power Chords killing zombies.
- Hurtlin' Hurdles practices alternate picking.  Pick as fast as possible to run, then mute to jump hurdles. Funner than it sounds!
- Temple Of Bends is a game of climbing descending ropes by bending strings up (or down on the top half of the fret board) to climb ropes.
- Scale Racer is playing scales to dodge around cars by playing the correct scale notes while being chased by the Fuzz.
- Star Chords is a space shooter that requires playing open string chords to advance.
- Harmonic Heist is playing harmonics to sneak past security to steal objects.
Score Attack:
There are 4 levels to each song in your library: Easy, Medium, Hard and Master.  Master does not unlock until a Platinum score is achieved in hard.  Every song has these levels and scores are accumulated by hitting the right notes on time.  The harder the skill, the more difficult.  It is a mix between lead and rhythm, so it's a challenge all the way around.
Of course, we're all competitive, when it comes right down to it.  Leaderboard Challenges allow you to better your own score by making you score better than other RS14 players all over the world.  They'll show you a score of someone higher than yourself and the object is to beat that score and get higher up in the rankings.
As mentioned before, the game is full of video lessons from simple accents to syncopation and vibrato.  The lessons are either basic, amateur or advanced, and there is a test with each class to make sure the player is doing it right... which can be frustrating when I'm bending freaking notes for 15 minutes trying to bend it tot he perfect pitch.
All in all, I've eschewed all other games at this point because it is that much fun, and honestly, playing songs like Whipping Post or Cliffs of Dover or Redneck, all in the exact tone is awesome, with the actual band recording playing is just that much better. Instead of playing along with a CD, the tone being wrong, and trying to balance the volumes, this will do it all for the player, and they are effectively taking over the role (lead, rhythm or bass) for the band, so the player is the one filling that role.
I'm nto gonna lie, hitting the notes, hearing it come through perfectly and knowing that's me jamming along with Duane Allman or K.K. Downing or Dave Murray, it's just feels freaking awesome!!! If you own a guitar, buy this game, buy the cable (it's needed to play and is only $10), and have a freaking ball.
The 60 Day Challenge is kind of a bust for me.  It's not been recording my days, and the hours seem off, but it is accurately recording all the songs, arcade games, lessons and everything else I am doing in game.  I'm not the only one with this issue, the boards are rife with complaints about the 60 Challenge not accurately keeping track of time, but at this point, I'm just loving playing Boston or Kansas or Megadeth and rocking the ♥♥♥♥ out!!

Almost seven years have passed since Vanquish was released on Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3. This PC port and remaster I’m writing about today, has been a pleasant surprise since I honestly didn’t expect it. 2010 also marked the year in which I bought a PS3 and I’m proud to say that Vanquish was among my first video games on that console. I do have fond memories with it, yet some lingering issues related to the frame rate still haven’t been fully fixed. In anycase, developer PlatinumGames proves that originality can still be implemented even when a game’s topic is as SciFi and Japanese as they come.
I’m not even talking about stereotypes here. Vanquish is a love letter to Japanese game development and a perspective into what makes robots/cyborgs so enticing. This title’s story is filled with plot twists, intricate (and fairly long) cutscenes and as much attention to detail as in its gameplay. If the Metal Gear series still has the longest between-mission animations, well I can only say that Vanquish inspired to some degree, Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance. While focusing more on the shooting from cover part than techno katanas, of course.
In the near future, a US space station/orbital laser gets hijacked by a separatist faction within the Russian Federation which proceeds to destroy San Francisco and threatens to attack New York. The Unites States Marine Corps gets tasked with recapturing the massive facility before it can recharge its weapon and DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency) lends a hand by sending in one of their elite operatives. Sam Gideon is the protagonist in Vanquish and he looks like Adam Jensen’s younger brother while his exoskeleton would put the ones in the Crysis series to shame. Too bad Sam can’t fly, or he’d give Iron Man a run for his money.
Gideon gets assisted by both fellow US troops and his trusty DARPA handler while he’ll fight against mostly robots of different shapes and sizes. Saying that the plot shall thicken, would be an understatement. Alas, I shall not spoil anything. Suffice to say that it’s a strong narrative regardless of some clichés. The villains are well motivated and the enemy types (plus boss fights) prove to be a real challenge when in sufficient number. Most battles take place in large, open areas so the very scale of Vanquish’s set pieces, is something to consider. It won’t be Dark Souls in space but it is definitely a cover-based shooter for a good reason. Advanced suit prototype or not, Sam won’t be able to take many direct hits and engaging in melee combat should only be used when low on ammo or when battling larger (and thus, slower) mechanized opponents.
Much like in Bayonetta’s case, Vanquish is powered by PlatinumGames’ proprietary graphics engine. I like referring to Vanquish as a remaster and not just a PC port, since it looks and runs much better than I recall playing and finishing it on my PS3. I remember that during intense fighting, 30fps was a luxury and I had to contend with micro stuttering as well. I endured, since the game is captivating enough. Considering my current PC, I’d never wish to play in those conditions ever again. As for the PC remaster I’m writing about today, it features ambient occlusion, better shadows and the textures are crisper and more detailed. There are sporadic low-res assets but overall, on PC you’ll experience the ultimate Vanquish version if it’s eye candy you’re after.
In pure Japanese video game tradition, the majority of the game’s file size is reserved by its frequent full-motion video sequences. For screenshot enthusiasts out there, F8 is gonna be you new best friend in Vanquish. You can instantly hide the User Interface by pressing that button and even play the game like that, if you wish. It does involve an extra layer of challenge, having to aim with no crosshair or any sort of pointers and visual aides, but I believe the added immersion is worth it in the end. The first person cutscenes & visor feedback seem locked to 30+ frames per second.
One weird thing I noticed is that once I deactivated the in-game Vertical Sync option and enabled the one from the Nvidia Control Panel, I had no more frame rate dips when playing maxed out on 4K resolution. Stable 60 fps, unlike the rare dips to 50s and 40s experienced before I found the work-around. Playing completely without any Vsync method, was out of the question since I despise screen tearing almost as much as unstable frame rate. On a capable system (i7 6700K, 32GB RAM and GTX 1070), this has to be a technical bug related to the native Vsync support, not my hardware. If you’re running Vanquish on 2K res or just 1080p, no worries. You’ll see 100+ frames per second even during the most heated battles.
Simply superb. I have yet to meet a Japanese title, regardless of its gaming genre, which would feature a weak or non-existent OST. Sound effects and the soundtrack are important, but the voice acting was the one which really stood out. Full emotional range and the occasional joke thrown in for good measure. Absolutely nothing to complain here.
The classic third person cover-based shooter formula which features some nice extra elements into the mix. Sam’s powerful suit has a propulsion system which allows him to rapidly slide for brief periods of time and thus enabling him to engage his robotic nemeses through all sorts of stunts. The second special element is a form of “bullet time” which automatically triggers once the protagonist is either low on health or attacked by something far deadlier than small caliber. We’re talking of shooting down missiles as they approach you kind of stunt. And that shall happen more often than not. Whether he’s backed up by AI-controlled marines or not, Gideon shall always be outnumbered and outgunned.
Without the use of tactics and patience (by carefully moving from cover to cover), you won’t last long out in the open. Luckly, DARPA has provided Sam with an extended and complex arsenal. Any type of projectiles you may think of, it’s probably included in Vanquish. The scarcity of the ammo is never a real issue since you can either loot neon-lit weapon crates or assist fellow soldiers by healing them and they shall happily share mags or grenades. Some boss fights follow a strict pattern, but most allow enough strategic freedom to approach from multiple locations. Quick Time Events are usually the culminating point for your aggressors. Without a proper coup de grâce it really wouldn’t feel rewarding at all, defeating an enemy several times bigger than our cybernetically enhanced hero.
An already excellent third person shooter even on last gen consoles, the PC version of Vanquish does not disappoint in any capacity. We’ve all heard or saw firsthand what a disastrous PC port can do for a gamer’s perception and even motivation. Seeing the favorite game you once played on a console, perform far worse on a PC, can really make a gamer question the support for his or her hobby of choice. All things considered, the Steam version of Vanquish is fully worth its price tag. You can always wait for a quality bundle or Steam Sale and pick it up at a nice discount, but know that even if you pay the full price, you won’t regret it.

I would describe Rocksmith as a learning tool disguised at a game. I have used it for practicing guitar and bass, and my skills have developed a lot since I started playing the game.
There is a plethora of features to be found in Rocksmith 2014, the most prominent being Learn a Song mode. In Learn a Song mode, the game basically plays similarly to Guitar Hero, except the notes may span the entire fretboard of the actual instrument you are playing (guitar/bass). When you are first beginning, the songs are watered-down. Rocksmith decides to just throw a few notes at you at a time, until you get the hang of it, then it gradually increases the complexity until you are playing it just the way it was recorded. The game registers all kinds of techniques that are used with a guitar, such as hammer-ons pull-offs, slides, bends, harmonics, palm-mutes, etc. The Real-Tone cable just knows. You can unlock new songs by doing missions, you can also buy song-packs as DLC.
Another feature I enjoy is Session Mode. It allows you to program a backing band that plays according to the scale that you are playing. It sounds really sweet and gives you a feel of playing with an actual band. Session mode also gives you some pretty good tutoring about scales, and playing with a band if you follow the in-game missions. Also, the game offers a huge amount of video based, interactive guitar lessons, to help out the newbies, and experienced players too.
Rocksmith has local multiplayer for Score-Attack mode, Session mode, and Learn a Song mode. It works great, you just need to have two of the Real-Tone cables (and two guitars, of course.)
There is a tone designer within Rocksmith, which basically allows you to choose equipment and effects for the game to synthesise. Allow me to say, the game sounds almost as good as my amplifier through my stereo, and the latency for playing a note is unnoticable. You can unlock new sounds for your guitar, just by playing the game.
Rocksmith also offers arcade-style games to help you practice with techniques, which are pretty fun, to say the least. I have put in a lot of hours just trying to get the achievements in these, and I'm still working at it.
Does anyone else play this? Add me through Steam if you do, I would love to have some friends to compare scores with and stuff. I got it around Christmas time and I'm up to 250 hours through Steam (only counting online sessions.)
