Stories Untold presents as a text adventure with graphical elements, but is primarily a first person puzzle game akin to
, with the occasional text adventure or first person exploration section. It contains some really great writing and atmosphere.
The story starts out strong but eventually undermines itself with a twist which is less interesting than what was originally presented. The final episode is tedious as hell. It explains what's going on in the first 5 seconds, yet proceeds to drag you through an extensive exposition which just feels like going through the motions.
There are technical issues. The system requirements are very high for an adventure game, especially one which appears to be a text adventure. The text prints out very slowly on the screen with a typical laptop CPU. This game should have been optimised before release.
There are design issues. In text-adventure scenes, you have to wait for the same text you've already read to slowly print out every time you return to a location you've already been. There is no way to skip this animation. There is also no way to skip any cutscenes or dismiss any dialog. Compounding this, there is no save game feature - you have to play each episode in a single sitting.
In the final episode, the text parser becomes very pedantic about which keyword you need to progress. The designers did not try very hard to make it robust to synonyms. Therefore, this game suffers from an issue which has plagued text adventures since the 1970's - the player knows exactly what to do to progress, but the game frustratingly won't allow them to do it.
There are show-stopping bugs. There is a point in episode 4 where a required switch becomes inoperable if you hit it too early. But because the game revolves around switch and lever puzzles, it's not apparent there's even anything wrong. This bug has affected many people, according to the forums, yet wasn't fixed. I had to restart the episode over from the beginning. Twice. This sealed my opinion of the game.
I enjoyed this game up until the final episode, where a combination of design oversights, dull writing and bugs infuriated me. Logical or not, we tend to enjoy an experience as much as we enjoy how it ends.

It's probably the most impressive and captivating experience I've had playing an "adventure" game. I've bought it after having read a lot of praises from various sources but without knowing exactly what to expect. The fact that it was inspired by old text adventure games immediately captured my attention, having played a lot of them during the eighties. The presentation and attention to detail is incredibile, a work done clearly by people of superior talent. But after the first chapter a big "meh" resounded in my head, mainly for two reasons. First the parser was very poor, I was expecting a lot more in this regard and second the story itself, while somewhat original, in the end appeared to me no more than a spooky novel for teenagers. I decided to move to the next chapter anyway and luckly my first impressions were totally wrong. Everything is connected and is a part of a bigger scheme, as the story unfolds everything start to make sense and literally makes the player live a surreal and disturbing experience. Nothing must be taken for granted in this game and the ability to constantly surprise the player without cheap "methods" is one of its most amazing aspects. In the end Stories Untold is the most refreshing and "mature" (from a design, aesthetic and narrative point ov view) that I've played during 2017 and I highly recommend it to everyone but especially to older players who can understand all the references and the zeitgesit that the game so masterfully depicts.

Most games have you playing as the hero of the story which is fun, but you know what is a nice change of pace? Being the villian, with your army of weird, big eared minions you aim to take over the world.
The game combines elements of rts and makes them a lot simpliar and mashes it with some spice adding some RPG and loot collecting in their too, just for good measure. This game is incredibly fun, from everything like the minions short dialogue saying weird things like "cheese" and "for you master" to the simple but fun combat using spells and your handy war axe. ANother interesting system they have in play for this game is the castle design. Through-out the game you are gathering money to upgrade and build up your castle to make it the evil pent house that you dreamed it would be. Which honestly.....is a lot of fun. I found myself striving to get the new banner to add to my collection.
The game also has a bit of puzzle solving inside it's depths, now if you dont like puzzle solving, these are really quick and easy, but satisfying puzzels. Most of the time you will have to move something out of your way or building a wheel by using your minions, this honestly didnt feel out of place in this game, it wasnt random it made you feel like the evil leader you wanted to feel like. Watching your minions strive in and out, straining their back and arms to move things for you. They will even die for you if there is the promise of restoring health or mana. There are different types of minions that you can unlock, at first you start out with the standard brown minions, which are your main source of attack. You then have your blue minions which can move through water and heal other minions, you also have your red minions which are basically pyro's slinging flames like the little bosses they are. This brings more variety into the gameplay, I feel like if these different types of minions wernt there the gameplay would get stale pretty fast but luckily they are there.
You will encounter many bosses that stand in your way of becoming overlord of the world. They each have different attacks and look extremly different from one another. Something I would say that enoys me is that for atleast an hour into the game i still hadnt encountered any different enemies, all i was fighting was these little dwarf characters called halflings and the occasional boss, but if you stick with it like I did, you will find that there is a larger enemy variety later on in the game which motivates you to keep on playing. There is a bunch of quests in the game, this includes sidequests for you Wow fans. These were fun and gave me an excuse to go attacking halfling stongholds which honestly is always fun. I can see this game lasting around 16-24 hours, 24 if you complete all sidequest's and randomly generated strongholds. But i can see the average player who does some sidequests getting around 14 hours from it which for 5 dollars is insane, then  you also have the multiplayer which i havnt even delved into yet, i will update this review with my response to the multiplayer once i have gotten a solid feel of it.
I addore this game and after i beat it will be getting Overlord 2 because well so far im loving this one, if you have even the slightest interest in being a deathly overlord but also like a bit of humour from your main advisor and minions in general then please get this game, it is worth your money.
-Joshua Upham

I had such high hopes for this after the first two episodes. They were short, tense, and just the right amount of interactive, and fascinating to boot. Unfortunately, the third episode was a ♥♥♥♥ing disaster, an exercise in pointless frustration. If you like squinting at a blurry microfilm and working out what to do next based on elaborate code protocols I can't stop you, but it absolutely broke immersion for me and by the end of the episode I didn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the plot. By the way, you can hold the right mouse button to zoom, which they don't tell you in the game, and which only helps a little. Fourth episode provided totally unnecessary exposition on the first three episodes, and provided an overarching story that the game didn't need and that I didn't care much about. It mainly frustrated me some more. If you're going to get this game anyway, get it on sale and play only the first two episodes.
Other qualms: a text-based game that doesn't account for alternative keyboard layouts, and doesn't let you change the keybindings for first-person movement controls. I had to switch to QWERTY for the first-person sections and then back to Dvorak for text entry. The game also doesn't respect basic conventions of text interfaces, like Tab switching text fields, so I had to move to mouse and then back to keyboard quite a bit while I was figuring out the puzzles. A weirdly specific final puzzle that requires you to
. No way to save in the middle of an episode, so if you quit, you have to start over. And the cutscenes are unskippable.
Basically a 4/10, 9/10 if you ignore the ending half of the game. It's a terrible missed opportunity -- a series of four independent episodes that were only thematically connected would have been much better.

In addition to the mobs are the other players and if you're not playing a PVE server then an additional layer of mistrust and trepidation of dying is added to the game.
It's safe to stay in the Safe Zones, and it's safe to camp atop a multi-story building.  But the hunger bar, loot drops and nether protection device failures are a sufficient motivator to keep the player moving and to keep them tense and twitchy.

I recommend this game to people, but I also recommend NOT reading the reviews. Especially the positive ones. This game is very well made, beautiful beautiful beautiful, and thought-provoking! But the hype from all the positive reviews and the trailers set the bar so high before experiencing the game, that I was somewhat dissapointed after finishing it.
There are a couple things they did with this game that I reallyyy appreciate. The monsters. I'm a wuss. Unlike games like Deadspace, Outlast, etc. you didn't dread moving onto the next level stressing about what type of OP monsters would threaten your survival. Throughout most of the game, you could relax, explore the environment, appreicate the underwater beauty and if you came across a chapter that featured a monster(s), it was really no big deal. They were deadly and ugly, yes. And there were some chase scenes, yes. But you didn't get bombarded by them every single minute of the game, which I thought was nice. You could actually focus and follow along with the story. Not really any cheap scares. The monsters were very well done. You would get hints about their characteristics (to survive) and you always were notified when they were nearby (screen would blur/get static-ey). On another note, your source of light is infinite. In Amnesia you needed to always find lamp fluid to be able to shed light to survive. In Outlast, you needed batteries for your camcorder to survive.
Your companion. Catherine, your "AI" companion was a very nice addition. In these types of games, it's always nice to have someone to talk to on the other end of the radio. It's a bit overused, but in this genre it really is comforting psychologically to hear banter between your character and the other person. I really cherished the few interactions the protagonist had with other NPCs in the game. I wanted more of that. It was extremely interesting interacting with the few bots.
I personally couldn't get attached very much to the story like the other reviewers have. I got super attached to Catherine, and I liked the story in general but the main protagonist just wasn't a good fit. I just couldn't quite connect/get hooked. And believe me, I wanted to. I just didn't like the dialogue written for some of the characters. The dialogue could have been much better for a game with a premise such as this one. Choices were alright. There were times where I wanted to be able to make a choice, but the story couldn't progress any other way. There were other times when you made a choice, but it didn't really affect the story at all. It was just to make a choice with no outcome, which I guess is refreshing from most games nowadays.
If your computer can handle high texture settings, boy, get them as high up as possible. I slightly lowered my resolution so I could bump up the texture effects and wow, what a world of difference. I spent a lot of time in the game just admiring the stunning attention to detail they put into the atmosphere. The lighting was spectacular. The progression was perfectly paced and not rushed or overly lengthy. I just sincerely wished I played the game without reading the reviews or viewing the trailers.

Orwell. If you've read the description of the game you probably know basically what it is about. You are an investigator for Orwell, a government project to spy on citizens in an attempt to stop terrorist attacks. You are tasked to investigate the bombing of the Freedom Plaza. Anything I say after that is entering spoiler territory which I won't do in this review because the story an important part of what made this game so good. But I'm getting a little bit ahead of myself.
Before I go into the nitty gritty of why I really enjoyed the game, I will give a very quick summary of why I think you should purchase this game if you have the money, whether it's on sale or not.
Pros:
- The Art Style is Fitting For The Game.
- The Gameplay is Innovative and Overall Fun.
- The Story is In-Depth and Intriguing The Whole Way Through.
- The Characters are Well Written and Feel Real.
- The Game Doesn't Drag On.
Cons:
- The Game Only Lasts About 5 Hours.
- The Ending Feels Like It Came A Bit Too Soon.
- The Twists In The Story Were A Mixed Bag, Some Good, Some Bad.
So that is my very brief review of the game. I think the thing you need to know the most is this is 100% a story game. The gameplay is fun but it's just a means of getting more of the story. But goddamn the story is fantastic. So, if you are looking for a game that you can get 100s of hours out of, this is not the game. But if you are looking for a story which makes you question what's right and wrong and overall just think, this is a must buy.
That wraps up my brief summary of the game, now I am going to go more in depth on why I think the game worked as well as it did. However I am not going to spoil the story at all because it is extremely important that you go in blind. If you know what happens, you are not going to have as good of an experience that I did. Lastly, a quick disclaimer. When I played this game, two of my friends were watching. This is a doubled edged sword because on one hand, it made my experience better and I got to examine multiple perspectives. But on the other hand, it may not be possible for you to have friends with you as you play. I don't think this is crucial to enjoy the game but I also think it does help at least a little. So, without further ado, this is my review of Orwell.
Gameplay:
The game does an outstanding job of making you feel like you really are an investigator. It does this by letting you find the story for yourself by letting you search through all the files for yourself. It does guide you a little bit by locking who you are allowed to collect information on by chapter but I feel like this was a fair balance of gameplay and immersion. There had to be a line between the two and I felt this was completely reasonable. However I do have some gripes with the gameplay, one specifically. For example while I played there were multiple instances where it wouldn't let me progress because I hadn't added something the game deemed important. The problem is, it doesn't do a great job telling you what is important and what isn't. Sometimes it felt like I'd just have to add random bits of information just so I could find actual important information later on. Other than that problem though, there wasn't really anything else gameplay wise that annoyed me. Overall, I think that the gameplay was solid for what it was, a story game.
Art Style:
This is going to be shorter than the other sections because it is the thing I have the least to talk about. The art was fine. It wasn't outstanding but it also wasn't terrible. There were certain instances where the art did subtract from the game though, especially with some of the characters (Josef's picture while fishing). However, the few times it did subtract from the game were made up by the dozens of times it made the characters feel more like people. Overall, the art was decent.
Story/Characters:
This is going to be hard to talk about because of the fact that I am not going to spoil anything so I’ll make it pretty quick. The story is pretty great, mainly because of the fact that you never are 100% sure who the bombed the Plaza. Sure as I played I suspected people but it kept changing over and over. I went from one person to the next to the next back to the first one and in the end, it was a huge surprise. It kept you thinking the whole time and that was extremely well done. One of the reasons it kept you thinking was because of the characters who are all written really well. They all feel like real people because they aren’t only doing things that relate to what you are looking for which makes sense. It’s something that I think a lot of games forget to do. Real people have lives outside of the one story that is being told to you. I’ve played games where the characters only seem to exist in the bounds of the story you are being told. They literally don’t do anything but help you on your quest which, in the moment, sounds fine but when you look back at it, it makes no sense. But I’m rambling longer than I need to. Basically, the characters are well written and feel real and the story is compelling.
That’s basically all I have to say. The only point I didn’t cover is the fact that the game doesn’t drag on and there isn’t that much to talk about. It was a quick game but it didn’t feel too quick and that’s really it. Orwell is a game that, if you have the money to buy it and are fine with buying a short game, I highly recommend it.

Orwell is one of the most interesting games I've played in a while; it's well thought out, the game experience is smooth and natural and the core elements are solid. It's arguably not a game for everyone but it's a fantastic achievement, that should be beyond doubt.
So who is it for? I guess that's the core question for an indie, niche production such as this so let's get right to it: Orwell is for the player looking for a contemplative, narrative-driven challenge that you can play on your own time. If you like unravelling a mystery carefully, if you like narrative driven games or if you really like surveying people, then this is definitely for you. Who's it not for? It's not for players looking for explosions, fast-paced action or who don't like to read. You read in this game, quite a lot. It's not like reading a novel but expect reading.
In Orwell, you take on the role of an analyst who's trying to unravel a terrorist plot using the governments newest super-surveillance tool, Orwell. The system highlights 'datachunks' in POIs internet activity, chat activity, phone activity, anything really, and it's your job to decide what information is pertinent and what isn't. You build files on suspects while you slowly expand the network of POIs and what you choose to include is what decides the 'system's' attitude towards groups and individuals. Of course, the question soon beckons; should you be doing any of this?
As the story moves forward, the player is confronted with many choices and they have real consequences for the story, not merely symbolic ones. Furthermore, while the system highlights important information, some decisions can only be made accurately through the players own memory and deductions from text pieces that at the time perhaps seemed inconsequential. It's a game that rewards the player for keeping up and thinking for themselves.

I kind of wish I could put a "Wait and see" option instead of yes or no for recommending the game. Scroll past the lists to see why you should keep an eye on it.
Would I recommend this game to the average player? Not really, mostly because there are just better shooters out there. What this game has over other shooters comes down to three things right now at the current version:
Right now the game is just a basic team shooter, much like Counter strike or Call of Duty.
1-Faction/gear system and a leveling of gear more than just your guns. 4 factions to choose from each with different priorities/styles for how they fight.
2-The setting. If you like post apocolyptic settings this game does it well. Any STALKER fans out there will be right at home.
3-Anomalies and Artifacts. If you have played STALKER, you know what these are, if you havent... They are basically these spots/areas of the maps that will hurt/kill you. The catch is you can harvest artifacts from the Anomalies that give you powerful bonuses like increased health regen, reduce damage, etc.
Thats really it, when it comes down to it thats all it offers and the grind for new gear is extremely long.
Four main issues with this game:
1- the shooting is a little wonky, because they are framework they are setting up there is this delay and sway of the game kind of like ArmA but not in a good way. CS:GO has a much better responsiveness.
2- The game is grindy, and I mean seriously grindy. When I play Im always at the top of the scoreboard but I havent put a single dime into the game and I have two of the four factions to tier 6 out of 10. You get to a certain point where getting new guns/armor just has such a large gap that one of its main attractions is lost.
3&4- Lack of players and a tier system: these issues kind of chew into each other.... Basically there are 10 tiers of gear in each faction. The highest piece of gear equipped is what the matchmaker bases your matches on. Which is cool but it has this added issue where most of the players you fight against will either have worse or better gear than you. Now why this isnt much of an issue compared to games like World of Tanks. You still will lose out on fights purely because the guy you are fighting has better armor and a better gun than you. Add this in where the player base is split up based on tiers and the small player base gets smaller. Which the match maker will expand the search. So if you arent careful you can be a tier 4 player fighting against players with tier 8 or 9 gear because there was no one to play against. The player base is so small they only have EU and RU servers.
REASON TO WATCH THE GAME: One reaosn and one reason only, Free Play. basically STALKER but open world with other players in a pvp and pve enviorment. Where you can actually escape with your gear and not lose it as horribly as you do when you die like in games like DayZ. Here is there run down on how free play will work:
The issue with free play? they promise to have a playable version of free play at the end of each year, and fail to meet it. This has been going on for years.

I picked up Delicious - Emily's New Beginning after watching someone online play it. I wasn't familiar with the franchise at all, but that didn't take away from my enjoyment of the game. Other things almost did though.
Emily's New Beginning follows Emily, who opens her cafe again after having her daughter, Paige. Although her family comes in to help her with the restaurant, conflict ensues between them. They also start having conflict with another restaurant owner in town. The version available on Steam has 50 levels, where the player goes through time management tasks that get steadily more complex as the game goes on.
Pros:
- Silly game that doesn't take itself seriously.
- Cute, smooth graphics.
- Tasks start easy but get more complicated.
- Controls are simple - everything is done with the mouse.
- Most achievements are easy, but some offer a little bit of a challenge.
- Family friendly.
Cons:
- Others have stated that there's another version with 10 extra levels. Could be a downside for people who love the franchise.
- There are earlier Delicious games that aren't available on Steam as well. This can make the player feel a little lost in regards to the story and character relationships.
- Taking care of Paige during the game is irritating most of the time.
- Challenges aren't really all that challenging.
- Story is cheasy and some-what dull.
Emily's New Beginning is a fun time management game for people who enjoy that sort of thing. People who enjoy the Delicious franchise will enjoy this addition. Those new to time management games may one to try a different Delicious title before jumping to this one. Even though it's the first in the series available on Steam, there are later games that are better.

I liked Delicious Emily: Message in a Bottle well enough to buy the gamehouse bundle. I was looking forward to more of the DE addictive gameplay and ludicrous storylines.
Delicious Emily: New Beginnings is the earliest game in the series to be ported to steam, and it's just missing a fair few QOL features. The entertainers often get in the way and block the customers, you don't get a "quick" bonus, different customers like different food and your menu has to account for that (a feature that adds complexity but no actual rewarding gameplay or challenge), you can't see which levels you've aced while finding the mouse, and there are a few bugs. The game also thinks that the best way to make you identify with Emily as a new mother is to make "mind the baby" a constant, draining, infuriating task. Which... true to life, I guess?
The plot isn't even satisfyingly insanely sitcom-ey. Literally the wackiest thing is a stuffy chef who keeps stubbing his toes on a series of objects you can't actually stub your toes against. Emily just juggles a series of restaurants along with a baby (sadly, she doesn't actually juggle the baby), then ends up buying a home. Which leads to the start of the next game - Emily's Home Sweet home. A game which (hopefully) features all the quality of life features I've been missing, as well as the sitcom stupidity I've been looking forward to.

I do recommend this game overall, although I beat it in two hours.

This was not my favourite of the series, the story felt like filler and I never found it that compelling. The story, for what it is, is Emily has decided to go back to work in her restaurant after having her baby Paige, and the series of events that push her from one restaurant to another because there's always a problem, usually stemming from her insistence in bringing baby Paige to the restaurant every day. Fortunately Paige is a magic baby and rarely cries (and then only when you've let her wonder round for too long) and entertains most (but not all) guests. The central tension of the story is between Emily's family focused style, and her competitor Wu's non-family friendly style. And instead of recognising that hey, both restaurant styles are valid there's nothing but competition and bickering with Wu being a child-hating card-board cut-out.
But that's enough critiquing the story of a cooking time-management sim. As to gameplay it's enjoyable enough, the usual 'grab the required dishes, throw them at customers, get their money at the till' fair. It's usually challenging enough to be fun but easy enough to not get frustrating.
All in all a decent game, though I didn't find the story engaging the gameplay was enjoyable.

You can skip to the bottom of the review for the TL;DR
The Darkness 2 is one of my personal favourites in a long list of games on my steam account. It is everything you could possibly want from a first person shooter that has a noire feeling to it, with light horror elements and an interesting story that will keep you hooked.
The story, without spoiling anything, is a direct sequel for the first part, meaning eveything ties up and the timelines are logical. Basically: you are Jackie Estacado, a young mafia member with dark powers beyond control,that seeks vengeance.The plot gets better and makes more sense as you play through the game. You have choices, tough it's not a primary element of the game and the story and levels are rather linear, choices only representing the question "do you want one more cutscene?", most of the times.
The gameplay is where this game really excels at. You have the basic fps mechanics with a strong emphasis on the signature dual wield of Jackie, which can carry 3 weapons with him- a primary, a secondary and another secondary, with the option to dual the secondaries or carefully aim with them. Besides that, the power of the darkness system is truly a breath of fresh air for the genre. Jackie has, at all times, 2 demon arms besides him that, if controlled right, can do huge amounts of damage just on their own. Tactically combined with the generic fps mechanics, they can adapt to any situation and turn the tides of battle in a second with specific skills. They can slash, execute enemies in exchange for health, ammo, etc, grab objects from the enviroment to use them as either defense or gory offense. Your godly powers go away in the light tough, as the game offers dynamic light gameplay elements, requiring you to think strategically before encounters as you shoot lights out and cut down heads.
The game also has a skill tree system, featuring 4 different skill trees that all branch out from a primary ability and that can be leveled simultaneously. The primary skill adds a new mechanic, eating the hearts of enemies (dead ones, of course) and replinishing health by it and gaining more points towards the purchase of your next skill. Every skill tree has a speciality and any skill you get can drastically change the gameplay and your methods of brutally murdering bad guys, making the end game the most fun of all, as you got so many tools in your arsenal that every situation is your playground. The skills you get also scale with your own, as you learn to further multitask the demon arms while still keeping concentrated on the basic firefights and making the ultimate killing machine out of you. That's why even the hardest difficulty doesn't feel unfair in any way, but challenging and forcing you to sharpen those reflexes make use of everything you learn. It's a masterpiece to be quite honest with you.
Just so you can get the idea of how deep this game can be (story-wise), before the TL;DR, I'll leave you with my favourite monologue of Jackie Estacado: "Time slips away from you. And then, all of a sudden, it's like you're sitting in a theatre, watching a movie of your own life. You're a fu**ing movie star. And you're killing all the bad guys-tearing them limb from limb.And you feel good, you look good. F**k, you ARE good. And then you realize something: everyone else in the theatre? They're screaming, because they're watching a horror movie...and you're not the hero...you're the monster..."
TL;DR: A great atmospheric game, filled with gore and overall dark themes. One of the best story-driven first person shooters out there, featuring great, complex and innovative gameplay mechanics by using the power of the darkness. A solid 10/10 in my opinion, at least for the singleplayer.

Rocksmith is a great great if not the best starting point for learning the electric guitar in my opinion. Yes, a personal guitar teacher would be great. It would also be great if you could study music and art at the same time and tour with a band to learn your instrument.
the problem is, not everybody has the time and oportunity to do this kind of stuff, it also involves quite a commitment. This is where rocksmith shines, it gets you playing. Despite all the flaws and the lack of theory it teaches you it gets you started soemwhere you gain not only an understanding on how to play the instrument but also an actual feeling for it.
I'm looking back on playing the guitar for around 1000 hours now thanks to rocksmith, whereas in total the rocksmith hours float around 300ish i think... the other hours i played outside of rocksmith using whatever rocksmith taught me to understand and work on music theory to become an actual musician the way i like it.
Rocksmith will teach the fastest and the most effective on how to improve technically on the guitar. How your fingers move on the fretboard, how to hit your stuff. It won't teach you how to compose a song, or what actual music theory is, but let me tell you this:
it's great WHEN you decide to dip into music theory that your hands are not holding you back anymore because you can translate what you learn so much faster than if you had to learn this from scratch as well. (and THAT is boring as hell).
10/10 for this life changing game.

I really don't understand why this game gets as much hate as it does, I rarely write reviews for any games but after looking at all the negativity this game has gotten I figured i'd chuck in my few cents.
So basically this game is at its core a Fighting game, it essentially is a Hybrid between a Fighting game and your standard Multiplayer options, such as Team Deathmatch - Skirmish, Domination - Dominion - Elimination - 4v4 with one life and then your Fighting game modes like 2v2 and 1v1.
The fighting mechanics are quite unique and it can be very engaging trying to outsmart your opponent and adjusting to their playstyle, learning new techniques you can string together and of course can be very satisfying if you come up against a decent player and manage to win the fight.
The problems lie mostly with connection issues and the way certain people like to troll and cheese, however this can be countered once you learn the pattern and how to adjust to people who play like this, but it will still be frustrating when you come across these kind of players, and really these type of players are in every game.
As for the connection issues I find that the majority of the time its perfectly fine, I rarely get disconnected or have any problems, sometimes it will have to re-adjust mid-match but its not really a big deal, and it will probably be improved down the road, as it already looks like it has since season 2.
The game itself like I said is very unique and if you like a difficult game with a large learning curve then I would urge you to give this game a shot.
Story mode is also quite fun, has a different feel to multiplayer and isn't just multiplayer modes in a story setting, I would of liked the campaign to be abit longer not gonna lie, but overall I did enjoy playing it and it has quite abit of replay value due to the fact you can find crates, steel and emblem pieces to use for multiplayer, it can also be COOP with a friend.
As for the Season Pass, this has been something alot of people have moaned about and it is another thing I do not understand, as unlike other games, such as Call of Duty, Battlefield or anything with a season pass, instead of giving any DLC exclusively to season pass owners and splitting the community and forcing you to fork out more money to obtain the DLC.
This game has done it like Rainbow Six, where if you get the Season Pass, you will get access to things sooner, and you won't have to pay for the new characters or anything with Ingame currency, which I might add can be a fair bit, on top of that you get free champion status from time to time as i did at the beginning of Season 1 and 2, I chose to get the Season pass to support the game and because i wanted to get 110% out of it and I personally don't regret it.
But anyway, thats my opinion of the game, as you can see i've gotten alot of hours in and definitely got my moneys worth, I hope this review helps atleast one of you to give this game abit of a chance.

What is Vanquish? Vanquish is a Gears of War and Devil May Cry (DmC) lovechild with a healthy helping of japanime exaggeration.  Does that sound appealing?  If so, then you'll like Vanquish.  As far as the game goes, however, don't expect overwhelming value or playable sustainability.  As such Vanquish (great name) is a mixed bag of contradictions.  The game is possessed of solid graphics (for 2010-11) and often visually-interesting character/weapon/map design.  The characters animate fluidly and dynamically.  Weapon play is fantastic and the actual combat is by far the greatest element in Vanquish.  It is, in fact, the combat and visceral animations that carry an otherwise mediocre (at best) game.
The game packs a variety of weapons and many feel really good and are justified by their varying effects.  Melee is also competently executed and the game's primary slide movement adds a speed and impetus that few games can hope to match.  In a way, this game feels like Mass Effect 2 on fast forward xx4.  The game runs well and is well composed, rarely exhibiting slow downs and never crashing.  However, the game is fraught with an avalanche of flaws that would bury any normal title.  Platinum's impeccable work on combat keep the title from becoming a putrid mess.
The game lacks any multiplayer and, instead, encourages logevity by replaying chapters to find limited easter eggs and to best your previous performance.   However, many maps are very samey both in appearance and in objective and while the combat feels great, replaying the same maps over and over can quickly feel staid, unless you are an avid gamer completionist.  Therefore, one quick, 6 hour play through Vanquish will display 85% of what the game offers and value becomes a tough sell for the title.  While the game runs well, it is not super optimized for PC, despite mouse and keyboard gunplay being mostly superior to a gamepad/controller.  Twenty USD is a comparatively big price to demand for a game that is almost a decade old and that only fashions about 4-8 hours of play value for most gamers.
The music in the game is forgettable at best and obnoxiously laughable at worst, bad textures abound and the maps are extremely linear.  The game has only marginally more exploration than something like House of the Dead.  Even Gears of War had multiple routes you could occasionally take.  Some weapons are significantly weaker/less useful than others and the AI as a whole is as dumb as a box of rocks.  Don't expect intelligent response from enemies and look forward to increasing waves of often cheap mobs that shoot almost a dozen missiles/rockets/grenades/bullets/lasers et al at you at any given time.  The game is rife with quicktime events which showcase some very cool cinematic events.  However, those same cinematic events come at the expense of gameplay as players often don't have a choice in how to proceed during a fight.
Those same quicktime events will, of course, lead to several deaths.  And those events, when coupled with some admittedly cheesy bosses that fire half a dozen wide-range AoE weapons at you at once, will require you to play certain battles over and over.  And over.  And over.  Especially at harder difficulties.  Again, if this is something that you like and you derive satisfaction and achievement from such difficult gameplay executions, you'll probably enjoy it.  However, if you are like me, and just want to enjoy the game's best elements: the combat, without constantly replaying areas and you have better things to do both online and in real life, the game can become obnoxious quickly.
No critique of Vanquish can exist without a short detail of how attrociously juvenile and flat-out dumb the plot is.  As an action game, Vanquish shouldn't be expected to ponder weighty concepts.  The gameplay doesn't have to be remarkably deep either.   However, characters in this game are an insult to "cardboard cutouts" and they act with volatile inconsistency, attempting to kill each other one minute and *literally* protecting each other the next.  The hero protagonist is charged with saving a space colony from destruction and yet the game's end hardly gives you a feeling of success or accomplishment.  The story is hackneyed and, created by a predominantly Japanese developer, is very anti-American in both its context and writing.  There are probably only 6 truly unique characters all game and, therefore, Vanquish feels more like a carnival shooting gallery than a living, breathing world.
In short, after playing hundreds of games on a variety of platforms over the last few decades, I can clearly profess that Vanquish has perhaps one of the top five *worst* plots I've ever encountered.  We're talking Transmorphers/Sharknado/Piranha II plotting bad.  Like, laughably bad.  Ridiculously bad.  And yes...insultingly bad.  The game lacks even a proper ending and instead gives you a chopped, deformed cliffhanger ending.  When considering the music, the shallow gameplay mechanics and horrendous plot, it is almost easy to bash Vanquish. However, the combat, coupled with the visceral graphics keep pulling the player through the game and it's hard not to fall in love with a shooting gallery that feels this good.  I purchased the game for 20 USD and I feel that it was a bit pricey for what I got.
If, however, you can find this title on sale for 10-15 USD, I recommend you pick it up.  It's a solid game that does twitch gallery shooting as well as any other title out there.
Recommended.

I was skeptical at first about spending $60 on For Honor. I took the risk, knowing full well what I might be getting. And I do not regret my purchase one bit. What I don't understand is why it's so loathed...
That's going to be the general gist of my review of For Honor. I know it's going to bring cries that I'm just shilling for Ubisoft or that I'm some rabid fanboy on the defensive, clutching desperately at straws in an attempt to excuse otherwise inexcusable faults in For Honor... but really? Mostly Negative? If you're interested in For Honor, I urge you to take a few moments to read this before deciding to avoid the game yourself because of the negative reviews.
I don't think it really needs repeating, but I'll give a brief overview on the points that I think have been covered well in other reviews already left here on Steam:
Gamplay is incredibly fun, the combat system mixing the simplicity of spectacle fighters with the complexity of traditional fighting games.
The Campaign is nothing to really write home about. It serves the purpose of acting as a sort of extended tutorial/practice mode before you dive into multiplayer, but aside from the occasional DAUBENY! meme, there's nothing too memorable about it. It's not really like we needed an excuse for them to be beating the crap out of each other to begin with.
Matchmaking needs some refining. It's not uncommon for new players to get paired up with veteran, well-geared players in the Dominion, Elimination, and Skirmish matches, where gear actually matters beyond just looking pretty.
Game balance is very much a work in progress. At launch, some characters (Raider and Lawbringer, notably) were rather lacking and difficult to contend against while others (Peacekeeper and Warden, notably) had some insane balance issues that made them outright broken and frustrating to fight against. While several of those issues have been taken care of, there are still some balance concerns in the game.
"But why is this game then listed as Mostly Negative under reviews? This doesn't sound so bad!" you may ask. And you're right, it isn't. But there's some misinformation and bad publicity that has hit For Honor that's swaying people away from it. In reality, For Honor is not as terrible as many of the reviews would have you believe. And -that's- what I wanted to focus my review on. So let's start.
Peer-to-Peer Connectivity and Network Issues: Was Ubisoft Too Cheap or Lazy to get Dedicated Servers?
According to Betteridge's Law of Headlines, No. Many reviews point to peer-to-peer connectivity as some sort of nail-in-the-coffin for For Honor, stating that it makes the game unplayable in its current state and many even suggesting that Ubisoft was either too lazy or too cheep to invest in dedicated servers.
These people have never worked in networking or touched video game netcode in their life.
If they had, they would understand that For Honor, being a fighting game, requires peer-to-peer connectivity. Dedicated servers, which require time to update based on information each client (people playing) sends to them. In a game with so many reaction-based actions, a dedicated server would require netcode which would either make the game a total spamfest of swings with little point in parrying or blocking, or a war of the turtles where attacks that would actually land would be few and far between due to the need for compensation on the part of the netcode to account for the server update rate. Would it be more stable? Yes. Would it be more secure? Yes. But it would not work nearly as well with For Honor's current mechanics. If dedicated servers are needed, then the game is going to need a ground-up overhaul of the gameplay, something that really does -not- need fixing as For Honor's fighting system is an incredible one.
Peer-to-Peer is a necessary evil of For Honor's mechanics and, thankfully, Ubisoft had the foresight to fix the long-loathed "host advantage" of peer-to-peer multiplayer by distributing out the load amongst all players in the session. There are still issues, and you may face problems with connectivity and latency, but these are not problems that would be immediately fixed by a dedicated server. At best, they'd happen slightly less often, and the game would run like a brick in a washing machine. So no, peer-to-peer is not an issue.
Microtransactions?! In my $60 game?! UNACCEPTABLE! - ... Except not really.
I'm sure we're all well acquainted with Ubisoft's usual greed when it comes to games. Especially their rampant use of season passes and half-baked DLC as attempts to milk every nickel and dime they can out of a game before they're outright forced to publish another game. One would think the addition of microtransactions into the game would be just a continuation of that, right? Well, no... and that's the part that kinda terrifies me because, for once, Ubisoft actually didn't make the greedy decision here...
I know, I know, it sounds hard to believe, but bear with me while I explain. In For Honor, Steel is the currency used to buy just about everything. Gear, outfits, emotes, executions... all bought and paid for with Steel. You can earn Steel by playing games, completing daily challenges, or doing the campaign and snagging the collectibles hidden throughout it. However, you also have the option to buy packs of Steel from Ubisoft. "PAY TO WIN!" shrieks the crowd that has never touched a Korean MMO before and wouldn't know what "pay-to-win" was if it actually ate their wallet. The only "power" one can really buy comes in one of two forms: a feat pack for heroes (which you'll unlock for each hero with just a few hours of gameplay, it really doesn't take that long), or gear (which only really matters in Dominion, Elimination, or Skirmish modes. If you're dueling or brawling, gear is just for show). Even the gear, however, doesn't give a definitve advantage, as each gear piece comes with a bonus to one stat (like revenge duration or attack damage) at the cost of another (like increasing cooldowns on your feats or increasing the stamina it costs to use each attack). This is, of course, all subject to balance problems, but that will come with time.
In what little time I've played (yes, 100 hours [at time of writing] is not that much compared to what a LOT in the community have put in), I've earned probably upwards of 50,000 steel. Just doing dailies and playing matches. this is more than enough to purchase whatever goodies in game you'd like.
Ubisoft was actually not greedy about this. Purchasing Steel is simply an option left to those who play a bit more casually and think that the time they'd spend earning that steel is worth more than the money they'd spend to get the same amount. It's a convenience, nothing more.
Balance, Patches, and... Ubisoft actually listening to the community?!
Again, I know, reading that must have felt like reading the headline "Lasting Peace in Middle East Achieved," but I'm actually serious. While it has taken some time, between launch and now, allow me to go over some of the community complaints that have been had regarding For Honor:
Peacekeeper light attack spam is annoying and overpowered - Addressed
Warden vortex is unfair and not fun to go against - Addressed
Lawbringer is too weak for the job he's expected to perform in the meta - Addressed
Netcode is unstable and a lot of disconnects have happened - Addressed; Ongoing patches still occurring to optimize
Steel is too difficult to earn outside of buying it - Addressed; rewards increased up to 50% just for playing
Revenge stats on gear are too strong - Addressed
This is just a small sample of the issues For Honor players have brought up, and many of them have already been addressed!

Review:
Orwell is a love letter to Orwellian fiction. It is a plot filled with mystery and intrigue that evolves fast enough so you will never think about getting bored. I especially enjoyed how the game doesn’t paint the organization you work for as inherently bad/evil. Flawed, but in a way that makes it real, not malicious. This gives each individual person the chance to come to their own conclusions about this potential future.
There are a few issues with this game such as certain data chunks having potentially vague outcomes (much like a Bioware dialog wheel). Also the slow writing in personal messages, while realistic, did get a bit tiresome where you can read the text 3 times faster than they can type. And sadly you cannot walk away, wait for the convo to finish, and then come back, as certain data chunks are time sensitive (I learned this lesson the hard way). All those issues are trivial however and I did not feel that they ever interfere with my ability to play and enjoy the game; a minor annoyance. The ending however, did rub me the wrong way.
Without spoiling anything, I will just say that the ending is multiple choice depending on how you act. Initially I enjoyed this reveal, yet ended up accidentally choosing an ending I did not want, after not being bale to figure out how to select the one that would make the most sense with my character/play style. Then once I realized what I had done I tried to go back, however once you beat the game that save file is forever stuck at the epilogue after the choice. This requires you to complete an additional play through.
With all that said I would definitively recommend this game!

Rating:  8/10 for story/gameplay, 6/10 for game length
Summary: A pretty good game that makes you think about how people see things from different perspectives. From the Government's point of view: you're doing a good thing. From the citizen's point of view: invasive and controlling. As you play this game you will constantly think about this as you go through your work. As far as I'm aware, there are 3 endings to the game, and make for roughly 3-5 hours playthrough depending on how quickly you work through it.
Positives:
-A game that makes you think. If you're like me and you try and solve the game before it's over, it will have you guessing yourself over and over, because the ending is not quite who you suspect. (Even if you do guess correctly - it's not likely through the means that you're thinking.)
-The style of the game is very pretty and modern, with the futuristic features being clean and eye catching. Personally, I loved the layout and setting of the game.
- Time IS important! Like in real life, if you find critical information that might affect something in your life and don't immediately act to stop it, you may face consequences. (I learned the hard way when I Alt + Tabbed out of the game for a minute.)
Negatives:
-Not many, honestly. The story was great and consistent and always had you going back to double-check your infirmation. (Great thing imo, but I guess people can see this as tedious.)
- There are occassionally blips where it says there is more possible information for you to look at, but there isn't.
- It's too short in my opinion. You only really play 'one' story, and I feel like you should be able to play a couple more than that, and the ending you get should influence it too.

Jazzpunk is a difficult game to review, but I'll give it my best shot.
Wow would be a simple word to describe this game. If there is such a thing as a God, it is Jazzpunk.
Jazzpunk is a very much experimental game, infusing just about everything under the sun with puns. Alot of puns. Jazzpunk also incorporates just about any game you can think of into one neat little package. Pizza version of Nazi Zombies. Here. Quake game based around weddings. Here.
The story line, while short, is funny and compelling at the same time. The story focuses on espionage, set in a bright world that enfuses new technology with a background of bright, and colourful Art Deco motifs. There is a ton of exploring to do, easter eggs to find, and whole new games to play! If you follow the main story path, you're looking at 2, maybe 3 hours of gameplay. But combined with all the secrets, achivements and down right silly side-quests, you could easily extend your playtime to 4-5 hours or even more!
I expected a more Thirty Flights of Loving feel to Jazzpunk, but I was mistaken. Jazzpunk (it's just such a fun word to say) is it's own game, heck, it's own genre. It's much more "in your face" than Thirty Flights of Loving, but that isn't always a bad thing. Jazzpunk is just a silly, good time, but doesn't take it too far but actually making all these silly things funny. Granted, you'll need an acute sense of humor to enjoy this game. But I sure enjoyed the hell out of it, and I hope too again soon.
+ The jokes are actually funny. No Duke Nukem Forver nonsense.
+ The music, art, character and charm of the game are all fantastic.
+ Incorporates lots of secrets, mini-games, this game has it all. Seriously.
- Story is short
- The ending is a bit abrupt/cheap
- The very fact that it does end.
9.5/10.

I recommend this game to people, but I also recommend NOT reading the reviews. Especially the positive ones. This game is very well made, beautiful beautiful beautiful, and thought-provoking! But the hype from all the positive reviews and the trailers set the bar so high before experiencing the game, that I was somewhat dissapointed after finishing it.
There are a couple things they did with this game that I reallyyy appreciate. The monsters. I'm a wuss. Unlike games like Deadspace, Outlast, etc. you didn't dread moving onto the next level stressing about what type of OP monsters would threaten your survival. Throughout most of the game, you could relax, explore the environment, appreicate the underwater beauty and if you came across a chapter that featured a monster(s), it was really no big deal. They were deadly and ugly, yes. And there were some chase scenes, yes. But you didn't get bombarded by them every single minute of the game, which I thought was nice. You could actually focus and follow along with the story. Not really any cheap scares. The monsters were very well done. You would get hints about their characteristics (to survive) and you always were notified when they were nearby (screen would blur/get static-ey). On another note, your source of light is infinite. In Amnesia you needed to always find lamp fluid to be able to shed light to survive. In Outlast, you needed batteries for your camcorder to survive.
Your companion. Catherine, your "AI" companion was a very nice addition. In these types of games, it's always nice to have someone to talk to on the other end of the radio. It's a bit overused, but in this genre it really is comforting psychologically to hear banter between your character and the other person. I really cherished the few interactions the protagonist had with other NPCs in the game. I wanted more of that. It was extremely interesting interacting with the few bots.
I personally couldn't get attached very much to the story like the other reviewers have. I got super attached to Catherine, and I liked the story in general but the main protagonist just wasn't a good fit. I just couldn't quite connect/get hooked. And believe me, I wanted to. I just didn't like the dialogue written for some of the characters. The dialogue could have been much better for a game with a premise such as this one. Choices were alright. There were times where I wanted to be able to make a choice, but the story couldn't progress any other way. There were other times when you made a choice, but it didn't really affect the story at all. It was just to make a choice with no outcome, which I guess is refreshing from most games nowadays.
If your computer can handle high texture settings, boy, get them as high up as possible. I slightly lowered my resolution so I could bump up the texture effects and wow, what a world of difference. I spent a lot of time in the game just admiring the stunning attention to detail they put into the atmosphere. The lighting was spectacular. The progression was perfectly paced and not rushed or overly lengthy. I just sincerely wished I played the game without reading the reviews or viewing the trailers.

At first glance, this game seems just like any other puzzle platformer game that uses squares a a lazy excuse to not have art direction. But it's amazing what this game turns into when you add a simple yet interesting story, an excellent narration set, and one of the best damn soundtracks I've ever heard.
You follow the story of Thomas, and AI inside a network that spontaneously gains a personality. He starts to explore the levels, as he notices that they are suited to his abilities, like the world is testing him. Along the way, you meet other AIs that all have very unique personalities, and all of them relate to their abilities. There's John, an arrogant egotist who can jump higher than any other AI. There's Claire, someone who is convinced she's a superhero because of her ability to float in water. I'll leave it at that due to spoilers, but I assume you get the idea.
The gameplay is also very good. Of course, like I said, it's very basic, you just move around with the arrow keys, up to jump, you know the drill. The difference here is that the jump for each character is very distinct, adding to their sense of personalities. They are well animated, and you always feel in control of the characters. The puzzles are also well designed, always giving a fair challenge, and only  in 2 levels did I feel as if the game was unfair. Trust me, you'll know them when you see them.
Another interesting aspect of the game is the art style. Obviously, it doesn't look like much, but the jump animations are superb, the water looks very cool and stylized, the lighting effects in some levels are unbelievable, and it overall just looks so much better than your average flash box platformer.
However, I think the highlight of the game is the sound design. The soundtrack is absolutely superb. It fits the tone perfectly, it's catchy as hell, and it always made you feel like a part of the game. The narration is also excellent, giving a hilarious British accent as the thoughts of every single character, yet somehow being able to easily distinguish between the characters, even when their names aren't mentioned.
However, the game is not without faults. The first one is that it feels way too short. It's only about 4 hours long, and while it is a marvelous story, it's also pretty forgettable, and there's next to no replay value. There are no unlocks, no level designer, nothing but a 4 hour story. Another problem I noticed is that some of the puzzles take FOREVER. There are often times when you have to control 6 or 7 little rectangles at once, and trying to orient them all to jump on top of one another to finish a puzzle is not only boring, but highly tedious. There are even some parts where you have to go through a level 6 or more times with the different rectangles just to get them all to their respective portals. It honestly feels lazy, and takes a lot out of it.
Overall though, the game is very damn good. While it isn't nearly long enough, I feel the puzzles are creative, the characters are unforgettable, the sound design is beautiful, it controls fairly well, and it feels like a much-needed step up from your average platformer. 8/10

If you are a child of the early 80's or late 70's, you may remember Master's of Orion II. It was, for lack of a better term, a masterpiece. The graphics were worse than the modern game FTL, but at the time that was the standard. And in this game, that didn't matter: You were the commander of a space empire with distinct characteristics. You designed spaceships, sent them into battle, researched exciting new technologies, and negotiated with other empires for exchange of goods, technologies and money.
The Good: Stardrive II is a modern reinvention of that game. It does nothing to reinvent the 4X genre, but the execution is the closest thing to the old Masters of Orion II that any game has in recent history. Trust me, I've played them all. This game gets some things brilliantly right, however: Turns play out at a pace you set, either calculated and one at a time, or mash the turn button and let it run for a few turns. Space combat is semi-real time, while ground combat is turn based. Outside of certain scenarios, they are also auto-calculable, which is nice at times-- Battle can feel slowly paced, and skipping it can be appealing.
The Bad: The game is also riddled with bugs and poor interface decisions. Hero's skills, like "Bloodthirsty," which allows a hero to gain passive governing bonuses for every enemy defeated in ground combat, doesn't work at all. Loot, which gives you bonus BC (money) doesn't either. Occaisional crashes happen, and the game doesn't support multi-monitors or borderless windows. Ground combat is also tedious, and it can be easy to make an uncorrectable mistake that costs you a battle due to the poor interface.
MOO Fans will enjoy the fact that most of the old species play style can be recreated, despite certain traits not being present in the default characteristics. Creativity, for example, allows you to research every technology in a tier, just like MOO2 Psilons-- but requires taking a lot of negative traits to achieve, like low gravity homeworld.
I can't say that this game will be appealing to a newer audience. But if you loved MOO2, you'll love Stardrive 2.

It's maybe 3 hours of play, and still excellent value for money. Control rectangles with different relationships with gravity; one can double-jump, one can float in water, one falls up, and more. Get them to their little portal at the end of each level using clever teamwork.
While you're enjoying the puzzles and crisp, responsive controls and mechanics, be soothed by the lovely soundtrack, and moved by a very well-told story about artificial intelligences becoming self-aware, as read by a delightfully reassuring voice along the lines of Steve Merchant of Portal 2 fame. Rarely has a game packed so much character into its short life, each of the rectangles has a very distinct personality and some very endearing thoughts and reactions to the world and their allies.
It's short, yes, but it doesn't overstay its welcome and it's cheap. Well worth the asking price.

"I guess the bottom line is that I would've rather had a remake than this version of the game. "
For the purposes of this review, I'm going to ignore the fiasco that happened with the first game. From here on out, let's continue with the assumption that had the first game been finished as it was intended, it would have gone on to become a great game - if you don't already consider it to be one. Why am I bringing this up? Stardrive 2 is a sequel. It is NOT a remake of the first game. And as a sequel, I"m going to compare it to the first one just like I would any other sequel.
So first things first:
Stardrive 2 is turn based - not real time. While some people might like this change, I for one HATE it. I personally feel that a sequel should try to be somewhat similar to its predecessors and this change is a bit overwhelming for me. I mean we went from RTS to Turn Based, and while I do genuinely like some turn based games (Civilization comes to mind), it felt very awkward for this game because I just wasn't expecting it I suppose.
The planetary menu/information screen has changed quite a bit. All the planets have hexes (instead of tiles) you can build on now and all hexes are unlocked where before Biospheres were important for unlocking all tiles on any given planet. I actually like this change quite a bit. Tiles that were disabled seemed too arbitrary before and this hex system seems much more balanced. Furthermore I LOVE the citizen/workers. You can now quite easily reassign any citizen(s) to a different role (Farmer, Scientist, etc.) and I think overall this change was extremely well done. It is far less tedious trying to get a new planet established than the original Stardrive which had major issues when you got "Bad Starting Territory."
Of course the space battles and ship design have always been the major attraction to the Stardrive series and this game does not fall short in that department. I feel like the ship design has been tweaked slightly from the first game and I also consider this to be an improvement. Since the game is now turn based, you get encounters when engaging in space combat. There is first a deployment stage where you can move your ships around and decide what positions/formation you want them to be in, followed by the actual battle. You may NOT give attack orders during the initial phase. I find this to be quite frustrating for someone who likes to micromanage the entire fight but overall combat is still done very well.
Now on to a few matters that really drive me nuts!
CP stands for command points. Ships cost command points to maintain every turn and if you go over your CP limit, you now have to pay a heavy BC fee (BC stands for Billions of Credits IIRC). This forces one of two things: you either maintain an ENORMOUS empire, or you are forced to have a small fleet. Small as in compared to the first game. Hell I remember the nerf from the original Stardrive. I never actually looked up the patch notes, I just remember loading up one of my files where a had a huge fleet and looking at my massively negative income. I don't know if credit income was nerfed or ship maintenance fees were increased but I truly loved the massive fleet sizes you could attain in the original Stardrive before that patch. Even after it you could still field a somewhat large fleet. But that's the problem. I played the Original first and I know how much fun it is to watch that many ships having a chaotic space battle. In Stardrive 2 a LARGE battle is something like 20 vs 20. CP is a soft cap due to BC paying for ships but.... your economy probably can't handle even tens of ships past the limit.
The best way to increase your CP is to build new starbases (or their upgrade/Battlestations) on all your planets. So what this comes down to is not how much money you make, but is much more about how many planets you control. Therein lies another problem.
I feel like the interface isn't very good for managing a large empire. After playing a few games I quickly learned I was having more fun on cluster settings with the minimum number of systems - 20.  Even at 5 systems you typically control somewhere around 10-15 planets. I can't stand just using the galaxy map at that point. Maybe I'm missing something or maybe the layout of the Empire Overview just isn't what I"m looking for. But ultimately in the original game I wanted a HUGE, MASSIVE EMPIRE! ...But in this game I just want to be small civilization :(
Last but not least due to the fact that the number of ships for each race is so small, the initial fight seems to decide the outcome of the entire war. You kill their fleet, you go on to take over all their planets with little difficulty (Neuro Toxic Bombs quite easily wipe out the local ground oppostion). The last thing I want in a 4x game during combat is to have only ONE definitive space battle against any one race. Ships are hard to spam fast enough to recover from a loss that quickly, even with a Gaia world.
Overall I feel the original game was much better, though there were obvious problems completing the game due to what happened. I guess the bottom line is that I would've rather had a remake than this version of the game.
Note that I didn't quite go over EVERYTHING (like leaders) but this review is already long enough and I want anyone who takes the time to read it to make up their own mind.

That one planet at the back of your nation that has never been scouted, the one without a star base, yup every enemy you have will attack it again and again and again.  Combine that with the ability for the AI to build huge fleets in a handful of turns, and sneak them around, and the inability to intercept said fleets because they go right past yours without combat, it totally ruins the experence. Only a short review since there is a character limit and my last atempt run out of space half way through.
It's a good game for the MoO2 fans. If you liked MoO2 this game will scratch that itch, however it is a bit different.
Each race has different ships which means different sizes and so some races are just better for having bigger ships, in fact some races has cruisers as big as some other races battleship so there is a bit of inballance there, looking up the wiki to find which race to play is definitly advised at least for the first playthroughs.
Spaceship combat is interesting, it allows for some things that MoO2 didn't since it's in real time. For example I can fit a few fast ships with cruise missile and run circles around enemy slow ships avoiding slow moving rockets and out of range of their guns. on the other hand the turn based combat of MoO2 was more strategic allowing you to chose what weapon to fire so you could make sure that point defense weapons wouldn't be wasted on enemy ships just because they got close. Differences aside, long range weapons are incredibly overpowered. Mass drivers and guass cannons are pretty much the metagame because not only they are incredibly powerful, but they are also very easy to research.
There are some inbalanced in the perks, creative is too bad because it's very expensive to justify learning all tech but on the other side subterranean gives you so much population that it's nearly a crime not to take it with how overpowered it is.
The diplomacy system leaves a lot to desire, it is in fact the one thing I'd say is straight up worse than MoO2. Trading depends on tolerance, you spend tolerance to do a trade and have to wait for it to refil. Tolerance limits also depends on how much the enemy likes you. This leads to trades often being impossible. Add that the hardest difficulty makes the AI want 70% gain on trades and that's that for diplomacy. Obviously because of this system nothing lasts forever. Trade agreements last 50 turns, so do pacts and there are no alliances (not that i think alliances were needed).
I could keep going on but the bottom line is. The game has a MoO2 feel to it while still managing to be it's own thing. I feel however that at this point a lot of balance improvements are required and a lot of quallity of life improvements too are needed.
If I had to rate this game I'd give it a 7 out of 10. Definitly a game which is above average, but with a bit of a road ahead to become really good. An rpg that takes you back to the old school style of gameplay (that I personally enjoy very much), this offering tells the story of a witch (Rowan or whatever name you choose) that has been robbed and left for dead by a mysterious thief who is part of a larger group of very bad people with evil designs on the world.
And, as the story moves along Rowan meets other characters that join her on the overall quest to set things right.
As with all of these adventures the story itself is fundamental to the success of the game, and this is one that is interesting and well told. It is direct enough so as to keep the player on track, but there are plenty of diversions and secrets to investigate and discover that you will stay busy and involved. It has that "one more area" pull that the successful titles seem to have. I intended to just take a quick look, and stayed in over two hours.
Art work and music are pleasing with an assortment of scenes and themes that help propel the game.
Battle encounters are side view with some creative and interesting monsters that have not been seen before (and I've played a lot of these).
The overall mechanics are good, with easy controls using either the keyboard or the mouse.
The game appears to have a very good length. As I indicated, I'm in for over two hours and can see that even though there has been much to do, lots to explore, many characters to talk to, and several battles to fight I am just getting started ---- and that's on easy mode.
So if you are a fan of these games, you don't want to miss this one ---- it is reasonably priced and will take a big chunk of your game time. Recommended.

On a whim, I picked up this cheap RPG that came out not even a week before writing this review. Now, I'm against the idea of people charging anything for the games they've made in RPG Maker, but they rarely charge more than $5-$7, which I suppose isn't objectionable. What is objectionable, however, is Onyx.
Onyx is about a world where witches are a regular part of life, but are being hunted down and slaughtered like lambs by a rebel sect known as the "Nimrod Brotherhood." Yes, that is what they're called. No, I don't believe they're named after the Biblical Nimrod. I think they're named Nimrod because it's a JOOOOOOOOOOOOOKE.
That seems to be half the reason for the game's existence, really. There can't be three lines of dialogue without some character or other cracking what they must think is the wittiest jest in their lifetime, and while some will get a chuckle out of you, others fall flat on their face. Not helping matters is the lack of any editing or spellchecking going into the product before release, leaving horrendous typos everywhere and sometimes incomprehensible sentences, problems that could easily have been fixed prior to release.
That's another problem I have with the whole RPG Maker business model. Due to the ease of cranking out games when you have very little to do yourself aside from place assets and write a story, it creates an environment where you could easily release two or three games a month, given enough free time. With that capability at your fingertips, it can become easy to give in to apathy, and start cutting back on things like QA testing or caring at all about the products you sell your customers.
Speaking of not giving a♥♥♥♥♥♥ the game focuses on a character named Rowan, though you can rename all playable characters anything you see fit within the 8-or-9 character limit. Rowan is Velvet Crowe from Tales of Berseria. That's her character. A poorly written Velvet Crowe. She's joined by a character who is basically Komoto Raynar from this site, a mother and daughter with serious familial issues, a Mystic Knight from Final Fantasy V, and some other character I couldn't be bothered to play long enough to meet. None of them are interesting enough to get invested in, Vel- I mean, Rowan is a selfish witch, and they are all groan-worthy at various points.
The maps you'll be spending most of your time travelling around are some of the clunkiest and poorly designed maps I've ever seen. Back in my Ar tonelico review, I threw some serious shade at its maps, but I feel I now owe it an apology. At least Ar tonelico had maps with rules. Onyx has no rules. One bush might block your progress, while the very same bush in a different location you might be able to pass over. Sometimes the ground covers up half your character's sprite, as if they are slowly sinking into the abyssal quicksand that is this game. Take two steps and they are suddenly freed, allowed to suffer the torment of fourth wall breaks and petty intra-party drama. This will occur even if you are standing on the exact same kind of floor tile after moving.
Battles are just a visual nightmare. Your party appears as RPG Maker sprites, obviously, but enemies are these weird, watercolor portraits superimposed over Earthbound's battle background. They look horrendous, have a tendency to blend together or hide each other, and, given enough enough enemies on the screen, can even impose themselves over your own character sprites. And once you have a fourth party member, you might not realize it, because the UI is so tall and the characters are situated in such a way that the UI will cover your fourth member. It is negative fun to get into a fight in this game. Anti-fun, if you will. It actively sucks joy from your life.
You're allowed to save anywhere in the game, but outside a tent early in the game, there's a save point. It has no reason for existence. I can only assume that an early version required save points, and they failed to dummy them all out. It's extremely inconsistent.
Near the end of my play time, I also stumbled across The End of Ti- I mean, a magical museum that is not totally a ripoff of Chrono Trigger right down to name-dropping Melchior as the inspiration. It definitely also does not have the Hylian shield (which can be seen in other places within the game, as well) and Prince of Persia's scimitars hanging in a hallway. This game is wholly original and will not fall back on using nostalgic images in order to garner favor from its players. I hate this game and my life because of this game.
I don't understand why this exists. I don't understand how it has the right to charge money. But since it is charging money, it deserves to be criticized like anything else we have to crack open our wallets for, and even at a $7 price tag, this one is not worth your time or money. Even if you are an avid follower of RPG Maker enterprises, steer clear of this one.
