Okay, so there are problems with this game. My main two are the Matchmaking system and the Gear system. Luckily, the new update has remedied the Gear system, while the Matchmaking may suck for all eternity. BUT, I have a TON of good things to say about this game. Strategy is required for this game, both for the 1v1 and the entire battlefield. You have to use tactics to beat your bigger opponents, and you have to manage your health against the smaller ones. The directional blocking system is a breath of fresh air in an industry dominated by Hack 'N Slash or Point 'N Shoot mechanics. The classes have been balanced for the most part (I'm looking at you, Warden) and each feels slightly more unique than the other, although there are overlaps. So, I recommend any gamer to at least try this game and try each class, find one you like, get good at it, then find another two or three so that you can be versatile. Happy gaming, everyone!

Stories Untold is many things, most prominently a text-based adventure game. It weaves a wonderful tale, meshing gameplay and story in a way that many developers dream of. The final act, particularly, is astounding. Production values and sound design are high, and I can recommend the game without too much hesitation.
However, Stories Untold contains the most irritating aspects of adventure games. Often you'll find yourself typing various commands in at the prompt, over and over, without any of them being the ones that the game is looking for. Sometimes, most notably in a scene taking place at a party, it's entirely unclear what your character is supposed to be doing. In one particular instance, I was supposed to go into the kitchen from a hallway. However, the description of the hallway, even with additional details gleaned from using the "look around" command, made no mention of a kitchen. Another irritation was the usage of a microfiche in episode 3. Even after optimizing the focus, I was unable to make out many of the characters I was supposed to input into the computer. The game mentions in a tooltip that finding the right command is "part of the fun," but I certainly wasn't enjoying myself.
One could make an argument that the adventure style of the game ties in with the story as a whole, and that might be a compelling argument. However, I think the game might've been just as powerful if the developer used a "multiple choice" technique at each prompt.

I originally purchased Kotaro's, Masamune's and Hanbei's routes on the mobile version, but I didn't think twice when I saw this released on Steam and immediately purchased it.
The art is extremely beautiful, although I'm sad there is no e-mote system. The music is okay. The writing and localization, for what originally was a mobile otome, are really good. The translation flows really well and is very modern ('okay', 'jeez') which is a good thing. Like all Forbidden Romance games, the writing can get a little steamy (bonus points). The interactions among the characters were well done and the hints to solve the bigger mystery spread throughout the various routes, although only in Nobunaga's we can see resolutions.
Be warned, all the routes have two endings, one in which the guy stays in the Princess' world, one in which the Princess goes into the guy's world. Not all the characters have happy endings. Some are just doomed.
As MC, the Princess isn't half bad. Really depends on the route and the ending. She could have been worse for an otoge MC. Also, she has eyes in the CGs, which is a HUGE bonus :)
Now, let's talk about men :> and trigger warnings.
My suggestions regarding route orders are as follow: Masamune = Yukimura > Kotaro = Hanbei > Nobunaga; the first two routes focus heavily on romance and less on plot, order can be switched up. The second two routes give more hints regarding the bigger picture, again order is up to preference. Nobunaga's route has all the answers and as the game tell you, is very spoiler heavy.
- I really liked Masamune's route. He's a very cute guy and a genuine good person. He's also very respectful of the Princess' wishes, and his narrative is a take on the 'different social classes' trope. One of my favorites.
- Yukimura's route dealt with 'incest'. Of course, Yukimura is not the real twin brother of the Princess, but he is convinced he is for 95% of the time and still rolls with it. Incest is not my thing so it made me slightly uncomfortable.
- Kotaro's route was extremely refreshing because he appears so mischievous and carefree, but of course he's not, being a ninja and all. They had many sweet, sweet moments together. Should probably warn for one of his ending, in which he's 'so caught with passion that he has to satiate his lust RIGHT NOW', which personally makes me eyeroll every time. The other ending was cute tho.
- Hanbei's route should have a big warnig for♥♥♥♥♥♥and abuse. Which kinda gets brushed off in the end by the Princess. Otoge MCs... nevertheless, I did enjoy his route.
- Now, Nobunaga. Ooh boy. Where to start. The man is a pig and acts sleazy despite the fact that everybody around you sees him as your father. Also the writing seems to push you to like him. Uhm not really. I did enjoy the spoilers (some were pretty OMG WTF and made so much sense) and the endings were wicked good. But as I stated early, incest and play-pretend incest are squicky to me so I was uncomfortable playing his route. Also♥♥♥♥♥♥warning.
In conclusion, it's a solid port of a good mobile otome. The price is amazing considering it has all the main scenarions, all the sequels and the date scenarios. Does it have flaws? Certainly. I still found it an enjoyable read. Recommended :)

It would be easy to be critical of this game - so here goes:
You play as Nuna, who cannot swim and will die within 1 second of contact with water, unless the plotline determines this to be inconvenient, in which case she can hold her breath underwater forever. Her friend, a happy companion fox, also cannot swim until it's convenient for the game to do so, and then is a slippery ice weasel.
The game will not progress until you do things the right way, specifically, the way the game's makers played it, presumably this being a game which had no QA testing, because in it's functional capacity as a platformer it is pretty darn broken. If, for example, you jump at the wrong time and land on a platform the game will not allow you to land on that platform because you jumped at the wrong time according to Game.
If you placed one of your characters too far away from the other, then the game won't allow your other character to complete certain jumping tasks, despite there being no obvious reason why this should be.
As a lesson in Inupiat culture, art, madness and wisdom, it's pretty darn solid. In fact, it's beautiful graphics are one of the better examples of matching mood to content that I've seen, and are culturally-appropriate. As a platformer however it's fairly simplistic, clumsy, and it did not surprise me that it was made in Unity - that being the Great Maw from whence all unpolished content which looks good ensues.
Other beefs: There's no option to change controls, meaning the game is barely playable for left-handers. There's no real 'flow' of direction to the game, and finding out what you're meant to do is more-or-less trial-and-error most of the time. And occasionally Fox will just wander off in the opposite direction to yours, for no apparent reason. In certain areas, if you are controlling the fox instead of Nuna, you'll insta-fail. The game uses 100% of all cores on your CPU at all times.
What's astonishing is that this game has been out several years - would be relatively easy to fix - but hasn't been. The new steam review system would make sure that it got the attention it deserves, if the issues were resolved.
So if you don't care about 'game', play this game - it's a good learning experience.
If however you're the type that gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off with clumsy controls and simplistic puzzles, give this one a miss.

As a huge fan of Sierra and FMV (full motion video), I was very excited to play this one--but came away disappointed and irritated for several reasons:
1) the bugginess (my cursor would get stuck and I would have to exit and relaunch the game)
2) the single save file
3) the lack of player direction throughout the game (there are several points where you don't have an objective and have to wander around in hopes of triggering a cutscene in order to advance the game)
4) the need to search
every day to make sure nothing has changed (some opportunities are only available at a single arbitrary point in the game)
5) the irritating heroine (she does everything very slowly and spends a lot of time primping her hair--you can't move or do anything until her primping animation has finished playing. She also has serious trouble opening unlocked doors; she stands there jiggling the handle for 5+ seconds on some of them)
6)
--when you reach the finale, the game converts your save file to a movie file, so if you screw up and forget to pick up an item before entering the finale,
. This is particularly infuriating because there is no reason to search for or pick up one of these items in particular (the glass shard). The in-game hint system doesn't mention it and tells you to head straight for the finale. I fell into this trap and had to start a new game on the last chapter (if I'd had to restart from the beginning, I wouldn't have bothered at all).
Besides all that, I guess there are worse ways to spend an afternoon. At the very least, I enjoyed the novelty of the FMV.

Firstly, this is an unusual game and, looking at the forums the developers are very happy to tweak and improve.  Their obvious intent is to make it as good as it can be.  For this reason I’m recommending it.  There isn’t a lot of experimentation with genre these days and they deserve the credit for having a go and persevering.  I hope that one day my game will be better as they patch it.  And the overall feel is such that even though the gameplay is driving me to distraction I’m still trying!
However, there are some cons that are close to game breakers for me.  It feels as if it should be a happy, casual game with a few teeth to make it a bit more exciting – storms, pirates etc.  It also feels as if the random tasks you have to do while trying to get your passengers from A to B within a time frame should be fun and lift the pace a bit.
Unfortunately, as it stands at the moment playing this game is a chore purely because, despite experimenting with lots of different combinations of settings, the controls are, quite frankly, awful.
With my basic gaming computer set up, the boat controls are fine and as they should be, as long as you realise that these are boats and not racing cars.  However the big problem is the camera and mouse controls which are fantastically erratic.
The mouse control is laggy, which means that you have to spend way too much time trying to hit a button resulting in loss of control of your boat. I have since found that if you go into your computer control panel and turn the mouse sensitivity down to the slowest you can, the situation - although not perfect - improves dramatically. The camera angles are poor.  On the face of it, as you are given 4 different camera positions, you should be able to easily see whatever you need to.  Unfortunately 2 of them have very limited use – why would I want to see inside the boat unless I’m happy to crash?  The third, I haven’t been able to find a use for and the default one, the one that you are almost constantly using, is a nightmare.
In order to look around, you have to hold the left mouse button down and move the mouse in the direction you want to see (up, down and around).  This control varies wildly from fair, where you can see everything with very little effort; to ultra sensitive where the slightest touch leaves you looking at a scene and you have no idea where you are (please remember the boat is still moving at this point - well until the harbour wall stops it).  Alternatively you can end up looking at the bottom of the sea.  The problem here is that it seems to become ultra sensitive when you need it to behave most – such as when you’re trying to dock. Compare this with the lagginess of the mouse when you need to use it to click on things and the whole thing just doesn’t make sense.
The sensitivity is an issue when you are trying to take photographs. You find your bird.  You point your boat in the right direction and hold the right hand mouse button down.  Sadly you see a piece of blue sky with absolutely no idea where in the sky you are.  You wave your mouse about in the hope you might catch the bird.  No luck.  You go into the normal view and find the bird again – to be fair not very far from where it was initially.  Try again.  No luck.  Eventually you glimpse the tip of the wing and you realise how fast your mouse is scanning the sky – you’re hardly touching it but it’s going so fast that by the time you realise you’ve seen the tip of the wing, you’ve got no chance of backtracking and finding it again. Rinse and repeat until you luck out.  Absolutely no way can you do this when you’ve got a passenger on board.
Having said all this everything else is lovely – which is why, along with the developers, I’m persevering with it.  It’s just that this could easily become my favourite casual game and it’s frustrating to have it spoilt by the controls.

Rocksmith 2014 is the latest version of the Rocksmith brand musical simulation games. Ever wanted to learn to play guitar? What about bass? One thing this game misses out on that the first game had is a campaign mode, which is a real shame, since it gave the game a lot more focus. This game just throws you into individual "play a song" mode instead.
It does, however, have a virtual band session mode. Have no friends? Cant get together with anyone but want to play in a band? Well, session mode caters to that. It allows you to pick a selection of different instruments, and play along, with the game generating music from the selected instruments based on what you play.
All in all, really good game, especially if you like either the idea of, or actually playing music.

SOMA, a game from Frictional Games, the makers of Amnesia (what better guarantee..). A first-person, sci-fi adventure with elements of survival horror. The latter constits of scary moments but it is more based on the aspect of phychology with pertinent questions about existence, life and the state after life. Not sure if the title is based on the greek word about "body" but I can not find a better fitting title.
Pros:
+ amazing depressing atmosphere, which is greated enhanced by the dialogs between the protagonist and Cathrine.
+ story is unravelled beautifully and so effectively that leaves you a desire to continue only to learn what happened to the station and to the world in general. You start by visiting a doctor for a scan only to end up in a sub-water base not being able to understand what is going on. You are motivated to keep continuing also to find out what will happen in the story.
+ awesome sound effects and music, definitely matching the tone of the game
+ very nice representation of the base turned into ruins but also of the aqueous environment
+ all puzzles have solutions based purely on logic or physics, almost no backtracking is required to solve them
+ very easy interface to interact with the environment
Cons:
- perhaps some levels outside the parts of the basis are a bit repetitive and require walking from one point to the other without interacting with anything
- some encounters with the enemy can be a bit frustrating
- perhaps it could include more puzzles to be solved
All in all, a brilliant game not to be missed. This is a game to show to the non-believers to prove that games are art. Definitely recommended for all those who want to participate in a very engaging, story-based experience of high-quality, existential science fiction blended with horror.
Can not wait for the next creation of Frictional Games.

Frictional Games outdid themselves - again
SOMA starts off with a 26 years old man waking up and going to get his head examined after a tragic accident. But things take an unexpected turn when he wakes up alone and confused in an underwater installation about a hundred years later into the future. Telling anything more would just spoil the game for you, but know that SOMA is not the next installment in Amnesia series, but Frictional Games' first foray into scifi-horror which takes you about 8 hours to complete.
The game consists of walking and solving puzzles in an atmospheric, at times spooky and downright chilling, environment packed with all sorts of hazards. Graphically the game is not very demanding, but can still strike you with awe the moment you least expect it. The underwater segments are especially noteworthy, and the atmosphere is even stronger at times than in Amnesia: The Dark Descent. There are monsters, but they are not the main attraction this time, but only a sideproduct of the story. Unlike in Dark Descent, here the monsters pose no such a dire threat as they can be maneuvered with relative ease. It may be a bit of stating the obvious, but there really is no fighting back, either. Your best option is to run away and hide.
The fulcrum of SOMA is its story, which is more like a synthesis on what it means to be a human, how we define existence, and what is real for whom. As weird as it may sound, after the credits roll, you are left with feelings of loneliness, sadness, and even anxiety. Make no mistake, SOMA is a game for mature audiences because of its gripping dissection on the human mind and how we perceive ourselves in relation to time and space.
Very few games in existence as of today have managed to tackle above mentioned subjects with such grace as SOMA. I congratulate Frictional Games for their succesfull effort and cannot wait for their next game(s).
SOMA nails its targets at nearly every turn, but there a couple of niggles here and there. Real-world pictures of cats, trees etc. are used in the game, but all human faces are not animated, but hand-drawn. Consequently, whenever there is dialogue, you may find yourself just looking at a hand-drawn image of a person's face which breaks the immersion severely. Another small negative is the fact that there is no replay value whatsoever. There are no secrets to find or achievements to unlock, and no multiplayer.
Pros:
+ A captivating, chilling take on transhumanism and existence
+ Level design is outstanding ranging from mundane appartments to derelict underwater bunkers
+ Sound design fully supports the atmosphere and kicks it up a notch
Cons:
- Drawn faces of characthers take you out of the immersive game world
- No replay value
SOMA costs only half of what a typical triple A game does, but delivers more in terms story. This is a game you don't want to miss, and one which you'll remember for all eternity. Good job, Frictional Games!

this will be short but I want tog ive my two cents in.
I know people were clamoring for a multiplayer aspect to be added but in all honesty I don't know how it would work, especially with waiting for real time battles to finish up, unless all real time battles happen at the end of a turn which can seriously derail someone's strategy even moreso if other players are allowed to do things while a real time battle is going on.
Stardrive 1 was fun but it had issues, primarily with the bland proceduraly generated race descirptions and while a fully real time setup was a novel idea it presented too many issues to work around vs the traditional 4X turn based game. AS it stands, making Stardrive 2 into an equivalent of "Total War in Space" was probably the best idea, yest you can't reinforce fleets in battle anymore but at least the game kept it's staple of real time combat scenarios to help it stand out.
My only major compaints with the game are as follows: the lack of victory conditions and no sandbox ship editor. There's no turn limit (at least not that I've found) and no other way to win excepyt total military conquest. I'd like to see a return of the "ascendence" victory from the first Stardrive as well as diplomatic or science based victory options. As for the second, I want to be able to experiment with ship designs freely outside the game and, most importantly, figure out wxactly what layouts each of ships for each race have, I want to say I love that each races' ship has a unique style and design to it that is more than just aesthetics but even with that I can't help but wonder how it will affect my ship designing when I can't figure out ahead of time which ship layout I prefer.

So, I'm a very old gamer, but I've never written a Steam Review before.  This game needs more good reviews, so I'll make it my first.  As a veteran of every major 4x and strategy game since I played the first Civilization as a teenager, Stardrive 2 stands out as a real gem.  Major pluses:
+Depth and complexity in race and game setup without endless sliders and checkboxes.  You have several meaningful choices, which can be combined in complex ways to make for a very different play experiences, but customization isn't a total swamp of minor adjustments.
+The planet characteristics (Size, Type, Gravity, Mineral Abundance, Strategic Resources, Special Features) can be combined in an absolutely cool and endless number of ways to create a very unpredictable variety of planets.  This makes for great choices to make on the strategic map.
+The graphics are effective and evocative, and the game text and lore have a sense of humor matching the gamestyle.  This is an unusual and really beneficial thing - too many games have beautiful art that's not so evocative, or err on the side of grim-and-serious when that is not a needed aesthetic for their other choices.
+Ship design is fun, deep, and offers many ways to optimize your ships together or individually, while refit system encourages you to redesign when needed without a major gameplay penallty.
+Battles are pretty, quick, and offer an appropriate level of micromanagement.  They break the turn cycle with a real-time experience, tracking individual ships with medals and such for accomplishments is also a nice touch.
+Tooltips abound, meaning the complex mechanics can be explored and understood easily.
+Ongoing patching seems to indicate developer involvement and dedication.
+Diplomacy system uses trade, different weights for different groups and players, and a "tolerance" mechanic in an effective and interesting way - but see below for critiques of diplomacy.
No game is perfect, though:
- UI could use improvement and efficiency, with better keyboard commands and such.  This includes things like idle planet notifications.
- More and more interesting random events are needed to keep the universe outside of the AI players more alive.
- Some races feel less balanced than others, in the area of advantages and ship designs.  Same with weapon designs.
- Total randomness of setup can create very unfun initial game conditions, or conditions where you don't realize how much better other player's starting areas were until you're already a ways into the game.
- More diplomatic options and win conditions could make this feel more like a "complete" 4x game.  The AI's tendency to want to kill you at first sight could also be watered down a wee bit, at least for the 'not genocidal' races.
This is not a complete review, just a few isolated thoughts.

Survarium is a nice deviation from the usual PvP team shooter. There's a lot of complexity and flavor to it, as it is set in the STALKER universe and has a few unique systems on top of the usual shooter game.
You have a lot of customization options with the 4 factions that each offer 10 tiers of weapons, armor and items. You can upgrade up to three (out of 10 or so) stats on your gear and also unlock weapon attachments like scopes, silencers, grips for your weapons by getting kills with said weapons. The game has a lot for you to do when it comes to such progression, leveling up your profile for skills that increase your weapon handling, artifact interactions or mobility by tiny increments, and of course ranking up in the faction of your choice, which you can switch at any point unlimited times, to rank up in whichever of the factions you want.
Premium items only have unlocks ready and income & exp boosts, but have the same stats as their normal counterparts, so the game isn't Pay2Win, but simply SkipAhead. If you buy for example Tier7 premium weapons and expect to do well outright, you're going to get wrecked because others got to said high tier by playing and getting better at it.
The gameplay is otherwise solid, slight minus points for jumping and other such player collision stuff with world objects. Gunplay is absolutely great, especially shotguns finally having a pretty realistic spread with chokes, which is rare in shooter games. Weapons feel very unique and the sound design is amazing, it makes for very intense firefights.
Maps are very different from eachother, a couple of them pretty large maps with a lot of open ground, all of them have a lot of paths around and a lot of terrain and objects to hide behind. All in all very good maps and they feel well designed for the 3 man squad gameplay, which is the maximum you can have in your party of friends.
On top of the great gunplay and the usual deathmatch you've got three other gamemodes; point capture, artifact hunt and battery hunt. The capture mode is called research for flavor, but it's the same as with many other games, you hold three points on the map and gather points for your team. The other two make things interesting:
Artifact hunt has a mysterious artifact spawn in a random location of the map after a while, players can pick it up and try to carry it to their base, it's a spin on capture-the-flag, except the spawn point of the "flag" is random and it's a round ball shaped, so dropping it will have it roll down hills etc. making for interesting tactics.
Battery hunt is another cool gamemode, where both teams are trying to find batteries from multiple spawn points on the map, you'll only get a notification that one of the spawn points has a battery for your team, but you don't know which one. You also won't see where the enemy's battery spawns. You can also steal batteries from the enemy team etc. So this spin on capture-the-flag type gamemodes is very good, frantic action when looking for the batteries or trying to protect them, and intense stealth gameplay when trying to sneak a battery out of the enemy's battery rack.
Been playing the game for a few weeks now, and it's clear that the negative reviews are older ones, by people who have been waiting very long for some big features that haven't yet come to the game. But trust me, this game is very fun for new players, perhaps for multiple years, it's a free game in any case, so try it out if you like PvP shooters. I like this especially because I'm bored of years and years of different versions of Counter-Strike, which are all the same game, this one has a lot more flavor and complexity, albeit it comes with the price of getting less balanced matches, but having a shooter this good in the STALKER universe is amazing.
Slight minus points for sometimes buggy UI, lack of player guidance with the game's systems and features, the jumping wonkiness that I mentioned. Otherwise highly recommended, because this is a very solid PvP shooter game to have fun in with your friends.

I spent the weekend binging through the title, and I must say that after having finished the routes, I fairly enjoyed the game. I may go further into detail later on, but for now I'll give a brief review and explaination at the end.
Pros:
-Great artwork
-Beautiful soundtrack
-Varied character archetypes
-Fairly interesting story
Cons:
-Some QC errors with a good chunk of typos, missing grammar, and awkward sentences. (Still better than Kikuya's QC problems though)
-Game fell short of a good bit of potential the story and characters had
-Became somewhat dull in places
Overall, for the price, I'd highly recommend the game for otome fans. While there's better titles out there if you're new/just getting into the otome scene, Destiny's Princess was an enjoyable play for its length. However, there is quite a lot of sad/bittersweet endings, so If you're looking for a very "feel good" otome, then you should probably look elsewhere.
I've seen a few people comment negatively about the fact that there are two "incest" routes, but what a lot of people fail to mention is that, while there is quite a lot of incestual context, the two routes in question are not true incest routes. The male characters in those routes have "taken the place" of the protagonist's twin brother and father, but they are not actually related in any way. This is explained right off the bat in every route.

In
, you are the princess of a country in a world based on ours during the Warring States period of Japan (1467-1603). Overrun by demons, the country is slowly falling into ruin -- but your family has an age-old heirloom that is known to grant wishes only in the most difficult of situations. Desperate for help, you call to the heirloom for aid, which puts five heroes at your beck and call... But every wish has its price. Will you be able to save your country and will the hero you love stay by your side?
Brought to you by the same studio that was responsible for
, this game is a definite improvement compared to that one in many ways, and certainly not just a copy. Almost no grammar/editing/translation errors anymore, a better soundtrack, higher quality images, and a full-screen option that is actually viable -- though it does have slightly less content than
.
+ Interesting underlying story about the demons & the heirloom
+ Character personalities are fairly consistent but a bit boring
+ Pretty art and nice character designs
+ Almost impossible not to get together with the man of your choice
+ Short sequel stories & date scenarios to play after unlocking the main ending(s)
- Your choices do not seem to affect the story much
- Creepy sexual behaviour from groping to forcing the heroine into doing sexual stuff, though this is not present in all romance routes
- Endings with low likeability don't really differ from the ones with high likeability
- There are a couple of incestual angles to the story
- No voice-acting
All-in-all, this game doesn't shy away from tragic endings and drama, and I thought it was nice how differently the heroine develops throughout the different romance routes. And a tragic ending with a lot of death doesn't necessarily mean it's all over... illustrated very nicely by ending B with Nobunaga (save him for last!) which is probably my favourite one. I wouldn't necessarily buy it at full price, though, since there are romantic visual novels/otome games with a better story and better characters (such as
), but you can definitely get some enjoyment out of this one, too!

The entire game, minus the cutscenes, can run well over 60 FPS depending on how strong your rig is and loads incredibly fast between loading screens as a result.
Originally a console game, the controls were designed for such and controller play is very much do-able. Coming to PC however and with it being an incredibly fast third-person shooter it's obvious that KB+M are more viable as that new playstyle has been implemented nicely here as well.
I've only played the demo way back on PS3 so I'm not sure how good this port looks graphically in comparison, though it still looks great on high resolutions.
The plot is that cliche'd America VS. Russia thing and the EN voice acting is just as corny. It's a placeholder for the game itself if anything.
There are 5 acts and a varied number of missions in each one, but the game itself is incredibly short like many other Platinum games.
QTEs exist here; most are simplistic but the button mashing ones can be physically tiring, worse if you're attempting them on a keyboard.
The game's a fast third-person cover shooter that's actually designed to encourage mobility and not be behind cover very often. A lot of cover options are destructible depending on what kind of damage is done to them and there are plenty of enemies that will, in one way or another, close in on you making the stationary option a poor choice eventually.
The key features for the mobility are the game's slow motion feature known as AR mode and the ability to power slide, Boosting. You can't do either forever and they both use up the same bar on the UI which indicate how much heat the protagonist's suit can take before it overheats & needs to cool down for a lengthy period. While it's cooling down, you won't be able to use Boost or AR mode during that time so you're encouraged to manage them properly; making constant use of both features extensively without overheating the suit.
The AR mode is essentially the "bullet-time" in the game and can only be activated manually through varied means. The game doesn't just go into slow motion during this, but you also move and shoot faster, giving more reason to use it frequently. AR mode can also be triggered automatically by taking too much damage which is meant to be a moment for you to get to safety, but it can't be turned off as a result thus forcing the suit to overheat. It's a bit jarring that you can't turn it off manually if that kind of situation occurs since more often than not you'll already be in a safe situation before you need it on any longer.
Boosting allows you to slide with decent control at high speeds for as long as the gauge on the UI allows it. It's one of the main features that make the game be as fast as it looks and it feels cool doing it, especially whilst simultaneously shooting. Aiming or just shooting while Boosting turns on AR mode for as long as you're shooting or aiming, even with a sniper and a rocket launcher. It makes sense with aiming but I don't think it activate if you're just firing without aiming. If you're playing with a mouse, you can make complete u-turns with ease while sliding.
The shooter part is decent. The primary enemies in the game are a fair variety of robots and they all hit pretty hard, at least on Normal and Hard mode, and even harder when they use close-ranged attacks. Most of them can have their limbs shot off or disabled if damage is dealt enough on that part. I find that bit of info only really useful if you don't know how to or can't avoid some attacks properly and you're aware of what can be shot off, but nonetheless it's a great mechanic to have.
The friendly soldiers you fight with are virtually useless. They don't hit their targets very often, they die fast, they can sometimes obstruct your view, and there's no penalty for them dying in any way save for some point deductions at the end of a mission. The best use I ever have for them are for them to be distractions and if you revive someone when they've got a marker on them that indicates you can do so, you're rewarded with a weapon. Whether or not the weapon they drop is random, I didn't check.
There are eleven weapons in total you can find throughout the game and you're only allowed to carry three at a time excluding the frag & EMP grenades as seen on the d-pad-like interface. The assault rifle is probably the most common gun in the game as it damages decently, is fairly accurate, and has a sizable ammo count. While everything else is useful in their own right, the other weapons feel more situational than overall practical since in comparison to my time with the assault rifle, I barely had a need to use anything else.
The sound of the weapons don't feel very impactful either; they're low in volume and feel incredibly weak, even the shotgun, rocket launcher, and sniper. The melee attacks in the game sound harder than the guns but that's not saying a whole lot.
Some neat little things about the weapons you use are that you don't actually use or even pick up weapons on the field, but rather your suit scans them, thus forming it on your hands. If ammo for a held weapon is full and you pick up the same type of weapon somewhere, it gets upgraded. Most upgrades are only useful when they reach certain ranks as nothing actually gets upgraded until those points. Dying on Normal mode or higher downgrades the currently held weapon, though exiting to the main menu while your dying animation is occurring and continuing from the checkpoint renders the downgrade feature null, and that exploit is far more convenient on PC.
Melee attacks exist in the game but are extremely limited. They're incredibly powerful and are different depending on what weapon you're currently holding while you perform it. I guess for balancing purposes your suit overheats instantly as a result if you hit an enemy with a melee attack.
People say that this game has a lot of "depth" and I've been using the "hidden" things I've seen people do to my advantage, but the game doesn't give much incentive to go that far save for the very last difficulty that can be unlocked maybe. As satisfying as it may be to use these things, the primary functions work well enough to get you from point A to B. Scoring exists in the game and results appear after the end of each mission. There's no real reward for doing well in any regard meaning it's all just there for bragging rights.
The game's a great take on the third-person shooter genre given how fast & arcadey it is but, one, it's an incredibly short game where the story is only around five or so hours long and, two, I don't see much replayability in it outside of those that are maybe willing to dig deeper, especially with an unrewarding scoring system such as this.

An interesting point-and-click artifact from the '90s heavily inspired by
.  I never played this back in the day, but looking at it now, I'm really impressed with just how well Sierra was able to integrate FMV with 3D models at the time.  The acting and story are just like what you'd find in a (pretty amusing) B-movie, so don't expect to be deeply spine-tingled, though it must be said that a couple of the practical gore effects toward the end look really great.
Roberta Williams designed the game so that it would be winnable by casual players, but she couldn't help but toss in one little piece of design hatefulness from the "golden age" (or what I like to call the "mixed feelings age") of adventure games:  the dreaded
.  For those who have never experienced it, this is when your adventure has entered an unwinnable state because you failed to pick up some bit of flotsam or perform some insignificant action earlier on.  Now, the game block only strikes in the final chapter of this game, and you
go back and play the previous chapter to pick up the stupid McGuffin if you missed it, but it'll still cost you 30 minutes of pointless. infuriating repetition.  That's one reason why I think the true golden age of point-and-click adventure is now.
Despite suffering a fit of pique at the game's end, I definitely enjoyed it enough to justify my playthrough.  My favorite character is the sleazy realtor who sells the haunted manse to the beautiful protagonist and her husband; he taught me that the fishnetted legs of toothsome floozies may be referred to as "getaway sticks," and I shall never forget him for it.

For Honor Review
Pros
Decent Skill Ceiling
Fighting Game Esc Inspiration (Combos, Mix-ups)
Most Realistic Medieval Combat In A Game To Date 5/17/2017
Devs Listen to Player Concerns (so far it seems for the better)
Large Roster of Easy to Hard Characters with Varied Playstyles
Satisfying Executions
Gear Unlocks
Loot Boxes (for me that's a con but majority would say its not)
Intuitive Keyboard and Mouse Controls (switching guard with mouse is responsive but takes a bit to get used to)
Devs continued support, increased XP gain, two new characters (DLC), two new maps (DLC), bug fixes for several characters moves and added mix-ups to a few characters that had too predictable move sets so every character can be viable
Continued Patching, not Dota 2 patching every day to maintain balance and bug free but hey, not everyone can be Dota 2
Emphasizes Focusing On One Character and Mastering That Character (The Steel complaints are mainly of people trying to play six different heroes and get fat loot for all of them)
Play For The Game - The gear unlocks are there, but if you want to play the game and play really competitvely there should be no issue. Duel, Brawl = No Gear Stats| Dominion, Elimination, Skirmish = Gear Stats| Gear in Duel and Brawl are just cosmetic
You can play any of the heroes in the game (except Shinobi and Centurion due to DLC) without having to use 500 steel to unlock them. The only point to unlocking them with steel is to equip: Gear, Emotes, and Ambient Effects. Along with customizing feats which are special abilities in Dominion which I still debate the balance of.
Campaign is a decent length, I went through it with a friend on Realistic Difficulty. The hardest difficulty in the game that gets rid of guard and parry indicators that you will learn to really appreciate if you play on Realistic. As you will have to just where an attack is coming from, and the parry timing just from sight alone.
Co-op Campaign
Easy To Learn Hard To Master - You'll find this out very quickly and need to study up on how to get the most out of your Hero's playstyle. I've seen some people say they don't do Warden Shoulder Bash because its seems cheap; but I try to explain that its avoidable and leaves them wide-open for an attack if they enemy just dashes to the sides (left or right). High level play wise you will need to use all the tools in your hero's toolbox.
Cons
I have a Nvidia GTX 970 and never drop below 60 frames (but the game is locked at 60 fps), you will experience the occasional desync and people dropping from matches in Dominion mainly. I have seen people and heard of people that are experiencing it in 'every' dominion match they play; but I have not experienced this issue. It's annoying when you're mid way through a match or winning a match and the game just suddenly ends and doesn't count due to desync but it happens very rarely due to patches that dropped by the devs to soften the issue.
Some good explainations for how characters work are hidden behind How To Play, and I believe its called Hero Fight Videos. I recommend watching Basic and Advanced for every hero so you know what they are capable of then settling down to master one after trying them all out in practice against AI
Story for the Campaign is lack luster in my opinion but will have you hating the right characters to hate and making you want to kill them when you get your final showdown.
Playing gear-focused modes as a noob to the game will leave you feeling outclassed by maxed out gear stat players who can three or two shot you
Matchmaking is indiscriminate and matches you with random skill level people, from someone who just started the game. To someone who has been playing non-stop since the game came out. Gear wise this is a nightmare for newer players but in Duels and Brawls gear doesn't matter but you'll have to contend with their skill difference. Facing these better people in Duel and Brawl will most likely make you a better player if you are okay with getting beat quite a few times to learn.
Corner Traps - It is very possible for another hero to stand in front of you while you are in a corner and stop you from moving out of that corner. This can be devastating when up against a valkayrie, warden, warlord or any good player as you'll be forced to fight them two inches from your face and block everything much sooner. You'll also have to dash from left to right to avoid grapple and unblockable moves, as well as guardbreak at perfect times instead of being able to use spacing and manueverability. (If a valkayrie sweeps your legs in a corner and you dash to the left or right at the right time you will avoid it, same with Warden shoulder bash so you haave some chance)
Ledge or Environmental Kills - This game has maps that are far from OSHA compliant. There are broken railings or no railings at all on bridges that you can fall off into instant death. You can't throw yourself off or walk off, but you can however be full health and your enemy on low health can throw you off killing you instantly. Keeping in mind this is the guard break system by which when they contact with guardbreak you need to guardbreak as soon as they to which will shove them back and stop them from shoving you or going into a grapple move. It can feel really cheap when you are parrying everything your opponent throws at you and dealing massive damage (basically outplaying them heavily) and because you miss one guardbreak you fall off an edge or get thrown into spikes on the wall that instant kill you. Negating any advantage you worked so hard to secure.
Limited Soundtrack - They added a new japanese esc flute tune with the DLC, but the original theme is still there which will have you remembering the part where the violin gets really deep over and over and over. Because there's only one menu track and the DLC gave us one more menu track. I don't know combat tracks wise, it so far seemed to be just amped up war drum beats that scale with the momentum of situations.
Easy To Learn Hard To Master - You'll find this out very quickly and need to study up on how to get the most out of your Hero's playstyle. I've seen some people say they don't do Warden Shoulder Bash because its seems cheap; but I try to explain that its avoidable and leaves them wide-open for an attack if they enemy just dashes to the sides (left or right). High level play wise you will need to use all the tools in your hero's toolbox.

This game is very similar to the old flash "Epic war" series. So go find that on kongregate if you want to figure out if you want to spend money on this or not. At first the game feeIs slow and sluggish, and I got a bit disappointed with the length of the game since it ends very quickly. But I figured I'd try for the harder difficulty as well and and I found that much more interesting. Honestly it's quite the grind on the harder difficulty - but it's pretty interesting finding out that more than one strategy is viable.
You get less and less experience from monsters you have beaten earlier (monster have levels I guess, but nothing that is displayed to the player), so soon you'll run out of places to grind experience, which makes it possible to gimp yourself. So the progression feels a little bit diablo-esque: Try a build, mess it up, try something better. There is not an endless amount of strategies though, but I think it holds up pretty good for a few play throughs.
Some less pretty things:
There are some entirely untranslated pages, and others that are almost incomprehensible because of the bad translation job.
Then there are some issues that seems to be smartphone related. Like do we really need to open up a modal window to spawn units? On a pc-screen surely you can fit in a bar with 10 buttons to spawn your warriors? Mystery-meat menus and camera panning are other things that feels suspiciously like it was made for smartphone (or perhaps made with some smartphone framework). But it's not too bad, there are keyboard shortcuts for most things (except the unit spawning).
I think you need something like 10-12 hours to complete 100% achievements in this game. (Which ends up being about two play throughs, normal and hard.)
All in all, it's a solid game. Probably worth it's price tag.

So I've just finished one route and it's taken me 3 hours, as an avid manga/anime reader/watcher so assume what you will time wise.
This is made by the team that brought you "The Men of Yoshiwara" but let me tell you, it is definitely not a simply re-skin of that game. The drawing is better, the facial features are brilliant, the writing is very polished in this game - and the text flows a lot easier than in Yoshiwara. I would sometimes trip over words playing Yoshiwara because they weren't correct, but this was great.
I chose to romance Date Masamune, a man that takes after his feudal lord name, and I was not disappointed. Unlike Yoshiwara, I got a very "Amnesia: memories" feel from this game, and my relationship with the men felt a lot more genuine. I wasn't looking at guides to help me decide how to respond because I understood the characters and knew how to push their buttons this time around - I was given a load more time to fall in love with the characters. Albeit that there are only 8 chapters in this game whereas Yoshiwara had 13 as I recall.
Furthermore there are two different happy endings, provided you get the happy endings, so I recommend you go back and play both, as they differ immensely. I like the music a lot more this time around, too. The yoshiwara one started to grate on me halfway through my first playthrough.
I definitely recommend you walk into this game blind. The first time I played and I woke up in the castle, I was seriously confused alongside the Princess. Also, I get the steam store's language in the "about this game" is pretty naff, but if you're an otome fan, and if you like manga like tsuki no shippo, crazy girl shin bia or Goong, you'll like this. I thouroughly enjoyed it and I'm off to play the next man.
Get it whilst it's on offer too. Sadly, I don't think it's quite worth £12 - If you have £12 I'd recommend stardew valley or something instead, but this is neat for £7.19

When the game works, it is quite fun.
I always have a sense of unease while playing PvP, for fear not of monsters, but of players.
Probably because most of them are hackers who have a "Shoot-on-site" mindset and will not hesitate to one shot you if they see you.
PvE is a much different experience, since it adds an element of cooperation between players, but also makes the game much easier since the Nethers aren't too difficult to evade. PvE also removes the threat of hackers, since they cannot harm you in PvE.
If you want a challenging PvP survival experience that comes with hackers (free of charge!) then I certanly recommend this game. If you are looking for a cooperative, PvE survival experience with little challenge (if you know what you're doing), I also recommend this game. But be warned, hackers are an issue in PvP, and the development team seems to have dropped off the planet, so it's unlikely this will be fixed soon, if ever.
Overall: The development team should be more active, and should be more diligent with anti-cheat. But it looks unlikely they will be back soon, if ever.

The Darkness feels like a stylistic continuation of that cell-shaded beauty from 2003,  XIII. While it does have style to spare and you can have fun mowing down enemies, I still wish there were more depth.
Some of the set pieces and scripted sequences are both enjoyable and memorable. Those moments - along with the boss fights - are the best in the game. Most of the rest of it is a repetitive slog with the same weapons through enemies that pose no threat, even on the highest difficulty.
There is a skill tree, but beyond unlocking a few new basic skills I found most of it to not matter that much. Likewise, while the supernatural abilities you're granted are interesting at first, most of them can't be used beyond a short range, which definitely limits them in a game where the levels are based around gunplay and finding cover.
The story has a couple neat twists, but most of those are early on. I felt that the second half was largely a rehashing of the first, only moving things forward at the very end. And that ending doesn't really offer any kind of a conclusion. The fact that the series hasn't continued leaves the plot in a frustrating position.
If you want an FPS that you shouldn't take seriously then you should certainly give this game a whirl. Just be ready for repetition, and a story that doesn't fully satisfy.

A gem from my old 360 days. Vanquish is the first game I ever played from Platinum Games and made me a big fan of theirs even to this day, was so looking forward to Scalebound :(.  I was very excited to hear that Vanquish was coming to Steam. I just finished it and it is even better than I remember!
Pros!
- Framerate & Resolution!  Running around 100-120 FPS at 1440p on Ultra setting on my rig. Beautiful game and a smooth run throughout the entire game
-Action!  Just about nonstop action throughout. Slow-mo ability with the suit lets you zip around with your boosters and then destroy enemies with ease!
- Length - It isn't crazy  long by any means but it has a good length. I believe I beat it in about 7-8 hours. There are trials you unlock and new difficulties to test your skill against that will give you several more hours worth of fun.
- Audio!  Guns sound really awesome, each one is distinct, enemies, bullet and bomb hits, all sound really great.
Overall gameplay is just amazing. You have a boost slide and dodge roll mechanics that go into a dead eye slow-mo kind of ability. This lets you quickly take out several enemies who are pretty much stuck in place and feels great! Otherwise the game has your basic cover based shooting mechanics which work really well. You don't feel hindered by the controls with a keyboard or a controller. Boss fights are epic and they are usually HUGE!
Cons
- Difficulty  - I am still new to playing shooters on PC so chalk it up to scrubbiness. I don't remember dying so much on the 360 version. I heard there was a glitch causing you to take more damage at higher framerates which has been promptly fixed so perhaps this was the case for me as well.
- First Person Parts -  The game does drag sometimes during these first person parts with just some story and talking. Not really sure what purpose they are serving, perhaps loading the next part of the level. I felt like they broke the flow of the game and the fast pace nature of the combat.
- Menus - They are all controlled with keyboard or controller. I would have preferred to be able to use my mouse to select options and such.
- Melee -  Really the only terrible part of the combat. Melee is fairly weak and you only get 1 melee attack and it uses all of your suits energy leaving you vulnerable to attack. It does provide some cool moments where you slide kick into a slomo however.
These are all pretty minor gripes though. The price is great, the game is amazing from beginning to end. Definetely pick this baby up. Hopefully Platninum does a sequel someday. :)

Owners of Friday the 13th: The Game have the every right to say what the game is, but most of it is Dilly propaganda and issues with people that I would discuss. This is simply my experience with this game.
This game, as some matches would be fun, is not a solo playstyle game but I'll give the exception of you having a mic to coordinate. You see all those Youtubers and Streamers that are getting viewed from playing Friday the 13th? That's because they have friends and people to play with hence they have an enjoyable and cooperative time, and again I'll make the exception if they're running solo with a mic.
I mostly play Jason, so it would make sense for me to talk about him first.
When I played the game when it was released I mostly played Savini, and it was hellish as Savini is the "One" Jason as he has the best qualities of all the Jasons. The reach, the Destruction, the weapon strength, and Shift which I believe is useless but hey, if you need that extra recovery rate go for it.
When I unlocked Part 8, I knew that I needed to tone down the Savini, pretty much afterwards I toned him down all the way that I barely play him anymore due to the fact that people just know they won't have a chance. Sure it could happen to all the Jasons too but Savini is the one you paid for... and people can't buy him now and if they don't have them why even bother play against him? That isn't my only reason though, he's just a paywall that if someone doesn't have they shouldn't really have to play against him since he is especially just powerful in the aggressive ways. That's one of the problems that is most likely permanent now.
So Part 8 Jason, think of him as the water version of Savini, more of a toned down version. He is the aggressive "legit" Jason with Destruction so you could pressure like Savini, that's how I want to play after all. Better yet, he was the Jason I more aspired to want for his Water Speed, many people underestimate Water Speed as it could pretty much allow you to catch up with the escape boat and 1-2 kills. Those are the prime reasons why I enjoy Part 8, and I see his Weaknesses not all really bad at all.
But then there's always the feud of people saying that Part 9 Jason is the best Jason, and I beg to differ. From all the Jasons like they're meant to they are very much situational, and Part 8 Jason fits the universal tag for most situations. I won't lie, you can still kill but the likelihood is very low but I still believe you have a chance since getting Counselors in cabins is fairly simple. But that's an opinion for anyone, and if you believe something is best atleast hear others out and let evidence solve it if you ever get into these scenarios. Me? Nah I really don't care unless someone asks.
Counselors, yeah.
There is a range of Counselors you could choose from filling roles that you really want to do, you'll find one don't worry. This is the area where the whole group thing comes in, as it would be more enjoyable knowing that you could trust someone. Simple escapes; by a four seater car, two seater car, boat, police, or defeating Jason. Generally the police escape is hard to do as Jason could trap it, same thing with all these escapes but it's mostly leanient to the police box and four seater car. Best part is that Jason hears an audio cue if you decide to walk on a trap of his near an objective which will ultimately lead to your demise. This is where again the group thing comes in handy, as people could take watch for Jason while you force yourself into the trap, or pocket knife it, then someone on the phone calling for the police. The same thing can go for any escape but you mostly want to get a number of Counselors out. The other option is a step proccess to kill Jason which begins with taking off Jasons mask, acquiring Pamela's sweater,(Jason's dead mum) stunning Jason with the sweater after his mask is off, hitting Jason to get him to his knees, and have Tommy Jarvis with a machete or axe to defeat Jason when he is on his knees. It's hard if the Jason is good, but awarding if you live or perish.
Bugs, insects, and exploits.
The game of course like many people say has bugs that could end up killing you. But I'd like to talk about the exploits that people say are ruining the game in general which some I do agree on.
First is about Jason.
Jason can combat stance and slash at a door, effectively breaking it down quicker than the "normal" way. Keep in mind Jasons with the short range axe/machete, excluding Part 9's double axe, are more capable to being stunned during this breaking, though people have problems with this as Jasons with longer range can do this safely but are still vulnerable. I do this move all the time and people claim that it is bannable, I've read on the forums that it is not a bannable offense at all so please don't threat anyone like that.
Jason can combat stance BLOCK flare shots and firecrackers. This is one I myself had a habit of, but this is being outlawed as flares and firecrackers can all make the difference and Jason can instantly break that by blocking. This is a definite exploit that shouldn't be used.
Jason can combat stance BLOCK Counselor set traps. People say that this is a problem, but blocking traps don't give that much time for Counselors to escape and prove to do little other than award points for trapping Jason. It's still an exploit, but I don't feel as many people should get pissy about it as much since Jason was probably getting ready to block a strike from a Counselor and accidently blocked the trap.
Jason can get out of a stun from interacting with various things. I don't use this fairly too much as all you have to do is be near knives or a breakable object but it won't stop the stun duration at all.
Jason can BREAK a kill attempt by placing a predicted beartrap or interacting with something to cancel the on-his-knees stun. This is obviously an exploit as it completely just destroys a kill attempt by breaking the sweater in a fair way.
Those were some Jason exploits, I know more and probably all of them to be honest but Counselors have their own as well. Not much, but some that could end a game as a win.
Counselors can kill Jason with a killbox from stunning him while he is on the car's hitbox. This one is complicated to state, but the premis is that there is a thin line across the sides of the car that Counselors get on to prevent the car clipping through objects and plant the Jason-grab-Counselor out of a car action. But if he is on it and someone stuns him, he gets pushed at light speeds that if he touches a wall of a map it could kill him, ending the game as a win for the Counselors which is obviously broken. To be honest this is mostly accidental, and should really just be fixed.
Counselors could avoid traps by pushing eachother. Now as cool as it is, avoiding by collision hitboxes of other players isn't cool. You could do this like at a car and if the trap is where a Counselor needs to put fuel/battery/entry you could sit next to a Counselor on the side of a trap to move them away from it, effectively avoiding the trap altogether.
Those are the lighter ones, the bigger ones surely are to be kept shut, but otherwise than not this game is a group game. If you have friends that want to play this and enjoy the concept then this is a nice one to play around in.

I recommend this not as a game, but as a great opportunity for education.  As a game alone, I would not have gotten very far, and would be hesitant to recommend it.  However, when examined as a whole, this product delivers on what it sets out to do - and that is bring life to the stories and culture of the Kisima Ingitchuna people.
If you're looking for just gameplay, and don't really feel any excitement over the prospect of learning about a native american culture, then I would say this is probably not a game for you, you would be better off playing something else (Limbo has similar gameplay and is probably a bit more polished when it comes to the gameplay mechanics themselves).
If you are interested in learning about the Kisima Ingitchuna culture, this will be a unique experience,one that is much more interesting than just walking into a museum.  The Kisima Ingitchuna described themselves as a "living culture", and this game certainly exemplifies that.  I would love it if more native american tribes would create something similar, as this type of storytelling has tremendous potential to bring education and appreciation of native american culture, bringing it to life more than the still displays of a museum could.

TLDR: The game starts off with pleasing, cute graphics and a very solid atmosphere, but the lacking gameplay quickly overshadows all the nice things.
The game is tailored to be played in co-op but in case you don't have a co-op partner you can switch characters. The problem is that the AI controlling the other player is bad. The AI will follow you wenn you need it to stay where you left it, and will stay put whey you need it to follow you. Having plattforms fade in/out depending on your AI partner being in the right spot also caused me some deaths.
There is also the problem that the escape sequences often require you to quickly move plattforms and jumping over them, resulting in frequent character switches and more "Actions per Minute" than healthy for this genre.
The game feels a lot like LIMBO, it is a very simple plattformer that mostly focuses on atmosphere. The gameplay seems to have been secondary. I sometimes teleported to edges, sometimes made Jumps I shoudn't have (felt like glitches but I couldn't reproduce them). Navigating plattforms that are moving (which happens a lot) is even less responsive. It just didn't feel very good. The fact that the wind changes constantly doesn't help to make this platformer feel more solid. The schooting mechanic input doesn't work great and shooting with a great angle can be difficult. The projectile has ballistics and is therefore very inacurate, it is often just trial and error.
I hated every scriped sequence that'll eventually kill you on a timer because it is never apparent if you have to wait on the sinking ice floe and a path to safety will appear just in time, or if you should have jumped on a branch 5 seconds ago. (Playing singleplayer, e.g. having to sometimes move these plattforms to you, doesn't help here).
I also got softlocked once in my playthrough  after a cutscene, but that is just a minor issue, but I felt like mentioning it.
Again, there is just too much wrong and the experience is all in all not good enough to reccommend this.

I absolutely loved this game. Granted, it's not very long, but it's fun! I love the story, and the ability to unlock videos so you can learn more about the Iñupiat culture (and these videos relate to what's happening in-game). It's great being able to play through a traditional story and experience it for yourself. The characters are great too, and while there isn't any dialogue besides the narrator, you can get quite attached to Nuna and Fox.
I greatly enjoyed the art-style in-game, as well as the more traditional story-teller drawings in the cutscenes. The portrayal of the spirits was beautiful, and so was the scenery. The music was also well done and fitting for each area.
The weapon in the game can be a bit tricky to aim at times, but once you realize that her free hand will point to where she's aiming, it gets much easier. It's also very interesting to use it and see the video explaining how it was traditionally used.
Arguably, the puzzles weren't always that hard, but for this game I didn't find that to be a mark against it. I've played puzzle gams like Ori and the Blind Forest where, though I loved it, I was sometimes pushed to wanting to throw my controller during some rushed events or puzzles. I liked being able to approach this game with a little less frustration and a bit more consistent enjoyment. The puzzles are enjoyable, and while they can sometimes be a bit of a challenge they won't cause a rage that would cut into the enjoyment of the story being told (or cause such a long stall in gameplay that the flow of the story is lost).

FMV games are an obsolete game genre from the 1990s. They existed to try and bridge the gap between the 16 bit sidescrollers people were used to, and the high detail polygons of the future. They also helped popularize CD drives. Although while FMV games were impressive at the time, they did not age well and are generally derided online due to the lackluster acting and simplistic gameplay.
Enter Phantasmagoria. Phantasmagoria is a very bizarre FMV game (although tame compared to something like Harvester). It was created by Roberta Williams with her company Sierra On-Line. It takes a huge amount of influences from classic Stephen King stories like the Shining although does its own unique spin on things.
In Phantasmagoria, you play as Adrienne Delaney. A writer who moves into a strange house owned by a man with a dark past. The story starts out very slow and relatively dull. With time spent exploring her relationship with her husband and her relatively quirky personality. However the game gets progressively more and more surreal and bizarre as the storyline goes on. It's generally paced similarly to a Stephen King story and keeps your attention really well. It helps that the game was not afraid of controversy and doesn't shy away from scenes involving♥♥♥♥♥♥and dismemberment.
At the time Phantasmagoria was a relatively simple game to play. Almost the entirety of the game is played using the mouse. This was done to appeal to people who don't normally play video games. But actually really helped the game age better compared to other adventure games at the time. The game also runs in Dosbox so it should run relatively well, barring a few tweaks here and there.
It's a classic 90's game from yesteryear that was not afraid to offend and push the envelope. And it comes highly recommended.

Can't tell if this game is a puzzle platformer or one of those rage quit games. With that out of the way, gameplay is very simple; you will control a girl and a fox, both of them has different abilities in their skill sets that you will have to use with combinations of both of them to get throught the levels. Puzzles are simple enough and throughout the game they will keep adding up. Towards the end of the game one of the characters will get a major change in it's gameplay mechanics but it's not better in anyway, I found the change just as frustrating as it was before. However i will have to state that, game explores  the Alaskan culture in a beautiful way. This and the story alone makes this game a total win. Alaskan culture and their stories that are meant to prepare you for life are told beautifully and from metaphores to gameplay transitions are very well made. Some of the elements from the stories that are told by the narrator makes their way into the game such as enemies or platforming items and they blend in perfectly with the game it self. These Insights will unlock whenever you encounter a specific object, a place or a being and i highly recommend everyone to watch these as they unlock. I found myself being very eager to unlock the next one after I watched a few of them and they are definitely the highlights of the game. On the surface it is pretty standard Horror game fare. Without any means to defend yourself you play a deadly game of hide and seek with quite frightening biomechanical monstrocities at the bottom of the ocean, in the underwater facility PATHOS-II.
Interestingly, the encounters with said creatures are probably the least interesting part of this game. It certainly is not an action title, so if you want action survival horror this isn't it. I think that it would be possible to lose most of the monsters altogether without impacting the game much. However that by no means makes this bad, what would be standard horror hide and seek with sci fi monsters, is elevated by a compelling story and a hauntingly evocative setting.
I can't say too much about the protagonist or the setting, because to talk about either would be going into spoiler territory and this is a game that benefits greatly from going in without a plot synopsis.
Highly atmospheric and mood setting, PATHOS II looks like the 80s Sci Fi of the ALIENS franchise, by way of Bioshock's rapture. SOMA has a fantastic command of lighting, sound design and visual design that really sell the setting as you creep around its broken halls.
Gradually piecing together who the protagonist is, and what happened to PATHOS II was altogether the best part of this game. To begin with I wasn't particularly connected with the characters within the story, but as time went on I became quite attached to them and their plight.
Like good sci fi, it leaves you thinking and pondering long after the credits roll (word of note, there IS a post credits scene that is pretty essential).

The problem with free to play games is that anyone can download the game, play it for a while and then write a nasty review simply because they can, and have an agenda to destroy a title based on their petty little narrow-minded beliefs or prejudice. People who latch onto trend memes such as this I call 'fad bandwagonists'.
The problem in general is that people will tend to gather around and perpetuate a particular opinion, merely because they wish to feel that they belong. It is a universal herd mentality that we all can observe in ourselves, not just here, where people are reviewing PC games.
And so it is, that I come to write a review for a game that I like.
I also have an agenda, I wish to keep on playing this game, would like more people to try it, and I have the hope that it is/will receive further development into a more open world PvE/PvP game similar to that other one, but with better graphics, where you can't just turn off bushes/foliage/cover with the click of a mouse.
If you think Survarium is pay to win then you are mistaken. It is free to play, that does not, in this instance mean pay to win. The modifications you make to your weapons and gear do not have to be paid for, but you will find, more grind, if you are not prepared to pay a few Euros. A handful of Euros.
Gambling can be fun! Spending £0.08p to get a maximum modifier you just rolled instead of grinding for hours is not as bad as I had originally thought. But herein lies the problem, if you think you can buy your way through to the top in this game, you are mistaken. The modifiers make a very small difference to your game performance, well, most of them.
I'm not going to tell you here which are the best, most efficient modifications and which are the ones you maybe shouldn't bother with, it should become obvious to those who are just reasonably intelligent, and will be based on your playing style. So you'll just have to play the game to find that out.
Another good thing about this game is that you can very quickly rep up with the four factions, to low tier levels, if you want more variety of gear. And it doesn't matter if you only got to tier 6 in one or several of them, you can still build your character with tier 3 or lower gear, and get an easier game. And this helps me tremendously, being only an above average player, as it means I can win more often!
Don't download this game if all you want to do is carry on with another baseless crap review because you're a fad bandwagonist.

Back in the day when Guitar Hero and Rock Band became popular, I used to think how cool it would be if you could do the same thing but with real instruments.  Well, I've only put 10 hours into this so far, but it's very useful for learning to play guitar.
The starting selection of songs is OK with at least one or two songs I wanted to learn to play.  The prices for some of the DLC songs is a bit much for my liking but assuming they keep adding to the list of songs it may very well prove to be a case where I'd actually WANT to purchase and use the DLC.  Right now I think I can live without them (especially since I'm still very much a beginner).
You've got basically a set of lessons for everything from how to hold the guitar and manually tuning it all the way up to some complicated techniques.  These include practice lessons so you can demonstrate to the game that you've mastered it (except for the first few lessons that don't include actually playing).  From what I've seen, most of these lessons can be taken from 0% to 100% mastery in no time at all, though some of the techniques are tricky enough that it could take some hard work to get it down.
The Voice Over/Teacher in the game does his best to sound non-intimidating, but can instead come off sounding insincere, especially when you know that you flubbed the lesson and he says "good job!" at the end.  Then again, at least one point he told me I needed more work and yet another time I was told "it could be worse".  Gee, Thanks.
Your other options include "Learn a Song", Session Play (where you have a virtual backup band play for you), and the guitarcade.  Learn a song is self-explanatory, Session Play could be fun when you're ready to jam assuming you can tell the backup band just which chords you want to play, and the Guitarcade is a great way to practice without it feeling dull.
I've played a bit of the guitarcade to help familiarize myself with the guitar and it's slowly helping.  I can feel myself reaching for the right strings more often, and hitting the proper frets without having to look quite as much.  I am not sure I exactly agree with their system of levelling up on these games, but that helps to give you a secondary goal to just increasing your score.
Speaking of goals, this game is chock full of them.  Sometimes the game will decide it's time you looked at a new song, or tried a new mode, and other times the game considers you need more practice with chords and sends you to the guitarcade to work on it.  This is kind of a nice feature, but it feels too random at some times.   Other times the goals make more sense, like when you're learning a song, it may recommend you work on a particularly hard phrase.
However, It can be rather demanding for a newbie.  When you first learn a song, it tells you to play one note on one string and that's it.  After you demonstrate you can do this ONCE it may decide to up the ante and now you're playing two notes on two strings.  Just when you think you're getting the hang of it, it throws more at you until you feel like you're overwhelmed again.  I would like to feel like I've made progress first before going into the harder territory.  I think there's a way to reset progress on a song but that could put you too far back.
At least when you're using the "Riff Repeater" you can choose how much it throws at you, for how long, how many times you have to play it before it moves on, if it should get harder or not, etc.  The riff repeater is probably the best thing about learning a song since you can customize it fully.
The store has tagged this mistakenly as having Uplay.   The game itself does not require Uplay at all though.  It doesn't show up in my list of games on Uplay when I do launch it, and even though I am given the option of logging into Uplay, it's through the game with an email and password only...No Client running in the background.
Also, the Rocksmith website offers a "60 day Challenge", where you can show your progress from complete beginner to novice guitar player in just 60 days.  The caveat to this is that they expect you to play at least one full hour per day, and the timer doesn't run unless you're actively in a lesson, learning a song, doing the guitarcade or whatever.
Steam at this time says I've played for 11.4 hours, Ubisoft says I've played for 3 hours and 44 minutes and the 60 day challenge website says I've done 2 days worth of practice. :(
I was going to update this at 60 game hours but that  blew right by so fast I had no idea it was gone. Instead I'm editing this at the 60 day mark since I got the game.  Can I play a song 100% No... almost though.  I've got a couple in the 80%-90% range right now.
Next update when Ubisoft thinks I've completed their challenge.  It seems to only record 1 day of the challenge if I've spent at least 2 hours in game (not in menus).
