The long answer:
The Good: there are 9 races with unique traits and you can make your own custom race traits. The empire management is simple and easy to learn. The ship combat is a simple order you ships to attack this target or move here, BUT each ship takes damage to a certain part, front back left or right and once all the modules are destroyed, they can attack the core. Destroying the core destroys the ship. So you can maneuver your ships so that they last longer. The ship desgining is easily the most fun part of the game, you drag modules onto a layout of a hull and the positioning can change the part of the ship the shield will protect, the firing arc and more. There are also cool events that can happen, such as an infested ship or finding a planet of dragon people.
The Bad: the only victory is to exterminate all the other empires, and the AI acts like they know this. Diplomacy is tough, as the AI tends to ask you for your stuff and threaten war otherwise. Some of the races hull designs are certainly better than others, as the Kulrathi and Opteris Hive seem to have larger ships than the other races. Ground combat is kind of clunky and slow, and I find myself autoing the invasion, even if it makes me lose troops. The Mac version also crashes quite a bit, but it is getting less and less common.
BUY this game!

For a game of this caliber, the graphics are decent – I’m running the game on the “Fantastic” setting @ 1920 x 1080 and I maintain around 60 fps; your mileage may vary. The sound is acceptable, although several recording loops can be heard within the engine noises and the background ambients. In my opinion, the game feels a bit unfinished, and could definitely benefit from more "tweaking" work.
One of my early frustrations with this game, was getting the controls on an Xbox One controller all sorted out. Specifically the thumbsticks which control driving and camera movement. You can change the axis settings via the configuration pop-up before starting the game and this helps. After I made a few minor tweaks, I really began to enjoy it more.
All in all, it was quite fun cruising around ferrying passengers, and all the while building up my water taxi/property tycoon business within the given tropical setting of the Jo Jo Islands. I would recommend this game and I do think it’s reasonably priced for what it is. I say pick it up if you’re looking for a simple, relaxing, no brainer-time killer!

I got this game when it first came out, 7 dual-layer CDs (each chapter was a disc) and loved it (back then it would have been impossible to install this game on your HD... it was about the size of the average HD, if not larger!) As to the story, our heroine Adrienne Gordon and her loving husband Donald move into an old mansion that used to belong to a famous magician, Zoltan Carnovash. Thomas Was Alone is a game that has you control a band of suddenly sentient AIs roaming around the computer world stacking, jumping in portals and looking for an exit of their quadrate prison. Originally conceived during a personal 24-hour gamejam by Mike Bithell in 2010, the game, of course, has undergone much polishing and has definitely been deepened as an experience. The finished product is not only a simple platforming game in which you have to use different characters to progress through the level but also an interesting experiment in storytelling and, for the most part, characterization.
As you would expect, the core of Thomas Was Alone is jumping and using the right character for the right job, which the game handles in a very standard manner. The Blocks (characters) are of different width and height and also sometimes possess specific abilities – one can float on water, another acts as a trampoline – which is all what you would expect from a single-player puzzler. When you are given the right combination of unique characters the game truly shines. Combining the abilities of the anti-gravity James with the double-jump Sarah is immensely fun and, while the levels are rather easy, it is still very satisfying to see this small ensemble prevail. Sadly, most of the time, and especially in the levels that use a large amount of characters, the cooperation feels like a chore as many of the obstacles put before you are of a very artificial nature.
Thomas, the main character of the game, is an all-rounder and it feels like you could finish most of the levels using just him but the game imposes you with other characters that sometimes serve only as stepping stones once or twice, only to be left waiting for the player to finally switch to them and perform the menial task of controlling their useless, hard-edged bodies to the teleport. Most of the other puzzler games have the main character utilize tools, levers or switches to get to the end of the level, which then serve no other purpose. In Thomas Was Alone the tools are the characters and it simply does not work well. I assume the developer wants us to care about the characters, something that would create a natural drive to get them to safety, but the style of characterization makes this impossible.
Before I explain what exactly is wrong with the characterization and effectively flaws the whole design, I have to mention the base that drives the narrative in Thomas Was Alone – the narrator. The game, as many others after the success of Bastion, employs an all-knowing entity that outlines what is happening throughout the 5-hour journey. There are no visual cues, no gameplay mechanics that would serve to push the narration forward, so we have to rely on the voice of the British comedian Danny Wallace (who also helped with the script) and, as much as I loathe the idea of a narrator in a video game, he does that quite well, effectively adding to the overall soothing mood of the game. In the end though, one has to wonder if the inclusion of an external voice was, in fact, necessary. Would it not be better to make the narrator be the voice of Thomas, the main hero of the game, thus fleshing him out into a full character instead of the shell that he is now? Instead, the narrator provides us with bits and pieces of characterization for every AI we encounter, making the overall narrative heavily lean onto “telling” instead of “showing”. This makes the whole design fall flat as, in result, we do not really care about any of the controllable Blocks as they are not correctly shaped into characters. The narrator might tell you that X is feeling morose/happy/excited/etc., which is fine and dandy, but when it does not have any effect on the game you are playing, it makes the information completely pointless. The best example would be (and I hope you will not regard this as a spoiler) the situation when we are told that one AI is in love with another and… that is all that happens. No new mechanics are introduced, the Blocks do not suddenly work together in perfect harmony nor do they change their normal behaviour. The information changes nothing. To give credit where credit is due – the characterization of James is perfect. He is introduced as a lonely soul, forever ridiculed for being different from the rest and this actually translates to the gameplay – he is the only one that can, and even has to, move upside down. Unfortunately, no other character, maybe with the exception of the late-game Sarah, is crafted so well, making the platforming aspect loose most of its appeal.
Thomas Was Alone is certainly an experiment in the field of narration. Have everything that Mike Bithel designed clicked, it might have been a unique experience marrying the retro nostalgia with charmingly quirky modern storytelling. Sadly, it falls short of its noble goal, ultimately ending in a product that would be best labeled “style over substance”.

So I never got to play a lot of the cool point and click horror games in the 90s, I was a console gamer and didn't own a gaming PC. I was aware of a lot of them, though, and finally, in 2016, I can say I played one of the most legendary: Phatasmagoria.
I can see what the fuss back then was about. FMV of acting the caliber of a local puppet show and CG animated backgrounds with the same intensity as watching the door open during a Resident Evil load screen. All of this helps to create an unparalleled moody atmosphere and intriguing mystery around the enormous mansion where a famous magician violently died...and possibly worshiped Satan.
The story, which is very similar to The Shining, but better, revolves around a pony tailed dweeb, turning from clueless dork to nasty, possible wife beater husband, demanding drain cleaner and getting angry at pots in the barn. You play as his bra hating waifu, writing her next novel while trying to avoid her newly abusive husbando's verbal attacks by making him food and having picnics. She also talks to a classy realtor gentleman and numerous old people in the town shopping center consisting of exactly 3 stores for any general goods, antique, or realty needs.
If you like horror, pointing and clicking, 1995, women named Lou, or The Shining, I'd highly  recommend this game.

The Good Life description says that this is a game about building a "commercial empire" while becoming "rich and famous". However in reality, the game is so shallow that these descriptions are bordering on false advertising and misrepresentation. I'll briefly explain how the description provided is just barely met by the reality of what the game actually gives you.
Do you build a commercial empire? Well, you do have a box that pops up occasionally to allow you to buy property. But that is the end of it, no further interaction from the player. I wouldn't call it management at all since you cannot even set a charge for renting these properties or influence them at all. What these do is function as bonus cash after you taxi clients from port to port. This brings me nicely onto the boating business aspect.
When someone says the game is about running a business, there are some key elements required for that to really apply. Budgets, marketing, customer relations and employee relations are the core things which come to mind.  Well, The Good Life does require you work to a budget but everything else is absent. You apparently have employees because boats you own, but don't personally use, generate income like your other investments. But again, you don't actually influence any of that. Essentially your 'empire' consists of you personally picking up customers and taking them from A to B. Now this wouldn't really be too bad since games like Crazy Taxi actually made this kind of thing enjoyable but sailing empty waters in largely straight lines gets dull very fast and the highlight of the journey is the challenge of docking the boat without damaging it. One of the biggest mistakes the developers made is to give you the slowest boat in the game at the start and not explain that they can instantly buy a speed-boat instead. The developers should have simply provided the speed boat right away to avoid frustrating players.
The description also says that this has exploration, treasure hunting and other activities. Well, since you cannot ever leave your boat the exploration is limited to looking at islands from the coast and while the diving sections do allow you to very slowly move around freely, there is only 1 small map which is used for every diving mini-game. There is fishing, but it is a mini-game that just generates some more cash and isn't profitable or serve any purpose in the larger scope of the game. There isn't any complexity to fishing other than pushing the up and down arrows keys to reel the line in or loosen it to stop the line from breaking. There are other trivial events which happen at random as well. Such as tossing life-preservers to rescue people in the water, the occasional pirate speed-boat for you to avoid and the laughable 'tornadoes' which appear from time to time. But none of these are very interesting.
I can honestly say that while The Good Life sounds good on paper; what it gives you is a shadow of what it promises. Paying money for this game would be a big mistake even if it was on sale due to the limited entertainment value and what basically boils down to as leveling system where you invest time and energy to just see your bank balance grow. It lacks personality, a sense of progression or achievement and it just barely manages to even qualify as a game at all, due to how shallow the content is.

I received this game as a gift from a friend, but I would absolutely recommend paying money for Never Alone at its full price. It has a rich, powerful story that is captivating, fun, and a bit sad, narrated in Iñupiaq.
I remember growing up in the Pacific NW and Alaskan Natives would travel to our schools to share their language and tell us stories; this is a strong reminder about the intense need to preserve Native language and culture.
PROS:
-Awesome design work. I'm not a fan of side scrollers, but this felt very three-dimensional. I could get lost in the world for fun.
-Incredible storytelling.
-The 'Cultural Insights' videos. If you skip them during gameplay, go back and watch them at the end. They are well worth it.
CONS:
-Clunky gameplay. Nuna doesn't always respond to cliff edges and Fox didn't always seem to want to jump up a high wall, among other things. I'm not mad about it, though; it's obviously far more heavily invested in its story and that's what I came for.
-Felt too easy at times, but again, it was a story-game.
Please buy Never Alone! You will not regret it!

I picked this game up as part of a Humble Bundle earlier this year and to be honest I wasn't expecting a lot. I was plesantly surpised by the quality of this game.
The story itself is interesting, albeit a tad short. As a puzzle-platformer the game plays relatively well, despite the occassional control issues or graphical glitches (sometimes it was funny to see exactly where my character would get stuck in a wall, though I did really only experience this in the games later levels).
My one complaint about the game is that about halfway through the mechanics between the fox and the girl change significantly and it felt to me like this change was more geared towards co-op gameplay, as opposed to a single player campaign. Overall I found the game to be very enjoyable.
The game also contains cultural insights that give you a look into the culture behind the game. I haven't had a chance to actually watch these yet but they do look like they will be interesting and I look forward to checking them out, as well as the game's DLC "Foxtales".
One final note is that the game has a very enjoyable soundtrack. It's calm and peaceful when it needs to be but also kicks it into high gear when the time comes for it to. On the surface it is pretty standard Horror game fare. Without any means to defend yourself you play a deadly game of hide and seek with quite frightening biomechanical monstrocities at the bottom of the ocean, in the underwater facility PATHOS-II.
Interestingly, the encounters with said creatures are probably the least interesting part of this game. It certainly is not an action title, so if you want action survival horror this isn't it. I think that it would be possible to lose most of the monsters altogether without impacting the game much. However that by no means makes this bad, what would be standard horror hide and seek with sci fi monsters, is elevated by a compelling story and a hauntingly evocative setting.
I can't say too much about the protagonist or the setting, because to talk about either would be going into spoiler territory and this is a game that benefits greatly from going in without a plot synopsis.
Highly atmospheric and mood setting, PATHOS II looks like the 80s Sci Fi of the ALIENS franchise, by way of Bioshock's rapture. SOMA has a fantastic command of lighting, sound design and visual design that really sell the setting as you creep around its broken halls.
Gradually piecing together who the protagonist is, and what happened to PATHOS II was altogether the best part of this game. To begin with I wasn't particularly connected with the characters within the story, but as time went on I became quite attached to them and their plight.
Like good sci fi, it leaves you thinking and pondering long after the credits roll (word of note, there IS a post credits scene that is pretty essential).

Here's a truthful review... no biases (until the end)
For Honor has an in-depth fighting system that is unlike any before. The immersion to this combat can be very fun, but also very stressful which could be the reason why some people don't like it. The learning curve, especially as the game gets older, is super high and some new comers don't understand that going into a 4v4 player vs player match as your first game will not end well. The servers are buggy, but on good wifi, crashes only occur 1-3 times per 50 sessions (doesn't crash the whole game, just the match). Character balance, while not perfect, is being improved by the devs, and as a player gets more skilled, these unbalances go away. The community can be cancerous, but most times it's either funny or they are bad and you can mine salt from them. Vortexes are a major problem, especially in duels (vortxes are infinite attack chains). The devs have made little acknowledgement to this issue, but they are involved in their community on reddit, so the fix may come eventually.
Bias:
If you like medeival combat, get the game. Even if you absolutely can't handle multiplayer for some reason, the campaign has a pretty solid story and is a challenge to new players (and realistic mode is a challenge to all players). I don't see how anyone could not get some fun out of this game. Server issues are being exaggerated by a handful of players, and character balance is being exaggerated by new, salty, or bad players.

Patch H has really messed this game up. The AI does not respect Core Space. I've started several games and the narrative is always the same. Opteris colonizes beside me, sends a colony ship to Sol system. If I try to block it, its war and it sends wave after wave of fleets 7 and 8 ships strong.  Even if I manage to build a fleet of ten ships it always has more. If I allow it to build the colony then soon after I get a message telling me that I am in its space and need to vacate.  In which case its war and I have fight wave after wave of superior ships.
The AI seems to muster resources quicker that I can ever manage.  In all, these are 15 to 45 minute games with the outcome always the same.  It does not seem to suffer the same penalties for building ships as players do. The only weapon that was somewhat effective, the mass driver, now is useless because of the newly introduced aiming penalty.
One of the missions right off the bat is to colonize three systems for which you get 500 bc. However it seems that colonizing three systems really pisses the AI off and so it makes a bee line to my cololnies to take care of business. Doing this takes away valuable resources that could be used to build fighters.  However not  colonizing only postpones the inevitable.
It is obvious that there is no fog of war for the AI as it always goes for the weakest colonies and when it knows it has the advantage it swoops in and destroys everything.

I like where the game is going but hope some of the AI related issues get worked out. I feel that backing things off to give players time to figure things out a little more would make the game that much more enjoyable.

I bought Stardrive 2 with a 33% discount since I own Stardrive 1. I don't mind dropping 20 bucks on a game I'll play for 20+ hours. Stardrive 2 is a game I'm enjoying more than some of the other stuff out there. Even the "tacked on" ground combat isn't as bad as everybody is saying it is. Overall, I like the game.
If you can't afford or want to pay for this kind of game because you hate the dev or whatever, then don't, or wait for a Steam sale. Or, if you're like me and don't really care to light the torches and grab a pitchfork because a dev moved on from his former project, buy it for what it is: a decent single player 4X space game with tactical ground combat elements.
Pros
+ Ship customization is awesome
+ Ship combat is interactive RTS unlike other games where you just watch the results (Gal Civ II)
+ You can't research everything, so you need to make strategic choices in the best research options
+ You can acquire tech that you can't research through trade, racial traits, or assimilating planets.
+ Cool events and side quests
+ Races are varied and interesting
+ Other subtle nuances in game that show care and thought went into it
+ The price is definitely worth it. I could easily see myself putting well over 100 hours into this game over time.
+ Replayability
+ Steam workshop (future mods!)
+ Music (I just like it)
+ Tutorial is well done
Cons
- Some useful shortcuts are lacking, such as the ability to set fleet engagement ranges, instead, you have to set the optimal engagement range for each and every ship.
- Damage to specific systems and the effects of such are not shown, rather it shows colored damage to ship sections instead, leaving you guessing as to what is or is not working in that section of the ship.
- Ground combat feels incomplete, but I'm glad its there rather than not. Hopefully, future patches will improve it.
- Cannot customize fighters beyond simply researching tech and having them auto upgraded
- The community (Many people are griping about Stardrive 1 being abandoned too early.)
Overall, I give Stardrive 2 a 7.5 out of 10, and I expect it will likely improve over time with modding and content patches or DLC.

Pros:
- Amazing gameplay. The mechanisms are completely different from pretty much any other game
- Community. Honestly 60% of them are toxic but in my experience they are all joyfully easy to mess with. The other 40% are tremendously friendly and a real pleasure to play a game or two with.
- Gear system. People hate it and I can see why, but honestly I think it's better than anything. It makes the game unpredictable and keeps it from getting bland. (Plus despite what people say, it's really not game-breaking).
-Not P2W. A LOT of people will disagree here. Steel can be used to buy experience boosters and gear, but its purposes are mostly cosmetic. You can drop an extra $40 on this game to max out a hero's gear, but all that really does is make the learning curve a LITTLE bit easier. This game is fairly difficult, having higher stats comes nowhere close to knowing what you are doing. Play the game a bit, accept that you will not be the greatest player ever, and that you will probably get wrecked a lot when you start.
Cons:
- As everyone else here will say, the servers are crap. What should be dedicated is peer to peer, with a tendency to throw random people together and not actually find the people closest to you. Personally I only have a real issue every 5 games or so, but other people seem to have more.
- Low playerbase. It seems like it's mostly caused by the servers being crap and ample connectivity issues. I love the game and I can deal with the occasional outage, but the lack of players has made several game modes unplayable (Such as brawl, which is a 2v2 game mode and also my favorite). The only really viable mode now is Dominion, which is a point control game.
- No penalty for leaving matches early. It's a common thing, one guy will ragequit in a match and suddenly the advantage shifts heavily, and then everyone on their team will waterfall into quitting and the winning team gets stuck with bots. Eventually new players replace the bots and get stuck in a game which they are losing at the start. I've had 6 hour binges where literally every game I played was joining in late.
- Matchmaking. It's a pathetic attempt at it. For example, occasionally games will start without the lobby being full (Oh well) so the missing players are played by bots. Sometimes, it will be a 4v4 and one team will have two bots and the lowest levels in the match at the start. It also doesn't include gear level. Gear is not the tide-turning, end-all be-all thing people make it out to be, but it does make enough of a difference to need to be accounted for.
- "No Honor". The community can be garbage. People complain about spam constantly and can't handle the "Dishonorable" kills. As a heads up to anyone reading this who owns or wants to buy the game, every spam combo can be easily ended by the touch of one button, either dodge, parry, or guardbreak. There are very rare instances where you are 100% helpless against an attack, and those situations only occur when you screw up.
- Revenge/Gear. Revenge is a mechanic meant to make a gank possible to survive; your defense goes up, health is partially restored, and you do a LOT more damage. In a 3v1 the lone player can get revenge and at the very least give himself some breathing room. The problem with this is that gear (Which I also consider a pro) can be leveled into giving you revenge faster, which goes as far as people getting it twice in a 1v1.
The last one is more of an opinion. When you get into a good game it's a ton of fun, but getting into a game alone is difficult, and getting into a well-matched game is nigh impossible. Might be worth buying on sale, but for full price I would laugh at you.

Stardrive 2 is what Master of Orion 3 should have been.
The space combat engine is probably the best ever created, the space battles are spectaculars, and once you know what you are doing with the ship designer, the tactical part is really present. It's a pure jewel. The economy and research system are an improved and modernised copy/paste from Master of Orion 2, so it's very good and also very solid. This part of the game is also quite well balanced for release, that's worth mentionning.
However, as all 4x release, it's not perfect, the game has also some flaws due to its youth. The different ship modules are not as well balanced as the economy, some work is still needed here. The ground combat system is not as bad as it could look, but still, it need some work also (espescially the ground combat IA). The diplomacy lack some obvious options, like the 'Alliance' and 'Declare war to' ones. There is also some small bugs here or there (quite rare, no crash), and some optimisation to do for big battles.
On the overall, despite its youth's flaws, Stardrive 2 is wonderfull. Since release I have put nearly +70hrs in it, and enjoy it like crazy. It reminds me of the MoO2 birth in the old days : the game had lot of bugs (far more than SD2), and still I couldnt stop playing during nearly a month, it was a so good time.. as it is now with SD2 actually!
To end this review, and to be fair with you, readers, I would not say that it is the best space 4x ever created yet, as for me Distant Worlds, which is in real time and quite different on many aspects, has still the title. But trust me, considering all the passion Zero (the lone dev) put in SD2, it's only a matter of time before Stardrive 2 take the title. Six months? One year? I dont know, but for sure, it will happen! ;)
Thank for reading.

Anyway, I played Worms Armaggedon like 20 years ago when it first came out, and it was such a blast.  I compare Forts a lot to that game, because there's so much back and forth and skill involved, but rather than being turn-based, it is real-time.  There's resource management, but it doesn't get in the way of the gameplay (it compliments it well).
I defintely recommend this game, there is more than enough content for a full release.  There are some balancing issues that are being worked (a few mid-late game weapons are rather OP), but the Devs are active and have done multiple balancing fixes throughout the game's life.

One of the better FMV adventure titles from the golden age of adventure games. It plays just as well as it did when I owned it around the time when it originally released. Some people may be turned off by the dated graphics or may not enjoy FMV visuals, but back in the day the visuals were mind-blowing, and to me it still looks good. The storyline is still interesting and well-done. Some of the characters are played out as kooky 90's stereotypes, and that's ok with me. Some of the acting is well done, while the rest of the acting is so bad it's good, in a cheesy b-movie horror kinda way that complements the atmosphere/story.
The atmosphere and music are still pretty scary and well done. I still love how the game starts off slow in the first chapter with not a whole lot of scares going on while still effectively building tension/suspense, while the game progressively gets more and more intense and disturbing as you work your way towards the final act. The game takes between 5-15 hours to complete, depending on how good you are at the puzzles and whether this is your first time playing or not, which is pretty good value for a $13 or lower game. I only have two problems with the game: first, most of the puzzles are easy to figure out. Second, I didn't like the ending.
In conclusion, Phantasmagoria is still great to this day; I am glad to have rekindled my past with it. I recommend it to any adventure gaming completionists, or people looking for a great old-timey, spooky/retro good time. 8/10.

So I might be a little bias to this game given that it was one of the very first point and click adventure games from my childhood and I've always had very very fond memories of this game.. Now that I've gone back and played it a bit, I remember why I loved it as much as I did when I was a kid.
To start off this is a point and click adventure game that features a actors over a green screen in a 3D rendered background. It's got a strangely charming feeling when I go back to play this game at nearly anytime with the way the actors need to interact with the enviroment around them.
Our story is about a Novelist named Adrienne and her photographer husband Don who purchase a mansion nearby a small town. The previous owner of the mansion was a magician named Zoltan Carnovash. The very first night after arriving towards their new home Adrienne experiences a nightmare but that is only the start of her worries, as her curiosity and the forces at work within the house hold much worse horror than a simple nightmare.
To be completely honest, doing a pro/con list would be kind of useless for me and my love for this game since I'm just so happy that it has come to steam and a digital format where someone could randomly obtain this game and maybe enjoy it as much as I do. The start is a little campy as you explore the house and just obtaining your first set of items and figuring how to use them and meeting the characters and the story progresses for the better as you complete each chapter. There are probably guides that you could use on the internet to get through if you got stuck but the hint system in game has helped me out enough, even today if I  get a little stuck to find out what I need to do or if I had forgotten something.
Once again, I am just highly pleased that this game has 'come' back and I hope other people are able to enjoy it and its mystery as much as I did over a decade and a half ago.

Review for Vanquish (PC)
Well here is a bit of background, I played this game on PS3, I thought it was fun but I hate playing shooters with analog control and the framerate was simply awful so I just stopped playing around half way in the game. But hearing the game was going to be on PC was the greatest news since all my issues are fixed simply by being on this particular platform.
[Gameplay] 9 / 10
I'm not someone who plays many cover shooters because I honestly find it being a slow process of poking out of walls over and over which seems like a matter of time till I win deal. Vanquish if you really want to you can do this but it's not an optimal way to do this if you want those high score time bonuses. On top of aim, shoot and cover you're also given a rocket slide, multiple melee options which can change based on your current weapon, smoking behind cover and then tossing the♥♥♥♥♥out into the battlefield and have that distract all opposition and access to bullet time.
Bullet time, dashing, all melee except from disklauncher and access to the one unlimited ammo weapon in the game all cost boost guage which very quickly regenerates to give you as constant access to it but if you run out you're not just out of these benefits till it returns which compared to how fast the game makes you feel, makes it feel like an eternity but you're only 30% as fast in movement making getting gunned down a simple task, it really makes it feel justified having so much in way of abilities where an instant of over exerting what's allowed can set you up to be killed in an instant.
This is the sort of gameplay you may feel a bit odd at the start and maybe even over punishing when you're still learning how to manage boost guage but playing with a mindset of what you can possibly do and constantly trying to do it will leave you by end game feeling like the super power mech suit soldier doing a awesome slide through enemies just like on the box.
A last touch about this game's gameplay is that it coulds the % of time you spend behind cover which I personally see as the game as judging me so it felt like it was heavily encouraging me to play faster, but half of me thinks it was to hide the one issue I had with the gameplay which is when on cover the times I eventually try to use it I get A. Stuck on the side of the wall instead of being behind it so the fire I attempted to avoid just finished me while I hug the side of the cover that I just made a last stand trying to get behind. B. Trying to strafe on it makes me just stand up and I get shot. C. When there is a soldier where I want to get cover which is very common as they're hugging all cover, the cover and revive soldire he'll like a nice guy revive then when he could just as easily do it after he's safe behind cover without even leaving it. These issues are there but they're no where near deal breakers for something according to my end screen only took up 5% of my action.
[Difficulty] 10 / 10
This would also be a good place to talk about to design of enemies and the levels, every segment in the game is a straight up harder part then the last offering more in both quantity and variety and stronger enemies, it leads to the difficulty going up a slow incline of it going up more and more but you're gaining experience of dealing with more and more making it never feel like the game is suddenly now tossing too much at you.
A good example that I'm sure others will use but let that be a sign of how much the game respects your skill.
Here are 3 acts from level 1, 2 and 3, there are more then these segments in each level
Level 1 - Early on you fight a Spider tank boss with a later phase where it becomes a mecha after launching missles everywhere in a massive barrage which can hit you easily, not just a stylish form change, you start on an advantageous platform with an option to go to the more wider spaced arena with 2 turrets to also take advantage of to deal the massive damage to the weakpoints.
Level 2 - Now in a massive arena with no turrets or advantageous spot you must now fight both phases of that previous boss fight at the same time, these aren't nerfed versions of the boss either, they're both exactly like in level 1 but now fight at the same time.
Level 3 - After fighting 3 of a super soldier version of the basic enemy it makes you fight a new mini boss in the form of a hover craft tank, then it leads you to a cramped arena that at first seems like only a few enemies, but in the time it takes to dispatch them that Spider tank boss appears again now in a cramped smaller arena, in this cramped arena it still does that large rocket barrage form change which is really hard to dodge in a crammped arena (With a safe zone only if you chose to keep the boss where he entered and make quick work of this phase) and again you have to fight this second form with now a super lazor desperation attack. Level isn't even over yet, now fight 2 of the strongest main enemy in the game in an arena with no cover (like it helps vs this enemy)
Still 2 more levels in the game after this, and the later challenges are all straight up spikes from there but they're optional extras after.
There's a level of respect for your skill with this sort of design where they can keep handing you the first boss of the game over and over and I really like this, I'd describe it as a fair arcade game, it's hard to take your money but still builds up how hard it's going to be later giving you time to get hooked first.
[Graphics] - 6 / 10
What is in the game looks nice, really damn nice, but I'm not sure if that's because of time into making look this nice through out or because of recycling because like 80% of the game is the same theme with only a segment of level 4 and the ending of level 5 really changing the look of the game.
Until the game outright through a menu gives a score screen which it doesn't always do to sign an end of act you might not even be able to tell unless you die and reset to find out, honestly one of the best parts is when the colour pallet changes late game just looks so nice on the eyes to have a time to be washed from the whites and silvers all over the game otherwise.
[Story] ? / 10
Characters are our main Sam who you'll enjoy jetstreaming through the game with, Elena the scientist who comments on if you're rushing areas and comments on suit performance in segments where it's being pushed and progress like Hannigan from RE4 and also like Hannigan she is a QT 3.14, Burns who is Sams OTP in levels he has pretty good banter with Sam while they work together and low key giving objectives in mission acts and last but not least Hillery Clinton who opens up by telling Russia she'll attack them (great plan) and acts suprised when they attack first by stealing their moon sized microwave.
Pretty solid cast who you hear comments from while you play but they never feel like they're ever in the way of you which is a good point to have.
The plot is some people say some things then "Tab to skip" comes up and the gameplay starts again, funny that. :^) It ends fighting some Russians with large knifes so I take it we're were all this time playing the worlds largest CS:GO match for ownership of the planet.
I don't think the story is importent and skipped it but it's there if you want it but I can't comment on it as I'm not a professional and skipped it to keep feeding my need to play.
I had a segment about music next but steam is limiting my sucking off of this game short of the climax so I had to cut it out. TL:DR music is forgetable but sound effects being clear and distinct is top notch.
[Overall]
This is a game that you can pick up and play have a lot of fun, and then do it again and again because it's that accessible, feels nice to play a game with no downtime and keeps scaling up and up and then end feeling like you simply had fun and would want to experience it again, hope this PC port puts in encoragement to make a sequel.

Why don't "they" make more games like this? I really like this game a lot!
Basically, this is a game about moving to the tropics and taking over a small boat transportation enterprise. You spend most your time transporting people from island to island (for a fee), while acquiring the money to help build your tourist industry empire (via bidding on properties that pay rent). There are also missions that have you skin diving to collect treasure and find downed vintage helicopters, etc... You also have the opportunity to fish (which I have yet to get the full hang of). As you gain money and property, you also gain reputation. And yes, you can buy different boats and so on as you increase your funds (and it is all fairly open ended). The game apparently ends when (you go broke or) you drive all of your competitors out of business. Haven't got to that point yet...  :)
The game takes a little getting used to as far as the controls, but its smooth sailing (sorry) once you do. There are some minor issues that the developer is on top of and he has already released a patch addressing some of them and adding improvements (literally acknowledging the individual players who suggested them). He is very engaged on the "discussions" board and obviously, is very open to those of us who have made suggestions. THIS is the kind of communication that you hope for from a developer!
I'm really excited about the possibilities that might be included and the tweaks that will be made. Because this game is really fun to me .... And I believe it can be even more fun as its further refined. If the game is not going to be undated further, I would love to see a "The Good Life 2."

I reviewed the game a year and a half ago while it was on Desura and for the most part had a positive experience.  However, there are some glaring flaws that I'm sorry to say haven't been fixed.
*There are no audio sliders in the option menu.  Granted, this can be worked around by using your desktop's audio mixer, but you really shouldn't have to.
*At present, there are certain situations in which the "save" button will not appear when you hit "esc" to view the in-game menu.  This can be a bit inconvenient for when you need to leave in a hurry.
*I like the addition of the new red quest line telling you where to go on your map, though for whatever reason it displays a line from the last port I've been to rather than the current port to which I'm currently docked.  It's worth noting that this only happens before you accept the quest (when you check to see where the destination port is on your map) - 11/30/14 Update: This appears to have been fixed.
*Safari and photo missions tend to pop up at the worst times (like when on a timed ferry mission) and skipping it so as to deliver the person on time will actually penalize you.
*On the plus side, new fishing missions have been added though reeling in a fish takes some getting used to.  The water effects are superb but the rest of it (character & cloud models, etc.) could use work.
For now, the game is simply "good" for the asking price, though it could have been better.

I really wanted to like this game. It's a budget title so I went in with what I think are fair expectations. The problems are fixable so I'll start with the good, end with the bad. Maybe they'll get fixed! Edit: The developers have noted that they're working on some of the negatives in my reveiw. This game is NOT shovelware, it's just rough. It's November now, if you're reading this review a few months from now, check the forums to see if my concerns have been fixed. Edit2: Pirate issues have been addressed. I can safely give this game a thumbs up. It's ROUGH, but still good if you like this kind of game.
The graphics are a mixed bag, the models for people are so bad, but it's not really a big deal because the game is about boats, water and scenery. I think they did a pretty good job on that although there is definitely some improvement with weather effects.
I really liked the physics for waves. You can't just point your boat in a direction and go, you've got to be active on the helm like in a real boat.
The controls for everything except steering your boat are awful. Trying to aim when throwing life rings is nauseating. Trying to use the diving controls is a nightmare, fishing is confusing and unfun even once you know what you're supposed to do.
The random event generator is unbalanced, a random Hurricane is awesome. Two in a row is dumb.
Pirates, at least early in the game are a death sentence. I got two pirate events in a row before giving up on this game.
Edit!!: Boat Damage has been addressed and fixed---
Boat damage is economically crippling. A trip taking about 10 minutes might pay for 10% of your ship's damage. A single crash can cause that much, pirates might cause 50% damage. Damage also slows you down so good luck earning your way back to 100% health after a pirate hits you.
Edited on 25 Nov 2014: Made a note that the developer has acknowledged some of these problems.
Edit: 26 Nov 2014: Repair damage has been rebalanced and pirate areas are now marked. This was the thing that made me feel like the game was unplayable. The other issues are still being worked on.

So after a few months playing this, I'm giving it a positive review.
PROS:
- Excellent animations. What you'd want to expect from a AAA company
- Art direction and game just looks nice. High quality textures, and models
- Fluid combat. In combination with the animations, the combat looks and feels great.
- High skill ceiling on most characters means there's a lot to learn about playing a single character.
- The AI is for the most part pretty good. While level 1 and 2 bots are fairly easy, level 3 bots will eat your face. The AI is sophisticated enough that I enjoy playing them, even if they are easy to manipulate.
- 1 male, 1 female, 2 male/female character options per faction is awesome to see.
- Armour customisation is great. Could always use more stuff.
MEH:
- It has a story. It's not that good, but the fact that it’s there and attempts to follow into the multiplayer is something.
- Ornaments are very meh on most characters. Mythic outfits sometimes look rediculous.
CONS:
- P2P connections. It took about two months for patches to come out that made 4v4 modes not a total mess of instability. Even now, moths later, someone leaving the game can cause no end of problems. If they don't have permanent servers for any ranked games they hope to have, then the game will die.
- Revenge in 1v1 modes. The fact it exists in this mode is ridiculous, and it either immediately causes an imbalance of character power, or the other player simply avoids them until its over, doing nothing.
- Character balance. Obviously in fighting games you're going to get an imbalance of some characters, however some characters you have to wonder who pushed them out the door. PK lights are so fast that she's been banned on console tournaments. Warlord has a ridiculously bloated kit that can handle almost any match up, while Raider and Conq have tiny kits. Warden 50/50 vortex is something that no other character has and makes him incredibly imbalanced in 1v1 situations.
- Ubisoft community interaction. The first few weeks of the game launch had next to no contact with the devs about balance and performance issues. It took a boycott over server outages to get them starting a more constant stream of communication.
-Matchmaking. The system always seems to prioritise nearby people over skill. While this may be more stable in terms of speeds, it does mean that as an Australian, ♥♥♥♥ing NO ONE play Elimination except during 5-7 pm AND there's an elimination contract. I would like to see an option to allow the search to expand just so people can still play the game even when the in game count inevitably lowers. (Yes I know this would wreak havoc across the p2p system, hence why ubisoft should get ♥♥♥♥ing dedicated servers)
Overall the fact I have 240 hours in this means that I enjoy this game immensely. However, it has some glaring problems that could kill the entire community if not address. Primarily character balances and dedicated servers.

A little bit about me, I have played probably every major space 4X game made. MoO1-3, Space Empires 2-5, Galactic Civilizations 1-2, Sword of the Stars 1-2, Sins of a Solar Empire, Imperium Galactica 2, Endless Space, Distant Worlds, and many many more. I also was a Beta Tester for a couple of the Distant Worlds expansions and you can see my name in the credits. So you could say that I have been around the space 4X block, and I really enjoy this game, warts and all. Let me break it down a little. Keep in mind the next few things throughout my review:
A - this game is made by one developer (goes by the handle "Zero"), and he contracts out art, music, and other assets. So very indie.
B - this game is only $20+ at time of review, and as an owner of StarDrive1 I got a discount (so no ♥♥♥♥♥ing about having to pay for a new game if you bought SD1, and yes this game is a huge leap forward and worth the price). What's my point? This game is arguably as interesting as Civ Beyond Earth, and a fraction of the price, so lots of value for the money.
C - I am comparing this game to other space 4X games in each category, not other genres.
D - I have read some reviews where players claim that the AI is cheating, I think they just didn't RTFM and don't realize that there are mechanics like TAXATION that can net players and AI lots of cash to supports massive fleets and cash negative planets with.
Graphics 9/10 - This isn't Halo4, but man this game LOOKS GOOD for a space 4X! Great colors and effects, and the ships and artwork are clean and stylish. Explosions and weapon effects are slick. IMHO best looking space 4X in a while. The only weak point is the ground combat doesn't look very good. Would have preferred the ground combat from MoO2, even now the most epic looking space 4X ground combat.
Sound 8/10 - This game has an epic sound track that I didn't tire of easily. Weapon effects like different thuds as mass drivers hit armor or shields brings the combat to life. Quite adequate.
Diplomatic AI 7/10 - This game has a great feature where there is a threshold on how many deals you can make with another faction that keeps you from spamming tech trades or going from being complete strangers in to becoming instant besties like in the Master of Orion series and most 4X games. The main drawback here is that the other empires just don't feel as alive as they could, but to be honest this is a huge problem with most 4X games. The main one that does it better is GalCiv2, man that AI was dastardly! I will note that as of yesterday (4/24/15) Zero released a patch that works on my of the Diplo AI's issues so this is definitely something that will get better with time.
Strategic Fleet AI 8/10 - Your opponents don't quite feel as alive as they could, but man are they AGGRESSIVE, and I am not just talking about declaring war. This is the first space 4X in a long time where the AI contantly pounces on my undefended systems (and INVADES the planets successfully) and aggressively engages my fleets. Enemy fleets could coordinate a little better, and upgrade their ships more often, but overall the Strategic Fleet AI is solid.
Ship Customization 9/10 - Dude this game is seriously cool, like Gratuitous Space Battles mixed with Master of Orion. Love the ship customization, the only drawback here is that SOMETIMES the AI doesnt pick great ships to build. The other minor gripe is that not every race's ships are created equally, some races have more spaces on their ships for components, etc.
Map 9/10 - Two of the four "X"s are Explore and Exploit, well this game has fun mechanics that really support this. Meaningful wormholes with interesting placement, space monsters, pirates (human themed space monsters), Orion... I mean Master raiders are there and there are rewards to be gained once they are defeated. Also, planets can have specials like having deep caves, dangerous fauna, strategic resources that give your empire a boost, etc. In addition there are minor races that you can trade with, hire mercs from, or attack and subjugate.
Ground Combat 6/10 - This feature just isn't there yet. It has the potential to be very advance wars or XCOM, but instead it is just kinda underdeveloped and a bit of a slog. I would suggest Auto-Battling until this is fixed in a patch or in a Mod, which is sure to happen and would be pretty easy to flesh out.
Tech Tree 9/10 - This is very closely based on the Master of Orion model, including the core concept that you can only research one of three techs at each level of research and can only trade or steal for the ones that you didn't research. This is assuming that someone researched a tech, and often one tech isn't researched and so you can have a game where some techs aren't available. There are a few nice features that earn this high score. One, you can often unlock secret research projects by doing things like killing a space monster and dragging it's corpse in for research. Two, each race has hidden techs specific to it.  Three, at the end of each tech tree are a choice of two advances that you can take over and over again that give you meaningful benefits like increased ship speed, weapon damage, diplomacy boosts, shield strength, etc. There are also references to one of my favorite scifi book series "Old Man's War", so kudos to the dev.
End Game 8/10 - Currently there is no allied victory condition, but Zero posted as of the latest patch that he will be adding that in. No victory animation or movie (like the slick one in Master of Orion 2), or Civ style map replay (which would be really cool to relive the adventure), nor a power graph screen, but it does rank you versus fictional SciFi chracters (I was ranked Picard); funny I dont recall seeing Kirk or Blackjack Geary listed, what a shame.
Modding Support 8/10 - As of right now the game has Steam Workshop but it isn't listed like normal, you have to navigate to the Workshop tab and search plug-ins to see them. Alternatively you can head over to the game's forums on the dev's website. StarDrive1 benefitted heavily from player made content and I suspect that this game will too. Unfortunately at time of review there is no integrated mod loading menu like in SD1, not sure of dev plans but I hope this is added sooner than later and that the Steam Workshop works correctly soon.
Stability and Bugs 8/10 - Small bugs, but no crashes, and not too surprising considering that the game is so indie but looks and feels so high budget. Some people report framerate issues, but I have experienced none. I have an i7 processor, 16 gigs of RAM, Nvidia card. Make sure to keep your drivers up to date!
There is more here than I have listed, like a really in-depth medal and experience system where your ships can level up and earn medals through various combat exploits, which give them relevant bonuses (ie: Purple Heart, if your ship survives after being reduced to 35% health, whenever that happens in the future it takes 10% less damage). There are fun missions, and funny alien empire dialogues, overall this game is really great for around $20 at time of release.

Pros:

- Family forget who you are

A perfect example of why some game mechanics, no matter how old, shouldn't be changed.  The real-time "pause every 3 seconds to stop your fleet's ai from being dumb" is just clumsy and aggravating in my opinion; and I think alot of old school 4x fans (and those new to 4x who love the MOO2 gameplay) feel the same way.  It just gives a better foundation for all aspects of the game.
From the reviews that I've passed by, almost all had a critique similar to "Diplomacy underwhelming... too much focus on combat".  ...Of the game's major aspects, diplomacy does pale to the rest when it comes to the matter of depth and detail.  However, I'm one of those that prefers to blast my way through and spend hours mastering my own path down the tech-tree.  (Not to mention the new and more fun to use ship editor). And I'd much rather see the devs focus on more tech-tree additions, new random events, and stuff like RTS'able special skills I can unlock and use during combat!
Making the ships fun and exciting to watch as they destroy each other seems to be a lost artform. I've been dissapointed countless times with poor or flat out missing combat graphics.  If my end game death-ray has the same graphic as every single beam type weapon in the game, then I'm going to have a bad time.  It's a perfect example of why some gameplay fundamentals just shouldn't be messed with... only added to and refined... and as long as Zero Sum doesn't read to far into today's under-experienced, generic, newgen gamer mentality and pull a "Diablo III", then they will be the first among a painful amount of failed attempts to finally revive and modernize that epic 4x I fell in love with nearly 20 years ago.

First and foremost, is forts a good game?
Yes, it's great.
However, there are quite a few balancing issues that really are annoying right now.
Honestly, the worst thing for me right now is the warhead. If you've played forts you know what I mean. I can completely destroy a well built base and can sometimes oddly soak up bullets. With the addition of seep, i think it's definitely too powerful now, it was powerful before, but not too bad. Really? When it gets destroyed it splits into swarm missiles, which essentially makes it's earlier upgrade obsolete.
On a different note, the EMP Rocket. It's not that bad mid-late game but early game when you still have a small base and limited defenses, it's just ridiculous. It can disable your reactor (Temporarily) which is your main source of power early game and, by the time the stun has expired, it can be fired again. Because of this, it can be spammed to an extreme amount and you can only really sit there and hope your 3 or so machine gunners (Because it's still so early game) can get a lucky shot. To add to this, it's upgrade is basically a mini warhead, which costs the same as an emp to fire, and can also be spammed to a stupid amout.
There are some other balancing issues that I won't go into right now, but honestly those are only the two weapons I think are definitely in a bad place.
However just to list some pros;
-Great building allows for some really cool base setups
-A variety of weapons to choose from (Even if some are unbalanced)
-Several tech buildings allow you to choose what type of weapon you want
-Good resource management
-Great amount of building materials and gadgets to choose from
-Overall, a well paced and good feeling game
So, I'd have to say forts is definitely a 8/10 or 9/10 without the balancing issues, but is still a really good game for it's relitively low price, probably more like a 7/10 right now.
(P.S. I apoligize for any grammar or spelling issues in my review)
I'd definitely still recommend the game for anyone who likes building or rts games.
(P.S. 2 Please let me know if there was any issues in my review, i'd love to hear them!)

Stories Untold is a short narrative presented through 4 episodes, each with varying gameplay. These segments range from text-based interactions, to performing experiments, to deciphering morse code (with a lookup chart available, of course). Many gameplay elements are similiar to those you'd find in a puzzle game, and I'd say gameplay was probably the best part of this game.
The story itself wasn't anything special (it didn't have to be) but the game tried to present it in a way that made it seem more interesting. I personally don't think it worked; I wasn't involved or invested in any of the characters (because, for one, there weren't really any characters presented) so I didn't particularily care about the outcome. I was actually enjoying the red herring plot more.
Overall, I'd say it's a decent game worth picking up while on sale. It's style and presentation are great, and it tries out some interesting ideas, but full price cannot be justified by these things alone for a game that took me only a little over 2 hours to beat. Get upwards of 66% off.

I spent years waiting for this to come to the PC, but I never expected that it actually would. Vanquish is Platinum Games' take on a third person shooter, for better or worse. It has a few actiony moves like being able to jump and dodge around, and instead of sprinting you jet around the level on rockets, shooting around in slowmo in the process. It's overall pretty smooth, and it would be a lot of fun, but the level design is mostly just boxes and bridges, and there are only a few moments where it feels like Platinum knew what they were doing in terms of designing the levels around the mechanics. The story is also more or less half-finished, and the backstory you get in the loading screens is illegible because of how fast the game loads, which admittedly isn't a terrible problem to have. The game is also only around 4 hours long, and the only reason I have so much time in it is because of forgetting it was running in the background. If you're a Platinum fan then Vanquish is worth playing, and it's not a terrible game either way, but even though it has impressive ideas the game as a whole is kind of unimpressive, so you may want to wait for a sale unless you're sure you want to give it a go.

Stories Untold is part suspense, psychological horror, sci-fi, and mystery.  It has an authentic, light-handed 80s nostaglia vibe; it harkens back to the days of cassette tapes, text adventures, and alien conspiracy theories.  It takes place in 4 episodes.  Three of these episodes are different set pieces with a common thread.  It is not readily apparent what the common thread is, but it is substantial enough to feel as you progress.
The first episode is presented as a creepy text adventure being played by the protaganist.  The is a psychologicqal twist to it that puts you on the edge of your seat, on pins and needles as it draws to a concolusion.
The second episode is an alien conspiracy/sci-fi light scenario.  It has an X-Files flavor to it.  Again you play as the main character carrying out experiments of questionable nature.  You are left to wonder why your are doing this, and being pushed to continue... It leaves the player wondering what the connection is, if any.  It ends on a very alarming and suspenseful note.
The third episode takes place at a remote arctic weather station.   Questions start to mount as you are taked with decrypting and relaying coded messages for an unkown reason.  Something has gone very wrong and you are left to simply do your job as things unravel.  The conspiracy theorys and sci-fi elements come crashing back, and there is significant tension leading to the end of this episode.
FInally, the last episode ties it all together.  There is no way to review the story here without spoiling it.  This episode also briefly revisits individual gameplay elements from the first 3 set pieces.  The game allows the player a chance to start making the connections before it is pieced together in front of them.  It is an uncomfortable, grim, and somewhat moving climax.  You may find yourself fighting the inevitable as you see it bearing down.  For me, the ending didn't quite take the direction I would have expected considering the previous set pieces, but that was OK.  The game doesn't give away what it is until this final episode when you realize what has happened and why you are doing these things.
Of particular note is how powerful it can be when seemingly inconsequential details from the previous episodes suddenly become meaningul in the light of the final revelations.  I found the game to be very clever when it came to these small details which it intentionally does not attract attention to, but if you find yourself immersed in the mystery of each set piece, you will likely spot and question them yourself.
Gameplay is at your own pace.  There is a small amount of learnings to use the mechanics of each episode, but this element is not overbearing.  Some may find it tedious to a small degree, but this process has a purpose to the story.
The mechanics themselves are mostly simple point/click/drag , with some text inputs and some FPS walking simulation.
Graphics are solid, as is expected from Unity.  Some portions seem to have an intentionally downgrapded quality to them, which can be attributed to story elements; or at least they can be excused under the guise of story.
Sound and music are good.  There is a solid early 80s synth vibe to the spacey music.  Voice acting ranges from the immersive feeling of the radio chatter at the polar station, to some almost typical deadpan British delivery.  Note that the deadpan delivery again can be attributed to story and may have been intentional.
Stories Untold is an experience.  It's also a short experience at about 3 hours to complete without a guide.  However, these 3 hours keep the story moving at a good pace and wrap it all up in a decent time.  Quality over quantity:  Stories Untold should leave a mark on you by the time it is finished.  After the game is over, the experience lingers as you reflect on all those clever details you either overlooked or dismissed as inconsequential at the time.  Like any finely crafted mystery, you can replay the story and really see that it was all right in front of you the whole time, but you simply had no idea.  It took time to put the pieces together and for the light to shine on the truth.
If you like psychological thrillers, creepy sci-fi horror with an 80s falir, point & click adventures, or emotionally charged stories, Stories Untold is a worthwhile journey.  Just remember to pay attention and question why, because the more you invest into the game, the more you'll walk away with when it's all over.

This is a disappointing review for me to write. I was enjoying the game very much during the first couple of levels, but then the oddities and bugs started stacking up and tipped the scale in the other direction.
On a positive note, the graphics were clear, and the controls were very responsive. I liked the appearance of the main character and the scenery. It seemed like a nice little fantasy world to dive into. I'm an avid fan of straightforward platformers, so I love to see a well-done platformer that hasn't been muddied up with puzzles. If I can find one that incorporates real-time combat, then it immediately goes to the top of my list.
Wicce is a side-scrolling platformer. The character is a witch, and the combat is limited to a melee attack with a broom with charged special attack. Throughout the game, you obtain gold and red gems as drops for breaking destructibles and defeating enemies. However, there doesn't seem to be a purpose to the gold, and the game doesn't provide nearly enough of the red gems for healing, considering that I've encountered no other healing mechanism in the game.
One of the oddities is encountering characters where you're directed to press the up arrow and "X" at the same time. The purpose of this is unknown to me. At first, I thought it would heal my character or provide some type of upgrade or item, but I've seen no evidence of that. My second thought was a save point, but that didn't prove to be the case, either, as the character always goes back to the beginning of a level upon death.
It's worth noting that sometimes I would restart a level after death with the same number of red gems I had upon death, and sometimes I started with much less. I could find no rhyme or reason to this, making me think it was either a development issue or very unclear game mechanics. There doesn't seem to be an upgrade mechanism anywhere in the game, and I've encountered no other items. Even so, I kept playing.
The third boss is where things got out of hand for me. I was beginning the level with very little health and no more than 2 red gems, which only heal partially. You can't go backwards to other levels, and I encountered no merchants of any kind to obtain these items. No matter how hard I tried, I couldn't beat this boss, so I posted in the discussion forum for help, as well as the developer's profile, but haven't received any response yet from either the dev or the apparently minimal player base.
Out of options, I started a whole new game with the intent to save up every red gem I could find so I could beat the third boss. With 7 gems, I was able to just barely beat this boss, but my frustration didn't end at this point as another "oddity" comes into play after a boss is beaten.
Once a boss battle is won, a paper scroll comes up on the screen with arrows on it. It took me a bit to figure out what this was, but after repeatedly getting tossed right back into boss battles, I figured out that you're supposed to use the appropriate key, d-pad or joystick to correspond to the direction that the arrow is pointing. However, I found that the last arrow in the sequence, a down facing arrow, wasn't registering when I'd point my left joystick (xbox360) down. I tried multiple times but was tossed back into the boss battle anyway. Again, I beat the boss, this time with 6 health points remaining, only to have the same game-breaking bug prevent me from progressing.
I don't see how I can possibly recommend a game that can't be completed. It's for that reason that I'm choosing not to recommend the game. The lack of developer feedback and support is disappointing, and I was surprised that I couldn't find a single guide or walkthrough anywhere.
Overall, the game has definite potential. With some rebalancing, fixing of bugs, and introduction of more items and content, this game could be great. I sincerely hope that the developer will put the necessary effort into these changes. I would gladly give the game another go at that point.

Thomas Was Alone is not good. I'll give it credit for being pretty to look at and modestly pleasant to listen to. Aside from that it's simply a really poor gaming experience. First of all, it's way, way too easy: I think I was only briefly challenged on maybe 5 levels. That leaves 95 that were a total breeze. Even if a solution to a particular puzzle is obvious you still have to waste time wrangling the imprecise controls and swapping between polygonal "characters" as you move them into position over and over again. Towards the end I even ran into a bug that got one block stuck. I had to restart the whole level and painstakingly move around 10 different blocks step by step into the correct spots.
The less said about the "story" the better. The volume level of the narrator's voice fades in and out, making him hard to understand. The script's attempts at humanizing a bunch of polygons is laughable and fails miserably. The ending is a complete enigma, and not in a good way.
In short, skip Thomas Was Alone unless you like games that are short, easy, buggy and generally irritating.

So after a few months playing this, I'm giving it a positive review.
PROS:
- Excellent animations. What you'd want to expect from a AAA company
- Art direction and game just looks nice. High quality textures, and models
- Fluid combat. In combination with the animations, the combat looks and feels great.
- High skill ceiling on most characters means there's a lot to learn about playing a single character.
- The AI is for the most part pretty good. While level 1 and 2 bots are fairly easy, level 3 bots will eat your face. The AI is sophisticated enough that I enjoy playing them, even if they are easy to manipulate.
- 1 male, 1 female, 2 male/female character options per faction is awesome to see.
- Armour customisation is great. Could always use more stuff.
MEH:
- It has a story. It's not that good, but the fact that it’s there and attempts to follow into the multiplayer is something.
- Ornaments are very meh on most characters. Mythic outfits sometimes look rediculous.
CONS:
- P2P connections. It took about two months for patches to come out that made 4v4 modes not a total mess of instability. Even now, moths later, someone leaving the game can cause no end of problems. If they don't have permanent servers for any ranked games they hope to have, then the game will die.
- Revenge in 1v1 modes. The fact it exists in this mode is ridiculous, and it either immediately causes an imbalance of character power, or the other player simply avoids them until its over, doing nothing.
- Character balance. Obviously in fighting games you're going to get an imbalance of some characters, however some characters you have to wonder who pushed them out the door. PK lights are so fast that she's been banned on console tournaments. Warlord has a ridiculously bloated kit that can handle almost any match up, while Raider and Conq have tiny kits. Warden 50/50 vortex is something that no other character has and makes him incredibly imbalanced in 1v1 situations.
- Ubisoft community interaction. The first few weeks of the game launch had next to no contact with the devs about balance and performance issues. It took a boycott over server outages to get them starting a more constant stream of communication.
-Matchmaking. The system always seems to prioritise nearby people over skill. While this may be more stable in terms of speeds, it does mean that as an Australian, ♥♥♥♥ing NO ONE play Elimination except during 5-7 pm AND there's an elimination contract. I would like to see an option to allow the search to expand just so people can still play the game even when the in game count inevitably lowers. (Yes I know this would wreak havoc across the p2p system, hence why ubisoft should get ♥♥♥♥ing dedicated servers)
Overall the fact I have 240 hours in this means that I enjoy this game immensely. However, it has some glaring problems that could kill the entire community if not address. Primarily character balances and dedicated servers.

I have put 58 hours into this game on steam and thousands more on the phone. While the impressive graphics and enjoyable space combat are enormous plusses, this game needs a lot of work to be enjoyable.
First off, it shouldnt be so intimidating for new players. The tutorial is simple enough, and the way the game works is easy to understand, but once you are done the tutorial it all goes crazy. The game itself doesnt change a bit, no, but the difficulty certainly does. You are thrown into a sea of players that are way too strong, and there is no attempt made to cordon off the weak ones from the big ones, its just one big slaughter. There is always a bigger player. Even I, after having pumped gosh knows how many hours over the last for 3 years, am on the weaker side. I always get disenfranchised, leave for months, and return hoping to see that the game is better. But alas, it is always worse, and I always feel as meek as I did when I began playing. I can only imagine what it is like for new players now.
One of the most annoying things for me is how long everything takes. You will spend a month upgrading your fleets only to lose them all in 2 minutes to better players. Then it takes up to a week to repair your ships. All of the while, you try your best to upgrade your base to defend yourself from these big players, but the stronger it is, the bigger the fleet they can use to attack it. And the cycle never ends. Now I am at the point where many of my upgrades take weeks, or even months. That is far too long to be enjoyable.
The problems I mentioned before are what motivates people to pay for this game. Some people literally spend thousands to play this game, which makes it very fun for them, but it only aggrivates the issues already present for everyone else.
For starters, if I want to experiment with a new type of fleet, it can take weeks for it to be prepared. Then once im done preparing it, i might find that it is insufficent, so i need to try again, spending many more weeks. While this is happening, another player might attempt the same thing, but they instead will pay for it all to be done instantly. If an experimental new fleet fails, they will simply pay and try a new one within a few minutes. Eventually they will be on a whole new level of ship and fleet design, and players like me will have no hope of catching up.
The game makes it super tempting to pay to play. When presented with a 3 week wait you cant help but want to pay for it to be done immediately. You are presented with situations like this constantly. In fact, there are always 4 or 5 unique ways presented on the screen to spend money. It crowds the UI too much.
In all fairness, the combat is exciting to play and to watch, and you will make many freinds in this game. That is why i keep playing, but that really doesnt seem like enough to draw in new players.

Thomas Was Alone. On paper it looks rather simple: You take control of a small rectange called Thomas, and you solve puzzles by running...er... sliding and jumping.
What is this, 1980?
But the game quickly becomes more intricate, introducing a small host of other 'characters' whose movements all differ slightly, and your goal becomes one where you have to get all of your new friends 'safe' by taking control of them one at a time and positioning them appropriately.
Yes, this still doesn't sound like the most thrilling game ever, does it..?
But wait! There's more!
Behind all of this camaraderie lies a twisting 'plot' for want of a better word. Who created Thomas and his friends? Will they achieve their goals of becoming independent from the levels they find themselves in, progressively getting harder and harder, as if testing them to their limits? Suddenly narrative is an enormous part of the game, a disembodied voice narrating the thoughts and feelings of your crew.
Underlaying this beautifully-imagined game is a truly inspired soundtrack, which I believe could be prescribed to people with anger management issues. It really does need its own billing on the game's box art.
Don't just take my word for it - this game does not take up a vast sum of your hard disk, and those on the slowest connections will find themselves playing in no time. Which is good, because you'll find you rarely want to stop. Though I'm sure it says game manuals everywhere about taking frequent breaks....
Stop reading this, go buy it. Download it, and spend the next few hours of your life (it's not terribly long) basking in the warm embrace of a magnificent gem of a game.

Remember, this game is already old - yet it also is a classic game of the genre "Play Evil". The graphics are still fresh and crisp even on newer machines, the game is also less laggy now - because of the better hardware.
The story is told fast, you are an "evil" Overlord, who uses his horde of Lackeys to the best effect of his own will, get as corrupt as you like and fight against... Well... Who would have thought: Maneating Hobbits, Bloodthirsty Unicorns and other vile stuff of ...
Well you see already where this is going, Hobbits and Unicorns normaly are considered good or heroic creatures, but not in this game, not at all. You'll meeting some of the most original character in any Fantasy game that was published over the years, and you'll be surprised by the sometimes black humor, irony and sarcasm that this game has to offer to the player.

Kick your Jester, punish him for good... Be as cruel as you can be against your enemies, and frighten the masses by displaying the most cynic abuse of power. And don't wince, because you don't look powerful when you wince, you just look foolish.
Have I forgotten something? Oh yes, the recomendation.
If you are not into this kind of genre you will find the game maybe a little frustrating, even ridiculous. Even it is not new, it still has it's bite... and once it's poison is in your veins ... you're poisoned! You won't get away from it, at least not without solving the game.
