Video games usually aren't the first place to if I want a learning experience.  I do however enjoy documentaries and in many ways Never Alone is a hybrid video game/documentary.  This original story of a young girl and a friendly fox has been cleverly designed to cover the life and legends of the Inuit people.  The game lets the player go back and forth from the gameplay to mini-segments of a documentary covering various aspects experienced through the game.  It is really cool to be able to discover the different parts of this rich culture and go on to experience them hands-on.  If you're curious to learn about the native Alaskan people or you're looking for a light co-op experience Never Alone might be worth checking out.
In this story you play as a young girl named Nuna.  With a relentless storm threatening Nuna's village she decides to head out to find what the origin of the storm is.  Nuna doesn't quite realize what she is getting her self into.  Thankfully she quickly finds a Fox who will help protect and guide her.  Both Nuna and her Fox have different abilities that require them to work together.  You can control both characters or you can play co-op with each player controlling one character.  On Nuna's adventures you'll come across different elements of Inuit culture which are explained in detail via the documentary.  The story is definitely the focus of this experience and its quite fun to learn about all the different legends and beliefs of these natives.
Game-play wise this is a pretty straight forward side-scroller.  The two characters will need to avoid or maneuver around various hazards such as Icebergs and Polar bears.  When there is no immediate danger the levels often turn into puzzles.  You'll need to take advantage of Nuna's bola and the fox's ability to climb to navigate and progress to the next area.  The game isn't particularly challenging which isn't too surprising since this is an educational game and was designed with children in mind.  That being said there are a couple parts especially in the later half of the game that can get quite tricky and may require multiple attempts.
Never Alone is very pretty game.  As one may imagine there is only so much variety of things to see in this snowy paradise but what there is to see looks nice.  The cut scenes are particularly interesting as they borrow the look of traditional Inuit art.  To farther enhance the immersion the narration is voiced by a native in the native language.  This game is all about spreading and promoting Inuit culture and it does everything it can to be authentic.
How much you'll enjoy this game really comes down to how open minded you are.  If you enjoying learning new things there is a lot to appreciate.  However, more "hardcore" gamers find the gameplay a bit too lax.  That isn't to say there is anything wrong with the gameplay, in fact I found the difficulty quite appropriate for the experience.  This game also is a good example of proper asymmetrical multiplayer for those who enjoy couch co-op games.  Find any reason to play Never Alone and I'm sure you'll walk away contented and a lot more knowledgeable about this fascinating culture.
(Note: Low hours on record because I finished playing the game on my Playstation 4)

(edit) After more play, I have changed my review to thumbs down. We are to version 1.0h, and none of the bugs mentioned below have been addressed. Meanwhile the developer has plans to release a named patch with new features while balance issues still exist. This misplaced sense of priorities makes me think the game will never be balanced, or patched, correctly.
The good: It's an addictive 4X game that steals a lot from MOO 2. Many of the tech are taken directly from MOO 2 and choosing one topic locks you out of other choices, just like MOO 2, forcing you to use diplomacy to acquire them. It's a pretty game overall. The switch to turn based play for the galaxy map is a good one. The real time ship battles look great. It has that one more turn feeling. This is Moo 2 brought up to date. That should be good, right?
The bad: Here are just some examples to give you an idea of what I'm complaining about.
Ship design: it's a fiddly process. The game doesn't remember your previous choices in terms of size and quality of your components, forcing extra clicks as you fine tune your design. Also I have had the game simply refuse to save designs I've spent 10 minutes making, losing my work. Speaking of losing my work, the game will erase your work if you click a new hull. There is no 'mirror mode' that would allow you to quickly apply armor to 2 sides of a ship.
The game's soundscape is poor. Some sounds are simply not mixed correctly. The game released with serious balance issues in terms of the different difficulty levels. This has been addressed somewhat in a patch, but still needs work. When being attacked, you can't see the components the enemy ships have. Listening posts and refueling stations have the same icon on the galaxy map, making it impossible to tell which is which at a glance. At the moment, listening posts are bugged and acting like refueling stations. When one of your planets lacks something to build, the on screen notification of that is ridiculously tiny and tucked in the bottom right, making it easy to miss.
I hope this gives you an idea of the general state of the game. There are bugs, and there are things that are either just plain wrong, or clunky, when managing your empire. As I said above, the deveoper seems to be more interested in 'building buzz' by releasing a 'superpatch' than polishing his game.

Stardrive 2 has more than few influences from grandfather of space strategies, Master of Orion 2. If you have played it you will feel instantly at home with how colony building and allocating population works, switching them between farmers, workers and scientists.
Planets themselves come from several types, from Toxic wasteland to Gaia type planets and asteroid fields which can hold different amounts of population, which can be upgraded with technology. Tech tree itself is set so you have several fields to pick from and you can only pick one, leaving the other two to be obtained other ways, namely diplomacy and spying.
Diplomacy itself gives you "point" limit with determines how much you can do with other races which increases as you do deals with the race. Eventually allowing you to do treaties such as non agression pact and alliance. Unfortunately AI and limited amount of victory conditions ingame undermine diplomacy a bit and sooner or later (usually sooner, due aggressive AI). You will end up fighting with the AI, which especially at harder difficulties can be brutal. On my playhtoughs I saw AI wield sneak attack fleet that was larger than my entire fleet.
Space combat itself is a mix original Master of Orion 2 and rts, you equip your ships with different equipment and then command them in real time view which for the most part works smoothly but one of games issues is that it does not have reinforcement system, so with larger battles your computer can slow down to a crawl. Once you win space battle it's time to bring in the ground troops, which too can be equipped and heroes to be hired who can directly help you with ground combat.
Ground combat itself is turn based system bit like X-Com except much simpler where you command your troops and your mechs until one side gets killed, problem with ground combat is AI is bit stupid and it can be easily exploited, I had same squad of 6 timid warriors (they receive penalty to hitpoints) and I was still able to eliminate most of enemy fights without losing single soldier due AI being poor at ground combat. It really needs to use it's special abilities and formations better.
Lategame when your empire starts to expand on several starsystems and you have lots of colonies one of games biggest issues start to shine, there is no way to have manager for colonies which would build stuff based on your preferences, so you end up changing build orders a LOT, even when you have them queued it gets tedious and you really wish for some kind of governor system.
Overall good game that could use some polish, especially quality of life improvements.

There's still lots of bugs and the dev seems to be pumping out patches but there's just lots of strange behavior in the game, an enemy caught me spying and I have -675% diplomatic approval, but I'm always under constant assault by the ai's legion of spys which apparently cost the ai nothing to produce or upkeep despite having huge costs for the player to upkeep. The AI likes to request trades but you don't have good enough relations with the ai to request something in return so obviously you decline, which incurs a penalty. There are lots of descriptions that are filled out for some weapons that seem like they could benefit from someone re-reading them now that the game has been published so they could be clearer, lots of weapons that have slightly different terminology to describe them. My most recent game loaded up and my tooltips weren't displaying all my racial bonuses and I couldn't save ship designs after I spent 10 minutes customizing them so thats fun. Bugs I'm sure will be patched some day. Also, the AI seems to have unlimited fuel range and your ships can barely get to the neighboring system, but when I inspec the enemy ships... they have no extended fuel cells. Also, if you auto resolve combat, you lose about 20 troops even if you went up against 4 guys despite the enemy not being that much better at ground combat, so you have to play through each ground combat which is basically waiting for 3 turns then firing missiles from your mechs you bought on the black market, but if you autoresolve you somehow lose half of your 20 infantry, makes sense. Combat is so laggy during these mega combats that you can't tell whats going on, but if you auto resolve then you lose, if you circle the canopy shield wagons then you win but you have to watch combat for half an hour.
The game is fun when things work within reason, but I just spent a day playing through and all the enemy races declared war on me simultaneously after I killed the vulfars which is a race that declares war on you for the sake of declaring war. I managed to kill their bigger fleets which occupy the entire deployment area (which should also bankrupt the ai due to how fleet sizes should work) but then I have to play whack a mole with every other AI's mega fleet while they cherry pick my star systems with a mix of omniscience and unlimited fuel range and poorly designed ships and for every mega fleet I send my entire fleet after I lose 3 planets to bombing or invasion.

This is a review from the opinion of an absolute guitar novice who never seriously played the guitar before getting Rocksmith 2014. At the time of this review Ive played around 70 hrs of Rocksmith and have been playing the guitar just over a month.
So what's it all about?
The main part of the game is similar to the Guitar Hero / Rockband  where you play along to songs based on notes streaming down the stream although played with a real guitar not a plastic one with coloured buttons. It's like guitar tab but upside down (you can reverse it I think). No career mode, just select the song and start playing. Good choice of song from the 60's right up to modern day with some well known bands and some I've never heard of.  You can choose lead, rhythm or bass guitar and the tones are the same as the ones used in the original songs.  If you don't like the songs you can also import songs through a mod on the pc version.
The game will automatically sense how well or badly your doing and adjust the amount of notes you have to play in the song accordingly. If you really struggle on one part of the song you can enter rift repeater mode and slow the song down and adjust difficulty, looping the rift over and over till you get it right.

There are a multitude of tutorial videos you can watch with practice sessions for each one right from basic stuff like how to hold the guitar to some very advanced stuff.
It has a selection or "very retro 90's games" which teach you things like chords, string skipping, scales and accurate fretting. This is the part I use the most at the moment and is a fun and enjoyable way to learn essential skills as opposed to sitting there with repeating stuff over and over which can become boring pretty quickly.
The tone designer is great too. Has a selection of effects and amps from a multitude of manufactures and it allows you to play around and create your own tones. Ive not really delved too deeeply into this much so cant comment and further.
It's also got a session mode although this is a bit above my abilities as of yet. In this you can create a band and they will sense what you're playing and play along with you. I can see this as something I'll use more as I progress.
There is no rigid learning structure to this game though. Apart from some missions it gives you it's not going to tell you to do this and then that. You use it as you want to use it. At the moment I don't really want to use it to learn song s so much but mainly use games such String Skip Saloon, Ducks Redux and Castle Chord Dead games to improve my technique to supplement my Rockschool studies.
It's also not going to replace a real teacher by all means as it's not going to see physical things such as your posture being wrong  or your left hand technique is wrong etc. But is a great supplemental tool to help anyone learn the guitar and adds a little more spice the equation.

I love the concept, but did not enjoy the execution.
The dialogue of the characters during the campaign missions was clearly intended as a parody of action movie dialogue, but came across too cringey. The humour just seemed like it was pitched to a very young audience, which doesn't match up with what I'd expect from what is clearly meant to be a base-building/strategy game.
In addition I felt unmotivated and uninspired by the campaign. After each mission is completed, some amount of oil is awarded. Collecting enough oil unlocks later missions. But in some way I can't see the point of this. As a player I need a clear long-term goal, reason to want to complete the levels. In this game though, the level cycle just felt like a trudge. Get some oil, unlock a level. Now I need some more oil to unlock the next level... ok but why? What's the end-game? What am I heading towards? Either a player should be rewarded with something like upgrade points, to give a sense of long term progression, or simply motivated by the love of unfolding the plot. Sadly Forts provides neither of these.
I can't quite put my finger on it, but the pacing of base development/reasource acquisition felt off. I appreciate that creating a power curve that is neither too steep nor too shallow is hard, but it just felt like the balance wasn't quite right. I suspect this is a symptom of having too many different branching ways to develop turrets. Having multiple different 'technology' buildings that work independently of one another, and having per turret upgrades as well... well it could work, but honestly it should be stripped back to a basic Rock-Paper-Scissors balance, and play tested to hell first. Then if and only if that goes well should the power dynamics be made any more complicated.
It felt like the game couldn't make up it's mind if towers were 'meant' to be autonomous or not. Some turrets fire autonomously in self-defence, but not others. All can be fired manually. It's not clear to me whether the intent of the game is to micromanage the firing of many turrets simultaneously. If it were my game to design, I'd favour taking a much more pro-autonomous route. That way the player can focus on base building and development and not the more tedious act of firing turrets one by one.
I think there is a lot of potential here, and games of a similar nature have been very enjoyable to me. Most of all Redcon is a great fort vs fort game. This game needn't be a cookie cutter clone of Redcon, but this game should draw upon it as a guiding influence.

While it had a nice idea behind it, overall the games pacing and difficulty was ruined by the clunkiness of the controls and the glitches (thankfully it has very forgiving checkpints so +1 for that), maybe that might be better with two players though.
If you can see past that then it's a fun game but you might start getting frustrated later on by the responsiveness of some mechanics.
I do appreciate the effort they went to with the cultural accuracy however, 10/10 for that.

is a collection of short adventure/time management games -
and
- developed and produced by JoWooD in 2003-2004. They are the kind of perfectly silly games that you'd try during an initially boring afternoon with a mischievous smirk on the corner of your mouth.
Meet Woody, our main character, who has sworn to make every living moment hell for his despicable neighbor, Mr. Rottweiler in a 2D animated fashion. The whole concept of the game is based on a sitcom: cameras do follow Woody as he sneaks around to play juvenile tricks in ACME quality - like setting a banana peel on a slippery surface, drawing funny faces on family portraits or changing the coffee in your neighbor's pot with compost - on his nasty neighbor and dabble with which actually shouldn't concern him. On that manner, Woody is basically a human version of Bugs Bunny in plastic animations.
The second instalment of the series is basically same, with some more characters, a different environment and mini games thrown around. This time, Woody follows his neighbor to his vacation spots to show some personal attachment. Is he obsessive, or what? Oh, and Woody has given 3 chances to complete his series of trickeries before his neighbor catches him this time. Graphics are slightly better, yet the main idea is same.
In each episode of the show, you are given 5-7 minutes to follow your neighbor's pattern for the episode, discover and initiate a series of crude jokes and traps for him to fall for while avoiding getting caught sneaking around. The more you manage to lay the outcome of your tricks in short periods between, the better rating you get for the given episode - so your poor neighbor wouldn't recover from the joke before and lose his temper to display funnier poises.
is a cute, yet not very imaginative game with crass jokes. The concept is interesting, yet it is not particularly funny. Once you complete each episode with 100% rating, - which is real easy if you follow the patterns - there is no replay value at all. Go for it when it's on discount, and either spare a lazy afternoon to try and enjoy it or offer the idea to your kids in case you have any. Do I recommend it? Well, not particularly good but, hey! At least it's kid friendly... if your kid is into ACME humor, that is.

Alright, I've played this one for a little bit and I guess that I can write something about this game so it won't look like another refund request or some sort of.
Nether gave me quite unique experience. Yes, it's buggy as hell. Yes it may be P2W(there's cash shop where you can buy stuff and go on murdering while others will have to scavenge loot on their own). Yes it feels unfinished( like it came from late 2000s lol). But still.
I can't write about how I felt when I was crouching while trying to not get spotted by monsters that can easily wreck me out with teleportation powers or rude force, or by numbers. Or that feeling when you're going by wastelands, hiding by every corner that you can find just not to get sniped. But the most exciting time I've spent below the city, in the metro tunnels. Oh my, you just going there, without any source of light(however there is some bug that makes these tunnels brighter than it would be on the surface, but its pretty rare), trying to not be shooted by another survivor or eaten by monsters. And all those burned skeletons, corpses, furniture, abandoned barricades, stations turned into field hospitals and refugee camps that were overruned... That is what this game have. Dark, hard atmosphere, without any hope. And this is the reason why I love this game.
I really want to play the finished, polished version of this game; that would be a facsinating experience for me. But things ain't going so well - there are some cheaters on servers, the game itself looks unfinished, raw and kinda outdated. Playerbase is pretty low, servers may be downed for some time(check out steamcharts or something like that for details). Also some people reported about problems with synchronizing this game with Steam, so be careful with buying it - you may consider reading out the content in local Steam community or watching videos, gathering info on social networks etc.)
This game is really not for everyone, at least, in that kind of shape. But still this one have things to offer - open world, perma - death which works with RPG system(you can develop your character by purchasing different perks and attribute points with your XP to make your own build, plus you can't unlock every skill), co - op thing works well here, plus there's not only PVP, but PVE servers too(I hope they are still around here).
Buying this game is a hard decision, so consider anything here. But I am satisfied with it. This game gave me what I wanted - maybe it wasn't a perfect experience, but still I love it.
You've been warned! Hehe...

Never Alone is such a beautiful little platformer based on insightful folklore and fascinating storytelling. Playing through it, I was captured by the story and actively looked for the owls to unlock short clips that peeked into the interesting life/culture of the iñupiaq people.
Gameplay time!
Playing single player is probably harder than playing co-op due to the A.I's clumsiness in some areas and positioning in others so your experience would likely be more enjoyable with a friend. That said, if you can get through the frustration from the A.I this game is quite enjoyable. The puzzles are relatively easy, the environment is interesting, the graphics are simple but still nice, and the story (and it's insights) is truly a work of art.
Keep in mind this game is mostly a narrative so the gameplay is slow paced. There are some occasional bugs in the game but nothing terrible that a simple restart of the checkpoint/game can't fix. The A.I controls the character you don't play and can sometimes get itself killed, stuck, or wondering away from the place you want it to stay. You may have to micromanage a little.
The overall play time is quite short, but I took my time to explore and enjoy the environment. The DLC however is incredibly short, going on a very short story separate to the main storyline. As short as it was, the puzzles in it were nice and the concept of the story quite intriguing. This game would be even better with more story driven DLCs.
I recommend Never Alone if you love story/culture driven games. However I don't think it's quite worth the $15 price tag simply because it's a little too short.

There is a difference between a game being good and a game being fun. I cannot recommend For Honor saying that it is a good game. You will be constantly getting kicked out of multiplayer matches and occasionally be faced with unfair situations where there is nothing you can do but watch as your character dies. Since Ubisoft had it's hands in this, as I'm sure every other user review on this site will tell you, there's really not much that can be done in that regard. Along with that, the toxicity of the community is beyond comprehension, the vast majority of the time. However, even with all that in mind, I can't deny that For Honor is fun. It's enjoyable to fight against other players and feels rewarding when you win an uninterrupted battle. The combat system is quite good, even if it's sometimes abusable, in its current state. I can tell a lot of effort went into the creation of this and it truly seems like the developers genuinely just wanted to make a good game. I can't say they succeeded but, in any case, I can say they made something that's fun to play. I read a review once that summarized For Honor perfectly; "Playing this game is like eating great steak with a plastic fork." When it works and you have those moments of triumph, whether you outskill someone in a one-on-one duel or just throw a guy down a hole, you really don't regret your purchase.

A couple years ago during a Steam Sale, I purchased two games against my better judgment. That is, according to some negative reviews I had read, I probably should not have bought them. But I personally felt they had potential and were worth giving a shot. One of them exceeded my expectations more than I could have ever possibly imagined. The other…did not. The former I will review at a later date. The latter is Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna).
To start on the positive: the main reason I decided to give Never Alone a chance was because of the setting. In real life, I absolutely love everything about Native American culture, people, and even religion. In the world of video games, these elements have rarely ever been explored. This almost ingenious tapping of unused, fresh, and exciting material is Never Alone’s biggest strength. The completeness and wholeheartedness that Never Alone embraces its focal point really clicks with me. I love the legend-esque story, the way it is told, (by an Inupiaq elder), and the cave drawing-like animations that accompany it. The subtitles and translations of the elder are a little awkward, but not terrible. I also love all the documentary extras, and genuinely wanted to unlock and watch each one.
Aside from the setting, almost every other part of Never Alone struggles at least partially. The models, environments, and visual effects are all passable, but not noteworthy. Some of the level designs have interesting moments, but the puzzle designs don’t do anything we haven’t seen before. Part of this is due to the fact that Nuna’s Bola, her “weapon” and tool that allows her to shoot objects and orbs (that summon spirits) in the environment, isn’t interesting enough in it’s own right, and the game never asks the player to use it in any interesting ways. The spirits are the best parts of the overall design of the game, but their help usually turns into hindrance due to the poor platforming controls. Seeing spirits that you must jump between is a disheartening sight. Seeing a spirit Nuna must climb like a ladder is groan-inducing. Trying to get Nuna to jump to a platform FROM a ladder spirit (or vice-versa) is absolutely infuriating.
Poor controls and puzzle design are probably the worst criticisms that a puzzle/platformer could ever deal with, but those complaints I have about Never Alone are not the games’ worst fault.
A big part of Never Alone is being able to switch between Nuna and her companion in order to solve puzzles. Unless you are playing with another human, the game’s A.I. controls whichever character you are not. I’m going to give the developers the benefit of a doubt that Never Alone was developed primarily with couch co-op in mind, because the A.I. in this game is some of the worst I have ever seen. I frequently set up one character for his or her role in the puzzle, then swapped to the other…only to have the A.I. character start moving away. Swapping back to rein in him or her would make the now A.I. character move away. The A.I. character also has the extremely nasty habit of getting him/herself killed or stuck on the environment. The latter results in frustrating babysitting, the former in many unnecessary deaths.
It only took me about 3 hours to finish Never Alone. I know in my mind that is an extremely short length for a video game, even an indie game. Sometimes I wonder if my play through would have been even shorter if my A.I. companion had not been so stupid. But because of that, and the poor controls, 3 hours felt like an absolutely eternity. In all fairness, Upper One did release a patch for Never Alone in an attempt to address some of these issues. Unfortunately, however, I did not notice much of a difference, and the issues still remain. Unless you are going to play this game with a human partner, the bad outweighs the good here--and I cannot, in good conscience, recommend this game. Even then, you both are going to grapple with the poor controls, which may end up being worse than an A.I. partner.
Kisima Ingitchuna, the Inupiaq translation of the game's title, translates to “I am not alone.” In both the game and real life, this is a very special idea. Although the ultimate plot of the game revolves around Nuna saving her village from danger, the moral of this legend is that, as we live our lives and overcome obstacles, we are never truly alone. Much like how Nuna is surrounded by the Helping Spirits and her faithful companion throughout her adventure, in real life, we too are surrounded by our friends and, perhaps, even the spirits of those who have gone before. But if my friends and companions were as incompetent as the ones “helping” Nuna on her journey, I would much rather take my chances on mine… alone.

Absolutely beautiful game and thought provoking story that's an experience to remember. I recommend playing it with "the monsters don't attack mod" at least once -- perhaps after one play-through, but that's up to you. I say this not because the game is too hard or stressful but being able to actually look at the monsters and fully explore the scene and environment made the game even better in my opinion. This isn't jumpscare or cheap thrills horror, but a slow building existential and psychological dilemma that sticks with you well after completion.
The story is so well crafted that it could have easily been a book or movie instead. I recommend Soma for anyone that wants to explore a deep and well crafted narrative, and is probably my favorite game of all time. The only negative about Soma at all is perhaps its replay value, but that's because the plot is everything, here.
On a final note, the graphics, effects and soundtrack also blend wonderfully together and the atmosphere is so thick you could cut it with a knife. I look forward to seeing what Frictional do next. Their titles have always been quality, but Soma is by far the best yet.

This is one of those games that needs your attention. You cannot really play it while idly waiting for the AI to do something threatening. Honestly it feels a bit more realistic in the way it portrays aggresive expansionism.
A strong focus on one sole aspect of the game can yield some good results (economy, research or military), but learning to balance the three of them while sending out scouts and forming a good set of core worlds is key to building up the strength to be able to stand toe to toe with an AI that makes calculated decisions every single turn.
Is it an easy game? No.
Is it a thinking man's game? Yes.
If you're looking for a quick game you can beat in a relaxing afternoon, maybe look outside the 4X genre.
All that said, I truly enjoy the challenge, and it makes the victories feel real and well earned. Combat is more meaningful and making otherwise "boring" decisions about your economy, research and politics is a tense and exciting process within the context of the larger game.
With a few more options for better difficulty scaling and some great steam workshop support, this will definitely be a mass hit. But until then, enjoy the challenge!

The game is very Masters of Orion-esc.  I have played stardrive and many many other 4x games.  Probably my favorite Genre.  Honestly i was on the fence about this one.  I didn't know if i wanted to spend the money and jump in, but after watching some lets plays, I had to try it.
The Good:
Stardrive ship customization. Probably the biggest thing here.  You can literally make any ship you want and make it work, Its based on these little squars blocks outlining your ships interior and its 4 quadrents.  Each quadrent having a different gun facing and its own hps.
The 4x-ness- spying, diplomacy, trading, combat. Multiply paths to victory.  Side missions and quest.  Which i might add can be harder than some of the AI players.
The fact that there is ground combat. So, This is also a negative but still the fact they they at least have something representing ground combat is good from the point of future development.
They game iteslf is Turnbased, but the combat is real time in an instanced battlefield.  I really like this!  One thing I didnt like about Stardrive 1 was that a battle would be really messy and meander all over the place. Some might like that, but for me having an actually formal engagement really made this fun for me. It also opens up battle arena that is also in the game.  So less persistant RTS and more Gratuitous space battles.
The look and asthetic is well done. Hard to believe they have such a small team working on it.
The bad:
Some things are half done or not fully fleshed out.  Ground combat needs a lot more love, but it is still enjoyable for me.
There are some bugs here and there that need fixing
Many racial weapons/tech/ship layouts are unbalanced or non existant.  I.e Kulrathi have their own melee weapon and defensive skill for ground combat, and they have tech that furthers this in the ???? tree for research. Pollops and Squids have it also, but races like human Vulfar chukk are kind of out in the cold.  Not to mention an optri cruiser has almost 2x the space to put modules on it than the vulfar.  I know that this is being looked at but for now its in the negative column as it directly effects the game in a big way.
The game to me seems more like a beta, but I am a purist that believe games are not launched until they are ready and polished.
Conclusion: ok so I would not have recommended this game when it launched, but in just a few days the developer released so many big changes in under a week that I had to take the plunge.  Sure, is it not finished and buggy. Yes, but I would rather have a game where the developer is constantly updating it to make it better than a ok game that gets and update every 6 months to a year.

Building an evil empire is hard work. Fortunately, minions love to do trivial tasks such as carrying heavy things, beating sheep to death with sticks and blades alike, putting stuff on their heads, immolating halflings, and smashing, well, everything in sight. It makes the tedium of smiting and being feared much more enjoyable.
Between Steam and my console version of this game, I probably have about 100 hours in it, and every playthrough was fun. The four kinds of minions (conveniently color coded for an Xbox controller, which I do recommend using a controller given how laid back this game is, but it is hardly required) add a great layer of strategy to the game if you take the time to utilize them to their maximum efficiency. Of course, you can always just send them all rushing in to smash smash smash, and they will happily die for you, but they will die quite often this way. And you just don't want that when they're so adorably evil. Unless maybe you're just extra evil, and that's actually encouraged around here.
I would not call this game particularly challenging (although Legendary mode added in the Raising Hell expansion surely amps up the difficulty), but it is pretty forgiving overall. This is definitely a pick up and play game that is not going to drown you in the details of lore, equipment, crafting, etc., but it has just the right amount of strategy involved to keep it interesting while allowing it to remain a game you can lounge back and play just to unwind and enjoy the ride.
Fact is, sometimes you just want to be the bad guy. This game lets you be a brutal tyrant, but does so in such a charming way it just feels so right to be evil. So pick it up, build a horde, claim a mistress, restore your Dark Tower to all it's inglorious..er...glory, literally fill a room with gold and treasure, and sit back on your sweet evil throne, sipping wine made of fermented peasant tears, and debate how to punish your godawful jester.

This is a review from the opinion of an absolute guitar novice who never seriously played the guitar before getting Rocksmith 2014. At the time of this review Ive played around 70 hrs of Rocksmith and have been playing the guitar just over a month.
So what's it all about?
The main part of the game is similar to the Guitar Hero / Rockband  where you play along to songs based on notes streaming down the stream although played with a real guitar not a plastic one with coloured buttons. It's like guitar tab but upside down (you can reverse it I think). No career mode, just select the song and start playing. Good choice of song from the 60's right up to modern day with some well known bands and some I've never heard of.  You can choose lead, rhythm or bass guitar and the tones are the same as the ones used in the original songs.  If you don't like the songs you can also import songs through a mod on the pc version.
The game will automatically sense how well or badly your doing and adjust the amount of notes you have to play in the song accordingly. If you really struggle on one part of the song you can enter rift repeater mode and slow the song down and adjust difficulty, looping the rift over and over till you get it right.

There are a multitude of tutorial videos you can watch with practice sessions for each one right from basic stuff like how to hold the guitar to some very advanced stuff.
It has a selection or "very retro 90's games" which teach you things like chords, string skipping, scales and accurate fretting. This is the part I use the most at the moment and is a fun and enjoyable way to learn essential skills as opposed to sitting there with repeating stuff over and over which can become boring pretty quickly.
The tone designer is great too. Has a selection of effects and amps from a multitude of manufactures and it allows you to play around and create your own tones. Ive not really delved too deeeply into this much so cant comment and further.
It's also got a session mode although this is a bit above my abilities as of yet. In this you can create a band and they will sense what you're playing and play along with you. I can see this as something I'll use more as I progress.
There is no rigid learning structure to this game though. Apart from some missions it gives you it's not going to tell you to do this and then that. You use it as you want to use it. At the moment I don't really want to use it to learn song s so much but mainly use games such String Skip Saloon, Ducks Redux and Castle Chord Dead games to improve my technique to supplement my Rockschool studies.
It's also not going to replace a real teacher by all means as it's not going to see physical things such as your posture being wrong  or your left hand technique is wrong etc. But is a great supplemental tool to help anyone learn the guitar and adds a little more spice the equation.

I have played a lot of 4x games(Master of Orion, Master of Orion 2, Ascendency, Master of Magic, Fantasy Empires, The Civilization Games, Heroes of Might and Magic 1-5, Galactic Civilizations, Imperium Galactica II, and probably a bunch more that I don't remember right now), and the reviews for this one seem a bit more enthusiastic rather than accurate.
It borrows heavily from other games but to the point where it feels derivative of them rather than being a synthesis of them. Moreover it is so blatant about it that it feels like it is flirting with the breaking the fourth wall not something I am a huge fan of.
The game has a lot of potential in the ship design and strategic aspect of space and ground combat and the level of depth that it allows you to manipulate your empire.
I will say that it was better than MOO III in general fun and striking a balance between allowing depth and getting carried away with it.
My big gripes about the game are as follows.
Technological advance doesn't yield significant upgrades until you get very very far along in the trees. I almost always had better luck researching a few basic (tier one or two technologies), the pumping everything into producion ships and troops and conquering the galaxy without ever doing more than cursory reasearch.
The AI literally cheats on basic settings, I have tested rich homeworlds on small maps with optimized industrial output and the AI will invariably massively outcolonize me and outproduce me (in terms of fleet and fleet size) very quickly in the early game. You can still win by being clever or cheesy in your builds, but the fact that it literally plays by a different set of rules on default settings really really bothers me.
The technologies are poorly balanced to create a stable empire. The game forces you specialize each of your planets because of prohibitive maintanence costs (making one planet that has all upgrades and buildings your empire is capable of will put a big dent in your wallet). Basically I find myself skipping almost all of my unlocked buildings on most colonies just because of what it costs to maintain them. The way various technolgies interact and overlap with each other just makes a lot of them feel useless or redundant or only of use on a very small proportion of your colonies.
I do think the game has a whole lot of potential and with some patches or balance changes could be more fun. Essentially my complaint it that it forces you to play in one of a few very specific ways if you want to avoid getting wiping out quickly on default difficulty. It felt more like how well can I implement this strategy which I know will be the only viable one for this map/race selection rather than what type of empire would I like to build this time. It feels like the game has mechanics for amazing strategies and fun but makes it impossible for you to implement them before you have already taken control of the map.
Bottom Line I just didn't have fun playing it.

This is a phenomenal game if you're just starting out, or if you're already rocking out but want to practice stuff outside of your comfort zone, in alternate tunings, or just practice and jam and have fun. I sprinkle songs from this game throughout my practice sessions to liven things up and cut loose. Otherwise you're sitting there practicing scales or other songs with a metronome. Not as much fun.
That said, the game has some very important limitations (though I still recommend it):
1) If you're serious about music and want to play professionally, you're going to need a GOOD teacher anyway. Get a guitar teacher if you're playing guitar and a bass teacher to teach you bass (whatever you do, do not get a guitar teacher to teach you bass, trust me on this one).
2) This game is missing one very important feature and a related feature: the little boxes that come down indicating which note to play should actually SHOW you which note you're playing (i.e., "A", "E", "G", "Fb", "C#" etc.). Otherwise you're just exercising your fingres and learning the song by sound and muscle memory which is ultimately not that helpful if you later try to play this song with others (with exception of the guitar which at least does show you the chords). I am hoping Ubisoft ultimately does provide an option for this. Related to this should be a feature that lets you download and print the music. I'd settle for the bass/guitar tabs, but really it should have standard notation on top and tab on the bottom. Again, so you can go play the song with other people. If you want a quick fix for this, get the lead sheet, and then just fill it in with the riffs/licks you learn in the game. That's what I'm doing now. You're relying on memory and ear though which isn't ideal since you need to be able to do all 3: ear, memory and reading.
3) The lessons are good, but have a very important limitation in that you still need to ask your teacher and/or look at other videos online to figure out what they're talking about for the more difficult techniques. For example: I can tell you that if you rely on the ingame lesson on ghost notes, I'll die of shock if you get it right just from the game itself but maybe you're way smarter than me which I'm ok with. There is also no particular one way to do something and you may need to adjust to your own physical limitations. A good teacher will help with that. And I would add, be very very careful developing bad technique. Bass is a great example of this becuase it is a deceptively "easy" instrument, and by that I mean: it's not, but most people THINK it is. And I learned the hard way when I started playing bass: a bad left or right hand technique can pretty much cripple everything you're trying to learn down the road.
4) Further on the lessons: what is missing is a more detailed lesson on rhythm and meter encompassing time signatures and note durations (they do have one lesson on syncopated rhythm but it's not that great and doesn't explain how it all ties into the rhythm section of a band, time signatures, etc.). Why is this important? Well, because you will note that some of the songs you play either have a different time signature or syncopated rhythm (i.e., notes that fall on off-beats or weak beats or just unexpected places in the measure). Since the game already HAS the measures in it (those are the horizontal lines that move towards you as you play), why not explain what it all means so you can get the rhythm right from the beginning instead of wondering why what you're playing just isn't grooving right. If you're the lead guitar, YOU can go nuts. But if you're playing bass or rhythm guitar, YOU are holding the rhythm (meaning you're locking in with the rest of the rhythm section of the band to hold the lead guitar and the rest of the band together) so if you can't figure out what the rhythm is, you'll drive yourself up the wall.
Hope that was helpful!

Before you purchase read the reviews. Be mindful when reading both positive and negative and look at the paterns, praises and complaints in both.
Pros:
Visuals are ok
Space and ground combat can be challenging but fun for a time if you design your ships/troops correctly.
Ground combat is way better and more visually appealing than SD1
Several aspects add immersion and more challenge to the game, ie pirates, crystals entities, wormholes so on.
Ship desing is more simple with less modules and less options than SD1. This can be both good and bad.
You can disable GNN!!!!
Cons:
Interface is awkward and confusing. Devs should have stuck to what they had in SD1 bcs this attempt to change things up made the interface awkward and not user friendly. This is not a game breaking feature but it is definitely frustrating and disapointing. Sometimes the interface sounds will make you think you are playing FF7 all over again.
Economy is punitive, confusing and awkward. Good luck trying to figure out what to build in order to make a profit and not plunging you planets into a Chernobyl like state. The money making builings are scarce and you are also limited by the tech tree as to which buildings can be built. Which brings me to the next point.
Diplomacy is mediocre. Your military, financial or technological might or lack thereof does not seem to influence or sway the AI one way or the other. Basically what it comes down to is dont colonize too many planets or you will never be able to negotiate anything with anyone. All the while they will keep asking you to give them stuff for free but God forbid you ask them for the equivalent of a slab of bread in return to  make the deal fair somewhat... They will not have it.
Tech tree is very restrictive and confusing (at first). The Tech tree is divided into 6 main categories each with 10 sub categories. Each sub category has 2 to 3 techs in it and you only get to pick one. Once researched you move to the next and cannot research anything else in the prior category. VERY limiting especially since some sub categories have your Titan, the best starbase and the best armor in game. Guess what, you only get to pick one. There are several other categories like these that limit you significantly although with very good planning this can be overcome.
The Command point structure is extremely punitive and borderline game breaking. Why is this? Because this is what limits how big your fleet can be. Go over it and the game will be over for you in no time. This is a borderline moronic feature that was poorly implemented ESPECIALLY since the AI does not abide by it. To put it into perspective lets say you have a decent size empire with several planets, you can probably squeeze out 13 to 15 ships. Sometimes maybe a bit more if you reduce the amount of battleships and titans to 1 or 2. Not bad not bad right? This means absolutely nothing when not even the most powerful AI comes at you with 2 full fleets of 40 plus ships. Keep in mind your empires are similar in size and you are relatively equal in tech lvl. No.. im sorry.. No
AI does not seem abide by any of the restrictions and/or  limitations you will be put through. They are not attacked by the other forces (ie pirates and such) and they do not seems to have a fleet or ship cap (aka comand points). Their only limitation is tech, which they will steal from you no matter how many counter spies you have.
AI will violate your territorial integrity regardless of treaties (which is expected) but will immediately declare war the minute you go an inch into their space.
Wormholes will pop randomly all over your territory (usually right by your planets). This would not be a problem if they would connect to other wormholes across or near your turf. Sadly they lead right into the gates of oblivion at the heart of the enemy empire. They will use this repetadly to move their superfleets through you territory regardless of any treaty in effect. They also use this to teleport their main fleets right next to your main planets. This pretty much renders borders useless.... Maybe tone down the amount of wormholes a bit.
There is no "bounce back" or "come back" in this game. Once you are brought to your knees you might as well quit. You can have better ships than the enemy and you may be able to repell their attacks but they will continue to send those endless waves of superfleets at you with no detrimental economic impact to them or no replenishment time of their fleets. Even if you beat them every time single time you will go bankrupt = game over.
Summary:
Game is not bad but its just not good either. I feel it is a stepdown from SD1. In its current state it is good to play in the long term if you are a masochist. Otherwise wait till they patch it and purchase only at a reduced price. Like when its 40-50% off.

I consider myself a novice/intermediate guitarist, and this game is great. I like Rocksmith since its catalog of songs provides much-needed variety in the absence of a real instructor. Splitting up the Learn to Play and Score Attack modes makes a lot of sense, and I like the mechanics of the new riff repeater a lot more. It's also probably almost worth buying this game just for the amp modeling (Orange and Marshall, and some generic clones).
Potential cons: I expected to hate Uplay, but so far it hasn't really posed a problem. The computer-controlled instruments in session mode also fell apart as soon as I started playing some swinging blues. It works better if you stick with 4/4 quarter notes.
Overall, I think RS2014 is great for all levels of guitarists. If you're starting from square one, you'll probably still want some in-person lessons to progress faster, but RS2014 is definitely a great supplement to a routine.

I have played Worms Ultimate Mayhem 3 hours and counting. I wanted to write this review well after Worms had been released, all of the DLC had been released, and when the modding community had really had a good opportunity to get a foothold in. Worms is an amazing game all in all. To those people who were giving this game 0's and 10's on the very first day it was released, within the first 10 minutes of playing, all I got to say is that those reviews don't help ANYONE. A game like this takes time to grow.
Gameplay
Gameplay probably features the biggest changes and improvements of the worms series. Improvements can be found from various aspects of the game, from combat, exploration, crafting and character building. Compared to Worms Reloaded, the combat is much more responsive, faster and dynamic. Enemy variation is amazing in WUM and it was often surprising to see new features and abilities added to already known enemy types. Crafting is one of the biggest and greatest part of WUM. As soon I saw the new crafting system of WUM in E3, I knew it was going to be great and sure wasn’t disappointed. With More Worms DLC you can also build your own robots, and go far as building your own kickass Sentry Bot. With the improved crafting looting and exploration became more important and rewarding. Junk rarity was also in great balance, I often found myself missing needed materials which then motivated me go out to explore the wasteland. With the new crafting system also came the settlement mode, which allowed players to create their own towns and settlements. To me the vanilla settlement mode was dull in many ways. Either way the settlement mode can a lot of fun with mods, allowing you to actually craft something genuine and incredible. The leveling and perk system was also redesigned. While there was nothing wrong with the previous system, the new system was a welcome change.
Atmosphere
In general, the atmosphere in WUM is subtler than in previous entries. Fast Food Dino felt much brighter and hopeful than the desolate Gibbon Take or Monster Bash. This is likely due to the more vibrant weathers. To improve immersion, team17 did a nice job of reducing the amount of loading screens. Abandoned towns now could be explored without having to struggle through the 5 second loading screen every now and then.
Story and Quests
I personally enjoyed the main plot, mainly because I didn’t expect much of it I got what I expected. Most of the main storyline was very good, it definitely had some memorable moments, difficult choices and the total length of the story wasn’t too bad. As for side content and quests, which were usually good but often hard to find. Radiant quests in WUM have a large role. The highly criticized voiced protagonist and the new dialogue system didn’t bother me, which did undoubtedly pose problems. But to me they were welcome changes, which felt like taking one step back and two steps forward.
Overall
While WUM did sacrifice some of its predecessors RPG elements, it still turned out to be one of the best open-world shooter that I’ve played. Worms did change for better or worse, but as for me, it’s still a Worms game, and a damn good one.

So, I bought this game out of, more or less, scientific curiosity, as back when I was studying I also took a course on cellular automata, which are basically a generalisation of Conway's Game of Life (i.e. 'games' based on the same principles, but with different rule sets). I was curious as to how one would game-ify this principle, as Game of Life (and CAs in general) tend towards chaotic behaviour, that is behaviour that is technically strictly deterministic, but happens at a scale that to humans it must seem almost completely random.
And as you may guess, so is this game. Don't get me wrong - it's a very decent Game of Life simulation, but gamification on a highly chaotic system just doesn't work. Your best bet when trying to play this game is to set the difficulty to easy (as that lets you manipulate the whole "board") and then add single cells to the complex structures (or take a few away) and watch the levels collapse on themselves. The higher difficulty levels, in which you have to rely on "gliders" (specific cell configurations that result in a moving mass of basically stable size) to help you clear the board, are basically just click-and-pray, unless you really love the underlying computational model and spend a few hours to find a proper solution starting from the limited starting space you have.
So yeah, as a game, I can't recommend Bacteria. If you always wanted a decent simulator for Conway's Game of Life, however, feel free to spend that Euro. I don't regret buying it, but I certainly won't recommend it for the "game" part.

It actually really pains me to not recommend this game, because the story is fantastic, and with the help of the Insights, I felt that I actually learned quite a lot in a very short time. So what's the problem?
From a gameplay and mechanics standpoint, this platformer is a masterwork. It's simple, but just intuitive and unique enough to set itself apart. The problem comes with how well those mechanics work.
All too often, I found the controls to be sluggish, or unresponsive altogether. My AI character would occassionally get caught in the textures, release a ladder or ledge for no reason, or just plain refuse to move. It would be one thing had I been playing with another person, but when this game moves pretty quickly (even for a platformer), it's unacceptable for an AI character with basic pathfinding to fail so hard.
And this just wasn't a once or twice deal either. These issues, glitches, and other technical hiccups peppered what would have otherwise been a memorable experience with frustration. It took me roughly 3 hours to beat, but I can't even bring myself to play through the Foxtales DLC, because I can't think of a good reason to subject myself to the same frustrations and shortcomings I experienced in the main story.
Again, it's so sad to not be able to recommend this game, but without additional polish and maybe some QA oversight, it's just not worth experiencing the otherwise unique offerings this game brings to the table.

I picked up this game in a Humble Bundle and just got to playing it recently. I heard lots of good thiings about this game from other reviews, but to be honest, I wasn't really impressed by this game. It wasn't terrible, but it definitely wasn't something I enjoyed. I finished this game not because I really enjoyed it, but just because I wanted it finished.
The platforming was not really a challenge and required little skill or thought. In the three hours or so it took to finish the main game and the "Foxtales" DLC, the only times I felt challenged were because the controls were not responsive enough or the other AI-controlled character jumped off of a ledge, causing more rage than enjoyment in these parts. If you're looking for solid platforming, look somewhere else. Also, The story and the characters were semi-forgettable. It was not really a bad story, just not something I "got into."
However, as an educational experience, this game did manage to provide an window into the culture of the Inupiat. The collectible "insights" explained various details relating to parts of the story. If this is what you are looking for, the game may be worth it, but I can't recommend it on gameplay alone.
This game is not worth it for the platforming, but the story and the cultural background might make it worth it for some people.
Gameplay - 4/10
Story - 7/10
Educational Value - 9/10
Overall - 6/10
Value for price - $15 is a lot for 3 hours of gameplay. If I were considering buying this game, I'd definitely wait for a sale.

I rarely leave reviews, but I think this deserves one. As a horror game, It's quite solid. Story is absolutley terrifying if I'm honest. The way it presents the world, characters and It's theme is one of the best I've witnessed in a game. All these features are great, delivered with some really good voice acting too. The gameplay doesn't really compliment the creepy vibe though, I feel. Mostly just stealth and walking. The scenery is awesome, and it's interesting to explore for a while. I do feel that the game would have been better suited with a more linear structure, since the environments can get confusing and sometimes frustrating to navigate. Everytime I had a big area to explore I was both glad, and put off at the same time, as I'd know that I would have a little trouble making my way to the next scripted section. The few choices at the beggining of the game were very dull to me, it would usually consist of something that I had not much control over; luckily in the second half, a few moral choices were given with such disturbing theme's that it took me some time to make a choice that probably would have no effect later on. Not because I was given an annoying timer, or gimmicky button prompt. I was usually shown a choice, and then that was it. I could make my own mind up with the material I had. I feel the game works better as a phycological horror game, which is overshadowed at times by the sneaking gameplay that felt like a chore. I wasn't too scared of getting caught at the later stages, because all that happened was slightly laughable. I only died once in the game, just because I thought I could wait a few more seconds rather than run. So I feel that the story was the best feature of this game. I'm all for story driven games, but I don't feel this could be considered flawless when the gameplay is uninspired at best, and boring at worst. If you're more into being scared long after the game is over, then get this immediatley without getting spoiled. I wish they focused more on the phycological terror at times, but even with saying that, this game left me shaking my head at the end. I won't ruin it, but I'll just say it was... bitter sweet. Overall: 8/10

Stardrive 2 is a fun 4X with a focus on combat, ship design and exploration. Think Total War in space: turn based strategy map with real time space battles.
Lots of good humour and references to SciFi in the game, as well as colourful characters / races / art. Lots of random events and anomalies to explore - the galaxy is a big place.
Ship designer is quite deep and uses a module based system where you drop and drag engines, weapons etc onto your ship. Everything is directional, so shields placed on the left side will only shield the left side, and weapons have firing arcs depending on where they are placed etc. For those who don't like making ships, the game comes with default designs.
This game is heavily inspired by MoO2. If you are looking for a massive complex game like Distant Worlds or Europa Universalis, you won't find it here. Ground combat is turn based tactical similar to Xcom or Advance Wars. I would say the ground combat is alright but not great.
Some of the menus need polish which I expect will come as the dev tweaks the game post-release. I have not encountered any game-breaking bugs, but the game did freeze once and the one time the UI disappeared while I was in the ship designer. There are also some game balance issues which are of course being worked on by the dev.
Even still, it's worth picking up.

I somewhat enjoyed playing it, when I could play it that is. So do I recommend this game? Meh. Since there is no Meh button I say “No”, but what I really mean is “if you have free time play and write a review”. You're out zero dollars. but a preface to the entire thing is, you may not be able to find players on your desired servers. I think there was less than 700 people playing across all servers yesterday (7/16/16)
I've been following this game since they announced its development back in whenever. Followed them on facebook, visited their website, watched the development videos. I've finally gotten around to playing it at 0.43. So here we go with the good.
The environments and levels in this game a pretty excellent. Seriously if you can get into a match they are very pretty to look at. you can see the attention put towards these levels. The combat lanes have the right amount of variation and cover to allow long, mid, and short range combat. The game gets this right on all the levels I’ve played so far. The sound seemed okay, because sound is something you don’t really notice unless it is way off. Like it is in the after mission reports, no bells and whistles there. The combat is there, it exists which I mean is good, but it doesn’t stand out that much. The bullets do actual damage that you can't just walk off. You can damage parts of a person’s body making it more difficult for them to fight, which is pretty interesting. Because of this your guns feel like you’re actually shooting. The recoil is manageable and everything falls in line pretty well. The game modes a pretty standard and honestly that’s okay.
That’s it with the good, so let’s look at the bad.
It says I've played the game for two hours, but honestly that is probably about half true? Mostly what I did was wait to get into a match on the NA server. Never did manage to, so I've been playing pretty exclusively against EU RUS players. This is in no way ideal, because even with the management system you can unload an entire magazine into these guys and then suddenly you both die. Not great. The anomalies seem pointless in this game, and the artifacts don’t really seem to have that great of an outcome on play. Mostly what you’ll be doing is sneaking around in tall grass, popping your head up to get shot or shoot someone. Or if you play close in, mostly what you’ll be doing is running around from cover to cover to pop your head out to get shot, or spray someone down. There isn’t a high enough population to create a match control system, So you’re going to run into a people with pretty high level of skill, gear, and investment in the game. This makes the game pointlessly unfun at times. Sometimes someone will pull off a headshot and you’ll know it was crap but by toggling appropriately you can’t tell if they are just getting lucky or if they are hacking. But other times people will see you through multiple walls from across the map. They’ll worm their way all the way through a path bullets and other players, come around a corner tactically while aiming down their sights to shoot you will you hide behind a barrel in a bush in the corner of the map. Many players are just idle because they’ve sat so long trying to find a match. So you might find yourself in a shootout with a team that isn’t napping with one or two other players.
All around though the game isn’t done, and there are lots of promises to be delivered on. Hopefully this game makes a lot of improvements and I look forward to playing it as it progresses to see if it improves.
TL;DR
No I don’t recommend this game, except it is free so try it out and tell us what you think.

Alright, so vanquish, a Title that i wouldn't expect to show up on steam's store front, and like all port, the first thing that i'd want to talk about is the performance, how is it ?, well unlike bayonetta where your frames would randomly drop and stutter, vanquish actually performs great, even better than some AAA games that wasn't a port, and this is because the game is ported by little stone software, the same studio that's responsible for the Valkyria chronicles port for PC, and credit where credit is due, they done something that not many studio did, even though there are still a couple of bugs which i'll talk about later,
[Gameplay]: 8/10, Imagine Gears of war and binary domain had a rowdy night on a motel with 60 cans of red bull,
[Graphics]: 9/10, Simply beautiful without excessive use of effects (would suggest turning off blur because its annoying)
[Story]: 7/10 as generic as you can get, with basic characters, but let's be honest, if we want to see pointless expositions then we'll just go play something like life is strange, and it is enough to keep you entertain,
[Music]: 7/10, well there's not much, but what's there is enough
[Bugs]: 6/10, while it doesn't affects the performance you're getting, there is one bug that might screw you over, when your framerate went above 60fps, the damage that enemies inflict significantly increased, which might seems like a good thing for those who are looking for a challenge, but not necessarily for those who aren't, a simple patch should fix this and my potato can't reach higher than 60-70 anyway, but i'm holding my score until they do, just to be fair
so overall, would i recommend Vanquish ?, yes, especially for that price, at least they're not selling old games for full price *Cough Cough* Bethesda *Cough Cough*

StarDrive 2 is a complete rip off of Master of Orion 2 without any of the good and all the bad.
A lot of people on here are writing reviews either praising the game or telling you it is too difficult. I doubt anyone praising it has actually beaten it or plays many 4X titles. I could write a long list about why you should avoid this game, but I will keep it short. Here is the breakdown:
1. There is no ending. A silent video is all you have to indicate you have won the match. The game will continue even once finished. You have to exit to the main menu, quit to desktop, or keep playing.
2. Conquest is your only victory condition. You cannot have allies, so there is no diplomatic option.
2. The UI is a direct copy from MoO2 in every way. Managing colonies at the late game is tedious, and will take up almost all of your time unless you ignore them.
3. The AI is terrible. If you need proof, go read any of the other 500+ reviews telling you it is terrible.
4. Diplomacy is pointless. The AI will only use diplomacy to threaten you. Once again, you cannot have allies.
5. The ground combat is terrible. It is similar to XCOM in style, but is devoid of any strategy. There is no cover, and only a few weapons / items in the entire game. You take over entire planets with small squads of marines.
6. The game is too quiet. The only sound is the music (which is very lackluster especially in combat), and basic UI / combat sound Fx. There are no voice overs except for the tutorial. It truly feels desolate and without character.
There are a multitude of other issues, but I will not burden you with them. The end all be all is that the game is not what it should be. Your play experience will not be good, and when you finally beat a match you will be extremely disappointed by the ending assuming you survived the boredom of the late game.

Overall, if you're interested in fun, spooky games and think this looks interesting to you, it's definitely worth playing through without knowing anything else about it. Otherwise here's my review.
The first chapter of this game is the best. It's one of the most fun horror experiences I've had in a while. Atmospheric and eerie, I jumped out of my seat, had dawning realizations and at moments I dreaded having to reach out and type even another word. I loved it. The developers knew how to use this medium effectively and it really shines.

The rest of the game, while I enjoyed it, was simply not as scary. The concept of switching settings multiple times and always having some kind of computer interface to interact with was neat, and they did do a good job. It was immersive, sitting at a computer and getting lost in the instructions and atmosphere (it's as if I have a lot of experience doing that in real life :D). The little vignettes unfolding where interesting and I grasped at every little bit of information in those first few chapters. Part of me wishes there had been ten chapters, draw out the stories with subtle hints and give us more vignettes in various horror scenarios, because what they did was fun and interesting. It just felt like a big genre shift away from horror and into (admittedly decent) speculative fiction. Maybe another, scarier vignette would have tipped the balance back to horror? I don't know. I do know that while enjoyable, the rest of the vignettes don't hit the same high. I think #2 and #3 aren't too bad but brought down a little by #4 tearing you out of the immersion completely for the story's sake. I was left craving more of The House Abandon, some kind of escape the room game switching you between finding clues in a house and doing a text adventure on an old computer.
There are other minor complaints and most other reviews cover them pretty well. Frustrating mechanics, instructions not telegraphed clearly, the overall story gives a YMMV vibe. For me that stuff keeps it from being an amazing game, but I'd still recommend it, because it was a really nice experience to play through. It felt kind of like reading a horror short story anthology, and I wish there was more. I don't see this as a game someone regrets playing, even if that first chapter truly is the best. If you are worried about enjoying it all the way through, get it on sale. Chapter 1 is more than worth the sale price.

This game is basically an interactive creepy story told in 4 episodes.  It's unique in how it tells it.  A lot of it is text commands like, "go outside", "use key", "look around", etc. while your character uses a computer and the story plays out on the computer.  The game isn't just typing on a computer.  Sometimes you have to tune a radio, flip switches, and turn knobs.  Some parts let you walk around in first-person.  The setting takes place in the mid-80's so the environment and music is retro. It's not a super scary story but will have you on edge at times.  This isn't a horror game where ghosts and monsters come after you.  This is all about an interactive story that lets you play the main character.  It's not for everyone but if you like interactive stories, 80's themed stuff and creepy stories you should give it a chance.  I enjoyed it!  It starts out a bit slow but you'll soon find out that this game will take you for a ride.
I will admit, I had to use a walkthrough on some parts.  It can be a little cryptic at times but just keep looking around your environment and when using text commands get used to using the "look around" command.
Pros:
Immersive storyline
80's themed
Interactive story (not a cheap point-and-click)
Can be completed in short time
Easy to get all achievements
Cons:
Had to use a walkthrough a few times.

Yes this is a game about squares and rectangles, but it's also so much more than that. The heart and soul of Thomas Was Alone is its story of friendship, learning to believe in yourself, and never settling for just OK. Groan worthy as that may sound, developer and writer Mike Bithell deftly avoids the pretentious and heavy handed pitfalls that have proven to be so easy to fall into, and manages to craft a narrative that is touching, funny, and unquestionably charming from start to finish.
Equal if not greater credit for this also has to go to Danny Wallace for his spot on voice acting which includes a liberal amount of British wit, that brought to life these quadrilateral characters in a way that despite being a tired phrase, can only be described as a triumph! When the end came after just over two hours, I was saddened not because I felt unsatisfied or that it was too short, but merely wanted to spend more time with these characters I had so quickly come to love.
Even if forgoing the story, TWA is still a very clever puzzle platformer that near perfectly balances the difficulty to rarely be frustrating but always satisfying. The levels have been thoughtfully planned without any filler to speak of, which made for no obvious stopping points and instead keep the adventure rolling. What I feel is most remarkable though is how ingeniously gameplay is blended with story, building upon each other and proving impossible to separate without sacrificing what makes the various components so great. This to me is what defines a great videogame story; something that couldn't be achieved the same way in any other medium and was built with this understanding in mind.
Unlike the dozens of simplistic flash games that use similarly primitive shapes as placeholders or out of sheer laziness, here much care has been put into each block and area to make them both unique and memorable, result is not the least bit unpleasant to look at. From the subtle jump animations to the impressive lighting, upon further inspection TWA is much more detailed than it first appears, and with the engrossing soundtrack the presentation across the board is simply a treat.
I'm sure if I tried I could find something to nitpick about, but there's no need for me to as that is all it would be. I absolutely loved every moment of Thomas Was Alone, and you would be hard pressed to stop me from recommending to almost everyone. Mike Bithell did a cracking fine job in every regard, and I'm ever so thankful he was able and willing to share it with me. Now I hope to do the same and that this prompts you to take a moment if you haven't to meet Thomas, who as it turns out was most certainly not alone.

I've had a lot of fun playing this game. The combination of a leveling system, crafting system, and some basic quests, makes it an enjoyable way to spend spare time. You're in the apocalypse. Actual guns are rare and always will be.
Enemies are made challenging by their ability to teleport. Little buggers love just jumping around you and I find that makes it an interesting and fulfilling experience when you kill them. Random raids on your "Safezones" make it even more interesting as you have to fight off a nonstop wave of enemies and repair the boundaries.
Some bugs I have noticed are things such as:
Getting caught on pieces of terrain and bouncing all over the place and attracting attention.
Nether teleporting onto you instead of on the ground below you when you find that rare spot where you're out of reach.
Some issues with hitboxes in melee.
Water that goes over your head kills you. Instantly.
Unexplained cooldown on medical supplies.
On the cons side, I do wish there was more to do. Quests that take you halfway across the map to deliver boxes are fun and all... but I wish there were campaign type quests or something. More weapons would also be nice or better yet armor. Because what survivor wouldn't want a good suit of scrapmetal armor when fighting beasts that want to gnaw your face off? Or Kevlar for PVP?
All in all, as a game it's fun and interesting. But DO NOT BUY until it's clear that the devs are back up and working again instead of just sitting on their cash mound smoking crack and laughing as Steam users can't log in to their game and hackers run rampant on the PVP servers.
