It is a good game to play with lots of different setups and tactics, with a good selection to chose from and unlock as you progress, it is just a shame you need big wallets to catch up or be competitive.
Pros,
A nice paced game both combat and learning. (accept build times later in tier).
A good variety in ship modules, weapons armor shields etc for each own purpose, so theres many different stratergies to use.
Some good events that cycle around with slightly different content and prizes.
Getting help from alliance members to shave off 10% from total build time, if you're there to finish it.
Lots of PvE & PvP but remember this is a PvP game so that takes presidence.
Can get 'up to' 25 free coins daily but it's hardly a substitute for the cost to get it there and the cost off speeding certain things up or unlocking content.
There is a gating system which means no fleets 5 levels above or below you're base level, can attack you're base.
Cons,
Build times, repair times, refit times etc start to get drastically stupid in time or cost to complete the further you progress in tier. Basically to put into perspective the game is STUPIDLY expensive (so much emphasis on that if i haven't said before ;)), unless you want to wait 1-3 months for at least 1 out of 7 fleets to be fully built.
The combat servers AI does some funky things when its peak time and the servers are laggy.
You also cannot man you're own base turrets while being base attacked which i find odd for a pvp game.
Two different AI setups or servers for vega fleets/own combat AI and alien fleets/outposts.
If Kixeye made things cheaper all round and less time to build everything (say 50%) , meaning lower the cost of coins in game then more people would probably spend a bit and have a bigger player base, then i think the game would be in a much much better place for us customers/consumers, right now it sucks but it has a lot of potential.
They have also said on the forums, that they will be making changes to the current system to help speed up tier 1-5, but that also means no changes to T6 and what changes they do to the other tiers ?, we shall see.

I rarely leave reviews, but I think this deserves one. As a horror game, It's quite solid. Story is absolutley terrifying if I'm honest. The way it presents the world, characters and It's theme is one of the best I've witnessed in a game. All these features are great, delivered with some really good voice acting too. The gameplay doesn't really compliment the creepy vibe though, I feel. Mostly just stealth and walking. The scenery is awesome, and it's interesting to explore for a while. I do feel that the game would have been better suited with a more linear structure, since the environments can get confusing and sometimes frustrating to navigate. Everytime I had a big area to explore I was both glad, and put off at the same time, as I'd know that I would have a little trouble making my way to the next scripted section. The few choices at the beggining of the game were very dull to me, it would usually consist of something that I had not much control over; luckily in the second half, a few moral choices were given with such disturbing theme's that it took me some time to make a choice that probably would have no effect later on. Not because I was given an annoying timer, or gimmicky button prompt. I was usually shown a choice, and then that was it. I could make my own mind up with the material I had. I feel the game works better as a phycological horror game, which is overshadowed at times by the sneaking gameplay that felt like a chore. I wasn't too scared of getting caught at the later stages, because all that happened was slightly laughable. I only died once in the game, just because I thought I could wait a few more seconds rather than run. So I feel that the story was the best feature of this game. I'm all for story driven games, but I don't feel this could be considered flawless when the gameplay is uninspired at best, and boring at worst. If you're more into being scared long after the game is over, then get this immediatley without getting spoiled. I wish they focused more on the phycological terror at times, but even with saying that, this game left me shaking my head at the end. I won't ruin it, but I'll just say it was... bitter sweet. Overall: 8/10

Star Drive 1 was better. This one doesn't feel very unique. It's like Galactic Civilisations 2 lite. It tries to do a bit of everything in GC2, but doesn't excel in anything.
Prepare to go to war from the start of the game. There is no diplomacy in this game. AI will come knocking as soon as they meet you.
The space combat is average. Not like the first game where you can have hundreds of ships duking it out.
Ship design is like the first game. But your choices are simpler because you're not faced with as many units as the first game. You just have to kill whatever is in front of you before they close the distance to your ship, so mounting an array of long range rail guns and flak cannons (for point defense) = like shooting fish in a barrel.
The ground assault is meh. It's like XCOM but there isn't much variety in units, gear or abilities even with full tech research. The limited amount of troops (only 4 units) permitted in ground assault is a let down. I ended up bombing from orbit rather than deal with the frustrating ground assaults.
Planetary invasions are buggy. You clear out the sector of enemy ships, but then you can't invade or bombard. The only way is to leave the system and come back and try again. Annoying.
For $20... its ok. Not great but ok.

pros: its got an interesting faction based system where each faction has different strengths and weaknesses, it has skill trees allowing you to customise your character to suit your play style but it also forces you to compromise in some areas as there is a max of 100 skill points available meaning that you cant go crazy and there wont be some people who play more getting more perks/ skills.
cons: the movement of the characters felt slow and clunky and at times unresponsive, the game overall seems to be in favour of guns that have higher fire rates this lead to me not seeing many people using rifles, snipers, semi automatics and seeing SMG's and automatic rifles being used by most people, this could be attributed to the slow reaction timing of players that dont have time to aim or to the maps which prodominantly take place in close quarters, in buildings and factories. it takes a while to get to the better weapons and customisation which might put off casual players who dont have time to pour into leveling up.
what i liked: the map design was very detailed and thought out and it definatly felt like this is what a post apocaliptic world would look like. the different factions being very distinguishable from one another with their different outfit styles, the game modes were fun and specific modes such as battery retreival and research mode make you feel like these are tasks people would have to do in a post apocaliptic world.
what i didnt like: for some of the game modes the maps felt too big for the amount of players in the game, i would only see one or two enemies every couple of minutes and only on the objectives so even though i liked the map design i felt it was wasted as i didnt see enemies anywhere other than the objectives. on maps that would be more suited to snipers/ long range weapons the distance you could see was limited by fog making the snipers even more irrelivant.
in conclusion this game was fun in short play sessions and shows lots of promise, i would recommend it to anyone who has lots of time to spare but doesnt necissarily have the funds to actually buy games.

SD2 is a difficult 4x strategy game with homicidal AI and some very good game mechanics. Overall the game is very solid but in its current state if falls just short of a classic. A must have for space strategy fan boys, not a good buy for a casual gamer or those new to the genre.
The Good:
* Customizable options for the factions and starships lends to great immersion. I have made plenty of flagship battle heavy titans that get smashed because I didn't place armor in the right places or had too many spinal mounts that could hit anything far away but the big ship couldn't turn fast enough to handle flank attacks.
* Graphics are awesome. Clicking on planets and watching the cities light up on the dark side increase with population is a nice touch. Ships blow up into several smaller pieces and actually come apart instead of an explosion cloud animation.
* Space battles tend to devolve into choatic melees despite the most careful planning and ship design ( I consider this a realistic plus some micromangers may get frustrated with the lack of form in battle) A formation button would be a plus.
The Bad:
* Homicadal AI that will attack at immediately when weakness is shown
* AI sends massive doom fleets that are kinda of fun to destroy with some well built smaller fleets, but it is easy to be get overwhelmed
* Some characters cause some serious headaches. Watch your♥♥♥♥♥if you hire Zapp Groening, because the AI will go ape♥♥♥♥♥♥ (-20 diplo for a 30% firepower bump)
* Ground combat seems a bit underwhelming. Troops are determined by population so 6 soldiers defending a world of 6 billion doesn't seem right in scale.
* Tech tree are based on difficult choices. Each category has one of three options. If you just start playing and researching blind you will find that you have a broken economy and a disfunctional empire mid game.
Summary:
* Active community with a developer who reads the damn forums and reacts with frequent patches
* Hard but satisfying when you develop a winning reciepe
* A beautiful game with great FPS for the graphics (34 hours in no CTD)
* A lot of bang for 30 bucks

This is a pick-up and put-down game. It's good if you only have 5 minutes to spare. I wouldn't spend more than $2-$3 for it.

October 12, 2017 Update: The big patch and content update just released appears to have made major positive improvements to the Friday the 13th game, including fixing balance issues and finally addressing some very annoying bugs. The new rainstorm weather option increases the creepiness factor by 10X at least, Part IV Jason is a bad mother-("shut your mouth"), and the Jarvis House map has a great layout and feels very unique compared to the original 3 camp locations, posing cool challenges to both Jason and counselors.
There's still some lingering technical issues the devs admit they need to address, but this has been an impressive step in the right direction, including improving frame rate performance, and I'm happy to now change my review from negative to a very solid thumbs up.
(My original review is below for context about the issues with glitches and problematic patches during the first months after launch, but my opinion about the game has now clearly improved considerably.)
-----------------------------------------------------------
I wanted to leave a positive review, but simply can't bring myself to do it. The core premise of Friday the 13th: The Game is very solid and I've had a decent amount of fun playing it. The game is basically hide and seek with brief flashes of extreme violence.
As a fan of the film series, mainly the 80s entries, I really appreciate how well they recreated the locations in the movies and they did a generally great job with the characters, both counselors and Jason choices. The in-game music also perfectly captures the mood of the early films. However, the makers seem to have no clue on how to engage in a constructive way with their player community, the game currently has many broken components, lacks basic customization features, and I've lost faith that they'll turn things around in a meaningful way.
If they release patches that fix the problems with perks, people flying out of the maps, vital items glitching in the ground, and provide some decent free DLC, I'll happily change this review to positive. However, it appears that their current focus is on luring new buyers with exclusive content for the physical version (currently only announced on console) and leaving the fans who already ponied up high and dry with an incomplete game that should be clearly flagged as Early Access and priced substantially cheaper.
Lastly, I must confess that I have very little interest in the single player component they talk about as coming soon, especially if it's focused on Jason and NPC counselors. I'll try it, sure, but the multiplayer is what I purchased this for and I want that fixed above all else. After that, then please add more maps and characters to add variety to the experience. In my mind, the single player mode is dead last in terms of priority given the state of the game and its quickly dwindling player base.

I only played one more platformer which savaged my keyboard worse than Shio. And that was the one and only Super Meat Boy. I’m not going to complain (not a lot, anyway) since I am fully aware that ridiculously difficult games are a mark of distinction for independent development and that there’s a real demand for such titles. Coconut Island Studio made their Steam debut with just the kind of video game that you’ll either love or hate, the minute you realize that getting passed the tutorial level, won’t be a breeze. I have to review it, so expect me to refrain from stonger words in describing my Shio experience. Also, I didn’t dislike the game enough to rate it down.
You don’t purchase or play platformers for their “charming” storylines, right? Shio still features one, yet it is quite ambiguous and I presume that was on purpose. You control the Masked Man who remains silent at all times and somehow still runs errands for his sensei or the village elder. An old guy sends him off for some reason and our mysterious hero has to travel across the levels by hopping from one floating lantern to another. It’s not a lot to talk about in terms of the narrative, but I didn’t expect much to begin with. Ironically, “shio” means “salt” (塩) in Japanese. Salt is one of Super Meat Boy’s mortal enemies.
I did find it odd that Shio seems to feature all sorts of Japanese leitmotifs (such as the advertising posters found on certain buildings) yet I couldn’t help but notice that the writing is in Mandarin instead. I know for certain that the dev team comes from mainland China, Shanghai. At least the Korean writing has those circle patterns which are unique to their culture and thus, you can’t mistake it for another Asian alphabet. Most players won’t even bother or care what those many in-game signs are all about, plus there are English subtitles for the few occasions during which some NPCs interact with the protagonist.
Another 2D platformer made with Unity Engine assets. Not too shabby, yet the visuals did lack both sufficient diversity and that certain something to draw attention to them. It all looked the same, even after playing for 3 hours. Same colours, same trap types and just some backgrounds which would occasionally follow a day/night cycle. It only starts raining towards the end. Devs, where's my mouse peripheral support in the main menu?
Since the protagonist remains silent throughout the entire game, don’t expect any form of voice acting. The soundtrack is comprised of Oriental songs which were the only relaxing part in Shio. I did appreciate the OST, since the rest of the title really went the extra mile in stressing me out.
Getting stressed by Shio is actually an understatement. I reckon that I must have suffered at least 100 in-game deaths before seeing the 3-hour mark. And players have no way of dialing down on the difficulty scale. Depending on your choice to remap the jumping button or not, you’ll be hitting that default “J” key until it wishes to cut-and-run. The annoying  one-hit KO traps in Shio will require precise keyboard strokes as if rehearsing on a piano. You know what? I hated playing the piano in my childhood. Far better off to listen to others play than doing it yourself, in some cases.
Watching gameplay vids of Shio off YouTube, I really have to admire the nerves of steel and  stoicism exhibited by some of those players. I did the same thing with Super Meat Boy once I figured that it was simply wasting my time, when I was trying it myself.  Still, there’s no more Meat left on that Boy. Shio and I'm certain many similar titles to follow, have to keep alive this “tradition” for difficult 2D platformers which mainstream development refuses to promote out of (partially understood) fear that there’s not a lot of demand for such games. Regardless of my own experience and opinion, Shio fully deserves its place in the Steam Store.
Shio may not be overpriced, yet it should include Trading Cards at some point. I’m not even sure that’s easily achievable, with Valve’s ever-stricter policy in this matter. For example, new Steam games that fail to sell a certain quota, no longer have access to Cards but perhaps this won’t apply to older releases, before Steam Direct. If you’re still not convinced, wait for a Steam Sale or bundle and you won’t regret trying out Shio. I don’t, despite the fact that I’m not gonna play it again for the next few years. Or sooner. Maybe that’s Shio’s ultimate lesson to its players. You can’t stay :steamsalty: forever, can you?
EDIT: Trading Cards have been added after two weeks from the publishing of this review.

Non-Combat Skill-based Platformer
Medium-Hard
You play as a silent, masked man whose job is to light lanterns. Who you are and why you do what you do is what you will discover in Shio.
There is no combat in Shio, your only enemy is the environment. Nearly everything will kill you in one touch. You can only do two things, run and jump. While that sounds simple enough, the architects of the towers you have to traverse have placed all sorts of obstacles in your path, such as, but not limited to, spikes, lava floors, fireball cannons and swinging pendulums. At certain points there is also gates which has to be opened by lighting certain lanterns. As if the tower itself was not enough to be in your way, the weather will also try to stop you, from sun-beam lasers to razor-leaf-carrying wind-canons.
There are 4 chapters and each chapter has roughly 30 levels and a different season. Each season determines what type of weather obstacles are present in each level. The levels gets gradually harder as you progress through each level in chapter. Some levels can be completed in the matter of seconds, while some of the later levels might take you several minutes to complete, after you have trial-and-error'ed your way through it.
The narrative is delivered through interactions with characters you meet on your journey through the different towers.
Shio has a 2D painting-like art-style and is well optimized, so it will probably run on slightly older machines.
The game has a mix between eastern-inspired combat music and relaxing zen-like music.
Shio has nearly infinite replayability, as you can speed run each level, competing against a character in the game called "old friend", who has some fairly good times. Even if you do not try to speed run Shio, you will challenge yourself to get through all the levels to discover who you, the silent, masked man, are and why you do what you do. The game is truly challenging, especially when you get further into the game. The game can be frustratingly hard at times, but that only drives you to perfect your timing and skills to get past it, even if it is only by the skin of your teeth with 0.1 second from death.

"Oh, no worries," you naively say. "I just won't get those packs and play without spending money."

What's that? The new laser beam annihilates enemy ships in 3 seconds? I want it! And what a steal, it only costs $500!
Shame on you Kixeye for turning my favorite free to play game into a smoldering pile of nerd sweat and blood money. You are a symbol of everything wrong with the video game industry.

I... I seriously don't know what to make of this game. I wanted to like it, I really did, but perhaps, just perhaps, I expected it to be something it was never meant to be in the first place. It certainly has a lot of good will in it, that's for sure – but does it make for a fun game? It's a co-op experience, but does it compliment it? It has a unique (culturally) story, but does it work?
Let's try breaking it down into what's good (+) and what's bad (-).
(+)
Although the full effect is reached by having a fairly simple geometry (it's mostly snow and water, but the water looks really great) covered in a generous amount of blur and bloom, it does create an atmospheric eye-pleasing image.
(+)
A game based on genuine eskimo stories? Count me in!
(+)
Yes, I just listed that as a pro.
(+)
Although they are often misused or not implied clearly enough. No one wants their hand held, but come on, you can't just invent a completely new puzzle type 5/6 into the game and expect it to be figured out instantly, which is a cause for frustration.
(+)
Genuine eskimo narrator, how neat is that? But, despite the claim in the extra footage that eskimo stories were like movies, the narrative is not movie-like, not by a long-shot.
(+)
It gives away a certain educational vibe, but the extras, which are picked up as collectibles in the game, are actually documentary shorts (24 one-to-two minute pieces in the main game, and 5 more in the DLC). They are missable, however, and the game weirdly does not encourage you to seek any hidden areas, so I missed about 6-7 shorts total, and I had no desire to replay the whole game in order to find them.
(-)
Judge it as you will – it could be seen as an advantage in a game like this, but there certainly could've been room for more story. It's barely 3 hours long, +1 hour max for the DLC.
(-)
The story is akin to the myths of how things came to be, such as old ethnic mythos of how sun came to be etc. That doesn't necessarily translate to a satisfying story. Don't look for motivations in some events that happen here. Some could enjoy it, I, however, didn't.
(-)
It could slip past your eyes, but we played it co-op, and encountered quite a few geometry bugs, bugged spawn points skipping whole sections of game after dying etc.
(-)
Reminds a lot of Deadlight in that regard... You'd want that extra content, because finally for once the extras are great, but you're not willing to go through the increasingly exhausting game for them. So you just YouTube them.
(-)
It's short and underdeveloped, it doesn't utilize mechanics from the main game enough, and it has a really bad ratio of new environments to playtime you spend in them. You just get stuck in a screen-size room, only to move on to a similar screen-sized room meters away.
As a part of a bundle? Yes. As a huge, 75-90% discount? Yes. Full price? I would never pay full price for a game like this, I just couldn't.

Having played StarDrive one and being pretty impressed (After all, lets consider both of these games are by a one man band who gets alittle bit of art help on the side) but left wanting more, I had been following StarDrive 2 with alot of interest. I bought it day one, and started playing.
As evidenced by nearly 90 hours into the game over the last week, I have been blown away. As many have noted, there's a real "hardness" level to the AI - even on easy; recent patches (which by the way, what developer do you know puts out 4 patches in 2 days, and works over a weekend?) have added a true easy mode, but I was honestly unchallanged by it - even normal mode with special events turned off felt too easy. Having a real challenge is fun - regardless (again to the folks complaining about the AI cheating) of how the AI accomplishes the challenge. I actually have to design ships specifically to take out each race's ships - its pretty neat in my mind that I can tool up a bunch of ships with long range weapons, shred the enemy, and then get owned by the next group because I don't have enough point defense and they have tons of carriers with swarms of hundreds of fighters.
The graphics are outstanding; the game is filled with easter eggs to various Sci-Fi tropes; almost to the point I'm afriad some annoying lawyer will pop up and sue Zero. Some of them are aboslutely hysterical - such as the human fighter pilot hero.
Sound is good; the real time battles are fun and engaging, and tactics really do matter.
There's some bugs in Stardrive 2, but I'm confident Zero will get rid of them, and I also believe he will update and improve the already outstanding game over the next 6 months. I'm looking forward to modding it and doing some neat things.
My final comment on StarDrive 2 is this - it is the kind of game that makes me say "5 more minutes", and in my mind, the best compliment a game can be payed is the "5 more minutes" feeling - its the halmark of a great game.
There are many games out there that cost 50 bucks and are nowhere near as fun, enjoyable, technically sound, and replayable. Get StarDrive 2 today!

The learning curve is what threw me off so many 4x games in the past but this game has such a great tutorial (voiced over too!) that I felt like I picked it up in 15 minutes. Anything else I couldn't figure out what easily learned from the help menu which covers extra details like food and transports etc, maybe 10+ minor topics.
Building your own ships is super intimidating at first because you have no idea what counters what, but once you get the hang of it (make a save a few turns before a battle and experiment!) it's super fun to see what you can cook up! TIP: You eat the infinite missile stream of death a few times before you figure out ~3 or so tiny laser turrets can pick them off before they hit your ship.
Custom races traits are also REALLY great. Want to make a cybernetic race of bears that lives underground? It's possible. And it's fun!
Most addicting game I've played in space in a long time.
The one CON I can list for this game is that their are Command Points limiting your # of ships, but each race's ship layouts are unique, and some races get significantly more tiles to build on per ship type than others. This could be turned into a plus if you decide you want to play the easiest race (cybernetic guys) first then move on to the hardest (bugs/wolves, etc)...

I remember way back getting into the disc boxes of my father and catch the demo of this gem for the first time. This is a really genuine game that surprised me on my childhood. I remember to play the demo over and over because there was no way to get this game from a retailer near my old home. In this game you play as a charismatic dude that needs to annoy his neighbors in the most humiliating ways possible. It take me a smile every time I hear the old dude screams. The game puts the player in a live-show at the shows of Paul. The star of the show and the one that needs to humiliate his pals on live-cam. It's just hilarious.
This comedy is worth a try, no matter how old you are, this game will steal a laugh from your soul. Sometimes you need to annoy the old dude by putting soap into his bathroom floor, or maybe a dynamite on his birthday cake. The possibilities are limited, but the combinations are up to the player. It is the same thing always, the old dude gets humiliated, but the way in which the actions are performed is up to the player. Sometimes in bizarre ways, sometimes in really weird ways, but he always gift the player his screams.
This is a game which you play by point and click objects. You have a scene in 2D and the player needs to search for objects around the area to interact with other objects, and perform an action. This action is to humiliate specific npcs in the game. But generally the old dude is the one that gets all the tragedy. Anyways, the game also allows the player to hide, because if the old dude, or another "rival" npc discover you in-fraganti. He or she pwns you on live cam. There is a score for each level. You get a percentage depending on how bad you humiliated the target. The player also gets a bar in which counts how many times you got the target beyond the line of awkward fury. The old dude gets his back hurt every time the player makes him really mad. Also, the player can combine the actions to make the target in constant madness.
It is a really hilarious game and it is really fun. It is super old, but still is amazing today. Look at the trailer to see more about this game. It really worth a try.

StarDrive 2 impresses me in a lot of ways.  Firstly, the music and graphics are outstanding.  Secondly, the ship editor is both in-depth and intuitive...though I'm still trying to figure out optimal designs as the default ones don't seem to last very long in combat.  The races themselves have unique personalities and I appreciate their quirks and dialogue.  The tech tree is different in the sense that you have to pick between 2-3 techs every tier, meaning you'll pass on the others and may never get them.  This made me really think about what kind of empire I wanted.  Combat was also very fun and satisfying...I liked watching my creations attempt to work with what I gave them (shields and beam weapons, mostly).
As far as what I don't like: the game doesn't tell you when a planet is not producing anything (it does tell you when new research is available) and the AI is still too difficult, even on "Easy".  I am not ashamed to say that I could be playing better and designing my ships more efficiently, but I'd also like to see "Easy" made even easier...that is, I'd like to build up my empire in relative peace and then attack when I'm ready. It would be great if there was a way to turn off the AI's ability to attack altogether and instead have it play a defensive game. Either that, or limit their CP in some way.  Of course, there are those that think "Brutal" is too easy and don't want the developer to change anything. That's why there are multiple difficulty levels...I'm sure it's possible to change one difficulty setting without touching the others, making the "don't nerf the AI for the casuals" complaints irrelevant. Some of us don't want a challenge, just a way to unwind after working 10 hour shifts. I'm just the type that prefers a "light" challenge...*shrug*, everyone's mileage will differ.  If some feel that "Easy" is just right, then perhaps an "Easier" difficulty setting could be added.
Long story short, casual 4X players may get frustrated (like I have) at times when the AI decides to come at you with a vengence despite your attempts to be passive.  Difficulty aside I'm really enjoying this one and I can easily recommend it to 4X fans.

It's good. It's very good. In my opinion it doesn't (yet) surpass the incredible MOO2 but it might be the best space 4X to come out since then. That said it is still something of a rough diamond and there is definitely room for improvement, fortunately the developer is generally responding to constructive criticism and I am hopeful that he will continue to refine the game.
The good -
The whole game oozes personality, ships look amazing, races are well designed and battles are really impressive.
There are some really nice innovations. Designing ships is great fun. Interactions with events and minor races are on the whole well implemented and the way these elements play out is both interesting and rewarding.
The diplomacy system - it's innovative and I really like it in principle. Although this is countered somewhat by the limited number of diplomatic interactions.
The basic game mechanics are a lot like MOO2 and that, for me at least, is a very good thing.
The space battles are a great spectacle and a lot of work has clearly gone into them. There are some weapon balance issues but these are already being looked at and patched.
It's generally stable, I have experienced no crashes so far and have encountered only one bug, which has already been fixed. As far as I can tell it's in a much better state than SD1 was on release.
The bad -
There's only one victory condition and it's via the total elimination of all opponents. I have some concerns that the need for complete eliminations will make the late game a boring grind, this is one of the biggest issues with 4X games in general and I am disappointed that SD2 has not addressed it, at least not yet.
There's no benchmarking mechanism to see how you compare to your opponents, there's not even a basic score counter. I realise this is personal taste, to an extent, but for me it is a significant issue and I hope to see it addressed soon.
The lack of fleet formations, you fleets turn up for battles in any old shape. This means you can either manually arrange every single ship before any battle or just don't bother, I found my approach quickly became the latter option, and that is irritating and immersion breaking.
On the whole the bad bits haven't (so far) detracted from my overall enjoyment of what is a fun game with huge potential. I would unquestionably recommend Stardrive 2 even as it is at present and if improvements continue to be made it could just be the true MOO2 successor that many people have been waiting nearly 20 years for.

Excellent software for practicing guitar and bass (pronounced /bās/), it's like having your very own practice coach in your computer!
It's more of a tool for honing your guitar skills than an actual game, though the original Rocksmith was more of a game than this version is. It needs to be coupled with other material to give you music theory, but it does try to cover some of this itself. If you are just interested in playing with little care towards learning to play outside of Rocksmith, then it's certainly completely capable of providing an experience like that without having to learn anything more than what Rocksmith 2014 can teach you.
But if you treat Rocksmith 2014 as a practice coach and find yourself a good theory coach, then you can fully expect at some point to be playing music outside of the game with relative ease. I've found a good place to start in getting that theory coaching is the Hal Leonard FastTrack Guitar (or Bass)  Method Starter Pack that includes a book, CD & DVD. It can be had for under $15 and covers the basics fairly succinctly.
But like in the old joke "How do you get to Carnegy Hall?", the answer is "practice!", and that's what Rocksmith 2014 really brings to the table. It coaches you on new techniques and ramps up the difficulty as you get better at playing, but it provides an interactive environment that stimulates you and challenges you WHILE you get in that all so important practice time. It deals with the single biggest barrier to becoming musically adept, namely the 'grind'. You may never get to Carnegy Hall, but with Rocksmith 2014 practicing is no longer a drudge!
If you intend to play songs outside of Rocksmith then you may want to invert the view of the strings on the screen, putting the low E on the bottom to match the way tab is written. Once you are used to this orientation, then downloading guitar songs that are notated in tab will afford you the ability to play them without having to mentally flip what you see on the paper because you avoided instilling bad habits while using Rocksmith by orienting the display to match the way tab is written from the start. Of course, if you never intend to play music outside of Rocksmith then it shouldn't matter...
Multiplayer is pretty fun, though very basic in how it's done in Rocksmith. You can play any combination of guitar and bass, including emulated bass in multiplayer. If you haven't given this a try, you should! Multiplayer uses two separate profiles under the same account, we played at my friend's house so I had to start a profile under his account to do this. While I could also use this profile in single player, it's under his account and not mine so I can only use it when he's the one logged in. There doesn't seem to be a way to use my main profile under my account while we are logged in on his system, so any progress I make under the profile I use on his account is lost except when I'm playing multiplayer.
Playing emulated bass is pretty fun by itself, but doesn't hold a candle to playing with a real 4-string bass! It's worth the money to go to the local pawn shop and buy a used Ibanez GSR100 or Dean Edge 9 bass for under $100. Like the BC Rich Bronze Series Warlock, most pawn shops have these around and usually for less than $100, though any Silvertone, Jay Turser, SX, Gregg Bennett, Squier, etc.  guitar or bass can be had at a pawn shop for less than $100 are all well worth the cost and enhances the Rocksmith experience.

Do you ever wanted to be the bad guy? Do you ever admired the Dark Lord, looking badass, destroying world and killing those pesky heroes? Well, then, this game is for you! Without further delay, lets sink into the fantastic (and sarcastic) world of Overlord!
The "bad guy" game market is severelly limited. Everywhere we are feeded with either Goody McGood heroes, fighting to save the world or with shallow concept of being gray and developing our character the way we want to (shallow being either ♥♥♥♥ing rainbows knight in shining armor or baby killing maniac). You wont see that here. Instead, we are evil from the start. And that's what making this game fun.
Gameplay is really basic sadly. We are the Overlord. We need to rebuild empire. But Overlord doesn't just go around killing stuff, oh no. He have his minions for that. So we are running around with bunch of our Imps, killing things, collecting stuff to upgrade our tower and (of course) doing some fairly easy puzzles. The style is kinda like Zelda. We need some item or other thing to advance further, we collect it, defeat the boss with that, go to another area, rince and repeat.
Graphics are really beatiful. This game aged well, giving nice vibe even so long after the golden release. Locations are colorful and alive yet distinct, there are things moving everywhere, light effects are well made. The olny thing I can really dissaprove of are the overall sugar-like appearances of every single location, but the game have it's (gigantic dose) of humour, and exaggeration pays a big role in that.
Music is on par with graphics. Really exaggerated, yet well made and distinct. Sounds are great. Every single detal from random people dialogs to battle sounds are great.
Story is great. We are the Overlord, taking over the world yet again. At our path there will be much obstacles, including corrupted heroes, lack of resources and other natural or unnatural calamities. Narration is smooth and plot twists are well done. We even have the pleasure of having a wife here, and Overlord is not your average multihour RPG.
Bad things? Well, for starters all our work is done by minions. I won't say its technically bad, but our Overlord can't do crap. Its kind of stupid, we are the antihero of this world. The other thing, because the game is strongly influenced by Zelda franchise, we can't really talk about open world RPG or exploration all that much. Oh, we can go to the previous locations to loot additional stuff with our new powers (it's unattainable otherwise, the easiest example would be Imp Pillars in the water, we can't get them, until we get Blue Imps), but we need to go from point A to B on a series of semi-linear locations in order to progress with the story. Also our Overlord can't be developed all that much. More minions, stronger armor and weapon and minion types. Sadly that's all.
Well, if you we're spending all nights in Dungeon Keeper, this game is for you. It have great sense of humor (and a bit of self awareness), nice graphics, enjoyable and easy gameplay, and, of course, you play as the bad guy. Its a good piece, althou technically not a RPG, and sadly, kind of short. But hey, its Zelda on crack, so it can't be all that bad! I would recommend this game to anyone from new to experienced players. Go! Conquer the world, Overlord!
Zawisza out.

I love puzzle games and I've played a huge number. I consider myself pretty good at them but by no means an egg-headed expert boffin. I'd read lots of reviews for ECT, all talking about extreme difficulty, so with a bead of nervous sweat trickling down my neck I gulped, reached out a trembling hand and installed...
Each level is a 3D structure which you can rotate to view from all angles like a CAD model. You control a flat square which flips over and over to move around the grid of the puzzle. The early part of the game is mostly Sokoban based puzzles where you push balls and cubes towards exit squares or off the edge of the grid but before long you enter new worlds where the rules fly off at a tangent in totally unexpected ways.
Most puzzle games are based on a single concept that increases in complexity but the basic idea doesn't change. What sets this apart from other games is that a particular concept will increase in complexity only for a few levels before changing to something completely new. It's like having several different puzzle games all rolled into one.
Each puzzle is so cleverly designed that I often just sat there marvelling and admiring it from all angles before I even got around to tackling it. Conversely, some of the most difficult ones are the smallest, using only a few blocks.
Let me try and describe one just to give you a taste. Imagine an actual Egyptian pyramid with secret tunnels inside it. Right in the centre is a cube with beams of light shining out from each face. From outside the pyramid you can use these beams to push the cube through the passages, out of the pyramid and off the edge. If you take a wrong turn the beam will be blocked and the cube will get stuck.
Main level overview is a minimalistic 3D interconnected network with 17 coloured worlds, each with its own name to describe the types of puzzles within. You rotate the 3D network to select the world you want to enter and as you do so the puzzles are laid out in the same way, showing miniature versions of the actual puzzles, so you can easily identify them without any need for a numbering system. New puzzles are white and completed ones turn black. The network is expanded as you complete puzzles until the world is marked as completed and can be identified as such on the main world overview. This unusual system feels efficient, natural to use and just looks great.
Level designs I would describe as elegant rather than beautiful. Good use of colours highlight the special features of each puzzle and worlds all have their own colour themes. The plain backgrounds have what looks like tiny blurred leaves being blown in a strong wind. At first I thought something had blown onto my monitor, then I wondered what the purpose of this was, then I finally realised that it's a constant reminder to your subconscious brain that the 3D puzzle is suspended in an open space rather than on a flat background and these 'insects' also swarm around the uncompleted levels on the main overview to further highlight them. This attention to detail is a typical example of the care that has gone into the game.
Settings menu has everything you need and the screen resolution updates instantly without restarting the game, which is a nice touch. One minor problem I found is that on Linux the graphics quality doesn't persist, it reverts to 'good' on every game restart so I have to manually change it to my preferred 'fantastic'. A side effect of this is that I found out how active the dev is, who responded to my forum post within hours.
The game only has keyboard controls (arrow keys, Z to undo, R to reset, Shift to rotate) but I mapped my Steam controller and found it works really well. You can also set up your Xbox controller using the Guide on the community page - I would recommend doing so.
This is the only Steam game I've ever seen where the Linux version is better than Windows. In Win the screen is fixed to 4:3 ratio but in Linux you get full 1920x1200 widescreen. Yay!
The background music is the usual ambient relaxing sounds, nothing to write home about. I switched it off and listened to PiL instead, I think it suited the excitement and rebellious craziness of the puzzles better.
There are a few easy levels to introduce new mechanics and a few medium ones but the vast majority will test you to the limit and beyond. You need a high degree of spatial awareness at all times. There are no timers, difficulty settings, move counters or any other extraneous distractions, just pure unadulterated puzzling.
I'd like to comment on some of the negative reviews of this game complaining that it's "too difficult". I've never heard anything so ridiculous. Decent puzzles are supposed to be hard, isn't that the whole point of them? "I'm too stupid for this game" shouldn't be a reason to give it a negative rating, it's not the game's fault is it?
The only minor criticism I have is that you need to overcome a crescendo of difficulty in order to unlock new worlds which then start off with easier puzzles to introduce new mechanics. This unlocking method is done in such a way that you always have 2-3 different world types available so you can switch between them to refresh your thought process if you get bogged down on one particular puzzle, but it also has a bottleneck effect in that you can be struggling for some time with a small number of very hard puzzles, then you drop over a cliff to begin your climb again with new puzzle types. With that said, I can't really offer any solution to this issue. I suppose it does give you a bit of a breather after a hard slog.
100+ levels and these are not 5-minute jobs. Many of these will take hours, not minutes. It will take a long time - IF EVER - to complete the game, and you will not become so accustomed to the gameplay that it becomes easy, as with so many other puzzlers, so there is plenty of replay value. All in all, compared to other games in this price range the value here is outstanding.
No cards. No achievements. As the dev has noted on his discussion forums, this is a deliberate move. My understanding is that he's vehemently proud of his work and doesn't want it to be sullied by such trinkets. In my opinion he has earned the right to adopt this attitude. Besides, the game is hard enough already. I think the extra pressure of chasing achievements would tip me over the edge and the men in white coats would have to come and take me away to the funny farm.
It does have Steam cloud support which is very useful as it's the sort of game you'll want to carry around with you and do a level or two now and then.
As I said, I consider myself a bit of an aficionado when it comes to puzzle games so I don't say this lightly: this obscure, 5 year old, low cost game with an odd name is, beyond a shadow of a doubt, the best one I've ever played (yes, better than Portal 1 and 2!) After this I'm looking forward to Stephen's Sausage Roll, the newish title from the same dev.
Do not treat this like any other cheap casual puzzler to fill time without too much challenge when you're bored. This is a puzzler's puzzle game. It's a military grade assault course for your brain.

Heads up, this is one of the most fun games I've ever played, it takes a simple machanic and cranks it up to rediculous levels of fun.  Beat the whole thing through in a week I was that hooked.
Unfortunately it's a bit short, my first playthrough clocked in at about 3½ hours.  It wasn't especially hard either (on normal) as I never managed to die.  I do however now have a new "God Hard" difficulty to try out, as well as hidden objects to hunt (won't be doing that though), AND new challenge missions.
The ending feels a bit rushed (two bosses in a row?  when you only really had 4 notable bosses out of 8 in all?!)  Heavily sets up for a sequel that I worry won't come.  Story is kind of background fog, feels like the outtakes for Metal Gear Rising Revengeance were shoved over here as we still have the good old "War will stimulate the economy!" vs "War is bad!" narrative.
I should also note there are 11 different weapons *each with their own melee attack type as well* and two types of grenades.  I focused on the Sniper Rifle/Assault Rifle/Shotgun in my first runthrough.might try LMG/Rocket Launcher/Disk Launcher next run-through.  The weapon leveling system is a bit annoying though.  Fire one round off and picking up another gun of the same time will refill your ammo instead of leveling it up as normal.  (there is a workaround for this, equip the fully loaded one, then upgrade it with the spent one.  But still, feels it lacks polish) and maybe I'm just 'bad' or something, but I never got any use out of the frag-grenades.  EMPs were where it was at.  Also rarely (if ever) used the cigarettes as no enemies would trace them.
All in all though, despite my complaints, it's an amazing game, given the price and time I spent with it, I asked myself "Was this more fun than going down to the local theater and watching a double-feature?"
And the answer was "Definiately, at least Vanquish will buy me dinner after playing with it instead of demanding I pay $20 for popcorn and soda."

ECT has nothing to do with its title. I'm not sure where that comes from. It's a very tricky 3D puzzle game.
The puzzles themselves revolve around trying to move certain blocks into certain places, but where you have to consider their interactions in a 3D environment. The puzzles require a lot of thought and planning, so it's a good puzzle game in that respect.  You can't just randomly make moves hoping you'll get the solution.
It can be a bit tricky at first to get your head around the way things work, but once you understand, progressing through the levels will give an immense dose of satisfaction. There may come times when you are left completely stuck, however.
I can only really recommend this game to people who like hard puzzles. You'll hate it otherwise.

The visuals and art style reflect an oriental beauty – and at times, I felt like I was playing an art project. Some of the object animations are a bit funky. For example, in my opinion – the fire is poorly animated. It’s set on a 4-frame rotation and all the fireballs on screen are synchronized together. This is a small nit-pick, but it’s pretty visually present.
In terms of difficulty, I found this game hit me in the sweet spot. By no means is it easy, but, I didn’t find myself getting stuck on any single area for too long. It provided just enough challenge to keep me interested, while not frustrating me by a lack of progression.
All in all, if you’re a platformer fan, or even just a fan of games like super meat boy, I’d defiantly give this a shot!

Old Review:
Edit: Many fanboys are thumb downing my review, they have obviously never played any of the great old 4x games and I wish them well on their journey into the 4x space genre. The developer is working hard to rectify many of the detriments below so I may be changing this into recommended. Want to add like many other of the no fanboy reviews that long range cannons make the game very easy to exploit. Hope to see this change as well like the dev was hinting in the last update.
This is the best Strategy Starship customizer and battle simulator to date, sadly though I can't recommend the game as a full 4x product because of it detriments.
Here is a summation of the Detriments:
Ground Combat:
Awkward out of place RPG grid turn based board game that is slow, boring and does not belong in a 4x game ever. The customization of the soldiers is tedious, the limited amount of soldiers is stupid as it makes planetary defence which was a very cool aspect of the original Star Drive impossible. No more massing an armada on nearby planets planning your military invasion in steps in a grand strategy. Now its just 12 ground troops=automatic Win. If you need some inspiration then check out a old glory game called Imperium Galactica or it's prequel Reunion by one Hungarian team, or even better use the MASTER OF ORION II system with two armies basically just slugging it out on a battlefield referencing Empire Strikes Back battle on Hoth. Not a RPG slow grind that take ages for a simple comat which is in truth a wierd minigame within the game.
Note: The Diplomacy has been greatly improved in the last update, so this criticism is no longer valid.
Diplomacy:
Went from exploitable in Stardrive the original into plain stupid in Stardrive 2. In the original stardrive you could get any treaty if you just sprinkled it with enough techs or capital, which made it very easy to get a cease fire even when the Opteris or Rayleh had just destroyed your armada and they stand ready to commit genocide. Now even throwing everything at a normal trade treaty the AI just says "wow you are giving me too much, this would tip the balance of power too much in our favor and we are so for equality and fairness we can't accept this"...
Planetary Bombardment:
So I guess the developers wanted to go back to Master of Orion II, which would be great. But don't half♥♥♥♥♥it! The Planetery bombardment in MOOII was great visually and strategically with planetary shields, planetary hangars, orbital gun batteries etc. But no, none of the Master of Orion goodness instead it's just a text that appears "Your planet was bombarded *YAWN*". This is just plain boring, especially visually.
Races and the lack of Factions:
Instead of learning from other great 4x Games such as Distant Worlds where a limited number of races equal an almost endless number of factions, we are now stuck with the same 8 opponents forever, same personality, same lack of diversity and same predictable diplomacy in every game. Please add some randomness to the factions with different personality traits equaling different approaches to expansion, military and diplomatic behavior.
Limitation on fleet size:
The new system based on command points or whatever is not a bad system, it's just a step in the wrong direction from the first game. There is no rational or logical explenation given for why i.e 7 cruisers wrecks the economy whereas 6 cruisers is just fine, just fine. Why even have this system? Why not let each component have it's maintainance cost with ability to dock your ship at planets for lower maintainance? That would make sense.
Poor Camera in battle control:
This really bugs me, for a space battle simulator with excellent graphics you can't tilt the camera 360 degrees or even 180 degrees. Why? Even in old games such as IG2 or Homeworld you have this option, granted these games also let you change altitude of your spaceships but compare it to another game with same gameplay as Stardrive 2 which is Empire at War, where is the awesome battle cam?
Unit control:
In general the unit control is simple and good enough with the ability to give orders like target enemy with broadside or the bow depending on what type or role or guns the ship has, and if it should keep moving in order to avoid missiles, torpedos or artillery shots or stay stationary if it's a artillery gun in space ship design. But there is no attack move function and there is no attack everything or target enemy fighters option for your own fighters which leaves you micromanaging the fighters which is tedious at best and very very frustrating at worst.
Lack of Multiplayer:
Still no multiplayer for a game that in 2015 when everyone have high speed internet connection connected to steam 24/7 and would be perfect for multiplayer.
With all this being said this is still a great game, but I can't recommend it as a full fledged 4x product which it promises to be in the desciption. The humour is great, the space battles are awesome, especially the ship customizer and the general campaign is an okay game the fact that the campaign is more static than the first Stardrive and have horrible ground combat which is such an important aspect of the game leads me to the conclusion that this is not a recommended game.  It does space battles very well even with the bad camera and unit control but it is a step in wrong direction and is not an improvement over the original.

Oh. My god. I'm not saying it's a difficult game. I'm just saying that Dark Souls is like Kirby's Epic Yarn in comparison to this game. That said - once you realise that you need to play it smart and stop thinking in terms of this being a 4X game - the game becomes really interesting.
The only way to win is to take an intimate interest in your empire's stats. Like some kind of super micro managing mother. Use all the tools you are given to carve out a bloody path for your empire to success, because otherwise someone else will carve a bloody and desperate path right through your face.
Pros:
The UI is buttload better than most of the other space strategy games out there. It's not great. It's just better than most, which I call a pro.
The management of the planets and ships makes sense. I've yet to go "Oh. I wish I could do that."
Customising the loadout of your ships both works great and is absolutely vital to victory. Because only you know what kind of ship you need for what kind of scenario. Need a pure tank to absorb the initial attack and then a bunch of fighters slam into the enemy dealing the real damage? You gotta make it happen yourself. And you can. And it's awesome.
Cons:
The tutorial. I sort of didn't want to put it as a con, because it's not bad compared to other space strategy games. But it's still narration. "Do this, this happens." That said - it's short, to the point and gives you the important stuff. As someone who never pays attention to tutorials, this one worked well enough to get me into it.
The difficulty is a bit odd. On the lowest difficulty I got my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me. This was until I started customising my ships, but even so. The lowest difficult is supposed to be a "try this button and see what it does." kind of affair, not "you want easy? You can't handle easy. Here, have some insanity."
Overall - if you want a challenge, and a good space empire game, I say grab this one.

Review for those who are hardcore 4x gamers who play for the challenge:
Stardrive 2 is a phenominal game that will test your endurance, wits, and resource management skills from TURN 1.  There are a LOT of things you need to know to play this game, but if you have ever played Masters of Orion 2, you're ready to tackle this game on Normal.
Pros:
1.  Ship design - While some games allow you a fair deal of customization, Stardrive 2 allows you nearly 98% customization of your fleet.  The only thing you can't customize is which ship 'hulls' you use, as that is determined by the race you play as.  For those of you out there who played Stardrive 1, there have even been some hulls that were removed, but the selection is more than adequate and what you can do with your ships is peerless.
2.  Difficulty - This game is HARD.  VERY VERY hard.  I have beat Masters of Orion 2 (the game this game is effectively emmulating) countless times on the hardest difficulty.  The first playthrough I attempted in Stardrive 2, I tapped out as I had pirates, 3 races, space crystals, and the Remanent (The Antarans, if you're a MOO2er) all coming after my homeworld of Earth.  If you enjoy a TRULY dauntless and unforgiving game - this is IT.  That's not to say this game isn't beatable, but you can seriously lose this game on turn 1 if you don't know what you're doing.
3.  Graphics - Beautiful starship battles framed in slow-mo bullet-time-esque speeds await you.  Expertly drawn and animated unique races bring you into the rich universe.
4.  Gameplay - Everything you do is it's own task in this game - managing an intergalactic empire takes the form of many screens feeding you the information you need to make the correct decisions, star ship battles are done in a real-time strategy where you can control your AI's engagement ranges and behaviors, ground combat is done on a hex grid.
This game is definitely a must buy for you.
Review for the Casual gamer:
This game has far too many things that aren't explained or are intuitive enough for the casual gamer.  If you're looking for a game where you just build up ships and watch them clash - this is not the game for you.  If you see the pretty starship battles and think that is the majority of the game, I'm just going to say that isn't the case.  The game will be ludacrisly difficult for you, and you will rapidly become frustrated with this title.
Unless you are serious about entering the 4x genre, this title is definitely not for you.

A tough call to NOT recommend this game. At least until some more patches resolving critical issues on a otherwise very fun and solid game.
So after reaching 16 hours into this game I've decided to give some solid feedback. In it's current state, I do not recommend the game. I throughouly enjoyed my 16 hours and I like SD2's particular style of a space 4X game.
The ship design system actually means something. When you research shields further along you can then make a new design for researched and unlocked hulls (corvette up to titan) that include that technology. You can also look to retrofit now obsolete ships you've already built at a cost of production and recalling the ships or Fleets back to a planet with the facilities built to do so. It's very practical, has costs to consider at different levels. It gives you full control over what you want to do for your Fleets and tactics for combat. A huge focus on this game.
Unfortunately, despite the vast amount of different weapon technologies you can research most aren't effective enough to warrant their research or use. Mass drivers and gauss cannons blow any other weapon type out of the water. I would just mass build cruisers with 6 mass drivers each and I'd destroy anything before they even got into weapons range. This is just the most popular and easy example to give of the overall balance issue in combat. With soooo many different technolgy choices it makes things very complicated. For another example the AI likes to build hundreds of missile frigates and you will literally have hundreds of missiles imbound on your half a dozen ships or so. No level of flak cannons, vulcan cannons or ECMs will save you. So much for the mass drivers. The combat is really circumstantial when it comes to imbalances and you will always have that in a technological race for superiority but it becomes a serious playability issue when the AI cheats and/or doesn't seem to follow a strategy at all when it just builds 50+ missile frigates.
The diplomacy system is nice. I like it. It isn't as intricate as another games but it works with SD2. Different racial factors, perks and handicaps will influence your ability to negotiate. Previous interactions of all sorts will build a reputation with each Empire. So, you can literally develop a trust between others over time -- even with aggressive traited species. However, despite the solid diplomacy system it's all for naught when you consider how psyopathic the AI is. The AIs are hyper aggressive. Perhaps that's due to the fact SD2 has a focus on combat and military conquest. SD2 is NOT for you if you're the kind of person that would rather spend most of their 4X play time on the empire management side or would rather win through research and diplomacy. Nope. SD2's focus is combat.
I'm forcing myself to uninstall this game until several more patches have come out improving the AI, combat/technology balances and maybe some more features to really solidify a unique, fun game that is SD2.
I also must mention the Developer(s) have been giving constant feedback in the forums and has been pumping out patches since the release based on player feedback. That's great. However, I feel this should've been a thing done during a Beta -- I didn't pay to play an incomplete, untested game. I look forward to seeing where this game will be in 3-6 months!
TLDR - A fun, solid Space 4X game with a focus on combat whose favorable traits are undone by horrible AI, serious combat imbalances, large battle lag and did I mention the horrible, cheating and psycopathic AI?

Let's start with the most important.
I suggest that game for the lovers of RPG games but it's also a good strategic game where you can command a mini-army of minions,little monsters ready to follow your orders.
In the game are present 4 types of minions.
Brown Minions - The best minions for fighting,they got the highest health,armor and damage,but beside that,nothing special.
Red Minions - Ranged Minions wich attacks by throwing fireballs to the enemies,they got extremly low health and armor,and alone they are kinda weak,they are very good in groups,by attacking enemies while the brown minions defend them,they are also fire-resistant and can absorb fire from certain paths to leave you proceed.
Green Minions - Close combat minions,low attack but extremly deadly in backstabs,they can also turn invisible and are poison resistant,allowing them to destroy noxious-plants. Great for ambushes and traps.
Blue Minions - They are literally the worse for combat,they got extremly low health,armor and attack.The good side is the fact that they can actually swim in the water without drowning,that may allow them to follow you trough rivers and swamps,they also got some magical powers,wich allow them to resurrect dead minions,and they are the only kind of character wich can actually hurt magical beings like ghosts or whisps.

I played Neighbours From Hell way back when it first came out on CD-ROM, over ten years ago. I later bought the sequel (also on disc) after it came out. It seems to me like if these games had been first released within the past few years, they would have been more widely known. These sort of games seem like prime "meme material" and the kind of thing that would thrive on the modern internet.
Neighbours From Hell might as well be called "Trolling: The Game". The entire premise of the game(s) revolves around playing pranks on your fat alcoholic neighbour as part of the reality show in which you star. The whole objective of the game is essentially to make his already-miserable life even worse. The angrier you make him, the more points you get. The pranks start out relatively mild (drawing on family photos, egg in the microwave, clogging the toilet, etc.) but as you progress through the game they become more complex and unique (shorting an outlet and electrocuting him, for example). The game can get boring at times, but usually there is a new and unique prank right around the corner to keep you entertained.
The first game confines you to the neighbour's house, starting with just the first and second floors. As you progress through the game, you will unlock more floors and rooms to access. The second game, however, is far more expansive and takes you to multiple places as you follow the neighbour on his vacation.
Overall, these games are great for some stupid fun. Replay value is unfortunately pretty minimal, as once you've discovered everything you can do, there is limited enjoyment in re-watching the effects of the same pranks over and over again. But the first time through each game is well entertaining, and figuring out the various pranks definitely incorporates a fair amount of puzzle-solving elements (especially in the second game). While these elements are not overly-expansive, they do force you to think a bit. I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a few hours of cheap and stupid fun.

Excellent software for practicing guitar and bass (pronounced /bās/), it's like having your very own practice coach in your computer!
It's more of a tool for honing your guitar skills than an actual game, though the original Rocksmith was more of a game than this version is. It needs to be coupled with other material to give you music theory, but it does try to cover some of this itself. If you are just interested in playing with little care towards learning to play outside of Rocksmith, then it's certainly completely capable of providing an experience like that without having to learn anything more than what Rocksmith 2014 can teach you.
But if you treat Rocksmith 2014 as a practice coach and find yourself a good theory coach, then you can fully expect at some point to be playing music outside of the game with relative ease. I've found a good place to start in getting that theory coaching is the Hal Leonard FastTrack Guitar (or Bass)  Method Starter Pack that includes a book, CD & DVD. It can be had for under $15 and covers the basics fairly succinctly.
But like in the old joke "How do you get to Carnegy Hall?", the answer is "practice!", and that's what Rocksmith 2014 really brings to the table. It coaches you on new techniques and ramps up the difficulty as you get better at playing, but it provides an interactive environment that stimulates you and challenges you WHILE you get in that all so important practice time. It deals with the single biggest barrier to becoming musically adept, namely the 'grind'. You may never get to Carnegy Hall, but with Rocksmith 2014 practicing is no longer a drudge!
If you intend to play songs outside of Rocksmith then you may want to invert the view of the strings on the screen, putting the low E on the bottom to match the way tab is written. Once you are used to this orientation, then downloading guitar songs that are notated in tab will afford you the ability to play them without having to mentally flip what you see on the paper because you avoided instilling bad habits while using Rocksmith by orienting the display to match the way tab is written from the start. Of course, if you never intend to play music outside of Rocksmith then it shouldn't matter...
Multiplayer is pretty fun, though very basic in how it's done in Rocksmith. You can play any combination of guitar and bass, including emulated bass in multiplayer. If you haven't given this a try, you should! Multiplayer uses two separate profiles under the same account, we played at my friend's house so I had to start a profile under his account to do this. While I could also use this profile in single player, it's under his account and not mine so I can only use it when he's the one logged in. There doesn't seem to be a way to use my main profile under my account while we are logged in on his system, so any progress I make under the profile I use on his account is lost except when I'm playing multiplayer.
Playing emulated bass is pretty fun by itself, but doesn't hold a candle to playing with a real 4-string bass! It's worth the money to go to the local pawn shop and buy a used Ibanez GSR100 or Dean Edge 9 bass for under $100. Like the BC Rich Bronze Series Warlock, most pawn shops have these around and usually for less than $100, though any Silvertone, Jay Turser, SX, Gregg Bennett, Squier, etc.  guitar or bass can be had at a pawn shop for less than $100 are all well worth the cost and enhances the Rocksmith experience.

Neighbors From Hell! A charming point and click game which, also happens to be one of my favorite game genres.
To start off this review lets take  a look at the concept of this game. You play as Woody, a content young fellow who is terrorized by his dispicable neighbor Mr. Rottweiler. You start to skulk around his house as the star of a T.V show. Your job is to set up traps in his house to terrorize Mr. Rottweiler and enact your revenge. One of the things that I love about this game is the creativity of the traps and the strategy that's behind them. A lot of the traps in this game are clever and took me a while to figure out. Timing also plays a huge role, especially if you want a percentage of over 90% (Like me). It really does keep you on your feet as you have to be aware of Mr. Rottweiler. Also, there are no lives in this game. If you're caught, you have to restart the whole level. While these aspects have drawn me towards loving the game, there are some factors I can't stand. Mainly the immature humor. Now, listen. If done correctly, immature humor can trigger a laugh here and there but, in this game it feels a tad bit forced and monotonous. 3D Sokoban with complex rules. There aren't very many types of blocks to get used to, but the rules governing each of them are surprisingly deep, and even at the beginning of the game, you really have to understand all of the subtle rules thoroughly in order to plan ahead and complete each level. For example, the "larva" blocks are pushed around when you run into them. But gravity applies to them selectively, and you absolutely must understand how gravity works in order to get them to fall into the right positions.
Because of the complex rules, you need to plan ahead - guessing rarely gets you to the correct solution. And as a result, completing a hard level, at least to me, gives a Dark Souls-like satisfaction. You *earn* your victories!
