For Honor is a fantastic game. The core mechanics are strong, the character and general art design is phenomenal, and there are a variety of different modes to play. Now sporting a roster of 18 characters, 50% more than launch, there's much more content, including tons of new customization options. So why is my review negative? Because this game has absolutely no future under the development team working on it. I don't think it's ever all that justified to directly call out the studio creating the game, but it's 100% the case with this one. Let me explain.
For Honor was released 9 months ago in February, and since then the game has gone through the wringer of the same problems over, and over, and over again. Rather than fix these main issues, the development team simply acknowledges them and never does anything about it. The best example of this is the balance of the game. To be completely blunt, this game is one of the most putrid piles of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I've ever seen from a balance perspective, but for all the wrong reasons. It isn't entirely a character balance issue (although that's a problem), it isn't a gear/stats balance issue (even though this is also pretty bad), it's a core mechanical issue. As it stands, defensive play will always win. No matter the character, no matter the mode. This is because parrying, a fairly simple and safe mechanic, rewards so much damage over offensive play.
Light attacks in For Honor are generally 500-600ms, or 30-36 frames. That's a pretty generous window, especially when compared to traditional fighting game frame data. Parrying a light attack gives you a heavy attack punish, most likely your most powerful tool. That means that a character like Valkyrie, who relies on light attacks, has to throw out incredibly risky 12 damage lights when the average mook can parry them and punish for three times the amount, so Valkyrie is forced to play defensively since all of her offensive options are absolute trash. This same exact scenario can be applied to nearly every character in the game, save the top tier characters.
And speaking of top tier characters, let's get into the one currently ruining the game. With every new season, two heroes get released. Season 2, Shadow and Might, introduced Shinobi and Centurion respectively. Season 3, Grudge and Glory, introduced Highlander and Gladiator. Season 4, Order and Havoc, introduced Aramusha and Shaman. With the exception of Aramusha, these characters have all been fundamentally BROKEN on release, while some, like Gladiator, CONTINUE to have their same exact problems. Saving Highlander who was fundamentally broken in a way that made him useless, each one of these characters has an issue that makes them a straight upgrade from any character in the base game.
While the development team claims they're working on "a big balance patch", they've been saying this for over six months now and have only done a couple public test servers to show off these changes, and from previous "big patches", it sounds like it won't amount to a lot. While a typical fighting game "new season" patch will change many things of almost every character, For Honor does not change one bit. The meta stays the same because they refuse to focus on the core mechanics of the game. If you're played Rainbow Six Siege, you probably know about Operation Health. For Honor NEEDS this more than anything. Whereas Operation Health in Siege was trying to work on netcode and lighting issues mainly, while improving user experience, For Honor needs a massive overhaul to have any sort of mainstream appeal.
While the team on Siege acknowledges a lot of issues with problems like peaker's advantage or 3-speed operators in general and work to counteract them, the development team of For Honor has no idea what they're doing. Time snap, a lag compensation mechanic, was removed from the game months ago and resulted in attacks being sped up by 100ms across the board, making things incredibly inconsistent and rewarding those with bad connections. There has been no effort to fix this since then, even though it's one of the biggest things the community complains about. If you're not convinced by now, just watch this video of a developer playing the game:
. Now watch a video of "high level" play just a month after the game came out:
. While the own dev team blindly throws out attacks and doesn't coordinate, but still manage to hit people, the players who have only had a month's experience with the full game already release that attacking is a bad idea and have developed great defense.
One of the other major gripes I have is the fact that the matchmaking is absolute garbage. DO NOT buy this game if you don't have friends that know what they're doing. You will have no idea what to do and you'll get stomped by people who have been playing since launch. It doesn't matter the mode, the same type of players exist in all of them. If you play Duel, you'll get matched up against people who only play Duel and just react to everything you try to throw at them. If you play Dominion, you'll get matched up against premades who have been grouping together since release and mindlessly roll through teams of randoms. It's complete chance if you get a good match or not, because a good portion of that chance relies on the player or players you're going up against to want to actually have some enjoyment and not abuse game mechanics.
The straw that broke the camel's back in regards to me finally uninstalling this game is the newest character, Shaman. Ubisoft has been incredibly open about the fact that they invite tournament players and "content influencers" to community workshops where they can test future updates months in advance. They give primary outside feedback on things like new characters or balance changes. And while everybody told the development team that Shaman was too good, they did absolutely nothing and released her in the broken state she has now. While other characters in the past like Centurion or Gladiator have been good because of a single move, Shaman is good because of every single thing in her kit. She blatantly steals concepts unique to other characters and in a better way.
Warden has an unblockable attack called the Shoulder Bash, which he can feint AND charge. While this move isn't super strong, it's a very viable part of his kit. Shaman has a straight upgrade of this move with her Pounce attack. It's faster, confirms more damage, and knocks you against walls without even having to charge. Also, if she inflicts a bleed on you, the pounce becomes a heatseeking missle that takes away half of your HP and heals her. This is similar to Shugoki's Demon's Embrace move, which does LESS damage and is much more punishable. It was also stealth nerfed in this patch. It's clear from♥♥♥♥♥♥like this that the team working on the game doesn't care. They're willing to give unique traits of characters away on a whim just so the character can be good so they sell season passes.
The issue that ties it all together though is the pace of the game. Not the actual game itself, but the speed at which Ubisoft works at. Patches come out at a snail's pace and do practically nothing to the game, and the new seasons don't even introduce much else other than the new characters. Certain heroes like Kensei or Conqueror have been bottom tier for over half a year, other heroes like Warlord or Peacekeeper have been top tier since launch with no serious efforts to nerf them, with the only one that actually happened to Warlord being overturned in less than a month. So even if For Honor has a chance of being good in the future, that future is far too long away for me to hold interest. I've spent far too much time in this game, been far too active in the community, and tried desperately to rationalize why they won't fix their game. Wait until it goes free to play in a few months.

A game that could be example of how to do good level design / challenges. The gamepad controls feel really lacking though (but not unbearable).
Shio is a platformer where your character jumps between lanterns to reach the unknown destination (which is gradually revealed to you by plot). If you have played “Ori and the Blind Forest” – remember the waterfall level? The one that did not have much checkpoints and was insanely hard to jump through? Yup, this game essentially evokes this same feeling, only gives different obstacles in much greater variety. You’ll often have to remember position/timing of every platform before you can succeed.
•	Great level design: each new mechanic is gradually introduced into the game. At first the jumping is trivial, but then it gives you much harder challenges that you have to complete using things that you’ve learned
•	Creative approach to obstacles: lots of variety that requires player to adjust his play style. Some notorious examples are lanterns that reveal obstacles for a small while, the ray that kills you if you stay in one place for too long, the platforms that you need to jump away from right before they disappear
•	The game is difficult, but because of that it is rewarding: you might want to smash your controller sometimes, but after 20 minutes of attempting the same challenge and completing it you’ll feel gratification. Completing the challenges is insanely rewarding
•	The graphics and style are captivating: the backgrounds are colorful and character animations are also well done.
•	Great ambient music that enhances level traversing experience
•	If you are playing with controller: left stick is used for movement (the usual way), but for some reason if you press up or down – your character keeps moving left or right (depending on your previous direction I think). It might not seem like a big deal, but you’re probably going to instinctively press “up-right” when you are jumping right for example. This is when it will get tricky, as the system somewhat gets confused if you’ve been going left before. Worse news if you are used to pressing “up” when jumping, since the character will simply divert to previous direction. I had to switch to d-pad, which was ok, because it’s easier to avoid up/down buttons.
•	The door-opening lanterns are often unresponsive: they just don’t activate the same way as the ones that help you jump. You’ll often miss them at first because they seem to require different timing when you jump towards them (which will mess up your mechanical memory / control expectations).
Apart from controls (which are troubling but not unbearable), the game offers a great jumping/platforming experience. It’s not for everyone, but if you enjoy high difficulty games which require perfect performance from the player– this one might just be for you.

Holy mother of base-building!
This game has got me completely hooked, and I'm warning you, if you enjoy the hectic nature of RTS games paired up with classic Worms-style combat, Forts is going to be your wet dream for the night.
We've got machine guns, snipers, mortars, swarm missiles, heavy-duty cannons, and freaking lazer beams! We've got resource management, clever construction mechanics, and nuclear reactors.
Do you want to pepper your enemies with gatling guns that set fire to everything they love and cherish? You can do that!
Do you want to rush the big toys and surprise your opponent by surgically removing his fort from the very cliffside he's anchored to with a giant lazer? You can do that!
Do you want to go head to head with a single opponent to determine which one is the better tactical mastermind? Or would you rather pair up with a bunch of madmen and join an all-out brawl in a 4-vs-4 firefight to the death? How about multiple players controlling the same fort? You man the guns, I'll get that economy up and running!
You can also choose to play with Commanders, which bring different bonuses and unique abilities to the table, allowing you to fine-tune your strategy and catch your opponents off guard. There are 9 commanders available, each one with a different passive and active ability.
There is a campaign that serves as a tutorial of sorts, which is filled with fun snippets and comments from the npcs. Where the game truly shines, though, is in multiplayer. It is fast-paced and fun as all hell. Even though the playerbase isn't the largest right now, I have never had the problem of not finding people to join. This afternoon I even had one of the developers join my lobby, and I got to chat with him on discord for a few hours. These people have done an outstanding job, and I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone and everyone! The sound design is amazing, every explosion feels impactful, and there are enough audio queues to let the attentive players know what's going on around the map without having to pan over and have a look. The artstyle is simple, elegant, and funny. It fits the tone of the game and really let's you know not to take a loss too hard or a win too seriously.
Forts is a game for people who like fun. And fun is definitely allowed!

The Darkness II is one of those random games that landed in my Steam library at some point that I totally forgot about. I vaguely knew what it was; a quad-wielding first person shooter with some kind of demon worms coming out of your shoulders. However, when I decided to try burning a few hours by giving this game a shot, I found that The Darkness II is a really surprisingly good game.
Now, it should be noted that it only took me about 5 hours to beat the single player campaign. There is a new game + option, but I don't see any reason to play the game a second time. There is also a serviceable coop campaign, but from the hour or so that I have played of that, it isn't as good as the main campaign.
What the game does with quad-wielding is over-the-top and fun. It took a little bit to get used to, but once I got into the flow of the game, I found that the various options available to me with weapons, projectiles I could throw, demon arm slashes, and other combos and abilities that I purchased throughout the game with currency that is earned through killing enemies provided plenty of fun as I plowed through admittedly narrow battlefields. The combat is fun and enjoyable, and for such a short game is enough of a reason to give The Darkness II a shot.
Where I was really surprised, though, was the quality story. The game has interesting characters, pretty much all of which are voice acted extremely well. The story itself was surprisingly engaging, with twists and turns that were very unexpected. The game does some interesting things with an "unreliable narrator" approach, and the relationship between your character and The Darkness is interesting.
In 2012 when this game released, I think it was probably too short on content to be worth a full asking price. However, in 2017, it is a game that can be purchased at a low price, and one that should certainly be played by fans of story-driven shooters.

I have played a lot of 4x games(Master of Orion, Master of Orion 2, Ascendency, Master of Magic, Fantasy Empires, The Civilization Games, Heroes of Might and Magic 1-5, Galactic Civilizations, Imperium Galactica II, and probably a bunch more that I don't remember right now), and the reviews for this one seem a bit more enthusiastic rather than accurate.
It borrows heavily from other games but to the point where it feels derivative of them rather than being a synthesis of them.  Moreover it is so blatant about it that it feels like it is flirting with the breaking the fourth wall not something I am a huge fan of.
The game has a lot of potential in the ship design and strategic aspect of space and ground combat and the level of depth that it allows you to manipulate your empire.
I will say that it was better than MOO III in general fun and striking a balance between allowing depth and getting carried away with it.
My big gripes about the game are as follows.
Technological advance doesn't yield significant upgrades until you get very very far along in the trees.  I almost always had better luck researching a few basic (tier one or two technologies), the pumping everything into producion ships and troops and conquering the galaxy without ever doing more than cursory reasearch.
The AI literally cheats on basic settings, I have tested rich homeworlds on small maps with optimized industrial output and the AI will invariably massively outcolonize me and outproduce me (in terms of fleet and fleet size) very quickly in the early game.  You can still win by being clever or cheesy in your builds, but the fact that it literally plays by a different set of rules on default settings really really bothers me.
The technologies are poorly balanced to create a stable empire.  The game forces you specialize each of your planets because of prohibitive maintanence costs (making one planet that has all upgrades and buildings your empire is capable of will put a big dent in your wallet).  Basically I find myself skipping almost all of my unlocked buildings on most colonies just because of what it costs to maintain them.  The way various technolgies interact and overlap with each other just makes a lot of them feel useless or redundant or only of use on a very small proportion of your colonies.
I do think the game has a whole lot of potential and with some patches or balance changes could be more fun.  Essentially my complaint it that it forces you to play in one of a few very specific ways if you want to avoid getting wiping out quickly on default difficulty.  It felt more like how well can I implement this strategy which I know will be the only viable one for this map/race selection rather than what type of empire would I like to build this time. It feels like the game has mechanics for amazing strategies and fun but makes it impossible for you to implement them before you have already taken control of the map.
Bottom Line I just didn't have fun playing it.

Outside of the bugs, some of which are game breaking (freezing on load screens) but mostly just annoying (shipyard bugs) you also need to deal with artificially inflated difficulty. If you invest in expanding you're just going to end up losing the expansions to random occurance since pirates and rebels will also randomly pop up with large fleets to take them over.
Over all it has potential but it's really more frustrating than it's worth to fight your way past the bugs just to have to try to game the inflated advantages that the AI gets.

This game is about how "life" achieves ballance. There are two modes, hard and very hard. In hard mode you are attempting to get equilibriam; no births, no deaths. In very hard you are attempting to get the number of "cells" down to a specific number.
The interface is straight forward. Right side has menu, run/pause, and speed. Left side has the buttons for adding cells. There is add one, and three patterns. The three patterns are designed to "crawl" across the play area by following the growth/death rules.
It can take a bit to understand how this all works together. It can also take a bit of time to actually achieve the goals for each level. But a bit of persiveriance and you will be able to work it out. After all this is a puzzle game.

SOMA, a greek word for ‘body’ used in the late 19th century.
Faithful to it's title, SOMA is a game that takes you ponder the significance of a body to a human being. You will question throughout the game, what makes 'You', 'You'.
Consider the following: What if we copied your mind and put it within another body. Is that simply a copy of you? Consider the ship of Theseus, where a ship gradually had it's old parts replaced until every plank of is new. You then take the old parts and put together a new ship. Which ship is the original? Such philosophical questions is what this game will make you question as you progress, you will also be made to make a series of moral choices of which will live with you (throughtout the game), though these choices do not influence the outcome of the story.
The world of SOMA has many objects of which you can interact. Most of them do nothing to the story and simply makes the world feel more real and allows you to learn more of what had occured in Pathos, the underwater station.
As SOMA is a horror game, there are mosnters in the world. Mechanical abominations that will try to kill you. All the enemies have a very distinct behaviour pattern in which you need to learn to be able to avoid them and sneak past them. Admittedly this is the part of the game I despise the most. Whilst it shows the player the extent to which the world has gone to hell and you are within this hell, seemingly out of place, in my opinion this hinders the narrative of the story, forcing the player go through with the tedious process of sneaking past enemies. Though death doesn't have much of a consequence as you'll just restart at an earlier point. The horror aspect of this game is bearable even for poeple who are not fans of this genre (personally I avoid horror games), but there are also mods that the player can use to remove the monsters etc, so you can focus solely on the narrative of the story.
In summary, SOMA is a horror game with a well written story containing ethical choices and philosophical questions that continue to resonate with the player for possibly days after completing the game. I recommend this to anybody looking for a story rich game and doens't mind a little horror aspect in the mix.
On a side note, youtuber Joseph Anderson created a critique of SOMA, which analysed the goods and bads of this game (Contains spoilers obviously), but I would recommend both poeple who have yet to play the game and people who've already completed the game to watch it as it really improves your understanding of this game. (It is what made me get this game to begin with).

That's going to be the general gist of my review of For Honor. I know it's going to bring cries that I'm just shilling for Ubisoft or that I'm some rabid fanboy on the defensive, clutching desperately at straws in an attempt to excuse otherwise inexcusable faults in For Honor... but really?
If you're interested in For Honor, I
you to take a few moments to read this before deciding to avoid the game yourself because of the negative reviews.
I don't think it really needs repeating, but I'll give a brief overview on the points that I think have been covered well in other reviews already left here on Steam:
you may ask. And you're right, it isn't. But there's some misinformation and bad publicity that has hit For Honor that's swaying people away from it. In reality, For Honor is
as terrible as many of the reviews would have you believe. And -that's- what I wanted to focus my review on. So let's start.
According to Betteridge's Law of Headlines,
Many reviews point to peer-to-peer connectivity as some sort of nail-in-the-coffin for For Honor, stating that it makes the game unplayable in its current state and many even suggesting that Ubisoft was either too lazy or too cheep to invest in dedicated servers.
These people have never worked in networking or touched video game netcode in their life.
If they had, they would understand that For Honor, being a fighting game,
peer-to-peer connectivity. Dedicated servers, which require time to update based on information each client (people playing) sends to them. In a game with so many reaction-based actions, a dedicated server would require netcode which would either make the game a total spamfest of swings with little point in parrying or blocking, or a war of the turtles where attacks that would actually land would be few and far between due to the need for compensation on the part of the netcode to account for the server update rate. Would it be more stable? Yes. Would it be more secure? Yes.
If dedicated servers are needed, then the game is going to need a ground-up overhaul of the gameplay, something that really does -not- need fixing as For Honor's fighting system is an incredible one.
Peer-to-Peer is a necessary evil of For Honor's mechanics and, thankfully, Ubisoft had the foresight to fix the long-loathed "host advantage" of peer-to-peer multiplayer by distributing out the load amongst all players in the session. There are still issues, and you may face problems with connectivity and latency,
At best, they'd happen slightly less often, and the game would run like a brick in a washing machine. So no, peer-to-peer is not an issue.
I'm sure we're all well acquainted with Ubisoft's usual greed when it comes to games. Especially their rampant use of season passes and half-baked DLC as attempts to milk every nickel and dime they can out of a game before they're outright forced to publish another game. One would think the addition of microtransactions into the game would be just a continuation of that, right? Well, no... and that's the part that kinda terrifies me because, for once,
I know, I know, it sounds hard to believe, but bear with me while I explain. In For Honor, Steel is the currency used to buy just about everything. Gear, outfits, emotes, executions... all bought and paid for with Steel. You can earn Steel by playing games, completing daily challenges, or doing the campaign and snagging the collectibles hidden throughout it. However, you also have the option to buy packs of Steel from Ubisoft.
shrieks the crowd that has never touched a Korean MMO before and wouldn't know what "pay-to-win" was if it actually ate their wallet. The only "power" one can really buy comes in one of two forms: a feat pack for heroes (which you'll unlock for each hero with just a few hours of gameplay, it really doesn't take that long), or gear (which only really matters in Dominion, Elimination, or Skirmish modes. If you're dueling or brawling, gear is just for show). Even the gear, however, doesn't give a definitve advantage, as each gear piece comes with a bonus to one stat (like revenge duration or attack damage) at the cost of another (like increasing cooldowns on your feats or increasing the stamina it costs to use each attack). This is, of course, all subject to balance problems, but that will come with time.
In what little time I've played (yes, 100 hours [at time of writing] is not that much compared to what a LOT in the community have put in), I've earned probably upwards of 50,000 steel. Just doing dailies and playing matches. this is more than enough to purchase whatever goodies in game you'd like.
Ubisoft was actually not greedy about this. Purchasing Steel is simply an option left to those who play a bit more casually and think that the time they'd spend earning that steel is worth more than the money they'd spend to get the same amount. It's a convenience, nothing more.

Speaking of attack, P2Ps are able to attack a player and do nothing else, because of the AI system, their top-tier ships with their overoveroverpowered weapons and armor too much for the next best tier of ships to leave a scratch.

This is a negative review, yes, but with caveats.
Pros:
- You can actually lose quite easily, making this qualify as a game more than most VN's on PC nowadays.
- Most of the character art is very gorgeous in all the places it can be seen.
- The setting is interesting and full of promise.
- English script is easy to read/follow.
- All the chibi Essi art is very cute and makes me want to get a little Essi doll.
Cons:
- The game refuses to provide any clues as to what training each attribute will do, or what the minimum stat required is to pass a scene, until after you get a bad ending. Getting a bad end is a matter of not having the information to prevent it, which is given after you get a bad end. This is probably by design since they want all players to get all the endings, but I still think there should be some subtle clues to prevent it.
- The game never tells you that you can hold down the down arrow key to skip text.
- Essi shows herself to be weak-willed, flighty, and unable to handle any kind of bad news, nor willing to listen to an explanation about it, causing all sorts of problems for others.
- The main story is about as rote as it gets.
- Guide is required to reach all the endings, even if that guide comes from the endings themselves.
- Lots of loading/reloading saves and skipping dialog to reach more than one ending.
- Password to the safe doesn't seem to be hinted at nor given during the route I played which asked for it.
- There doesn't seem to be a "best" ending. What I mean is you won't be able to finish a route and understand the very important plot threads that were started; important information is locked to different routes.
- At some points Essi does and thinks what she wants, regardless of what the player is thinking, cutting out possible interaction the player could have had and different paths to reach the different endings. Oh, here's a mysterious white-haired boy, I think I'll feel at ease and instantly trust him. Oh, here's a snarky information-gatherer type who notices I'm sexually attractive, I think I'll say and think bad things about him.
- There's a set way to reach the end of each path and if you veer more than slightly away from it you can't reach it. I guess that's fun for some people? Not for me.
- Arbitrary connection to phychic stats and story. Why would one more level in, for instance, clairvoyance, the ability to read the memories off of objects, suddenly make Essi not die, or change what the results were of an investigation Essi had no control over nor involvement in? If the skill itself was worked into the explanation for these story beats this wouldn't be a problem but it really pulls you out of the fiction.
----- Biggest cons of them all: The price and length for what is basically a VN flash game (think newgrounds), albeit a pretty and well-developed one. Nobody should pay full price for this, I don't think anyone should pay even a small fraction of the price; had it not been part of a bundle I wouldn't have had the chance to play through it.
Thank you for reading my review and have a good day.

I played Overlord back when it first came out, and remembered enjoying it quite a bit. I was excited to see it on sale here on Steam with its addon and sequel, so I picked them up dirt cheap.
The game is pretty fun, with the story being staged with you in the role of the villain out to subjugate any and all you come in contact with. You get the option to choose between good and evil, but it's more accurately evil and really, really evil. The game play is fun, though a bit frustrating when you can't quite find how to get to the next area. I realized how much I've come to rely on the objective markers in newer games (Skyrim and such), when I had to actually think about where to go. Once you get all four minion types, the game really starts to move, because more paths to success are open to you.
The primary negative to the game, I feel, is the minion control when using the keyboard and mouse. Controlling minions is often clunky, especially if you are standing just a bit too close to something you want them to interact with. It is exceedingly difficult to control the minions when they have to lure enemies to certain places or take timed explosives to certain points before they detonate (both happen a lot late in the game). It was really hard to move around while directing a minion, which made a couple of challenges lose their entertainment value quickly.
Besides those few specific examples, however, I found the game to quite fun all these years after my first playthrough. The graphics are dated, and the story is very shallow, but it was worth the couple of bucks I spent on it. Just remember you are playing an older game when you start!

The most important quality in a VN is story, in my opinion, and this game has a very interesting one. It blends mystery with romance although the latter is more subtle. I enjoyed playing through all of the good and bad paths of the possible guys, and I felt that there was a lot of emotion that could be evoked from reading the story. Not a lot of VNs can succeed in doing so. Of course, everyone who has played will have their own opinion on which path is their favorite but as for me, I liked Anon's the best although I liked all of them really. Also, the art in this game is beautiful and the music fit pretty well with the scenes, for the most part.
If there are any criticisms that I would give, they would be a couple. As I played through the paths, I noticed that there were minor grammar errors here and there although I haven't played the newest version yet where these errors have been corrected so my assessment may be outdated. Nevertheless, these errors didn't detract my enjoyment of the game. One other criticism I would give is that I would have liked for the image gallery to be unlocked on the main screen rather than having to enter a password to access it. Although I can understand why this feature was implemented, it would have been nice to have the gallery feature unlocked permanently on the main screen after playing through all or most of the paths.
Overall, I truly enjoyed X-Note and would highly recommend it to anyone who's a fan of VNs and a great story. :D

Anna is... weird. But a pretty fun kind of weird. A bit slow at parts, but enjoyable on the whole.
The key things to bring along when playing Anna are observation and inference. There are a lot of puzzles whose required solutions are fairly subtly hidden, so you'll need to keep an eye out for objects and/or connections between things you've seen or found most of the time. This is made that much more important by how Anna takes a lot of different occult material and remixes it into its own pocket mythos, making any supernatural points of reference the player may have a bit less useful here.
Speaking of remixes, if you've played the non-Extended edition before, there are some new and remixed puzzles from the original version, so keep that in mind. Solutions have changed slightly, or at least, it felt as such. To be fair, it'd been a while since I finished Anna originally, so it could just be failures on my memory's part.
Despite its occasional drifts into the obtuse, Anna - Extended Edition is a fun, sometimes frustrating romp through lingering dread and ambient menace. The encapsulated nature of the story presents something different from most rehashed horror trope-fests and is worth trying, if only to get your brainmeats flexing for a bit.
If you want a taste of the game, here's a -really- old clip of me exploring the starting area in the original version.

First, I love Rocksmith 2014. I am certain that in large part because of it, I will not be one of the 74 out of 75 that give up guitar. I'm advancing rapidly (in my opinion) in just three weeks. RS14 has excellent feedback mechanisms to point out what is right and wrong about my playing. Riff Repeater allows me to focus on the first part of a song, 100% difficulty and 1% speed, until I get it (I wish to learn it right the first time through, not add bits and pieces here and there).
While it has a scale game, I find it not very good for learning scales (maybe just me), so I augment my studies with the book "Fretboard Logic" in order to learn the logic of the fretboard. I recommend it. So I'd like to see much more done in the area of scale training. Yes, it can be picked up in Session Mode, but it will take a lot longer instead of having a focused scale training programming.
Session Mode: I like this part of the program perhaps the best, because it's like having a band that can tolerate me at my current low level of playing. Very impressive.
Riff Repeater: could use one improvement: the ability to control the transparency of the readout would be fantastic, as I often pause it to see what to do next with the finger placement, and sometimes the readout interferes with the process. I'm sure this will be fixed at some point. Once the Riff Repeater is set, it's function is somewhat unneeded until the next time one wishes to reset it. Right? Also, if paused, RR should be able to pick it up right from the point it was paused... it is very frustrating to have to wait for the music to pick up again, and learning could proceed much faster if this were implemented.
I realized I'll never make the 60 day challenge. Everyone there has an Epiphone, and I don't plan on purchasing one. I purchased a few junk guitars so as to learn the mechanical/electrical aspects of guitar without ruining a nice Epiphone. :)  So I'm posting my weekly progress and insights on YouTube: "A guitar path using Rocksmith 2014: Week 1 of 52". Yeah, I'm sure it will sell a lot of copies of RS14 without the Epiphone. :)
Overall, if you want to keep playing guitar without a major amount of frustration, get Rocksmith 2014. You'll be glad you did.

An enjoyable third person SHMUP, with a straight take on just about every American action movie trope from the 80s filling in for storyline.
Graphically the game is competent, it has some amazing set pieces and one or two awe inspiring cutscenes, but for the most part you'll be mowing down similar types of enemies in broadly similar terrain. Some dislike the soundtrack but I quite enjoy the 90s synth style. Sound design is competent, with the voice acting as gruff as it gets for the main characters. The entire visual and audio style is clearly designed to play to Red Alert 2 style sci-fi camp, although it falls a bit flat on the storyline and delivery.
As mentioned in other previews, the gameplay is where it shines through strongly - guns are highly upgradable and you'll get plenty of second chances in the form of bullet time when you're close to dying, while challenge scales up by varying available weaponry, providing some tactical choices (lots of chest high walls if that's your thing) and varying enemy force composition rather than type. The option to slow down time on a whim allows you to break through and destroy entire squads before they know you're there, at least once you learn not to overheat every time you try it. Combat is fast and fluid, and although you may find yourself dying (more so at over 30FPS as of release time), it never really feels unbeatable. Melee options are limited, and you'll usually be dodging back and going for a headshot instead of hitting a close range target. Combat feels enjoyable as well, which is good after you've died for the third time against a supposedly easy target.
Overall a solid 7/10 and worth a go. The softer aspects of the game are weak, but in technical terms it's polished and stable (if not cutting edge), and in gameplay terms it's a fun romp through action land with some replay value for added playtime.

Vanquish is an old PS3 game, one of the best PS3 games at that time (IMO). Its a 3rd person cover shooter with a cyborg suit and bunch of robotic ♥♥♥♥♥es to kill. I played this game quite a long time ago on my ps3, to be honest, I was having a hard time because playing this game with a controller is a big no for me, aiming is hard, and it could lead to frustration especially in Challenge Mode, the game has difficulty rating of 9.5 (10 is the highest in playstationtrophies website). Yeah, its a no joke if you want to get 100% it, I got my platinum in about 40-50 hours, I dont know how will I do with KBM though.
Story:
Its about a terrorist ♥♥♥♥♥ing about money or world domination, I am not sure which one, I didnt put much attention to the story. But one thing for sure, the final boss battle is my favourite.
Controls:
The controls can be remapped in the option, you can remap everything which can be remapped. No input delay, no double function in a same button. But I suggest to adjust the aiming and zooming sensitivity, if you leave it at default, when you zoom, its gonna get berserk like it moves so fast and makes it hard to aim.
Graphic:
We got quite an upgrade here in PC version. In the graphic option we got resolution, display mode, AA (Edge dan FXAA), filtering we got bilinera, trilinear and antisoptric, SSAO quality option (low, normal, high), HDR option, and LOD  ( I dont know what is this, please dont ask me about this). One more thing, there is a bug that tied to your fps, the high the fps, the more damage you received (aka the faster you die).
Gameplay:
Just like any other shooter, but what makes Vanquish different is the sliding, you can slide boost by kneeling, its cool, so dont worry. While slide boosting you can activate AR mode by aiming, its basically a slowmo mode, it also activated automatically when you are near death. For weapons, we got assault rifle, heavy and boosted machine gun, shotgun, AA pistol(my favourite), rocket launcher, LFE gun, disk launcher, lock on laser, EMP and HE grenade. Weapons can be upgrade when you're picking the same weapon (only when you already have full ammo on that weapon, if has less ammo, it will replenish the ammo instead of upgrading it), upgrading the weapon increase firepower and max magazines. Tips: stick with your assault rifle, its quite powerful when it has reached maximum level. Certain boss battles has QTE (a cool one). Enemies also has varieties, from grunts, jumping ♥♥♥♥♥es, huge robot with flamenwerfer, huge robot with rocker launcher on its back, balls, squares/rectangles, drill robots, etc.
Conclusion: This game worths full price, but its your money, your choice, but you have to get it. Its an amazing game. Support console port from SEGA, maybe someday we can get Persona on PC.

This game is by Stephen "Increpare" Lavelle, creator of PuzzleScript. That should be enough said but heres some information on the game.
English Country Tune is a sokoban puzzler similair to those you would see from PuzzleScript, but this one is in 3d. This game uses a large variety of creative elements. Watch which ones so you can unlock them first and have more choices if you get stuck. No achievements. I like acheivements I dont know why he doesnt want them but thats ok.

Ultimately, English Country Tune is a good quality experimental puzzler. Check out PuzzleScript if you havent. If you like that sort of thing this is basicly a must get.

One of the greatest games I have ever played. From start to finish I was being mind blown by the story, the atmosphere, the visuals, everything.
I'll break it down
The story: I can say much about the story that would do anyone who is blissfully unaware of it a big disservice. It's best experienced than discribed anyhow. What I will say is that it might be the most gripping story I have experienced in a game, ever. It'll make you think and feel more than most high budget drama movies, all while it scares the s*** out of you for good measure. My favorite part of the game was the story that unfolded before you.
The visuals: Very creepy, dark, detailed, and in someways, beautiful spectical to experience. Never experienced any significant frame rate drops which, for how good it looks, actually surprised me.
Sound: The music really stood out to me. Music can make or break a mood. In this game, it hits all the emotional points when your supposed to be experiencing them. The sound effects were great too. From the way sound changed when you were submerged in water and the shreeks of monsters, your ears will be fooled as much as your eyes.
Controls: Pretty simple controls very similar to amnesia and other puzzle games that didn't ever require me to look up controls or ponder on what it is I need to press. Basically felt natural to control the game instantly.
Overall: There really wasn't anything this game attempted that it didn't completely ace. If you ever were too buy a game at full price, this would have to be one of them. There is literally no reason not to own this game. So do yourself a favor, stop reading reviews and buy this game.

this is a puzzle game based around the game of life. im not going to go into what the game of life is exactly because the developer doesn't bother himself (just links to wikipedia from the game), so why should i? but, if you wanted an implementation of game of life to goof around with, buying this for a dollar is fine i guess.
as a "game" though there's not a whole lot to it. the strategy aspect is more trial and error, or "spam click until i win." the game allows you to place points on the grid mid-simulation, but doesnt let you go frame-by-frame in the simulation to accompany this, so if you were actually sitting down and doing the math and trying to figure this out, it seems like there's a need to rely on randomly getting the right frame by spamming pause. or maybe the point is to set it all up beforehand and hitting play and watching the game unfold is more the point, in which case why allow you to put down new life mid-game? the game doesn't really have its priorities straight and the fact that instead of explaining the intention the developer just opens the wikipedia page for conway's game of life in the steam browser is quite frankly insulting.
every menu button makes the same extremely high pitched squeak sound which is grating and started giving me a headache after 20 minutes so i stopped playing. on top of that, the whole game runs in 4:3 with black bars on the sides (who has a 4:3 monitor in this day and age), windowed mode didn't work, and the graphics are this muddy mix of a microscope and a CRT screen that just is unappealing and unnecessary. it actually has graphics styled more like a horror game which is ironic considering you'd probably go mad if you played this for longer than an hour. to top it off, even the achievements have this pretentious, "edgy" vibe to them and none of the six achievements tell you what you need to do, they're just "colors are the spice of life" or "a doctor gave a man six months to live, but he couldnt pay his bill so he gave him another six months." how hard is it to just have achievements that actually tell you what you need to do?
if you're a HUGE math nerd and love the game of life and actually have the time and ability to sit down and plan out every single point you put down on the grid, go for it, you'll probably have a lot of fun. or if you want something cool to put on your (4:3) monitor and just leave up, you can get some really cool patterns in the simulation mode that morph and change dynamically. i have nothing against the game of life itself, it's awesome, but THIS game is really really mediocre and will probably give you a headache, so this is a thumbs down from me.

The two 3D Worms titles (Worms 3D and Worms 4: Mayhem) packaged together in a collector's edition of sorts, which comes with many small improvements (mostly graphical). The 3D entries are typically held to be the weakest in the series, but I think they have been unjustly treated by most players. The game as a whole seems to lack the elegance (it does take quite a bit longer to learn the basics) of the 2D titles, and there's not much that can be done about that - It has less of that "pick up and play" quality of the other Worms games.
If you do get over the initial bump, you'll discover a rather charming turn based artillery game. All of the classic tactical considerations return in 3D (try having your bazooka shot be influenced by 3D wind!), and many new ones are introduced. Most of the old weapon and equipment dynamics remain, though to different degrees of fidelity and with an eye on enabling the new gameplay. Even terrain destruction is back, though the granularity of their weird "poxel" technology can often appear low (i.e. terrain and objects are composed of only a few large "chunks"), and the environmental damage always occurs in a distinctly "blocky" fashion.
It feels like a console port through and through (you cannot even select weapons with hotkeys - a staple of PC Worms), and the UI is rather garish. The game can be a bit unstable, and crashes when you minimize/maximize the game window are not unheard of.
Even if it didn't have a solid and enjoyable MP mode (if lacking in customization options), I would still recommend this game solely for its campaign. Worms 3D and Worms 4: Mayhem have by far the best SP missions of any Worms game, and they're all available in Ultimate Mayhem. A lot of variety and creativity on display, and it can be rather challenging to beat the par time on some of them. It really does seem like the SP was Team 17's main focus for the 3D games, which makes them even more unusual.

Bacteria or Conway's ''life'' or ''game of life'' is now in puzzle/game form and at your finger tips to experience! In the 1970 's british math guy Conway created this algorithom pattern game dealing with the simulation of cellular automation.  WHAT THE HECK DOES THAT MEAN ????!!!! Basically you have a blank screen and you use patterns and diffrent cell combinations to create and destroy life/cells. There is rules and help/simulations with a link to Wikipedia... that I actually think you need to AT LEAST glance over so you have an idea what is going on. There is basically the rule of life or rule of 3. IF there is more than 3, then your cells overpopulated and die. IF there is less than 3, than your cells cant populate and you die. SO, click on the screen and see what happens and click click and watch. ALOT. One click you are winning and close to the blank screen or the life/dead cells you are trying to get rid of are almost done, then BOOM life exploads forth as you tighten your grip on your mouse and start all over. The music is kinda hypnotic and soothing, but the game itself even though called relaxing.. isnt really. Have fun and actually learn a real science math concept. Life is hard. and Life finds a way and yeah your mind goes to all the awesome quotes about life while you do reliaze, its not as easy as it seems.

雖然這個遊戲仍在開發階段，但是復古可愛的畫風，
精緻但不複雜的系統，仍是非常推薦在現階段就入手支持作者。
以下簡單描述其遊戲內容，如一般角色扮演一定會有的
等級系統、技能以及天賦系統：
一樣有分近戰(單手或雙手武器)以及魔法，
但是並不局限於一定要走純戰士或是法師，
假如技能或天賦點錯了也能重新分配點數。
有招喚獸能幫忙攻擊以及捕捉寵物來提升角色的能力
有趣的點是不論走近戰還是魔法，
每個人都一定會有弓箭跟盾牌可以使用。
解謎：
不論是劇情或是地圖上都會有一些需要小小解謎的地方，
有些地方稍微有點難度，但同時也增加了耐玩度。
有一些地方有所謂的小彩蛋，可以讓玩家自己去尋找。
房屋系統：
儘管現在房價很高，但仍然可以在遊戲中擁有一棟屬於自己的歸屬，
隨著劇情推進，會獲得越來越多種不同的家具可供裝潢自己的房子，
有些可透過製作系統來得到，有些可用金幣跟NPC購買，
有些家具則是屬於在劇情推進時才有機會拿到的，
玩家在探索時可得仔細點才能得到這些有趣的家具。
釣魚系統：
打怪打膩了？何不到湖邊釣釣魚呢！？
透過簡單的釣魚方式即可收集每張地圖所擁有的專屬魚種，
而掉的的魚則能跟商人換取金幣或是用來餵食以及提升自己寵物的能力。
紙娃娃系統：
覺得屬性比較好的裝備不和自己的胃口嗎？
那就用自己喜歡的裝備來打點自己的行頭吧！
遊戲中有許多好看的裝備，隨時都能讓你的角色變的更加可愛，
城鎮也有髮型師能變換其他的髮型及髮色。
以下為筆者心得
筆者有實際去作者的開發日誌看過，作者的更新頻率是滿穩定的，
每周都會有遊戲開發的進度回顧，通常二到四周會有一次的版本更新。
劇情的部分筆者預估還有20~30%以上仍未完成，但就目前的劇情而言都是有品質。
角色上的互動也都滿有趣的，也能在某些NPC身上看到小小的致敬，
相信老玩家們應該更能體會其箇中滋味。

Bacteria is a casual puzzle game that has a retro/nostalgia feeling to it. The game itself consists of a few game modes, and 2 types of difficulty Hard mode and Harder mode. There is also another game mode called Simulation mode which is basically a sandbox mode to mess about with and see how things works.
When I first entered this game and started playing Hard mode it was rather confusing at what my actual object was, and what I actually had to do. There is no tutorial on how to play this game, only a link to a wiki page which explains how the game works. I am not one that really likes to read a lot of text before playing the game, so me being me I just went straight into the game with no knowledge of what I had to do or whatnot. So upon entering the first level I really wasn't sure what I had to do. I assumed that I had to make the unstable cells back to normal cells in order to progress. So upon hitting the unstable cells it split and it just caused chaos, and it caused more unstable cells to multiply and such. I guess the point I am trying to make with this first time experience with this game is that people don't really like to read a wiki on how to play as game. Possibly add a small tutorial to explain the basics on how the game works, this should be shorter than the wiki. Then if people are still confused redirect them to the wiki. From what I gathered from my first playing experience and reading the wiki the gameplay works as follows. It consists of a set of unstable cells that you need to be able to get them back to a stable state, or if you can't do that get them to a fixed repeating pattern. You have a specified area where you can plant your cells to direct them to the unstable cell and hopefully make them all stable again. Although, I really appreciate the simulation mode, it help me understand the game a little more and how each cell works. The game has some really relaxing music to complement the game itself in it's retro styled form.

This is, in essence, a text-based adventure game that is not necessarily limited to the text. There are also quite a few point-and-click elements to it, with a sprinkle of walking simulator.
But despite these simple mechanics, Stories Untold is one of the most immersive games that you will find in this genre. It uses the tools given
well, and even the limiting elements of a text-based adventure serve to spicen up the story. The mystery of every episode acculmulate and climax in the final epsode, but the episodes are well-strucutred enough to serve as standalone stories.
The only qualms I have about this game is the text-based system. Although Stories Untold is masterful at using this method, if one is unfamiliar to this kind of game, it takes some time to get used to the system. Even then, I sometimes struggled with trying to phrase things so that the game would "understand." The ambiance of the ending was a bit ruined for me as I struggled for five minutes phrasing my actions.
Still, Stories Untold provides an experience that no other game gives these days. The sheer novelty of its storytelling is captivating. To see if one would enjoy this game, I'd suggest downloading the first episode (I believe its free) and trying it out. If you enjoy it, then you'll enjoy the rest of the game.

So this girl comes up to you and grabs your phone. She says it's causing natural disasters in her house, on the other side of the state. You chase her through the town, across the park, and back to her house. When you get there you demand that she return your phone! She looks at you and throws it on the ground, cracking the screen.
And for some reason, you're so happy that you pick it up, SING A SONG, and walk home!
I appreciate that the game is based off of Alaskan tribal stories, but WTF? The way that this game was put together was very fractured and unsatisfying. It's obvious that they fused multiple tales together, and it really detracts from the cultural experience when you're trying to follow a cohesive storyline. Please give me my regular fox back.
And then there's the actual game. It starts off simple and relaxed, giving you some new mechanics here and there. The platforming is very forgiving, allowing you to climb up ledges that you might have fallen short from. There's co-op with AI that does its best to follow you, automating movement in non-essential areas while requiring you to switch when making a progressive jump or action.
There are "boss" battles, which mostly felt shoehorned in and sometimes unintuitive. One boss requires you to break branches, which killed me at first and then decidedly fell through my character in subsequent tries.
Swimming areas were beautiful, and seemed to work surprisingly well in static levels. However, in later levels where you're "swimming" while the stage is moving, it was very common to either get trapped thanks to the moving camera or in SOLID objects that were moving level pieces. Very buggy collision.
The only thing I really appreciated were the visuals. Very simple characters with beautifully crafted backdrops, shown in a variety of palettes that really make this game more of an artpiece than anything. I really wish they focused more on presenting the levels they created rather than trying to be mechanically innovative and share all the stories ever told by the Alaskan tribes. Overall, I could have skipped this one for sure.

If you heard anything about the developers of this game, it might be one of the games that is featured as the first story, The House Abandon. A horror text adventure that took 2016 by storm. A year later, we have an official Steam release with three other stories wrapped in mystery. They may have already made one great game, but can they keep it up for three more?
The House Abandon plays like any other text adventure. Though with a huge difference that might not look that substantial in the beginning. Instead of the screen equating your screen, you are instead seated like you are probably right now, at a desk. The computer actually containing the text adventure off to the left as your lamp shines on your keyboard and the lone photo frame directly in front of you. As you continue on through the seemingly innocent adventure of going back to your home that you moved away from, it quickly turns dark. The house you just went through is a twisted version of itself. And suddenly the text adventure isn’t just a game on the old computer. This might not even be located in an ordinary house as small changes continue to happen right in front of you as the text adventure continues.
The first story is a text adventure, so the other three must be as well right? Nope! The second story, The Lab Conduct, strays away and puts you in the shoes of someone performing experiments on an artifact. With a mysterious voice guiding you to what you need to continue as instructions come into a computer to the left of you. The computer also holding information to help you know which equipment is where and the information about specific equipment. Not having much choice to deviate from the guy that is the owner of the voice as you try to set the needed equipment correctly and turn off unnecessary equipment. The tension ramping up with each experiment.
I might have lied a little. After conducting multiple experiments, you do get back into a text adventure for a short time. Though, do keep in mind that before this, you are made to look into a bright, flashing light to advance multiple times. So if you are susceptible to this, you really should turn away from the game. You do get more story beats that are not entirely clear till you know the full extent of the story.
The next story is The Station Process. Once again, straying away from the previous story's gameplay to show different scenery and focusing more on codes. Stuck in a station placed in a frozen tundra with the only people that are conversing with you are not in the same building anymore. Everyone is isolated in their own station far away enough that going out is risking everything as everyone tries to stay in contact with each other through a radio. Trying to stay alive to not let the other be alone. Though, we can't all have what we want. You have an important role, you receive transmissions and in turn, you send them back. First required to get a passcode, which is attainable by going to the required radio frequency before continuing to send it back.
There is one small hurdle that may hinder you, the microfilm. The microfilm contains the required codes needed to input based on the code word. Little does the game let you to believe, you can zoom into, rotate, and focus so the microfilm can become easier to read. If the code word is “Chevron” after searching for the page titled with it, the lines of code you need to enter is placed here. There might also be values set that needs to be replaced with the corresponding place within the passcode, as it might ask for the second number to replace 'a'. The difficulty ramps up at a good rate, passcodes soon needing a key to decipher and more values coming in. The situation ramping up as we can finally walk away and explore what lies outside. And as you can tell, this chapter holds hints for the overall story, and with the other chapters under your belt, you can easily make some theories on what the next chapter will reveal.
Lastly, the fourth and last story is The Last Session. Where everything comes together and all of the hints from the previous stories are weaved together. The truth finally comes out. Everything coming to a full circle as the game comes to a close. The ending will have a chance of disappointing you. With three stories building it up, it is only normal to think that something big is going to be revealed. And with the overall moral being really overplayed so much that there is a guarantee people will whine in frustration in a room. Though, instead, it does show a different type of horror than it leads you to believe. The type we all fear deep down. I can’t spoil the ending for you, but it can definitely give you mixed feelings on it with how cliché it is.
This would be far from being terrifying if the sound design was horrible. Luckily, this is not the case as the sound design is great. The clank of the keyboard, the whirr of a machine, and a radio tuning in brings up the tension in their respective stories. Bringing life to the world that is subtle, but combined with the story brings fear. Fear of what's to come or the actions you are forced to complete. On this note, the voice work is great as well. Perfectly fitting into the grim world we are given. These voices easy to latch onto, but are they more than we seem? Can we trust them?
Stories Untold holds a mix of styles that mess with how the player needs to play. Going from a simple text adventure, to operating machinery, and lastly to entering codes and deciphering passcodes. Giving just enough information that you can get through all parts of the game with few hurdles while also giving out hints that only make sense when you go back and look. Even with the ending possibly being the one thing that can put a sour taste to the rest, everything before is great. Not relying on jumpscares but on the atmosphere as the goosebumps just keeps on coming.

It's a game; it's a book; it's an interactive story! Never Alone is a very interesting title, venturing about as close as I am comfortable to a 'visual novel'. The games creators did theri research, traveling to Alaska to speak with members of the Inupiat inuit tribe, gleaning knowledge of their traditions, their lifestyles, and their culture as a whole. They then used this information both explicitly and implicity through the (simple) puzzle platformer game they lovingly crafted and through the very well produced video documentary elements available for review after stumbling upon a particular theme in the game that relates to a particular snapshot of the documentary. This game was by no means challenging, and in a few points a little buggy (I would find myself trapped at the top of a ladder or in some other crevice), but for the three hours I put in to it beating the game and gaining a large amount of knowledge and a new respect for the inuit people, I would say Never Alone is definitely worth taking for a spin.
P.S. - Seems like a great learning game for kids too, I'm going to let my niece play through very soon.

UPDATE 5/27/16: There have been some changes/fixes/enhancements, but I wanted to let the original review stand, so I'll mention the new stuff here.
The Housing, Shops, Jobs, and Safety sliders now all work in the same manner and it's much more intuitive (no more confusion over when to build shops!) This was the one confusing point I had with the interface originally, but now that's been fixed.  In addition, the mousewheel zooming is more intuitive (up to zoom in, down to zoom out), and there is now a proper exit game button.
The dev has been kind and collaborative with players, and has asked for and considered (and in some cases, then implemented) player suggestions. Compared to most games on Steam, this is a game with a smaller scope, and a smaller price point, so having this kind of dev response to game issues is really refreshing.
PREVIOUS REVEW:
This game is cute and relaxing. I have to admit the negative reviews put me off, but I kept being drawn in by the screenshots and the videos. So, I decided to buy it and make my own decision. If it simply didn't work, I could get a refund.
I'm not going to refund. I've had a blast playing this game. As soon as I figured out how to manage the "Build Shops" meter, it's been very entertaining to place my colorful little isometric buildings and watch my city grow.
Basically, build housing. Build industry to gather materials. Build offices or factories for jobs. Then, when people start moving in (build a LOT of housing... that's the only way the population will start to really grow), your Build Shops meter will move. Build ONE shop, and give it about 15 minutes to let it get supplied with materials and then it'll start generating cash for you. Then, just build more when the meter moves to the right.
Beautify your city with parks and playgrounds, and make sure things are safe by placing your fire station and police station.
The larger your population gets, the more shops and different kinds of housing open up.
I enjoyed SimCity back in the day, but it was a little micromanagey for me what with the power grid and water pumps and zoning, etc. This little game is truly pick up and play, and you don't have to invest a lot of time into every session... but I can't help that I have. :)
I'm not going to say everyone else's negative reviews are wrong, but I sincerely don't understand what they were expecting... except for that one reviewer who was somehow expecting power and sewage and curved roads... all for under $4. Wut.
I love the game for what it is, but then... I have reasonable expectations.
UPDATE: Just hit 250 population and I got my first disaster! I about jumped out of my skin, because up until now, things have been calm and quiet and peaceful. I started hearing traffic noise, which was cool... and then *crash*! Looked like a traffic accident with the yellow triangle. Luckily, I had not one, but TWO hospitals at this point, and a little icon appeared on the hospital so I figured I'd try to click it. Well, the accident was cleared up with some pretty cool sound effects and I got some gold coins out of it. :)
UPDATE 2: Just hit 400+ population and my cops just busted a car thief! :D I've also had one apartment fire and one office fire. I built schools and schoolbuses are now driving around town with the cop cars and the fire trucks and the ambulances. I can finally build penthouses!

Summary: This game is quite the bore, and quite horribly designed all around.
Tutorial
---
The tutorial left much to be desired. It doesn't show you anything, it just gives you a description of what to click, and it's only about 15 messages or so long. The content itself doesn't actually describe what you need to do in order to get started in the game - it just gives you some basic information and tells you some things you need to click on.
After going through the tutorial, I was incredibly confused on what I even needed to do next. The messages lacked detail and I missed some very basic things (like auto-completing the building or *moving* the building to a different location on the screen). Then I sat there and wondered how I actually got people to come live there, as several of my homes had completed already but it still said I had no Free Homes. Eventually it just updated on its own, I have no real idea what caused it to do that though.
Controls
---
Terrible. You can only move around the map by moving your mouse to the edges of the screen, at least from what I can tell. I wouldn't be able to confirm because there is no actual Options menu which lists out controls, so I'm assuming you can only use your mouse for anything. I would have expected the minimalistic idea of using the arrow keys to move around easier, because using the mouse at the edge can be quite glitchy, and is pretty terrible in this game.
The clicking action is also horribly bound. Clicking on something will click on *every single thing* under your cursor. This gets especially annoying when there are any messages on the screen, or if you're trying to click on something that is below one of the buttons on the right - it will activate both things you clicked on. The mapping for the buttons seems to be off too, as there have been many times where I've clicked something on the map that was just near one of the buttons on the right, but it still activated the button.
Even worse, if you want to start over fresh to see if you can manage things better this time around - too bad, you can't. There is no restart feature. Once you've started, you keep that forever. As far as I can tell, all of the information for your city is stored on their servers, not on your computer, so you can't do squat.
Countdowns
---
The entire game is based on countdown timers for how long it will take for a building to complete or how long it will take for a new resource to appear. It's really quite boring, and all you can do is just sit there and wait. You can instantly complete your building if you have coins to do that, but if you run out you're boned.
Resources
---
The resource system is possibly the most annoying part of this game. They make it incredibly easy to get all the coins you could possibly need by building shops, but they limit you to only 5 of each type of resource miner, and some of them barely pump out squat. Nowhere near enough to keep up a steady building pace. I had all five brick builders constructed and I was still having to sit around and wait for more because even with all five, you still only get enough bricks each round to construct one, maybe two more buildings.
Further, I'm pretty sure the stone mining building is completely glitched. It keeps adding a bunch of squares where it looks like it's generating more stone, but near the end doesn't complete the task and just stops doing anything. I had to keep moving my brick buildings around to new spots of stone because the stone mining wasn't actually producing more stone for those buildings. Maybe I was doing something wrong. Maybe that was something that needed included in that crappy tutorial I mentioned.
Advertised Game Features
---
The description of this game is quite hilarious if you've actually been into the game to see how it works. Mainly, the list of "features" that this game has.
- High quality building graphics -- I wouldn't call any of them high quality. They look ok, but they're extremely basic and nothing to be excited about. There's also a lot of anti-aliasing issues that make some spots look pretty bad.
- More than 80 different types of buildings -- Most of which are the same. There are several different types of Apartments that all look similar, several Condos that all look similar, and several Row Houses that all look similar. You get the idea. There's a lot of different types of the *same thing* that are slightly modified to look different.
- Changing vehicle traffic on the roads, animated cars and buses -- There's traffic, that drives around pretty randomly and doesn't really add anything to the game whatsoever. Might as well not even be there.
- A unique road construction system -- Nothing unique about it. It's an incredibly standard "put a piece of road on the squares and they connect together" road system with no curves and no creativity to it.
- Fun game play in a unique tycoon game -- Fun is quite the overstatement. As is unique.
- City builder game for all ages -- Maybe elementary school students.
- Be a city building tycoon -- Were they just trying to make their description longer by adding bullet points?
- Artificial intelligence based on real simulation of in and out moving tenants -- None witnessed. It's just numbers that represent your population and then a couple of bars that represent the number of free homes and jobs. I'm not sure they know what AI means.
- Unexpected catastrophe simulations -- Never tried this because, well, why would you? It takes freaking forever to build anything up in this game, why would I want to destroy it all in a few moments?
- Travis the city adviser will give you hints -- He's about as useful as the Microsoft paper clip.
- Continuous updates and bug fixes -- Oh boy, I sure hope so.
---
---
They should have spent quite a bit more time on this game making sure it was actually ready and would be fun. Spelling mistakes in your text is a HUGE no-no. I mean, come on, really? That's so damn easy to catch. Hopefully this game gets a *lot* of improvements to make it more fun and live up to its description. But right now, it's not worth the $3 I paid for it.

X-Note is not a bad VN by any means, especially compared to many you can find on Steam, but I cannot honestly recommend it either. I wish there was an option to give a neutral review rather than just "recommended/not recommended".
The visuals and music are decent; not exceptional, but they work. However, there seems to be no way to skip dialogue you have already read, which is frustrating when doing multiple playthroughs or simply trying again after getting a bad end.
The story, while it has some surprises and good flow, especially when the pieces of the puzzle finally start to fall together, is sadly not very original. The writing is not bad, but nothing to write home about.
Now, for the gameplay.
The game is a mix of a classic mystery VN with choices influencing the story's direction and a "raising sim" which gives you the choice between three different statistics to raise, not unlike an RPG. I had never played such a game before, and was disappointed that X-Note does not make those elements work very well. Rather than influencing the path the story takes, the skills mechanic only seems to serve as milestones you absolutely have to reach before a certain point in the story, or else it's game over.
At least the game gives you pointers so that you can avoid doing the same mistakes over and over again without knowing what was wrong.
There are also a couple minigames thrown inside, but they aren't very interesting, and some tend to be frustrating.
But X-Note's biggest flaw lies in its pricetag; 20 dollars/euros for such a short VN is a hefty one, and the main reason I cannot in good faith recommend this game.
At the time of writing this, there seems to be a bug with its pricing; no pricetag is shown, and people have reported simply not being able to buy the game.

Overlord is an action/strategy hybrid that has you ordering masses of weak minions about as an equally weak evil (or just evilish, depending on how you respond to the binary "choice" system) Overlord (heh, eh). Without your minions you suck, and small masses or individual minions suck worse. However, together you and the little red/green/brown/blue imps can form an unbeatable team of chaos...so long as you can master the controls and don't have too many technical issues.
The worst thing about this game are the controls. Overlord is an experience that demands a level of precision and skill that my controller and I are incapable of. Initially pleasant and open levels give way to tight-corners and enemy puzzles that require quick and accurate adaptation on the fly, yet the camera is incapable of keeping up. On the controller, the stick you would normally use for controlling the camera is used to guide your brain-challenged minions around the environment. Using the mouse allows for easier camera control, but I couldn't "send" my minions at anything when I tried it. The camera follows either you or a minion you're controlling, and if you're trying to move and control minions at the same time in tight spaces it has a tendency to freak out or try abrupt and nauseating angles. The camera has two settings, behind the back and top-down, but neither is useful.
A terrible camera isn't a killer, but poor minion controls are. Later levels have you coordinating your four minion types by role: Greens back stab, Blues heal, Reds throw fireballs, and Browns soak up damage. You can pin and recall groups of minions to/from spots, but while the pin function is individual to your selected units the recall function will recall ALL units, which can easily and quickly ruin any plans you might have. The challenge of the game exacerbates this, as all minions but the Browns die extremely easily. The Blues are almost useless if not for their healing, and many enemies in later levels are entirely immune to the Reds. Additionally, the only way you may replenish your army is by killing certain enemies, while every new encounter seems designed to go through a sizable number of minions to just get it done (figuring everything out is usually the easy part). So, by the second to last boss fight I managed to run entirely out of the only minion who could do reliable damage to ANYTHING in the level, and the only way to earn my minions back would be through extensive, boring, stupid, ugly grinding.
Finally, the game lags on my computer. Mostly it seems related to if/when I run ANYTHING in the background, but other times it slows down for no apparent reason. It's extremely odd, and makes no sense given the number of things I can otherwise run just fine.
I want to recommend Overlord for the opportunity to play the leader of a mob of idiots, but the controls just ruin everything.

A mediocre 2-5 hour mystery VN (high variation in time based on pursuing multiple endings).
Where this VN does best is that it manages to work in some neat little surprises in how all of the dots connect together in such a short time frame. I definitely enjoyed the manner in which the story was exposed to the reader.
I felt the artwork was a lot less lazy in X-Note than what I've seen from many other VNs of the same caliber. Kudos to the artist offering up far more assets than would be considered the minimum.
Most of the other assets fit well into the passable category. For such a small VN, I still ended up finding the music mildly redundant. The engine could be better with offering better skip options through lengthy dialogs (pretty necessary for multi-path VNs, really) and options for scrolling up through previous dialog in case you missed something.
The mini-games are fairly petty, but I can't say that they detracted from my experience much.
The thing I hated the most about X-Note, are how the fail-states are constructed. There are 3 different character skills that you can upgrade, and those need to be at certain levels at certain milestones. There is very rarely any logic associated with why you need those skills to be at those milestones. Oh, you decided to shoot me in the gut because my clairvoyance skill wasn't high enough; thanks, game. The positive value of this unfairness is that you get to actually properly experience all the endings - whenever you get a bad ending, the game gives you tips on what you need to do to get the good ending.
The ultimate reason for this review being negative is the base price-tag of $20. Nobody in their right mind should pay more than $10 for this, and my personal cutoff point would be around $5.

I cannot emphasis enough just how good Stardrive 2 is. Apart from the similarities to MOOII it's ship design system is easily the best of any game I've seen so far yet. Ground combat is dealt with in a style similar to XCOM, sometimes I like it, other times I don't. Its good for the away team themed 'events' but lacks realism for planetary invasion.
The strategic layer and ground combat are turn based with ship combat being realtime. Ship combat needs a minimum of input generally your main input is to dictate which ships should focus on broadsides or frontal volleys. Really you should be able to default this in the design screen. You can micromanage as much as you like but I prefer to click begin and watch my ships crush the opposition. Speaking of which the workshop has already started to pump out ship models of the classic sci-fi races with the inclusion of the Federation fleet.
There are so many nods to the SciFi genre in this game. Especially in the achievements and in the tech tree. The game is a unabashed celebration of science fiction.
This may be my favourite 4x yet. It has some issues (see cons) but I'm hopeful they'll fix them soon.
Pro's:
Ship design
SciFi geek out
MOOII
Good AI opponent's
Excellent plot / event scripting
Con's:
Needs AI planetary governors
Needs auto colonise or 'Send Colony Ship' option on the Planets screen
A 2x or 4x speed would be nice in ship combat.
Ground combat doesn't feel right in planetary combat.
